### [1] [CLIR-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Question Answering over Irregular Clinical Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09880)
*Frank Nie,Ethan B. Liu,Yuan Zhu,Loe Yan,Wei Fan,Jindong Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CLIR-Bench is a new benchmark for irregular clinical time series QA, containing 6,600 instances across 11 clinical variables and 11 tasks, designed to evaluate whether models can faithfully ground answers in sparse, irregularly sampled temporal observations. Experiments reveal that existing models struggle with evidence retrieval and reasoning in this setting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical time series are often sparse, irregularly sampled, and asynchronous, posing challenges for temporal evidence identification in clinical QA. Existing benchmarks focus on regularly sampled time series or static medical data, failing to assess whether models can ground answers in irregular temporal observations.

Method: The authors construct CLIR-Bench from de-identified ICU records using a principled four-stage pipeline. The benchmark comprises 6,600 QA instances covering 11 clinical variables, organized into four capability dimensions and 11 tasks. Each question is explicitly linked to temporal evidence and answer derivation rules, enabling dual evaluation of answer accuracy and evidence usage.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that existing generalist models struggle to retrieve and reason over sparse clinical evidence, underscoring a significant performance gap in irregular time-series reasoning.

Conclusion: There is a clear need for stronger irregular time-series reasoning methods in clinical QA. CLIR-Bench provides a principled framework for benchmarking progress in this direction, with code and data publicly released.

Abstract: Clinical time series are central to patient monitoring, risk assessment, and clinical decision support. However, they are often sparse, irregularly sampled, and asynchronous, making it difficult for models to identify the temporal evidence required for clinical Question Answering (QA). Existing benchmarks primarily focus on regularly sampled time-series QA or medical QA over static data, and therefore rarely assess whether models can faithfully ground their answers in irregular temporal observations. To fill this gap, we introduce CLIR-Bench, a benchmark for irregular clinical time series QA constructed from de-identified ICU records through a principled four-stage pipeline. CLIR-Bench contains 6,600 QA instances spanning 11 clinical variables, organized into four capability dimensions and 11 tasks. Each question is linked to explicit temporal evidence and task-specific answer derivation rules, enabling evaluation of both answer accuracy and evidence use. Experiments show that existing generalist models struggle to retrieve and reason over sparse clinical evidence, highlighting the need for stronger irregular time-series reasoning methods. Our code and data are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/winall/CLIR-Bench.

</details>


### [2] [Index SLM Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09885)
*Lusheng Zhang,Shien He,Tianxing Yan,Mengran Yu,Ziang Cui,Kai Zhao,Xiaojing Liu,Tianjiao Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Index-1.9B is a series of small (1.9B parameter) open language models from Bilibili, featuring base, pure, chat, and character variants. The base model, trained on 2.8T tokens with a novel Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule and Norm-Head output layer, achieves competitive benchmark performance (avg. 64.92) against much larger models. The paper includes controlled ablation studies on depth, learning rate, data quality, and instruction data effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop and release a competitive, fully open small language model (~1.9B parameters) that achieves strong performance relative to models several times its size, while also providing controlled empirical studies on key pre-training design choices (learning rate scheduling, data quality, instruction data inclusion) that are rarely systematically examined in public literature.

Method: Four model variants: (1) Index-1.9B-Base: pre-trained on 2.8T tokens (Chinese + English) using a Warmup-Stable-Decay learning rate schedule with increased curated data concentration during decay, plus a Norm-Head output layer for training stability under large learning rates; (2) Index-1.9B-Pure: identical recipe but with all instruction-like data strictly filtered; (3) Index-1.9B-Chat: SFT + DPO alignment from base; (4) Index-1.9B-Character: Chat model augmented with retrieval-augmented generation for few-shot role-playing. Controlled ablation studies examine model depth, learning-rate magnitude/scheduling, LR decay × data quality interaction, and pre-training instruction data effects.

Result: Index-1.9B-Base achieves an average score of 64.92 across benchmarks (examination, reasoning, mathematics, code), competitive with or exceeding open models several times its size. Controlled studies reveal (a) an unexplained surge in benchmark performance midway through the constant-learning-rate phase, and (b) the interaction between learning-rate decay and data quality.

Conclusion: Small language models, when trained with careful learning-rate scheduling (Warmup-Stable-Decay), curated data strategies, and stabilizing architectural modifications (Norm-Head), can match or surpass much larger models. The inclusion of instruction data during pre-training and the interaction between LR decay and data quality are important design factors. All models and code are open-sourced.

Abstract: We present Index-1.9B, a series of open small language models developed at Bilibili. The series comprises four models: Index-1.9B-Base, a foundation model with 1.9 billion non-embedding parameters pre-trained on 2.8 trillion predominantly Chinese and English tokens; Index-1.9B-Pure, a control variant trained with an identical recipe but with all instruction-like data strictly filtered from the corpus; Index-1.9B-Chat, aligned from the base model with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization; and Index-1.9B-Character, which augments the chat model with retrieval-augmented generation for few-shot role-playing customization. Pre-training employs a Warmup-Stable-Decay learning-rate schedule in which the concentration of curated data is raised substantially during the decay phase, together with a Norm-Head output layer that stabilizes training under large learning rates. On a suite of standard benchmarks covering examination, reasoning, mathematics, and code, Index-1.9B-Base attains an average score of 64.92, competitive with or exceeding open models of several times its size. We further report controlled studies on model depth, learning-rate magnitude and scheduling, the interaction between learning-rate decay and data quality, and the effect of including instruction data during pre-training, and we document an unexplained surge in benchmark performance midway through the constant-learning-rate phase. All models, together with evaluation code, are released at https://github.com/bilibili/Index-1.9B.

</details>


### [3] [RouteRec: Strict Evaluation of Recommender-Agent Selection and Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09908)
*Kaiji Zhou,Vladimir Kalmykov,Yue Feng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RouteRec compares hard agent selection vs. learned item-level aggregation across four traditional recommender agents and one LLM reranker. Under a leakage-free protocol, hard selection underperforms BM25, while learned aggregation (especially gated all-agent) achieves stronger results, suggesting item-level fusion is more promising than request-level routing in sparse fixed-candidate settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recommender systems must choose among heterogeneous agents (collaborative filters, sequential models, content-based retrievers, LLM rerankers), but no single agent is universally optimal. The paper addresses how to best leverage multiple agents under cost constraints, framing it as task-aware agent ranking.

Method: RouteRec framework comparing two strategies: (1) request-level hard selection — picking one agent's full list per request, optionally escalating to an LLM reranker; (2) item-level learned aggregation — fusing items from multiple agents via cheap-only or gated all-agent variants. Evaluated on MovieLens-1M using a leakage-free 5-fold out-of-fold protocol, with cost measured by LLM call proportion.

Result: The full quality oracle achieves HR@10=0.584, confirming cross-agent complementarity. Under leakage-free protocol: hard selection (0.223 HR) underperforms BM25 (0.254); selective LLM escalation does not improve it. Learned aggregation's cheap-only variant matches BM25 HR with higher NDCG (0.123 vs 0.114). Gated all-agent aggregation reaches HR@10=0.295 with 70.2% LLM calls.

Conclusion: Request-level selection of a single complete agent list is too coarse for sparse fixed-candidate settings. Item-level aggregation represents a more promising action space for combining heterogeneous recommender agents. Routing remains unsolved, but the path forward lies in finer-grained fusion rather than hard agent selection.

Abstract: Recommender systems increasingly face a choice among heterogeneous agents -- collaborative filters, sequential models, content-based retrievers, and LLM-based rerankers -- yet no single agent is uniformly best. We study this choice as task-aware agent ranking under cost constraints using RouteRec, a framework that compares request-level hard selection with item-level learned aggregation over four traditional recommender agents and one LLM reranker agent. On MovieLens-1M, the full quality oracle has substantial headroom (HR@10 = 0.584), confirming that useful cross-agent signal exists. Under a leakage-free 5-fold out-of-fold protocol, however, hard selection remains below BM25 (0.223 vs. 0.254), and selective LLM escalation does not improve it. The same protocol yields a different outcome for learned aggregation: its cheap-only variant matches BM25 in HR and has a higher NDCG point estimate (0.123 vs. 0.114), while gated all-agent aggregation reaches HR@10 = 0.295 with 70.2\% LLM calls. The resulting lesson is not that routing is solved, but that request-level selection of one complete agent list is too coarse for this sparse fixed-candidate setting; item-level aggregation is the more promising action space.

</details>


### [4] [Global Merger-Arbitrage Forecasting with Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09921)
*Hinal Jajal,Michal Mucha,Charles Sweat,Chris Pulman,Charlie Flanagan,Peter Anderson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A fine-tuned LLM system for predicting M&A deal outcomes (close, higher bid, termination) outperforms market-implied probabilities, XGBoost, and frontier LLMs by combining expert-crafted long-context engineering with hindsight-guided reasoning traces, achieving a class-balanced Brier score of 0.151 on 400+ global deals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on judgmental forecasting with LLMs has focused on broad, short-context benchmarks (e.g., news snippets), leaving unexplored whether LLMs can succeed in specialized, high-stakes financial settings requiring long-context reasoning over hundreds of pages of technical documents. Merger arbitrage — predicting the outcome of announced M&A deals — represents such a setting where accurate probabilistic forecasts have direct financial consequences.

Method: The authors build a language-model forecasting system combining two key components: (1) expert-guided context engineering, which curates and structures hundreds of pages of technical deal documents for long-context consumption, and (2) fine-tuning on hindsight-guided reasoning traces — synthetic reasoning chains derived from historical deals with known outcomes. Given an announced deal, the system outputs a probability distribution over three mutually exclusive outcomes: closing at announced terms, a higher bid, or deal termination.

Result: On an out-of-sample set of 400+ large deals across 42 countries, the fine-tuned system achieves a class-balanced Brier score of 0.151. This represents a 24% reduction below calibrated market-implied probabilities, 19% below XGBoost, and 25–42% below frontier language models (tested zero-shot or with basic prompting). Ablation studies confirm that both hindsight-based supervision and expert-designed context are critical drivers of performance.

Conclusion: LLM-based forecasting can succeed in specialized, long-context financial workflows. The combination of expert-informed context engineering and hindsight-guided fine-tuning enables the model to reason effectively over complex technical documents, surpassing both traditional quantitative methods and market-implied estimates. This opens the door to LLM deployment in other document-heavy, high-stakes forecasting domains.

Abstract: We present a language-model forecasting system for merger arbitrage, a specialized high-stakes financial setting in which the task is to predict the outcome of announced M\&A deals. Unlike prior work on judgmental forecasting with LLMs, which has focused on broad mixed-topic benchmarks and short context such as news snippets, we study a setting that requires long-context reasoning over hundreds of pages of technical documents. Our system combines expert-guided context engineering with finetuning on hindsight-guided reasoning traces derived from historical deals. Given an announced deal, it outputs a probability distribution over three mutually exclusive outcomes: closing at announced terms, a higher bid, or deal termination. On an out-of-sample set of more than 400 large deals spanning 42 countries, our finetuned system achieves the best performance of any method we evaluate, reducing class-balanced Brier score to 0.151. This is 24\% below calibrated market-implied probabilities, 19\% below XGBoost, and 25-42\% below frontier language models. These results, together with ablation studies, show that LLM-based forecasting can succeed in specialized, long-context financial workflows, with hindsight-based supervision and expert-designed context playing a critical role.

</details>


### [5] [Faithful by Design: Evaluating and Improving LLM-Generated Clinical Trial Summaries for Multi-Stakeholder Audiences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09932)
*Robert Williams*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A benchmark of 200 clinical trials was used to evaluate faithfulness of LLM-generated summaries (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash) for three stakeholder audiences. Unsupported Claims was the dominant hallucination mode. A knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval system significantly improved faithfulness scores, with model-dependent improvement pathways (contradiction reduction for GPT-4o, entailment increase for Claude and Gemini).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed to summarize clinical trial results for healthcare providers, patients, and payers, but hallucination poses unacceptable risks in this high-stakes domain. There is a need for systematic, audience-specific faithfulness evaluation frameworks and mitigation strategies tailored to clinical trial summarization.

Method: The authors constructed a benchmark with 200 stratified trials from AACT, audience-specific prompt templates for three stakeholder groups, and a six-dimension faithfulness annotation schema. Baseline faithfulness was measured for GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Flash across 1,800 summaries using a cross-encoder NLI model. A knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval system was then developed and evaluated against baselines, with statistical significance testing on NLI-based entailment and faithfulness scores.

Result: Unsupported Claims was the dominant failure mode (mean score 1.55/3). The knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval system yielded statistically significant improvements: entailment +0.0125, faithfulness +0.0130 (p < 0.0001). Improvement pathways diverged by model — GPT-4o reduced contradictions, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Flash increased entailment.

Conclusion: Hallucination in clinical trial summarization is dominated by unsupported claims. Knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval offers a viable mitigation strategy with statistically significant gains, though the mechanism of improvement is model-specific, suggesting that remediation approaches may need to be tailored to individual LLM architectures.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to summarize clinical trial results for healthcare providers, patients, and payers, but their tendency to hallucinate poses significant risks in this high-stakes context. This study introduces a benchmark evaluation framework for measuring the faithfulness of LLM-generated clinical trial summaries across three stakeholder audiences. The framework consists of 200 stratified trials drawn from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov database, evaluated using audience-specific prompt templates and a six-dimension faithfulness annotation schema. Baseline measurements were established for GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Flash across 1,800 generated summaries scored using a cross-encoder natural language inference (NLI) model. Unsupported Claims was identified as the dominant failure mode across all three models, with a mean annotation score of 1.55 out of three. A knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval system was developed and evaluated against the baseline, producing statistically significant improvements in NLI-based faithfulness scores (entailment +0.0125, faithfulness +0.0130, p < 0.0001). Improvement pathways were model-dependent, with GPT-4o improving primarily through contradiction reduction while Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Flash improved through increased entailment.

</details>


### [6] [Workload-Driven Optimization for On-Device Real-Time Subtitle Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09957)
*Tsz-To Wong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A 0.6B on-device subtitle translation model with a 64k subtitle-domain tokenizer achieves 1.63× speedup over a 151k-vocabulary baseline and 59.2% tie-excluded win rate against Google Translate under GPT-4o evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-device English-to-Traditional-Chinese subtitle translation for Taiwan faces strict constraints: short inputs/outputs, batch-size-one inference, low latency, and privacy requirements. Standard LLM serving optimizations targeting long-context or high-throughput scenarios offer limited benefit. Profiling reveals that after GGUF quantization, vocabulary projection dominates decode-time cost, motivating vocabulary optimization.

Method: Starting from LMT-60-0.6B, the authors replace the original 151k-token vocabulary with a 64k-token subtitle-domain tokenizer. They migrate the embedding space and adapt the model via embedding calibration followed by full supervised fine-tuning. The resulting model is called LocalSubs.

Result: LocalSubs achieves a 59.2% tie-excluded win rate against Google Translate under GPT-4o pairwise judging on 500 OpenSubtitles2024 test examples. Performance is strongest on short cues and degrades as cue length increases. Preliminary Apple M2 Metal measurements show a 1.63× speedup over the 151k-vocabulary baseline, though the benchmark configuration is noted as incomplete.

Conclusion: Vocabulary reduction via a domain-specific tokenizer is an effective strategy for reducing decode-time latency in on-device NMT under tight constraints. The latency results are preliminary due to incomplete benchmarking, warranting further validation.

Abstract: This report studies on-device English-to-Traditional-Chinese subtitle translation for Taiwan under short inputs, short outputs, batch-size-one inference, low latency, and privacy constraints. These conditions limit the value of optimizations designed for long-context or high-throughput language-model serving.
  Starting from LMT-60-0.6B, preliminary profiling suggests that vocabulary projection becomes a more important decode-time cost after GGUF quantization reduces the relative cost of Transformer blocks. We replace the original 151k-token vocabulary with a 64k-token subtitle-domain tokenizer, migrate the embedding space, and adapt the model through embedding calibration followed by full supervised fine-tuning.
  On a fixed 500-example subset of the OpenSubtitles2024 test set, the LocalSubs achieves a 59.2% tie-excluded win rate against Google Translate under GPT-4o pairwise judging. Performance is strongest on short cues and declines as cue length increases. Preliminary Apple M2 Metal measurements on a 64k-vocabulary model show a 1.63$\times$ speedup over a 151k-vocabulary profiling baseline. The raw benchmark configuration is incomplete, so the latency result is treated as preliminary.

</details>


### [7] [Silent Failures in Quantized LLM Reasoning: A Taxonomy-Based Analysis of Hollow Convergence and Failure Mode Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09999)
*Renuka Oladri,Mohan Vamsi Varadaraju Priya,Jerry Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Post-training quantization alters LLM reasoning patterns (particularly "Hollow Convergence" — correct answers via flawed reasoning) even when accuracy remains stable. This effect is size-dependent (small models vulnerable, ≥12B robust), benchmark-specific, and undetectable via surface-level text features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training quantization is widely used to reduce LLM inference costs, but its impact is typically assessed solely via task accuracy. The authors hypothesize that accuracy metrics mask qualitative shifts in *how* models reason — changes that could have serious deployment consequences. They aim to uncover whether quantization silently degrades reasoning fidelity.

Method: The authors construct a six-category failure taxonomy for chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, validated by two annotators (Cohen's κ = 0.906). They apply it to 30,000 CoT outputs from five instruction-tuned LLMs (3B–14B parameters) across three quantization precisions (FP32, FP16, NF4) and four reasoning benchmarks. They analyze how failure categories shift across precision and model size, and test whether surface-level text classifiers can detect the key failure mode (Hollow Convergence).

Result: (1) Accuracy is robust across precisions (max 3.1 pp drop). (2) Hollow Convergence drops significantly under NF4 for small models (3B, 8B) but remains invariant at ≥12B. (3) Effects are benchmark-specific: GSM8K is immune; LogiQA and ARC-Challenge show largest shifts. (4) Under NF4, LLaMA 3.2-3B shows Shortcut Collapse rising from 44%→78% of wrong-answer failures and Confidence Snowballing collapsing from 15.8%→~0%. (5) Hollow Convergence cannot be detected from surface-level text features (best F1 = 0.53).

Conclusion: Post-training quantization induces qualitative reasoning shifts that accuracy metrics miss, particularly in smaller models. Hollow Convergence emerges as a critical, deployment-relevant failure mode that evades standard evaluation pipelines. Practitioners should not rely solely on accuracy when deploying quantized models, and benchmark selection matters significantly for detecting these effects.

Abstract: We show that post-training quantization can silently alter how large language models reason even when task accuracy is preserved. Using a six-category failure taxonomy validated by two independent human annotators (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.906), we classify 30,000 chain-of-thought outputs from five instruction-tuned LLMs (3B--14B parameters) across three quantization precisions (FP32, FP16, NF4) and four reasoning benchmarks. We find that while accuracy is robust across precisions (maximum 3.1 pp drop), Hollow Convergence (correct answers reached through incomplete or unverifiable reasoning) shows a significant size-dependent shift under NF4, dropping sharply for the two smallest models tested but remaining invariant for models at 12B parameters and above. This effect is also benchmark-specific: GSM8K is categorically immune while LogiQA and ARC-Challenge show the largest shifts. Furthermore, under NF4, Shortcut Collapse rises from 44% to 78% of wrong-answer failures in LLaMA 3.2-3B while Confidence Snowballing collapses from 15.8% to near zero, a qualitative shift invisible to accuracy metrics. Finally, we show Hollow Convergence cannot be reliably detected from surface-level text features (best F1 = 0.53), establishing it as a deployment-relevant failure mode that standard evaluation pipelines cannot catch.

</details>


### [8] [Robust, Scalable Detection of Text Containment in Large Web-Crawled Corpora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10020)
*Lars Henry Berge Olsen,Pierre Lison,Martin Jullum,Mark Anderson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FindMyText is an open-source Python tool for detecting near-verbatim text containment in large corpora, using chained fingerprint sequences to outperform existing methods across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing document fingerprinting techniques identify textual similarities but struggle to reliably distinguish near-verbatim copies from mere similarity. A tool is needed that explicitly captures sequences of matching fingerprints to verify the presence of copyrighted material in large-scale web-crawled corpora.

Method: The method extends document fingerprinting with a novel mechanism that captures chains (sequences) of matching fingerprints rather than isolated matches. It employs a distributed, disk-based indexing framework to handle large web-crawled datasets, and introduces a new benchmark for evaluating text containment.

Result: FindMyText outperforms alternative approaches across three diverse datasets: ArXiv papers, Wikipedia, and generic web content, as evaluated on the newly introduced text containment benchmark.

Conclusion: Chaining fingerprint sequences significantly improves near-verbatim copy detection over standard fingerprinting methods. FindMyText provides a scalable, practical solution for copyright verification in large corpora, with strong empirical performance across varied text domains.

Abstract: We present FindMyText, an open-source Python package designed to efficiently assess whether a given text appears, in part or in full, within a text corpus. The tool builds on prior techniques for document fingerprinting, but extends them with a novel mechanism to explicitly capture sequences of matching fingerprints. By identifying such chains, the tool can more reliably detect near-verbatim copies of a given text rather than mere textual similarities. This makes FindMyText particularly suited for verifying the presence of copyrighted material in a corpus. Leveraging a distributed, disk-based indexing framework, the system scales to large web-crawled datasets. Using a new benchmark for evaluating text containment methods, we show that FindMyText outperforms alternative approaches across three datasets (ArXiv papers, Wikipedia, and generic web content).

</details>


### [9] [Efficiently Adapting Spoken Language Models for the Singaporean Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10092)
*Ng Jia Sheng Jason*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Domain adaptation of a spoken language model to Singapore's Home Team context across four languages and five speech tasks, using LoRA fine-tuning, a surrogate text-QA dataset to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and a multi-task reweighting scheme. The resulting 5B model matches or exceeds models up to 7x its size, with minimal loss of original speech QA capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adapting spoken language models (SLMs) to sensitive, multilingual, spoken-query domains is underexplored, particularly when the original training data is inaccessible. There is a practical need for an SLM tailored to the Singaporean Home Team context, supporting Singapore's four official languages.

Method: The authors adapt an open-source SLM using: (1) Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, (2) a surrogate text-QA dataset to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of original capabilities, and (3) a multi-task objective adapting the CoBa reweighting scheme for speech. They also construct HTD-multilingual-QA, a 504,853-sample multilingual text and spoken QA dataset. The resulting model is named HT-Moonstone (5B).

Result: HT-Moonstone (5B) matches or outperforms SLMs up to 7x its size on most tasks, achieves the best accent and gender recognition among all evaluated models, and loses less than 2% of its original speech QA ability.

Conclusion: Effective domain adaptation of SLMs for sensitive, multilingual, spoken-query scenarios is feasible through a combination of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), anti-forgetting data surrogates, and multi-task reweighting, yielding strong performance and high retention of pre-existing capabilities.

Abstract: Spoken language models (SLMs) unify speech perception and reasoning, but adapting them to sensitive domains is underexplored, especially when the original training data is inaccessible and the use case demands multilingual, spoken-query interaction. We adapt an open-source SLM to the Singaporean Home Team context across five speech tasks in Singapore's four official languages, combining LoRA fine-tuning, a surrogate text-QA dataset that guards against catastrophic forgetting, and a multi-task objective that adapts the CoBa reweighting scheme to speech. We also build HTD-multilingual-QA, a 504,853 sample multilingual QA dataset in text and spoken form. The resulting HT-Moonstone (5B) matches or outperforms SLMs up to 7x its size on most tasks, attains the best accent and gender recognition among all models evaluated, and loses under 2\% of its original speech QA ability.

</details>


### [10] [Cost of Reasoning in non-English Languages: A Case Study on Japanese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10114)
*Yuu Jinnai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates training a reasoning language model (RLM) to reason in Japanese rather than English. Using GRPO on a Japanese continually pretrained variant of Qwen-3-8B, the authors find that language-controlled reasoning is feasible, but performance only matches—not exceeds—English-reasoning baselines, and Japanese cultural task performance does not improve automatically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLMs perform best when reasoning in English due to abundant training data, but reasoning traces are critical for interpretability, safety, and usability. Users and developers would benefit from models that reason in a language of choice while maintaining strong reasoning performance. This motivates exploring whether non-English reasoning (specifically Japanese) is practically achievable without sacrificing capability.

Method: The authors create a Japanese-reasoning variant of Qwen-3-Swallow-8B—a Japanese LLM continually pretrained from Qwen-3-8B—by training it with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). They evaluate the resulting model across coding, math, and science benchmarks, and additionally assess performance on Japanese cultural benchmarks.

Result: The Japanese-reasoning model demonstrates that reasoning-language control is feasible via GRPO training. However, its performance is at best on par with strong English-reasoning baselines across several benchmarks—it does not surpass them. Furthermore, on Japanese cultural benchmarks, the model underperforms relative to baselines, indicating that reasoning in Japanese does not yield automatic gains on culturally relevant tasks.

Conclusion: Language-controlled reasoning is achievable through GRPO on a continually pretrained target-language model, but it does not inherently boost performance beyond English-reasoning baselines, nor does it confer free improvements on culturally specific tasks. There remains a gap between enabling non-English reasoning and achieving superior or even competitive performance in that language.

Abstract: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) achieve their strongest performance when they reason in English, the language for which reasoning-oriented training data is most abundant. However, reasoning trace is a clue for model interpretability and safety, and useful in practice for both the model users and for model developers. Thus, it is desirable to be able to develop a model that reasons in a language of the user's choice, while still maintaining strong reasoning performance. To this end, we study the feasibility of training a model that reasons in Japanese. We develop a Japanese-reasoning variant of Qwen-3-Swallow-8B, which is a Japanese LLM continually pretrained from Qwen-3-8B, with GRPO and evaluate it across coding, math, and science benchmarks. The study shows that reasoning-language control is feasible by training a Japanese continually pretrained model with GRPO. However, its performance is at best on par with strong English-reasoning baselines on several benchmarks. We also evaluate the trained model on Japanese cultural benchmarks and observe that the model's performance is worse than the baseline models, suggesting that the reasoning in Japanese does not immediately improve performance on culturally relevant tasks for free.

</details>


### [11] [Instruction Set and Language for Hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10194)
*Mario Pascual-Gonzalez,Ezequiel Lopez-Rubio*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: IsalHG encodes bounded-arity connected hypergraphs as strings over a compact instruction alphabet using a virtual machine with a sparse hypergraph, a CDLL, and k traversal pointers. A greedy h2s algorithm produces a canonical string conjectured to be a complete isomorphism invariant, enabling native hypergraph isomorphism checking. Benchmarks against nauty, Traces, and bliss on Levi graphs show agreement on 600 verdicts but a 311×–117,672× wall-clock disadvantage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hypergraph isomorphism solvers rely on reducing the hypergraph to its 2-coloured Levi incidence graph and then applying graph isomorphism engines (nauty, Traces, bliss). The authors seek a native, representation-level approach that decides hypergraph isomorphism directly from a canonical string encoding, bypassing the Levi reduction entirely.

Method: IsalHG defines a virtual machine composed of (1) a sparse hypergraph, (2) a circular doubly-linked list of node references, and (3) k traversal pointers. A compact instruction alphabet Σ_HG encodes pointer movements and hyperedge insertions. Every string decodes to a valid hypergraph (closed alphabet). The greedy HypergraphToString (h2s) algorithm encodes any connected hypergraph; a backtracking variant seeded at lexicographically maximal structural-tuple nodes produces a canonical string w*, conjectured as a complete isomorphism invariant. Canonical-string equality decides isomorphism.

Result: Round-trip property s2h(h2s(H)) ≅ H verified on 150 random uniform hypergraphs and named combinatorial designs. Canonical algorithm benchmarked against nauty, Traces, bliss on a (n,c) grid with 10 seeds/cell: all four methods agreed on all 600 isomorphism verdicts. Levi baselines dominated wall-clock time by 311× to 117,672× (geometric mean).

Conclusion: The IsalHG framework provides a viable native string-based representation for hypergraph isomorphism, with experimental evidence supporting the canonical completeness conjecture. However, the current implementation is substantially slower than mature Levi-graph-based solvers, motivating future optimization.

Abstract: We present IsalHG, a method for representing the structure of any finite, connected hypergraph of bounded hyperedge arity as a string over a compact instruction alphabet $Σ_{\mathrm{HG}}$. The encoding is executed by a small virtual machine comprising a sparse hypergraph, a circular doubly-linked list (CDLL) of node references, and $k$ traversal pointers, where $k$ bounds the hyperedge arity. Instructions either move a pointer through the CDLL or insert a hyperedge, optionally together with new nodes, into the hypergraph. Every string over $Σ_{\mathrm{HG}}$ decodes to a valid hypergraph; the alphabet is closed. A greedy \emph{HypergraphToString} (h2s) algorithm encodes any connected hypergraph into a string; a backtracking variant seeded at nodes of lexicographically maximal structural tuple produces a \emph{canonical string} $w^{*}$, which we conjecture to be a complete isomorphism invariant. Canonical-string equality then decides hypergraph isomorphism natively, without the standard reduction to the Levi incidence graph followed by a graph-isomorphism engine. We verify the round-trip property $s2h(h2s(H)) \cong H$ on 150 connected random uniform hypergraphs and on named combinatorial designs, and we benchmark the canonical algorithm against the three practically available exact baselines -- nauty, Traces, and bliss operating on the 2-coloured Levi graph -- across a $(n, c)$ grid with ten seeds per cell. All four methods agree on every one of 600 isomorphism verdicts, consistent with the completeness conjecture. On wall-clock time the Levi baselines dominate every tested cell by three to five orders of magnitude (geometric-mean ratio $311\times$ to $117{,}672\times$), which we report as measured. We contribute the representation framework, a conjecture of canonical completeness, and the first native-versus-Levi benchmark for hypergraph isomorphism.

</details>


### [12] [Equal Accuracy, Unequal Evidence: Search APIs as Decision Surfaces for Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10198)
*Sriram Selvam,Anneswa Ghosh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Search APIs function as decision surfaces that shape agent behavior and token expenditure, not just retrieval tools. Testing three providers (Brave, Tavily, Firecrawl) with a fixed GPT-5.4 agent on 100 SEALQA-HARD questions reveals similar answer accuracy but sharply different "evidence economies" in how each provider's snippets and rankings influence agent actions, exploration breadth, and the contradiction-to-gold ratio in surfaced content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional search API evaluation focuses narrowly on answer accuracy, ignoring how the ranked snippets, URLs, and metadata constitute a "decision surface" that governs whether an agent answers immediately, re-searches, or expends tokens fetching full pages. The authors argue that in progressive-disclosure architectures, provider choice is better understood as a retrieval-budget and policy decision rather than a pure recall decision.

Method: A single frozen GPT-5.4 agent was given two tools (search_web, fetch_page) and tested on 100 questions from SEALQA-HARD. The only variable was the search provider: Brave, Tavily, or Firecrawl. A Kimi-K2.6 oracle labeled every content element (URLs, titles, snippets, fetched pages) visible to the agent, yielding 6,869 per-URL judgments. A semantic-match metric (preserving exact matches while tolerating harmless formatting/naming variants) was used as the correct-answer label. The authors also introduced a surface contradiction-to-gold URL ratio to quantify misleading content.

Result: All three providers scored closely on answer accuracy (25, 25, 26/100). However, their evidence economies diverged: Brave provided gold-answer-rich snippets directly in search results; Tavily concentrated gold-supporting URLs at rank 1; Firecrawl was associated with broader page-fetching exploration. The surface contradiction-to-gold URL ratio ranged from 0.92 to 2.59 across providers, indicating substantial variation in the proportion of misleading vs. helpful content surfaced to the agent.

Conclusion: Provider choice should be framed as a retrieval-budget and policy decision rather than solely a recall optimization problem. Different search APIs create distinct decision surfaces that materially affect agent behavior, token consumption, and the risk of encountering contradictory information, even when final answer accuracy appears comparable.

Abstract: Search APIs are the fundamental retrieval layer for many agents and are often their most frequently used tool. Traditional search APIs provide URLs, titles, and snippets that preview website contents. Because full-page retrieval is token-intensive, agent retrieval architectures increasingly use progressive disclosure: the agent first sees snippets and then chooses whether to fetch full pages. In such systems, search API performance is often evaluated primarily by answer accuracy. We argue that a commercial search API is better understood as a decision surface: the ranked snippets, URLs, and metadata that determine whether an agent answers immediately, searches again, or spends tokens opening pages. We test this claim with one frozen GPT-5.4 agent, two tools (search_web and fetch_page), and 100 questions from SEALQA-HARD, varying only the search provider (Brave, Tavily, Firecrawl). A Kimi-K2.6 oracle labels every content element visible to the agent (URL, title, snippet, and fetched page, when fetched), producing 6,869 valid per-URL judgments. We use an audited correct-answer label, semantic match, which preserves exact matches while accepting harmless formatting and naming variants. Under this measure, the providers remain close (25, 25, 26 / 100), but their evidence economies differ sharply: Brave offers gold-answer-rich snippets, Tavily concentrates gold-supporting URLs at rank 1, and Firecrawl is associated with broader exploration under this fixed agent policy. We also introduce a surface contradiction-to-gold URL ratio, which varies from 0.92 to 2.59. Provider choice is therefore a retrieval-budget and policy decision, not merely a recall decision.

</details>


### [13] [Consensus vs. Dissent: Dynamic LLM Modeling of Subjective Preferences in Group Recommenders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10235)
*Cedric Waterschoot,Nava Tintarev,Francesco Barile*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether fine-tuned LLMs can dynamically select optimal group recommendation aggregation strategies based on group preference distributions, using human survey data to align with perceptions of fairness, satisfaction, and consensus. The approach, validated in a user study (n=284), achieved the highest satisfaction and consensus scores, with LLM judgments most aligned with human perceptions when accounting for interaction effects with group configuration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work shows that group recommender systems benefit from adapting aggregation strategies to the distribution of preferences within a group. However, existing systems lack the ability to make such adaptations in a way that aligns with nuanced human perceptions of fairness, satisfaction, and consensus. The authors explore whether LLMs can fill this gap by mimicking human sensitivity to group configurations.

Method: The authors fine-tune LLMs (creating Judgmental Llama and Judgmental OLMo) using: (1) a reasoning dataset distilled from DeepSeek-V3.1 and (2) human ground truth survey assessments. These models serve as real-time judgmental components within a recommendation pipeline that generates multiple candidates via social choice-based aggregation strategies and dynamically selects the one maximizing predicted human-like evaluations. Validation is conducted through a user study with 284 participants.

Result: The methodology achieved the highest scores for satisfaction and group consensus in the user study. LLM judgments aligned most closely with human perceptions of fairness, satisfaction, and consensus when interaction effects between the LLM-based method and group configuration (e.g., minority or coalition presence) were explicitly considered.

Conclusion: The findings support dynamically adapting aggregation strategies to specific within-group preference distributions and highlight the advantage of using LLMs for adaptation that aligns with subjective human judgments. This reinforces the importance of group configuration-aware strategy selection in group recommender systems.

Abstract: Previous work in group recommender systems has demonstrated a sensitivity to the distribution of preferences within a group. Specifically, the selection of the preference aggregation strategy benefits from considering such group configurations. In this paper, we study whether LLMs are able to mimic this sensitivity and to select the ideal aggregation strategy (and corresponding recommendation) according to nuanced human perceptions of fairness, satisfaction, and consensus.
  We do this by fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on human survey data to serve as real-time judgmental models within the recommendation pipeline. Using a reasoning dataset distilled from DeepSeek-V3.1 and human ground truth assessments, we develop Judgmental Llama and Judgmental OLMo to simulate group assessments. Our pipeline successfully generates multiple recommendation candidates based on social choice-based aggregation strategies and dynamically selects the one that maximizes these predicted human-like evaluations. We further validate these suggestions in a user study (n=284) and find that our methodology achieved the highest scores for satisfaction and group consensus. Furthermore, we find that LLM judgments are most aligned with human perceptions of fairness, satisfaction and consensus when we also consider interaction effects between our LLM-based method and group configuration (e.g., minority or coalition). These findings give further support for dynamically adapting aggregation strategies to specific within-group preference distributions, and highlight the advantage of using LLMs for an adaptation that is aligned with subjective human judgments.

</details>


### [14] [PTEI: Integrating Personality Traits to Enhance Emotional Intelligence in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10245)
*Amir Reza Jafari,Praboda Rajapaksha,Reza Farahbakhsh,Noel Crespi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PTEI is a framework that enhances LLMs' emotional intelligence by integrating MBTI and OCEAN personality traits extracted from emotional scenarios into prompts, using contrastive learning for optimal retrieval, significantly improving emotional understanding accuracy, especially when combined with Chain-of-Thought reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs significantly underperform humans in complex emotional reasoning partly due to limited incorporation of individual differences, particularly personality traits, which are fundamental to human emotional inference.

Method: PTEI framework extracts MBTI and OCEAN personality traits directly from emotional scenarios, uses them as contextual knowledge in personality-aware prompts, and employs Contrastive Learning to build an optimized retrieval system that surfaces emotionally and personally aligned scenarios for enhanced reasoning.

Result: PTEI enhances Emotional Understanding capabilities across various LLMs, with strongest improvement in GPT models; combining PTEI with Chain-of-Thought reasoning yields an additional 4% accuracy increase on established EI benchmarks.

Conclusion: PTEI demonstrates that integrating personality traits into LLM-based emotional reasoning advances AI systems toward more sophisticated social and psychological grounding, narrowing the gap between human and machine emotional intelligence.

Abstract: Despite advances in Emotional Intelligence (EI), Large Language Models (LLMs) still significantly underperform humans in complex emotional reasoning. This gap originates partly from the limited incorporation of individual differences, particularly personality traits, which are fundamental to human emotional inference. To address this, we propose PTEI, a novel framework for integrating Personality Traits into Emotional Intelligence tasks using LLMs. In PTEI, MBTI and OCEAN personality traits are first extracted directly from the given emotional scenarios and then utilized as contextual knowledge within personality-aware prompts, guiding LLMs to accurately infer emotions and their underlying causes. To ensure optimal contextual grounding, we employ Contrastive Learning to construct an optimized retrieval system that surfaces emotionally and personally aligned scenarios, enhancing reasoning quality. Extensive experiments on established EI benchmarks show that PTEI enhances the Emotional Understanding (EU) capabilities of various LLMs, with the strongest improvement observed in GPT models. Combining PTEI with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning yields an additional 4 percent increase in accuracy. These findings underscore PTEI's contribution toward advancing AI systems with more sophisticated social and psychological grounding.

</details>


### [15] [One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10248)
*Oliver Steele,Jiangtao Wen,Yuxing Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Transformer language models implement a unified mechanistic version of Fauconnier's mental-space theory, using a reusable router/slot architecture where a single space-index mechanism controls counterfactual, belief, fictional, and temporal contexts interchangeably, challenging formal semantics' treatment of these as distinct logical domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formal semantics treats different discourse contexts (modal, temporal, doxastic, depictive) as having distinct logics, while Fauconnier's mental-space theory unifies them as a single space-building operation. The authors investigate which approach transformer LMs implement mechanistically.

Method: The authors use Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) to train subspaces that control specific mental space types (counterfactual, belief, fictional, temporal) and test cross-type generalization across three model families. They analyze the router's causal manipulability, rank, composition with entity identity, and localization to specific attention heads in late layers.

Result: A single router/slot format underlies all space types: a reusable value slot stores attributed content, and a causally manipulable router (space index) selects which space is read. Subspaces trained on one space type generalize to others well above chance. Belief is not specially separated. The router is low-rank, composes additively with entity identity, and operates through a few late-layer attention heads. The mechanism drives inference (flipping conclusions while dissociating from reports) and composes across space-builders.

Conclusion: Transformer LMs mechanistically implement Fauconnier's unified mental-space theory rather than formal semantics' fragmented treatment. The cross-type generality of the router/slot mechanism is established, with a companion paper addressing belief in depth due to its special philosophical and linguistic status.

Abstract: Language builds discourse contexts other than the actual: a painting, a belief, a memory, a hypothetical. Each is a mental space in which the same entity can take a different value, as when a flower is red in reality but purple in a portrait. Formal semantics keeps these contexts apart because their logics differ (modal, temporal, doxastic, depictive); Fauconnier's mental-space theory treats them as one space-building operation. We ask which of these a transformer language model implements, and find a mechanistic version of Fauconnier's unification. The model uses one router/slot format across the inventory: a reusable value slot stores attributed content, and a causally manipulable router (the space index) selects which space is read. A subspace trained with Distributed Alignment Search to control one space type, counterfactual, belief, fictional, or temporal, also controls the others, well above a random floor, on three model families; belief, which formal semantics marks as a distinct case, is not specially separated. The router is low-rank, composes additively with entity identity, and acts through a few late-layer heads. Two further results show the mechanism drives inference and composes: a subspace trained on a rule-derived conclusion flips what the model infers while dissociating from what it reports, and composing space-builders mints a fresh router over the shared slot. This paper establishes the cross-type generality. A companion paper develops belief in depth, because of its special status in philosophy, psychology, and linguistics (epistemology, theory of mind, and propositional attitude reports).

</details>


### [16] [Which Languages Transfer Best to Warlpiri? A Similarity-Based Study for Low-Resource ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10256)
*Pravina Mylvaganam,Eliathamby Ambikairajah,Ting Dang,Vidhyasaharan Sethu,Tuende Szalay*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework that ranks high-resource languages for cross-lingual ASR transfer to extremely low-resource languages like Warlpiri by combining acoustic similarity from pre-trained speech models with linguistic similarity (typology, phoneme inventories, grammar, syntax). Experiments with Whisper show acoustically/typologically similar languages (Assamese, Hindi) outperform baselines, with acoustic similarity being the strongest predictor for fine-tuning and phoneme/typological similarity better explaining zero-shot performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Warlpiri, an Australian Aboriginal language, suffers from an extreme scarcity of transcribed speech data, making monolingual ASR training infeasible. Cross-lingual transfer from high-resource languages is essential, but selecting optimal source languages remains an open challenge. The authors aim to move beyond ad-hoc language selection by systematically leveraging both acoustic and linguistic similarity metrics.

Method: The authors propose a two-pronged similarity framework: (1) acoustic similarity computed via distance metrics on embeddings from pre-trained speech models (Whisper), and (2) linguistic similarity derived from typological databases (e.g., WALS, PHOIBLE) covering phoneme inventories, grammatical features, and syntactic properties. These similarity scores are used to rank candidate high-resource languages. Fine-tuning experiments are conducted with Whisper across multiple source languages, evaluating both zero-shot and fine-tuned ASR performance on Warlpiri using word error rate (WER) and character error rate (CER). Correlation analyses assess which similarity dimensions best predict transfer outcomes.

Result: Assamese and Hindi — languages identified as acoustically and typologically similar — achieved substantial WER and CER reductions compared to monolingual and multilingual baselines. Correlation analysis revealed that acoustic similarity is the strongest predictor of fine-tuning performance, while phoneme inventory overlap and typological similarity better explain zero-shot transfer effectiveness.

Conclusion: Combining acoustic and linguistic similarity provides a principled, effective strategy for selecting source languages in cross-lingual low-resource ASR. The approach is generalizable to other endangered languages and highlights distinct predictive roles for different similarity types depending on the transfer regime (zero-shot vs. fine-tuning).

Abstract: This paper investigates how language similarity can improve cross-lingual transfer for automatic speech recognition (ASR) in extremely low-resource settings. Warlpiri, an Australian Aboriginal language, has very limited transcribed speech data, making transfer learning essential. We propose a framework combining acoustic similarity from pre-trained speech models with linguistic similarity based on typology, phoneme inventories, grammatical, and syntactic features to rank high-resource source languages and evaluate their effectiveness for ASR transfer to Warlpiri. Experiments with Whisper show that acoustically and typologically similar languages outperform monolingual and multilingual baselines. Assamese and Hindi achieve substantial reductions in word and character error rates. Correlation analysis further indicates that acoustic similarity is the strongest predictor of fine-tuning performance, while phoneme inventory and typological similarity better explain zero-shot transfer.

</details>


### [17] [Language Re-generation: An investigation into information locality effects on reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10268)
*Amirhossein Mohammadi,Laurence E. Frank,Albert Gatt,Robert A. Bagheri*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fine-tuning GPT-2 models pre-trained on impossible languages to reconstruct natural English reveals that information locality acts as a strong architectural bias. Recovered structures show shorter dependency lengths, recovery difficulty tracks locality disruption, and structural/surface recovery can dissociate, with sentence length modulating performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work examined whether LMs can *acquire* impossible languages, but it remains unclear whether they can *recover* natural language from such perturbed input, and what this reveals about their inductive biases. The authors aim to complement learnability approaches with a reconstruction framework to probe the architectural bias toward information locality in GPT-2.

Method: GPT-2 models are pre-trained on three types of perturbed (impossible) English: (1) local swapping of adjacent words, (2) local scrambling within spans, and (3) global shuffling of entire sentences. These pre-trained models are then fine-tuned on natural English to reconstruct the original text. Recovery is evaluated using Exact Match (surface), dependency Triple F1 (structural), and fluency metrics, with analyses across perturbation type and sentence length.

Result: Recovered structures exhibit shorter dependency lengths than original text, mirroring locality preference in unconstrained generation. Recovery difficulty increases with locality disruption degree. Structural recovery (Triple F1) dissociates from surface recovery (Exact Match); fluency and faithful reconstruction dissociate under global shuffling. Longer sentences facilitate recovery when local structure is preserved but cause collapse under global shuffling. Recovery difficulty tracks learnability difficulty across perturbation types.

Conclusion: Information locality is the shared constraint governing both learnability and recoverability in language models. The reconstruction paradigm reveals an architectural bias toward locality that learnability experiments alone cannot detect, providing a quantitative signature of the inductive biases that shape LM behavior.

Abstract: Information locality, the tendency for syntactically related words to appear close together, shapes both human language processing and language model learning. While prior work has examined whether language models can acquire impossible languages, it remains unclear whether they can recover natural language from such input and what this reveals about their inductive biases. We address this by complementing learnability-based approaches with a reconstruction framework: fine-tuning GPT-2 models pre-trained on impossible languages to reconstruct natural English from three perturbation types. Our findings show that the recovered structures exhibit shorter dependency lengths than the original text, mirroring the locality preference observed in unconstrained language model generation and providing a quantitative signature of an architectural bias that learnability experiments alone do not reveal. Recovery difficulty increases with the degree of locality disruption. Structural recovery (dependency Triple F1) dissociates from surface recovery (Exact Match), while fluency dissociates from faithful reconstruction under global shuffling. Sentence length further modulates performance: longer sentences facilitate recovery when local structure is preserved but lead to complete collapse under global shuffling. Finally, recovery difficulty tracks learnability difficulty across perturbation types, suggesting that information locality is the shared constraint governing both.

</details>


### [18] [MafiaScope: Non-Invasive, Time-Resolved Belief Probing for LLM Agents in Social Deduction Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10645)
*Ilia Karpov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MafiaScope is an open testbed that uses the social deduction game Mafia to measure machine Theory of Mind by privately probing agent beliefs after every public utterance, revealing that LLM agents exhibit poor calibration and systematic biases in their social reasoning despite superficially competent public behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: An LLM agent's observable behavior reveals little about its internal social reasoning — correct votes may be guesses, and successful deception leaves no trace of actual beliefs. There is a need for an instrument that can measure what agents truly believe during social interactions, rather than merely evaluating their surface-level performance.

Method: MafiaScope transforms the game Mafia into a measurement framework where, after every public utterance, each agent privately answers structured probe questions scored against known ground truth. The system includes: (1) configurable probes that never re-enter gameplay, (2) an interactive visualizer with impersonate mode, timeline-aligned accuracy/calibration panels, and counterfactual replay via forking any recorded step. A case study ran 32 DeepSeek games yielding 13,815 parsed probe answers and a 30-fork replay experiment.

Result: In the DeepSeek case study, stated confidence was poorly calibrated (expected calibration error = 0.17), agents over-predicted being suspected by a factor of 1.5×, and the 30-fork replay experiment successfully demonstrated the end-to-end counterfactual replay workflow. The engine, viewer, and a corpus of 200+ cross-model games are publicly released.

Conclusion: MafiaScope provides a principled framework for measuring machine Theory of Mind through private belief probing, revealing that LLM agents' social reasoning is significantly miscalibrated despite outwardly competent play. The open release of the testbed, visualizer, and multi-model corpus enables systematic benchmarking and deeper investigation of social cognition in language agents.

Abstract: An LLM agent's public behaviour reveals little about its social reasoning: an agent that votes correctly may be guessing, and an agent that lies well leaves no trace of what it actually believes. We present MafiaScope, an open testbed that turns the social deduction game Mafia into a measurement instrument for machine Theory of Mind. After every public utterance, every agent privately answers a configurable set of structured probe questions; the answers never re-enter the game and are scored automatically against the ground truth the engine knows. An interactive visualizer renders the belief trajectories: impersonate mode shows the game as one agent sees it, panels chart timeline-aligned accuracy and calibration, and counterfactual replay forks any recorded step. In a 32-game DeepSeek case study with 13{,}815 parsed probe answers, stated confidence is poorly calibrated, with expected calibration error 0.17, agents over-predict being suspected 1.5 times, and a 30-fork replay experiment walks the counterfactual replay workflow end to end. Engine, viewer and a corpus of 200+ cross-model games are released under an open licence; live demo: https://karpovilia.github.io/mafiascope/; screencast: https://vimeo.com/1208920221.

</details>


### [19] [PolyInterview: An LLM-based Platform for Immersive Mock Interview Practice with Comprehensive Multimodal Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10310)
*Zhiyuan Wen,Jiannong Cao,Zijian Wang,Chen Chen,Xiaoyun Liu,Jianing Yin,Zhuo Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PolyInterview is an LLM-powered mock interview platform featuring a lip-synced digital human interviewer that generates tailored questions, conducts multi-turn spoken interviews with follow-ups, and delivers multimodal feedback (content, vocal, non-verbal) grounded in KSA and STAR frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Realistic interview practice is inaccessible: real interviews are rare, expert coaching is expensive, and self-practice lacks adaptive dialogue and structured assessment. Existing systems offer only partial solutions—fixed questions, limited modalities, or evidence-weak feedback.

Method: PolyInterview takes a job description and CV as input, generates role-tailored questions, and conducts spoken interviews via a lip-synced digital human that asks answer-aware follow-ups. Four parallel evaluators extract 13 behavior-level features, aggregated into 10 assessment aspects across two competency tracks. KSA and STAR frameworks link scores to behavioral evidence and actionable recommendations.

Result: The platform has 101 accounts, 1,564 sessions, 7,665 questions, and 1,422 five-stage question sets. Generated questions aligned better with matched vs. cross-role job descriptions in 93.7% of sessions. Ten expert evaluators judged question plans and feedback as strong.

Conclusion: PolyInterview demonstrates a scalable, evidence-grounded approach to multimodal mock interview practice, combining adaptive LLM-driven dialogue with comprehensive behavioral assessment to make realistic interview preparation widely accessible.

Abstract: Preparing for job interviews is important for securing desired positions, yet realistic practice remains difficult to access: real interviews are infrequent, expert mock coaching is costly, and self-practice offers neither adaptive dialogue nor structured assessment. Existing systems typically address only parts of this need through fixed question sequences, limited communication channels, or feedback with little supporting evidence. We present PolyInterview, an LLM-based platform for immersive mock interview practice with comprehensive multimodal assessment. PolyInterview uses the target job description and CV to generate questions tailored to the role and candidate, conducts multi-turn spoken interviews with a lip-synced digital human interviewer that asks answer-aware follow-up questions, and evaluates response content, vocal delivery, and non-verbal behavior. Four parallel evaluators produce 13 behavior-level features that are aggregated into 10 assessment aspects and two competency tracks. Guided by the KSA and STAR frameworks, the report links each score to behavioral evidence and actionable recommendations. PolyInterview is publicly accessible. Its current all-account snapshot contains 101 accounts, 1,564 interview sessions, 7,665 generated questions, and 1,422 five-stage question sets. Generated questions are more closely aligned with their matched job description than with cross-role job descriptions in 93.7% of sessions. An evaluation by ten experts found strong question plans and actionable feedback.

</details>


### [20] [Polarization Detection: A Hybrid Approach with AfroXLMR-Social and DeBERTa for Low- and High-Resource Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10312)
*Muhammad Abdullahi Said*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A hybrid modeling approach (DeBERTa for English binary detection; AfroXLMR-Social for Hausa and fine-grained tasks) with LoRA adaptation and text augmentation achieves competitive results across all POLAR Shared Task 2026 subtasks on polarized discourse detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online polarization is rapidly proliferating and threatens social cohesion, creating an urgent need for automated detection systems that work across diverse linguistic contexts — particularly under-resourced ones like Hausa alongside English.

Method: A hybrid strategy: DeBERTa (monolingual) for English binary polarization detection; AfroXLMR-Social (domain-adapted multilingual model) for Hausa and all fine-grained subtasks (Types and Manifestations). Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) addresses computational constraints, and nlpaug-based textual data augmentation mitigates data scarcity.

Result: Competitive results across all three subtasks (binary detection, Types, and Manifestations) in both English and Hausa, demonstrating that task-specific model selection balances performance effectively.

Conclusion: Tailoring model selection to specific subtask requirements — monolingual models for high-resource binary tasks and domain-adapted multilingual models for low-resource fine-grained tasks — yields optimal performance. LoRA and data augmentation are effective strategies under computational and data constraints.

Abstract: The rapid proliferation of online polarization threatens social cohesion, necessitating robust automated detection systems that operate effectively across diverse linguistic contexts. This paper presents our system description for the POLAR Shared Task 2026, focusing on the detection and characterization of polarized discourse in English and Hausa. We propose a hybrid modeling strategy: for English binary detection, we leverage the monolingual strength of \textbf{DeBERTa}, while for Hausa and all fine-grained subtasks (Types and Manifestations), we utilize \textbf{AfroXLMR-Social}. This domain-adapted multilingual model proved critical for capturing the nuances of polarization in social media text. To further address computational constraints and data scarcity, we implement Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and textual data augmentation via \texttt{nlpaug}. We report competitive results across all three subtasks, demonstrating that model selection tailored to specific subtask requirements yields the best balance of performance.

</details>


### [21] [Automated Textbook Auditing with Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11276)
*Ciprian Cristescu,Adrian-Marius Dumitran,Angela-Liliana Dumitran,Gabriel Stefan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AI Textbook Auditor is a modular multi-agent LLM pipeline that automates quality assurance of educational textbooks by combining factual/technical error detection with grammar checking, producing structured reports for human reviewers. Tested on two Romanian textbooks (CS and history), it identified 56 and 72 issues respectively, with a validated precision of 62.5% on the CS domain, serving as a triage tool to reduce manual audit effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Educational textbook auditing demands simultaneous verification of factual accuracy, domain-specific technical correctness, and linguistic quality — a combination that general-purpose grammar checkers cannot handle. Manual expert review is time-consuming and expensive, motivating an automated triage system that surfaces candidate issues for human validation.

Method: A modular multi-agent pipeline with two parallel tracks: (1) a Factual and Technical Track using an ensemble of specialized LLM agents to detect factual errors, code errors, incorrect definitions, and conceptual inconsistencies, augmented with web search for humanities; (2) a Grammar Track operating PDF-natively to preserve diacritical encoding. A Judge Agent filters false positives using domain-specific rules. The system supports two PDF ingestion modes (vision-native rendering and PyMuPDF text extraction) and is domain-adaptable via custom prompts encoding subject-specific error taxonomies.

Result: On a Romanian CS textbook, the system found 56 technical findings across seven categories with expert-validated precision of 62.5%. On a history and social sciences textbook, it identified 72 findings spanning factual errors, ideological bias, and grammar issues.

Conclusion: The system functions effectively as a triage tool that significantly reduces the manual effort of locating candidate issues in textbook auditing. However, human expert validation remains essential before any editorial decisions are made, and the 62.5% precision indicates room for improvement in false-positive filtering.

Abstract: Ensuring the quality of educational materials requires more than standard proofreading: textbooks must be audited for factual accuracy, domain-specific technical correctness, and linguistic quality simultaneously -- a task that general-purpose grammar checkers cannot address. We present \textbf{AI Textbook Auditor}, a modular multi-agent pipeline for automated quality assurance of educational materials across subject domains. The system accepts a textbook PDF and produces a structured, human-reviewable report via two analysis tracks: a \textbf{Factual and Technical Track} in which an ensemble of specialized LLM agents detects factual inaccuracies, code errors, incorrect definitions, and conceptual inconsistencies, augmented with web search for humanities domains; and a \textbf{Grammar Track} operating PDF-natively to preserve diacritical encoding. A \textbf{Judge Agent} filters false positives using domain-specific rules before presenting findings to a human reviewer. The pipeline supports two ingestion modes -- vision-native page rendering and PyMuPDF text extraction -- and is domain-adaptable via custom prompts encoding subject-specific error taxonomies. We demonstrate the system on two Romanian upper-secondary textbooks: a CS textbook (56 technical findings across seven categories, with an expert-validated precision of 62.5\%) and a history and social sciences textbook (72 findings spanning factual errors, ideological bias, and grammar). The system is designed as a triage tool that reduces the manual effort of locating candidate issues, with human expert validation required before any editorial action.

</details>


### [22] [Neutralizing Structural Inequality in the Nigerian FinTech Sector](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10317)
*Muhammad Abdullahi Said*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a hierarchical human-AI triage system for fraud detection in Nigerian FinTech that corrects algorithmic bias. Using a three-tier routing policy, dynamic shadow pricing for human attention, and random audits, the model reduces regional performance gaps from 19.43 to 2.88 percentage points and improves fraud recall by 24.79% over autonomous baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Algorithmic fraud detection systems in financial services often engage in "discrimination laundering," where infrastructure-related noise (e.g., rural network timeouts) is misinterpreted as fraudulent intent. This disproportionately excludes rural users in Nigeria from the digital economy due to structural inequalities encoded in data proxies. The authors aim to operationalize a "We Are All Equal" fairness worldview to ensure substantive equality of opportunity.

Method: The authors design a hierarchical human-AI triage model with three tiers: (1) a calibrated ensemble model as primary filter, (2) specialist analysts handling epistemic uncertainty cases (e.g., cold-start new accounts), and (3) a senior supervisor for high-stakes cases. A dynamic shadow price mechanism rations finite human attention, and random audits prevent human skill atrophy.

Result: The model achieves a statistically significant 1.88% complementarity gap and a 24.79 percentage-point gain in fraud recall over the autonomous baseline. The regional performance gap drops from 19.43 to 2.88 percentage points, demonstrating effective neutralization of structural bias against rural accounts.

Conclusion: Hierarchical human-AI collaboration, when designed with explicit fairness constraints and attention-rationing mechanisms, can robustly deliver substantive equality of opportunity. The approach ensures rural account holders are not penalized by environmental brute luck, enabling inclusive participation in the digital financial ecosystem.

Abstract: Algorithmic decision systems in financial services often rely on data proxies that inadvertently encode structural inequalities. This paper introduces a hierarchical human-AI triage model for Point of Sale fraud detection in the Nigerian FinTech sector. Adopting a We Are All Equal worldview, we address the challenge of discrimination laundering, wherein the system misinterprets infrastructure related aleatoric noise such as rural network timeouts as fraudulent intent. We implement a three-tier routing policy utilizing a calibrated ensemble model as a primary filter. The policy routes transactions characterized by epistemic uncertainty such as cold start new accounts to specialist analysts while reserving high stakes cases for a senior supervisor. To manage finite human capacity, we utilize a dynamic shadow price to ration human attention and implement a random audit mechanism to prevent human skill atrophy. Our experimental results demonstrate a statistically significant 1.88\% complementarity gap and a 24.79\% percentage point gain in fraud recall over an autonomous baseline. Crucially, the model reduces the regional performance gap from 19.43 to 2.88 percentage points, neutralizing structural bias. Hierarchical collaboration provides a robust mechanism for substantive equality of opportunity, ensuring that rural accounts are not excluded from the digital economy due to environmental brute luck.

</details>


### [23] [CAFE: A Compound-AI Factorial Evaluation Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10380)
*Fabian Lukassen,Christoph Weisser,Thomas Kneib,Alexander Silbersdorff*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CAFE is an open-source platform that applies factorial experimental design to evaluate compound AI systems, identifying which interchangeable components (retrievers, models, prompts) most affect answer quality through mixed-effects modeling, significance testing, and cost/latency trade-off analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practitioners building compound AI systems face many swappable components but lack systematic methods to determine which ones drive answer quality. Existing tools either search for optimal configurations or score outputs in isolation without explaining which components matter or whether observed differences are statistically significant.

Method: CAFE implements a factorial design framework where practitioners register swappable pipeline components as factors, run all resulting configurations, and score outputs using a configurable LLM judge combined with human raters. Mixed-effects models then decompose answer-quality variance across components and interactions, reporting effect sizes, significance levels, best configurations, cost/latency trade-offs, and judge-human reliability.

Result: Validation on a retrieval-augmented QA pipeline over HotpotQA shows CAFE recovers planted factor effects and remains calibrated under a permutation null, confirming its statistical validity.

Conclusion: CAFE fills a gap between pure search-based optimization and isolated scoring by providing statistically rigorous attribution of quality variance to specific components, released as both a Python package and a web application.

Abstract: We introduce CAFE (Compound-AI Factorial Evaluation), an open-source platform that brings design of experiments to the evaluation of compound AI systems (CAIS). Such systems expose many interchangeable choices - e.g. which retriever, model, or prompt - and practitioners rarely know which of them most affects answer quality.
