With CAFE, a practitioner registers each swappable component of a pipeline as a factor to build a factorial design over the chosen factors, run the resulting configurations, and score the answers on a shared rubric using a configurable LLM judge together with human raters. From these ratings it attributes answer-quality variance to the components and their interactions with mixed-effects models and reports effect sizes, significance, the best configuration, cost and latency trade-offs, and judge-human reliability. Whereas existing tools mostly either search for a good configuration or score outputs in isolation, CAFE also explains which component drives quality and whether an observed difference is significant. We validate CAFE on a retrieval-augmented question-answering (QA) pipeline over the HotpotQA benchmark dataset, where it recovers planted factor effects and stays calibrated under a permutation null. CAFE is released as a Python package and as a Web application.

</details>


### [24] [Structured Thoughts For Improved Reasoning And Context Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10386)
*Zain Sarwar,Supriyo Chakraborty,Berkcan Kapusuzoglu,Chia-Hsuan Lee,Anirban Das,Stephen Rawls,Kartik Balasubramaniam,Sambit Sahu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Structured Thoughts introduces a framework that segments LLM reasoning into alternating <try> (exploratory work) and <outcome> (distilled conclusion) blocks. Fine-tuning on this structured data yields up to 8.08% benchmark improvement over standard SFT, and the structure enables context pruning with ~85% memory savings at an 8.67% performance cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long reasoning traces from LLMs are verbose and memory-inefficient. The authors seek to both improve reasoning performance and enable more efficient context usage by imposing explicit structure on chain-of-thought reasoning.

Method: The framework organizes reasoning into alternating <try> and <outcome> blocks. A dataset is constructed by segmenting existing reasoning traces into <try> blocks and prompting an LLM to summarize each into a corresponding <outcome>. Foundation models are then fine-tuned on this reformatted data to adopt the structured reasoning style. Additionally, a proof-of-concept pruning mechanism removes <try> blocks after each pair, retaining only <outcome> conclusions.

Result: Fine-tuned models achieve up to 8.08% improvement on reasoning benchmarks compared to standard SFT. The pruning implementation achieves ~85% memory/context savings with only an 8.67% performance drop across mathematical tasks.

Conclusion: Imposing a structured <try>/<outcome> format on chain-of-thought reasoning improves both model accuracy and memory efficiency. The approach demonstrates that explicit reasoning structure enables effective context pruning with minimal performance degradation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating long chains of thought, but long reasoning traces are often verbose and memory-inefficient. In this work, we introduce Structured Thoughts, a framework that organizes reasoning into alternating <try> and <outcome> blocks: <try> captures exploratory scratch work, while <outcome> contains the distilled conclusion of that step. We construct a dataset of structured thoughts by segmenting reasoning traces into <try> blocks and prompting an LLM to summarize each step into its corresponding <outcome>. Fine-tuning pretrained foundation models on this reformatted data produces models that adopt the structured reasoning style, leading to performance gains of up to 8.08\% on reasoning benchmarks compared to standard SFT. The explicit structure also enables context pruning: after each <try>/<outcome> pair, the <try> can be pruned, allowing the model to retain conclusions without keeping the full scratch work in the context. A proof-of-concept pruning implementation achieves an average of 85\% memory / context savings with an 8.67\% performance drop across mathematical tasks.

</details>


### [25] [A Stepwise Questioning Expert-Editor Multi-Agent Framework for Long-Document Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10390)
*Lingyun Shen,Xuejia Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes an expert-editor multi-agent framework for long-document summarization, where two specialized agents (expert and editor) iteratively refine summaries by posing aspect-specific questions and providing revision clues, demonstrating effectiveness on scientific datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with long-document summarization because document lengths frequently exceed context window limits. While agent-based approaches offer a way to augment LLM capabilities, existing methods lack structured, stepwise refinement mechanisms for summary improvement.

Method: A stepwise questioning multi-agent architecture involving two roles: an "expert" agent and an "editor" agent. These agents guide a third summarization agent by asking questions targeting different content aspects and supplying targeted clues to iteratively revise and improve the generated summary.

Result: Experiments on two representative long-document scientific datasets, evaluated using widely recognized automatic metrics, demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Conclusion: The expert-editor stepwise questioning multi-agent method effectively addresses the challenges of LLM-based long-document summarization by enabling structured, iterative refinement through role-specialized agents.

Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have shown promising potential in news summarization tasks, their performance on long-document summarization remains challenging as their length often exceeds the input limits. As the agent investment, which provide possibility to improve the inherent capabilities of LLMs. To enhance the effectiveness of long-document summarization based on LLMs, this paper proposes an expert-editor stepwise questioning multi-agent method, in which the expert and the editor guide another agent to refine the summary by posing questions on different aspects of the content and providing targeted clues for revision. We conducted experiments on two representative long-document scientific datasets and evaluated the results through widely recognized automatic metrics. The results demonstrated the effectiveness of our method.

</details>


### [26] [Enjoy Your Talk: A Human-Centered Benchmark for Multi-Turn Dialogue with Decoupled User Simulation, Target Modeling, and Judging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10428)
*Jinglan Gong,Jiefan Lu,Hewei Guo,Kehan Li,Zhiyuan Han,Jihang Jiang,Wenwen Tong,Lewei Lu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EYT-Bench is a human-centered multi-turn dialogue benchmark using a three-party decoupled design (persona-grounded user simulator, target model with separated intent perception/response generation, and third-party LLM judge) to evaluate persona consistency, intent tracking, emotional dynamics, and goal completion. Key findings: open/closed models converge on subjective metrics but diverge 9x on objective intent tracking; reasoning modes improve intent tracking without affecting subjective scores; persona format dominates trajectory spread; and 16/17 models show robust warm-up effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing single-turn benchmarks fail to capture critical multi-turn conversational capabilities: persona consistency, evolving intent tracking, emotional dynamics, and goal completion. There is a need for a human-centered evaluation framework that disentangles these dimensions while minimizing LLM-induced biases from synthesized personas.

Method: EYT-Bench employs (1) a three-party decoupled architecture: a persona-grounded user simulator, a target LLM with separated intent perception and response generation modules, and an independent third-party LLM judge with optional multi-judge ensembling; (2) personas sourced from public human-curated corpora (Nemotron-Personas-USA, PersonaMem-v2) rather than LLM-synthesized; and (3) two trajectory-level metrics: embedding-based intent drift and final-intent completion rate (FICR), inspired by tau-bench. Evaluation spans 17 target models × 200 dialogues.

Result: Four key findings: (i) SOTA closed- and open-source models are statistically close on subjective dimensions (empathy/persona/anthropomorphism vary ≤0.3) but differ up to 9× on objective intent tracking; (ii) reasoning ("thinking on") improves objective tracking on long-context personas (+0.47–0.50 latent-intent accuracy on Gemma-4) while subjective scores remain nearly unchanged; (iii) persona format dominates trajectory spread, with FICR >0.95 on Nemotron-USA but ranging 0.53–0.88 on PersonaMem-v2; (iv) warm-up effect is robust across 16/17 models (GPT-5.5 is the sole outlier, reversing the effect), with stable rankings across α ∈ [0.05, 0.15]. Cross-judge ablation with deepseek-v4-pro confirms target rankings and final-intent satisfaction are preserved across judges.

Conclusion: Multi-turn conversational evaluation requires decoupling subjective and objective dimensions, as models converge on subjective qualities but diverge sharply on intent tracking. Persona source and format critically affect trajectory spread, and reasoning modes provide targeted gains in intent tracking without inflating subjective scores. The warm-up effect is broadly robust, and cross-judge consistency validates the third-party judging framework.

Abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) as multi-turn conversational partners requires probing capabilities that single-turn benchmarks miss: persona consistency, evolving intent tracking, emotional dynamics, and goal completion. We introduce EYT-Bench, a human-centered benchmark built around a three-party decoupled design: a persona-grounded user simulator, a target model that separates intent perception from response generation, and an independent third-party LLM judge with optional multi-judge ensembling. Personas are sampled from public human-curated corpora, Nemotron-Personas-USA and PersonaMem-v2, rather than synthesized, reducing LLM-induced persona bias. EYT-Bench also introduces two trajectory-level metrics: embedding-based intent drift and final-intent completion rate (FICR), inspired by tau-bench. In a 17-target x 200-dialogue evaluation, EYT-Bench reveals four findings: (i) state-of-the-art closed- and open-source models are statistically close on subjective dimensions (empathy / persona / anthropomorphism vary within <= 0.3), but differ by up to 9x on objective intent tracking; (ii) reasoning ("thinking on") sharply improves objective tracking on long-context personas (+0.47-0.50 latent-intent accuracy on Gemma-4) while leaving subjective scores nearly unchanged; (iii) persona format dominates trajectory spread, with FICR saturating above 0.95 on Nemotron-USA but spreading from 0.53 to 0.88 on PersonaMem-v2; and (iv) the warm-up effect is robust on 16/17 models (one outlier, GPT-5.5, reverses the effect), with stable rankings across alpha in [0.05, 0.15]. A cross-judge ablation using deepseek-v4-pro confirms that target rankings and final-intent satisfaction are preserved across judges.

</details>


### [27] [Anamnesis: An Open-Source Platform for Large-Scale Backstory-Conditioned Survey Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10628)
*Song-Ze Yu,Joseph Suh,Serina Chang,David M. Chan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Anamnesis is an open-source, interactive system that uses LLMs to simulate demographically controllable survey responses. It operationalizes the Anthology and Alterity frameworks via structured narrative backstories, supports multimodal surveys, and produces opinion distributions that more closely match real-world data than standard persona-prompting baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based survey simulation tools are often proprietary, lack demographic controllability, and use simplistic persona prompts that fail to capture the nuance of real human opinion distributions. There is a need for a transparent, reproducible, open-source platform that allows researchers to prototype and stress-test survey instruments on virtual populations with realistic demographic conditioning.

Method: Anamnesis implements the Anthology (structured narrative backstories) and Alterity (probabilistic demographic resampling) frameworks within a unified web interface. The system supports: (1) open-ended text generation conditioned on backstories, (2) probabilistic demographic resampling to capture distributional properties, and (3) multimodal surveys including image and audio inputs. Evaluation is conducted via two case studies: replicating Pew Research Center's ATP on political typology and biomedical issues, and emulating human preferences in the New Yorker Caption Contest, with comparisons against standard persona-prompting baselines.

Result: In both case studies, Anamnesis-produced opinion distributions more closely matched real-world survey data than standard persona-prompting baselines. The system demonstrated improved fidelity in replicating political typology segments and biomedical opinion distributions from the Pew ATP, as well as human preference patterns in the Caption Contest.

Conclusion: Anamnesis offers a transparent, reproducible, and open-source alternative to proprietary simulation services, demonstrating that structured narrative backstories and probabilistic demographic resampling significantly improve the alignment of LLM-generated survey responses with real human opinion distributions.

Abstract: We present Anamnesis, an interactive system for demographically controllable survey simulation using large language models. Open-source, and designed for non-technical users/researchers, Anamnesis enables the prototyping and stress-testing of survey instruments on virtual populations rather than real human subjects. The platform operationalizes the recently introduced Anthology and Alterity frameworks, which use structured narrative backstories to condition model responses, within a unified web interface. It supports open-ended generation, probabilistic demographic resampling, and multimodal (image and audio) surveys. We evaluate the system through two case studies: (1) replicating segments of Pew Research Center's American Trends Panel (ATP) on political typology and biomedical issues and (2) emulating human preference in the New Yorker Caption Contest. In both cases, Anamnesis produces opinion distributions that more closely match real-world survey data than standard persona-prompting baselines, offering a transparent, reproducible, and open-source alternative to proprietary simulation services.

</details>


### [28] [Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models Using Diversion Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10476)
*Basel Abdeen,S M Tahmid Siddiqui,Meah Tahmeed Ahmed,Anoop Singhal,Latifur Khan,Punya Parag Modi,Ehab Al-Shaer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces "diversion decoding," a novel, computationally efficient method for detecting hallucinations in LLMs by actively challenging model-generated responses during decoding and using the resulting resistance features to train a machine-learning model that measures uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucination (fabricating factually incorrect statements), undermining trustworthiness. Existing hallucination detection methods are probabilistic and computationally expensive, limiting practical deployment. There is a need for an efficient, robust uncertainty heuristic.

Method: The authors propose diversion decoding, which actively challenges model-generated responses during the decoding phase. Features are extracted that capture the LLM's resistance to producing alternative answers. These features are then used to train a machine-learning model that yields a heuristic measure of the LLM's uncertainty.

Result: Diversion decoding outperforms existing hallucination detection methods while requiring significantly lower computational complexity.

Conclusion: Diversion decoding offers an efficient, robust, and practical solution for evaluating LLM hallucination detection, addressing the computational limitations of prior probabilistic approaches.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a powerful tool for retrieving knowledge through seamless, human-like interactions. Despite their advanced text generation capabilities, LLMs exhibit hallucination tendencies, where they generate factually incorrect statements and fabricate knowledge, undermining their reliability and trustworthiness. Multiple studies have explored methods to evaluate LLM uncertainty and detect hallucinations. However, existing approaches are often probabilistic and computationally expensive, limiting their practical applicability. In this paper, we introduce diversion decoding, a novel method for developing an LLM uncertainty heuristic by actively challenging model-generated responses during the decoding phase. Through diversion decoding, we extract features that capture the LLM's resistance to produce alternative answers and utilize these features to train a machine-learning model to develop a heuristic measure of the LLM's uncertainty. Our experimental results demonstrate that diversion decoding outperforms existing methods with significantly lower computational complexity, making it an efficient and robust solution for evaluating hallucination detection.

</details>


### [29] [When Reasoning Hurts Legal Drafting: The Verbalization Bottleneck in Patent Claim Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10480)
*Lekang Jiang,Wenjun Sun,Stephan Goetz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting benefits patent claim generation, finding that implicit CoT (internal reasoning) consistently outperforms explicit CoT (verbalized reasoning), which can harm output quality through abstraction of details, disruption of generation patterns, and cascading error propagation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Patent claim drafting is a complex legal task requiring technical precision, formal conventions, and logical consistency. While CoT prompting improves LLM reasoning broadly, recent evidence suggests it may be ineffective or detrimental in highly structured, pattern-sensitive tasks. The authors seek to empirically determine whether CoT benefits or harms patent claim generation specifically.

Method: The authors propose a task-specific CoT method for patent claim generation and evaluate it through both automatic metrics and human expert assessment. They systematically compare explicit CoT (verbalized reasoning chains) against implicit CoT (internal reasoning kept latent), analyzing failure modes through three identified mechanisms.

Result: Reasoning-enhanced prompting can improve patent claim quality. However, implicit CoT consistently outperforms explicit CoT. The authors identify three mechanisms by which verbalized reasoning degrades output: (1) abstraction of critical details, (2) disruption of internalized generation patterns, and (3) cascading error propagation, collectively forming an unnecessary information bottleneck.

Conclusion: Explicit CoT introduces an information bottleneck that can compromise patent claim generation quality, challenging the assumption that verbalized reasoning is universally beneficial. The findings offer new insights for applying CoT to legal and other highly structured, convention-bound NLP tasks.

Abstract: Patent claim drafting is a challenging legal drafting task that requires technical expertise, precise linguistic control, strict adherence to formal conventions, and the preservation of complex logical relationships among claim elements. While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been widely used to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), recent evidence suggests that its benefits may be limited, or even negative, in highly structured or pattern-sensitive tasks. Therefore, this paper investigates whether CoT prompting benefits patent claim generation. We propose a task-specific CoT method for patent claim generation and evaluate its effectiveness through both automatic metrics and human expert assessment. Our results show that reasoning-enhanced prompting can improve claim quality. Moreover, we demonstrate a counter-intuitive but important empirical finding: implicit CoT, where reasoning is kept internal rather than explicitly verbalized, consistently outperforms explicit CoT. Through systematic analysis, we show that explicit CoT can introduce an unnecessary information bottleneck for claim generation. Verbalized reasoning may compromise the quality of final outputs through three specific mechanisms: abstraction of critical details, disruption of internalized generation patterns, and cascading error propagation. Our findings provide new insights into legal tasks and CoT applications.

</details>


### [30] [Articulate Intuition or Genuine Analysis? Benchmarking Epistemic Reliability in LLM-as-a-Judge Peer Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10511)
*Nuo Chen,Qian Wang,Qingyun Zou,Bingsheng He*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Kahneman4Review, a benchmark operationalizing dual-process theory to evaluate peer review quality across nine textual dimensions and eight bias diagnostics. It reveals that decision tier does not align with epistemic quality, LLM-generated reviews score higher on surface features but gaps are explained by length and venue, and ICLR review diagnostics shifted around 2022–2023, coinciding with LLM availability. The authors argue that trustworthy LLM-judge benchmarks must separate analytical form from epistemic function.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observe a philosophical disconnect: "analytical" in form (as LLM judges assess) may not equate to genuine epistemic quality in peer review. This motivates a structured, theory-driven benchmark grounded in Kahneman's dual-process theory (System 1 vs. System 2 reasoning) to disentangle surface-level analytical appearance from substantive critical thinking in reviews.

Method: The authors operationalize Kahneman's dual-process theory into a structured review rubric with nine theoretically motivated textual dimensions and eight bias diagnostics. They construct Kahneman4Review, a benchmark of 3,563 rated peer reviews, and compute a continuous reasoning-quality (epistemic) score. They analyze alignment between decision tier and epistemic quality, compare human vs. agentic LLM reviews, and conduct temporal diagnostics on ICLR review texts (pre/post-2022). A matched function-probe pilot contrasts genuine fault-finding with surface fluency.

Result: Three key findings: (1) decision tier is not detectably aligned with the rubric's text-grounded epistemic-quality proxy; (2) public-showcase agentic reviews score higher on raw metrics than pooled human reviews, but length and venue largely explain the gap and samples lack paper-pairing; (3) ICLR review-text diagnostics shift around the 2022–2023 boundary, temporally coincident with widespread LLM availability. The function-probe pilot confirms the rubric distinguishes genuine fault-finding from mere surface fluency.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that a trustworthy reliability benchmark for LLM judges must explicitly separate analytical form from epistemic function. They propose concrete design choices toward this goal and provide an interactive demo for the benchmark.

Abstract: When an LLM judge calls a peer review analytical and a human committee calls another review high quality, are they tracking the same thing? We argue they are not, and that the difference matters philosophically. We operationalise Kahneman's dual-process theory into a structured rubric for peer review and release Kahneman4Review, a benchmark of 3,563 rated reviews scored along nine theoretically motivated textual dimensions, eight bias diagnostics, and a continuous reasoning-quality score. Three findings bear on trustworthiness: decision tier is not detectably aligned with the rubric's text-grounded epistemic-quality proxy; public-showcase agentic reviews receive higher raw scores than pooled human reviews, but length and venue explain most of the gap and the samples are not paper-paired; and ICLR review-text diagnostics shift at the 2022--2023 transition, temporally coincident with widespread LLM availability but without identifying its cause. A matched function-probe pilot further shows that the rubric distinguishes textual probes designed to contrast genuine fault-finding with surface fluency. We argue that a trustworthy reliability benchmark for LLM judges must separate analytical form from epistemic function, and propose concrete design choices toward that goal. An interactive demo is available at https://huggingface.co/spaces/nuojohnchen/Kahneman4Review.

</details>


### [31] [LightMem-Ego: Your AI Memory for Everyday Life](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11487)
*Yijun Chen,Boyi Xiao,Yixian Zhao,Haoting Xia,Buqiang Xu,Jizhan Fang,Yanya Li,Yaqi Zheng,Xuehai Wang,Zirui Xue,Liuxin Zhang,Hui Li,Ningyu Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LightMem-Ego is a lightweight, streaming multimodal memory system for mobile/wearable AI assistants that continuously captures, aligns, and hierarchically organizes egocentric visual-audio streams to answer user queries about past experiences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile and wearable AI assistants continuously perceive visual and audio streams, but answering queries about past experiences requires a lightweight multimodal memory system capable of continuously accumulating, organizing, and retrieving long-term experiences — a capability that remains challenging with existing approaches.

Method: LightMem-Ego captures egocentric visual and audio streams, aligns them on a shared timeline, and organizes them into a three-tier hierarchical memory structure: current memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory. Query answering is performed by dynamically routing retrieval to the appropriate memory level and generating responses grounded in multimodal evidence.

Result: The system is deployable on smartphones and AI glasses, demonstrating capabilities including object finding, conversation recall, life summarization, routine discovery, and personalized assistance.

Conclusion: LightMem-Ego demonstrates a practical solution for lightweight, streaming multimodal memory on resource-constrained devices, enabling everyday-life assistance grounded in continuously accumulated egocentric experiences.

Abstract: Personal AI assistants on mobile and wearable devices continuously perceive users' daily lives through visual and audio streams. However, answering queries about past experiences requires lightweight multimodal memory that can continuously accumulate, organize, and retrieve long-term experiences, which remains challenging. To address this challenge, we present LightMem-Ego, a lightweight streaming multimodal memory system for everyday-life assistance. The system continuously captures egocentric visual and audio streams, aligns them on a shared timeline, and organizes them into a hierarchical memory consisting of current, short-term, and long-term memory. Given a user query, LightMem-Ego dynamically routes retrieval to the appropriate memory level and generates answers grounded in multimodal evidence. The demonstration can be deployed on smartphones and AI glasses, supporting object finding, conversation recall, life summarization, routine discovery, and personalized assistance. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/LightMem-Ego.

</details>


### [32] [UNIBROWSE: A Data-to-Agent Framework for Multimodal BrowseComp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10557)
*Xiyu Wei,Qingwei Zong,Zhuocheng Yu,Sujian Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: UNIBROWSE introduces a unified data pipeline that generates training data covering all three web browsing information-flow patterns (text-only, image-to-text, text-to-image) for the first time, and trains a 35B-scale agent that achieves state-of-the-art performance on multimodal BrowseComp benchmarks, surpassing closed-source competitors like GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5 Pro.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal browsing data construction methods only cover text-only and image-to-text information-flow patterns, neglecting the text-to-image pattern (e.g., searching for images based on textual queries). This gap limits agent generality and robustness in real-world multimodal browsing scenarios that require all three patterns.

Method: The authors propose UNIBROWSE, a unified data pipeline with three key innovations: (1) simultaneous generation of training data across all three information-flow patterns (text-only, image-to-text, text-to-image); (2) augmentation of curated knowledge graphs with live web retrieval for improved fidelity; (3) a novel "exploration degree" metric to filter low-signal instances for efficient reinforcement learning. The pipeline produces cold-start tool-use trajectories and exploration-rich QA pairs, used to train a 35B-scale agent via supervised fine-tuning and exploration-aware RL.

Result: The UNIBROWSE agent achieves an average accuracy of 54.4 across five diverse multimodal BrowseComp benchmarks, outperforming its base model Qwen3.5-35B-A3B by 10.5 points, and surpassing closed-source agent workflows including GPT-5 (42.9), Gemini-2.5 Pro (44.8), and Gemini-2.5 Flash (41.3).

Conclusion: By unifying all three information-flow patterns in training data and incorporating exploration-aware reinforcement learning, UNIBROWSE significantly advances the state of the art in multimodal web browsing agents, demonstrating that comprehensive data coverage and efficient RL filtering are critical for robust, general-purpose browsing agents.

Abstract: Multimodal BrowseComp tasks require agents to combine perception, tool use, and long-horizon reasoning over dynamic web content, challenging their ability to handle compositional structure, open-world uncertainty, and multimodal integration across extended interactions. Crucially, real-world multimodal browsing involves three distinct information-flow patterns: text-only, image-to-text, and text-to-image, yet existing data construction methods cover only the text-only and image-to-text patterns, leaving text-to-image largely unaddressed and limiting agent generality and robustness. We introduce UNIBROWSE, a unified data pipeline that for the first time simultaneously generates training data covering all three patterns, augments curated knowledge graphs with live web retrieval for improved fidelity, and introduces a novel metric of exploration degree to filter low-signal instances for efficient reinforcement learning. Through this pipeline, we produce high-quality cold-start tool-use trajectories and exploration-rich QA pairs, and train a 35B-scale agent via supervised fine-tuning and exploration-aware RL.The resulting UNIBROWSE agent achieves state-of-the-art performance on multimodal BrowseComp benchmarks, attaining an average accuracy of 54.4 across five diverse benchmarks -- an improvement of 10.5 points over its base model Qwen3.5-35B-A3B -- and surpassing serveral closed-source agent workflows such as GPT-5 (42.9), Gemini-2.5 Pro (44.8), and Gemini-2.5 Flash (41.3).

</details>


### [33] [PaperRouter-Agent: A Content-Grounded LLM Agent for Personalized Hierarchical Paper Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11564)
*Keshen Zhou,Lintao Wang,Suqin Yuan,Zhuqiang Lu,Yu Luo,Zhiyong Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PaperRouter-Agent is a training-free LLM agent that routes new papers into user-specific folder hierarchies by grounding decisions in folder member papers rather than folder names alone. It uses evidence retrieval, member inspection, and rejection feedback, boosting Recall@1 from 0.39→0.61 on personal libraries and accuracy from 44.5%→51.5% on LaMP-2.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hierarchical text classification assumes fixed, shared taxonomies. Real users organize papers into private, evolving folder hierarchies (folksonomies) where folder semantics are implicit, multi-faceted (topical, venue-based, process-oriented), and defined by the papers inside them. Standard classifiers fail here, especially on organizational (metadata-based) folders. The authors aim to solve personalized hierarchical paper routing (PHPR) without requiring per-user training.

Method: PaperRouter-Agent is a training-free LLM agent with four stages: (1) Candidate Set Generation—narrow the hierarchy to likely folders via LLM reasoning over folder names and structure; (2) Evidence Retrieval—retrieve representative member papers from candidate folders as grounding evidence; (3) Verification & Routing—inspect member papers to verify fit and assign the paper; (4) Similarity-Gated Feedback—incorporate past user rejections via similarity comparison to avoid repeating mistakes, without explicit training.

Result: On real personal libraries (formative study): Recall@1: 0.39→0.61; Recall@3: 0.57→0.83. Largest gains on organizational folders (venue/year-based): Recall@1 from 0.09→0.50. On LaMP-2 benchmark: accuracy 44.5%→51.5% (+9.0 macro-F1). The method remains low-cost for practical use.

Conclusion: LLM-based agents can effectively solve personalized hierarchical paper routing by grounding decisions in folder membership evidence rather than relying on folder names. The approach is training-free, handles folksonomies, and particularly excels where single-shot methods fail—on organizational folders defined by metadata. The method is practical, low-cost, and validated on both real-world personal libraries and public benchmarks.

Abstract: Researchers organize the papers they collect into personal folder hierarchies in reference managers, and route each new paper into the folder where it belongs. This task differs from standard hierarchical text classification. A user's folder hierarchy is not a fixed, shared taxonomy but a private and evolving folksonomy whose folder meanings may be topical, shorthand, venue-based, or process-oriented, and are often defined by the papers already stored inside them. We formalize this setting as personalized hierarchical paper routing (PHPR): assigning an incoming paper to folders in a user-specific hierarchy without per-user training. We propose PaperRouter-Agent, a training-free LLM agent that grounds routing decisions in folder members rather than folder names alone. The agent first narrows the candidate hierarchy, retrieves folder-specific evidence, verifies fit by inspecting member papers, and incorporates similarity-gated feedback from past user rejections. A formative study on real personal libraries shows that PaperRouter-Agent raises overall Recall@1 from 0.39 to 0.61 and Recall@3 from 0.57 to 0.83, with the largest gains on organizational folders defined by metadata such as venue or year, where single-shot methods collapses (Recall@1 0.09 to 0.50). On the public LaMP-2 benchmark, the same approach improves accuracy from 44.5% to 51.5% (+9.0 macro-F1) over a single-shot baseline, while remaining low-cost for practical use.

</details>


### [34] [Demographic Prompting at Scale: When More Attributes Hurt LLM--Human Agreement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10590)
*Mahammed Kamruzzaman,Shrabon Kumar Das,Gene Louis Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study shows demographic cues in prompts improve LLM-human alignment up to 1–3 high-signal attributes, but full demographic sets degrade performance. Alignment depends on attribute signal learnability and coherence, not just demographic influence magnitude. Neuron probing confirms specialized activation correlates with alignment only under coherent signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how and when providing annotator demographic attributes as prompt cues affects the alignment between LLM predictions and human annotations, moving beyond treating demographic prompting as a uniform strategy.

Method: Five open-source LLMs tested across five tasks. Systematically varied demographic attribute combinations in prompts from single-attribute to full-set configurations. Neuron probing used to examine activation patterns underlying alignment effects.

Result: (1) Alignment peaks at 1–3 high-signal attributes and declines with full attribute sets (over-specification threshold). (2) Demographic influence magnitude alone does not predict alignment improvement; both learnability and directional coherence matter. (3) Neuron activation volume does not imply steerability; specialized activation correlates with alignment only under coherent signals.

Conclusion: Demographic prompting is highly context-dependent, not monolithic. Its effectiveness hinges on attribute signal quality, task characteristics, and model architecture, requiring joint consideration of learnability and directional coherence.

Abstract: We investigate how annotator demographic attributes, supplied as prompt cues, shape the alignment between large language model (LLM) predictions and human annotations across five tasks. Using five open-source LLMs, we systematically vary the number and composition of demographic components in the prompt, spanning every combination from single-attribute through full-attribute configurations. Our experiments reveal three principal findings. First, alignment consistently peaks with one to three high-signal attributes and degrades under the full attribute set, establishing a clear over-specification threshold. Second, the overall magnitude of demographic influence on human annotations does not predict which attributes improve LLM alignment; instead, both the learnability and the directional coherence of each attribute's annotation signal need to be considered jointly. Third, neuron probing reveals that specialized activation correlates with alignment gains only under coherent annotation signals, and that activation volume alone does not imply steerability. Together, these results demonstrate that demographic prompting is not a monolithic intervention: its utility is highly context-dependent, shaped by attribute signal quality, task characteristics, and model architecture.

</details>


### [35] [Non-binary bottom-up constituency parsing without arity actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10591)
*Jungyeul Park,Eunkyul Leah Jo,Zihao Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that arity (number of children) in non-binary bottom-up constituency parsing is not a necessary action primitive. By introducing constituent labels separately and using delimiter-bounded stack configurations to recover reduction spans, arity becomes a derived property rather than an action label, reducing action inventory while maintaining competitive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional non-binary bottom-up constituency parsers require Reduce-X#k actions that jointly specify the mother label and arity (number of children). This leads to a large, sparse action inventory, especially for high-arity constituents. The authors question whether arity truly needs to be an explicit action parameter, seeking to simplify the action space without losing the ability to construct non-binary trees directly.

Method: The proposed delimiter-guided parser separates constituent label introduction from reduction span recovery. Constituent labels are introduced independently. Reduction spans (arity) are recovered from the stack configuration, which is bounded by delimiters. In a well-formed reduction configuration, the active delimiter and label marker uniquely determine arity, making it a derived property of parser state rather than an explicit action label. This factorization eliminates label-arity-specific reduce actions.

Result: Experiments on the Penn Treebank (PTB) and Chinese Treebank (CTB) show the delimiter-guided parser remains competitive with an arity-specific bottom-up baseline under the same implementation framework, while having a substantially smaller action inventory. The predicted arity profile remains close to gold treebanks, and high-arity constituents do not collapse when arity actions are removed.

Conclusion: Arity is not a necessary transition primitive in non-binary bottom-up constituency parsing. Factorizing label and arity through delimiter-guided stack configurations yields a more parsimonious action space without degrading parsing accuracy or distorting the arity distribution, including for high-arity constituents.

Abstract: Non-binary bottom-up constituency parsing is usually taken to require arity actions: reductions such as \(\textsc{Reduce-}X\#k\) specify both the mother label and the number of children to be composed. We show that this arity parameter is not a necessary transition primitive. Our parser introduces constituent labels separately and recovers reduction spans from delimiter-bounded stack configurations. In a well-formed reduction configuration, arity is uniquely determined by the active delimiter and the label marker, making it a derived property of parser state rather than an action label. This factorization removes label--arity-specific reduce actions while preserving direct construction of original non-binary trees. Experiments on PTB and CTB show that the delimiter-guided parser remains competitive with an arity-specific bottom-up baseline under the same implementation framework, with substantially smaller action inventories. Analyses further show that its predicted arity profile remains close to the gold treebanks and that high-arity constituents do not collapse when arity actions are removed.

</details>


### [36] [Eval-Pair Matrix: Answer-Paired Meta-Evaluation of LLM Judges for Grounded RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10626)
*Sriram Selvam,Anneswa Ghosh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Eval-Pair Matrix, a controlled meta-evaluation protocol revealing that apparent self-leniency in LLM-as-a-judge RAG evaluation disappears when judges are paired on identical answers, with the only robust effect being lower flagging when answers avoided induced contradictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is widespread in RAG, but reusing models from the same family as both generator and judge risks self-leniency bias that is hard to detect. Existing evaluation protocols lack controlled, answer-paired comparisons to isolate same-model effects from other confounds.

Method: The authors construct the Eval-Pair Matrix protocol: starting from GaRAGe questions and grounding passages, they induce one hidden answer-causal contradiction per record, generate answers from perturbed passages using GPT, Grok, and Gemini models, then use the same models as blind judges. The crossed 3×3 design (300 core records, 897 labeled outputs, 2,683 verdicts) pairs judges on the exact same candidate answer to estimate same-model effects, rather than comparing diagonal/off-diagonal cells across different answers. A targeted human evaluation adjudicates apparent false positives.

Result: Diagonal and off-diagonal F1 scores are similar under answer-paired analysis. The paired same-model recall effect is near zero (-0.5 pp; 95% cluster bootstrap CI [-2.7, +1.7]). The only robust paired gap is a -4.3 pp difference in matching-judge flagging for answers that avoided the induced contradiction. Human evaluation found that reviewed apparent false positives were alternate source-error detections, labeling mistakes, or unclear cases — none were genuine false alarms.

Conclusion: The self-leniency concern in RAG judge evaluation is largely a methodological artifact of confounded answer comparisons. The authors recommend that RAG judge studies report full matrices, answer-paired effects, behavior strata, and label-task alignment to ensure valid meta-evaluation.

Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is widely used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but reusing the same model family as both generator and judge makes self-leniency difficult to identify. We introduce Eval-Pair Matrix, a controlled meta evaluation protocol for source-grounded RAG. Starting from GaRAGe questions and grounding passages, we induce one hidden answer-causal contradiction per record, generate answers from perturbed passages with GPT, Grok, and Gemini models, and then use the same models as blind judges to evaluate each answer against the original passages. The experiment contains 300 core records, 897 labeled generator outputs, and 2,683 judge verdicts in a crossed 3 x 3 matrix; the primary analysis uses 275 fully validated records. Instead of comparing diagonal and off-diagonal cells across different answers, we estimate same-model effects by pairing judges on the exact same candidate answer. This changes the interpretation: diagonal and off diagonal F1 are similar, and the paired same-model recall effect is near zero (-0.5 pp; 95% cluster bootstrap CI [-2.7, +1.7]). The only robust paired gap is lower matching-judge flagging for answers that avoided the induced claim (-4.3 pp). A targeted human evaluation finds that reviewed apparent false positives are alternate source-error detections, mistakes in labeling whether the induced claim was adopted, or unclear cases; none were adjudicated as genuine false alarms. The lesson is methodological: RAG judge studies should report full matrices, answer-paired effects, behavior strata, and label-task alignment.

</details>


### [37] [Characterising AI Models for Cataloguing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11353)
*Miguel Arana-Catania,Neil Jefferies*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper evaluates the application of AI models for automating catalogue record creation in digital collections, comparing different implementations through both qualitative and quantitative analyses, and provides generalizable recommendations for AI model usage beyond the specific digitization use case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The creation of catalogue records for digital collections is a slow, costly, and often-overlooked task that currently relies on expert manual effort. Automating this process with AI could significantly reduce time and expense.

Method: The authors conducted experiments comparing different AI model implementations for catalogue record generation, followed by both qualitative and quantitative evaluations of the results.

Result: The paper presents findings from the comparative evaluation of various AI models on the cataloguing task, though specific performance metrics are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: The work offers practical recommendations for deploying AI models in cataloguing workflows, emphasizing that these insights are applicable beyond the specific use case examined.

Abstract: The creation of digital collections involves not only the digitisation of content, but also the creation of catalogue records for it. This often-overlooked task requires slow and costly expert manual work. In this project, we have evaluated the application of AI models to this task, comparing different implementations and models. This work includes a qualitative and quantitative evaluation of the experiments carried out, as well as recommendations on the use of AI models that go beyond the specific use case.

</details>


### [38] [Knowledge Distillation for Automated AI Tutor Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10647)
*Tahmid Al Hannan,Diego Garcia,Alex Njoroge,Suha Al Juboori,Tarek Sakakini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces FATE, an 8B-parameter model fine-tuned via knowledge distillation from a frontier LLM to evaluate AI tutors across four pedagogical dimensions. It achieves up to 22.63 pp gains and benchmarks commercial models, with Gemini 2.5 Flash ranking highest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are rapidly being deployed in K-12 and higher education, but reliable, automated methods for evaluating their pedagogical quality have lagged behind. There is a lack of specialized tools and limited labeled data for assessing how well AI tutors perform on educationally meaningful dimensions.

Method: The authors build FATE, a specialized 8B-parameter language model aligned with the four BEA 2025 Shared Task evaluation tracks: Mistake Identification, Mistake Location, Guidance, and Actionability. To overcome scarce labeled data, they use knowledge distillation from a frontier LLM to generate auxiliary supervision, yielding significant performance improvements.

Result: Knowledge distillation yields absolute gains up to 22.63 percentage points. In benchmarking commercial models as AI tutors, Gemini 2.5 Flash scores highest (82.88%), followed by ChatGPT 5.5 Instant (80.75%), DeepSeek V4 Flash (80.13%), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (74.00%).

Conclusion: FATE demonstrates that a relatively small, purpose-built evaluator model, trained with distilled supervision, can serve as an effective automated judge of AI tutor pedagogical quality, offering a scalable alternative to costly human evaluation.

Abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into K-12 and higher education has outpaced the development of reliable methods for evaluating their pedagogical quality. As the research community starts to explore the space of automating evaluation of AI tutors, we introduce FATE (FLC AI Tutor Evaluator), a specialized 8B-parameter language model designed to evaluate AI tutors. Aligned with the four core evaluation tracks from the BEA 2025 Shared Task, our model assesses pedagogical ability across Mistake Identification, Mistake Location, Guidance, and Actionability. Because pedagogical evaluation is a specialized task with limited labeled data, we leverage knowledge distillation from a frontier LLM to generate additional supervision, yielding absolute performance gains up to 22.63 percentage points. Finally, we demonstrate FATE's utility as an automated evaluator by benchmarking instructional responses generated by popular commercial models, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek. On average, we have found that Gemini 2.5 Flash perfomed best (82.88%), then ChatGPT 5.5 Instant (80.75%), followed by DeepSeek V4 Flash (80.13%) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (74.00%).

</details>


### [39] [Unlocking Parallelism in Autoregressive Language Models via Speculative Decoding with Progressive Tree Drafting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10661)
*Zipeng Gao,Zhi Zheng,Qingrong Xia,Junda Lin,Ziwei Zhao,Tong Xu,Zhefeng Wang,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Progressive Tree Drafting (PTD) is a training-free, model-agnostic speculative decoding method that uses a guided parallel drafting strategy with a progressive tree structure and stepwise pruning to achieve up to 2× decoding speedup in LLM inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional speculative decoding relies on auxiliary draft modules that incur training and communication overhead. Recent self-drafting methods fail to fully exploit the target model's latent parallel capacity due to a lack of structural coordination in the drafting process.

Method: PTD employs a progressive tree structure coupled with a stepwise pruning mechanism to guide the LLM in exploring multiple semantic paths within a single forward pass. The progressive tree enables structured parallel drafting, while stepwise pruning ensures draft diversity and coherence by iteratively refining candidate sequences.

Result: PTD achieves up to 2× decoding speedup across various benchmarks while remaining training-free and model-agnostic.

Conclusion: PTD effectively unlocks the parallel capacity of LLMs for speculative decoding without requiring auxiliary models or additional training, offering a practical and efficient solution for accelerating LLM inference.

Abstract: Speculative decoding has significantly accelerated Large Language Model (LLM) inference by alleviating memory-bound bottlenecks. However, traditional speculative decoding typically relies on auxiliary draft modules, incurring significant training and communication overhead. Although recent methods attempt to generate drafts within the target model itself, they often fail to fully exploit its latent parallel capacity due to a lack of structural coordination. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Progressive Tree Drafting (PTD)}, which employs a structured, guided parallel drafting strategy to harness the model's parallel potential. By coupling a progressive tree structure with a stepwise pruning mechanism, PTD actively guides the LLM to explore multiple semantic paths in a single forward pass, ensuring both draft diversity and coherence. Experiments demonstrate that PTD achieves up to $2\times$ decoding speedup across various benchmarks while remaining training-free and model-agnostic. Our code is available at: https://github.com/MINE-USTC/PTD.

</details>


### [40] [A Corpus of Persuasion Techniques in Slavic Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10715)
*Jakub Piskorski,Dimitar Iliyanov Dimitrov,Marina Ernst,Jacek Haneczok,Michał Marcińczuk,Arkadiusz Modzelewski,Roman Yangarber*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A new multilingual persuasion techniques corpus for Bulgarian, Polish, and Russian, annotated at span and sentence levels with 25 fine-grained techniques across 6 rhetorical categories. The paper provides baseline detection results using classical ML and generative AI models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persuasion techniques are widely used to shape public opinion, yet NLP resources for detecting them in Slavic languages are scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a richly annotated corpus spanning three Slavic languages, enabling computational analysis of rhetorical persuasion in under-resourced languages.

Method: Corpus construction: 222 documents (~7500 text spans) in Bulgarian, Polish, and Russian annotated at coarse-grained text-span level and fine-grained sentence level using a taxonomy of 25 persuasion techniques grouped into 6 rhetorical strategy categories. Baseline experiments employ classical machine learning models and generative AI-based approaches for both detection and classification tasks at both annotation granularities.

Result: The paper presents a fully annotated corpus with detailed statistics and topic-technique correlation analyses. Baseline benchmark results for persuasion technique detection and classification are reported for both text-span and sentence levels using classical ML and generative AI models.

Conclusion: The corpus provides a valuable resource for multilingual persuasion detection in Slavic languages. The baselines establish initial benchmarks and highlight challenges in fine-grained persuasion technique classification, paving the way for more advanced models in this domain.

Abstract: Persuasion techniques are powerful rhetorical devices used to sway public opinion in a wide range of media. We present a new corpus of persuasion techniques, focusing on Slavic languages. The corpus contains documents in Bulgarian, Polish, and Russian, annotated with persuasion techniques at the coarse-grained text-span level and fine-grained sentence level. The techniques are drawn from a taxonomy of 25 fine-grained persuasion techniques, grouped under six broad categories of rhetorical persuasion strategies. The corpus contains approximately 7500 text spans from 222 documents that cover topics hotly debated at the national and international levels. We describe the corpus creation process, provide detailed statistics, and examine correlations between topics and persuasion techniques. We use classic ML-based and generative AI-based models to provide baselines and benchmark results for the detection and classification of persuasion techniques at the text-span level and sentence level.

</details>


### [41] [The First ChineseBabyLM Challenge: training data-efficient and cognitively plausible language models for Chinese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10745)
*Siyuan Song,Zhiheng Qian,Yunhao Zhang,Linyang He,Xiaozhe Ji,Yingxin Lin,Hongao Zhu,Chongtian Shao,Chuhan Lang,Luan Li,Rui Wang,Renfen Hu,Shaonan Wang,Hai Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first ChineseBabyLM challenge at NLPCC 2026, where participants train language models from scratch using only 100 million Chinese tokens and are evaluated on NLU, cognitive alignment, and Hanzi knowledge tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The challenge is motivated by the BabyLM initiative, which advocates for sample-efficient language learning — training models on limited data to better understand how humans (and potentially machines) can acquire linguistic competence from a developmentally plausible amount of input. By focusing on Chinese, the challenge addresses the under-explored domain of low-resource, cognitively plausible modeling for non-English languages.

Method: Participants must train language models entirely from scratch using a fixed corpus of 100 million Chinese tokens. There are no constraints on tokenizer choice, model architecture, or number of training epochs. Models are evaluated across three tracks: Natural Language Understanding (NLU), cognitive alignment (measuring how well model representations align with human cognitive data), and Hanzi knowledge (assessing character-level understanding of Chinese writing).

Result: This is a challenge proposal paper; no experimental results are reported. The paper outlines the competition setup, tracks, and evaluation framework to be used at NLPCC 2026.

Conclusion: The ChineseBabyLM challenge aims to foster research on data-efficient language acquisition in Chinese, bridging the gap between cognitive modeling and practical NLU under strict data constraints. It extends the BabyLM paradigm to a non-Latin script language with unique typological properties.

Abstract: This paper describes the first ChineseBabyLM challenge, which will be held in the 2026 NLPCC conference. The challenge calls for researchers to train language models from scratch with 100 million Chinese tokens and evaluates the models on 3 tracks of tasks: NLU, cognitive alignment and Hanzi knowledge. There is no restriction on tokenizer, model architecture and the number of training epochs. Details of the challenge can be found in https://chinese-babylm.github.io/.

</details>


### [42] [Trust Before Fusion: QIMG-7 and Source-Aware Resolution for Polluted Multimodal RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10798)
*Saadeldine Eletter,Owais Aijaz,Preslav Nakov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: QIMG-7 is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal RAG under retrieval pollution (7 image-attack types across 4 datasets). The authors show naive fusion is brittle when images are misleading, and propose SATR, a training-free trust-resolution method that selectively relies on Parametric, Text-only, or Full-MM sources, achieving an 0.816 balanced score vs. 0.490 for polluted Full-MM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal RAG systems are typically benchmarked with clean evidence, but real-world retrieval often returns unreliable content—misleading images from corruption, adversarial edits, or metadata swaps. The authors aim to systematically study how such retrieval pollution degrades multimodal generators and to design a robust mitigation strategy.

Method: The authors construct QIMG-7, a controlled benchmark with 7 image-attack families (corrupted metadata, entity swaps, typographic overlays, semantic edits, adversarial patches, blends, style transfer) across 4 datasets in 16 clean/polluted regimes. They evaluate 4 generator/gate stacks. They then propose Source-Aware Trust Resolution (SATR), a training-free method that compares candidate answers from Parametric (no retrieval), Text-only, and Full-MM modalities, using a Field-Selector variant to choose or fall back based on estimated source reliability.

Result: Under the main gpt-4o-mini stack, Full-MM support drops from 0.908 (clean) to 0.490 (polluted). Parametric fallback is often safer than polluted retrieval. SATR's Field-Selector achieves a 0.816 balanced score, improving over Full-MM by +11.7 points and over a Cascaded Router baseline by +2.7 points. Ablations reveal explicit text-reliability modeling as the dominant performance driver in this text-first setting.

Conclusion: In text-first factual QA with multimodal retrieval conflict, selective trust (via SATR) outperforms unconditional fusion. The results advocate for source-aware gating rather than naive multimodal integration when retrieval evidence may be polluted.

Abstract: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is often evaluated with clean evidence, yet real retrieval can return topically relevant but unreliable content: false text and misleading images from corrupted metadata, entity swaps, typographic overlays, semantic edits, adversarial patches, blends, or style transfer. We introduce QIMG-7, a controlled benchmark for multimodal retrieval pollution in multi-sentence factual QA, spanning four datasets, seven image-attack families, and 16 paired clean/polluted regimes, for 1,760 evaluation rows per method. Across four generator/gate stacks, naive multimodal fusion is brittle: in the main gpt-4o-mini stack, Full-MM support drops from 0.908 with clean text to 0.490 with polluted text, often making Parametric fallback safer than retrieval. We propose source-aware trust resolution (SATR), a training-free approach that compares Parametric, Text-only, and Full-MM candidate answers and selects among candidate answers or falls back based on source reliability. The Field-Selector variant achieves the best balanced score, 0.816, improving over Full-MM by 11.7 points and over the Cascaded Router by 2.7 points. Ablations show that, in this text-first setting, explicit text-reliability modeling is the dominant driver of these gains. Overall, in text-first factual QA with multimodal retrieval conflict, our results support selective trust rather than unconditional fusion. Artifacts are available at https://github.com/SaadElDine/Trust_Before_Fusion.

</details>


### [43] [Diagnosing and Mitigating Thinking Collapse in On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10805)
*Keqin Peng,Chen Li,Yuanxin Ouyang,Yancheng Yuan,Liang Ding*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Standard On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) degrades complex reasoning in LLMs due to "Thinking Collapse" — a sharp drop in epistemic-token density caused by aggressive teacher gradients suppressing student epistemic tokens. The authors propose Adaptive Dual-Perspective OPSD (AD-OPSD), which anchors high-suppression-risk tokens to a frozen base model prior via an asymmetrical divergence gate, improving accuracy by up to +4.1% across math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD is widely used to enhance and align LLMs, yet paradoxically degrades performance on complex reasoning tasks. The authors aim to systematically diagnose the root cause of this degradation and develop a solution that preserves reasoning capacity while retaining OPSD's error-correcting benefits.

Method: First, the authors define and measure "Thinking Collapse" via epistemic-token density (ET per 1k). Using entropy-based gradient masking and token-level analysis, they identify that collapse originates from aggressive teacher gradients at high-student-entropy decision forks, where student epistemic tokens are suppressed into teacher non-epistemic targets in regions of high pointwise divergence. To address this, they propose AD-OPSD: a control framework that dynamically moderates self-distillation by selectively anchoring high-suppression-risk ("sandboxed") tokens to a reference prior from the frozen base model, gated by an asymmetrical pointwise divergence measure. This preserves native thinking while maintaining error correction.

Result: AD-OPSD achieves up to +4.1% absolute average accuracy improvement over standard OPSD across diverse model scales and competitive mathematical benchmarks. It effectively mitigates thinking collapse and generalizes robustly to different post-training paradigms.

Conclusion: Thinking Collapse is a critical optimization pathology in OPSD for complex reasoning. AD-OPSD provides an effective solution by dynamically balancing knowledge distillation with native reasoning preservation, demonstrating strong empirical gains and cross-paradigm robustness.

Abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for enhancing and aligning Large Language Models (LLMs). However, in complex reasoning tasks, OPSD paradoxically degrades downstream performance. In this paper, we systematically investigate this pathology and identify a severe optimization trap we define as \textbf{Thinking Collapse} -- a sharp decline in the model's native intermediate reasoning behavior, measured by epistemic-token density (ET per 1k). Through entropy-based gradient masking and token-level target analysis, we show that this collapse is triggered by aggressive teacher gradients at high-student-entropy decision forks, where student epistemic tokens are frequently suppressed into teacher non-epistemic targets and are highly concentrated in high pointwise student-teacher divergence regions. To resolve this optimization pathology, we propose \textbf{Adaptive Dual-Perspective OPSD (AD-OPSD)}, a robust control framework that dynamically moderates the self-distillation objective. AD-OPSD selectively anchors high-suppression-risk sandboxed tokens to a reference prior derived from the frozen base model via an asymmetrical pointwise divergence gate, preserving native thinking capacity while retaining OPSD's error-correcting power. Extensive experiments across competitive mathematical benchmarks show that AD-OPSD improves over standard OPSD by up to \textbf{+4.1\%} absolute average accuracy across diverse model scales and datasets. Further analysis demonstrates that AD-OPSD mitigates thinking collapse and generalizes robustly to different post-training paradigms.

</details>


### [44] [Abstractiveness Metrics for Evaluating Text Summarization: A Refined Formulation with Empirical Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10806)
*Praveenkumar Katwe,Rakesh Chandra Balabantaray,Kali Prasad Vittala*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces three heuristic metrics — Reference Abstraction (RA), Summary Abstraction (SA), and Abstraction Ratio (AR) — that quantify how abstractive a summary is by measuring its divergence from extractive copying. Evaluated on 100 XSUM documents across four models, the metrics effectively discriminate extractive from abstractive summarizers and flag summaries potentially requiring manual hallucination review.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing summarization evaluation relies heavily on surface-level metrics like ROUGE, which fail to capture the degree of abstractiveness in generated summaries. There is a need for principled, interpretable metrics that quantify where a summary falls on the extractive–abstractive spectrum and can help identify outputs that may contain hallucinations.

Method: The authors propose three metrics: (1) Reference Abstraction (RA), measuring divergence of the reference summary from the source; (2) Summary Abstraction (SA), measuring divergence of the generated summary from the source; and (3) Abstraction Ratio (AR), the ratio of SA to RA. The formulation uses the harmonic mean of document lengths modulated by a cubic non-overlap factor, producing dimensionally consistent, bounded outputs with non-linear sensitivity at the extractive–abstractive boundary. Evaluation is conducted on 100 XSUM documents using four models: BART-large-cnn, Pegasus-xsum, DistilBart, and MT5-small.

Result: The metrics successfully discriminate between extractive models (SA ≈ 0.12–0.26) and abstractive models (SA ≈ 0.96–1.77). The Abstraction Ratio effectively identifies summaries that warrant manual evaluation for potential hallucination.

Conclusion: RA, SA, and AR provide a principled, interpretable framework for quantifying summary abstractiveness, enabling finer-grained evaluation beyond ROUGE and assisting in hallucination detection workflows. Code and results are publicly available.

Abstract: Quantifying abstractiveness in generated summaries is essential for evaluating summarization models beyond
  surface-level metrics like ROUGE. We introduce Reference Abstraction (RA), Summary Abstraction (SA), and Abstraction
  Ratio (AR) -- a set of principled heuristic metrics that measure how much a summary diverges from extractive copying
  of the source text. The formulation uses the harmonic mean of document lengths modulated by a cubic non-overlap
  factor, yielding dimensionally consistent, bounded output with non-linear sensitivity to the extractive-abstractive
  boundary. Evaluation on 100 XSUM documents across four summarization models (BART-large-cnn, Pegasus-xsum, DistilBart,
  MT5-small) demonstrates that the metrics successfully discriminate between extractive models (SA ~ 0.12-0.26) and
  abstractive models (SA ~ 0.96-1.77), and that the Abstraction Ratio identifies summaries requiring manual evaluation
  for potential hallucination. Code and results are available at https://github.com/katweNLP/AbstractionStudy.

</details>


### [45] [Large Language Models for Token-Efficient and Semantic-Preserving Opinion Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10825)
*Fabrizio Marozzo,Stefano Iannicelli*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A framework that uses multidimensional classification and stratified sampling to select compact, representative opinion subsets before LLM prompting, achieving token-efficient summarization that preserves semantic diversity, coverage, and balance across product, hotel, and social media domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale opinion corpora (reviews, social posts) suffer from scale, redundancy, and imbalance, making it difficult to generate summaries that faithfully represent the diversity of viewpoints without incurring excessive computational cost and token usage.

Method: The framework combines multidimensional classification (e.g., sentiment, topics) with a family of stratified sampling strategies to select compact yet representative opinion subsets. Tailored prompts are then used with an LLM to generate balanced summaries that highlight salient aspects such as strengths and weaknesses.

Result: Experiments on Amazon product reviews, Tripadvisor hotel reviews, and X/Twitter posts show significant reductions in token usage and computational cost, while consistently outperforming traditional AI-based and standard LLM summarization baselines in content coverage, balance, and semantic preservation.

Conclusion: Stratified sampling guided by multidimensional classification is an effective strategy for making LLM-based opinion summarization both cost-efficient and semantically faithful, enabling balanced summaries that capture diverse viewpoints without exhaustive processing of full corpora.

Abstract: Opinionated text - spanning product reviews, hotel feedback, and social posts - captures rich signals about user experiences, preferences, and concerns. However, the scale, redundancy, and imbalance of such corpora make it challenging to analyze opinions effectively, particularly when the goal is to generate summaries that remain faithful to the diversity of viewpoints expressed. This paper presents a framework that preserves semantics in LLM-based opinion summarization while minimizing token usage. We combine multidimensional classification (e.g., sentiment, topics) with a family of stratified sampling strategies to select compact yet representative subsets of opinions before prompting the LLM. Tailored prompts then produce balanced summaries that surface the salient aspects expressed in the opinions (e.g., strengths and weaknesses of products/hotels). Experiments on Amazon product reviews, Tripadvisor hotel reviews, and X/Twitter posts demonstrate that our method significantly reduces token usage and computational cost while consistently outperforming traditional AI-based and standard LLM summarization baselines in terms of content coverage, balance, and semantic preservation.

</details>


### [46] [Quantifying the Sources of Instability in LLM-Based Stance Analysis of Public Discourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10846)
*Bo Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces a diagnostic framework that disentangles two sources of instability in computational social science pipelines — preprocessing (e.g., diarization) versus measurement instruments (LLM vs. keyword lexicons) — showing that while aggregate metrics appear stable, cross-dimensional relationships like valence–modality coupling are sensitive to both pipeline choice (especially for low-sample speakers) and, more systematically, to measurement method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computational social science pipelines that convert raw media into analyzable text can produce divergent outputs from the same input, but researchers lack a systematic framework to distinguish whether such variation originates from the preprocessing pipeline or from the downstream measurement instrument. This ambiguity threatens the reproducibility and validity of findings based on automated text analysis.

Method: The authors analyze 256 YouTube interviews of 41 public figures across five domains, systematically comparing two speaker-diarization pipelines and two measurement methods (LLM-based annotation vs. keyword-lexicon), all targeting the coupling between affective valence (positive/negative) and epistemic modality (certainty/hedging). They quantify pipeline-induced changes via mean absolute differences in correlation coefficients and assess cross-method agreement.

Result: Key findings: (1) Pipeline sensitivity is concentrated in speakers with ≤5 videos; for well-sampled speakers (N≥16), the mean absolute change in r(neg, emph) is only 0.13. (2) Cross-method disagreement is larger and systematic — LLM and lexicon methods assign opposite coupling directions even within the same pipeline. (3) Aggregate valence proportions are highly stable (|Δp(neg)| < 6pp) regardless of pipeline or method, masking both sources of instability.

Conclusion: The authors contribute a diagnostic framework that separates pipeline effects from measurement effects, urging researchers studying cross-dimensional relationships in interview data to verify robustness against both sources of variation, with particular attention to measurement method choice, since aggregate metrics alone can conceal significant instability.

Abstract: Computational social science increasingly relies on automated preprocessing pipelines -- speaker diarization, ASR transcript cleaning, sentence segmentation -- to convert raw media into analyzable text. When these pipelines produce different outputs from the same input, two distinct sources of instability can arise: the preprocessing pipeline itself (diarization method, segmentation rules) and the downstream measurement instrument (LLM annotation vs.\ keyword lexicon). Using 256 YouTube interviews across 41 public figures from five domains, we compare two speaker-diarization pipelines and two measurement methods, all targeting the coupling between affective valence and epistemic modality. We find that (1) preprocessing pipeline sensitivity is concentrated in speakers with limited video samples (N $\leq 5$); for the four best-sampled speakers (N $\geq 16$), the mean absolute pipeline-induced change in $r(\text{neg}, \text{emph})$ is only $0.13$; (2) cross-method disagreement is larger and more systematic -- the LLM and keyword-lexicon methods assign opposite coupling directions to several well-sampled speakers, even within the same preprocessing pipeline; and (3) aggregate valence proportions are highly stable ($|Δp(\text{neg})| < 6$pp) regardless of pipeline or method, masking both sources of instability. The contribution is a diagnostic framework that separates pipeline effects from measurement effects: researchers studying cross-dimensional relationships in interview data should verify that their conclusions are robust to both sources of variation, with particular attention to measurement method choice.

</details>


### [47] [Capabilities of Claude Fable 5 on Biomedical Challenge Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10849)
*Dominic Okonkwo,Magnus Hodgson,Temitope I. David,Susan Adanna Ihejirika*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Claude Fable 5 exhibits unprecedented refusal rates (8–99.4%) on biomedical benchmarks, but once refusals are excluded, it matches or exceeds all other models. Two distinct refusal patterns are identified: content-based (basic science/mechanism) and disease-domain (inborn metabolic diseases). Willingness to engage, not capability, is the limiting factor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two methodological problems plague biomedical LLM evaluations: (1) legacy benchmarks are near-saturation, and (2) open-ended responses are graded by other LLMs, introducing evaluator bias. This study addresses both by using deterministic scoring against fixed answer keys across eight benchmarks (four text, four multimodal), and by systematically tracking refusals as a distinct outcome.

Method: Evaluated Claude Fable 5, two Claude predecessors, and GPT-5 on eight biomedical benchmarks (four text-based: MedQA, MedXpertQA MM, RareBench, and one unnamed; four multimodal). Used deterministic scoring against fixed answer keys throughout. Refusals tracked as a distinct outcome category in every result table. Analyzed refusal patterns using benchmark-provided category labels to identify content-domain and disease-domain clusters.

Result: Fable 5 refused 8.0%–99.4% of questions depending on benchmark, a pattern absent in predecessors and GPT-5. When refusals excluded, Fable 5 matched or exceeded every other model on every benchmark. Two refusal patterns emerged: (1) concentration in basic-science/mechanism content on MedQA and MedXpertQA MM, independently confirmed across both benchmarks; (2) near-universal refusal of inborn metabolic disease presentations on RareBench, while adult-onset autoimmune presentations were answered normally.

Conclusion: Fable 5's biomedical constraint is willingness to engage, not capability—overturning the standard assumption that accuracy alone measures clinical utility. Systematic refusal tracking should become standard practice in biomedical LLM evaluation.

Abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly evaluated on biomedical benchmarks, but two problems undermine most published evaluations: legacy benchmarks are near-saturated, and open-ended responses are graded by other language models. We evaluate Claude Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable publicly available model, across eight biomedical benchmarks, four text and four multimodal, using deterministic scoring against fixed answer keys throughout. We include two Claude predecessors and GPT-5 as baselines. Refusal is tracked as a distinct outcome in every result table. That decision produces the paper's central finding. Fable 5 refuses between 8.0% and 99.4% of questions depending on the benchmark, a pattern absent in both predecessors and in GPT-5. Once refused items are excluded from the denominator, Fable 5's accuracy exceeds or meets every other model on every benchmark in this study.
