We identify two distinguishable refusal patterns: one concentrating in basic-science and mechanism content across MedQA and MedXpertQA MM, confirmed independently on two benchmarks using each benchmark's own category labels; and a separate disease-domain pattern on RareBench, where inborn metabolic disease presentations are refused near-universally while adult-onset autoimmune presentations are not. The primary constraint on Fable 5's biomedical usefulness is willingness to engage, not capability once it does.

</details>


### [48] [The Nuts and Bolts of Natural Language to SQL Translation: A Systematic Analysis of Model Pipeline Optimisation Approaches and their Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10911)
*Filip Klubicka,Vasudevan Nedumpozhimana,Sneha Rautmare,Bora Caglayan,Mingxue Wang,John D. Kelleher*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Explores NL2SQL pipeline extensions (NatSQL, preprocessing, synthetic data fine-tuning, and a novel reranker) with SmBoP and RASAT backbones. Finds that combining all components does not yield optimal results; their effectiveness depends on interactions with the baseline and each other, supported by ablation and Shapley analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NL2SQL remains an open problem despite advances in LLMs. The authors aim to inspire development of lightweight models by systematically studying how various pipeline extensions interact, rather than simply stacking them together.

Method: Integration of four components: (1) NatSQL intermediate representation, (2) a preprocessing step, (3) fine-tuning on synthetic data, and (4) a novel beam-level reranker for SQL selection. Ablation study and Shapley value analysis are used to assess component contributions and interactions across two backbone architectures (SmBoP and RASAT).

Result: Combining all extensions naively does not yield the best performance. Component impact varies significantly depending on the underlying backbone system and on pairwise or higher-order interactions between extensions.

Conclusion: NL2SQL pipeline design must account for component interactions rather than assuming additive benefits. The interplay between extensions and backbone architecture is critical for optimizing lightweight models.

Abstract: In the age of large language models, Natural Language to SQL (NL2SQL) translation remains an open problem with many useful applications. We explore interactions between several NL2SQL pipeline extensions to inspire development of more lightweight models. Specifically, we integrate the NatSQL intermediate representation, include a preprocessing step and a fine-tuning step based on synthetic data, and develop a novel reranker model to improve SQL selection in the final beam. We perform an ablation study supplemented by a Shapley analysis of these different components integrated with two backbone architectures, SmBoP and RASAT. We find that simply combining all of them does not lead to best results, but that their impact depends on their interactions with the baseline system, as well as each other.

</details>


### [49] [EasyOPD: An Easy-to-use On-Policy Distillation Framework for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11012)
*Jie Sun,Mao Zheng,Mingyang Song,Qiyong Zhong,Gengsheng Li,Zhepei Hong,Chang Wu,Pengfei Liu,Junfeng Fang,Xiang Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EasyOPD is a unified on-policy distillation framework built on verl that standardizes disparate OPD methods through modular extension boundaries, enabling reproducible implementations across cross-tokenizer, self-distillation, and step-wise OPD settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy distillation methods differ greatly in supervision form, tokenizer compatibility, teacher access, and granularity, resulting in fragmented, hard-to-reproduce implementations. A unified framework is needed to standardize these approaches.

Method: EasyOPD decouples user configuration, method-specific supervision logic, and verl-based distributed execution. It defines extension boundaries for loss construction, rollout metadata, reward processing, tokenizer alignment, and teacher-side computation. Three OPD settings are instantiated: cross-tokenizer OPD, on-policy self-distillation, and step-wise OPD.

Result: Experiments on reasoning, code-generation, scientific-knowledge, and tool-use benchmarks demonstrate that all three OPD instantiations can execute through the same verl backend while preserving their method-specific objectives and task-dependent performance characteristics.

Conclusion: EasyOPD provides a reproducible, extensible foundation for on-policy distillation research, released with YAML configurations, documentation, an installable demo package, and a demonstration video.

Abstract: Conventional language-model distillation often relies on fixed teacher-generated data, which may not cover the states encountered by an evolving student policy. On-policy distillation (OPD) instead collects teacher or evaluator supervision on student-generated rollouts. However, existing OPD methods differ substantially in supervision form, tokenizer compatibility, teacher access, and supervision granularity, leading to fragmented implementations that are difficult to reproduce and extend. We present \textsc{EasyOPD}, an on-policy distillation framework built on verl, a distributed reinforcement-learning framework for large language models. \textsc{EasyOPD} separates user-side configuration, method-specific supervision logic, and verl-based execution. Its method modules connect to the shared backend through extension boundaries for loss construction, rollout metadata, reward processing, tokenizer alignment, and teacher-side computation. We instantiate representative methods for three OPD settings -- cross-tokenizer OPD, on-policy self-distillation, and step-wise OPD. Experiments on reasoning, code-generation, scientific-knowledge, and tool-use benchmarks show that these implementations can be executed through the same verl-based backend while retaining their method-specific objectives and task-dependent performance profiles. We release \textsc{EasyOPD} with runnable YAML configurations, documentation, and an installable demonstration package and video.

</details>


### [50] [Can a Language Model Learn Facts Continually in Its Weights?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11020)
*Charles O'Neill*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether continual learning in language models can support knowledge accumulation through weight updates. Using Qwen3 models, the authors find that training data diversity critically determines knowledge quality: bare statements produce recitation, while diverse restatements enable genuine use. However, even with broad data, later writes cause catastrophic interference — earlier facts become "question-keyed" (stored but unreachable), and no intervention tested preserves access to them. The reliable channel for composable, durable knowledge is context rather than weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether sequential weight updates in continual learning can truly accumulate knowledge in language models, or whether later writes inevitably impair access to earlier facts — addressing the undecided question of whether weight-based knowledge accumulation is viable.

Method: The authors write invented facts into Qwen3 models across sequences of 20–100 sequential updates. They evaluate using five question types with held-out questions, using the original model (with facts supplied in-context) as a reference baseline. They compare bare-statement training against diverse-restatement training, measure log-probability retention of forgotten facts, test recovery when forgotten facts are supplied in prompts, track KL divergence from the original model, and test various interventions (including local gradient measurements) to preserve earlier facts.

Result: Diverse restatements reduce the recitation-to-use gap from 27.4 to 5.4 points. After 20 sequential writes, bare-statement facts retain only 1% accuracy vs. 46% for broad-study facts. Forgotten facts retain most of their log-probability increase; under bare-statement training, 70% of wrong answers contain the most recently written fact. Supplying a forgotten study fact in the prompt recovers 77–80% accuracy. Later writes cause interference regardless of how earlier facts were stored, and no tested intervention keeps earlier facts reachable.

Conclusion: Broad training data enables usable knowledge, but later writes inevitably disrupt access to earlier facts through a "question-keyed" storage phenomenon. For knowledge that must be composed or survive subsequent updates, context — not weights — is the reliable channel.

Abstract: Continual learning promises a language model that keeps acquiring knowledge after training, with each new fact written into its weights. Whether weight writes can support accumulation remains undecided. We follow invented facts written into Qwen3 models from creation through sequences of twenty to one hundred later writes, using held-out questions of five types, with the original model given the fact in its prompt as the reference. Across these experiments, the breadth of the training data determines the kind of knowledge created. Bare-statement training produces recitation, while diverse restatements reduce the recitation-to-use gap from 27.4 to 5.4 points without showing the model a conclusion. This difference carries into later writes: after twenty sequential writes, bare-statement facts retain 1% accuracy while facts written from broad study data retain 46%. We also find that facts can be behaviourally forgotten without being erased. Forgotten facts keep most of the log-probability added by their write, and under bare-statement training 70% of wrong answers about them contain the most recently written fact. The same writes barely degrade the model's use of facts in context, and a forgotten study fact supplied in the prompt recovers to 77-80% on its questions. These results describe knowledge that is stored but question-keyed: later writes redirect the questions that reached it. Damage to unrelated abilities tracks KL divergence from the original model, and the later writes cause interference regardless of how the earlier fact was stored. Broad data can create usable knowledge, and a frozen reference can preserve capability, but no intervention we tested, including those built on accurate local measurements of each write, keeps earlier facts reachable. When facts must be composed or survive later writes, the reliable channel is context rather than the weights.

</details>


### [51] [Dimensionality in Satisfaction Ratings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11026)
*Andrew Hong,Jason Potteiger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GPT-4.1 was used to annotate ~9,000 customer-support conversations across five satisfaction axes (overall, agent, outcome, product, effort). LLM annotations aligned well with self-reported ratings (r ≈ 0.65), with disagreements concentrated in a small tail of divergent sessions. The decomposition's value lies in attribution and coverage, not incremental prediction. Full-census satisfaction (2.91/5) was markedly lower than survey-only satisfaction (3.62/5), revealing a response-bias gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional customer satisfaction measurement relies on surveys with low response rates, introducing selection bias and limiting coverage. The authors aim to demonstrate that LLMs can decompose satisfaction from conversational text across multiple axes, providing broader coverage and more nuanced insight into drivers of customer experience than survey ratings alone.

Method: GPT-4.1 was used to annotate ~9,000 customer-support conversations from a global consumer-goods firm across five satisfaction axes: overall, agent, outcome, product, and customer effort. Annotations were validated against customers' self-reported satisfaction ratings. Correlation analysis assessed alignment, with attention to divergent cases. Collinearity among axes was examined, and full-census satisfaction scores were compared against survey-only scores to quantify response bias.

Result: Four of five axes tracked self-reported satisfaction closely: overall, agent, and outcome ~0.65 unadjusted correlation; effort at -0.54. Product satisfaction showed weak alignment. Disagreements concentrated in a small, readable tail; excluding severe divergences raised overall correlation to 0.811, and excluding the full tail reached 0.914. Axes were highly collinear, so adding them did not improve predictive power — the value is attributional, not incremental. Full-census satisfaction averaged 2.91/5 versus 3.62/5 from surveys, a substantial gap driven by response bias.

Conclusion: LLM-based decomposed satisfaction annotation is a viable methodology that matches self-report reasonably well and, more importantly, extends coverage to un-surveyed interactions. The primary value is attributional — identifying nuanced drivers of satisfaction across conversations — rather than improving predictive accuracy. Full-census measurement reveals satisfaction levels significantly lower than survey-only estimates, underscoring the importance of coverage in customer-experience analytics.

Abstract: We used a large language model (GPT-4.1) to annotate the text of about 9,000 support conversations at a global consumer-goods firm, decomposing customer-care satisfaction into component axes (overall, agent, outcome, product, and customer effort), and validated the LLM annotations against the satisfaction ratings customers gave themselves. Four of five axes track self-reported satisfaction closely (overall, agent, and outcome near an unadjusted 0.65; effort -0.54), while product satisfaction is weak against the available proxy. The unadjusted correlation also understates the alignment: the disagreements concentrate in a small, readable tail of divergent sessions rather than in general drift, and the overall correlation rises to 0.811 when only the severe divergences are excluded and to 0.914 when the full divergent tail is excluded. The axes are also highly collinear, and adding them to the overall score does not improve prediction of the customer's rating, the decomposition's value is not incremental prediction but attribution and coverage. And, with greater coverage the picture of the data changes. Read on every contact rather than the few that return a survey, satisfaction is markedly lower than the survey reports (a full-census 2.91 against the surveyed 3.62 on a five-point scale). The promise of decomposed satisfaction as a methodology is the ability to identify more nuanced drivers of customer experience in conversational data.

</details>


### [52] [Flout at Your Own Risk: LLMs Struggle with Pragmatic Cooperativity Under Epistemic Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11053)
*Hannah VanderHoeven,Abhijnan Nath,Nikhil Krishnaswamy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Investigates whether LLMs can engage in pragmatic, cooperative communication under partial information in multi-party collaborative tasks. Finds LLMs show some pragmatic ability (enhanceable via prompting/post-training) but still struggle with incomplete information, with failures correlating to unrecognized violations of Grice's maxims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in collaborative, multi-agent pipelines where information asymmetry is common. It is unclear whether LLMs possess the pragmatic reasoning capabilities needed to communicate cooperatively under partial information — a fundamental requirement for successful human-like collaboration grounded in Gricean cooperative principles.

Method: The authors formalize "collaborative epistemic asymmetry," linking objective task success to Grice's cooperative principle. They design a multi-party collaborative task with partial information conditions and empirically evaluate LLMs as both speakers and listeners, testing various prompting strategies and post-training approaches. Failure modes are analyzed through the lens of Grice's maxims (quantity, quality, relation, manner).

Result: LLMs exhibit measurable pragmatic capabilities in collaborative settings, and these can be improved through targeted prompting and post-training. However, LLMs still face significant challenges in pragmatic communication under incomplete information. Critically, certain failure modes correlate with floutings of Grice's maxims that the models fail to recognize or repair.

Conclusion: While LLMs demonstrate emergent pragmatic reasoning, they remain unreliable in cooperative communication under epistemic asymmetry. The alignment between failure modes and Gricean maxim violations suggests that deeper integration of pragmatic principles into LLM training and architecture may be necessary for robust multi-agent collaboration.

Abstract: Fruitful collaborations rely on cooperative communications, including of contextual cues to incorporate into reasoning. The increasing use of LLMs in collaborative and agentic pipelines raises questions about the extent to which they exhibit these pragmatic capabilities, especially in scenarios where they may not have access to the same information as their collaborators. In this paper, we perform a novel investigation into the pragmatic reasoning capabilities of LLMs in a multi-party collaborative task under partial information conditions. We formalize a notion of collaborative epistemic asymmetry that explicitly connects objective task success to Grice's cooperative principle and empirically assess various LLMs' abilities to act cooperatively as both speakers and listeners, including both prompting and post-training strategies. Our results show that while LLMs exhibit certain pragmatic capabilities in collaborative settings, and these can be elicited through prompting and post-training, they still face challenges in pragmatic communication with incomplete information, and that certain failure modes do correlate with floutings of Grice's maxims that go unrecognized.

</details>


### [53] [MJ: Multi-turn LLM Jailbreaking via Decomposed Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11070)
*Junyoung Park,Namgyu Park,Sechan Lee,Yoon-Chan Jhi,Jihoon Cho,Sangdon Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DC-GRPO introduces turn-level credit assignment for multi-turn jailbreak attacks using Group Relative Policy Optimization, achieving ~98% ASR5@3, significantly outperforming prior methods by assigning separate learning signals to each dialogue turn instead of broadcasting a single trajectory-level score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-turn jailbreaking is a realistic threat model for LLMs, but existing methods suffer from coarse credit assignment — a single trajectory-level reward is broadcast across all turns, obscuring which turns actually contributed to the jailbreak. This makes it difficult to learn effective multi-turn attack policies.

Method: DC-GRPO is a unified turn-level credit assignment framework built on Group Relative Policy Optimization. It assigns a separate group-relative advantage to each turn by decomposing credit into immediate reward and future credit. The framework is instantiated with two weighting variants: static (fixed balance between immediate and future credit) and dynamic (adaptive weighting), both sharing the same turn-level structure.

Result: Dynamic-weighted DC-GRPO achieves 98.26% ASR5@3 and static-weighted achieves 97.88%, substantially outperforming SOTA baselines SEMA (86.58%) and TROJail (86.23%). The consistent performance across both variants suggests the key benefit stems from turn-level group-relative credit assignment rather than any specific weighting rule.

Conclusion: Turn-level credit assignment is the primary driver of improved multi-turn jailbreak attack learning. The framework's effectiveness generalizes across multiple victim LLMs and benchmarks, establishing DC-GRPO as a new state-of-the-art for automated multi-turn red-teaming.

Abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) operate in interactive multi-turn settings, making multi-turn jailbreaking a realistic threat model and an important setting for automated red teaming. A core challenge in learning multi-turn jailbreak attackers is credit assignment: different turns contribute differently to the final outcome, yet existing learning signals are often too coarse to identify their individual contributions. We propose decomposed credit GRPO (DC-GRPO), a unified turn-level credit assignment framework for Group Relative Policy Optimization in multi-turn jailbreak learning. DC-GRPO assigns a separate group-relative learning signal to each turn by combining immediate and future credit, avoiding the credit misassignment induced by broadcasting a single trajectory-level score across the dialogue. We instantiate this framework with static and dynamic weighting rules that differ in how the two credit sources are balanced while sharing the same turn-level structure. Across multiple victim LLMs and benchmarks, the dynamic- and static-weighted variants achieve average ASR5@3 scores of 98.26% and 97.88%, respectively, substantially outperforming the state-of-the-art methods, including SEMA (86.58%) and TROJail (86.23%). Their consistently strong performance indicates that the central empirical benefit comes from turn-level group-relative credit assignment rather than a particular weighting rule. Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful content.

</details>


### [54] [ResearchQA: Benchmarking Citation-Grounded Question-Answering on Scientific Papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11074)
*Saba Imran,Debanjum Singh Solanky*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ResearchQA is a benchmark of 6,211 QA pairs from 494 papers across 8 domains, designed to evaluate whether model answers are supported by verifiable citations. It introduces citation-grounded evaluation that rewards grounded refusal and permits multiple valid supporting passages. Evaluation of 8 models reveals citation-based metrics separate systems better than LLM-evaluator scores, and open-weight models approach closed-model citation accuracy with 3-6x lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation methods for LLM-assisted scientific reading fail to verify whether generated answers are supported by actual, verifiable citations from the source paper. There is a need for a benchmark that enforces citation-grounded evaluation, including the ability to detect unsupported claims and reward appropriate refusal to answer.

Method: The authors construct ResearchQA, comprising 6,211 single-paper QA pairs from 494 open-access papers across 8 scientific domains, with four question types (lookup, comprehension, multi-hop, adversarial). The benchmark permits multiple valid supporting passages per claim and supports grounded refusal. Eight closed- and open-weight models are evaluated in a citation-grounded chat-with-paper setting using a deterministic citation matcher and an LLM-based rubric evaluator. Citation-based metrics (section coverage, citation accuracy) and latency are measured.

Result: Citation-based metrics (section coverage, citation accuracy) reveal substantial variation across models and separate systems more clearly than LLM-evaluator scores, which remain tightly compressed. Open-weight models approach the citation accuracy of the best closed models while achieving 3 to 6 times lower per-example latency.

Conclusion: ResearchQA provides a more rigorous, citation-verifiable framework for evaluating scientific QA systems. The compression of LLM-evaluator scores highlights the limitations of judge-based evaluation alone. Open-weight models offer a compelling efficiency-accuracy trade-off, nearing closed-model performance at significantly lower latency. The benchmark is publicly released.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to assist scientific reading, but existing evaluation methods often fail to detect whether answers are supported by verifiable citations. We introduce ResearchQA, a benchmark of 6,211 single-paper question-answer pairs from 494 open-access papers spanning eight domains and four question types: lookup, comprehension, multi-hop, and adversarial. ResearchQA is designed for citation-grounded evaluation: it permits multiple valid supporting passages for a claim and rewards grounded refusal when the source paper does not support an answer. We evaluate eight leading closed- and open-weight models in a citation-grounded chat-with-paper setting using a deterministic citation matcher and an LLM-based rubric evaluator. Citation-based metrics separate systems more clearly than LLM-evaluator scores: section coverage and citation accuracy vary substantially across models, while evaluator scores remain tightly compressed. We further find that open-weight models approach the best closed-model citation accuracy while achieving 3 to 6 times lower per-example latency. We release the benchmark, evaluation harness, and evaluator prompt.

</details>


### [55] [Do LLMs Fabricate Legal Citations? A Bilingual Benchmark on Saudi Data Protection Law and the GDPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11127)
*Noura Suliman Alrajeh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A bilingual benchmark of 120 questions (Arabic/English) tests whether three free LLMs fabricate article citations for GDPR and Saudi PDPL. Results reveal near-perfect GDPR accuracy but 60-77% fabrication on Saudi PDPL, with fabricated citations delivered at high confidence (≥0.8). The jurisdiction, not query language, drives fabrication, underscoring the need for verbatim-verification safeguards over model self-confidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations and regulators increasingly rely on LLMs for regulatory-compliance questions, yet a wrong statutory citation can silently propagate into binding legal advice and policy. No systematic bilingual benchmark existed to quantify whether LLMs fabricate citations differently across jurisdictions, languages, and under adversarial probe conditions (false premises, unanswerable "trap" questions).

Method: The authors construct a bilingual (Arabic/English) benchmark of 120 questions targeting two data-protection laws: the EU GDPR and the Saudi PDPL. Question types include direct citation retrieval, false-premise verification, and deliberately unanswerable trap questions (e.g., about a repealed article or deadlines from implementing regulations rather than statutory text). Three freely accessible models — Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-OSS-120B, Nemotron-3-Super-120B — are evaluated. All scoring is fully automatic against a manually verified gold reference.

Result: A dramatic jurisdiction gap emerges: near-ceiling GDPR citation accuracy (94–100% on direct retrieval) versus majority fabrication on Saudi PDPL (60–77%). The highest fabrication rate (67%) stems from statute-versus-regulations confusion. 91% of fabricated citations are asserted with confidence ≥ 0.8. Fabrication tracks the law's jurisdiction rather than query language, and model confidence fails as a reliability indicator.

Conclusion: Verbatim-verification safeguards must gate any institutional reliance on LLMs for compliance screening, as model self-confidence provides no meaningful protection against confident fabrication in lower-resource jurisdictions.

Abstract: Organizations and regulators increasingly consult large language models (LLMs) for regulatory-compliance questions, yet a wrong statutory citation can silently propagate into legal advice, compliance documentation, and policy decisions. We introduce a bilingual benchmark of 120 questions probing whether freely accessible LLMs fabricate article citations for two data-protection instruments: the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Saudi Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL). The benchmark pairs direct citation retrieval questions with false premise verification probes and deliberately unanswerable "trap" questions -- including questions about a repealed article and about deadlines that exist only in implementing regulations, not in the law itself. Every question is posed in both Arabic and English, and all scoring is fully automatic against a manually verified gold reference. Evaluating three freely accessible models (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-OSS-120B, Nemotron-3-Super-120B), we find a dramatic jurisdiction gap: near-ceiling citation accuracy on the GDPR (94-100% on direct retrieval) against majority fabrication on the Saudi PDPL (60-77%), invariant to query language; the highest fabrication rates (67%) arise from statute-vs-regulations confusion, and 91% of fabricated citations are asserted with confidence >= 0.8. Fabrication tracks the jurisdiction of the law, not the language of the query, and model confidence provides no protection -- indicating that verbatim-verification safeguards, rather than model self confidence, must gate any institutional reliance on LLMs for compliance screening.

</details>


### [56] [TIGER: Text-Conditioned Visual Gated Routing with Acceptance Alignment for Multimodal Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11131)
*Quynh Vo,Cong-Duy Nguyen,Ponhvoan Srey,Luu Anh Tuan,Thong Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TIGER introduces a text-conditioned visual gated routing framework for multimodal speculative decoding in VLMs, dynamically selecting sparse context-relevant visual tokens and optimizing the drafter with acceptance-aligned group-based policy training to maximize verifier-accepted prefix length, achieving consistent speedup gains without sacrificing accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding in vision-language models (VLMs) suffers limited speedup because drafters diverge on vision-critical content, and existing methods fail to (1) directly address irrelevant visual evidence that distracts the drafter, and (2) explicitly optimize for the verifier-accepted prefix length — the key metric governing actual decoding speedup.

Method: TIGER employs two core techniques: (1) a text-conditioned visual gated routing mechanism that dynamically selects a sparse subset of context-relevant visual tokens based on the drafter's current textual state, avoiding full or fixed-compressed visual input; (2) acceptance-aligned group-based policy training with verifier-derived rewards that directly optimizes the drafter to produce token continuations maximizing accepted prefix length, initialized via distillation warm start with KL anchoring.

Result: TIGER achieves consistent improvements in accepted prefix length and speculative speedup under exact verifier-side speculative decoding, with favorable quality-latency trade-offs and comparable downstream accuracy in visual-routing analyses.

Conclusion: By dynamically routing visual tokens and optimizing the drafter for acceptance length rather than mere imitation, TIGER effectively bridges the gap between speculative decoding's theoretical promise and practical gains in multimodal settings, enabling faster VLM inference without degrading output quality.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose multiple tokens that are verified by a larger target model. Although effective for text-only LLMs, speculative decoding yields limited gains in VLMs because drafters often diverge on vision-critical content, while existing multimodal acceleration methods do not directly address irrelevant visual evidence or optimize the verifier-accepted prefix length that governs speedup. We propose TIGER, a Text-conditioned vIsual GatEd Routing framework for multimodal speculative decoding. TIGER dynamically selects a sparse set of context-relevant visual tokens based on the drafter's current textual state, rather than expose the full visual token set or a fixed compressed interface. To better align training with inference-time efficiency, we optimize the drafter with acceptance-aligned group-based policy training using verifier-derived rewards based on accepted prefix length, built on top of distillation warm start with KL anchoring. This encourages the drafter not only to imitate the target model, but also to produce speculative continuations that survive verification for longer prefixes. Experiments show that TIGER yields consistent gains in accepted prefix length and speculative speedup under exact verifier-side speculative decoding, while achieving favorable quality-latency trade-offs with comparable downstream accuracy in visual-routing analyses.

</details>


### [57] [Unified Gradient Projection: Language-Balanced Continual Learning for Multilingual Low-Resource ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11163)
*Ziang Ren,Guodong Lin,Yuchen Ai,Kaize Tan,Wei-Qiang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: UGP (Unified Gradient Projection) addresses catastrophic forgetting in multilingual ASR fine-tuning by constraining parameter updates via language-balanced reference gradients in a unified projection space, reducing dominant-language bias and achieving near-zero forgetting on Whisper-large-v3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning large pretrained ASR models (e.g., Whisper) on low-resource languages causes catastrophic forgetting of previously learned languages. Existing continual learning methods fail in multilingual settings because dominant languages bias gradient optimization, leading to cross-task interference and degraded performance on underrepresented languages.

Method: UGP constrains parameter updates by projecting gradients onto a unified space defined by reference gradients computed from language-balanced replay data. Per-language contributions are explicitly equalized within this projection, reducing dominant-language bias. The approach combines gradient-level projection with data-level replay, yielding complementary benefits in stability (retaining old knowledge) and plasticity (learning new tasks).

Result: UGP enables effective adaptation across diverse low-resource language groups and model scales while substantially mitigating forgetting. On Whisper-large-v3, it achieves near-zero average forgetting, demonstrating strong cross-lingual stability without sacrificing adaptation performance.

Conclusion: Unified Gradient Projection effectively resolves the dominant-language bias problem in multilingual continual ASR fine-tuning. The synergy between gradient projection and data replay provides a robust framework for adapting large pretrained speech models to low-resource languages while preserving previously acquired multilingual capabilities.

Abstract: Large-scale pretrained ASR models such as Whisper exhibit strong multilingual capabilities. However, fine-tuning on low-resource languages often causes catastrophic forgetting. Although continual learning mitigates this issue, existing methods struggle to regulate cross-task interference in multilingual settings, where dominant languages bias optimization. We propose Unified Gradient Projection (UGP), which constrains parameter updates using reference gradients from language-balanced replay in a unified projection space. By equalizing per-language contributions in the projection, UGP reduces dominant-language bias and improves cross-lingual stability. We further show that combining gradient-level projection with data-level replay yields complementary gains in stability and plasticity. Across diverse low-resource language groups and model scales, UGP enables effective adaptation while substantially mitigating forgetting. On Whisper-large-v3, it achieves near-zero average forgetting.

</details>


### [58] [Query-Focused Event Summarization: A Dataset and Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11166)
*Chenyu Hu,Bang Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces Query-Focused Event Summarization (QFES), a new task and dataset (QFESum) for generating query-focused summaries from large thematic event corpora, along with a two-stage framework (RAT + SHC) that outperforms baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current QFS datasets lack event-oriented summarization, and existing methods cannot handle large-scale thematic corpora effectively. Users need multi-dimensional, query-specific summaries from event collections containing hundreds or thousands of documents.

Method: Proposes a two-stage framework: (1) Query-Focused Retrieval with Adaptive Thresholding (RAT) to filter relevant documents from large corpora, and (2) Query-Focused Summarization based on Hierarchical Clustering (SHC) to generate the final summary. The QFESum dataset is constructed with 8 thematic events, 16,684 documents, and 104 queries.

Result: RAT and SHC consistently outperform baseline methods on the QFESum dataset, demonstrating their effectiveness for the QFES task.

Conclusion: The QFES task, QFESum dataset, and the RAT+SHC framework effectively address the gap in event-oriented query-focused summarization for large-scale thematic corpora.

Abstract: A thematic corpus is a collection of semantically coherent documents that collectively describe different aspects of a shared thematic event. Such a corpus typically contains hundreds or even thousands of documents. While users' interests in a thematic event often span multiple dimensions, Query-Focused Summarization (QFS) aims to generate summaries tailored to users' queries. However, existing QFS datasets lack event-oriented summarization, and most QFS methods struggle with large-scale corpora. To address these challenges, we propose the Query-Focused Event Summarization (QFES) task and construct the QFESum dataset, which contains 8 thematic events, 16,684 documents, and 104 queries. Furthermore, we introduce a two-stage QFES framework consisting of Query-Focused Retrieval with Adaptive Thresholding (RAT) and Query-Focused Summarization based on Hierarchical Clustering (SHC). Experimental results on QFESum show that RAT and SHC consistently outperform the baselines, demonstrating their effectiveness for QFES. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://github.com/sarcasm-hcy02/QFES-QFESum.

</details>


### [59] [Amplitude-Only FFN Intervention for Tool-Structured LLM Inference Method: Gated Evaluation Protocol, and Cross-Model Empirical Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11183)
*Sheng Xu,Boyuan Huang,Ke Jia,Jiadun Zhu,Zhen Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces Amplitude Gating (AG), a non-destructive FFN intervention method that modulates activation magnitudes during inference to improve structured outputs of LLMs. It outperforms the destructive Orthogonal Residual Projection (ORP) baseline, with learned gates yielding up to +11.36 points on tool-structured tasks across Qwen models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs operating as tool-using agents frequently produce format, argument, or function-call errors that invalidate otherwise correct responses. The authors seek inference-time intervention methods that improve structured output reliability without requiring retraining of model weights.

Method: The authors first explored Orthogonal Residual Projection (ORP), a direction-changing repair approach that identified sensitive SwiGLU FFN sites but proved destructive overall. They then proposed Amplitude Gating (AG), which preserves pretrained FFN weight directions and only modulates activation magnitudes. The intervention system spans fine-grained site categories (P1/P2/P3 and branch-specific P1s/P2a/P2b). An evaluation protocol was introduced using combination-oracle vs. fixed-configuration separation, sample-level accounting, and task-aware metrics. Both entropy-based and Newton-Schulz-windowed AG variants are compared. Experiments cover Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B.

Result: AG is weakly positive in aggregate but strongest on tool-structured tasks. On Qwen3.5-9B, a category-level learned gate improves tool/structured/agentic performance from 38.66% to 42.92% (+4.27 pp), with Hermes function-calling gaining ~+7.6 points. On Qwen3-8B, Hermes JSON mode improves by +11.36 points. Qwen2.5-7B retains oracle headroom but learned gates fail to capture it, indicating model-specific and category-specific routing is necessary. Neither entropy AG nor Newton-Schulz-windowed AG is uniformly dominant.

Conclusion: Tool-structured inference is the most credible first target for safe FFN-level inference optimization. Deployment requires model- and category-specific routing strategies. Prospective online validation and broader cross-model evaluation remain necessary future work.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly operate as tool-using agents, where small format, argument, or function-call errors can invalidate otherwise plausible responses. We study inference-time feed-forward network (FFN) intervention for improving structured outputs without retraining model weights. Our project began with Orthogonal Residual Projection (ORP), a direction-changing repair attempt that revealed sensitive SwiGLU FFN intervention sites but often caused more harm than fixes. We therefore propose Amplitude Gating (AG), a non-destructive alternative that preserves pretrained FFN weight directions and modulates only activation magnitudes during generation. We define a fine-grained intervention system spanning P1/P2/P3 and branch-specific P1s/P2a/P2b sites, and introduce an evaluation protocol that separates combination-oracle headroom from fixed configurations and learned gates, enforces sample-level accounting, and uses task-aware metrics for binary and partial-credit datasets. Across Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, AG is weakly positive in aggregate but strongest on tool-structured tasks. On Qwen3.5-9B, a category-level learned gate improves tool/structured/agentic performance from 38.66% to 42.92% (+4.27 percentage points), with Hermes function-call tasks reaching about +7.6 points. On Qwen3-8B, Hermes JSON mode improves by +11.36 points. Qwen2.5-7B retains oracle headroom but current learned gates fail to capture it, showing that deployment requires model- and category-specific routing. Comparisons of entropy AG with Newton-Schulz-windowed AG show that neither family is uniformly dominant. These results identify tool-structured inference as the most credible first target for safe FFN-level inference optimization, while prospective online validation and broader cross-model evaluation remain necessary.

</details>


### [60] [ProgramTab: Boosting Table Reasoning of LLMs via Programmatic Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11207)
*Pei Guo,Enjie Liu,Yunzhi Tan,Mochi Gao,Jianxin Zhang,Ruichao Zhong,Juntao Li,Bo Hu,Zang Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ProgramTab uses LLMs with in-context learning to preprocess tabular data via Python code and extract key content through row/column selection and SQL generation, outperforming baselines on table reasoning tasks, especially with large or unstructured tables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based table reasoning methods degrade significantly with large tables due to long-text modeling difficulties and input length constraints. While text-to-SQL approaches can extract sub-tables, real-world tables (especially web tables) often lack the structure and consistency required for SQL-based mathematical logic operations.

Method: The ProgramTab framework leverages LLMs with in-context learning to: (1) preprocess tabular data using Python code to handle structural inconsistencies, and (2) extract momentous contents via row/column extraction combined with SQL generation for efficient sub-table construction.

Result: Experiments on table reasoning datasets show that ProgramTab effectively handles table-based reasoning tasks and outperforms all LLM-based baselines.

Conclusion: ProgramTab successfully addresses the limitations of both pure LLM reasoning and text-to-SQL approaches by combining Python-based preprocessing with SQL extraction, achieving state-of-the-art performance among LLM-based methods for table reasoning.

Abstract: Table-based reasoning with large language models (LLMs), which requires reasoning based on natural language questions and structured tabular data, has gained widespread attention. However, a series of issues still constrain the application of this task. The previous approaches suffered from significant performance degradation when faced with large tables due to the difficulty of long text modeling and the limitation of input length for LLMs. The text-to-SQL approach is used to efficiently extract key information from tables and generate smaller sub-tables. However, tabular data, especially web tables, often lack the necessary structure and consistency, making them unsuitable for performing mathematical logic operations using SQL queries. We propose the ProgramTab framework, which guides LLMs employing in-context learning to perform tabular data preprocessing with Python code, as well as the momentous contents extraction with row and column extraction and SQL generation. The experiment results on table reasoning datasets demonstrate that the ProgramTab framework effectively deals with table-based reasoning tasks and outperforms all LLM-based baselines.

</details>


### [61] [When the Target Domain Changes: AI-Mediated Construct Drift in High-Stakes English Language AssessmenW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11213)
*Yi Gui*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Generative AI is reshaping academic communication, creating a validity problem for high-stakes English tests that rely on unaided performance. The paper introduces "AI-mediated construct drift" and proposes "bounded AI mediation" as a design principle to realign test constructs with AI-mediated target domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Target language use domains increasingly involve generative AI, yet high-stakes English proficiency tests continue to interpret unaided test performance as evidence of academic communicative readiness. This extrapolation is becoming less defensible, and AI has been underexamined as a construct validity and score-interpretation problem rather than merely an operational concern.

Method: The paper presents a conceptual validity argument that synthesizes current literature across three layers. It defines the novel concept of "AI-mediated construct drift" and proposes "bounded AI mediation" as a validity-oriented test design principle, specifying standardized conditions with institutionally controlled AI assistants, predefined assistance boundaries, logged interactions, and tasks distinguishing comprehension support from answer generation.

Result: The literature synthesis reveals an uneven distribution: most work treats AI as assessment infrastructure (scoring, feedback, security), while far less theorizes its implications for construct validity and extrapolation warrants. The paper argues that score interpretations must be narrowed and supplemented when used to support claims about AI-mediated academic communication.

Conclusion: As AI mediation becomes normative in academic communication, language testing must evolve from treating AI solely as an operational issue to addressing it as a core validity concern. Bounded AI mediation offers a principled path for realigning test constructs with real-world communicative demands while preserving standardized, defensible score interpretations.

Abstract: High-stakes English proficiency tests treat standardized, unaided performance as evidence for score interpretations about academic English proficiency. This interpretation remains meaningful, but as target language use domains increasingly involve generative AI, the extrapolation from unaided test performance to academic communicative readiness becomes less self-evident. This conceptual validity argument reframes AI as a score-interpretation problem in high-stakes language testing, not only an operational issue of scoring, feedback, security, or misconduct. Synthesizing current literature in three uneven layers, the paper shows that most work treats AI as assessment infrastructure, while far less theorizes its implications for construct validity and extrapolation warrants. It defines AI-mediated construct drift as the misalignment that arises when communicative abilities required in the target domain change through AI mediation while test constructs remain anchored to an unaided-performance model. It proposes bounded AI mediation as a validity-oriented design principle: a standardized condition in which all test takers access the same institutionally controlled AI assistant, with predefined assistance boundaries, logged interactions, and tasks that distinguish comprehension support from answer generation. The paper argues that score interpretations should be narrowed and supplemented when used to support claims about AI-mediated academic communication.

</details>


### [62] [Q-BridgeNet: A Quantization Network for Cross-Lingual Sign Language Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11215)
*Liqian Feng,Lintao Wang,Xiaochen Liu,Anusha Withana,Ken-Tye Yong,Dehui Kong,Zhiyong Wang,Kun Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Q-BridgeNet is a unified multilingual sign language translation framework that uses discrete Q-units (learned via adaptive segmentation and residual vector quantization) to disentangle language-agnostic semantics from language-specific variations, combined with a fine-tuned multilingual LLM, achieving SOTA on multiple benchmarks and generalizing to non-native sign-spoken pairs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multilingual SLT methods fail to effectively balance shared cross-lingual semantics with language-specific variations, leading to cross-lingual conflicts. A unified model is needed that can serve multiple sign language communities without performance degradation from these conflicts.

Method: Q-BridgeNet uses a two-sided approach: (1) On the sign language side, adaptive segmentation and residual vector quantization learn discrete Q-units — a shared base codebook captures language-agnostic semantic primitives, while language-specific residual codebooks refine heterogeneous signing semantics. (2) On the spoken language side, a multilingual LLM is fine-tuned to operate in this Q-unit space, leveraging cross-lingual priors for unified translation.

Result: Experiments on PHOENIX14T, How2Sign, and CSL-Daily demonstrate SOTA performance on native sign-spoken pairs and strong generalization to non-native pairs, validating effective mitigation of cross-lingual conflicts.

Conclusion: Q-BridgeNet successfully addresses cross-lingual conflicts in multilingual SLT through discrete Q-units with shared and language-specific codebooks, enabling a unified model that serves diverse sign language communities with both strong native performance and cross-lingual generalization.

Abstract: Most sign language translation (SLT) methods focus on isolated native sign-spoken pairs (e.g., American Sign Language - English). Extending language-specific SLT models to multilingual translation would improve accessibility by enabling communication across diverse sign and spoken language communities. However, existing multilingual SLT approaches still struggle to learn a unified model that minimizes cross-lingual conflicts while capturing shared cross-lingual semantics and preserving language-specific variations across different sign languages. Therefore, we propose Q-BridgeNet, a unified framework for multilingual SLT that jointly mitigates cross-lingual conflicts across both the sign language and spoken language sides. On the sign language side, Q-BridgeNet learns discrete Q-units via adaptive segmentation and residual vector quantization: a shared base codebook provides language-agnostic semantic primitives, while language-specific residual codebooks refine heterogeneous signing semantics. On the spoken language side, a multilingual LLM is fine-tuned to operate in the Q-unit space, leveraging cross-lingual priors to enable a unified SLT model. Experiments on PHOENIX14T, How2Sign, and CSL-Daily show that Q-BridgeNet effectively mitigates cross-lingual conflicts, achieving state-of-the-art performance on native sign-spoken pairs while also demonstrating strong generalization to non-native pairs. Our source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/FengLiQ/Q-BridgeNet

</details>


### [63] [TreeThink: A Modular Tree Search Library for Mathematical Reasoning with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11258)
*Burak S. Akbudak,Zeynel A. Uluşan,Can S. Erer,Gözde Gül Şahin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TreeThink is an open-source Python library that provides modular, fully asynchronous tree search for neural theorem proving, integrating vLLM inference with formal verifiers (Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle/HOL) and achieving up to 6.3× wall-clock speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM tree search libraries focus on natural language reasoning and lack native integration with formal verifiers, while theorem-proving systems rely on task-specific, non-reusable search implementations. There is a need for a unified, modular framework that bridges tree search algorithms, LLM inference, and formal verification across multiple proof assistants.

Method: TreeThink is implemented as an open-source Python library featuring: (1) modular architecture supporting established tree search methods; (2) fully asynchronous execution via vLLM-based inference pipelines; (3) diverse node evaluation techniques from lightweight heuristics to neural evaluators; (4) direct connection to each language's REPL server for real-time verification and proof state extraction; and (5) support for Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle/HOL, and natural language.

Result: Evaluated on miniF2F and MATH500 benchmarks, TreeThink demonstrated cross-language formal proof search, natural language reasoning support, and up to 6.3× wall-clock speedup from asynchronous execution compared to synchronous baselines.

Conclusion: TreeThink fills a critical gap by providing a reusable, modular, and efficient tree search infrastructure for neural theorem proving, released under MIT license as both a GitHub repository and a PyPI package.

Abstract: Tree search algorithms enable systematic exploration of the proof space in neural theorem proving. Existing LLM tree search libraries primarily target natural language reasoning and do not provide native integration with formal verifiers, while theorem proving systems often rely on task-specific search implementations. We introduce TreeThink, an open-source Python library for modular, fully asynchronous tree search in neural theorem proving. It integrates established tree search methods with vLLM-based inference pipelines and diverse node evaluation techniques, ranging from lightweight heuristics to neural evaluators. We support Lean~4, Rocq, and Isabelle/HOL alongside natural language. It connects directly to each language's Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL) server for real-time verification and proof state extraction. We evaluate TreeThink on miniF2F and MATH500, demonstrating cross-language formal proof search, natural language reasoning support, and up to 6.3$\times$ wall-clock speedup from asynchronous execution. Source code is released under the MIT license at https://github.com/GGLAB-KU/treethink , and the library is accessible as a downloadable package at https://pypi.org/project/treethink/ .

</details>


### [64] [FAD-SA-GRU: Enhancing Hate Speech Detection in Algerian Dialect Through Feature-Augmented Self-Attention GRU Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11279)
*Sara Yakoubi,Ikram Khalfallah,Kenza Khelkhal,Dihia Lanasri*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents FAD-SA-GRU, a hybrid architecture that fuses multiple embeddings (DZ FastText, DZ AraVec, DziriBERT) with a self-attention-enhanced GRU for hate speech detection in Algerian Darija, achieving 93.2% accuracy on an annotated social media dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of hate speech on social media platforms poses serious social and ethical risks. Detecting hate speech in Algerian Darija is particularly challenging due to the dialect's linguistic complexity — it mixes Arabic, French, and Arabizi — and the scarcity of resources for low-resource dialectal Arabic, necessitating robust automatic detection methods.

Method: The authors benchmark four categories of approaches on an annotated Algerian Darija dataset: (1) traditional ML with TF-IDF features, (2) RNN-based deep learning models, (3) Transformer-based models (DziriBERT, multilingual BERT), and (4) a novel FAD-SA-GRU architecture that fuses DZ FastText, DZ AraVec, and DziriBERT embeddings via multi-embedding fusion, followed by a self-attention-enhanced GRU encoder for binary hate speech classification.

Result: FAD-SA-GRU outperformed all baselines, achieving 93.2% accuracy, 93.4% precision, 91.0% recall, 92.1% F1-score, and 97.0% ROC-AUC on the annotated Algerian Darija social media dataset.

Conclusion: Fusing complementary embedding representations — capturing morphological, semantic, and contextual information — with attention-based sequence modeling yields robust hate speech detection in low-resource dialectal Arabic, and the FAD-SA-GRU architecture sets a strong benchmark for future work on code-switched, linguistically diverse dialects.

Abstract: The widespread adoption of social media platforms has transformed online communication by enabling users to exchange information and opinions instantly. However, these platforms have also facilitated the dissemination of abusive and hateful content, posing major social, psychological, and ethical challenges. Hate speech can incite discrimination, harassment, and violence against individuals or communities based on attributes such as ethnicity, religion, gender, nationality, or political affiliation. Consequently, automatic hate speech detection has become a major research topic in natural language processing (NLP) and an essential component of content moderation systems.
  This paper investigates automatic hate speech detection in the Algerian Arabic dialect (Darija) on social media. This task remains challenging because of the dialect's linguistic diversity, characterized by the coexistence of Arabic, French, and Arabizi (Arabic written using the Latin alphabet). We compare four categories of text classification approaches: (1) traditional machine learning models using TF-IDF features, (2) deep learning models based on recurrent neural networks, (3) Transformer-based language models, including DziriBERT and multilingual BERT, and (4) a novel hybrid architecture, FAD-SA-GRU, which combines semantic representations from DZ FastText, DZ AraVec, and DziriBERT through multi-embedding fusion, followed by a self-attention-enhanced GRU encoder.
  Experiments on an annotated dataset of Algerian Darija social media comments for binary hate speech classification show that FAD-SA-GRU outperforms all baselines, achieving 93.2% accuracy, 93.4% precision, 91.0% recall, 92.1% F1-score, and 97.0% ROC-AUC. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining complementary embedding representations with attention-based sequence modeling for robust hate speech detection in low-resource dialectal Arabic.

</details>


### [65] [The In-Car Sign Language Corpus (ICSL): A Multi-Modal Resource for Constrained-Space Sign Language Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11341)
*Raviteja Boddu,Guilherme Vieira Leite,Joed Lopes da Silva,Ângelo Benetti,Isabela Barbieri,Natália de Melo Afonso,Thyago Santos,Helio Pedrini,Felipe Venâncio Barbosa,José Mario De Martino,Munir Georges,Alessandro Zimmer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ICSL, a multimodal dataset for Brazilian Sign Language (Libras) recognition in vehicle interiors, combining MoCap baseline data with real in-car recordings (2D camera + 3D ToF sensors) to advance SLR research in constrained, occluded environments for improved Deaf accessibility in shared mobility services.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sign language recognition has largely been unexplored in confined real-world environments like vehicle interiors, creating a gap in accessibility for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing individuals using shared mobility services (taxis, rideshares, carpools). The authors aim to motivate research into robust "in-the-wild" SLR under constraints such as occlusion, non-frontal viewpoints, and limited space.

Method: The authors constructed the ICSL dataset with two components: (1) high-precision laboratory MoCap data serving as an idealized linguistic baseline via synthesized signing avatars, and (2) real-world multimodal in-car recordings using synchronized 2D cameras and 3D Time-of-Flight sensors. The corpus contains over 1.5 million frames with gloss annotations for both lexical signs and non-lexical elements, recorded across diverse in-car scenarios with Libras users.

Result: The resulting ICSL dataset exceeds 1.5 million frames of synchronized multimodal data, with gloss-level annotations designed for training and evaluating deep neural networks. It provides a foundation for comparative analysis between avatar-synthesized signing and real interpreter videos, enabling future work on domain adaptation and robust constrained-space SLR models.

Conclusion: In-vehicle signing represents a technically significant constrained recognition scenario. While acknowledging existing Deaf communication strategies, identifying automotive-specific limitations serves as a stepping stone for research into enhancing in-car accessibility and passenger quality of life.

Abstract: This paper addresses the challenges of using sign language within shared mobility services, such as taxis, carpools, or ride-sharing platforms. The use of sign language recognition (SLR) in real-world, confined environments, specifically vehicle interiors remains largely unexplored. To motivate research in this area, we present the In-Car Sign Language (ICSL) dataset for Brazilian Sign Language (Libras), with the long-term goal of improving public transport accessibility for the Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing community. The dataset consists of: (1) high-precision laboratory motion capture (MoCap) data to establish an idealized linguistic baseline and (2) real-world multi-modal in-car recordings captured using a 2D camera and 3D Time-of-Flight sensors. The dataset provides a basis for comparative analyses between synthesized signing avatar animations and recorded real signing interpreter videos, which enable future research into robust "in-the-wild" SLR models and domain adaptation. We describe in detail the use cases, the setup, the data collection protocol, and the metadata structure of the corpus. In total, we recorded a multimodal dataset exceeding 1.5 million frames, comprising the synchronized multimodal streams described above featuring Libras users across various in-car scenarios. The corpus is provided with gloss annotation of lexical signs and non-lexical sign language elements specially designed to support the training and evaluation of deep neural networks for constrained space recognition. In-vehicle signing offers a technically significant example of a constrained, occluded, and non-frontal environment. While recognizing the diverse communication strategies already employed by the Deaf community, identifying automotive-specific limitations provides a useful stepping stone for research into enhancing in-car accessibility and passenger quality of life.

</details>


### [66] [RefineEvo: Planning-Guided Heuristic Evolution with Bidirectional Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11358)
*Yang Wu,Junran Pan,Yifan Zhang,Ning Xu,Fanshuo Zeng,Jian Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RefineEvo proposes an LLM-based evolutionary framework for automatic heuristic design that uses a Planner to dynamically schedule operators and a Reflector with a Bidirectional Experience Pool to learn from past search trajectories, outperforming fixed-operator baselines on combinatorial optimization benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based AHD methods rely on fixed evolutionary operators and fail to accumulate or reuse historical search experience, limiting adaptability and efficiency.

Method: RefineEvo introduces a dual-component architecture: (1) a Planner that dynamically schedules evolutionary operators and triggers refinement based on search state, and (2) a Reflector that distills both positive insights and negative pitfalls into a Bidirectional Experience Pool, enabling trajectory-aware, situation-conditioned guidance for heuristic generation.

Result: RefineEvo consistently outperforms strong baselines on classic combinatorial optimization benchmarks, achieving superior solution quality while improving token efficiency.

Conclusion: By transforming AHD from static trial-and-error into a planning-guided, experience-driven system, RefineEvo enables more efficient, adaptive, and autonomous heuristic design.

Abstract: Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD) has emerged as a transformative approach for solving combinatorial optimization problems. While recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise, they predominantly rely on fixed evolutionary operators and struggle to effectively accumulate and reuse historical search experience. This paper proposes RefineEvo, a novel evolutionary framework that transforms AHD from a static trial-and-error process into a planning-guided, experience-driven system. RefineEvo introduces a Planner to dynamically schedule evolutionary operators and trigger refinement based on the current search state, and a Reflector to distill valuable lessons into a Bidirectional Experience Pool containing both positive insights and negative pitfalls. This synergistic framework enables the system to adapt its search tools to the evolving complexity of the problem and leverage trajectory-aware, situation-conditioned insights to guide generation. Experiments on several classic combinatorial optimization benchmarks demonstrate that RefineEvo consistently outperforms strong baselines. In particular, RefineEvo delivers superior solution quality while improving token efficiency, enabling more efficient and autonomous heuristic design.

</details>


### [67] [Beyond Sally-Anne: Evaluating Theory of Mind in LLMs using Epistemic Schelling Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11363)
*Roberta Rocca,Sami Boukortt,Geoff Keeling,Winnie Street*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces EAST, a dynamic two-player dialogue game that tests LLMs' functional Theory of Mind through coordination under varying epistemic transparency, revealing that even frontier models struggle with epistemic tracking despite performing well on static ToM benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing text-based ToM evaluations (e.g., Sally-Anne task variants) are susceptible to data contamination from pre-training and fail to test functional, generalizable ToM abilities in naturalistic, interactive settings.

Method: The authors propose the Epistemic Asymmetry Schelling Task (EAST), where LLM-LLM dyads must converge on semantic Schelling points under different conditions of epistemic transparency (private vs. mutual knowledge). Coordination success and reasoning traces are analyzed to assess ToM and epistemic tracking.

Result: Only frontier LLMs successfully navigated the tasks. Primary failure mode across models was epistemic tracking errors, specifically conflating private knowledge with mutual knowledge, highlighting a significant gap between static benchmark performance and functional social reasoning.

Conclusion: Robust social reasoning and epistemic tracking remain critical bottlenecks for LLMs. The EAST framework provides concrete, ecologically valid targets for future evaluation and development of ToM capabilities in language models.

Abstract: Text-based evaluations of Theory of Mind (ToM) in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involve cognitive tests akin to the Sally-Anne task that can be gamed due to exposure to relevantly similar tasks in pre-training and do not obviously test models' functional ToM abilities in ways that generalize to naturalistic settings. To address these issues, we introduce the Epistemic Asymmetry Schelling Task (EAST), a two-player dialogue game designed to benchmark robust and generalizable ToM abilities. By requiring LLM-LLM dyads to independently converge on semantic Schelling points under varying states of epistemic transparency, we evaluate whether models can robustly apply ToM to achieve coordination. Our results reveal a significant capability gap in functional social reasoning, with only frontier models successfully navigating the varying epistemic demands of the tasks. Analysis of reasoning traces shows that coordination failures are primarily driven by epistemic tracking errors, such as conflating private knowledge with mutual knowledge. Despite high performance on traditional static benchmarks, our study shows that robust social reasoning and epistemic tracking remain a critical bottleneck, providing concrete targets for future LLM evaluation and development.

</details>


### [68] [Agentic Routing: The Harness-Native Data Flywheel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11399)
*Xinchen Liu,Hang Zhou,Yingjie Zong,Yuchuan Tian,Liuyang Song,Shuo Zhang,Yulong Li,Wei He,Mengyu Zheng,Runke Liu,Siyang Cheng,Xiang Kuang,Hailin Hu,Kai Han,Yunhe Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Harness-Native agentic routing, a step-level paradigm that selects optimal models per agent execution step based on full harness state, generating structured execution traces that fuel a data flywheel for training progressively better routers and agent-native models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing routing methods optimize single-turn cost-quality trade-offs and ignore execution state, intermediate failures, and feedback loops inherent to agentic workflows. As models become structurally specialized (code, tool use, reasoning, latency), model selection within agent execution harnesses becomes a core systems problem requiring step-level, state-aware decisions.

Method: The authors propose a four-layer routing stack (OpenSquilla) using an open LightGBM cold-start ranker. Routing decisions produce structured records (query, harness state, model choice, trace, outcome, cost) labeled by the environment, forming a harness-native data flywheel. The system supports both singleton (best-fit) and multi-model (ensemble) routing, with staged policies trained iteratively from logged arena records.

Result: The approach is evaluated on agentic benchmarks including DRACO and PinchBench, studying both singleton and multi-model routing configurations. Execution traces train better routers and harness-native models, improving cost-quality trade-offs and generating more traces under fixed budgets.

Conclusion: Agentic routing transcends cost control — it functions as a data engine for agent-native training, where execution traces continuously improve routing policies and downstream models in a self-reinforcing flywheel.

Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly executed not by a single model call, but by an execution harness that manages observation, context, control, action, state, and verification. At the same time, frontier and open models are becoming structurally specialized: a model that is strong at code editing, long-context recovery, tool use, mathematical reasoning, or low-latency response may not dominate on the other axes. This makes model selection inside an agent a core systems problem rather than a per-query serving trick. Existing routing methods mostly optimize single-turn cost-quality trade-offs and therefore miss the execution state, intermediate failures, and feedback loops that make agents different from chat completion. We propose Harness-Native agentic routing, a step-level routing paradigm that selects either a single best-fit model for cost-effective execution or multiple complementary models for ensemble-style accuracy improvement, conditioned on the full harness state. The key insight is that every routing decision naturally produces a structured data record -- consisting of the query, harness state, model choice or model set, execution trace, outcome, and cost -- whose labels are supplied by the environment rather than by the router itself. These records form a harness-native data flywheel: execution traces train better routers and harness-native models, which improve cost-quality trade-offs and generate more traces under the same budget. We instantiate this idea in OpenSquilla with a four-layer routing stack, an open LightGBM cold-start ranker, and a staged router-model path that turns logged arena records into progressively stronger routing policies. The report studies singleton and multi-model routing on agentic benchmarks including DRACO and PinchBench, and argues that agentic routing is not merely cost control, but a data engine for agent-native training.

</details>


### [69] [Cross-Architecture LLM Ensembles, Feature-Based Reranking and Retrieval-Augmented Prompting for Legal Information Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11400)
*Amal Saad Alshehri,Nelly Bencomo,Amir Atapour-Abarghouei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Team DU's COLIEE 2026 submission across all five legal AI tasks, achieving 1st place in statute entailment (96.3% accuracy) via cross-architecture ensembling, with significant post-competition improvements through prompt engineering and model scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal information processing requires text matching, reasoning, and robust generalization under limited supervision. The work explores which inductive biases—cross-architecture ensembling, feature-based reranking, or retrieval-augmented prompting—are most effective for distinct legal tasks including retrieval, entailment, and judgment prediction.

Method: For Task 1 (case retrieval): learning-to-rank with 34 features combining lexical/semantic retrieval, structural, citation authority, and temporal features. For Task 2 (case entailment): prompt engineering from single- to multi-selection prompting. For Task 3 (statute retrieval/entailment): Qwen3-235B with structured legal reasoning prompt. For Task 4 (statute entailment): cross-architecture ensemble of 9 models from 3 families. For Pilot Task (tort prediction): multi-view system with 5 claim-level models plus verdict refinement using claim-derived features. All models are open-weight; Tasks 3-4 use pre-July 2025 models per competition rules.

Result: Task 4: 96.3% accuracy, 1st of 33 submissions (11 teams). Pilot Task (unofficial): 73.1% TP accuracy, 68.2% RE F1, exceeding all official TP scores and matching best RE. Task 2 (post-competition): F1 improved from 0.343 to 0.555, surpassing best official (0.490). Task 3 (post-competition): accuracy improved from 79.3% to 91.5%. Task 1: F1=0.314, rank 11 of 54 submissions.

Conclusion: Different legal information processing tasks benefit from distinct inductive biases: cross-architecture ensembling excels at statute entailment, feature-based reranking suits case retrieval, and retrieval-augmented prompting improves entailment and judgment prediction. No single approach dominates across all tasks.

Abstract: Legal information processing spans retrieval, entailment and judgment prediction problems, requiring text matching, reasoning and robust generalisation with limited supervision. We report Team DU's participation in all five tasks of COLIEE 2026, using open-weight systems for legal case retrieval, case entailment, statute retrieval and entailment, and legal judgment prediction. For Tasks 3 and 4, all models predate the 15 July 2025 cutoff required by the rules. For Task 4 (statute entailment), a cross-architecture ensemble of nine models from three families achieves 96.3% accuracy, placing first among 33 submissions from 11 teams. For the Pilot Task (tort prediction and rationale extraction), a multi-view system combining five claim-level models and refining the verdict using features derived from the claim predictions achieves 73.1% TP accuracy and 68.2% RE F1 as an unofficial submission, scoring above all official entries on TP and matching the highest on RE. For Task 2 (legal case entailment), changing only the prompt from single- to multi-selection raises F1 from 0.343 to 0.555 in post-competition evaluation on released gold labels, exceeding the best official submission (F1 = 0.490). For Task 3 (statute retrieval and entailment), replacing the entailment model with Qwen3-235B and a structured legal reasoning prompt raises accuracy from 79.3% to 91.5% in post-competition analysis. For Task 1 (legal case retrieval), a learning-to-rank system combining lexical and semantic retrieval with structural, citation authority, and temporal features (34 in total) achieves F1 = 0.314 (rank 11 of 54 submissions from 22 teams). Overall, legal information processing benefits from different inductive biases across tasks, with cross-architecture ensembling, feature-based reranking and retrieval-augmented prompting each proving most effective in different settings.

</details>


### [70] [Confidently Wrong: Detecting Hallucinations in Financial Question Answering from LLM Internal States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11414)
*Richard Zhe Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs in finance often produce confident but wrong answers (confident hallucinations). This paper trains linear probes on model residual streams to detect such errors, finding probes significantly outperform baselines like token log-probabilities and model self-assessment (0.68-0.77 vs 0.55-0.63 AUROC) across three models on FinQA/TAT-QA benchmarks, suggesting probing as a cost-effective triage mechanism for human review.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Confident errors (hallucinations) from LLMs in high-stakes financial applications are especially dangerous because they fail silently without warning, unlike hedged/uncertain answers that invite scrutiny. The authors aim to determine whether internal model activations carry reliable signals for detecting such confident hallucinations, beyond what observable outputs alone can provide.

Method: The authors train linear probes on the residual stream activations of three LLMs (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B). Behavioral confidence is quantified via answer agreement across eight resampled responses to the same question. Probe effectiveness is benchmarked on FinQA and TAT-QA (real financial filing QA datasets) and compared against baselines including token log-probabilities and the model's own True/False self-assessment.

Result: Among high-confidence answers (all eight resamples agree), 15-23% are wrong on FinQA. Probes achieve 0.68-0.77 AUROC for detecting these confident hallucinations, substantially outperforming the best baselines (0.55-0.63 AUROC) across all three models tested.

Conclusion: Probing internal activations serves as a cost-effective triage mechanism for routing LLM answers to human review and quality control in high-stakes financial settings, capturing error signals that are not accessible from observable outputs alone.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in financial applications fail most consequentially when they are confidently wrong.
