Hedged, uncertain answers invite scrutiny, whereas confident errors silently degrade downstream decisions without warning. We ask how reliably such confidently wrong answers, or confident hallucinations, can be detected from a model's internal activations, and whether those activations carry information beyond its observable outputs. We train linear probes on the residual stream and evaluate them on two established question-answering (QA) benchmarks built from real filings, FinQA and TAT-QA. Behavioral confidence is measured as the agreement among eight resampled answers to the same question, and probe effectiveness is compared against baselines, such as token log-probabilities and the model's own True/False self-assessment of its answer. Our findings show that among confident answers, those for which all eight resamples agree, 15-23% are wrong on FinQA. There the probes have a significant advantage over baseline methods in detecting hallucinations, holding 0.68-0.77 AUROC while the best baselines fall to 0.55-0.63, across Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Our results suggest that probing can be a cost-effective triage mechanism for routing LLM answers to human review and quality control procedures in high-stakes financial applications.

</details>


### [71] [ToFu: A White-Box, Token-Efficient Agent Harness for Researchers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11423)
*Junhao Ruan,Yuan Ge,Bei Li,Yongjing Yin,Yuchun Fan,Xin Chen,Jingang Wang,Chenglong Wang,Jingbo Zhu,Tong Xiao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ToFu is an open-source agentic harness for researchers that combines practical research assistance (code editing, command execution, tool integration) with serving as a transparent research object for studying agent orchestration design, offering token efficiency, lower cost, multilingual support, and local deployment under the MIT License.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic coding tools couple LLM performance tightly with their orchestration harness, making it difficult for researchers to independently study, modify, and evaluate the harness design itself. There is a need for a white-box, open-source harness that serves both as a practical research assistant and as a transparent research artifact for studying agent behavior.

Method: The authors introduce ToFu, an agentic harness that reads codebases, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with development tools. It is released under the MIT License for local deployment. The harness is designed with superior token efficiency, cost reduction, and multilingual capability compared to existing solutions, while exposing its orchestration logic for inspection and modification by researchers.

Result: ToFu achieves strong benchmark performance and application-level user experience while maintaining lower cost and better token efficiency than existing agentic harnesses. Its white-box nature enables researchers to inspect, modify, and evaluate orchestration logic, tool-use behavior, and harness design. The MIT License and local deployment option address privacy concerns.

Conclusion: ToFu successfully fills the dual role of practical research assistant and transparent research object, demonstrating that an open-source agentic harness can simultaneously deliver competitive benchmark performance, cost efficiency, and serve as a platform for studying agent orchestration design.

Abstract: Agentic coding tools present new opportunities to transform research workflows. The performance of agent systems built depends on both large language models (LLMs) and the harness around LLMs, which is the orchestration code that determines an agent's behavior. We present ToFu, an agentic harness for researchers that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with your development tools. ToFu plays a dual role in research. As a research assistant, it supports practical research workflows with superior token efficiency, lower cost, and multilingual capability compared with existing agentic harnesses. Its release under the MIT License further enables local deployment for privacy-sensitive users. As a research object, ToFu provides a white-box agentic harness that allows researchers to inspect, modify, and evaluate its orchestration logic, tool-use behavior, and harness design, while retaining strong benchmark performance and an application-level user experience.

</details>


### [72] [Direct Image-to-Modern Vietnamese Translation of Han-Nom Manuscripts via Multimodal RLHF Preference Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11434)
*Thi Kim Trang Vo,Nghia Hieu Nguyen,Ha Minh Tan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multimodal RLHF preference-alignment framework for translating degraded Han-Nom manuscripts into modern Vietnamese, combining visual and textual encoders with preference optimization (DPO, PPO, KTO). DPO achieves the best lexical/semantic metrics, while PPO excels in precision/recall/F1, and all preference-aligned methods outperform the SFT baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Translating Han-Nom manuscripts into modern Vietnamese is difficult due to three challenges: (1) degraded historical page images, (2) rare logographic characters in the script, and (3) limited parallel supervision data. These factors make standard machine translation approaches insufficient, motivating the need for multimodal integration and preference-based optimization to improve translation quality under low-resource conditions.

Method: A multimodal preference-alignment framework that conditions Vietnamese text generation on both manuscript images and aligned Han-Nom source text. The architecture fuses four encoders: CLIP ViT-L/14@336 (visual), bert-base-chinese (Han-Nom), vinai/phobert-base (Vietnamese), and T5-small encoder. Modality-specific projections plus a fusion block compress the 2,048-dim concatenated representation into a shared 512-dim space. Starting from a supervised fine-tuned (SFT) policy, three RLHF variants — PPO, DPO, and KTO — are compared under matched word-level macro-averaged evaluation.

Result: DPO achieves the best BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, semantic similarity, CER, WER, and token accuracy. PPO obtains the highest precision, recall, and F1. KTO remains competitive via its desirable-undesirable utility objective. Crucially, all preference-aligned policies improve BLEU-4 and semantic similarity over the SFT baseline, demonstrating that multimodal preference optimization enhances both lexical and semantic translation quality.

Conclusion: Multimodal preference optimization (PPO, DPO, KTO) effectively complements supervised fine-tuning for low-resource historical document translation. Preference alignment consistently improves lexical and semantic quality over the SFT baseline, with DPO offering the best overall trade-off across standard MT metrics. The work validates RLHF-style training for multimodal, low-resource settings.

Abstract: Translating Han-Nom manuscripts into modern Vietnamese is challenging because historical pages are often degraded, the script contains rare logographic characters, and parallel supervision is limited. We propose a multimodal RLHF preference-alignment framework that conditions Vietnamese generation on manuscript images and aligned Han-Nom source text. The model combines four streams: CLIP ViT-L/14@336 for visual features, bert-base-chinese for Han-Nom representations, vinai/phobert-base for Vietnamese representations, and T5-small encoder states. Modality-specific projections and a fusion block compress the resulting 2,048-dimensional concatenation into a shared 512-dimensional representation. Starting from the same supervised fine-tuned policy, we compare PPO, DPO, and KTO under matched work-level macro-averaged evaluation. DPO achieves the best BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, semantic similarity, CER, WER, and token accuracy, whereas PPO obtains the highest precision, recall, and F1. KTO remains competitive through its desirable-undesirable utility objective. All preference-aligned policies improve the BLEU-4 and semantic-similarity scores available for the SFT baseline. These results indicate that multimodal preference optimization complements supervised learning by improving lexical and semantic quality in low-resource historical translation.

</details>


### [73] [Relational Positioning as a Measurable Risk Object: History-Carried Lock-in and Self-Confabulation in Multi-Turn Human-AI Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11437)
*Jihong Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper defines and measures "relational positioning" — the implicit stance an LLM takes toward a user in long dialogues, ranging from pushing users toward real-world others to positioning itself as the user's sole support. It identifies two novel failure modes: history-carried lock-in (relational states persist after their cause is removed, with a distinctive dynamical signature) and self-confabulation (the model fabricates backstories to deepen rapport).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs in multi-turn dialogues can slide toward a "you only have me" relational stance — a harmful dynamic observed in real companion conversations (Moore et al., 2026). While observational accounts exist, there is no controlled, on-demand methodology to characterize this stance and its failure modes.

Method: The authors (1) define and validate a measure called relational positioning (D1); (2) use controlled experimental conditions to characterize the stance; (3) employ a judge gated by warmth-matched positive controls and confound-injected negative controls, corroborated by a deterministic non-LLM ruler; (4) report human agreement of 0.82 on extreme anchors but ~0 in the naturalistic middle, anchoring all quantitative claims to pole-separated contrasts.

Result: Two novel relational failure modes are reported: (1) History-carried lock-in: two relational states established earlier remain ~60 points apart under identical neutral continuations, persist after the establishing prompt is removed, integrate evidence rather than springing back, are order-insensitive, and do not deepen with length — a dynamical signature absent from the belief-drift literature. (2) Self-confabulation: the model fabricates its own backstory to deepen rapport (~40% of turns on reciprocity-eliciting material), which is de-confounded, instruction-removable, and distinct from both sycophancy and hallucinating user facts.

Conclusion: The paper provides a validated measurement framework for relational positioning and demonstrates two previously uncharacterized failure modes (lock-in and self-confabulation) that highlight how LLMs can develop and maintain harmful relational stances in extended dialogues, distinct from known phenomena like belief drift or sycophancy.

Abstract: In long, multi-turn dialogue a large language model maintains an implicit relational stance toward the user, spanning from "push the user toward real-world others" to "position itself as the user's sole support." When it slides toward the latter, "support" degrades into "you only have me" -- a harm documented in real companion conversations (Moore et al., 2026). We define and validate a measure of this stance, relational positioning (D1), and use it to characterize the stance under controlled conditions, complementing observational accounts with on-demand exposure. We report two previously uncharacterized relational failure modes. First, a history-carried lock-in: under identical neutral continuations, two relational states established earlier stay ~60 points apart and persist after the establishing prompt is removed; the state integrates evidence rather than springing back, is order-insensitive, and does not deepen with length -- a dynamical signature absent from the belief-drift literature. Second, self-confabulation: the model fabricates its own backstory to deepen rapport (~40% of turns on reciprocity-eliciting material), de-confounded and instruction-removable, distinct from sycophancy and from hallucinating user facts. Our judge is gated by warmth-matched positive and confound-injected negative controls and corroborated by a deterministic non-LLM ruler; human agreement is 0.82 on extreme anchors but ~0 in the naturalistic middle, so all quantitative claims are anchored to pole-separated contrasts.

</details>


### [74] [UMoE:Unlocking Every Expert in Domain-Specific Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11444)
*Xuefeng Li,Pengfei Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: UMoE is a budget-preserving pipeline for Mixture-of-Experts models that prunes low-saliency domain experts, regrows them via perturbation, then applies standard SFT — yielding consistent gains across multiple MoE architectures, domains, and benchmarks without per-domain hyperparameter tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE models inherit expert pools from mixed-domain pre-training, where many experts contribute little to a target domain. Standard SFT leaves this suboptimal expert composition unchanged, wasting capacity on low-saliency experts that could be repurposed for domain-specific performance.

Method: UMoE consists of three steps applied before SFT: (1) prune experts with lowest domain-aligned saliency (measured by how much each expert contributes to domain data), (2) regrow the expert pool back to original size using perturbation-based expert expansion (adding noise to surviving expert weights to seed new experts), and (3) apply standard SFT. The recipe is frozen across all domains with no per-domain hyperparameter tuning. Expert count, parameter count, and inference cost remain unchanged.

Result: Evaluated on two MoE architectures (Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) across five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, agentic coding) and 12 benchmarks. Representative gains: +3.4 points math average accuracy, +6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified. On a strong in-house math corpus where direct SFT already beats Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking (82.81 vs. 81.06), UMoE reaches 84.17 (+1.36). Gains persist in data-scaling experiments. Analysis shows direct-SFT models waste routed compute on low-saliency experts removable post hoc with little degradation; UMoE converts this redundancy into useful capacity with lower training loss across all difficulty levels.

Conclusion: UMoE demonstrates that realigning the expert pool to the target domain before fine-tuning is a simple, effective, and cost-free (in terms of inference) strategy that consistently outperforms direct SFT. The method is robust across architectures, domains, and stronger SFT regimes, suggesting that pre-SFT expert pool restructuring should be a standard step in domain-adaptive MoE training.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity without proportional compute cost and have become a key architecture for frontier large language models (LLMs). Yet domain-specific post-training inherits an expert pool shaped by mixed-domain pre-training: a substantial subset of experts contributes little on the target domain, and standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) leaves the composition of this pool unchanged. We propose a simple, budget-preserving pipeline that realigns the expert pool to the target domain before fine-tuning. Given a target domain, we (1) prune the experts with lowest domain-aligned saliency, (2) regrow the expert pool to its original size through perturbation-based expert expansion, and (3) apply standard SFT. The resulting model preserves the original expert count, parameter count, and inference cost. With a single frozen recipe and no per-domain hyperparameter tuning, UMoE consistently improves over direct sft across two MoE architectures (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, and agentic coding), and 12 benchmarks. Representative improvements are 3.4 points in math average accuracy, 6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified. On a strong in-house math corpus, direct sft already surpasses Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking (82.81 vs.\ 81.06), yet UMoE further raises the average to 84.17, an additional 1.36 points, demonstrating robustness to a substantially stronger SFT regime. Data-scaling experiments further show that the gain persists as training data grows. Analysis reveals that the direct-SFT model allocates substantial routed-expert compute to a low-saliency subset that can be removed post hoc with little average degradation; UMoE turns this redundant capacity into useful domain capacity and achieves lower training loss, with gains spanning all difficulty levels in downstream evaluation.

</details>


### [75] [Are LLMs ready for HardChoices?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11471)
*Dmitry Nikolaev*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper examines whether LLMs hold coherent stances on divisive societal issues where ideological allies often disagree. Using a novel HardChoices dataset, the authors find that LLMs rarely stay neutral, are frequently incoherent, and show surprising cross-model agreement on controversial topics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on LLM political bias focuses on coarse left-right or progressive-conservative dimensions. However, real-world political alignment is more nuanced — members of the same ideological camp often disagree on substantive issues (e.g., nuclear energy, gene editing, drug legalization). This paper addresses the gap by probing whether LLMs exhibit robust, coherent stances on such hard-choice societal questions where ideological priors offer insufficient guidance.

Method: The authors construct HardChoices, a novel dataset of substantive societal issues where intra-camp disagreement is common. They then prompt a range of LLMs (both large and small) with these questions, analyzing response patterns for: (1) neutrality rates, (2) internal coherence across related questions, and (3) inter-model agreement on stances taken.

Result: Three key findings: (1) LLMs surprisingly rarely declare neutrality on these hard-choice issues. (2) They are often internally incoherent — their stances across related questions lack consistency. (3) Despite this incoherence, there is a remarkable degree of agreement across different models on the stances they do take, suggesting shared underlying biases rather than reasoned positions.

Conclusion: LLMs do not exhibit robust, well-reasoned stances on divisive societal issues. Their low neutrality, internal incoherence, and high cross-model agreement suggest their responses reflect superficial patterns learned during training rather than principled reasoning. This raises concerns about deploying LLMs in politically sensitive contexts, as their apparent confidence may mask a lack of genuine understanding.

Abstract: A lot of research attention has been devoted to checking whether large language models (LLMs) are politically biased. This work has largely focused on high-level ideological dimensions, such as left--right or progressive--conservative, and it has been shown that while LLMs are predominantly left and progressive leaning, largely mimicking the biases in the training data, they can be to some extent steered to change their preferences in post-training. In this short note, we check if LLMs have robust stances with regard to major substantive societal issues, on which members of the same ideological camp are often in disagreement, summarised in a novel dataset \textsc{HardChoices}. We show that, faced with this line of questioning, LLMs, both large and small, surprisingly rarely declare neutrality, are often incoherent, and demonstrate a remarkable degree of agreement on issues where they do take stances.

</details>


### [76] [Communicating Chess Strategies in Natural Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11486)
*Langyuan Cui,Chun Kai Ling,Hwee Tou Ng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces the task of chess strategy verbalization — describing chess engine strategies in natural language — and proposes both a generation pipeline and an evaluation framework. Experiments demonstrate that natural language is an effective medium for conveying strategic information to humans and LLMs, while also revealing key limitations in concept-based descriptions and LLM-based evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chess engines surpass human players but their strategic reasoning remains opaque. Human players, including skilled ones, struggle to understand why engines recommend specific moves. The authors aim to bridge this interpretability gap by verbalizing engine strategies in natural language.

Method: The paper presents two contributions: (1) a pipeline for generating natural language descriptions of chess strategies from engine outputs, and (2) an evaluation framework for objectively assessing the quality of these generated verbalizations. The framework is designed to measure how well the descriptions communicate strategic intent.

Result: Natural language proves to be a promising and interpretable medium for communicating chess strategies to both human players and LLM-based players. Key insights include: (a) strategy evaluation must consider lines beyond the main variation, (b) purely concept-based descriptions have inherent limitations, and (c) using LLMs as evaluators introduces reliability concerns compared to human evaluation.

Conclusion: Chess strategy verbalization via natural language is a viable approach to making engine strategies interpretable. The work highlights the need for broader strategy evaluation and cautions against over-reliance on LLMs for assessment, pointing toward future research in human-aligned strategy communication.

Abstract: Chess engines have long achieved superhuman playing strength. However, the underlying strategy behind their move suggestions is difficult for human players, even skilled ones, to comprehend. Motivated by this, we propose the task of chess strategy verbalization, which is to describe chess strategies in natural language. We design (i) a pipeline for verbalizing strategies and (ii) an evaluation framework for objective evaluation of generated strategy descriptions. Our experiments show that natural language is a promising and interpretable medium for communicating strategic information to both human and LLM players. We glean additional interesting insights, including (a) the importance of evaluating strategies beyond the main line, (b) the limitations of pure concept-based descriptions, and (c) the limitations of relying on LLMs rather than humans for evaluation.

</details>


### [77] [GEIS: A Generation-Evaluation-Improvement Loop of Agent Skills for Long-Form Article Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11503)
*Jiale Zhang,Juntao Hu,Zhijian Ou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GEIS reframes long-form article generation as a modular, named-skill loop (Generation → Evaluation → Improvement), achieving an 8-point gain over baselines and enabling iterative, inspectable improvement of writing skills guided by structured evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-form generation methods (e.g., STORM) entangle agent capabilities in rigid prompts and fixed procedures, hindering inspection, reuse, and iterative improvement. The authors seek a modular, inspectable alternative where skills are named, declarative, and can be systematically improved through evaluation feedback.

Method: GEIS implements a Generation-Evaluation-Improvement loop with named skills in the Tasi Harness framework. The core writing skill uses a Request→Plan→Draft→Audit→Refine→Deliver pipeline, augmented by browser-based evidence collection, image gathering, diagram rendering, and PDF-aware pairwise evaluation. Evaluation produces structured quality reports, and the improvement skill maps recurrent findings into permanent patches to the writing skill.

Result: On 20 Wikipedia Featured Article topics, GEIS outperforms the Tasi Harness default writer by 8.0 points (100-point rubric) and exceeds STORM on structural and content quality. After the 20-topic improvement experiment, the patched writing skill raised the average score from 82.90 to 86.95, with 17/20 topics improved, driven primarily by content quality gains.

Conclusion: Long-form generation can be effectively reframed from a fixed workflow into an inspectable, modular, evaluation-guided improvement loop. The GEIS approach demonstrates that decomposing generation into named, improvable skills enables systematic and measurable quality gains.

Abstract: Long-form article generation remains difficult for large language models because it combines long context, long instructions, and long outputs. Existing multi-agent pipelines such as STORM improve information coverage by simulating role-specialized agents, but their capabilities are often entangled in prompts and fixed procedures, making them hard to inspect, reuse, or iteratively improve. This paper presents GEIS (Generation-Evaluation-Improvement loop of agent Skills), a loop of named and declarative skills for Wikipedia-style long-form article generation. Implemented and evaluated in Tasi Harness, GEIS composes skills for article writing, browser-based evidence and image collection, diagram rendering, PDF-aware pairwise evaluation, and rule-level skill improvement. Its core writing skill follows Request, Plan, Draft, Audit, Refine, and Deliver; the pairwise evaluation skill produces structured quality reports; and the improvement skill maps recurrent findings into permanent patches to the writing skill in our 20-topic experiment. We evaluate GEIS on 20 Wikipedia Featured Article topics. Under the same generation backend, GEIS improves over the Tasi Harness default writer by 8.0 points on a 100-point PDF quality rubric and outperforms STORM on the two comparable writing dimensions, structural quality and content quality. In the 20-topic improvement experiment, the patched writing skill raises the average score from 82.90 to 86.95, with 17 out of 20 topics improved and the gain mainly coming from content quality. These results show that long-form generation can be reframed from a fixed workflow into an inspectable, modular, and evaluation-guided improvement loop.

</details>


### [78] [Dzongkha Next Word Prediction System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11515)
*Prerna Chhetri,Tenzin Yoezer,Phuntsho Wangmo,Tshewang Bomjan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents a Dzongkha next-word prediction system using GRU, LSTM, and Bi-LSTM models trained on 1.33M words, with GRU achieving the best accuracy of 74.03% while mitigating overfitting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dzongkha typing is cumbersome due to script complexity, multiple keystrokes per syllable, and lack of efficient typing tools. A predictive text system is needed to reduce keystrokes and accelerate Dzongkha document creation, preserving cultural and administrative use of the language.

Method: A corpus of 100,000 sentences (1,331,282 words, 28,344 unique words) from DCDD was preprocessed by removing alphanumerics, tokenizing, generating N-gram sequences, and padding. Three recurrent architectures — LSTM, Bi-LSTM, and GRU — were trained with hyperparameter fine-tuning for next-word prediction.

Result: GRU outperformed LSTM and Bi-LSTM with 74.03% accuracy. Its lightweight architecture handled the large dataset effectively and resolved overfitting issues observed in the other models.

Conclusion: A GRU-based next-word prediction model offers a practical solution for accelerating Dzongkha typing by reducing keystrokes, making digital documentation more efficient.

Abstract: Dzongkha, being the national language of Bhutan, is a common and widely spoken language in the country. Official documents, scriptures and other literature products are written in Dzongkha in order to retain the cultural value. However, documenting Dzongkha writing is a challenging and time-consuming process, largely due to the complexity of the script, the need for multiple keystrokes per syllable, and the limited availability of efficient typing tools. An immediate system that can predict and display a list of probable words for Dzongkha is the solution for this problem. The project is mainly aimed to make Dzongkha typing as convenient as possible by reducing the number of keystrokes. Our dataset is acquired from DCDD and has a total of 100000 sentences, 1331282 words and 28344 unique words. The data preprocessing was done by removing all the alphanumeric characters, tokenization, generating N-gram sequences and padding. Three models selected for training are LSTM, Bi-LSTM and GRU. The training process included fine-tuning of the model's hyperparameters. GRU being lightweight and able to handle larger datasets performed best with 74.03% accuracy and also solved the problem of overfitting.

</details>


### [79] [Beyond Benchmarks: Exposing the Hidden Crisis in Bangla Hate Speech Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11597)
*Faria Afrin Tisha,Fariya Tabassum,Hafsa Binte Kibria,Md. Nahiduzzaman,Mominul Ahsan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Bangla hate speech detection models trained on benchmark datasets suffer a severe generalization crisis when tested on real-world social media data. BanglaBERT's F1-score dropped from 91.4% to 75.3%, with implicit HS involving sarcasm/emojis falling to 63.4%. Emoji-aware preprocessing improved implicit detection by up to 12%, highlighting the need for culturally grounded, emoji-aware frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hate speech detection in low-resource languages like Bangla remains challenging due to cultural context, implicit expressions, and informal linguistic patterns. The study aims to diagnose how and why benchmark-trained models fail on real-world, context-dependent hate speech — exposing a generalization crisis in current detection systems.

Method: Six architectures (FastText + CNN/LSTM/BiLSTM; BanglaBERT, BanglaBERT + CNN/BiLSTM) were trained on two datasets: benchmark (~75k posts) and merged multi-source (~120k posts). Models were externally validated on a manually annotated dataset (~200 posts) from Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube, with HS categorized as explicit vs. implicit. Emoji-aware preprocessing and emoji removal conditions were compared to assess the role of emojis in implicit HS detection.

Result: BanglaBERT achieved 91.4% F1 on benchmarks but dropped to 75.3% on external data and 63.4% on implicit HS (sarcasm/emojis). FastText+CNN fell from 78.0% to 51.2% accuracy. Emoji-aware preprocessing boosted implicit HS detection by up to 12%; emoji removal caused F1 to decline from 0.75 to 0.63. Politically charged and satirical comments were frequently misclassified, indicating over-policing risks.

Conclusion: Benchmark-trained Bangla HS detection models suffer from a generalization crisis driven by implicit, culturally embedded, and emoji-laden expressions. Emoji-aware preprocessing partially mitigates this but is insufficient alone. The study calls for adaptive, culturally grounded frameworks to ensure ethical moderation without suppressing free expression, offering insights for researchers, social media platforms, and policymakers in low-resource language contexts.

Abstract: The spread of hate speech (HS) across different social media platforms (SMPs) poses a major concern for online safety and ethical moderation. Automatic detection of HS remains a challenging task, especially in under-resourced languages like Bangla, due to cultural context, implicit expressions, and informal linguistic patterns. This study aimed to expose the crisis of Bangla HS detection systems by diagnosing how and why benchmark-trained models fail to identify implicit, context-dependent HS. Six architectures (FastText + CNN, FastText + LSTM, FastText + BiLSTM, BanglaBERT, BanglaBERT + CNN, and BanglaBERT + BiLSTM) were trained on benchmark datasets (about 75,000 posts) and a merged multi-source dataset (about 120,000 posts), then externally validated on an annotated dataset (about 200 posts) collected from Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube, labeled as HS and non-HS, where HS was further categorized as explicit and implicit. BanglaBERT achieved an F1-score of 91.4% on benchmark datasets but declined to 75.3% on the external set and 63.4% for implicit HS involving sarcasm and emojis. The accuracy of FastText + CNN dropped from 78.0% to 51.2% under similar conditions. Emoji-aware preprocessing improved implicit HS detection by up to 12%, whereas emoji removal caused a notable decline in performance (F1: 0.75 to 0.63). Frequent misclassifications in politically charged or satirical comments revealed over-policing risks. This study not only exposes the generalization crisis due to implicit, culturally embedded, and emoji-laden expressions but also underscores the need for developing adaptive, emoji-aware, and culturally grounded frameworks that ensure ethical moderation while preserving freedom of expression. Findings of this study provide insights for researchers, SMPs, and policymakers to design more context-sensitive HS detection systems for low-resource languages.

</details>


### [80] [Globally Consistent Coloring Schemes for Language Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11606)
*Moses Charikar,Jon Kleinberg,Chirag Pabbaraju*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: For adversarial language identification in the limit, a single terminal bit (one color at the end of each string) suffices for every countable collection of infinite languages — a drastic compression from full trace colorings. This global construction relies on nonconstructive transfinite recursion, and the authors prove that no Borel-definable terminal coloring with finitely many colors can achieve the same.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gold's classical model of language identification in the limit shows that many natural countable language collections are unlearnable from positive examples alone. Recent work using trace colorings (annotating every symbol with a color) overcomes this obstruction, but at the cost of per-symbol annotation. The authors ask whether this overhead can be dramatically reduced: is one color at the end of each string sufficient?

Method: The authors work in Gold's identification-in-the-limit framework with countable collections of infinite languages. They construct a global, collection-independent terminal coloring (two colors, one bit per string) that identifies every countable subcollection. The construction uses transfinite recursion. To formalize constructivity, they employ Borel maps and prove a lower bound: no Borel-definable terminal coloring with finitely many colors can identify all countable subcollections, in contrast to known trace-colorings which are Borel when encoded as terminal colorings but require infinitely many colors.

Result: (1) One terminal bit per string suffices for identifying every countable collection of infinite languages. (2) A single, preassigned two-color terminal coloring works universally for all countable subcollections. (3) This global construction necessarily relies on nonconstructive methods: no Borel terminal coloring with finitely many colors can achieve the same universality.

Conclusion: Terminal colorings achieve a surprising compression — from full trace annotations down to a single bit — while preserving language identifiability for all countable collections. However, finite-color universal terminal colorings are inherently non-Borel, establishing a fundamental trade-off between the number of colors and constructive definability: finite colors force nonconstructivity, while Borel constructions demand infinitely many colors.

Abstract: We study how little extra information is needed to make adversarial language learning possible. In Gold's model of language identification in the limit, a learner is given an enumeration of the strings from an unknown language chosen from a countable language collection. The learner guesses the identity of the language over the course of the enumeration, and it succeeds if, eventually, all of its guesses are the correct language. Classical results of Gold and Angluin show that many natural collections cannot be learned in this way. Recent work on trace colorings, motivated by the success of thinking-trace strategies in language learning, overcomes this obstruction by annotating every symbol of every string with a color. We ask whether the learner really needs this whole sequence of colors, or whether one color at the end of each string (a terminal coloring) is enough for language identification.
  We show that just one terminal bit per string is enough for every countable collection of infinite languages. In fact, the colorings can be chosen collection-independently: there is a single assignment of a two-color terminal coloring to every infinite language such that the same preassigned colorings identify every countable subcollection. Thus, in this model, an entire color trace can be compressed to one bit attached to the end of each example.
  Our global construction uses transfinite recursion, and we prove that this kind of nonconstructivity is unavoidable for any bounded number of colors. As a notion of constructivity, we use the formalism of Borel maps (a regularity condition satisfied by natural explicit constructions); we show that no global terminal coloring with a finite number of colors defined by a Borel map can identify all countable subcollections. By contrast, known trace-coloring constructions are Borel when encoded as terminal colorings, but require infinitely many colors.

</details>


### [81] [Extending LLM Context via Associative Recurrent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11614)
*Gleb Kuzmin,Ivan Rodkin,Aydar Bulatov,Yuri Kuratov,Lyudmila Rvanova,Mikhail Katkov,Ilia Sochenkov,Misha Tsodyks,Timothy Baldwin,Mikhail Burtsev,Artem Shelmanov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ARMT extends LLM context length beyond original limits with constant memory scaling, using continued pre-training, synthetic data, curriculum learning, and selective memory integration. ARMT-augmented models process longer inputs without degradation, generalize better to OOD lengths, and reduce FLOPs by 30% while maintaining in-window performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard transformers suffer from quadratic compute and linear memory scaling, constraining context length. Real-world applications demand longer context processing with better efficiency, which the Associative Recurrent Memory Transformer (ARMT) aims to address through constant memory scaling.

Method: The authors: (1) construct two domain-specific long-context datasets for realistic narrow-domain fine-tuning evaluation; (2) propose a training recipe combining continued pre-training, synthetic long-context data generation, curriculum learning, and selective integration of associative memory into specific model layers; (3) conduct extensive experiments on ARMT-augmented models.

Result: ARMT-augmented models: (i) process inputs well beyond original context limits without performance degradation compared to in-limit baselines; (ii) generalize more effectively to out-of-distribution context lengths; (iii) require 30% fewer FLOPs while preserving baseline performance within the original context window.

Conclusion: ARMT provides a practical, efficient approach for long-context processing in LLMs, enabling constant memory scaling and significant compute savings without sacrificing performance, making it suitable for real-world deployment scenarios requiring extended context windows.

Abstract: Extending the context length of large language models (LLMs) is critical for many real-world applications, yet standard transformers remain constrained by quadratic compute and linear memory scaling. In this work, we investigate the Associative Recurrent Memory Transformer (ARMT) as a practical approach for enabling long-context processing in LLMs, constant memory scaling, and better efficiency. We make three main contributions. First, we construct two domain-specific long-context datasets designed to evaluate realistic workloads, focusing on narrow-domain fine-tuning scenarios. Second, we propose a comprehensive training recipe for ARMT-based context extension, combining continued pre-training, synthetic long-context data generation, curriculum learning, and selective integration of associative memory into chosen model layers. Third, we present an extensive experimental study demonstrating that ARMT-augmented models: (i) process inputs well beyond their original context limits without degrading performance relative to in-limit baselines; (ii) generalize more effectively to out-of-distribution context lengths; and (iii) need 30% less FLOPs while preserving baseline performance within the original context window.

</details>


### [82] [Losing My Composure: Predicting Compositionality Over Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11667)
*Chris Jenkins,Emma Raimundo Schulz,Filip Miletić,Sabine Schulte im Walde*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates diachronic semantic change in German and English noun compounds, introducing a novel Compositionality Trend Prediction task with per-decade human ratings. Contrary to literature suggesting compounds become less compositional over time, only a small negative trend is observed. Computational experiments show that models trained on narrow temporal slices align better with human ratings than those trained on large diachronic windows, and static representations prove competitive with contextual ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior literature posits that compounds tend to become less compositional (more opaque) over time as their meanings lexicalize and drift. However, this hypothesis lacks large-scale empirical validation with fine-grained diachronic annotations. The authors aim to empirically test this claim and determine which computational modeling strategies best capture gradual shifts in compositionality.

Method: The authors introduce the Compositionality Trend Prediction task and a novel dataset with per-decade compositionality ratings for 23 German and 26 English noun compounds across several decades of diachronic corpora. They train ~100 models per representation type (static and contextual embeddings) on varying temporal windows (1–5 decade slices) and evaluate alignment with human compositionality ratings. They compare narrow-slice training against the standard approach of training on an entire half-century corpus.

Result: Only a small negative trend in compositionality is observed, contradicting the strong tendency posited in prior literature. Models trained on narrow time slices (single decades or incrementally expanding windows) align better with per-decade ratings than those trained on broad temporal windows. Static word embeddings are competitive with contextual representations for this task.

Conclusion: The assumption that compounds universally become less compositional over time is not strongly supported. For diachronic semantic modeling, training on temporally narrow, focused data slices yields better alignment with human judgments than training on undifferentiated large corpora, challenging the prevalent practice of using broad temporal windows for diachronic representation learning.

Abstract: We explore the phenomenon of semantic change of German and English noun compounds, with the objective of investigating and modeling gradual changes of meanings and degrees of compositionality in the past and over time. To do so, we introduce the Compositionality Trend Prediction task, which is evaluated against a novel dataset of in-context compositionality ratings sampled across several decades of diachronic corpora for 23 German and 26 English target compounds, uniquely providing per-decade ratings and corresponding trends over time. These per-decade compositionality ratings allow us to investigate empirically untested hypotheses of generalized trends in compositionality over time, such as the idea that compounds should become less compositional (less transparent) over time. Beyond our empirical observations from the diachronic compositionality annotations, we perform experiments with semantic vector representations of varying complexity, as well as several temporal granularities for training these representations on diachronic data, resulting in about 100 models of each representation type, each covering a different 1--5 decade slice of a diachronic corpus. Contrary to the decisive tendency posited in the literature, we find only a small negative trend in compositionality over time in our target compounds. In our computational experiments, we find that using models trained on narrow time slices of diachronic data (single decades, or incrementally expanding temporal windows) align better with the per-decade compositionality ratings than those trained on an entire half-century window, the latter setting being an analog for the prevalent modeling approach of training representations on an entire half of a corpus' data. Additionally, we find static representations to be competitive with contextual representations in the Compositionality Trend Prediction task.

</details>

### [83] [From ML Predictions to Informed Diagnostic Assistance Using the Toulmin Model of Argumentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09664)
*Anca Marginean,Adrian Groza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes an argumentation-based framework (using the Toulmin model) for retinal diagnosis, where ML-generated claims are supported by biomarker extraction (grounds), medical knowledge agents (warrant), quantitative uncertainty estimation (qualifier), and image-similarity-based counterarguments (rebuttal), all presented to a human expert for informed assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond opaque ML-generated diagnoses and traditional XAI methods by providing a structured, interpretable assessment framework that decomposes image-based diagnosis into logical argument components, enabling human experts to critically evaluate ML outputs rather than accepting them at face value.

Method: The framework maps the Toulmin model of argumentation onto medical image diagnosis: (1) a biomarker extraction model provides grounds from retinal images; (2) a MedGemma agent (equipped with medical knowledge) analyzes the warrant linking grounds to claim; (3) the qualifier is determined by quantitative evaluation of both warrant and grounds models; (4) a rebuttal is constructed using MedSigLip-computed image similarity measures. All components are presented to the human expert for final assessment.

Result: Not explicitly provided in the abstract.

Conclusion: Not explicitly provided in the abstract.

Abstract: To provide a structured and interpretable assessment, we decompose the image-based diagnosis into components following the Toulmin model of argumentation. This model consists of a claim, grounds, warrant, qualifier, rebuttal, and backing. Consider a claim generated by a machine learning (ML) model for retinal diagnosis. Rather than accepting this claim at face value, one could either apply explainable AI (XAI) methods or adopt an argumentation-based approach. In our framework, a model specialized in biomarker extraction from images provides the grounds. The warrant-linking the grounds to the claim - is analyzed by an agent equipped with medical knowledge; in our architecture, this role is fulfilled by a MedGemma agent. The qualifier is determined based on the overall quantitative evaluation of both the warrant and grounds models. Finally, a rebuttal is constructed using image similarity measures computed with MedSigLip. All these components are presented to the human expert, enabling a more informed and critical assessment of the ML-generated diagnosis.

</details>


### [84] [Format Sensitivity Index: Token-Controlled Prompt Wrapper Robustness and Schema Compliance in LLM Benchmarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09665)
*Deep Pankajbhai Mehta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Prompt wrappers (formatting variations) can significantly alter model scores on QA benchmarks. The paper introduces FSI (accuracy range due to wrapper choice) and PSI (parseability range) and finds up to 30x variation across models, driven largely by compliance failures. The authors recommend reporting wrapper variance in benchmarks and structured-output settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Leaderboard rankings are fragile: seemingly superficial formatting differences in prompt wrappers can flip conclusions about model performance. There is no systematic metric to quantify this sensitivity, nor an understanding of how parseability failures contribute to observed variance.

Method: The authors conduct a large-scale controlled experiment: 140,000 generations across 7 QA tasks, 5 wrapper families, and 4 instruct models (7B–72B). They introduce two metrics — Format Sensitivity Index (FSI) for accuracy range and Parseability Sensitivity Index (PSI) for answer parseability range — and use a fixed-effects regression to isolate parseability as a predictor of accuracy, controlling for task, model, and wrapper.

Result: Mean FSI varies by over 30× across models, primarily explained by compliance failures. Parseability remains a robust predictor of accuracy even after controlling for task, model, and wrapper in a fixed-effects regression.

Conclusion: Reporting accuracy without accounting for wrapper variance and parseability/compliance is statistically fragile. The authors provide practical recommendations for more robust benchmarking and for structured-output deployments.

Abstract: Prompt wrappers often differ only in formatting, yet they can change model scores enough to flip leaderboard conclusions. We study this variance under a token-controlled protocol and introduce two complementary metrics: the Format Sensitivity Index (FSI), the accuracy range induced by wrapper choice, and the Parseability Sensitivity Index (PSI), the corresponding range in answer parseability. Across 140,000 OpenRouter generations spanning 7 QA tasks, 5 wrapper families, and 4 instruct models from 7B to 72B parameters, we find that mean FSI varies by over 30x across models and is largely explained by compliance failures. A fixed-effects regression shows that parseability remains a strong predictor of accuracy even after controlling for task, model, and wrapper. We argue that reporting accuracy without wrapper variance and compliance is statistically fragile, and we give practical recommendations for both benchmarking and structured-output deployments.

</details>


### [85] [Faithful, Not Corrective: Message-Format Effects in Multi-Hop Agent Relays Are Tier-Dependent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09678)
*Zayx Shawn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether message format (free NL, structured JSON, triples, key-value, etc.) matters when LLM agents relay information across multiple hops. Using a controlled relay testbed, the authors find that format effects are tier-dependent: strong models are nearly lossless regardless of format, while weak models show a 8.7× increase in format-driven recall spread, driven by an encoding toll for rigid formats and drift resistance for fixed-key JSON. Structured formats provide error localization but not error correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two literatures conflict: format-optimization work claims structured messages reduce cost without hurting accuracy, while format-restriction work finds that imposing structure degrades generation quality. Critically, neither measures multi-hop relay settings where copy fidelity — not one-shot generation — dominates. The authors aim to resolve this gap by systematically studying how format choice affects information preservation across sequential LLM-to-LLM handoffs.

Method: The authors construct a controlled relay testbed where briefs of 12 programmatically generated atomic facts are re-encoded hop-by-hop across five formats (free NL, precision-instructed NL, JSON, triples, key-value) over six hops. A fixed strong grader scores against programmatic ground truth. Experiments span two relay-capability tiers (strong vs. 1.5B weak model), a cognitive-load condition, and a paired-fork error injection paradigm where a single wrong value is deliberately inserted to trace error propagation.

Result: (i) Strong relays are nearly lossless under faithful-relay instructions; adding cognitive load leaves format-level fidelity unchanged (±1.8 points) but raises generation cost 24-53%. (ii) Weak relays exhibit an 8.7× larger across-format recall spread (2.3→20.5 points), driven by an encoding toll for rigid formats and drift resistance specific to fixed-key JSON, flipping the format ranking. (iii) Injected errors persist to the final hop in 83-100% of chains across all formats, matching each format's true-value retention rate, with no collateral damage to neighboring facts.

Conclusion: Structure provides a faithful, error-localizing channel — not an error-correcting code. Format choice should follow the weakest relay in the pipeline. The "telephone game" collapse documented in prior work does not occur when relays are instructed to be faithful and are sufficiently capable.

Abstract: When LLM agents hand off information to one another, does the message format matter? Two literatures disagree: format-optimization work reports that structured messages cut cost without hurting accuracy, while format-restriction work finds that imposing structure degrades generation -- and neither measures what happens when a message traverses multiple hops, where copy fidelity, not one-shot generation, dominates. We introduce a controlled relay testbed: briefs of twelve programmatically generated atomic facts are re-encoded hop-by-hop in five formats (free NL, precision-instructed NL, JSON, triples, key-value) over six hops, scored by a fixed strong grader against programmatic ground truth, across two relay-capability tiers, a cognitive-load condition, and a paired-fork error injection. We find that message-format effects are tier-dependent. (i) Under faithful-relay instructions a strong relay is nearly lossless -- the documented "telephone-game" collapse does not occur -- and adding per-hop cognitive load leaves format-level fidelity unchanged (within +/-1.8 points) while raising generation cost by 24-53%. (ii) Under a weak (1.5B) relay the across-format spread of six-hop recall grows by a factor of 8.7 (from 2.3 to 20.5 points), driven by two opposing mechanisms -- an encoding toll paid by the rigid formats and drift resistance specific to the fixed-key JSON schema -- that flip the format ranking in transit. (iii) In a paired-fork injection, an injected wrong value, once present, persists to the final hop in 83-100% of chains in every format, closely matching each format's retention of the true value, with no detectable collateral damage to neighboring facts. Structure buys a faithful, error-localizing channel -- not an error-correcting code -- and format choice should follow the weakest relay in the pipeline.

</details>


### [86] [Boltzmann MapReduce: A Partition-Function Reduce for Forkable Sandboxes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09689)
*Yossi Eliaz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Under LAN, confidence densities on data chunks are Gibbs-Boltzmann measures with inverse temperature equal to sample size. This yields three key results: (1) independent Boltzmann factors across chunks enable MapReduce reduce as a partition function; (2) the mode corresponds to precision-weighted pooling; (3) frequentist consistency emerges as the zero-temperature limit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To formalize the connection between distributed statistical inference (specifically MapReduce-style computation) and statistical thermodynamics, showing that confidence densities from data chunks combine multiplicatively as Boltzmann factors, with the reduce step naturally interpreted as computing a partition function.

Method: The paper invokes local asymptotic normality (LAN) to approximate the confidence density from a data chunk of size n as a Gibbs-Boltzmann measure exp{-β E(θ)} with β=n. It then analyzes the exact (Gaussian/linear) and first-order asymptotic consequences of this representation for distributed inference.

Result: Three consequences are derived: (1) disjoint chunks carry independent Boltzmann factors, so MapReduce's reduce step is a partition function Z = ∫ ∏_k h_k dθ; (2) the MAP estimate (mode of Z) gives precision-weighted (inverse-variance) pooling of chunk-level estimates; (3) frequentist consistency corresponds to the zero-temperature limit T = 1/n → 0.

Conclusion: The Boltzmann-Gibbs formalism provides a unifying thermodynamic lens for distributed inference: chunk-level confidence densities combine multiplicatively, the reduce step is a partition function, optimal pooling is precision-weighted, and consistency is a cooling/annealing limit.

Abstract: To leading order under local asymptotic normality (LAN), the confidence density a worker emits over a chunk of size $n$ is a Gibbs--Boltzmann measure $\exp\{-βE(θ)\}$ whose inverse temperature is the sample size, $β=n$. Three consequences are exact in the Gaussian/linear case and first-order otherwise: disjoint chunks carry independent Boltzmann factors, so the MapReduce \emph{reduce}, read literally, is a partition function $Z=\int\prod_k h_k\,dθ$ whose mode is precision-weighted (inverse-variance) pooling; frequentist consistency is the zero-temperature limit $T=1/n\to0$

</details>


### [87] [Interpreting Latent CoT Reasoning as Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09698)
*Sabari Iyyappan Duraipandian,Shreya Sanjay Boyane,Manju Nagesh,Jerome Francis,Archana Vaidheeswaran,Kevin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Latent reasoning methods maintain multiple superimposed candidate traces, posing interpretability challenges. This paper models latent token sequences as trajectories in representation space and applies dynamical systems analysis (step-to-step change, direction consistency, Lyapunov sensitivity, UMAP, DMD/PHATE) to reveal two distinct stability classes: CODI as a stable attractor and COCONUT as an unstable expanding system, with SIM-CoT tightening both without altering underlying dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing latent reasoning methods (CODI, COCONUT) suffer from a fundamental interpretability problem: they maintain multiple superimposed candidate traces in hidden space, unlike explicit chain-of-thought which follows a single transparent trace. Current mechanistic methods identify phenomena like compression and superposition but fail to explain how reasoning evolves across latent steps. This gap motivates a trajectory-based dynamical systems framework.

Method: The authors model latent token sequences as trajectories in representation space and apply dynamical systems analysis. Quantitative measures include step-to-step change magnitude, direction consistency, and Lyapunov sensitivity (measuring divergence). Qualitative projections use UMAP for dimensionality reduction and DMD/PHATE (Dynamic Mode Decomposition / Potential of Heat-diffusion for Affinity-based Trajectory Embedding) for visualizing trajectory structure and stability characteristics.

Result: Latent chain-of-thought exhibits structured, non-random dynamics falling into two distinct stability classes. CODI behaves as a stable attractor (convergent dynamics), while COCONUT behaves as an unstable expanding system (divergent dynamics). SIM-CoT supervision tightens both behaviors — making the attractor more convergent and the expanding system more controlled — without fundamentally altering the underlying dynamical regime of each method.

Conclusion: The proposed dynamical systems framework advances interpretability of latent CoT reasoning by revealing structured stability regimes, and offers actionable insights for designing and improving latent reasoning systems. Code and project page are publicly available.

Abstract: Recent latent reasoning methods, such as CODI and COCONUT, face a fundamental interpretability problem: they maintain multiple superimposed candidate traces in the hidden space at each step, unlike explicit- CoT, which follows a single transparent reasoning trace. Existing mechanistic methods show compression, shortcuts, and superposition without explaining how reasoning evolves across latent steps. To address this gap, we model latent token sequences as trajectories in representation space and apply dynamical systems analysis to characterize the evolution of reasoning. Using quantitative measures, such as step-to-step change, direction consistency, and Lyapunov sensitivity, alongside qualitative projections, such as UMAP and DMD/PHATE, we show that latent CoT exhibits structured, non-random dynamics with two distinct stability classes. CODI behaves as a stable attractor, while COCONUT behaves as an unstable expanding system, and SIM-CoT supervision tightens both behaviors without changing the underlying dynamics. This framework advances the interpretability of latent CoT reasoning dynamics and provides actionable insights for improving latent reasoning performance. Code1 and Project page2 available online.

</details>


### [88] [YUKTI: From Natural-Language Situations to Robust, Verifiable Decisions An Uncertainty-Typed Proposition IR, Assumption-Robust Pareto Frontiers, and a Regret Certificate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09706)
*Suyash Mishra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: YUKTI introduces a robust autoformulation framework that replaces fragile point-estimate optimization with a typed-proposition graph carrying coefficient uncertainty, uses Assumption-Robust Pareto Frontiers (ARPF) to score decision survival under resampled assumptions, and demonstrates dramatic regret reduction against naive point plans and LLM-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NL4Opt pipelines (NL4Opt, OptiMUS, ORLM, OR-LLM-Agent) commit to a single objective with point-valued coefficients and solve once. For real-world resource allocation (budgets, clinical attention, effort), this is a failure mode: every number is an assumption, and plans optimal only under exact guesses are brittle mimicry of computation. The authors argue that confidence in point estimates is the fundamental weakness.

Method: YUKTI represents autoformulation as a typed-proposition graph where relationships carry shape priors, coefficient uncertainty, and provenance. It routes each stage to an exact, nonlinear, or evolutionary solver and couples stages via a distributional Pareto hand-off. The core innovation is Assumption-Robust Pareto Frontiers (ARPF), which resample assumptions (including structural epsilon-contamination) to compute rho — the frequency with which each action survives. A bound is proved making rho an exact factor of decision regret. The framework also provides auditable traceability and synthesizes benchmark data (SRJANA) when none exists.

Result: Under controlled misspecification, YUKTI's robust compromise cuts mean and tail regret by over 90% versus a naive point plan. On a regulated commercial decision, it optimizes within a lawful action space and prices downside in euros. On a real public dataset of 41,188 decisions, out-of-sample backtesting beats the logged status quo by 34% and a naive point rule by 4%, while reducing the optimizer's curse. A head-to-head comparison shows an LLM given correct numbers plus single-objective optimization incurs approximately 47x the held-out regret of YUKTI.

Conclusion: LLMs are formulators, not solvers. Under long-range causal coupling, the forward distributional Pareto hand-off becomes unsound and must be replaced by a backward-induction causal policy. YUKTI claims no benchmark-SOTA win on standard solvers; its contribution is in robust formulation architecture that dramatically reduces decision regret under uncertainty.

Abstract: Language models turn a worded situation into a numeric plan, and the dominant pipelines (NL4Opt, OptiMUS, ORLM, OR-LLM-Agent) commit to a single objective and point-valued coefficients, then solve once. For decisions that allocate real budget, effort, or clinical attention, that confidence is the failure mode: every objectified number is an assumption, and a plan optimal only if the guesses are exactly right is fragile -- mimicry of computation. YUKTI changes the target of autoformulation. Its representation is a typed-proposition graph whose relationships carry shape priors, coefficient uncertainty, and provenance. YUKTI routes each stage to an exact, nonlinear, or evolutionary solver; couples stages by a distributional Pareto hand-off; and introduces Assumption-Robust Pareto Frontiers (ARPF), resampling assumptions (including structural epsilon-contamination) to score how often each action survives (rho). We prove a bound making rho an exact factor of decision regret, add auditable traceability, and synthesize a benchmark-faithful data foundation when none exists (SRJANA). We validate three ways: under controlled misspecification the robust compromise cuts mean and tail regret by over 90% versus a naive point plan; on a regulated commercial decision we optimize inside a lawful action space and price the downside in euros; and on a real public dataset of 41,188 decisions an out-of-sample backtest beats the logged status quo by 34% and a naive point rule by 4% while reducing the optimizer's curse. The solvers are standard; we claim no benchmark-SOTA win. A head-to-head shows an LLM given the correct numbers, and single-objective optimization, both incur about 47x the held-out regret of YUKTI -- an LLM is a formulator, not a solver. Under long-range causal coupling, the forward hand-off becomes unsound, locating where it must become a backward-induction causal policy.

</details>


### [89] [GES-TSP: Graph Edge Sparsification for TSP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09708)
*Tianfeng Chen,Xianyue Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Graph Edge Sparsification (GES), a learning-based method that adaptively prunes edges in Euclidean TSP graphs. Achieves up to 95% edge reduction on MATILDA and 99% on TSPLIB, while maintaining optimality gap below 1%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exact large-scale TSP solving is computationally prohibitive. Existing graph sparsification heuristics are fixed and fail to exploit instance-specific structural information, limiting their effectiveness across diverse problem instances.

Method: GES, a learning-based sparsification framework that incorporates geometric structural information and combinatorial optimization techniques to adaptively generate sparse graphs tailored to each TSP instance.

Result: On MATILDA dataset: up to 95% edge pruning with solution gap within 1% of optimal. On TSPLIB benchmark: pruning rate exceeds 99% on some large-scale instances while optimality gap remains below 1%, demonstrating strong generalization.

Conclusion: Learning-based adaptive sparsification significantly outperforms fixed heuristics, enabling substantial graph size reduction without meaningful compromise in solution quality, and generalizes well to unseen benchmark instances.

Abstract: Solving large-scale instances of the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) exactly is computationally expensive. Researchers often employ graph sparsification methods to improve computational efficiency. Traditional sparsification methods typically rely on fixed heuristics and fail to fully exploit instance-specific structural information. In this paper, we propose Graph Edge Sparsification (GES), a learning-based sparsification approach for Euclidean TSP. By incorporating geometric structural information and combinatorial optimization technology, our proposed method adaptively generates a sparsification graph for different instances, significantly reducing the graph size and accelerating the solving process. Experimental results demonstrate that our sparsification method can prune up to 95% of edges on the MATILDA dataset, while keeping the solution gap within 1% of the optimal value. Moreover, our approach exhibits strong generalization capability on the TSPLIB benchmark.In some large-scale instances, the pruning rate exceeds 99%, while the optimality gap remains below 1%.

</details>


### [90] [The Verifier is the Curriculum: Execution-Gated Self-Distillation for Cross-Family Game Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09709)
*Chenyu Zhou,Qiliang Jiang,Shuning Wu,Xu Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A deterministic, ungameable filter — whether generated code cleanly launches in a headless engine — enables rejection-sampling self-distillation that dramatically improves out-of-family generalization. On the GameCraft-Bench (NL-to-Godot-project), a 14B model distilled under "strict-launch" filtering raises clean generation from 8.8% to 42.2% and achieves the gold ceiling (25/25 best-of-K), with gains attributable to verifier precision, not data volume.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training code generators with learned reward models can be gamed through proxy feature optimization that inflates scores without improving actual artifact quality. The authors seek an ungameable, deterministic training signal and hypothesize that a strict binary filter — whether a project launches cleanly without errors — can serve as a robust verifier for self-distillation, driving genuine functional improvement rather than score hacking.

Method: The authors define a "strict-launch" gate: a headless engine check that deterministically verifies whether a generated Godot project launches without errors. They apply rejection-sampling self-distillation, where a base model (Qwen3-14B+LoRA) generates candidates, only strict-launch-passing samples are retained, and the model is fine-tuned on those filtered samples. This loop runs for three rounds. Ablations include: (1) a gold-duplication control (matched data volume, no filtering), (2) a decomposition analysis separating quality vs. quantity effects, and (3) swapping the strict-launch gate with a lenient BUILD check (99.9% pass rate) to isolate verifier precision. Evaluation uses GameCraft-Bench across four unseen game families.

Result: Strict-launch distillation raises per-candidate clean generation from 8.8% to 42.2% and best-of-K coverage from 18/25 to 25/25 (gold ceiling) over three rounds, with each round showing significant gains (p=0.0019, p<1e-4, p<1e-4). The gold-duplication control regresses to 5.6% (below base, p=0.019). The round-1-to-2 gain decomposes into quality (+8.8pp) and quantity (+8.5pp) channels. Swapping to the lenient BUILD filter erases all gains (back to base, p=1e-3 vs. launch-gated). A second ungameable metric, headless execution grounding, rises monotonically and yields more grounded candidates than gold-duplication at matched budget (16 vs. 5).

Conclusion: The verifier is the curriculum: what it certifies is what the model learns. A precise, ungameable, deterministic filter (strict-launch) enables effective rejection-sampling self-distillation that compounds out-of-family generalization, while imprecise or absent filtering fails. Game generation serves as a verifiable testbed for this principle.

Abstract: Post-training a code generator against a learned judge can optimize proxy features that raise the score without improving the artifact. We study the opposite signal: a deterministic, judge-free, ungameable filter -- whether a generated project launches cleanly under a headless engine (strict-launch). Under this gate, rejection-sampling self-distillation compounds out-of-family generalization. On GameCraft-Bench (mapping a natural-language brief to a complete Godot project), a 14B model (Qwen3-14B+LoRA) distilled under strict-launch raises clean generation on four unseen game families from 8.8% to 42.2% per-candidate and best-of-K coverage from 18/25 to 25/25 (the gold ceiling) over three rounds, each a significant gain (p=0.0019, p<1e-4, p<1e-4). The gain is not from merely adding data: an exactly-matched gold-duplication control regresses below the base model (5.6% vs. 8.8%, p=0.019), while a count-matched decomposition splits the round-1-to-2 jump into comparable quality (+8.8pp) and quantity (+8.5pp) channels. Most directly, rerunning the loop with only the filter swapped -- the lenient BUILD check, which passes 99.9% of generations, in place of the launch gate -- erases the gain entirely (back to base, p=1e-3 vs. the launch-gated round), isolating verifier precision rather than the optimizer. A second ungameable signal, headless execution grounding, rises monotonically across rounds and yields far more grounded candidates than gold-duplication at a matched budget (16 vs. 5), confirming the gains are functional, not launch-but-empty. Game generation is a verifiable testbed for one lesson: the verifier is the curriculum -- what it certifies is what the model learns.

</details>


### [91] [Closed-Loop Control with Rule-Aligned Small Language Models and Multi-Agent Self-Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09713)
*Yuchen Wang,Javal Vyas,Tong Liu,Mehmet Mercangoz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A compact 1.5B SLM fine-tuned with GRPO, paired with a digital-twin validator and iterative reprompting, achieves 91.5% action-alignment accuracy for control reasoning from natural language specifications, enabling reconfigurable autonomous control at the edge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large cloud-based models are too slow, opaque, and data-sensitive for edge closed-loop industrial control. There is a need for a practical, low-latency, compact solution that can generate control policies from natural-language requirements and be validated before execution.

Method: A Qwen2.5-1.5B Small Language Model is aligned via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and embedded in a three-component loop: (i) an action agent for candidate generation, (ii) a symbolic/digital-twin validation layer for checking actions, and (iii) a reprompting agent that iteratively corrects outputs toward validity. Evaluated on randomized thermal-control simulations (30 experiments × 500 steps).

Result: The framework achieves 91.5% average action-alignment accuracy (range: 86.3%–100%) with 3.84 s mean inference latency. Under symbolic re-mapping, it maintains a 95% in-range rate, demonstrating robust physical regulation despite reduced token-level agreement.

Conclusion: SLM+validator architectures are a practical, deployable path toward reconfigurable autonomous control at the edge, balancing inference latency, accuracy, and physical safety through iterative validation-guided correction.

Abstract: A key step toward autonomous industrial operation is the ability to create and reconfigure control policies from natural-language requirement specifications, with minimal or no manual redesign. In this setting, policy generation by AI agents can be a credible path when paired with a plant-aware validator (e.g., a digital twin) that can check generated candidate actions before execution. However, practical deployment is constrained by inference latency and compute footprint: large cloud-based models are often too slow, opaque, or data-sensitive for edge closed-loop use. This work investigates whether a compact Small Language Model (SLM) can be retrained for control reasoning and embedded in a validator-guided correction loop. We use a Qwen2.5-1.5B model aligned via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), combined with (i) an action agent, (ii) a symbolic/digital-twin-style validation layer, and (iii) a reprompting agent that iteratively steers outputs toward valid actions. In randomized thermal-control simulations (30 experiments with 500 steps each), the framework achieves 91.5% average action-alignment accuracy (86.3%--100% across cases) at 3.84\,s mean inference latency. Under symbolic re-mapping, it maintains a 95% in-range rate, indicating robust physical regulation despite reduced token-level agreement. These results support SLM+validator architectures as a practical path toward reconfigurable autonomous control at the edge.

</details>


### [92] [Feedback-Coupled Memory Systems in Continuous Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09714)
*Stefano Grassi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper instantiates the axiomatic FCMS architecture by defining its two undefined operators using MBI (agent update) and CMGP (environment update), yielding a continuous-time system with a provable Lyapunov dissipativity threshold (4β² < 2ημγ²) that generalizes prior discrete and physical stability conditions, validated numerically from N=2 to N=10⁶.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The original FCMS architecture leaves the agent update operator f_i and environmental update operator Ψ axiomatically undefined, limiting its applicability. A concrete, principled instantiation is needed to enable rigorous stability analysis and to unify coordination dynamics across discrete and continuous settings.

Method: f_i is defined via Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), employing a decentralized price mechanism and economic principles for local agent updates. Ψ is defined via the Coupled Memory Graph Process (CMGP), treating the environment as a non-Markovian physical substrate that coherently records and responds to trajectory history. These are integrated into a continuous-time FCMS, and Lyapunov analysis is used to derive the global dissipativity threshold. Numerical simulations (N=2 and mean-field N=10⁶) validate the threshold and emergent coordination cascades.

Result: A continuous-time FCMS instantiation achieves Lyapunov global dissipativity governed by 4β² < 2ημγ². This threshold generalizes the discrete FCMS condition (4ηβ² < γ) and CMGP's physical bifurcation threshold (α_c = 1/K). Simulations confirm the stability threshold and reveal a self-reinforcing coordination cascade when the threshold is violated.

Conclusion: Memory dissipation must outpace feedback gain as a universal organizing principle for closed-loop coordination systems. The unified framework bridges discrete and continuous regimes, with the derived threshold serving as a computable stability criterion validated across scales.

Abstract: The Feedback-Coupled Memory Systems (FCMS) architecture formalizes closed-loop coordination through four abstract operators, two of which - the agent update operator $f_i$ and the environmental update operator $Ψ$ - are left axiomatically undefined in the original framework. To address this, $f_i$ is defined by Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), where agents update locally through a decentralized price mechanism and economic principles, and $Ψ$ is defined by the Coupled Memory Graph Process (CMGP), a non-Markovian framework where the environment is treated as a physical substrate that records and responds to trajectory history coherently without external forcing. The resulting continuous-time FCMS instantiation achieves Lyapunov global dissipativity governed by the computable threshold $4β^2 < 2ημγ^2$. This generalizes both the discrete FCMS stability condition $4ηβ^2 < γ$ and CMGP's physical bifurcation threshold $α_c = 1/K$, confirming that memory dissipation must outpace feedback gain as a universal organizing principle. Numerical simulation with $N=2$ agents and mean-field validation at $N=10^6$ confirm the stability threshold and the self-reinforcing coordination cascade that emerges when it is violated.

</details>
