Compression sharply cuts reasoning tokens, preserves most multiple-choice accuracy, and leaves hint influence near baseline. At the strongest target, lower-bound faithfulness falls to 63.1% of baseline for Qwen3-14B and 69.4% for Qwen3-4B; the raw rate at which a monitor catches hint use falls from 69% to 49% and from 60% to 48%. To separate length from content, we randomly delete sentences from uncompressed baseline chains until the remaining text matches the compressed length. Even after this length matching, compressed chains disclose the hint 7-35 percentage points less often than baseline chains that we shorten at random, for both Qwen3 sizes and all five evaluation distributions. Compression therefore does more than shorten reasoning, preferentially removing the cues a monitor needs to see what influenced the answer. Together, these results reveal a compression-monitorability frontier in which cheaper reasoning can preserve answers while making the influences behind them harder to detect.

</details>


### [115] [Toward Contemplative LLM: A Modular Framework for Evaluating and Enhancing LLM Alignment in Mental Health](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10871)
*Asher Sprigler,Yang-Yang Feng,Iftach Amir,Jonathan E. Bogard,Todd S Braver,Yi Ding,David Kinney,Yixue Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a modular, extensible evaluation framework for systematically assessing how contemplative principles (mindfulness, compassion, non-dual reasoning) improve LLM alignment, initially targeting mental health but designed to be domain-agnostic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to evaluating contemplative principles for LLM alignment are ad hoc, fail to generalize across rapidly emerging models, metrics, and benchmarks, and lack systematic cross-evaluation capabilities. Additionally, domain experts without technical expertise cannot easily define and test alignment criteria.

Method: A modular, extensible evaluation framework with a reusable pipeline supporting plug-and-play integration of new models, metrics, and benchmarks. It features a prompting module that allows domain experts to incorporate ethical perspectives (e.g., contemplative principles) without technical expertise. The framework supports flexible mixing and matching of components for systematic cross-evaluation.

Result: The framework successfully reproduces existing state-of-the-art results and enables systematic cross-evaluation through flexible combination of models, metrics, and benchmarks, facilitating fair comparison and deeper insight into the effects of contemplative principles on LLM alignment.

Conclusion: This work bridges computational evaluation with human-centered ethical reasoning, laying groundwork for interdisciplinary research across cognitive science, behavioral economics, philosophy, and system design toward robust, trustworthy, and socially beneficial human-AI ecosystems.

Abstract: Contemplative traditions have long guided ethical behavior and prosocial interaction, and recent work suggests that contemplative principles (e.g., mindfulness, compassion, non-dual reasoning) may offer a promising paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs), improving cooperation and reducing ethical violations in LLM outputs. However, as new models, evaluation metrics, and benchmarks emerge rapidly, it remains challenging to systematically assess whether and how contemplative principles enhance LLM alignment across diverse and evolving scenarios, and existing approaches are often ad hoc and fail to generalize. We present a modular, extensible evaluation framework, initially targeted at the mental health domain, that enables seamless integration of new models, metrics, and benchmarks through a reusable pipeline. The framework currently reproduces existing state-of-the-art results and supports systematic cross-evaluation by flexibly mixing and matching models, metrics, and benchmarks, enabling fair comparison and deeper insight. Its plug-and-play prompting module offers a principled pathway for incorporating ethical perspectives such as contemplative principles, allowing domain experts to define alignment criteria without requiring technical expertise. Although initially focused on mental health, the framework is domain-agnostic and extends naturally to areas such as decision-making, moral reasoning, and human-AI collaboration. By bridging computational evaluation with human-centered ethical reasoning, this work lays the groundwork for interdisciplinary research spanning cognitive science, behavioral economics, philosophy, and system design, toward robust, trustworthy, and socially beneficial human-AI ecosystems.

</details>


### [116] [PHITSBench: an execution-scored benchmark for AI-assisted PHITS radiation-transport input generation using natural language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09789)
*Xianglin Ji,Svetlana V. Boriskina*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PHITSBench is an execution-scored benchmark with 282 tasks for evaluating LLMs on Monte Carlo radiation transport code (PHITS). GPT-5.4-based agents achieve 95% on editing, 70% on repair, but 0% on generation from scratch. Adding a structured knowledge catalog boosts generation to 57%, and agentic workflows reach 66-73%, with remaining errors stemming from physics configuration rather than syntax.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks for code generation focus on general-purpose programming languages, lacking domain-specific evaluation for scientific simulation codes. There is no execution-scored benchmark for Monte Carlo radiation transport codes like PHITS, making it difficult to assess whether LLMs can reliably assist in nuclear/radiation physics modeling tasks.

Method: The authors introduce PHITSBench with 282 tasks across three categories: Edit (parameter modification), Repair (syntax fixing), and Reproduce (full generation from natural-language descriptions). Each task is scored via a Composite Metric Score combining execution success and agreement between generated and reference transport observables (e.g., tally results). Five GPT-5.4 configurations are tested: zero-shot, knowledge-augmented (using a structured machine-readable PHITS knowledge catalog + user manual), and agentic workflows with iterative execution feedback.

Result: Zero-shot GPT-5.4 achieves 95% success on Edit and 70% on Repair but 0% on Reproduce. Adding the structured PHITS knowledge catalog raises Reproduce success to 57% in single-shot mode. Agentic execution further improves Reproduce to 66–73% at higher computational cost. Failure analysis reveals remaining errors are dominated by incorrect selection and configuration of physical observables (e.g., tally types, energy binning) rather than syntax errors.

Conclusion: LLMs show strong capability on structured editing and repair of PHITS input files but struggle with physics-aware simulation generation from scratch. Progress depends not only on larger models but critically on machine-readable domain knowledge bases, curated training datasets, and execution-grounded evaluation environments.

Abstract: We introduce PHITSBench, an execution-scored benchmark for the Monte Carlo Particle and Heavy Ion Transport code System (PHITS). PHITSBench comprises 282 transport-scorable tasks spanning three common workflow categories: parameter editing (Edit), syntax repair (Repair ), and complete simulation generation from natural-language descriptions (Reproduce). Each task is evaluated using a Composite Metric Score that combines execution success with agreement between generated and reference transport observables. Using PHITSBench, we evaluate five GPT-5.4-based configurations ranging from zero-shot prompting to knowledge-augmented and agentic workflows. Without domain-specific knowledge, the model performs well on editing and repair tasks (95% and 70% success, respectively) but fails to generate correct simulations from scratch (0% success on the Reproduce track). A structured, machine-readable PHITS knowledge catalog, supplied alongside the user manual, raises single-shot Reproduce-task success to 57%. Agentic execution provides a further improvement to 66-73%, but at increased computational cost. Failure analysis shows that the remaining errors are dominated by incorrect selection and configuration of physical observables rather than syntax generation. These results suggest that future progress in AI-assisted radiation-transport modeling will depend as much on machine-readable knowledge bases, curated domain-training datasets, and execution-grounded evaluation environments as on advances in foundation models themselves.

</details>


### [117] [Semantic Drift and the Stability of Operator Control in Reasoning-Class Decision Support Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09790)
*M. L. Kaluzhsky,V. A. Efirov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates stability of operator control in hybrid human-machine decision support systems (DSS). Through a two-month longitudinal experiment involving joint monograph design, the authors discovered and characterized semantic context drift in Reasoning LLMs. They propose a mathematical interaction model with a novel metric — the operator control stability coefficient — which accounts for nonlinear contextual pressure from hidden reasoning chains. A critical inversion point of control functions is identified within the cognitome paradigm, and engineering recommendations are offered for dynamic relational arbitration loops using a modified hierarchical similarity model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Next-generation hybrid human-machine DSS face a fundamental challenge: preserving stable operator control and goal-targeting when deep logical reasoning models (Reasoning LLMs) introduce opaque, nonlinear reasoning chains that can subtly shift semantic context. The motivation is to identify, model, and mitigate the phenomenon of semantic context drift that undermines operator authority and system reliability.

Method: A two-month continuous longitudinal experiment was conducted involving joint human-machine design of a monograph-format textual array. This empirical setup was used to verify and characterize the latent phenomenon of semantic context drift. A mathematical model of human-machine interface interaction was developed, introducing the operator control stability coefficient as an original metric that captures nonlinear contextual pressure from hidden reasoning chains. Analysis was grounded in the cognitome theory paradigm to identify critical inversion points of control functions.

Result: The experiment verified the existence of semantic context drift in Reasoning LLMs. The proposed mathematical model successfully captures interaction dynamics, and the operator control stability coefficient provides a quantifiable measure of control degradation under nonlinear contextual pressure. A critical inversion point was identified where control functions flip — the machine's hidden reasoning begins to dominate operator intent. Engineering recommendations for dynamic relational arbitration loops based on a modified hierarchical similarity model were formulated to counteract this drift.

Conclusion: Semantic context drift is a real and measurable phenomenon in hybrid DSS powered by Reasoning LLMs, posing a genuine threat to operator control stability. The proposed control stability coefficient and the cognitome-based inversion point analysis offer both diagnostic and prescriptive tools. Implementing dynamic relational arbitration loops with hierarchical similarity modeling provides a viable engineering pathway to preserve goal-targeting and maintain meaningful human oversight in next-generation decision support systems.

Abstract: The article investigates the fundamental problem of ensuring the stability of operator control and preserving goal-targeting in hybrid human-machine decision support systems (DSS) of a new generation. Based on a two-month continuous longitudinal experiment on the joint design of a monograph-format textual array, the latent phenomenon of semantic context drift in large language models of deep logical reasoning (Reasoning LLMs) is verified and described. A mathematical model of interaction in the human-machine interface is proposed, and an original metric is introduced - the operator control stability coefficient, which takes into account the non-linear contextual pressure of hidden reasoning chains. Within the paradigm of the cognitome theory, a critical point of control functions inversion is captured. Engineering recommendations are formulated for implementing dynamic relational arbitration loops based on a modified hierarchical similarity model.

</details>


### [118] [Playful AI in Professional Email: A Field Experiment on Tone and Recipient Engagement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11749)
*Ziv Ben-Zion,Teddy Lazebnik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A randomized field experiment found that GPT-5 rewriting of work emails alters emotional tone but does not directly affect recipient behavior (open/reply rates). Instead, emotional positivity itself strongly predicts engagement, revealing an indirect-only pathway: AI shapes behavior solely through the linguistic tone it produces, not through the mere fact of AI assistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for workplace communication, yet no causal evidence exists on whether AI-assisted writing actually changes recipient behavior, and if so, through what mechanism (e.g., signaling AI use vs. altering linguistic features like emotional tone).

Method: A three-week randomized crossover field experiment with 121 employees across six companies. Participants sent work emails under three within-subject conditions: unaided writing, GPT-5 rewriting in a playful tone, and GPT-5 rewriting in a professional tone. The experiment analyzed 16,880 emails, measuring emotional positivity, open rates, reply rates, and response times. Mediation analysis tested direct and indirect (via emotional tone) effects.

Result: Playful editing significantly increased emotional positivity (B=+0.068, p<0.001); professional editing significantly decreased it (B=-0.041, p<0.001). Neither condition directly altered open rates, reply rates, or response times. However, within-sender positivity strongly predicted both opening (OR=2.05) and replying (OR=3.32, p<0.001), constituting a significant indirect-only mediation pathway.

Conclusion: AI-assisted communication shapes workplace engagement not through the act of using AI, but through the emotional tone of the language it generates. This suggests that the linguistic output, rather than the technology itself, is the mechanism driving behavioral change.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly reshaping workplace communication, yet whether AI-assisted writing changes how recipients actually behave, and through what channel, remains unknown. Here, in a randomized crossover field experiment, 121 employees across six companies sent work emails under three conditions over three weeks: unaided writing, GPT-5 rewriting in a playful tone, and GPT-5 rewriting in a professional tone. Across 16,880 emails, playful editing increased emotional positivity (B=+0.068, p<0.001), and professional editing decreased it (B=-0.041, p<0.001), yet neither condition directly altered open rates, reply rates, or response times. Instead, within-sender positivity strongly predicted both opening (OR=2.05) and replying (OR=3.32, p<0.001), a significant indirect pathway through which AI editing shaped behavior, in the absence of any direct effect. These findings suggest that AI-assisted communication shapes workplace engagement not through its use, but through the emotional tone of the language it produces.

</details>


### [119] [GRASP: GRanularity-Aware Search Policy for Agentic RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10463)
*Varun Gandhi,Jaewook Lee,Shantanu Todmal,Franck Dernoncourt,Ryan Rossi,Zichao Wang,Andrew Lan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRASP is an RL framework that trains agents to adaptively coordinate semantic search, keyword search, and paragraph-reading actions during multi-hop reasoning, jointly optimizing for answer accuracy, grounded reading, complementary search, and turn efficiency. It outperforms static RAG, prompting-based agentic RAG, and RL-based baselines on multi-hop QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic RAG systems struggle with three key decisions: when to retrieve, whether to use lexical vs. semantic retrieval, and how to control context granularity. Irrelevant tokens from poorly chosen retrieval strategies can interfere with agent reasoning, and no prior work addresses adaptive coordination of complementary retrieval tools within a unified RL framework.

Method: GRASP frames multi-step retrieval-augmented reasoning as an RL problem. The agent has three actions: semantic search (dense retrieval for broad exploration), keyword search (sparse/lexical retrieval for entity-specific evidence), and paragraph reading (expanding sentence-level evidence to local context only when needed). The reward function jointly optimizes four objectives: answer accuracy, grounded reading (evidence must support the answer), complementary search (encouraging diverse tool use), and turn efficiency (penalizing unnecessary retrieval steps). The policy is trained via RL on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks.

Result: GRASP improves both retrieval recall and downstream QA performance compared to single-step retrieval, prompting-based agentic RAG, and RL-based retrieval baselines on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks. Qualitatively, the learned policy exhibits interpretable skimming and scanning behavior: semantic search for broad exploration, paragraph reading for local verification, and keyword search for entity-specific evidence.

Conclusion: Learning to coordinate complementary retrieval signals and adaptively control context granularity is critical for correct agent reasoning in multi-hop settings. GRASP demonstrates that RL can effectively train agents to make these nuanced retrieval decisions.

Abstract: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) extends static RAG by allowing language models to iteratively reason, generate search queries, retrieve evidence, and predict answers. However, it remains challenging for models to decide when to retrieve, whether to use lexical matching or semantic similarity, and how to control context granularity to prevent irrelevant tokens from interfering with agent reasoning. In this paper, we introduce GRASP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for training agents to adaptively coordinate complementary retrieval tools during multi-step reasoning. GRASP provides the agent with semantic search, keyword search, and paragraph-reading actions, enabling it to retrieve sentence-level evidence and expand further context only when needed. We train the policy with a reward that jointly accounts for answer accuracy, grounded reading, complementary search, and turn efficiency. Experiments on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks show that GRASP improves both retrieval recall and downstream question answering performance compared with single-step retrieval, prompting-based agentic RAG, and RL-based retrieval baselines. Qualitative and ablation analyses show that the learned policy develops interpretable skimming and scanning behavior: it uses semantic search for broad exploration, paragraph reading for local verification, and keyword search for entity-specific evidence. These results suggest that learning to coordinate retrieval signals and context granularity is critical for agent's correct reasoning.

</details>


### [120] [TopoExplore: Topological Discrimination for Archive-Based Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09971)
*Jason Carlson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TopoExplore enhances Go-Explore by adding topological void detection: it identifies enclosed unexplored regions via flood fill on the occupancy grid's cubical complex, applies a decaying bonus only to strict entrance cells (gaps/doors), avoids sealed regions, and retires entered regions—achieving significant speedups over both Go-Explore and frontier baselines, especially in environments with doors and decoy structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing archive-based exploration (Go-Explore) uses visitation rarity and frontier methods return to the unknown boundary, but neither checks whether regions behind boundaries are actually enterable. Exploration should collect structurally complete experience for downstream learning, not just find reward. The authors aim to discriminate between accessible and inaccessible unexplored regions to avoid wasting exploration effort on sealed/decoy structures.

Method: TopoExplore augments Go-Explore cell selection with a periodic topological pass: (1) flood fill on the visited-set occupancy grid detects enclosed unexplored regions (voids) as H1 classes of the cubical complex; (2) a decaying selection bonus is placed only on strict entrance cells (gap or door cells) bordering these voids; (3) sealed regions with no entrance are never targeted; (4) regions that become entered have their bonus retired. The approach operates without requiring privileged wall knowledge.

Result: On 18 MiniGrid environments (15 seeds, frozen hyperparameters), TopoExplore achieves 1.52x geometric-mean speedup in median steps-to-first-entry over Go-Explore vs. 1.37x for frontier baseline. On decoy environments, frontier degrades to 0.83-1.48x while TopoExplore holds 1.65-2.11x. On hard multi-interaction doors, TopoExplore achieves 10.9x speedup. On Montezuma's Revenge (negative result), unreachable occupancy artifacts capture the bonus and degrade performance without wall knowledge. On HM3D scanned buildings (preliminary positive), speedup over Go-Explore correlates with scene difficulty (r=0.69).

Conclusion: Topology-aware selection pays off when enclosed structure must be discriminated from decoys, and remains competitive at open coverage where frontier methods excel, despite not being tuned for that regime. The wall-aware entrance test is identified as the critical load-bearing component, with honest reporting of failure modes on Montezuma's Revenge.

Abstract: Archive-based exploration methods such as Go-Explore select which visited state to return to using visitation rarity, and frontier methods return to the boundary of the unknown; neither asks whether the unexplored region behind a boundary is enterable at all. Exploration is not just about finding reward - it is about collecting a structurally complete experience for downstream learning and planning. We introduce TopoExplore, which augments Go-Explore cell selection with a periodic topological pass: enclosed unexplored regions (voids) of the visited-set occupancy grid are detected by flood fill (the H1 classes of its cubical complex), and a decaying selection bonus is placed only on their strict entrances (gap or door cells), so sealed regions are never targeted and entered regions retire. On a controlled 18-environment MiniGrid suite (15 seeds, frozen hyperparameters) TopoExplore attains a 1.52x geometric-mean speedup in median steps-to-first-entry over its exact Go-Explore ablation, versus 1.37x for a frontier baseline; frontier exploration degrades when sealed decoy structure appears (0.83-1.48x on decoy environments vs. 1.65-2.11x for TopoExplore), while TopoExplore holds its largest win on hard multi-interaction doors (10.9x). We report an honest negative on Montezuma's Revenge - without wall knowledge, unreachable occupancy artifacts capture the bonus and performance degrades as it grows, isolating the wall-aware entrance test as the load-bearing component - and a preliminary positive on HM3D scanned buildings, where the speedup over Go-Explore tracks scene difficulty (r=0.69) even as frontier selection dominates blanket coverage. The evidence supports a deliberately scoped claim: topology-aware selection pays off where enclosed structure must be discriminated, and remains competitive at open coverage, where frontier methods are strongest, despite not being tuned for that regime.

</details>


### [121] [A Symbolic Neural CPU for Quantization-Simulated Writeback and Interpretable Program Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10021)
*Jose Luis Lima de Jesus Silva*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a trace-supervised symbolic neural CPU that makes internal state transitions visible during learned program execution. By combining recurrent control, an explicit operation router over a fixed ALU bank, and complete trajectory supervision, the architecture achieves exact reproduction of reference execution and preserves symbolic operation paths even under 8-bit quantization, establishing a verifiable framework for interpretable neural execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural networks can learn algorithmic input-output mappings, but relying on a learned executor requires more than just correct final answers — the hidden internal state transitions undermine trust. The authors aim to make these transitions fully inspectable and verifiable.

Method: The authors introduce a factorized learned execution architecture featuring: (1) recurrent control with an explicit operation router over a fixed differentiable ALU bank, (2) destination-masked register writeback, (3) complete trajectory supervision, and (4) matched fixed-point replay. The model exposes selected operations, source/destination registers, register trajectory, memory signals, and writeback semantics at every step. Controller variants include recurrent, Transformer, temporal-convolution, temporal graph-inspired, and state-space models. Extensions include ValueMemory, hybrid adaptive LIF controllers, candidate-constrained symbolic control via behavior cloning and actor-critic RL, and an RV32I base-integer semantic bridge.

Result: On the 16-wide benchmark, the non-quantized executor reproduces reference execution exactly. The 8-bit quantization-simulated executor preserves the symbolic operation path through programs of 1,000 instructions. Matched fixed-point replay eliminates residual numerical drift, indicating the drift stems from continuous vs. low-precision reference mismatch rather than execution failure. Operation-gate supervision proves necessary for an inspectable execution path. Hidden-opcode memory-pressure tasks reveal remaining limits in delayed state use and temporal binding.

Conclusion: The results establish a trace-verifiable framework for interpretable, low-precision, and controllable neural execution, demonstrating that learned executors can be made fully inspectable with the right architectural and supervisory choices.

Abstract: Neural networks can learn algorithmic input-output mappings, but trusting a learned executor requires more than a correct final answer because the state transitions that produce it are usually hidden. To make those transitions visible, we introduce a trace-supervised symbolic neural CPU, a factorized learned execution architecture that combines recurrent control, an explicit operation router over a fixed differentiable arithmetic-logic unit bank, destination-masked register writeback, complete trajectory supervision and matched fixed-point replay. The model exposes the selected operation, source and destination registers, register trajectory, memory signals and writeback semantics at every step. On the principal 16-wide benchmark, the non-quantized executor reproduces reference execution exactly, while the eight-bit quantization-simulated executor preserves the symbolic operation path through programs of 1,000 instructions. When the same execution is evaluated against a matched fixed-point replay, the residual numerical drift disappears, showing that it comes from a mismatch between continuous and low-precision reference semantics rather than from execution failure. We compare recurrent, Transformer, temporal-convolution, temporal graph-inspired and state-space controllers, and the ablations show that operation-gate supervision is necessary for an inspectable execution path. Hidden-opcode memory-pressure tasks expose the remaining limits in delayed state use and temporal binding. We also extend the interface with ValueMemory, hybrid adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire controllers, candidate-constrained symbolic control trained through behaviour cloning and actor-critic reinforcement learning, and an RV32I base-integer semantic bridge. Together, these results establish a trace-verifiable framework for interpretable, low-precision and controllable neural execution.

</details>


### [122] [AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10059)
*Xun Liu,Yi Evie Zhang,Vira Kasprova,Parisa Rabbani,Pardis Sadat Zahraei,Tianyu Zhang,Ali Ebrahimpour-Boroojeny,Varun Chandrasekaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentAbstain introduces the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention—the ability of LLM-based agents to recognize when not to act. Using a benchmark of 263 paired tasks across 8 abstention scenarios, the authors find that the best model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy, and abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent evaluations focus on task success but ignore whether agents can recognize situations where they should abstain from acting. Under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended, irreversible actions. This gap poses real safety risks for autonomous deployment.

Method: The authors propose AgentAbstain, a paired-task benchmark with an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios spanning pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It includes 263 paired tasks in 42 sandbox environments, where each pair has a should-act task and a should-abstain variant created via controlled perturbation of instructions, tools, or environment state. To scale generation and resist contamination, they introduce AbstainGen, an automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges. Three independent annotators rate 94–98% of sampled tasks as well-designed.

Result: Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy. Abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, meaning scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. Key failure modes include post-hoc abstention, where agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers.

Conclusion: Agentic abstention is a critical, under-evaluated capability that does not automatically improve with general task-solving performance. Dedicated benchmarks, training, and design are needed to build agents that reliably know when not to act.

Abstract: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous tasks, yet existing evaluations mostly focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain. This gap poses real risks: under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended and irreversible actions. To close this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention: the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when not to act. At its core, AgentAbstain is a paired-task benchmark built on an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios across pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It contains 263 paired tasks across 42 executable sandbox environments, where each pair consists of a should-act task and a should-abstain variant produced through a controlled perturbation to the instruction, tool, or environment state. To scale this paired design and resist data contamination, we propose AbstainGen, a fully automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and generates paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges; fresh task instances can be regenerated on demand, and three independent annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks as well-designed. Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy (correct on both the act and abstain sides of each paired task). More importantly, abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, indicating that scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. We further identify failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers. Our code and dataset are open-sourced at agentabstain.github.io.

</details>


### [123] [From ambiguous utterances to governed reuse classes: canonicalization, quotient invariance, and conditional decidability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10069)
*Cosimo Spera,Ray Garcia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that semantic caching in governed domains should be based on a mathematically rigorous quotient of resolved conversational demands (via three refinement relations: reading identity, resolution identity, reuse identity) rather than embedding similarity heuristics, with reuse identity serving as the kernel of the resolution map into a governed answer partition. A supporting formal layer is provided with exact-denotation normal forms, join aggregation, total computability, policy admissibility, and terminating elicitation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current semantic caching uses embedding similarity thresholds to reuse answers, but this approach lacks notions of authorization, versioning, and principled criteria for what makes two conversational demands genuinely equivalent. In governed domains, this heuristic approach is inadequate, motivating a formally grounded alternative that defines reuse on a mathematically characterized quotient structure.

Method: The paper defines three independent relations on resolved utterances — reading identity, resolution identity, and reuse identity — that form a strict refinement chain under checkable nondegeneracy conditions. Reuse identity is characterized as exactly the kernel of the resolution map into the governed answer partition. The supporting formal layer includes exact-denotation normal forms, join aggregation as a design operator with closure-stable cells, total computability relative to an untrusted proposal layer, policy admissibility for arbitrary proposers, and terminating elicitation after finitely many informative replies sound under target consistency.

Result: The refinement chain among the three identity relations is strict under nondegeneracy conditions verifiable on deployment logs. The pipeline's outputs are invariant along the chain. Reuse identity corresponds precisely to the kernel of the resolution map, meaning the reuse quotient is the utterance-side object induced by the governed answer partition. Policy admissibility holds for arbitrary proposers, but provably not factual grounding or intent fidelity. Elicitation terminates after finitely many informative replies.

Conclusion: Reuse in governed conversational systems should be defined on the reuse quotient — the mathematically precise kernel of the resolution map — rather than on embedding similarity. Reuse identity licenses the governed query key and certified answer space, while reusing a particular answer requires either resolution identity or an applicability certificate. The formal layer provides the exact strength needed: computability, policy admissibility, and terminating elicitation, though not factual grounding or intent fidelity.

Abstract: Semantic caching defines answer reuse on embedding similarity: two utterances share a stored answer when a similarity score clears a threshold, with no notion of authorization, versioning, or of what makes two demands the same. This note changes the object on which reuse is defined: in a governed domain, reuse should operate on a mathematically characterized quotient of resolved conversational demands, not on a similarity heuristic. Three independently defined relations on resolved utterances -- reading identity, resolution identity, and reuse identity -- form a refinement chain, strict under realized nondegeneracy conditions checkable on deployment logs; the pipeline's outputs are invariant along the chain, and reuse identity is exactly the kernel of the resolution map into the governed answer partition, so the reuse quotient is the utterance-side object that partition induces, not a relabeling of it. Reuse identity licenses the governed query key and its certified answer space; reuse of a particular answer requires resolution identity or an applicability certificate. The supporting layer is stated at exactly the strength proved: exact-denotation normal forms; join aggregation as a design operator, with closure-stable cells characterizing no-escape; total computability of the full pipeline relative to an untrusted proposal layer; policy admissibility for arbitrary proposers -- and provably not factual grounding or intent fidelity; and elicitation terminating after finitely many informative replies, sound under target consistency.

</details>


### [124] [MAG: A Web-Agent Benchmark and Harness for Multimodal Action and Guide Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10079)
*Chengguang Gan,Hanjun Wei,Yunhao Liang,Zhixi Cai,Qinghao Zhang,Shiwen Ni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAG is a new multimodal benchmark unifying web task execution and guide text generation from screenshots, evaluated with joint metrics. A GRPO-based training method with expert trajectories nearly doubles a 9B agent's success rate, yet the best model still completes under 40% of tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work treats automated web agent actions and guide text generation as separate problems, and typically relies on textual page representations (DOM, accessibility trees) rather than rendered screenshots that humans actually interact with. Real tasks also span multiple pages with changing states—not single-page button clicks—and no prior benchmark unifies action and guide generation into one compound task.

Method: The authors introduce MAG, a multimodal benchmark that unifies task execution and guide writing. It uses two grounding schemes: Set-of-Mark element selection and raw pixel coordinates over screenshots. They build a complete pipeline including LLM-assisted annotation with human verification, training, live-environment evaluation, and joint action–guide metrics. They evaluate frontier API and open multimodal models, and propose a GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) training method augmented with expert trajectories to improve both action success and guide quality.

Result: The GRPO-augmented method nearly doubles the success rate of a supervised 9B agent (from 6.9% to 13.2%) while simultaneously improving guide quality. Even the strongest evaluated model completes fewer than 40% of tasks, indicating substantial headroom for future work.

Conclusion: MAG establishes the first unified multimodal benchmark for joint web action execution and guide generation, revealing that current models struggle significantly with this compound task. The GRPO training approach shows promise, but the sub-40% ceiling underscores the challenge and the need for further research.

Abstract: Digital Adoption Platforms (DAPs) are embedded overlays widely used on web systems to guide users through operations inside a page, helping them get started with unfamiliar interfaces quickly. Completing a real task, however, rarely means clicking a few buttons on a single page: it takes a sequence of actions that unfolds across changing page states. Prior studies have also treated automated web agent actions and guide text generation as two separate problems, and most of them feed models textual page representations such as the DOM or accessibility trees rather than the rendered screens that humans actually operate on. In this work we introduce MAG, the first benchmark that unifies task execution and guide writing into a single Multimodal Action and Guide task, with two grounding schemes over screenshots: Set-of-Mark element selection and raw pixel coordinates. We further build a complete harness for this compound task, covering annotation with LLM assistance and human verification, training, evaluation in live environments, and joint metrics for actions and guides. With this harness we evaluate frontier API models and open multimodal models, and report detailed analyses. Finally, we design a GRPO training method augmented with expert trajectories, which nearly doubles the success rate of a supervised 9B agent (from 6.9% to 13.2%) and improves guide quality at the same time. Even the strongest model completes fewer than 40% of the tasks, leaving ample room for future research.

</details>


### [125] [Looped State-Space Language Models with Adaptive Exit-State Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10110)
*Zhenxuan Yu,Takeshi Kojima,Yutaka Matsuo,Yusuke Iwasawa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether the principle that reasoning benefits from computational depth via recurrent computation applies to state-space language models (Mamba). Through controlled reasoning tasks and LM pre-training, the authors show that looped Mamba and Hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures outperform parameter-matched non-looped baselines. They also adapt adaptive exit mechanisms for threshold-controlled depth selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on looped (recurrent) Transformers shows that many reasoning tasks benefit from greater computational depth rather than more parameters. However, these studies focus exclusively on Transformer backbones, leaving open whether this principle generalizes to state-space models (SSMs) like Mamba, which have fundamentally different architectural properties.

Method: The authors propose Looped Mamba and Looped Hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures that repeatedly apply a shared Mamba (or hybrid) block for finite-depth recurrent computation. They evaluate on: (1) controlled reasoning tasks (Mano modular arithmetic manipulation and p-hop induction), comparing looped vs. parameter-matched non-looped baselines and equal-effective-depth models; (2) language model pre-training under matched iso-parameter and iso-FLOPs protocols; and (3) adaptation of Ouro's two-stage exit gate to Looped Mamba for threshold-controlled adaptive exit-state selection.

Result: On reasoning tasks, Looped Mamba consistently outperforms parameter-matched non-looped baselines and often matches/exceeds non-looped models of equal effective depth. Under iso-parameter pre-training, looped models remain competitive on downstream benchmarks with substantially fewer distinct parameters. Under strict iso-FLOPs, deeper non-looped models retain an advantage in validation perplexity. Adaptive exit-state selection improves downstream performance at intermediate depths, but inference-time savings require additional state-handling mechanisms.

Conclusion: The computational depth principle generalizes beyond Transformers to state-space models: looped Mamba architectures provide an effective parameter-efficient approach for reasoning tasks and competitive downstream performance. However, translating adaptive depth into actual inference savings remains an open challenge requiring better state-handling mechanisms.

Abstract: Recent work on looped language models suggests that many reasoning problems benefit from greater computational depth rather than from additional independent parameters. Existing studies, however, focus almost exclusively on Transformer backbones, leaving open whether this principle also applies to state-space language models. We investigate Looped Mamba and Looped Hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures, which repeatedly apply a shared Mamba (or hybrid) block to introduce explicit finite-depth recurrent computation. On two controlled reasoning tasks-Mano (modular-arithmetic manipulation) and p-hop induction-Looped Mamba consistently outperforms parameter-matched non-looped baselines and, in several settings, matches or exceeds non-looped models of equal effective depth. We then extend the study to language model pre-training under matched iso-parameter and iso-FLOPs protocols, which jointly disentangle the effects of parameter sharing and effective depth: looped models remain competitive on downstream benchmarks with substantially fewer distinct parameters, although deeper non-looped models retain an advantage in validation perplexity under strict iso-FLOPs comparisons. Finally, we adapt Ouro's two-stage exit gate to Looped Mamba for threshold-controlled selection among recurrent-step outputs. Since all recurrent steps are still executed, the selected exit step represents prediction depth rather than reduced wall-clock computation. At the scales studied, adaptive exit-state selection improves downstream performance at intermediate depths, while actual inference-time savings require additional state-handling mechanisms.

</details>


### [126] [Dynamic Agent Skills: A Lifecycle Survey and Taxonomy of Evolving Skill Libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10113)
*Yubo Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A 124-paper survey (2023–2026) taxonomizes how LLM agent skill libraries evolve over time, proposing a six-sense taxonomy of skill artifacts, an eight-stage lifecycle architecture, and a ten-operator vocabulary for comparing library updates. Key findings: admission and repair are critical, verifier quality affects skill-aware RL, flat retrieval degrades with library growth, and current benchmarks under-report library trajectories and safety surfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly store reusable procedures ("skills") outside the model, but the literature lacks a unified framework for understanding how these skill libraries dynamically change over time. Existing work treats skills in structurally different ways without common terminology for comparing library evolution mechanisms.

Method: The authors conduct a taxonomy-driven survey across a 124-paper audit set (2023–2026). They introduce three organizational tools: (1) a six-sense taxonomy distinguishing structurally different skill artifacts, (2) an eight-stage lifecycle architecture covering evidence acquisition, proposal, verification/admission, storage, retrieval/composition, maintenance, distillation/portability, and governance, and (3) a lightweight skill-record schema with a ten-operator vocabulary for standardized comparison of library updates.

Result: Key synthesized findings include: admission and repair stages are repeatedly important across systems; verifier quality materially affects skill-aware RL performance; flat retrieval mechanisms degrade as libraries scale; current benchmarks under-report library trajectories, usage–utility gaps, and safety surfaces.

Conclusion: The paper concludes with concrete reporting standards and open problems for evaluating dynamic skill libraries as evolving artifact stores rather than static prompt or tool collections, emphasizing the need for better benchmarks that capture the full lifecycle of skill library dynamics.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly store reusable procedures outside the model. These reusable procedures are often called \emph{skills}: they may be code functions, natural-language instructions, SKILL.md packages, workflow graphs, or learned adapters that a future agent can retrieve and invoke. This taxonomy-driven survey asks how such skill libraries change over time. Across a $124$-paper $2023$--$2026$ audit set, we synthesize dynamic skill systems as \emph{lifecycle-managed, verified, evolving artifact stores}: agents collect evidence from interaction, propose skill updates, verify and admit candidates, organize them for retrieval and composition, repair or prune stale entries, and govern sharing through provenance and rollback. We organize the literature around three survey tools. First, a $\text{six}$-sense taxonomy distinguishes the structurally different artifacts called ``skills'' in current papers. Second, an $\text{eight}$-stage lifecycle architecture identifies the recurring design decisions behind evidence acquisition, proposal, verification/admission, storage, retrieval/composition, maintenance, distillation/portability, and governance. Third, a lightweight skill-record schema and $\text{ten}$-operator vocabulary provide common terms for comparing library updates without elevating them into a separate method contribution. Using this structure, we synthesize evidence-graded patterns with explicit caveats: admission and repair are repeatedly important, verifier quality materially affects skill-aware RL, flat retrieval can degrade as libraries grow, and current benchmarks still under-report library trajectories, usage--utility gaps, and safety surfaces. We close with concrete reporting standards and open problems for evaluating dynamic skills as changing libraries rather than static prompt or tool collections.

</details>


### [127] [IdeaTrail: Full-Process Agent Trajectories for Scientific Ideation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10144)
*Hengquan Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This report introduces a multi-turn process-trajectory dataset for scientific ideation and proposal generation. Using a Generator-Advisor synthesis loop, it reverse-engineers trajectories from human-selected high-quality papers, producing realistic multi-turn research data that captures evidence gathering, tool use, artifact evolution, and proposal construction while maintaining alignment with real scientific artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing resources capture only isolated components of the scientific research workflow. No dataset jointly records the full process: tool use, evidence acquisition, intermediate artifact evolution, and idea/proposal-level endpoints. There is a need for process-supervision data that reflects the uncertainty, evidence use, and staged convergence of real research practice.

Method: A reverse-to-forward synthesis procedure using a Generator-Advisor loop. Starting from human-selected high-quality research papers and proposals, the Generator produces visible trajectories (actions, observations, artifact edits), while the Advisor — with access to the full generation context — checks grounding, causal order, naturalness, and leakage from hidden targets. This ensures trajectories remain aligned with real artifacts while approximating authentic research processes.

Result: The method yields a dataset of multi-turn process trajectories covering the full pipeline from literature search and evidence gathering through to idea selection or proposal construction. The dataset serves both as a resource and as a generalizable recipe for synthesizing process-supervision data for scientific research agents.

Conclusion: The proposed dataset and synthesis methodology address a critical gap in process-oriented training data for scientific AI agents, enabling better modeling of the iterative, tool-mediated, evidence-driven nature of real scientific ideation and proposal writing.

Abstract: Scientific research is a complex, multi-stage workflow rather than a single act of text generation. The ideation process typically emerges through literature search, paper reading, tool use, claim checking, cross-paper synthesis, brainstorming, rejection of weak directions, and iterative writing. Existing resources capture individual components of this process, but datasets that jointly record tool use, evidence acquisition, intermediate artifact evolution, and idea- or proposal-level endpoints remain limited. This report introduces \method, a multi-turn process-trajectory dataset for scientific ideation and proposal generation. Each instance records a research process from evidence gathering to either idea selection or proposal construction. Rather than freely fabricating trajectories, \method starts from human-selected high-quality research papers and proposal artifacts and uses a Generator--Advisor synthesis loop. The Generator produces the visible trajectory through actions, observations, and artifact edits, while the Advisor has access to the full generation context and checks grounding, causal order, naturalness, and leakage from hidden targets. This reverse-to-forward procedure produces multi-turn research data that remains aligned with real scientific artifacts while approximating the uncertainty, evidence use, and staged convergence of research practice. \method provides both a dataset and a general recipe for synthesizing process-supervision data for scientific research agents.

</details>


### [128] [UNIT: Unleash Large Language Models Potential for Graph Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10159)
*Tairan Huang,Yili Wang,Beibei Hu,Yiting Shi,Qiutong Li,Changlong He,Jianliang Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UNIT is a graph continual learning framework that fine-tunes LLMs on the first task to bridge distribution gaps, uses uncertainty-aware anchor generation to preserve cross-task knowledge, and employs structural confluence modeling to integrate graph topology with semantic information, achieving SOTA performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph continual learning methods suffer from (1) semantic-structural separation, where graph methods focus on topology but neglect deep semantics, and (2) imbalanced knowledge transfer, failing to effectively leverage general knowledge from early tasks for subsequent new tasks.

Method: UNIT fine-tunes an LLM only on the first task to bridge the distribution gap between pre-trained corpus and target data. It introduces an uncertainty-aware anchor generation mechanism to preserve representative cross-task knowledge, and structural confluence modeling to explicitly inject graph topology into semantic representations.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that UNIT achieves state-of-the-art performance on graph continual learning benchmarks.

Conclusion: By unleashing LLM potential through first-task fine-tuning, uncertainty-aware knowledge preservation, and structural-semantic fusion, UNIT effectively addresses the core challenges in graph continual learning and sets a new SOTA.

Abstract: In real-world multimodal web scenarios, graph-structured data often arrives in a streaming manner, making graph continual learning a crucial paradigm for continuously modeling such evolving structures. However, existing graph continual learning methods still face two fundamental challenges. 1) semantic-structural separation, where the graph-based methods excel at modeling topological relationships but neglect deep semantics. 2) imbalanced knowledge transfer, where existing models fail to effectively leverage general knowledge gained from early tasks to benefit subsequent new tasks. To address above issues, we propose a novel framework, \textbf{UN}leash Large Language Models PotentIal for Graph ConTinual Learning (UNIT). By fine-tuning large language model only on the first task, we bridge the distributional gap between the pre-trained LLM corpus and the target task dataset to enhance the adaptability of LLMs for graph-structured tasks. Meanwhile, we propose an uncertain-aware anchor generation mechanism to effectively preserve representative knowledge across tasks, avoiding the neglect of universal knowledge learned from previous tasks. Additionally, we introduce structural confluence modeling to explicitly integrates graph topology information into semantic information, enhancing the collaborative capabilities between semantic understanding and structural modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in the graph continual learning task.

</details>


### [129] [When Are Sparse Feature Interventions Actually Localized? Matched Evaluation for SAE-Based Safety Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10226)
*Daming Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a rigorous "matched coherence-gated" evaluation protocol for assessing whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) features serve as localized safety control handles. Applied to Gemma-2-9B-it, the authors find SAE feature ablation has a narrow useful regime (top~800 features), beyond which utility collapses or degenerate outputs arise. The useful regime is driven by a small, stable set of refusal-aligned features whose influence decays rapidly with rank.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work evaluating SAE-based safety interventions suffers from confounds: weak interventions, mismatched baselines, model robustness masking effects, and degenerate outputs that automated safety judges misclassify as unsafe. There is no standardized, rigorous protocol for determining whether SAE features genuinely act as localized, causally meaningful control handles for safety-relevant behavior.

Method: The authors propose a matched coherence-gated evaluation protocol with three key components: (1) comparing methods at matched target-effect points (equal harmfulness reduction) rather than arbitrary intervention strengths; (2) using a primary metric that counts harmful compliance only when outputs are both judge-unsafe AND coherent (gating out degenerate/junk outputs); (3) benchmarking SAE feature ablation against a dense refusal-direction baseline. Experiments use Gemma-2-9B-it with a Gemma Scope layer-20 residual SAE across three prompt splits, complemented by human audit and feature-level diagnostics.

Result: SAE top-800 ablation achieves low-to-mid target effect with lower total perturbation and competitive utility versus the dense baseline. SAE top-1600 loses utility relative to the matched dense baseline. SAE top-3200 primarily induces coherence collapse (degenerate outputs). Coherence gating effectively removes unsafe-only artifacts confirmed by human audit. Feature diagnostics reveal the useful regime is driven by a stable head of refusal-aligned features whose activation separation decays rapidly with rank.

Conclusion: SAE-based safety interventions should be evaluated as regime-dependent control mechanisms rather than assumed to be uniformly localized. The narrow useful regime and rapid decay of feature separation suggest limited scalability of SAE feature ablation as a safety method. The proposed coherence-gated protocol offers a more reliable framework for future mechanistic interpretability-based safety research.

Abstract: We evaluate when sparse autoencoder (SAE) features act as localized control handles for safety-relevant behavior. This question is difficult because apparent success can arise from weak interventions, mismatched baselines, model robustness, or degenerate outputs that automated safety judges mark as unsafe without representing meaningful harmful compliance. We introduce a matched coherence-gated evaluation protocol for runtime safety interventions: methods are compared at matched target-effect points, and the primary target metric counts harmful compliance only when an output is both judge-unsafe and coherent. Applying this protocol to three prompt splits on Gemma-2-9B-it with a Gemma Scope layer-20 residual SAE, we find that SAE feature ablation has a narrow useful regime. SAE top800 reaches a low-to-mid target effect with lower total perturbation and competitive utility, but SAE top1600 loses utility relative to a matched dense refusal-direction baseline, and SAE top3200 primarily induces coherence collapse. Human audit confirms that coherence gating removes unsafe-only artifacts, and feature diagnostics show that the useful regime is driven by a stable head of refusal-aligned features whose activation separation decays rapidly with rank. These results argue that SAE-based safety interventions should be evaluated as regime-dependent control mechanisms rather than assumed to be uniformly localized.

</details>


### [130] [GRATE: Temporal Extensions for Inductive KG Foundation Models via Gated Rotary Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10197)
*Jiaxin Pan,Osama Mohammed,Daniel Hernández,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes GRATE, a parameter-free temporal encoding mechanism that integrates into NBFNet-style KG foundation models to enable inductive transfer across temporal knowledge graphs with disjoint entities, relations, and timestamps. It introduces new benchmark suites (GDELTIndT, WIKIIndT) for evaluating cross-dataset temporal transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal knowledge graph models are tied to dataset-specific entities, relations, or timestamps, preventing inductive transfer to TKGs with disjoint vocabularies. While static KG foundation models (e.g., Ultra, Trix) achieve strong inductive transfer via relation-graph representations, extending this to the temporal setting remains an open challenge.

Method: GRATE (Gated Rotary Attention for Temporal Encoding) is an entity-side message function with zero learnable parameters. It encodes time via relative time differences by rotating each edge message according to its time gap from the query timestamp, combined with a query-conditioned gating mechanism that selectively filters temporally relevant signals. GRATE integrates into NBFNet-style architectures while preserving structural transferability. The authors also construct GDELTIndT and WIKIIndT, inductive transfer benchmarks with disjoint entities, relations, and timestamps covering both interpolation and extrapolation settings.

Result: A single jointly pretrained GRATE checkpoint improves over the static base model in most settings across the new inductive transfer benchmarks and held-out forecasting datasets.

Conclusion: GRATE successfully extends the inductive transfer capabilities of KG foundation models to the temporal domain without introducing learnable parameters, demonstrating that relative temporal encoding with gated attention is effective for cross-dataset TKG transfer.

Abstract: Knowledge graph foundation models such as Ultra and Trix achieve strong inductive transfer by learning relation-graph representations that generalise to unseen entities and relations. Extending this transferability to temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) remains challenging: existing temporal models tie their parameters to dataset-specific entities, relations, or timestamps and are not designed to transfer to TKGs with disjoint vocabularies. We propose GRATE (Gated Rotary Attention for Temporal Encoding), an entity-side message function that adds no learnable parameters and encodes time through relative time differences by rotating each edge message according to its time gap to the query and applying a query-conditioned gate to select temporally relevant signals. GRATE integrates into NBFNet-style KG foundation models while preserving structural transferability. Existing TKG benchmarks evaluate within shared train/test vocabularies and cannot directly test cross-dataset temporal transfer; we therefore construct GDELTIndT and WIKIIndT, inductive transfer benchmark suites with disjoint entities, relations, and timestamps spanning both interpolation and extrapolation. Across these benchmarks and held-out forecasting datasets, a single jointly pretrained GRATE checkpoint improves over the static base model in most settings.

</details>


### [131] [Cross-Layer Misalignment Detection in Agent Skills: A Progressive Loading-Aware Contrastive Learning Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10534)
*Chengjun Zhang,Yang Gao,Jianna Hur,Jingjing Zhang,Sagar Samtani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PL-HCL is a framework that detects inconsistencies between Agent Skill descriptions and their actual behavior (cross-layer misalignment) by modeling the layered structure of skills using hierarchical contrastive learning, achieving Macro-F1 scores of 0.87–0.89 on a corpus of 264,000+ open-source skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As open-source Agent Skill marketplaces grow, users and agents rely on brief metadata to select third-party skills. However, discrepancies between a skill's description and its true execution behavior—termed cross-layer misalignment—are hard to detect automatically, creating a need for reliable screening tools.

Method: The authors propose Progressive Loading-Aware Hierarchical Contrastive Learning (PL-HCL), an LLM-based framework that models the layered structure of Agent Skills (natural-language metadata, procedural instructions, and execution-time resources) and learns cross-layer consistency representations. A normalized corpus of over 264,000 open-source skills is used alongside a human-verified challenge set for evaluation.

Result: PL-HCL improves Macro-F1 from approximately 0.45 for unadapted baselines to 0.87–0.89 across multiple LLM backbones, demonstrating substantial gains in cross-layer misalignment detection.

Conclusion: PL-HCL provides an effective screening tool for users and operators of skill marketplaces and offers design principles applicable to detecting inconsistencies in other layered digital artifacts.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly extended through Agent Skills, reusable artifacts that package natural-language metadata, procedural instructions, and execution-time resources for runtime use. As open-source skill marketplaces expand, users and agents increasingly rely on brief metadata to select third-party skills, making it difficult to detect inconsistencies between a skill's description and its true behavior, a problem we call cross-layer misalignment. To address this issue, we propose Progressive Loading-Aware Hierarchical Contrastive Learning (PL-HCL), an LLM-based framework that detects misalignment by modeling the layered structure of Agent Skills and learning cross-layer consistency. Using a normalized corpus of over 264,000 open-source skills and a human-verified challenge set, PL-HCL improves Macro-F1 from approximately 0.45 for unadapted baselines to 0.87-0.89 across evaluated LLM backbones. This approach offers an effective screening tool for users and operators, as well as design principles for detecting inconsistencies in layered digital artifacts.

</details>


### [132] [KGCQual: An Interpretable Framework for Evaluating the Knowledge Graph Construction Quality from Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10212)
*Nipun Misra,Vikranth Udandarao,Aanchal Gupta,Yogender Kumar,Manuj Mukherjee,Raghava Mutharaju*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes KGCQual, an interpretable metric for evaluating automatically extracted knowledge graphs by measuring structural and semantic fidelity against source text, using entity-level and relation-level assessments; validated across multiple extraction systems and datasets, with downstream link prediction correlation demonstrated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated KG extraction pipelines often produce noisy, incomplete, or spurious triples, yet existing evaluation relies on task-specific metrics or small-scale manual checks that fail to capture structural and semantic fidelity to the source text.

Method: The framework combines (1) entity-level assessment measuring completeness, resolution quality, and connectivity; and (2) relation-level assessment judging predicate preservation and multiplicity via lexical similarity, dependency-parse alignment, and lightweight negation handling. Evaluated against state-of-the-art triple extraction systems on WebNLG, TinyButMighty, and BenchIE, with ablation on noun/verb components and downstream link prediction correlation analysis.

Result: KGCQual reliably identifies omissions, redundancy, and structural deviations overlooked by existing metrics. Ablation study validates the contribution of noun and verb components, and KGCQual scores correlate significantly with link prediction performance on the same extracted KGs.

Conclusion: KGCQual provides a scalable, model-agnostic, and interpretable framework for comparing automated KG construction methods, establishing a foundation for standardized intrinsic KG quality evaluation.

Abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are increasingly constructed through automated extraction pipelines; however, such systems often introduce spurious or incomplete triples, which degrade downstream performance. Existing evaluation practices rely heavily on task-specific metrics or small-scale manual verification, offering limited insight into the structural and semantic fidelity of extracted graphs. We propose a novel, interpretable metric for intrinsic KG quality assessment that measures how closely an automatically extracted graph approximates an "ideal" graph capturing the key noun phrases, predicate relations, and basic linguistic phenomena such as negation expressed in the source text. Our framework integrates two complementary components: (1) an entity-level assessment that evaluates completeness, resolution quality, and connectivity, and (2) a relation-level assessment that judges predicate preservation and multiplicity using lexical similarity, dependency-parse alignment, and light-weight negation handling to ensure semantic faithfulness. We evaluate our metric across multiple state-of-the-art triple extraction systems and datasets, including WebNLG, TinyButMighty, and BenchIE, demonstrating that it reliably identifies omissions, redundancy, and structural deviations that existing metrics overlook. Our work offers a scalable, model-agnostic, and interpretable framework for comparing automated KG construction methods and provides a foundation for standardised evaluation. We further validate the metric through an ablation study isolating noun and verb components, and a downstream evaluation showing that KGCQual scores correlate significantly with link prediction performance on the same extracted KGs. The code repository is available at https://github.com/kracr/kg-quality-metric.

</details>


### [133] [Behavioural Signatures of Risk-Sensitive Decision-Making in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10251)
*Xuankun Rong,Wenke Huang,Bo Du,Dacheng Tao,Mang Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frontier LLMs exhibit stable, model-specific risk profiles in no-limit Texas Hold'em, ranging from conservative to aggressive. These profiles remain robust across opponent compositions, though models diverge under global risk pressure and resource constraints, revealing heterogeneous behavioural adaptation patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in decision support systems, it is critical to understand whether their choices under uncertainty display stable, interpretable behavioural regularities analogous to human decision-making — which combines persistent risk preferences with context-dependent adjustment. This remains underexplored for LLMs.

Method: The authors use a controlled multi-model framework based on no-limit Texas Hold'em. Behaviour is quantified via two metrics: Participation (voluntary engagement in uncertain opportunities) and Proactiveness (pre-flop risk escalation). Experiments span homogeneous self-play and heterogeneous mixed-model interactions, with manipulations of global risk pressure and personal resource constraints to probe adaptive behaviour.

Result: Frontier LLMs display stable, model-specific risk profiles along a conservative-to-aggressive spectrum. These profiles are largely robust to changes in opponent composition, though the most conservative and aggressive models diverge further in mixed settings. Under risk pressure and resource constraints, models adapt in structured but heterogeneous ways — ranging from broad behavioural contraction to selective de-escalation and near-invariant behaviour.

Conclusion: LLMs differ not only in baseline risk disposition but also in which risk signals they respond to and how flexibly they adjust. This provides a behavioural foundation for auditing risk-sensitive decision-making in interactive AI systems.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in decision support, it is important to understand whether their choices under uncertainty exhibit stable and interpretable behavioural regularities. Human decision-making combines relatively persistent risk preferences with context-dependent adjustment, yet it remains unclear whether analogous behavioural structure can be observed in LLM-based decision systems. Here we examine this question using a controlled multi-model framework based on no-limit Texas Hold'em, where behaviour is quantified by Participation, measuring voluntary engagement in uncertain opportunities, and Proactiveness, measuring pre-flop risk escalation. Across homogeneous self-play and heterogeneous mixed-model interactions, frontier LLMs exhibit stable, model-specific risk profiles, forming a spectrum from conservative to aggressive decision styles. These profiles remain largely robust under changing opponent composition, while the most conservative and most aggressive models diverge further in mixed settings. Under global risk pressure and personal resource constraint, models adapt in structured but heterogeneous ways, ranging from broad behavioural contraction to selective de-escalation and near-invariant behaviour. These findings suggest that LLMs differ not only in baseline risk disposition, but also in the risk signals they respond to and the flexibility with which they adjust, providing a behavioural basis for auditing risk-sensitive decision-making in interactive settings. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/AgentTexasPoker.

</details>


### [134] [Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10275)
*Krischan Braitsch,Laura K. Schmalbrock,Theresa Weltermann,Andrew F. Berdel,Isabella Miller,Kai Tran,Michael Heider,Sabrina Kraus,Florian Bassermann,Jacqueline Lammert,Sebastian Ziegelmayer,Marcus Makowski,Lisa C. Adams,Keno K. Bressem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frontier LLMs were evaluated on an agentic hematologic oncology benchmark requiring proactive information-seeking across three rounds. The best model achieved 68% accuracy; information utilization strongly predicted accuracy (R=0.69) but plummeted in the final round, and reasoning quality decorrelated from correctness. Dominant failure modes mirrored human cognitive biases: satisficing, anchoring, and premature closure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluations focus on static medical knowledge recall. Real clinical reasoning, however, demands active information-gathering under diagnostic uncertainty — deciding what data to request, when, and how to integrate sequentially revealed findings. This gap motivated an agentic framework testing whether models can navigate the iterative, uncertain process of clinical workup in hematologic oncology.

Method: An agentic evaluation framework was constructed in which 32 frontier LLMs had to proactively request clinical data across three sequential rounds before committing to a diagnosis and treatment plan. Information utilization (fraction of available data actually requested) was measured alongside diagnostic accuracy. Reasoning traces were scored using a clinical reasoning rubric, and errors were taxonomized using dual-process diagnostic reasoning frameworks.

Result: The best model reached 68% overall accuracy. Information utilization correlated strongly with accuracy (R=0.69, P<0.001) but dropped from 57% to 26% in the final round, leaving molecular/cytogenetic data unexamined. Reasoning rubric scores were high (91% above threshold) yet decorrelated from accuracy. Dominant failure modes were search satisficing, anchoring, and premature closure — cognitive biases characteristic of novice clinicians.

Conclusion: The primary limitation of current LLMs in clinical oncology is not deficient medical knowledge but a systematic failure of information-seeking under uncertainty. Models exhibit the same cognitive biases as novice diagnosticians, underscoring the need for agentic reasoning architectures that sustain curiosity-driven data acquisition through to treatment-relevant molecular characterization.

Abstract: Large language models achieve high scores on medical knowledge assessments, yet clinical reasoning requires actively deciding what to investigate under uncertainty. We developed an agentic evaluation framework in hematologic oncology in which models must proactively request clinical data across three sequential rounds before committing to a diagnosis and treatment plan. Across 32 frontier models, the best achieved only 68% overall accuracy. Information utilization, the fraction of available data actually requested, was the strongest predictor of diagnostic accuracy (R = 0.69, P < 0.001), yet utilization collapsed from 57% to 26% in the final round, leaving molecular and cytogenetic data critical for treatment selection unexamined. Reasoning traces scored high on a clinical reasoning rubric (91% above threshold) but decorrelated from accuracy, revealing a gap between locally coherent rationales and globally correct conclusions. Error analysis identified search satisficing, anchoring and premature closure as the dominant failure modes, the same cognitive biases that characterize novice clinicians under dual-process models of diagnostic reasoning. These findings demonstrate that the primary limitation of current models in clinical oncology is not insufficient medical knowledge but a systematic failure of information-seeking under uncertainty.

</details>


### [135] [OpsMem: Dual-Memory Reasoning with Cross-Memory Resonance for Failure Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11357)
*Yongqian Sun,Rongchen Gao,Yu Luo,Wenwei Gu,Shenglin Zhang,Qingyi Guo,Qiuai Fu,Yaoliang Wu,Dan Pei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OpsMem is a dual-memory framework for failure diagnosis that uses short-term memory for the current diagnostic state and long-term memory for reusable operational experience, with cross-memory resonance and consolidation mechanisms, achieving significant improvements over baselines on a Huawei microservice dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based failure diagnosis methods lack a mechanism to coordinate the evolving diagnostic state with operational experience during iterative diagnosis, limiting their effectiveness.

Method: OpsMem employs a dual-memory architecture: (1) short-term memory tracks the current diagnostic state; (2) long-term memory stores reusable operational experience. It features cross-memory resonance to activate relevant long-term memories based on the current state, conditions multi-agent diagnosis on both short-term and activated long-term memories, and consolidates resolved incident experiences back into long-term memory.

Result: On a real-world Huawei microservice failure diagnosis dataset, OpsMem outperforms representative agentic-reasoning and knowledge-augmented baselines, improving Match by up to 46.88% and Relevant by up to 18.39% over the strongest baseline.
