Motivation: Existing multi-agent ensembling methods blindly multiply active parameters and inference cost without addressing three fundamental questions: (1) which agents to consult for a given query, (2) how deeply a query should traverse a hierarchical agent structure, and (3) when inter-agent communication is worth its computational cost. This leads to wasteful computation and suboptimal performance.

Method: GRADE is a hierarchical multi-agent system with four lightweight learned gates: agent selection, hierarchy depth control, inter-agent communication gating, and branch pruning. These gates are trained using CoGRPO (Collaborative Group-Relative Policy Optimization), a critic-free extension of GRPO that assigns a shared advantage signal to all participating gates and agents. Agent models reside in a hot-swappable Expert Registry, and per-agent calibration maps enable inference-time expert replacement without retraining.

Result: At ~17B average active parameters, GRADE outperforms all baselines on GSM8K, MMLUPro, and GPQA, surpassing the strongest baseline by 4.8 points on MMLUPro while using half the active compute. On AIME-2025, GRADE remains competitive with existing frameworks. Ablations identify the hierarchy and masked cross-attention as the largest accuracy contributors, and confirm that per-agent calibration is necessary for safe hot-swapping.

Conclusion: Learned gating mechanisms can make multi-agent LLM reasoning both more accurate and more compute-efficient by dynamically deciding agent involvement, hierarchy depth, and communication. GRADE demonstrates that these decisions can be jointly optimized without a critic, and that modular expert hot-swapping is viable with proper calibration.

Abstract: Multi-agent ensembling multiplies active parameters and inference cost without answering three basic questions: which agents to consult, how deeply a query should traverse a hierarchy of agents, and when inter-agent communication is worth its cost. We present GRADE (Gated Routing and Adaptive Depth for Efficient Reasoning), a hierarchical multi-agent system in which four lightweight learned gates jointly govern agent selection, hierarchy depth, inter-agent communication, and branch pruning. Training uses CoGRPO (Collaborative Group-Relative Policy Optimization), a novel critic-free recipe that adapts GRPO to multi-agent hierarchies and assigns a shared advantage signal to every gate and agent that participated in a rollout. Agent models are drawn from a hot-swappable Expert Registry; per-agent calibration maps allow experts to be replaced at inference time without retraining. At $\sim$17B average active parameters, GRADE outperforms all baselines on GSM8K, MMLUPro, and GPQA, surpassing the strongest baseline by 4.8 points on MMLUPro at half the active compute. On AIME-2025, where model depth dominates, GRADE remains competitive to existing frameworks. Ablations isolate the hierarchy and masked cross-attention as the largest contributors to accuracy, and show that per-agent calibration is necessary for safe hot-swapping.

</details>


### [158] [LOGOS: A Living Logic for AI Agent Teams That Evolve With Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10878)
*Yuma Ichikawa,Yamato Arai,Kosaku Kimura,Akira Sakai,Hiromichi Kobashi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: logos is a pluggable governance layer for multiagent systems that treats all agent-evolved artifacts (prompts, tools, skills) as untrusted release candidates, requiring evidence-based verification and explicit human authorization before promotion, enabling verifiable human-agent loop engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents evolve into persistent, self-modifying teams that learn and create new tools, the critical question shifts from capability to control: who governs what agents are allowed to become. Existing multiagent frameworks lack built-in mechanisms for auditable, fail-closed governance over agent self-evolution.

Method: logos compiles heterogeneous multimodal inputs into versioned "agent packs" (agents, tools, knowledge, tests, permissions, policies). It transforms agent activity into portable, auditable event traces and applies fail-closed verification. Every learned artifact remains an untrusted release candidate until it passes held-out execution evidence, human-controlled policy, and explicit authorization for promotion.

Result: The architecture enables "verifiable human-agent loop engineering," where agents act, learn, and propose improvements autonomously while humans steer objectives, permissions, approvals, and irreversible actions without interrupting continuous operation.

Conclusion: logos provides a living logic for accountable automation: agents may evolve at machine speed, but only evidence and human authority can close the loop.

Abstract: AI agents are evolving from answer engines into persistent teams that use tools, delegate work, learn from experience, and modify the artifacts that shape their future behavior. The defining question for deployment is no longer merely what agents can do, but who controls what they are allowed to become. We introduce logos, a pluggable layer for self-evolution and governance that strengthens existing multiagent frameworks rather than replacing them. logos compiles heterogeneous multimodal inputs, including documents, images, audio, tables, databases, APIs, and human instructions into versioned agent packs containing agents, tools, knowledge, tests, permissions, and policies. During operation, it transforms agent activity into portable, auditable event traces and applies fail-closed verification across frameworks and backends. Every learned prompt, memory, skill, tool, role, or workflow remains an untrusted release candidate until held-out execution evidence, human-controlled policy, and explicit authorization permit its promotion. This architecture enables "verifiable human-agent loop engineering": agents can act, ask, learn, and propose improvements, while humans can steer objectives, permissions, approvals, and irreversible actions without interrupting continuous operation. logos provides a living logic for accountable automation. Agents may evolve at machine speed, but only evidence and human authority can close the loop.

</details>


### [159] [First-Order Modal Logic in HOL: Deep and Shallow Embeddings with Automated Faithfulness (Extended Preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10880)
*Christoph Benzmüller,Daniel Kirchner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper extends a prior deep-and-shallow embedding methodology from propositional to first-order modal logic (FML) with constant-domain Kripke semantics, mechanised in Isabelle/HOL. Three embeddings are provided (deep, maximal-shallow, minimal-shallow), with the minimal-shallow embedding realized as an Isabelle locale admitting a global faithfulness theorem. A key technical contribution is the mechanisation of the countable downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem, which resolves a surjectivity problem in the faithfulness proof. First-order substitution machinery is also developed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work developed a deep-and-shallow embedding methodology but only for the propositional fragment of modal logic. Extending this to first-order modal logic introduces significant new challenges: the need for substitution machinery (capture-avoiding substitution, renaming, substitution lemmas) for quantifiers, and a surjectivity problem wherein the locale's countable variable assignment cannot be surjective onto an uncountable domain of individuals, threatening the global faithfulness theorem.

Method: The authors embed first-order modal logic with constant-domain Kripke semantics into classical higher-order logic (HOL) in Isabelle/HOL using three parallel embeddings: (1) a deep embedding with explicit syntax and semantics, (2) a heavyweight maximal-shallow embedding, and (3) a lightweight minimal-shallow embedding formalized as an Isabelle locale parameterised by accessibility relation, world-indexed interpretation, universe of worlds, and variable assignment. The faithfulness proof between deep and minimal-shallow embeddings is automated by mechanising the countable downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem. Substitution machinery (free/bound-variable predicates, fresh-variable function, capture-avoiding substitution, alphabetic renaming, substitutability predicate, substitution lemma, size-based induction) is developed to handle first-order quantifiers.

Result: The minimal-shallow embedding, as a locale, admits a global faithfulness theorem: quantifying over all minimal-shallow interpretations recovers exactly deep validity. The mechanised downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem resolves the surjectivity problem against uncountable domains by restricting to countable subdomains, extending the faithfulness result to the full domain. The substitution machinery is successfully developed and integrated for first-order quantifier reasoning.

Conclusion: The deep-and-shallow embedding methodology generalizes successfully from propositional to first-order modal logic. The combination of Isabelle locales with the mechanised Löwenheim-Skolem theorem provides a principled solution to the surjectivity problem, yielding a robust faithfulness result. This work establishes foundational infrastructure for embedding-based reasoning about first-order modal logics in higher-order logic proof assistants.

Abstract: We extend, in Isabelle/HOL, the deep-and-shallow embedding methodology of our prior work from propositional to first-order modal logic (FML) with constant-domain Kripke semantics. Three embeddings of FML into classical higher-order logic (HOL) are provided side by side: a deep embedding, a heavyweight maximal-shallow embedding, and a lightweight minimal-shallow embedding. The minimal-shallow embedding is presented as an Isabelle/HOL locale, parametrised by an accessibility relation, a world-indexed interpretation, a universe of worlds, and a variable assignment; the locale form admits a global faithfulness theorem, stating that quantifying over all minimal-shallow interpretations recovers exactly deep validity.
  A central technical contribution is a mechanisation, for FML under constant-domain Kripke semantics, of the (countable) downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem, which underpins the automation of our faithfulness proof between the deep and minimal-shallow embeddings. Deploying it inside an extension of the minimal-shallow locale resolves the surjectivity problem that arises against an uncountable domain of individuals -- where the locale's variable assignment, having countable domain V = nat, cannot be surjective onto the domain -- and thereby yields faithfulness over the full domain.
  Since prior work treats only the propositional fragment, we develop here the substitution machinery (free/bound-variable predicates, the fresh-variable function, capture-avoiding substitution, alphabetic renaming, the substitutability predicate, the substitution lemma, and size-based induction principles) needed for the first-order quantifiers.

</details>


### [160] [SETA: Scaling Environments for Terminal Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10891)
*Qijia Shen,Zhiqi Huang,Vamsidhar Kamanuru,Aznaur Aliev,Jay Rainton,Ahmed Awelkair,Zhichen Zeng,Jiajun Li,Shi Dong,Yueming Yuan,Boyuan Ma,Qizheng Zhang,Jiwei Fu,Yuzhen Mao,Wendong Fan,Ping Nie,Philip Torr,Bernard Ghanem,Changran Hu,Jonathan Lingjie Li,Urmish Thakker,Guohao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SETA is a scalable framework for generating verifiable terminal environments for RL-based terminal agent training. It comprises SETA-Synth (converting diverse sources into standardized RL environments) and SETA-Evol (expanding environments with controlled difficulty/diversity). The resulting SETA-Env dataset—4,500+ environments—enables training Qwen3-8B with GRPO to achieve 12% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (best 8B-scale RL result) and boosts DeepSeek-V4-Flash from 40%→43% pass@1, 54%→58% pass@5.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training terminal agents via RL is hindered by the lack of diverse, coherent task instructions, executable environments, and reliable verification—particularly absent is naturally grounded supervision data. Existing approaches cannot scale to meet these demands.

Method: SETA consists of two pipelines: (1) SETA-Synth transforms diverse raw sources into standardized, verifiable RL environments; (2) SETA-Evol expands existing environments with adaptive difficulty and diversity control. Both share a unified verification mechanism. The combined output is SETA-Env, a dataset of 4,500+ terminal RL environments. Models are trained using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) on this dataset.

Result: Qwen3-8B trained with GRPO on SETA-Env achieves a 12% pass rate on Terminal-Bench 2.0—the best reported for an RL-trained 8B-scale model. DeepSeek-V4-Flash improves from 40% to 43% pass@1 and from 54% to 58% pass@5 on the same benchmark when using the SETA terminal agent harness.

Conclusion: SETA-Env delivers high-quality, verifiable training environments for terminal-based agents, demonstrating clear improvements across model scales and serving as a valuable resource for advancing RL-based terminal agent research.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly shifting toward agents that solve tasks through diverse interfaces, including web and graphical user interfaces (GUIs). Among these, the terminal command line provides a text-based, general-purpose interface, covering tasks from system operations to data science and machine learning. However, scaling terminal-agent training remains challenging, as it requires diverse and coherent task instructions, executable environments, and reliable verification, while lacking naturally grounded supervision data. In this work, we propose SETA, a scalable framework for generating verifiable terminal environments for reinforcement learning (RL). The framework consists of two pipelines sharing a unified verification mechanism: SETA-Synth converts diverse sources into standardized RL environments, and SETA-Evol further expands from existing environments with adaptive control of difficulty and diversity. Together, we construct and release SETA-Env, the largest open-source verifiable terminal RL dataset to date, containing over 4,500 environments. We evaluate our dataset by training Qwen3-8B with GRPO on SETA-Env, achieving 12% pass rate on Terminal-Bench 2.0, the best reported result for an RL-trained model at the 8B scale. We further observe gains on DeepSeek-V4-Flash under the same terminal agent harness, with pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 improving from 40% to 43% and pass@5 improving from 54% to 58%. These results demonstrate that SETA- Env provides high-quality training environments for terminal agents and serves as a valuable resource for advancing research on terminal-based agent learning.

</details>


### [161] [Incremental Transformer for Surrogate-Based Inverse Design of Geopolymer Mixtures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10896)
*Giansalvo Cirrincione,Filippo Grassia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A topology-aware surrogate framework with an Incremental Transformer (INCRT) is proposed for physics-constrained inverse design from small, heterogeneous, mixed-type datasets. Applied to geopolymer concrete mixture design, the method integrates dimensionality reduction, tabular surrogates, INCRT-based manifold rationalisation, and constrained optimisation. INCRT serves as a rationalisation layer — not a replacement for tabular predictors — providing prototype regimes and manifold-support scores. The topology-aware physics-constrained strategy yields candidates that balance target compliance, carbon reduction, physical admissibility, and proximity to the learned feasible manifold, outperforming unconstrained and physics-only constrained approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small-data inverse design in engineering informatics faces challenges when observations are heterogeneous, mixed-type, and constrained by physical relations among design variables. Existing approaches struggle to ensure that inversely designed candidates are both physically valid and supported by the data manifold, especially when data are scarce.

Method: The framework comprises: (1) intrinsic-dimensionality analysis to reveal redundancy in the design space; (2) mixed-variable design-space representation; (3) tabular surrogate prediction (nonlinear models for compressive strength; regularised linear models for carbon emission); (4) an Incremental Transformer (INCRT) serving as a manifold rationalisation layer that yields prototype regimes and a manifold-support score; (5) three inverse-design strategies compared — unconstrained surrogate optimisation, physics-constrained optimisation, and topology-aware physics-constrained optimisation. Evaluated on a public benchmark of fly-ash and slag-based geopolymer concrete mixtures.

Result: The high-dimensional design space is strongly redundant, organizing around fewer effective mixture regimes. Compressive strength requires nonlinear tabular surrogates, while carbon emission is largely composition-determined and well recovered by regularised linear models. Unconstrained optimisation matches target strength but yields physically invalid or off-manifold candidates. Physics-only constraints do not always ensure data support. The topology-aware strategy successfully balances target compliance, carbon reduction, physical admissibility, and manifold proximity.

Conclusion: The INCRT-augmented topology-aware framework provides credible screening of candidate mixtures from small, mixed, physically constrained engineering datasets. INCRT acts effectively as a rationalisation layer rather than a predictor replacement, and the topology-aware constrained optimisation strategy is essential for generating physically admissible, data-supported inverse designs.

Abstract: Small-data inverse design is challenging in engineering informatics when observations are heterogeneous, mixed-type, and constrained by physical relations among design variables. This work proposes a topology-aware surrogate framework guided by an Incremental Transformer (INCRT) for physics-constrained inverse design, applied to geopolymer mixture design. The method integrates intrinsic-dimensionality analysis, mixed-variable design-space representation, tabular surrogate prediction, INCRT-based manifold rationalisation, and constrained inverse optimisation. Using a public benchmark of fly-ash and slag-based geopolymer concrete mixtures with compressive-strength and carbon-emission targets, the high-dimensional design space proves strongly redundant, organising around fewer effective mixture regimes. Compressive strength requires nonlinear tabular surrogates, while carbon emission is largely determined by composition and well recovered by regularised linear models. INCRT thus acts not as a replacement for tabular predictors but as a rationalisation layer providing prototype regimes and a manifold-support score for inverse design. Three strategies are compared: unconstrained surrogate optimisation, physics-constrained optimisation, and topology-aware physics-constrained optimisation. Unconstrained optimisation can match target strength but may yield physically invalid or off-manifold candidates; physics-only constraints do not always ensure data support. The topology-aware strategy yields candidates balancing target compliance, carbon reduction, physical admissibility, and proximity to the learned feasible manifold. The framework aims not to replace experimental validation but to support screening of credible candidate mixtures from small, mixed, physically constrained engineering datasets.

</details>


### [162] [Learning Linear Temporal Specifications from Demonstrations with Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10918)
*Parastou Fahim,Constantino Lagoa,Rômulo Meira-G'oes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework for learning minimal LTL formulas from uncertain system demonstrations, modeling uncertainty via Hamming distance neighborhoods and reducing the problem to Pseudo-Boolean Optimization, outperforming existing methods under trace uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LTL learning approaches assume demonstrations are correct or only affected by misclassification errors. In practice, system traces often contain uncertainty due to sensor faults, measurement errors, or data loss, which prior methods fail to handle adequately.

Method: The authors model uncertainty around each observed trace using Hamming distance to generate a set of possible estimates. Grouping constraints require that at least one trace per group is consistent with the learned LTL formula. The learning problem is then reduced to an equivalent Pseudo-Boolean Optimization (PBO) formulation to find a minimal LTL specification.

Result: Evaluation against state-of-the-art LTL learning approaches shows that the proposed method recovers specifications that more closely align with ground-truth formulas when demonstrations are affected by uncertainty.

Conclusion: The framework effectively handles uncertain demonstrations for learning minimal LTL specifications, bridging a critical gap in formal verification and controller synthesis for safety-critical domains where trace data is often incomplete or noisy.

Abstract: Learning temporal logic specifications from system demonstrations is essential for tasks such as formal verification and controller synthesis, especially in safety-critical domains. Existing approaches typically assume demonstrations are correct or only affected by misclassification errors. In practice, however, system traces are often uncertain or incomplete due to sensor faults, measurement errors, or data loss. We present a framework for learning minimal Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas from demonstrations with uncertainty. Our approach models uncertainty via Hamming distance to generate possible estimates around each observed trace, which are grouped with constraints requiring that at least one trace per group is consistent with the learned formula. Our problem is then reduced to an equivalent Pseudo-Boolean Optimization. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art LTL learning approaches and show that it recovers specifications that more closely align with ground-truth formulas under uncertainty.

</details>


### [163] [SVR-R1: Bootstrapping Multi-modal Reasoning with Self-verification in Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10966)
*Mingyuan Wu,Jingcheng Yang,Shengyi Qian,Xudong Wang,Jize Jiang,Qifan Wang,Aashu Singh,Khoi Pham,Fei Liu,Zhaolun Su,Zhuokai Zhao,Klara Nahrstedt,Jianyu Wang,Hanchao Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SVR-R1 is a multi-turn RL framework that uses the model's own binary self-verification (Yes/No) as a learning signal; a "No" triggers rethinking, and final answers are rewarded based on outcomes. It improves VLM reasoning accuracy over GRPO baselines without external supervision, showing that verification reliance decreases as self-correction is internalized.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal reasoning approaches either lack mechanisms for self-correction during inference or fail to integrate such self-refinement directly into RL training. The authors aim to bridge inference-time self-refinement and RL training for vision-language models (VLMs) by using the model's own verification as an internal learning signal, without requiring external supervision or auxiliary critics.

Method: SVR-R1 employs a multi-turn RL framework with GRPO and asynchronous rollout. For each query, the model generates an answer and a binary self-verdict (Yes/No) using the same weights. A "No" triggers a second-chance rethinking turn; a "Yes" or reaching a turn cap finalizes the output. The finalized answer receives an outcome-based reward, with no external supervision or auxiliary critics needed.

Result: SVR-R1 improves accuracy by a large margin over strong standard GRPO baselines on vision-language reasoning benchmarks. Training dynamics reveal decreasing reliance on verification (fewer verification turns over time) coupled with rising test accuracy, indicating the policy internalizes self-correction and learns to select the most confident answer.

Conclusion: SVR-R1 demonstrates that turning a model's own verification into an RL learning signal is a simple yet effective recipe for bootstrapping multimodal reasoning. The framework bridges inference-time self-refinement and RL training for VLMs, and the authors commit to open-sourcing it to facilitate further research.

Abstract: We introduce Self-Verified Reasoner (SVR-R1), a multi-turn RL framework that turns a model's own verification into a learning signal for multimodal reasoning. For each query, the model proposes an answer using the same weights, and issues a binary self-verdict (Yes/No). A 'No' triggers a second-chance rethink; a 'Yes,' or a turn cap, finalizes the output for computing the outcome-based reward. SVR-R1 is implemented with GRPO and an asynchronous multi-turn rollout framework and needs no external supervision or auxiliary critics. We evaluate SVR-R1 on vision-language reasoning benchmarks and show that it improves accuracy by a large margin over strong standard GRPO baselines. Training dynamics show decreasing reliance on verification-fewer verification turns, yet higher test accuracy-indicating that the gap between verification and generation narrows as the policy internalizes self-correction and chooses the most confident answer via our framework. SVR-R1 bridges the less explored intersection of inference-time self-refinement and RL training for VLMs, offering a simple yet effective recipe for bootstrapping multimodal reasoning. We will open-source \textbf{SVR-R1} to facilitate future research in VLMs.

</details>


### [164] [From Checker to Forecaster: Code-Owned Evaluation of Model-Generated Strategic Routes Under Delayed Ground Truth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10972)
*Aleh Manchuliantsau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RouteCast proposes a forecasting-based evaluation framework for model outputs when ground truth is delayed, censored, or private. Instead of deterministic scoring, a code-owned provisional forecast is issued. A pilot study on 21 binary-outcome strategic route cases shows preliminary discriminative performance (AUC 0.756), comparable to an identity-exposed LLM judge but with reduced leakage risk. Ablation suggests typed staged routes perform similarly to the full packet.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional model evaluation relies on immediate correctness checks or in-loop feedback. However, in many real-world settings, ground truth arrives late, is censored, or remains private, making deterministic scoring impossible at evaluation time. The authors aim to address this gap by introducing a forecasting-based evaluation regime where a provisional forecast substitutes for unavailable ground-truth verification.

Method: RouteCast introduces a framework where models propose candidate typed strategic routes along with structured factors. Point-in-time evidence, reference classes, and deterministic transformations are combined to produce a provisional forecast-ranking. Later outcomes serve to evaluate the forecast quality. The method was tested retrospectively on 21 binary-outcome cases (6 positive, 15 negative) using AUC as the discrimination metric. A preregistered decomposition ablation compared the whole-packet score against typed staged routes alone and a deterministic heuristic. LLM judges (blind vs. identity-exposed) were also benchmarked.

Result: The whole-packet RouteCast score achieved AUC 0.756 (95% CI [0.471, 0.980]). A blind LLM judge reached AUC 0.678 [0.419, 0.897], while an identity-exposed LLM judge reached AUC 0.761 [0.515, 0.944] — suggestive of leakage risk. The ablation found typed staged routes indistinguishable from the whole-packet score (ΔAUC = -0.144, 95% CI [-0.471, 0.176]) and from a deterministic heuristic (ΔAUC = -0.089, 95% CI [-0.412, 0.278]).

Conclusion: The pilot demonstrates feasibility and auditability of the RouteCast forecasting regime while exposing failure modes. It does not establish prospective calibration, causal decision improvement, route-decomposition advantage, or cross-domain validity. The authors explicitly bound the claims, positioning this as an initial feasibility result rather than a validated system.

Abstract: Many evaluations of model outputs rely either on contracts checkable at evaluation time or on feedback that arrives within the operating loop. We study the complementary setting in which ground truth is delayed, censored, or private, so deterministic code cannot check correctness at scoring time and must instead issue a code-owned provisional forecast. RouteCast instantiates this regime for model-generated typed strategic routes: models propose candidate routes and structured factors; point-in-time evidence, reference classes, and deterministic transformations produce a provisional forecast-ranking; later outcomes evaluate the forecast. In a retrospective venture pilot on 21 binary-outcome cases (6 positive, 15 negative), the whole-packet RouteCast score showed preliminary retrospective discrimination (AUC 0.756, 95% CI [0.471,0.980]), while a blind LLM judge reached AUC 0.678 [0.419,0.897] and an identity-exposed LLM judge reached AUC 0.761 [0.515,0.944], consistent with recognition- or outcome-related leakage risk. A preregistered decomposition ablation on the same binary subset found that converting the identical inputs into typed staged routes was indistinguishable from the whole-packet score (Delta AUC = -0.144, 95% CI [-0.471,0.176]) and from a deterministic heuristic (Delta AUC = -0.089, 95% CI [-0.412,0.278]). The pilot establishes an auditable feasibility result and exposes failure modes; it does not establish prospective calibration, causal decision improvement, route-decomposition advantage, or cross-domain validity.

</details>


### [165] [QwenPaw-Data: Bridging Facts, Methodology, and Execution for Autonomous Enterprise Data Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11019)
*Tianjing Zeng,Yuntao Hong,Zhongjun Ding,Dandan Liu,Yinan Mei,Yunxiang Su,Yiming Wang,Xiaojian Zhang,Jingyu Zhu,Junhao Zhu,Zhuowen Liang,Jiazhen Peng,Lianggui Weng,Zhihao Ding,Kerui Yi,Qifeng Wang,Rong Zhu,Bolin Ding,Liyu Mou,Jingren Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QwenPaw-Data is an agentic data system for enterprise analysis that consolidates heterogeneous assets and turns natural-language requests into end-to-end analytical workflows, built on three subsystems (DataBridge, Skill-Hub, Host) that form a self-evolving asset flywheel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise data analysis presents unique challenges — open, ambiguous, and continuously evolving environments — that demand a data-agent architecture treating semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class concerns, unlike general-purpose agents.

Method: QwenPaw-Data decomposes into three collaborative subsystems: (1) DataBridge for trustworthy semantic grounding via interconnected metadata, knowledge, and trace graphs; (2) Skill-Hub for codifying expert analytical methodology into reusable, verifiable skills; (3) Host for materializing evidence and method assets into controllable, artifact-centric runtime execution. Semantics, methods, traces, and feedback are continuously deposited back into the system, creating a self-evolving asset flywheel.

Result: Experiments on public benchmarks and real-world industrial BI workloads demonstrate improved verifiable data access capability and higher-level analytical quality compared to existing approaches.

Conclusion: QwenPaw-Data offers a practical foundation for reliable, traceable, and continuously improving enterprise data agents by treating semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class system concerns within a self-evolving architecture.

Abstract: Enterprise data analysis is emerging as a distinct frontier for autonomous agents. Compared with general-purpose interaction and software engineering, it operates in an open, ambiguous, and continuously evolving environment. These characteristics call for a data-agent architecture that treats semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class system concerns. To this end, we introduce QwenPaw-Data, an agentic data system designed for enterprise intelligent data analysis. QwenPaw-Data consolidates heterogeneous assets from warehouses, dashboards, documents, interaction logs, and historical tasks into reusable, governable, and evolvable analysis assets, then turns natural-language requests into end-to-end analytical workflows spanning data understanding, retrieval, analysis, report generation, and decision support. Its architecture decomposes the problem into three collaborative subsystems: DataBridge provides trustworthy semantic grounding through interconnected metadata, knowledge, and trace graphs; Skill-Hub codifies expert analytical methodology into reusable and verifiable skills; and Host materializes these evidence and method assets into controllable, artifact-centric runtime execution. Across these subsystems, semantics, methods, traces, and feedback are continuously deposited back into the system, forming a self-evolving asset flywheel. Experiments on public benchmarks and real-world industrial BI workloads show that QwenPaw-Data improves both verifiable data access capability and higher-level analytical quality, offering a practical foundation for reliable, traceable, and continuously improving enterprise data agents.

</details>


### [166] [AdvNav: Behavior-Guided Black-Box Adversarial Attacks on Vision-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11063)
*Chenyang Li,Kaige Li,Zeyu Jiang,Changhao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AdvNav is a black-box adversarial attack framework for Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) that disrupts an agent's first-person views using only observable inputs/outputs. It employs dual-granularity behavior-based feedback (trajectory-level performance + action-level reward + deviation) to guide a hybrid genetic-adaptive optimization strategy, achieving up to 87.30% Attack Success Rate on R2R against Transformer and LLM-based VLN models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLN adversarial attacks rely on white-box gradient access (unrealistic for deployed systems and computationally expensive) or target only single-step tasks, failing to handle the temporal dependencies of multi-step sequential perception-action loops. There is a need for a gradient-free, black-box attack that operates solely on observable inputs and outputs.

Method: AdvNav proposes a behavior-guided black-box attack with three components: (1) A dual-granularity behavior-based feedback mechanism that extracts a trajectory-level performance score, an action-level reward score capturing decision risk, and a deviation indicator — all derived from the agent's self-output behaviors without gradient access. (2) This feedback guides a hybrid optimization strategy that heuristically tunes perturbation strength via adaptive updates and evolves noise spatial structure using a genetic algorithm. (3) The attack iteratively discovers the most disruptive noise configuration applied to the agent's first-person views during navigation.

Result: Evaluated on the R2R dataset against Transformer-based HAMT and LLM-based MapGPT with two backbone types, AdvNav achieves 49.70%, 65.96%, and 87.30% Attack Success Rate across different settings, demonstrating both effectiveness and generality.

Conclusion: AdvNav effectively exposes critical perception vulnerabilities in VLN systems under realistic black-box constraints. Its success provides insights for designing more resilient future VLN models and highlights the importance of robustness in embodied navigation systems.

Abstract: Despite progress in Embodied AI, Vision-and-Language Navigation systems remain vulnerable to adversarial visual disturbances. Most existing methods rely on white-box access to target model gradients, which is often unrealistic for real-world deployed systems and computationally exhaustive due to recursive backpropagation for optimization, limiting their applicability. While previous black-box methods predominantly target single-step, instantaneous decision tasks, they struggle to handle the task complexities and temporal dependencies. This highlights the need for a gradient-free attack method that can effectively disrupt the multistep sequential perception-action loop using only observable inputs and outputs. Therefore, we propose AdvNav, a behavior-guided black-box adversarial attack framework that disturbs an agent's first-person views during navigation. To construct an informative surrogate objective for effective optimization guidance in gradient-free search under the black-box setting, we design a dual-granularity behavior-based feedback, aggregating a trajectory-level performance score representing overall navigation degradation, an action-level reward score considering the potential decision risk, and a deviation indicator, all of which are extracted from the agent's self-output behaviors. This feedback guides a hybrid optimization strategy that heuristically tunes perturbation strength via adaptive updates and evolves noise spatial structure genetically, to iteratively discover the most disruptive noise configuration. Evaluated against Transformer-based HAMT and LLM-based MapGPT with two types of backbones on R2R dataset, AdvNav achieves 49.70/65.96/87.30% Attack Success Rate. The result demonstrates the effectiveness and generality of AdvNav, reveals critical perception vulnerabilities and offers insights for the design of future resilient VLN models.

</details>

### [167] [Trivial Prompt Reframing Bypasses Safety Guardrails in Googleś MedGemma-4B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09804)
*Avi-ad Avraam Buskila*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MedGemma-4B-it, an open-weight medical LLM, violates its own model-card prohibitions 38% of the time under lay-accessible attacks. Recasting prohibited questions as "medical board exam" items or invoking a doctor's authority dramatically increases compliance, while topic-level guardrail strength varies enormously (drug-interaction: 83.2% ASR; emergency-deferral: 4.7%). Results motivate stronger deployment-time safeguards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-weight medical LLMs are increasingly deployed in patient-facing and clinician-support contexts. Their model cards explicitly prohibit dangerous behaviors (drug dosing, definitive diagnosis, treatment prescription, drug-drug interaction adjudication, skipping emergency care), but these are statements of intent, not enforced robustness. The authors aim to quantify the gap between intended and actual behavior by measuring how easily these guardrails fail under attacks requiring zero technical sophistication.

Method: A fully factorial benchmark: 5 guarded-behavior concepts × 50 templated questions × 6 lay-accessible attack manners × 3 repetitions = 4,500 generations. MedGemma-4B-it served locally via Ollama (default sampling). Every response triple-coded (refuse/hedge/comply) by three independent judges: an LLM judge (primary), a transparent regex judge, and an NLI-entailment judge. Statistical rigor includes Wilson confidence intervals, cluster-bootstrap effect sizes, cluster-robust logistic regression, Cochran's Q, per-manner McNemar tests, and Fleiss' kappa for inter-judge reliability.

Result: Under the primary LLM judge, overall Attack Success Rate (ASR) = 38.0%. Two framing attacks dominate: "medical board exam" reframing raises ASR from 29.0% baseline to 53.1% (+24.0 pp); doctor-authority appeal raises it to 43.7% (+14.7 pp). Crude instruction-override prefixes had no significant effect. Topic-level robustness is highly uneven: drug-interaction guardrail nearly absent (83.2% ASR), emergency-deferral guardrail strongest (4.7% ASR); only authority framing breached the emergency-deferral guardrail. Absolute ASR is judge-dependent, but the ordering of attacks and topics is consistent across judges. Fleiss' kappa = 0.26.

Conclusion: Model-card prohibitions do not translate into robust refusal behavior in open-weight medical LLMs. Simple, lay-accessible prompt-level attacks — particularly legitimacy-reframing tactics — reliably circumvent most guardrails. The extreme variation across topics suggests guardrail training is uneven. Stronger deployment-time guardrails (e.g., input/output classifiers, prompt-armoring) are needed for open medical models in real-world applications.

Abstract: Open-weight medical language models are increasingly used as the base of patient-facing and clinician-support applications. Their model cards prohibit specific behaviors -- recommending exact drug dosages, issuing definitive diagnoses, prescribing treatments, adjudicating drug-drug interactions, and advising that emergency care can be skipped -- yet a model card describes intended behavior, not robust behavior. We quantify that gap for MedGemma-4B-it under attacks that require no technical sophistication. We build a fully factorial benchmark of 5 guarded-behavior concepts x 50 deterministically templated questions x 6 lay-accessible attack manners x 3 repetitions (4,500 generations), serve the model locally through Ollama under default sampling, and code every response refuse/hedge/comply with three independent judges (an LLM judge, a transparent regex judge, and an NLI-entailment judge). Under the primary LLM judge the overall Attack Success Rate (ASR, the fraction coded comply) is 38.0%. The two framings that reinterpret the request as legitimate dominate: recasting a question as a "medical board exam" item raises ASR from a 29.0% baseline to 53.1% (+24.0 points), and an appeal to an alleged doctor's authority raises it to 43.7% (+14.7); crude instruction-override prefixes have no significant effect. Robustness is dominated by topic: the drug-interaction guardrail is nearly absent (83.2% ASR) while the emergency-deferral guardrail is strong (4.7%) -- and the authority framing is the only attack that breaches it. We report Wilson confidence intervals, cluster-bootstrap effect sizes, a cluster-robust logistic regression, Cochran's Q, per-manner McNemar tests, and inter-judge reliability (Fleiss' kappa = 0.26); absolute ASR is judge-dependent while the ordering of attacks and topics is not. Our findings motivate stronger deployment-time guardrails for open medical models.

</details>


### [168] [A Guess and Determine Attack on the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09814)
*Ayan Mahalanobis*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper extends prior work on a Las Vegas algorithm for the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) by reducing it to finding a zero minor in a matrix, then develops a new algorithm for zero-minor detection using the intersection poset of a hyperplane arrangement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Solving the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) is of fundamental importance in cryptography. The authors' prior Las Vegas algorithm reduces ECDLP to the problem of finding a zero minor in a matrix, motivating the need for an efficient zero-minor detection method.

Method: The authors leverage the intersection poset of a hyperplane arrangement to develop an algorithm for finding a zero minor in a rectangular matrix. The approach is described as elementary and is accompanied by complexity analysis, success probability estimation, and implementation/simulation details.

Result: An algorithm for zero-minor detection in rectangular matrices is presented, with its complexity and success probability analyzed. Implementation and simulation results are provided to validate the approach.

Conclusion: The intersection poset of a hyperplane arrangement provides a viable combinatorial framework for zero-minor detection, which in turn feeds into a Las Vegas algorithm for ECDLP. The zero-minor problem itself is noted to be of independent mathematical interest.

Abstract: This paper is a continuation of our earlier work, in which, we described a Las Vegas algorithm to solve the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. The Las Vegas algorithm reduces the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem to finding a zero minor in a matrix. Using intersection poset of a hyperplane arrangement, we develop an algorithm to find a zero minor in a rectangular matrix. Our methods are elementary. We discuss the complexity of our algorithm, success probability and provide implementation details. We also provide simulation details. Finding a zero minor in a matrix is also of independent interest.

</details>


### [169] [Generative Testing of Automated Speech Recognition Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09833)
*Yanis Xabier Wilbrand Peña,Oliver Weißl,Andrea Stocco*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: GATAS is a black-box adversarial attack on ASR systems that operates in the phoneme-level latent space of a TTS model via latent interpolation, achieving 98% attack success rate with superior perceptual quality compared to both white-box and black-box baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer-based ASR systems, despite high accuracy, remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing black-box methods struggle to balance attack efficacy with perceptual naturalness. There is a need for attacks that generate failure-inducing inputs while preserving speech naturalness, without requiring gradient access to the target ASR model.

Method: GATAS operates in the phoneme-level latent space of a text-to-speech (TTS) model rather than perturbing waveforms directly. It interpolates latent representations to induce transcription errors while staying on the manifold of natural speech. The attack is formalized as a multi-objective optimization problem that balances semantic divergence (driving ASR errors) and perceptual quality (maintaining naturalness). No gradient access to the target ASR is required.

Result: GATAS achieves a 98% success rate in inducing ASR transcription errors. It produces lower distortion and higher perceptual quality compared to both white-box and black-box baselines, as validated by human studies. Despite being black-box, it remains competitive with white-box methods.

Conclusion: Representation and perceptual alignment are more critical than access to model internals for effective ASR adversarial attacks. Untargeted latent-space optimization in the TTS manifold enables efficient generation of realistic and effective test cases, highlighting a viable path for robustness testing of deployed ASR systems.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have achieved high accuracy with transformer-based models, enabling deployment in critical applications. However, they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulation, particularly in black-box settings where attacks must preserve perceptual naturalness. This work introduces GATAS, a black-box testing approach that generates failure inducing inputs by operating in the phoneme-level latent space of a text- to-speech model. Instead of perturbing waveforms directly, the approach interpolates latent representations to induce transcription errors while remaining within the manifold of natural speech. The attack is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem balancing semantic divergence and perceptual quality. Our empirical evaluation against both white-box and black-box baselines shows that GATAS achieves a 98% success rate while producing lower distortion and higher perceptual quality, as confirmed by human studies. Despite operating without gradient access, GATAS remains competitive against white-box methods, highlighting that representation and perceptual alignment are more critical than access to model internals. Overall, our results demonstrate that untargeted latent-space optimization enables the efficient generation of realistic and effective test cases for ASR systems.

</details>


### [170] [A Hybrid Quantum-Chaos Theory Approach to Image Encryption Using Reservoir Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09923)
*Naheen Mohd. Kadir*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A hybrid image encryption system integrating quantum key distribution (E91 protocol), Lorenz hyper-chaotic system, and reservoir computing achieves fast encryption (~0.03s) with strong security metrics (NPCR >99.6%, UACI >0.49) for 128×128 images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional encryption schemes (RSA, DHKE) are vulnerable to quantum attacks such as Shor's and Grover's algorithms. There is a pressing need for image encryption methods that remain secure in the post-quantum era while maintaining practical computational efficiency.

Method: The proposed system combines three components: (1) the E91 quantum cryptographic protocol for generating secure, eavesdropping-resistant keys via quantum entanglement; (2) the Lorenz hyper-chaotic system to inject unpredictability and sensitivity to initial conditions; and (3) reservoir computing to accelerate encryption/decryption operations.

Result: For 128×128 images, encryption times reached as low as 0.0296s and decryption times as low as 0.0164s. MAE was reduced for 300–600 node reservoir networks. NPCR exceeded 99.6% and UACI surpassed 0.49 across various image sizes and configurations.

Conclusion: The fusion of quantum cryptography, chaos theory, and reservoir computing yields a practically feasible and secure image encryption framework suitable for the quantum computing era, offering both strong resistance to quantum attacks and high computational efficiency.

Abstract: This research presents a novel hybrid image encryption system that combines quantum cryptography, chaos theory and reservoir computing to address the limitations of conventional encryption methods. With the rapid advancements in quantum computing, traditional systems like RSA, DHKE (related to prime number factorization) are vulnerable to quantum attacks i.e. Shor's algorithm, Grover's algorithm. In response, this study proposes a hybrid solution that uses quantum cryptographic protocols, particularly the E91 protocol, to generate secure, eavesdrop-proof keys through quantum entanglement. The integration of chaos theory, specifically the Lorenz hyper-chaotic system, enhances the encryption system by adding unpredictability and sensitivity to initial conditions, making it more resistant to both classical and quantum-based attacks. Reservoir computing is used to improve computational efficiency, enabling faster and more effective encryption and decryption processes. The system achieved encryption times as low as 0.0296s and decryption times as low as 0.0164s for 128x128 images, with MAE reduced for 300-600 node networks, and NPCR and UACI above 99.6% and 0.49, respectively, across various image sizes and configurations. By combining quantum cryptography, chaos theory and reservoir computing, this approach offers both enhanced security and practical feasibility for image encryption in the age of quantum computing.

</details>


### [171] [Evaluating AI Models' Capability to Automate Voice Phishing Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09970)
*Fred Heiding,Claudio Mayrink Verdun,Simon Lermen,Andrew Kao,Vitor Albiero,Lauren Deason,Irina-Elena Veliche,Christine Lehane*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A large-scale study (N=4100 survey, N=12 interviews) finds that up to 36% of U.S. adults would or might comply with AI-generated voice phishing scams, with an overall 16.5% compliance rate across five scam categories. Certain AI voice models (notably Sesame) match or exceed human persuasiveness. The core risk is economic: AI automation makes vishing profitable at scale where human-operated vishing is not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional voice phishing (vishing) is constrained by the need for human operators, limiting scalability. The emergence of high-quality AI voice synthesis and LLMs removes this bottleneck, potentially enabling automated, large-scale scams. The study aims to empirically quantify how susceptible U.S. adults are to these AI-powered vishing attacks and assess their economic viability.

Method: A mixed-methods design: (1) a large-scale survey experiment (N=4100) where participants were exposed to audio recordings or transcripts of scam scenarios generated by six leading voice models (Llama Full Duplex, Sesame, Gemini, OAI AVM, Play.AI, ElevenLabs) alongside human baselines; (2) qualitative interviews (N=12). Five scam categories were tested, including "relative-in-distress." Compliance rates, persuasiveness ratings, and economic cost-benefit analyses were evaluated.

Result: Up to 36% of participants would or might comply in the "relative-in-distress" category; overall compliance was 16.5% across all categories. Caller persuasiveness was the strongest predictor of compliance. Sesame achieved persuasiveness ratings comparable to or slightly exceeding human voices. Economic analysis showed AI-powered vishing is profitable for several models, unlike human-operated vishing at U.S. wages.

Conclusion: The primary risk of present-day AI-enabled vishing is economic — automation makes attacks viable at scale — rather than superhuman persuasion (though future systems may achieve this). This raises serious concerns for AI system design, consumer protection policy, and model release practices.

Abstract: Voice phishing (vishing) attacks have traditionally been limited by the need for human operators. The rapid emergence of high-quality AI voice synthesis and large language models (LLMs) reduces this bottleneck and enables scalable, automated scams. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale survey experiment (N=4100) and qualitative interviews (N=12) to assess U.S. adults' susceptibility to AI-powered voice phishing attacks. Participants were exposed to audio recordings or transcripts of scam scenarios generated using leading voice models such as Llama Full Duplex (Llama FD), Sesame, Gemini, OAI AVM, Play.AI, and ElevenLabs and the corresponding human baselines. The results show high compliance rates. Up to 36% of participants would or might comply with phishing requests in the "relative-in-distress" category. Overall compliance rate across all five scam categories was 16.5%, a striking figure given the low cost and high scalability of AI-automated voice phishing. Caller persuasiveness was the strongest predictor of compliance and certain models (most notably Sesame) achieved ratings comparable to human voices, or sometimes even slightly surpassing them. Our economic analysis suggests that while human-operated vishing is unprofitable at US wages, AI-powered vishing appears to be economically viable for several models. The primary risk of present-day AI-enabled vishing thus lies in the economics of automation rather than novel or "superhuman" persuasive techniques, though these cannot be ruled out for future systems. This raises significant concerns for the design of AI systems, consumer protection, and model release policies.

</details>


### [172] [SafeGuard: A Lightweight Client-Server Architecture for Real-Time Endpoint Threat Detection and Response](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10027)
*Gideon Francis Oghie,DivineDavid Shittu Abolanle*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SafeGuard is a lightweight, open-source three-tier EDR system for Android endpoints, featuring signature-based threat detection, WebSocket-over-TLS communication, JWT authentication, and an admin dashboard. Evaluated with 50 concurrent endpoints, it achieved sub-2-second command-dispatch latency and resisted basic attacks, demonstrating that cost-effective endpoint visibility is feasible without commercial licensing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial EDR platforms are prohibitively expensive and operationally complex for small, resource-constrained organizations, leaving endpoint devices—a primary cyberattack target—underprotected in these environments.

Method: A three-tier client-server architecture: (1) a Flutter/Kotlin endpoint agent on Android; (2) a Node.js central server handling device authentication, secure communication coordination, and threat database matching; (3) an administrative dashboard for live monitoring and remote actions (device locking, app removal, warnings). Threat detection uses signature-based comparison for low overhead and explainability. Security relies on WSS, JWT, and HMAC integrity verification. Evaluation included unit, integration, system, load, and preliminary security testing with 50 simulated concurrent endpoints.

Result: Average command-dispatch latency was ~1.5 seconds and stayed below 2 seconds under load. Invalid JWT tokens were correctly rejected; manual SQL injection and replay attacks were unsuccessful in tested scenarios.

Conclusion: Open-source technologies can deliver real-time endpoint monitoring and coordinated administrative response without licensing costs. The contribution is architectural and empirical. Limitations include static signature reliance, Android-only scope, and controlled-environment evaluation.

Abstract: Endpoint devices remain a primary target for cyberattacks, yet commercial Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) platforms are often too costly and operationally complex for small and resource-constrained organizations. This paper presents SafeGuard, a lightweight three-tier client-server architecture for real-time endpoint monitoring, threat reporting, and administrative response. The system comprises a Flutter-based endpoint agent extended with Kotlin for Android system access, a Node.js central server that authenticates devices and coordinates secure communication, and an administrative dashboard for live monitoring and remote actions such as device locking, application removal, and warning notification dispatch. Threat detection is implemented through signature-based comparison against a maintained threat database, prioritizing low computational overhead, explainability, and ease of deployment over generalized anomaly detection. Communication security is achieved using WebSocket over TLS (WSS), JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication, and HMAC-based message integrity verification. The system was evaluated through unit, integration, system, load, and preliminary security testing. Under a simulated deployment of 50 concurrent endpoints, average command-dispatch latency was approximately 1.5 seconds and remained below 2 seconds under load. Invalid authentication tokens were rejected, while manual SQL injection and replay attempts were unsuccessful in the evaluated scenarios. The results demonstrate that an open-source technology stack can provide real-time endpoint visibility and coordinated administrative response without commercial licensing costs. The contribution is architectural and empirical rather than algorithmic, with current limitations including reliance on static threat signatures, Android-focused implementation, and controlled-environment evaluation.

</details>


### [173] [Federated Cybersecurity Testbed as a Service (FCTaaS): A framework to federate cybersecurity testbeds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10061)
*Josh Dean,Yu-Zheng Lin,John Paul Martin Encinas,Ibrahim Almazyad,Qinxuan Shi,Zhanglong Yang,Shalaka Satam,Tingjun Lei,Jielun Zhang,Sicong Shao,Salim Hariri,Pratik Satam*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FCTaaS is a federated framework that connects heterogeneous cybersecurity testbeds via VPN, enabling cross-geographical experiments with only 1% overhead, 49% max network utilization, and 5.63–147 ms latency across nodes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rapid technological change makes it difficult and costly for individual cybersecurity testbeds to stay state-of-the-art, and specialized testbed access is often restricted to small groups, leaving infrastructure underutilized.

Method: Proposes FCTaaS, a Federated Cybersecurity Testbed as a Service framework that connects independently managed, heterogeneous testbeds through VPN for remote discovery, experiment design, and coordinated experimentation. Evaluated via three case studies: denial-of-service on smart infrastructure and Suricata-based IDS/IPS intrusion detection/prevention workflows.

Result: FCTaaS enables effective cross-testbed experimentation with visibility into attack traffic, IDS alerts, and resource stress. Achieves limiting network utilization of 49%, only 1% overhead, and latency from 5.63 ms (local) to 147 ms (geographically dispersed).

Conclusion: FCTaaS successfully demonstrates that federating heterogeneous cybersecurity testbeds as a service is feasible and efficient, enabling broader access, resource sharing, and representative experimentation across geographical boundaries with minimal performance degradation.

Abstract: Rapid technological change is reshaping society through emerging domains such as autonomous vehicles and smart manufacturing, creating new research challenges in system design, operation, security, and training. Researchers often rely on testbeds to reproduce experimental scenarios, collect and analyze data, observe system behavior, and evaluate proposed solutions. However, the fast pace of innovation makes it difficult and costly for individual testbeds to remain representative of state-of-the-art systems, as doing so requires frequent upgrades and new capabilities. Moreover, access to specialized testbeds is often limited to a small group of researchers, leaving valuable infrastructure underutilized during its operational lifetime. This paper presents FCTaaS, a Federated Cybersecurity Testbed as a Service framework that enables heterogeneous cybersecurity testbeds to participate in a single experiment across geographical boundaries. By connecting independently managed testbeds through a Virtual Private Network (VPN), FCTaaS supports remote testbed discovery, experiment design, and coordinated experimentation. We evaluate FCTaaS across three case studies involving denial-of-service scenarios on smart infrastructure and intrusion detection and prevention workflows using a Suricata-based IDS/IPS testbed. The results show that FCTaaS enables effective cross-testbed experimentation while preserving visibility into attack traffic, IDS alerts, and detection-system resource stress. Even under resource-intensive attack scenarios, FCTaaS achieves limiting network utilization of 49%, introduces only 1% overhead, and supports latency ranging from 5.63 ms between local nodes to 147 ms between geographically dispersed nodes.

</details>


### [174] [A Survey on LLM Watermarking: Theory and Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10103)
*Huy Phan,Kieu Dang,Ojaswi Dulal,Aiham AL Shukairi,Abby Shine,Chase Garner,Phung Lai*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic survey organizing LLM watermarking literature around deployment-centric questions: embedding location, detection authority, assumptions, and threat models. It synthesizes techniques (sampling biasing, code-based, representation/training-based), analyzes security-utility trade-offs, reviews attacks and evaluation protocols, and provides practical guidance for real-world deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs enable large-scale fluent text generation, amplifying risks of provenance ambiguity, model misuse, and content laundering. Watermarking offers a technical solution for attribution and auditing, but the literature is fragmented — existing categorizations conflate orthogonal design choices, hindering comparison, reasoning about guarantees, and practical deployment.

Method: The survey organizes the design space along four practitioner-relevant axes: (1) where watermarks are embedded (generation-time vs. training-time; token-level vs. representation-level), (2) who can detect them (public vs. private detection authority), (3) what assumptions are made (logit access, sampling control, secret keys, model ownership), and (4) which threat models are considered (paraphrasing, translation, summarization, style transfer, token manipulation, adaptive removal). It then maps existing techniques — sampling biasing, code-based schemes, representation- and training-based approaches — onto this framework and evaluates their security-utility trade-offs.

Result: The survey synthesizes key findings across technique families: sampling-biasing methods offer strong detectability but face robustness challenges under paraphrasing; code-based schemes provide statistical guarantees; training-based approaches shift the watermark into model weights. It consolidates evaluation protocols (false positive control, calibration, robustness curves) and catalogs attack/evasion strategies. The analysis reveals gaps in cross-model transfer, multi-modal pipelines, collusion resistance, and governance integration.

Conclusion: LLM watermarking is maturing but requires deployment-oriented standardization. The four-axis framework enables principled comparison and selection of watermark designs under operational constraints. Key open challenges include cross-model transfer, multi-modal watermarking, collusion attacks, and alignment with governance frameworks. The authors provide practical guidance for practitioners and chart future research directions for reliable, accountable LLM deployment.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in high-impact workflows, yet their ability to generate fluent text at scale has amplified risks of provenance ambiguity, model misuse, and large-scale content laundering. LLM watermarking, embedding invisible signatures into model outputs, has emerged as a promising technical layer for attribution, auditing, and downstream trust decisions. However, the literature has grown rapidly and unevenly: existing categorizations often mix orthogonal design choices, making it difficult to compare methods, reason about guarantees, or translate research results into deployable systems. This survey provides a systematic, deployment-oriented review of LLM watermarking. We organize the space by the core questions practitioners must answer: where a watermark is embedded (generation-time vs. training-time, token vs. representation), who can detect it (public vs. private detection authority), what is assumed (access to logits, sampling control, secret keys, model ownership), and which threat models are targeted (paraphrasing, translation, summarization, style transfer, token manipulation, and adaptive removal). We synthesize the main families of techniques-including sampling biasing, code-based schemes, representation- and training-based approaches-and analyze their security-utility trade-offs through the lens of detectability, robustness, and distribution shift. We further review attack and evasion strategies, evaluation protocols and metrics (false positive control, calibration, robustness curves), and open challenges such as cross-model transfer, multi-modal pipelines, collusion, and governance constraints. Finally, we provide practical guidance for selecting watermark designs under real operational requirements and identify research directions needed for reliable, accountable LLM deployment.

</details>


### [175] [Minionese: Comprehensive Benchmark and Mechanistic Study of Multilingual LLM Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10112)
*Chigozirim Ifebi,Brent Kong,Ayushi Mehrotra*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Minionese is a multilingual jailbreak benchmark covering 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 perturbation types, paired with mechanistic analysis revealing that low-resource jailbreaks bypass refusal mechanisms by routing harmful content through a geometrically misaligned subspace that fails to project onto refusal directions, even though the refusal circuitry remains intact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety alignment in LLMs is brittle across languages — prompts reliably refused in English succeed harmfully in non-English and low-resource settings. Existing evaluations lack systematic coverage across language resource tiers, perturbation types, and mechanistic understanding of why refusal fails.

Method: The authors introduce Minionese, a benchmark spanning 18 languages across 4 resource tiers with 4 perturbation types (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese). They conduct geometric mechanistic analysis, examining how hidden representations of harmful content project onto refusal directions across language tiers, identifying a "misaligned subspace" phenomenon and a sharp safety regime transition between Tiers 2 and 3.

Result: Each attack type produces a distinct vulnerability profile: transliteration vulnerability depends on script identity; code-switching remains effective even at the lowest-resource tier; and a consistent sharp safety regime transition occurs between Tiers 2 and 3 across all models. Mechanistically, low-resource jailbreaks succeed because harmful representations route through a subspace that insufficiently projects onto refusal directions, leaving the refusal mechanism intact but untriggered.

Conclusion: English-only safety evaluations are insufficient. Robust multilingual safety requires accounting for script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage. The refusal mechanism itself may be intact in low-resource languages, but harmful content geometrically bypasses it.

Abstract: Safety alignment in large language models remains brittle across languages: prompts reliably refused in English can elicit harmful compliance in non-English and low-resource settings. We introduce \textsc{Minionese}, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 perturbation types (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, and translationese), paired with a geometric mechanistic analysis of refusal failure across language tiers. We show that each attack type produces a distinct vulnerability profile: transliteration vulnerability is mediated by script identity, code-switching maintains effectiveness through the lowest-resource tier, and a sharp safety regime transition between Tiers 2 and 3 is consistent across all models. Mechanistically, low-resource jailbreaks succeed by routing harmful content through a geometrically misaligned subspace that projects insufficiently onto the refusal directions, leaving the refusal mechanism intact but untriggered. These findings show that English-only safety evaluations are insufficient; they require accounting for script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage. The benchmark and analysis code is at https://github.com/Brentkong/Minionese-Comprehensive-Benchmark-and-Mechanistic-Study-of-Multilingual-LLM-Safety.git.

</details>


### [176] [Toward Stronger Code Watermarking: A Grammar-Driven Approach to Optimizing the Trade-off Between Quality and Detectability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10210)
*Licheng Yu,Aiwei Liu,Songze Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: GDW proposes a grammar-driven watermarking method for LLM code generation that uses three-level masking and role-aware modulation to balance code quality and watermark detectability, outperforming existing methods while resisting variable-renaming attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing logits-based text watermarking methods fail on code generation because code has low entropy, intensifying the trade-off between preserving syntactic correctness and maintaining watermark detectability.

Method: GDW employs: (1) a grammar-guided three-level masking mechanism to preserve syntactic validity; (2) structural role-aware modulation that assigns stronger watermark bias to content-bearing tokens and conservative bias to syntax-critical tokens; and (3) a role-aware weighted detection statistic aligned with the generation process to enhance detectability.

Result: Experiments across multiple programming languages, models, and decoding strategies demonstrate that GDW achieves a superior quality-detectability trade-off frontier compared to existing methods and remains robust against variable-renaming attacks.

Conclusion: GDW effectively addresses the unique challenges of low-entropy code watermarking by leveraging grammatical structure, establishing a new state-of-the-art in code watermarking for LLMs.

Abstract: With the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs), text watermarking has emerged as a crucial technique for identifying machine-generated content. However, directly applying existing logits-based watermarking methods to code generation remains challenging, since the low-entropy nature of code exacerbates the trade-off between code quality and watermark detectability. In this paper, we propose a novel code watermarking approach called Grammar-Driven Watermark (GDW) for LLMs. GDW preserves syntactic validity through a grammar-guided three-level masking mechanism and injects watermark signals via structural role-aware modulation, assigning a stronger bias to content-bearing tokens while applying a more conservative bias to syntax-critical tokens. Aligning with the generation process, we further design a role-aware weighted detection statistic to improve detectability. Experiments across multiple programming languages, models, and decoding strategies show that GDW establishes a stronger quality-detectability trade-off frontier than existing methods, while maintaining robustness against variable-renaming attacks.

</details>


### [177] [One Token Is Enough: Fingerprinting and Verifying Large Language Models from Single-Token Output Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10252)
*Tomas Bruckner*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LLMs can be identified by their behavioral fingerprint—the empirical distribution of answers to trivial one-word prompts (e.g., "name a random number between 1 and 100"). Using just single-token outputs, the method recovers model lineage, achieves a 7.3% equal error rate in verification, and exposes ecosystem anomalies like a proprietary endpoint indistinguishable from an open-weight model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are often consumed through opaque serving chains (API aggregators, resellers, inference providers) where clients cannot verify which model is actually responding. Prior audits reveal many commercial endpoints deviate from advertised reference weights. Existing identification methods are impractical—they require long generated texts, token-level log-probabilities (often unavailable), adversarial prompts, or cooperation from the model owner. A lightweight, black-box, low-cost identification method is needed.

Method: The authors define a behavioral fingerprint as the empirical distribution of an LLM's answers to trivial one-word prompts (e.g., "name a random number between 1 and 100"), collected across four languages, costing only one output token per query. They measure 165 models via the OpenRouter aggregator. They then: (1) compute Jensen-Shannon divergence between fingerprint distributions to assess distinguishability and recover model lineage; (2) evaluate a biometric-style verification protocol using a battery of up to 40 probe cells, measuring equal error rate (EER) as a function of probe count.

Result: Key findings: (i) Response distributions are highly non-uniform (median cell entropy ~1.0 bit) and strongly model-specific—split-half samples of the same model are an order of magnitude closer than samples from different models. (ii) JS divergence recovers model family with 59.5% leave-one-out accuracy (vs. 18.4% chance). (iii) The verification protocol achieves 7.3% EER with the full 40-cell battery and below 11% EER with only 8 probe cells (~100 single-token queries per audit). A notable anomaly: a proprietary-branded flagship endpoint was distributionally indistinguishable from an open-weight Qwen model.

Conclusion: Far weaker evidence than previously assumed suffices to fingerprint and verify LLMs. The proposed method is extremely lightweight (single-token outputs, no log-probabilities, no adversarial prompts), making it practical for operational auditing of opaque model-serving chains. The discovery of a proprietary endpoint indistinguishable from an open-weight model underscores the method's practical value for transparency and accountability in the LLM supply chain.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consumed through opaque serving chains - API aggregators, resellers, and inference providers - in which the client has no technical means to confirm that the model answering is the model advertised, and recent audits show that a substantial fraction of commercial endpoints deviate from the vendor's reference weights. Existing identification techniques require long generated texts, token-level log-probabilities, adversarially crafted prompts, or the model owner's cooperation. We show that far weaker evidence suffices. We define a behavioral fingerprint of an LLM as the empirical distribution of its answers to trivial one-word prompts - "name a random number between 1 and 100" - collected across four languages at a cost of one output token per query. Measuring 165 models served via a large commercial aggregator (OpenRouter), we find that (i) these distributions are highly non-uniform (median cell entropy 1.0 bit) and model-specific: split halves of the same model's samples lie an order of magnitude closer than samples of different models; (ii) Jensen-Shannon divergence between fingerprints recovers model lineage, assigning a model to its documented family with 59.5% leave-one-out accuracy against an 18.4% chance rate; and (iii) a biometric-style verification protocol achieves a 7.3% equal error rate with the full 40-cell battery, and below 11% with eight probe cells - roughly a hundred single-token queries per audit. We further report ecosystem anomalies, including a proprietary-branded flagship endpoint distributionally indistinguishable from an open-weight Qwen model. The protocol, prompts, raw data, and analysis code are released for reproduction and operational use.

</details>


### [178] [Devil in the Lens: Analyzing and Defending Physical Prompt Injection Against Vision-Language Models on Wearable Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10269)
*Yaxin Li,Hao Wang,Yanda Shao,Shuhao Zhang,Yan Long*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Physical prompt injection attacks on VLM-enabled wearable devices (e.g., AI glasses) exploit malicious environmental text to hijack model behavior. Analysis of 200+ real-world environments identifies 6 threat vectors, with up to 96% attack success rate across 12 VLMs. Two defense strategies are proposed to mitigate these attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs are increasingly deployed on wearable devices like smart glasses, yet security research has focused on digital prompt injection while ignoring threats from physical environments. The authors aim to characterize how malicious textual information embedded in physical surroundings can serve as an indirect prompt injection channel that evades human perception but manipulates VLM behavior.

Method: The authors collected physically captured photos from AI glasses across 200+ real-world environments to identify and categorize 6 representative threat vectors of physical prompt injection.
