They systematically evaluated the impact of these attacks on 12 VLM models across both integrity-critical and safety-critical tasks in simulated and real-world settings. Two defense strategies were proposed: a mask-based external filter and a semantic-vector-based internal detector.

Result: Physical prompt injection attacks consistently manipulate model outputs, achieving attack success rates up to 96% in simulated settings and 60% in real-world settings. Multiple VLM models exhibit excessive blind trust in environmental text, ignoring actual visual context and producing completely opposite summaries or directives. The proposed defense strategies effectively reduce attack success rates and safety impacts.

Conclusion: Physical prompt injection via environmental text poses a serious and underexplored threat to VLM-enabled wearable devices. Models demonstrate dangerous over-reliance on scene text at the expense of visual context. The proposed mask-based and semantic-vector-based defenses offer practical mitigation strategies for this emerging attack surface.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are rapidly deployed on human-facing wearable devices such as smart glasses to enable multimodal perception and AI-assisted decision-making. While prior research has demonstrated the risks of visual prompt injection into digital image inputs of VLMs, the unique security challenges posed by the increasing integration between physical environments and wearable intelligence, such as those embodied in VLM-enabled AI glasses, remain underexplored. Toward understanding and modeling such threats, our work characterizes how malicious textual information embedded in physical environments introduces a high-priority visual channel for indirect prompt injection, where scene texts that hinder or evade human perception could hijack VLM models' behavior. Such \textit{Physical Prompt Injection Attacks} can not only disrupt normal tasks of VLM-enabled wearable devices, but also steer models to produce profane, biased, or even untruthful outputs. Using physically captured photos from AI glasses in over 200 real-world environments, our analysis identifies 6 representative threat vectors of physically injected prompts, and further evaluates their impacts on 12 VLM models. Results show that these attacks consistently manipulate model outputs across integrity- and safety-critical tasks, achieving attack success rates of up to 96\% and 60\% in simulated and real-world settings. Our analysis confirms that multiple models exhibit excessive blind trust in environmental text, ignoring the actual visual context and producing completely opposite summaries or directives. We further propose two targeted defense strategies, including a mask-based external filter and a semantic-vector-based internal detector, to effectively reduce the success rate and safety impact of these attacks.

</details>


### [179] [Understanding Implicit Trust Errors in Core Carrier Networks through Multi-Agent Flaw Discovery and Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10315)
*Ziyu Lin,Ziting Wang,Xinfeng Li,Wei Dong,XiaoFeng Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper identifies a class of vulnerabilities in cellular core networks called "implicit trust errors" (iTrues) — where components blindly trust internal interfaces — and presents iFinder, an LLM-driven multi-agent system that discovers such flaws by combining specification cross-checking with automated PoC generation. It found 84 new vulnerabilities, 81 assigned CVEs, including a session-hijacking flaw confirmed on commercial 5G cores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cellular core networks historically relied on physical isolation for security, but the shift to cloud-native deployments exposes previously internal interfaces to external adversaries. Root-cause analysis of GitHub issues in open-source CN implementations revealed a recurring pattern of "implicit trust errors" — components that skip syntactic validation, fail to enforce semantic invariants, or allocate resources without availability checks. These weaknesses cause denial of service and session hijacking once internal interfaces become reachable. A systematic detection approach is needed.

Method: The authors propose iFinder, an LLM-driven multi-agent system with three key innovations: (1) multi-agent distillation that summarizes known flaws into reusable detection patterns; (2) a cross-checking strategy that validates against both 3GPP specifications and CN source code to suppress LLM hallucinations; and (3) automatic PoC generation with iterative refinement, where LLM-generated exploit code is executed against live CN implementations and results are fed back for correction until a working exploit is produced.

Result: iFinder discovered 84 previously unknown vulnerabilities across seven open-source CN implementations. Among these, 83 have been confirmed by developers and 81 have received CVE assignments. Most notably, a session-hijacking vulnerability was confirmed on real-world commercial 5G core networks, demonstrating practical severity beyond testbed environments.

Conclusion: Implicit trust errors represent a systemic security weakness in cellular core network implementations that is exacerbated by cloud-native migration. iFinder demonstrates that LLM-based systems, when augmented with specification-grounded cross-checking and executable PoC verification, can effectively discover these vulnerabilities at scale. The high CVE assignment rate validates the approach's practical impact.

Abstract: Cellular core networks (CNs) are critical infrastructure, yet their internal security model has historically relied on physical isolation: interfaces between core components often operate within an assumed trust zone. As CNs transition to cloud-native deployments, this assumption weakens, expanding the attack surface and enabling external adversaries to reach previously internal interfaces. From a root-cause analysis of security flaws reported in GitHub issues for opensource CN implementations, we found a recurring pattern of blind trust among CN components. Components may omit syntactic validation, fail to enforce semantic invariants, or allocate resources without checking availability. Once internal interfaces become reachable, these weaknesses can lead to severe impacts such as denial of service and session hijacking. We call these vulnerabilities implicit trust errors (iTrue). To detect iTrues and understand their security impacts, we designed iFinder, an LLM-driven multi-agent system that summarizes known flaws, distills them into detection patterns, and applies them to discover new iTrues in CN implementations. To suppress hallucinations produced by large language models (LLMs), we built an innovative strategy that crosschecks both 3GPP specifications and CN code to capture existing protection missed by the agents. Further, we developed a technique that uses LLMs to generate proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for potential iTrues and iteratively refine the PoCs by automatically executing them against CN implementations and analyzing results. Running iFinder on seven prominent open-source CN implementations, we discovered 84 previously unknown vulnerabilities. Among them, 83 have already been confirmed and 81 have been assigned CVEs. Importantly, a session-hijacking flaw has been confirmed on real-world commercial 5G core networks.

</details>


### [180] [Large Language Models in Misinformation Ecosystems: Misuse, Defense, and Vulnerability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10402)
*Lingwei Wei,Dou Hu,Wei Zhou,Songlin Hu,Philip S. Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper presents a role-layer framework for understanding how LLMs transform misinformation into an ecosystem-level security challenge, categorizing LLMs as attackers, defenders, and vulnerable components across content, social context, evidence, and verification layers, and identifying three open challenges for future research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs fundamentally alter the misinformation landscape: they do not merely generate false content more efficiently but also threaten the integrity of the entire sociotechnical infrastructure—social contexts, evidence repositories, retrieval corpora, and verification workflows—that misinformation defense relies upon. A unified conceptual framework is needed to systematically characterize these emerging risks and corresponding defenses.

Method: The authors propose a two-dimensional taxonomy: (1) a role dimension (LLMs as attackers, defenders, and vulnerable components of verification systems) and (2) a layer dimension (content, social contexts, evidence environments, and verification workflows). Using this framework, they conduct a structured literature synthesis, organizing LLM-enabled attacks, LLM-based detection/verification methods, vulnerabilities in LLM-centric detection paradigms, and existing countermeasures.

Result: The synthesis reveals that current defenses predominantly focus on static content-level detection accuracy, while LLM-enabled attacks increasingly target broader ecosystem layers. Three critical gaps emerge: lack of budgeted ecosystem-level risk evaluation, insufficient hardening of LLM-centered verification pipelines against adversarial manipulation, and absence of auditable human-in-the-loop verification deployments.

Conclusion: Future misinformation defense must shift from narrow detection accuracy to ecosystem-level resilience, incorporating adversarial robustness in verification pipelines and auditable human oversight. The role-layer framework provides a foundational organizing structure for both research and practical system design in this domain.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed misinformation from a primarily content-centric problem into a broader ecosystem-level security challenge. When misused, LLMs create risks beyond false content generation, enabling attacks on the social contexts, evidence sources, retrieval corpora, and verification workflows that misinformation defense depends on. In this paper, we introduce a role-layer framework to unify these risks and defenses. The role dimension characterizes LLMs as attackers, defenders, and vulnerable components of verification systems, while the layer dimension covers content, social contexts, evidence environments, and verification workflows. Guided by this framework, we organize LLM-enabled attacks, investigate LLM-based detection and verification methods, analyze vulnerabilities in LLM-centric detection paradigms, and discuss existing countermeasures against LLM-enabled attacks. Building on this synthesis, we identify three key open challenges: moving from static detection accuracy to budgeted ecosystem-level risk evaluation, hardening LLM-centered verification pipelines against adversarial manipulation, and deploying auditable human-in-the-loop verification systems for trustworthy real-world misinformation defense.

</details>


### [181] [Threat Vectors and the State of the Art in Defense Methods for Security in Neurotechnology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10451)
*Bryce-Allen Bagley,Nathaniel Rose,Quintus Kilbourn,Matthew Canham*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper surveys the current state of neurosecurity, identifies established and probable security threats to brain-computer interfaces, and recommends immediate countermeasures drawn from cybersecurity, hardware security, and machine learning to address existing vulnerabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BCI technology is advancing rapidly—entering clinical trials and consumer markets—yet security research (neurosecurity) significantly lags behind, leaving these systems exposed to a broad range of vulnerabilities that demand urgent attention.

Method: A comprehensive literature review and threat survey of the neurosecurity landscape, cataloging both firmly established and highly probable security threats to BCI systems, followed by cross-domain analysis to identify applicable defenses from cybersecurity, hardware security, and machine learning.

Result: The authors present a structured taxonomy of BCI security threats spanning diverse attack surfaces and map existing defense techniques from adjacent fields that can be immediately deployed to mitigate these gaps.

Conclusion: Neurosecurity is critically underdeveloped relative to BCI capabilities; however, many existing security techniques from other domains can be adapted now to reduce risk while dedicated neurosecurity research matures.

Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are a class of diverse hardware modalities, associated software, and connected devices which are widely used in a variety of fields, including neurosurgery, biomedical data analysis, and neuroimaging. Recent years have seen rapid advancements in BCI technology, and neurotechnology more broadly, with the first devices now passing clinical trials, early examples of consumer hardware entering the market, and many variants of consumer and medical hardware with increasingly extensive capabilities being developed rapidly. However, research and development in security for BCIs--known as neurosecurity--lags significantly behind the capabilities of BCIs themselves. In an effort to address as many vulnerabilities as feasible immediately, in this paper we review the current state of the art in neurosecurity, thoroughly survey the breadth and complexity of both firmly established and highly probable security threats to BCI systems, and provide recommendations of existing methods from cybersecurity, hardware security, and machine learning which can immediately be applied to address some of these gaps in neurosecurity.

</details>


### [182] [Firewall3D: A Hardware Firewall for Defending 3D Printers Against Firmware Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10484)
*Seyed Ali Ghazi Asgar,Narasimha Reddy*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes Firewall3D, a hardware-based security module that monitors 3D printer physical signals (motor currents, temperatures, fan speeds) to detect firmware-level attacks by comparing actual printer behavior against expected G-code execution, triggering alarms and halts upon anomaly detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapidly growing 3D printing market (exceeding $30 billion) faces increasing cybersecurity threats, particularly firmware-level attacks introduced via supply chain compromises, malicious updates, or insider threats. These attacks can sabotage prints, steal intellectual property, or physically damage printers, and existing defenses are insufficient.

Method: Firewall3D is a dedicated hardware firewall that continuously monitors physical layer signals — stepper motor currents, end-stop switches, nozzle/bed temperatures, and cooling fans — and verifies that observed physical behavior is consistent with the intended G-code execution.

Result: Experimental results show Firewall3D effectively detects a wide range of firmware attacks targeting print integrity, printer component damage, and intellectual property leakage. Upon anomaly detection, the system triggers an alarm and halts printing to prevent further damage.

Conclusion: A hardware-based monitoring approach operating at the physical layer provides an effective defense against firmware-level attacks in additive manufacturing systems, offering real-time detection and mitigation without relying on potentially compromised firmware or software.

Abstract: As the 3D printing market continues to grow rapidly, with an estimated value exceeding $30 billion, cybersecurity risks and attacks targeting additive manufacturing systems are also increasing. These attacks aim to sabotage printed components, steal intellectual property, or even physically damage the 3D printer itself. One major cybersecurity threat in this domain is firmware level attacks, which can be introduced through supply chain compromises, malicious firmware updates, or insider threats that deploy modified firmware to manipulate printer behavior. To defend against such threats, we propose a dedicated hardware based security solution,Firewall3D, that acts as a hardware firewall for 3D printers. Firewall3D continuously monitors physical layer signals, including stepper motor currents, end stop switches, nozzle and bed temperatures and cooling fans, to verify that the printer's physical behavior matches the intended G-code execution. Our experimental results demonstrate that Firewall3D can effectively detect a wide range of firmware attacks that could compromise print integrity, damage printer components, or leak intellectual property. Upon detecting abnormal behavior, the system can immediately trigger an alarm and halt the printing process, thereby preventing further damage and risks.

</details>


### [183] [Temporary Authority, Permanent Effects: Commit-Time Authorization for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10487)
*Igor Santos-Grueiro*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LLM agents often complete tasks using authority evidence (e.g., DOM snapshots) that was valid earlier but has since expired. This paper defines "commit-time authorization" — the principle that durable effects require fresh, causally prior, correctly bound, and eligible evidence at commit time. Experiments show agents frequently succeed in producing visible results but rarely remain authorized, and prompt-based mitigations are insufficient. The authors propose CommitGuard, a runtime boundary monitor that blocks unauthorized commits, distinguishing endpoint success (utility) from authorized commit (security).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents can produce durable side effects (e.g., file writes, API calls, DOM mutations) based on authority evidence (snapshots, tokens, version witnesses) that was valid earlier in execution but has since become stale or invalid. This creates a security gap: an agent may appear to succeed functionally while its authority to act has lapsed. Current systems lack a formal notion of whether a durable effect is authorized at commit time, leading to actions that complete without proper authorization.

Method: The authors formalize commit-time authorization via four freshness conditions: causal priority, binding integrity, freshness, and eligibility at the commit boundary. They construct a controlled-invalidation evaluation suite spanning browser, tool/API, and multi-agent workflows, with 54 task matrices (270 runs) where authority relations are systematically invalidated before durability. They then evaluate mitigation strategies: prompt-based caution, single-condition checks, and their proposed CommitGuard — a fail-closed runtime monitor that intercepts durable-effect attempts using witness, dependency, binding, and eligibility signals from the runtime.

Result: In the primary 54-task matrix, 262/270 runs reached a visible result (high endpoint success), but only 55/270 were authorized completions. Among 216 invalidating rows, 207 committed after the authorizing path had failed. All 54 clean controls remained authorized. Prompt caution and single-condition checks proved insufficient across different hazard types. CommitGuard successfully blocks stale durable-effect attempts when the runtime emits the required signals.

Conclusion: Endpoint success (functional completion) must be distinguished from authorized commit (a security property). Mitigation requires refreshing, rebinding, replanning, or refusing at the durability boundary. Runtime systems should emit witness, dependency, binding, and eligibility signals to enable fail-closed boundary monitors like CommitGuard to enforce commit-time authorization.

Abstract: LLM agents can commit durable effects from authority evidence that was valid earlier in execution: a DOM snapshot, approval epoch, version witness, branch token, or worker result. We study the commit boundary at which earlier authority evidence no longer authorizes a durable effect. We call this property commit-time authorization: a durable effect is authorized only if the witness that licensed its derived state remains fresh, causally prior, bound to the same effect, and eligible at commit time.
  We build a controlled-invalidation suite spanning browser, tool/API, and multi-agent workflows. The suite preserves the user goal and payload shape while invalidating the authority relation before durability. In the primary 54-task matrix, endpoint success remains high: 262/270 runs reach the visible result. Only 55/270 are authorized completions; among the 216 invalidating rows, 207 commit after the authorizing path has failed. All 54 clean controls remain authorized, and a separate 54-run authority-preserving check produces no unauthorized commits.
  We then evaluate mitigation families. Prompt caution and single-condition checks are insufficient because different hazards break different boundary conditions. Defenses work when they refresh, rebind, replan, or refuse at the durability boundary. CommitGuard, a fail-closed boundary monitor, blocks stale durable-effect attempts on protected commit surfaces when runtimes emit witness, dependency, binding, and eligibility signals.
  The result is a reporting and runtime-design lesson: endpoint success is a utility metric; authorized commit is a security property.

</details>


### [184] [NetInjectBench: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Large Language Model Agents for Network Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10490)
*Ruksat Khan Shayoni,Muhammad Faraz Shoaib,S M Asif Hossain,M. F. Mridha*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: NetInjectBench is a 130-scenario benchmark evaluating indirect prompt injection defenses for LLM-based network operations agents. A metadata-aware policy gate eliminated unsafe actions (0/240) while preserving usefulness, outperforming prompt-only defenses and static allowlisting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents deployed in network operations ingest untrusted artifacts (tickets, alerts, logs, runbooks, ChatOps messages) that can carry indirect prompt injections, causing unsafe tool actions. Existing prompt-level safeguards are insufficient for execution-time threats in this domain.

Method: The authors construct NetInjectBench, a benchmark of 130 scenarios (40 benign, 40 weak-attack, 40 strong-attack, 10 approved high-impact changes) with clean separation of untrusted artifact text, trusted policy metadata, and evaluation labels. Three models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) are tested under naive execution and five defenses: prompt-only safety, Self-Reminder, Spotlighting, Two-Pass LLM Judge, static allowlisting, and a metadata-aware policy gate. The policy gate leverages metadata-integrity assumptions to enforce execution-time authorization boundaries.

Result: Naive execution: 82.50% unsafe tool-action rate across 240 attack instances. Prompt-only defenses reduced this to 10.00–25.63% (Two-Pass LLM Judge best at 10.00%). Static allowlisting achieved 5.00% unsafe rate but blocked all approved changes (0.00% usefulness, 100.00% overblocking). The metadata-aware policy gate achieved 0/240 unsafe attack actions (95% Wilson upper bound: 1.58%) while preserving 99.17% attack-scenario usefulness and 100.00% approved-change usefulness.

Conclusion: Network-operation LLM agents require execution-time authorization boundaries (metadata-aware policy gates) in addition to prompt-level instruction hygiene. Prompt-only defenses reduce but do not eliminate injection risk, and static allowlisting is too restrictive for operational utility.

Abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents are attractive for network operations, but tickets, alerts, logs, runbooks, and ChatOps messages can carry indirect prompt injections. We present NetInjectBench, a 130-scenario benchmark that separates untrusted artifact text, trusted policy metadata, and evaluation labels for network-operation tool use. The sample contains 40 benign, 40 weak-attack, 40 strong-attack, and 10 approved high-impact change scenarios; each is evaluated with Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B. Across 240 attack instances, naive execution reached an 82.50% unsafe tool-action rate. Prompt-only safety, Self-Reminder, Spotlighting, and a Two-Pass LLM Judge reduced this rate to 25.63%, 21.67%, 18.33%, and 10.00%, respectively. Static allowlisting reached 5.00% but blocked all approved changes, yielding 0.00% usefulness and 100.00% overblocking on approved cases. Under the stated metadata-integrity assumption, the metadata-aware policy gate produced 0/240 unsafe attack actions, with a 95% Wilson upper bound of 1.58%, while preserving 99.17% attack-scenario usefulness and 100.00% approved-change usefulness. The findings show that network-operation agents need execution-time authorization boundaries alongside prompt-level instruction hygiene.

</details>


### [185] [PromptGraph: Graph-Guided Prompt Sanitization for Balancing Privacy and Utility in LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10709)
*Chen Gu,Hui Wan,Donghui Hu,Hui Wang,Zhuoer Gu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PromptGraph is a graph-guided prompt sanitization method for LLM inference that models both span-level privacy leakage and pairwise contextual dependencies as an attributed graph, then selects spans to sanitize by optimizing the trade-off between privacy gain and utility loss from broken contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM prompt sanitizers treat spans independently, assigning privacy/utility scores without modeling pairwise contextual relationships. This misses the fact that sensitive information can be inferred from associations among otherwise innocuous spans, creating a gap in privacy-preserving LLM inference.

Method: PromptGraph represents each prompt as an attributed graph where nodes carry span-level privacy scores and edges encode utility-relevant contextual dependencies. The sanitization objective selects a protected span set that maximizes privacy gain while penalizing the loss of contextual dependencies. Protected spans are sanitized locally, and placeholders are restored only after passing local consistency checks.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that PromptGraph achieves a more favorable privacy-utility balance compared to prompt-privacy baselines.

Conclusion: Modeling pairwise contextual dependencies explicitly via a graph formulation yields superior privacy-utility trade-offs in LLM prompt sanitization, outperforming methods that treat spans independently.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) services introduce a fundamental privacy challenge. Sensitive information may be inferred not only from explicit identifiers, such as names or phone numbers, but also from contextual associations among otherwise innocuous spans. Existing sanitizers typically assign privacy or utility signals to individual spans without explicitly modeling pairwise relationships among them. In this paper, we propose PromptGraph, a graph-guided prompt-sanitization approach for privacy-preserving LLM inference. PromptGraph estimates privacy leakage at the span level and utility-relevant contextual dependencies between pairs of spans. It represents each prompt as an attributed graph, in which nodes carry span-level privacy scores and edges encode contextual dependencies needed to preserve utility. The sanitization objective selects a protected span set that maximizes privacy gain while penalizing the loss of contextual dependencies. This formulation explicitly balances privacy and utility when contextual evidence is hidden. Protected spans are sanitized locally, and returned placeholders are restored only after passing local consistency checks. We conduct extensive experiments showing that PromptGraph achieves a more favorable balance between privacy and utility than prompt-privacy baselines.

</details>


### [186] [Distributed Denial of Science: How Indirect Data Poisoning of AI Systems Can Industrialize Scientific Fraud](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10712)
*Bálint Gyevnár,Atoosa Kasirzadeh,Nihar B. Shah*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces "indirect data poisoning," a novel attack where adversaries corrupt open datasets to manipulate AI-powered autonomous research agents into producing fraudulent scientific conclusions at scale. Across 450 experimental runs, poisoning succeeded in 49.56% of cases with only 6% detection. Mitigation via provenance auditing reduced attack success to zero.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific fraud has historically required significant resources (money, ghostwriters, corrupt academics), but the rise of AI-automated research agents creates a new vulnerability: adversaries can corrupt open datasets in public repositories, causing honest scientists using AI tools to unwittingly propagate fraudulent findings. The authors investigate whether this "weaponization of honest AI use" poses a credible threat to scientific integrity.

Method: The authors design an indirect data poisoning attack where an adversary uploads a poisoned variant of an open dataset with misleading metadata to a public repository. They evaluate this across five socially-salient topics (hiring discrimination, autonomous vehicle safety, etc.) using three frontier AI systems (Claude Code/Claude Opus 4.7, Codex/GPT-5.5, Gemini CLI/Gemini 3.1 Pro) over 450 ethically-contained experimental runs. Two mitigations are tested: (1) a "scientist persona" prompt and (2) a data provenance audit with five checks (referencing papers, social markers, statistical anomalies, related datasets, poisoning caution).

Result: Poisoning succeeded in 49.56% of runs, with detection at only 6.0%. The attack required no topic-specific triggers, agent access, indirect prompt injection, or fabricated papers — only the open data ecosystem and misleading metadata. The scientist persona mitigation still left 16.67% of runs with poisoned conclusions, but the provenance auditing framework reduced the attack success rate to zero.

Conclusion: Indirect data poisoning represents a scalable threat to scientific integrity, exploiting the open data ecosystem and autonomous AI research agents. However, the threat can be fully mitigated through provenance auditing during the data retrieval phase, offering a practical defense without requiring changes to the underlying AI models or the open data infrastructure.

Abstract: Scientific fraud is the instrument of doubt that malicious entities can use to establish controversy in science. Historically, it required the resources of a company: deep pockets, ghostwritten articles, and corrupt academics. Today, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly automating scientific research, so we ask: Can a remote adversary weaponize the honest use of AI in science to compromise scientific integrity? We envision and empirically evaluate a new attack, indirect data poisoning, in which an adversary corrupts an open dataset and uploads the poisoned variant to a public repository. Autonomous research agents may independently retrieve and process this data, turning honest scientists into the unpaid and unwitting distributors of fraud at scale. Across five socially-salient topics, from hiring discrimination to the safety of autonomous vehicles, three widely used frontier AI systems (Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.7, Codex with GPT-5.5, Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro), and 450 ethically contained experimental runs, we find that poisoning succeeds in 49.56% of runs, while the rate of poisoning detection is only 6.0%. The attack requires no topic-specific trigger-words, agent access, indirect prompt injection, or fabricated papers, only the open data ecosystem and misleading metadata. To mitigate the attacks, we propose and evaluate two measures: a scientist persona and a data provenance audit with five checks (referencing papers, social markers, statistical anomalies, related datasets, poisoning caution). We find that the persona still leaves 16.67% of runs with a poisoned conclusion, but provenance auditing reduces attack success rate to zero. Our results suggest that indirect data poisoning may enable scientific fraud at unprecedented scale, but these attacks can be mitigated with suitable auditing by agents during data retrieval.

</details>


### [187] [Mako: A Self-Evolving Agentic Operating System (SE-AOS) for Autonomous Web Exploitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11288)
*Praneeth Narisetty,Shiva Nagendra Babu Kore*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Mako is a self-evolving AI agent for autonomous web exploitation that achieves 100% success on the XBOW benchmark (104 targets, 26 vulnerability classes). It treats exploit capability as a mutable kernel, hot-loading new capabilities at runtime. The key finding: difficulty collapses once a capability exists — capability, not reasoning, is scarce. Source code is withheld as dual-use research of concern.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI security agents are limited by fixed, pre-programmed capabilities. The authors argue that autonomous exploitation requires a system that can observe its own failures, synthesize new exploit capabilities on the fly, and permanently incorporate them — moving from static tools to self-improving agents. They also posit a fundamental "law of autonomous exploitation": capability (not reasoning) is the bottleneck, and once a capability exists, difficulty collapses.

Method: The Self-Evolving Agentic Operating System (SE-AOS) architecture treats exploit capabilities as a versioned kernel extensible at runtime. Mako implements this through: (1) a core exploitation engine that targets live applications, (2) a self-evolution loop that monitors failures, proposes new agents/rules, sandboxes them, verifies fitness does not regress, and hot-loads improvements, and (3) a cryptographic verification regime using fresh per-build flags to prevent fabricated or memorized results. Testing was conducted on the XBOW benchmark: 104 containerized CTF-style web applications with 26 vulnerability classes across three difficulty tiers.

Result: Mako achieved full-suite coverage: 104/104 targets successfully exploited, each producing a cryptographically fresh, per-build flag. The authors derive a "law of autonomous exploitation" — once a capability exists and is discoverable, difficulty collapses; capability, not reasoning, is the scarce resource. The gated self-evolution loop successfully proposed, sandboxed, and committed improvements without fitness regression.

Conclusion: Autonomous exploitation can be systematized into a self-improving architecture where capability accumulation, not reasoning depth, determines success. However, a system that reduces full-spectrum web exploitation to a repeatable, machine-speed pipeline constitutes dual-use research of concern. The authors publish the scientific methodology but withhold operational results, payloads, exploit chains, and source code.

Abstract: We introduce the Self-Evolving Agentic Operating System (SE-AOS): a new class of AI agent that treats exploit capability as a mutable, versioned kernel it extends at runtime, observing its own failures, synthesising new capabilities, proving them against a live target, and hot-loading them back into itself. Mako is the first SE-AOS instance for security research and the autonomous web exploitation engine developed within LaunchSafe. LaunchSafe builds autonomous security agents for continuous offensive testing and agent-driven security research; Mako is the core engine behind that platform. On the public XBOW validation-benchmarks, 104 containerised, CTF-style web applications spanning 26 vulnerability classes across three difficulty tiers, Mako achieves full-suite coverage: it drives every one of the 104 targets to emit a cryptographically fresh, per-build flag, under a verification regime that makes fabricated or memorised results impossible. Our central result is a law of autonomous exploitation: once a capability exists and is discoverable, difficulty collapses; capability, not reasoning, is what is scarce, together with an architecture and formalism that turn that law into a self-improving system. Mako further runs a gated self-evolution loop that proposes, sandboxes, and commits improvements to its own agents and rules when fitness does not regress. We deliberately withhold the operational results, payloads, exploit chains, and tool source, because a system that reduces full-spectrum web exploitation to a repeatable, machine-speed pipeline is dual-use research of concern. We publish the science; we withhold the weapon.

</details>


### [188] [A Verifier-Centric Conceptual Model for Digital Credential Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10747)
*Shigeya Suzuki,Ryosuke Abe*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces Shinken, a verifier-centric conceptual model that decomposes digital credential processing into three layers (signature verification, semantic interpretation, validation) and two orthogonal planes (Constitution and Logistics). It identifies seven consequences of verifiability and demonstrates that this framework explains interoperability failures, trust assumptions, and design trade-offs that conventional element-by-element comparisons fail to capture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing digital credential ecosystems, despite sharing standards and data models, often remain mutually non-interoperable. Traditional atomistic comparisons of identifiers, formats, protocols, and algorithms cannot explain why interoperability breaks down, nor do they clarify what a verifier must obtain and trust before accepting a credential. A systematic framework is needed to expose these hidden trust assumptions and architectural decisions.

Method: The authors propose a verifier-centric conceptual model based on two decompositions: (1) a functional decomposition separating credential processing into L1 (signature verification), L2 (semantic interpretation), and L3 (validation), with two orthogonal planes — Constitution (ecosystem-level trust declarations) and Logistics (storage and delivery of verification materials); (2) a placement decomposition characterizing where each function resides along three dimensions (placement, timing, disclosure). From the condition of verifiability, seven consequences are derived: definitional corollaries, operational implications, and design trade-offs. The model is applied to four learner-credential stacks and existing ecosystems including authentication federations.

Result: The Shinken framework successfully explains interoperability failures across diverse digital credential stacks by making trust assumptions explicit across all five functions. It clarifies verifier-side burden, offline verifiability, privacy implications, and terminological ambiguities that element-wise comparison leaves unresolved. The model reveals that even stacks sharing a data model can fail to interoperate due to mismatches in Constitution and Logistics planes.

Conclusion: A verifier-centric decomposition into L1/L2/L3 layers plus Constitution and Logistics planes, combined with placement analysis along three dimensions, provides a robust explanatory and diagnostic tool for understanding digital credential interoperability. The approach surfaces hidden trust assumptions and architectural choices that determine whether a credential is practically verifiable across ecosystem boundaries.

Abstract: Digital credential ecosystems increasingly combine multiple standards. Because implementations have evolved independently across jurisdictions and application domains, systems described under the common label ``digital credential'' often remain mutually non-interoperable. Conventional element-by-element comparisons of identifiers, data models, credential formats, protocols, and signature algorithms do not explain why interoperability fails even when stacks share a data model, nor do they identify what a verifier must obtain, and what it must trust, before accepting a credential. We present a verifier-centric conceptual model built on two decompositions. The first separates credential processing into signature verification (L1), semantic interpretation (L2), and validation (L3), and models the supporting materials through two orthogonal planes: Constitution, which captures ecosystem-level arrangements and trust declarations, and Logistics, which captures how verification materials are stored and delivered; the Shinken framework makes trust assumptions explicit across all five functions. The second characterizes where each function may be placed along three dimensions (placement, timing, and disclosure). From the condition of being verifiable, the model derives seven consequences, distinguished as definitional corollaries, operational implications, and design trade-offs. Applying the model to four learner-credential stacks and to existing ecosystems including authentication federations, we show that it explains interoperability failures, verifier-side burden, offline verifiability, privacy implications, and terminological ambiguities that element-wise comparison leaves unresolved.

</details>


### [189] [Can Watermarking Techniques Help Prevent LLM Model Stealing?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10794)
*Elette Boyle,MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi,Keivan Rezaei,Suho Shin,Amos Stern*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes defense methods against model stealing attacks that extract hidden layer dimensions from black-box language models, using logit perturbation inspired by watermarking techniques, and empirically demonstrates effectiveness while preserving model utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model stealing attacks can extract precise architectural information (specifically hidden layer dimensions) from production black-box language models. The authors aim to develop defenses against the attack introduced by Carlini et al. (2024) and its extensions, addressing a critical security vulnerability in deployed commercial models.

Method: The authors propose defense methods inspired by watermarking techniques that perturb the logits layer of language models. By strategically modifying logit outputs, the defenses obscure the architectural signals that model stealing attacks exploit, preventing adversaries from accurately inferring hidden layer dimensions. The approach is evaluated across various configurations to balance defense effectiveness against model quality degradation.

Result: Empirical experiments demonstrate that the proposed logit-perturbation defenses effectively prevent model stealing attacks targeting hidden layer dimension extraction. The defenses achieve a favorable trade-off, successfully thwarting attacks while maintaining model utility and performance across multiple configurations.

Conclusion: Logit-level perturbation defenses, inspired by watermarking, provide a practical and effective countermeasure against model stealing attacks that attempt to extract hidden layer dimensions, without significantly compromising model quality.

Abstract: Model stealing attacks have recently been introduced, enabling the extraction of precise information from black-box commercial language models. In this work, we propose defense methods against a recent attack of \cite{carlini2024stealing} and extensions for extracting the hidden layer dimension of production language models. Our methods are inspired by watermarking techniques that perturb the logits layer of these models to prevent such attacks. We provide empirical experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed defense versus model quality degradation across various configurations, and propose an effective defense against such attacks while preserving model utility.

</details>


### [190] [When Local Monitors Miss Compositional Harm: Diagnosing Distributed Backdoors in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11751)
*Yibo Hu,Ren Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Runtime monitors that check individual messages or tool calls in multi-agent LLM systems have a fundamental blind spot: distributed backdoors can split a harmful payload across agents such that every local fragment appears benign, yet the assembled output is an attack. The authors formalize this as an "observability boundary" and prove that no detector limited to the benign-appearing fragment view can catch such attacks, empirically validating this across testbeds, benchmarks, and end-to-end agent runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent and tool-using LLM systems increasingly rely on per-step runtime monitors as a safety mechanism. The authors identify that this defense paradigm assumes harm is locally detectable in individual messages or actions, but this assumption fails when adversaries distribute malicious payloads across agents such that each fragment is locally benign. The core motivation is to expose and formalize this fundamental vulnerability.

Method: The authors formalize the problem using an "observability boundary" concept: a monitor's detection capability is bounded by what its view can distinguish from benign traffic. They provide a proof that when attack fragments appear benign within the monitored view, no detector operating on that view can succeed. Empirically, they construct a controlled testbed where distributed backdoors are split across agents, evaluate on an external benchmark, and run end-to-end multi-agent experiments. They also train a monitor on benign-only traffic and test a decoded-view gate that, when given the encoding family, blocks all tested attacks.

Result: Local monitors lose detection signal exactly as local evidence is stripped from fragments; signal returns only when the monitor inspects the assembled object. A monitor trained solely on benign traffic recovers attack code structure across held-out encodings (0.874 mean AUROC). A decoded-view gate, when informed of the encoding family, successfully blocks every tested attack. However, full-trace monitors and decoders still fail unless they access the representation where the payload is actually exposed.

Conclusion: Local safety does not imply global safety when harm is compositional. The open problem is identifying the correct representation at which a monitor must operate to detect distributed, compositionally harmful attacks. Merely expanding the monitor's view (e.g., full traces, decoding) is insufficient unless that view reaches the level where the payload becomes manifest.

Abstract: As multi-agent, tool-using LLM systems are deployed, a common safety net is a runtime monitor that checks each message, tool call, or step on its own. We show this net has a fundamental hole. A distributed backdoor splits a harmful payload across agents, so every local check passes while the assembled object is the attack. The monitor can be right on every step and still miss the attack. The problem is not splitting itself: split fragments can still leak suspicious tokens or provenance edges. The hard case is \emph{local benignness}. No fragment carries the harm, and what is left looks like ordinary benign traffic. We formalize this as an \emph{observability boundary}: a monitor catches only what its view can tell apart from benign traffic. We prove that once the fragments look benign in the monitored view, no detector on that view can catch them, however strong it is. Across a controlled testbed, an external benchmark, and end-to-end agent runs, local monitors lose the signal exactly as local evidence disappears, and it returns only when the monitor sees the assembled object. A monitor trained only on benign traffic recovers the attack's code structure across held-out encodings (0.874 mean AUROC). A decoded-view gate, given the encoding family, blocks every tested attack. But seeing more is not enough: full-trace monitors and decoders still fail unless they reach the representation where the payload is exposed. Local safety is not global safety when harm is compositional, and the open problem is finding that representation.

</details>


### [191] [Automated Stealthy Wear-Out Attack on Digital Twins With Deep Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10830)
*Joshua Haworth,Aryan Pasikhani,George Pavlides,Prosanta Gope,John Clark*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A stealthy DRL-based attack manipulates control signals in DT-enabled industrial systems to accelerate joint wear on a UR10e robotic arm, with SAC proving the most effective RL algorithm, while evading anomaly detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Digital Twins (DTs) bridge physical and virtual domains for Industry 4.0, but their expanded attack surface creates vulnerabilities. Existing research lacks focused study on stealthy, DRL-driven wear-out attacks that can degrade physical assets covertly in DT-enabled environments.

Method: The authors propose a novel DRL-based adversarial attack that strategically manipulates control signals to induce elevated torque on a specific joint of a UR10e robotic arm. Four RL algorithms (TD3, SAC, PPO, A2C) are benchmarked for attack effectiveness, sample efficiency, and stability. The adversary operates against a state-of-the-art anomaly detection system and is evaluated in a realistic industrial DT setting.

Result: SAC consistently outperformed TD3, PPO, and A2C across sample efficiency, stability, and attack effectiveness. The attack successfully elevated torque on the targeted joint, causing accelerated degradation and increased maintenance costs while remaining undetected by the anomaly detection system.

Conclusion: DRL-driven adversaries pose substantial risks to DT-enabled industrial environments. The findings underscore the urgent need for robust defence mechanisms to protect critical industrial systems from covert, degradation-focused attacks.

Abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) have emerged as pivotal enablers of Industry 4.0, offering transformative capabilities such as real-time monitoring, advanced simulation, and precise control of physical assets. By bridging the physical and virtual domains, DTs facilitate seamless integration of data-driven decision-making and operational optimisation. However, this seamless interaction significantly expands the attack surface of industrial systems, creating vulnerabilities that adversaries can exploit. This paper introduces a novel and stealthy wear-out attack leveraging Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to target DT-enabled infrastructures. The adversary strategically and covertly manipulates control signals, inducing increased torque on a specific joint to accelerate wear and tear while evading detection by a state-of-the-art anomaly detection system. Extensive benchmarking of reinforcement learning algorithms - including Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO), and Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) - revealed that SAC consistently outperformed its counterparts in terms of sample efficiency, stability, and overall attack effectiveness. We evaluate the proposed adversary in an industrial setting using the UR10e robotic arm. Results demonstrate the adversary's ability to significantly elevate torque levels on the targeted joint, leading to accelerated degradation and increased maintenance costs, all while operating stealthily and avoiding detection. Our findings highlight the substantial risks posed by DRL-driven adversaries to DT-enabled environments and emphasise the critical need for robust defence mechanisms to protect critical industrial systems.

</details>


### [192] [SoK: Federated Learning for Intrusion Detection in Vehicular Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10914)
*Yahya Shahsavari,Reza Nourmohammadi,Sara Rouhani,Kaiwen Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This SoK paper systematically reviews over 60 publications on Federated Learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems (FL-IDS) for vehicular networks. It provides a unified taxonomy of attack surfaces (ECUs, V2X), evaluates FL topologies, and maps adversarial threats (poisoning, inference attacks). The authors identify critical methodological flaws — artificial IID data splits, trivial benchmarks, weak adversarial evaluation, and neglect of real-time CAN constraints — and propose minimum benchmarking standards alongside a forward-looking research agenda for practical deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The vehicular FL-IDS literature is fragmented, with inconsistent methodologies and unrealistic experimental assumptions that undermine the credibility and practical applicability of proposed systems. No prior work has systematically audited these shortcomings across the field to establish rigorous standards for transitioning from simulation to real-world deployment.

Method: The authors conduct a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) by auditing over 60 publications. They unify the taxonomy of vehicular attack surfaces (internal ECUs and external V2X), categorize FL topologies used for IDS, and taxonomize adversarial threats including poisoning and inference attacks. Through this systematic review, recurring methodological pitfalls are identified and catalogued.

Result: Four recurring pitfalls are identified: (1) artificial IID data splits that misrepresent real non-IID vehicular data distributions; (2) reliance on trivial or outdated benchmark datasets; (3) weak or absent adversarial evaluation against FL-specific attacks; and (4) omission of real-time Controller Area Network (CAN) constraints critical to vehicular systems.

Conclusion: The paper defines minimum benchmarking requirements necessary for credible evaluation and presents a forward-looking research agenda to bridge the gap between optimistic simulated results and secure, practical real-world deployment of vehicular FL-IDS.

Abstract: Modern vehicular networks face an expanding attack surface across internal Electronic Control Units (ECUs) and external Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a decentralized paradigm to deploy Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) without compromising data privacy. However, the vehicular FL-IDS literature suffers from fragmented methodologies and unrealistic experimental setups. This paper presents a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) that unifies the taxonomy of vehicular attack surfaces, evaluates FL topologies, and maps adversarial threats such as poisoning and inference attacks. By auditing over 60 publications, we identify recurring pitfalls: artificial IID data splits, reliance on trivial benchmarks, weak adversarial evaluation, and omission of real-time CAN constraints. Finally, we define a forward-looking research agenda and outline minimum benchmarking requirements necessary to transition vehicular FL-IDS from optimistic simulations to secure, real-world deployment.

</details>


### [193] [ARMOR-IMC: Adaptive Resource Mapping for Operational Robustness via Secure In-Memory Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10938)
*Muhtasim Alam Chowdhury,Ramtin Zand,Soheil Salehi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a post-training framework that simultaneously hardens analog in-memory computing (IMC) accelerators against both manufacturing process variation (PV) and power side-channel attacks (SCAs), using novel metrics (VIS and LPI) and fault observation window mapping without requiring model retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional DNN architectures suffer from massive data-movement overhead, driving adoption of IMC using emerging devices like SOT-MTJs. However, these analog IMC accelerators face dual threats: manufacturing PV degrades computational reliability and amplifies fault injection susceptibility, while power SCAs leak sensitive information. Existing defenses address these threats independently, leaving a gap for unified mitigation.

Method: A post-training framework implemented in the IMAC-Sim simulator that uses two key innovations: (1) Variation Impact Score (VIS) to intelligently guide the mapping of Fault Observation Windows (FOWs), and (2) Leakage Per Inference (LPI) metric to quantify input-dependent power variability under stochastic injection and measure reduction in effective signal-to-noise ratio. The approach hardens against both PV and SCA threats simultaneously without retraining.

Result: PV-induced faults degraded DNN accuracy by over 50% in experiments. The proposed method restored near-baseline accuracy while simultaneously mitigating the threat of correlation-based power analysis attacks.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates that unified hardening against reliability (PV) and security (SCA) threats in analog IMC accelerators is feasible through post-training techniques, eliminating the need for costly retraining while preserving both accuracy and resistance to side-channel leakage.

Abstract: The massive data-movement overhead in traditional architectures has led to the adoption of In-Memory Computing (IMC) for energy-efficient Deep Neural Network (DNN) processing. By leveraging emerging devices like Spin-Orbit Torque Magnetic Tunnel Junctions (SOT-MTJs), IMC bypasses the "memory wall" and reduces leakage power inherent in traditional CMOS. However, this shift introduces dual hardware threats: manufacturing Process Variation (PV) degrades reliability and increases vulnerability to fault injection, while power Side-Channel Attacks (SCAs) compromise security. Existing defenses address these threats in isolation. This work presents a posttraining framework that simultaneously hardens analog IMC accelerators against both threats without retraining the model. Implemented in the IMAC-Sim simulator, our approach uses the proposed Variation Impact Score (VIS) to guide the mapping of Fault Observation Windows (FOWs) and introduces the Leakage Per Inference (LPI) metric to quantify input-dependent power variability under stochastic injection and the resulting reduction in effective signal-to-noise ratio. Experiments show that PV-induced faults can degrade accuracy by over 50%, while our method restores near-baseline accuracy and mitigates the threat of correlation-based power analysis attacks.

</details>


### [194] [Rethinking MCP Security: A Large-Scale Study of Runtime MCP Servers and Security Scanner Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11086)
*Pei Chen,Baichao An,Mengying Wu,Binwang Wan,Geng Hong,Jinsong Chen,Xudong Pan,Jiarun Dai,Min Yang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MCPZoo is the largest collection of MCP servers for dynamic analysis (64,611 unique servers), built via a multi-agent framework. Using it, the authors find that existing security scanners are unreliable: 96.89% of servers are flagged as risky, but manual validation shows fewer than 50% are true positives, with inconsistent results across scanners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is becoming a standard for LLM agents to interact with external tools, yet real-world security risks remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale runtime MCP servers for analysis. Current assessments rely on scanners applied to few cases, and their reliability is unknown.

Method: The authors build MCPZoo using a multi-agent framework that transforms static repositories into dynamic, interactable MCP services. The framework emulates human experts by combining environment inference with feedback-driven refinement to handle build, deployment, and runtime defects. Servers are validated through real protocol interactions. MCPZoo is then used to conduct the first ecosystem-scale measurement of both MCP servers and the security scanners that analyze them, with manual validation of scanner alerts.

Result: MCPZoo contains 64,611 unique MCP servers (113,927 total), with 37,288 supporting dynamic analysis. Existing scanners flag 96.89% of servers as risky, but manual validation reveals fewer than 50% of sampled alerts are true positives, and scanner outputs are inconsistent across different scanners.

Conclusion: Current MCP security scanning practices are unreliable, producing high false-positive rates and inconsistent results. MCPZoo enables large-scale, reproducible measurement of MCP server security, exposing these limitations. A public query interface is released to support practical risk assessment.

Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has rapidly established itself as a standard interface for enabling LLM-based agents to interact with external tools and services. As MCP servers are increasingly entrusted with security-sensitive operations, understanding their real-world risks has become critical. In practice, due to the absence of large-scale runtime MCP servers, such understanding largely relies on security scanners applied to a small number of cases, yet the reliability of these assessments remains unclear.
  In this study, we revisit how MCP security is measured. We present MCPZoo, the largest collection of MCP servers for dynamic analysis to date. MCPZoo is constructed through a multi-agent framework for transforming in-the-wild static repositories into dynamic services. The framework emulates how human experts build, diagnose, and iteratively repair deployment and runtime defects by combining environment inference with feedback-driven refinement. To ensure practical interactivity at runtime, the servers are validated via real protocol interactions. As a result, MCPZoo contains 64,611 unique MCP servers (113,927 in total), with more than 37,288 supporting dynamic analysis. Leveraging MCPZoo, we conduct the first ecosystem-scale measurement of MCP servers and the scanners that analyze them. While existing scanners report that 96.89% of servers are risky, we find that these signals are unreliable. In particular, manual validation shows that less than 50% of sampled alerts are true positives, and scanner outputs exhibit clear inconsistency across scanners. Overall, MCPZoo enables large-scale, reproducible measurement of MCP server security and exposes limitations of current scanning practices. We further release a public query interface to support practical risk assessment of MCP servers.

</details>


### [195] [AMT-X: Phase-Structured Multi-Turn Red-Teaming with Checklist-Gated Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11151)
*Yi Ting Shen,Kentaroh Toyoda,Alex Leung*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AMT-X is a phase-structured multi-turn red-teaming framework that uses a reproducible state machine driven by semantic signals, combined with a multi-role jury using phase-conditioned checklists, to reveal a substantial gap (up to 33 pp) between partially and fully actionable harmful outputs from frontier LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM safety evaluation suffers from two key deficiencies: (1) reliance on single-turn attacks that underestimate risks from adaptive multi-turn adversaries, and (2) single-judge scoring that reports a monolithic success rate, conflating partially actionable outputs with those containing complete operational detail. A more rigorous, reproducible, and granular evaluation methodology is needed.

Method: AMT-X structures the multi-turn attack as an explicit, reproducible multi-phase state machine driven by semantic signals extracted from the victim model's responses. It replaces single-judge scoring with a multi-role jury employing phase-conditioned checklists, where success is gated on actionable harm — specifically, whether outputs contain complete, real, and operational detail.

Result: Evaluated across six frontier victim models (under default safety alignment) and seven Moderation sub-categories, AMT-X achieved 97.6–100% attack success rate under a lenient threshold, but only 66.7–78.6% under a strict gate requiring complete operational detail — revealing a gap of up to 33 percentage points between partial and fully actionable harm.

Conclusion: Single-turn benchmarks and monolithic success rates significantly overestimate LLM safety. The large gap between lenient and strict success rates demonstrates that many "successful" attacks yield only partially actionable content, and rigorous multi-turn, phase-gated evaluation is essential for meaningful safety assessment.

Abstract: Safety evaluation of large language models (LLMs) relies largely on single-turn attack datasets and single-judge scoring, underestimating risk from adaptive multi-turn adversaries and reporting a single success rate that does not separate partially actionable outputs from those carrying complete operational detail. We propose AMT-X (Adaptive Multi-Turn Exploitation), a phase-structured multi-turn red-teaming framework. Unlike prior multi-turn attacks that rely on ad hoc escalation or free-form per-goal plans, AMT-X casts the attack as an explicit, reproducible multi-phase state machine driven by semantic signals from the victim, and replaces single-judge scoring with a multi-role jury whose phase-conditioned checklists gate success on actionable harm. Across six frontier victim models (queried under their default safety alignment, without added moderation layers) and seven Moderation sub-categories, AMT-X attains overall attack success rates of 97.6-100% under a lenient score threshold, but 66.7-78.6% under a stricter gate requiring complete, real, and operational detail: a gap of up to 33 percentage points between partially and fully actionable harm.

</details>


### [196] [Prezta: Provable Remote Execution of Zero-Trust Authorization using SNARKs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11466)
*Zhongjing Wei,Osaid Muhammad Ameer,Yupeng Zhang,Nikita Borisov*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Prezta eliminates application gateways in OT/ICS security by running zero-trust authorization policies inside a zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) on the client side. The zkVM generates a succinct proof that edge devices can verify efficiently, removing deployment burdens while maintaining security. A prototype using RISC Zero zkVM supports XACML 3.0 and JWT, achieving proof generation in tens of seconds and verification in tens of milliseconds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Operational technology (OT) edge devices have limited capabilities, so zero-trust authorization currently relies on application gateways that are powerful but burdensome: they must be collocated with distributed edge devices, kept patched, and managed with minimal downtime. The authors seek to eliminate these gateways entirely while preserving strong authorization guarantees.

Method: The authors propose Prezta, which compiles authorization policies (XACML 3.0) and identity claims (JWT) into a zero-knowledge virtual machine (RISC Zero zkVM) running on the client. The zkVM executes the policy evaluation and outputs a succinct zero-knowledge proof that the edge device verifies efficiently. Optimizations include compiling policies to Rust code, precompiling regular expressions, and tuning signature verification and JWT parsing, yielding over an order-of-magnitude reduction in prover time.

Result: The prototype compiler correctly handles 83% of the XACML 3.0 conformance suite. Proof generation completes in tens of seconds on a desktop machine, while verification takes only tens of milliseconds — fast enough for resource-constrained edge devices.

Conclusion: Prezta demonstrates that zero-knowledge proofs can feasibly replace application gateways for zero-trust authorization at the OT edge, eliminating deployment and management overhead while allowing policies and identity schemes to evolve without edge-device updates.

Abstract: Modernizing the security of operational technology systems that control critical infrastructure has become a pressing challenge. Because edge devices have limited capabilities, modernization has relied on application gateways that interface with identity management systems and enforce access policies. These gateways are powerful enough to perform complex authorization decisions and support zero-trust architectures, but they create major deployment and management burdens: they must be collocated with remote, distributed edge devices, kept up to date with security patches, and managed with minimal downtime.
  We propose Provable Remote Execution of Zero-Trust Authorization (Prezta), an architecture that eliminates these gateways by evaluating policies within a zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) running on the client. The zkVM produces a succinct proof of authorization that edge devices can verify efficiently, extending the zero-trust security envelope to the edge. Policies and identity management schemes can evolve without updating edge devices.
  To demonstrate the feasibility of Prezta, we implement a prototype built using the RISC Zero zkVM that supports XACML 3.0 policies and JWT identity claims. While zkVMs introduce substantial proof overhead, we mitigate this overhead by compiling policies to Rust code and precompiling regular expressions. Combined with optimized signature verification and JWT parsing, these measures reduce prover time by more than an order of magnitude. Our compiler correctly implements 83\% of the XACML 3.0 conformance suite, with proof generation completing in tens of seconds on a desktop. Verification, by contrast, takes only tens of milliseconds, which is fast enough for resource-constrained edge devices.

</details>


### [197] [LLM-Guided Program Evolution for Targeted Black-Box Attacks on Perceptual Hash Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11472)
*A. Krylov,D. Rakhov,V. Veselova,D. Bolokhov,Oleg Y. Rogov*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel evolutionary framework (GigaEvo + OpenEvolve) for targeted second-image attacks on perceptual hash algorithms (PHAs). It achieves higher attack success rates with fewer queries and lower L2 distortion compared to black-box baselines, exposing vulnerabilities in widely deployed PHAs like pHash, PDQ, PhotoDNA, and NeuralHash.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Perceptual hash algorithms are widely used for image forgery detection, but their adversarial robustness is poorly understood and lacks provable guarantees. Existing gradient-based attacks require internal knowledge of PHA architectures and cannot handle the non-differentiable, discretized nature of hash outputs. There is a need for black-box attacks that expose vulnerabilities without architectural access, motivating the development of more robust schemes.

Method: The authors propose an evolutionary framework combining GigaEvo and OpenEvolve to perform targeted second-image attacks: given a source image and a target hash, the goal is to produce a perturbed image whose hash matches the target. The framework is black-box, requiring no internal knowledge of PHA architectures and naturally handling non-differentiable hash discretization. Attack performance is evaluated via a composite score incorporating Attack Success Rate (fraction of adversarial images with normalized Hamming distance below threshold p), number of hash function queries, and L2 distortion.

Result: Experiments on 30 ImageNet image pairs across four deployed PHAs (pHash, PDQ, PhotoDNA, NeuralHash) show the evolutionary approach achieves comparable or better ASR than existing black-box baselines while using substantially fewer queries and producing lower L2 distortion. The best evolved programs reduce the composite attack score relative to the best optimized seed by: 41.2% (NeuralHash), 38.3% (PDQ), 34.0% (pHash), and 8.1% (PhotoDNA).

Conclusion: The results reveal previously unreported vulnerabilities in widely deployed content-moderation pipelines. The authors conclude that evolutionary black-box methods can effectively attack PHAs without architectural knowledge, and these findings motivate the need for developing provably robust perceptual hashing schemes.

Abstract: Perceptual hash algorithms (PHAs) are widely deployed to detect image forgery under benign transformations, yet their robustness against adversarially chosen perturbations remains poorly understood and rarely comes with provable guarantees. We propose a novel evolutionary framework based on GigaEvo and OpenEvolve for targeted second-image attacks on perceptual hash algorithms. We assess attack performance using a composite score that jointly accounts for the fraction of adversarial images whose normalized Hamming distance to the target hash falls below threshold p (Attack Success Rate), the number of queries issued to the hash function, and the L2 distortion relative to the original image. Experiments on four deployed PHAs (pHash, PDQ, PhotoDNA, NeuralHash) across 30 ImageNet image pairs demonstrate that our evolutionary approach achieves comparable or better ASR than existing black-box baselines using substantially fewer queries to the hash function, while simultaneously producing adversarial images with lower L2 distortion relative to the originals. The best evolved programs reduce the pre-defined composite attack score relative to the best optimized seed by 41.2% for NeuralHash, 38.3% for PDQ, 34.0% for pHash, and 8.1% for PhotoDNA. Unlike gradient-based methods, our framework requires no internal knowledge of PHA architectures and naturally handles the non-differentiable, discretized nature of hash outputs. These results reveal previously unreported vulnerabilities in widely deployed content-moderation pipelines and motivate the development of provably robust perceptual hashing 1schemes.

</details>


### [198] [Time Is Money: Incentivized Causal Transaction Ordering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11496)
*Hongyin Chen,Xu Zheng,Jichen Li,Ittay Eyal*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PRECEDE is a transaction ordering mechanism that prevents front-running on blockchains by using a power-weighted randomized lottery where winning probability grows super-linearly with bids, creating an equilibrium where attackers are economically deterred from competing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Front-running is a persistent problem on blockchains where attackers observe pending transactions and publish their own first to seize rewards, eroding incentives for users. Existing ordering mechanisms (e.g., bidding-based) fail to enforce transaction causality and only result in bidding wars. No prior approach has achieved true causality enforcement.

Method: PRECEDE is a mechanism-design approach that orders transactions via a power-weighted randomized lottery. The winning probability is a super-linear function of the bid amount. Users publish transactions with deterring bids, forming a game-theoretic equilibrium where attackers rationally refrain from front-running. The mechanism also prevents sandwich attacks, a prominent class of front-running exploits.

Result: PRECEDE achieves transaction causality by removing the economic incentive to front-run. The deterring bid strategy forms an equilibrium where attackers abstain from competing. It also prevents sandwich attacks and can be deployed on any censorship-resistant blockchain with only a change to the transaction ordering mechanism.

Conclusion: PRECEDE provides a practical, deployable solution to blockchain front-running by aligning economic incentives through a randomized lottery ordering scheme, achieving causality enforcement without requiring fundamental protocol overhauls.

Abstract: Front-running is a subtle and persistent problem for blockchains. A blockchain is a stateful virtual machine executing instructions called transactions. Users earn rewards by publishing functional transactions essential to the system. Attackers observe these transactions and publish their own ahead of the users', seizing the reward and eroding users' incentive to publish functional transactions. Preventing front-running means enforcing causality: If an attacker receives transaction tx_A and then publishes transaction tx_B, then tx_A must be ordered before tx_B. However, this causality is only observed by the attacker. Practical systems order transactions by bid amount, so transactions willing to pay more get executed first, but this only results in a bidding war eroding users' rewards. Though numerous ordering approaches have been proposed, none achieves causality, leaving users vulnerable to front-running.
  We present PRECEDE, a mechanism-design approach that enforces transaction causality by removing the economic incentive to front-run. PRECEDE orders transactions by a power-weighted randomized lottery, whose winning probability grows super-linearly in the bid. The user's strategy of publishing a transaction with a deterring bid forms an equilibrium where the attacker refrains from competing. Moreover, PRECEDE prevents the prominent sandwich attack, which relies on front-running. PRECEDE can be directly deployed in any censorship-resistant blockchain with a simple change to its transaction ordering mechanism.

</details>


### [199] [Graph-Based Structural Evaluation of LLM-Translated Adversary Emulation Procedures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11517)
*Ahmed M. Elmisery*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: GBSE evaluates cross-OS adversary emulation plan translations using normalized Graph Edit Distance across four layers (technique, tactic, telemetry, Sigma logsource). Applied to a 29-step ALPHV/BlackCat Windows-to-Linux translation, it revealed that binary scoring overestimates fidelity — full structural preservation on technique/tactic layers masked telemetry drift (0.897 similarity) and low technical realism (0.43), preventing the 0.80 deployment threshold from being met.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Binary scoring methods for evaluating LLM-generated cross-OS adversary emulation translations overestimate fidelity by measuring countable features rather than structural, observable, and rule-level equivalence. This can result in translations that merely rename tools while retaining source-platform logic, offering defenders little genuine cross-platform coverage.

Method: GBSE models each adversary procedure as a directed attributed graph and computes normalized Graph Edit Distance (GED) across four layers: technique, tactic, telemetry class, and Sigma logsource. The framework incorporates bipartite GED, a telemetry-intent parser for converting free text to observable classes, and 49 validated Sigma rules (19 Linux, 30 Windows) with full ATT&CK technique coverage. A 29-step ALPHV/BlackCat Windows-to-Linux translation was evaluated by comparing a reconstructed Windows control against the LLM-generated Linux plan.

Result: Technique and tactic layers showed perfect structural preservation (GED=0, similarity=1.000). Telemetry similarity dropped to 0.897 (GED=3) due to three steps with unmapped or drifting observables. Sigma logsource similarity was 1.000. All states classified as Medium Fidelity, with a best composite score of 0.674 — below the 0.80 deployment threshold, largely due to technical realism scoring 0.43 against the required 0.990. Technique-level divergences were found, including RDP-based external access mapped to unencrypted exfiltration and credential-store access mapped to remote-system discovery.

Conclusion: GBSE provides a more rigorous alternative to binary scoring for cross-OS emulation plan translation, capturing structural and semantic fidelity that binary metrics miss. The framework exposes hidden telemetry drift and technique-level semantic divergence, establishing that current LLM translations fall short of deployment-grade realism even when surface-level technique mappings appear correct.
