Abstract: Adversary emulation plans describe multi-step attacker procedures using MITRE ATT&CK techniques, privilege requirements, and observable telemetry. Translating them across operating systems supports cross-platform defender evaluation, and large language models (LLMs) can automate this task. However, a translation may only rename tools while retaining source-platform logic, giving defenders little target-platform coverage. Binary scoring can overestimate fidelity because it measures countable features rather than structural, observable, and rule-level equivalence. Graph-Based Structural Evaluation (GBSE) models each procedure as a directed attributed graph and calculates normalized Graph Edit Distance (GED) across four layers: technique, tactic, telemetry class, and Sigma logsource. GBSE was applied to a 29-step ALPHV/BlackCat Windows-to-Linux plan, comparing a reconstructed Windows control with the unmodified LLM-generated Linux version. Technique and tactic structure were fully preserved (GED=0, similarity=1.000). Telemetry similarity fell to 0.897 (GED=3) because three steps contained unmapped or drifting observables, while Sigma logsource similarity was 1.000. Every state was classified as Medium Fidelity, with a best composite score of 0.674. The 0.80 deployment threshold was not reached because technical realism scored 0.43 against the required 0.990. The framework includes bipartite GED, a telemetry-intent parser that converts free text into observable classes, and 49 validated Sigma rules: 19 for Linux and 30 for Windows. The rules provide complete ATT&CK technique coverage and pass validation with zero findings. Additional analysis reveals technique-level divergence, including RDP-based external access mapped to unencrypted exfiltration and credential-store access mapped to remote-system discovery. Results were reproduced and verified against recorded outputs.

</details>


### [200] [Linux disk encryption and self-encrypting drives -- A case study on Opal2 drives security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11563)
*Milan Brož,Tamara Čierniková,Ondřej Kozina,Vladimír Sedláček*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A black-box security analysis of 38 commercial Opal2 self-encrypting drives reveals firmware vulnerabilities and Linux integration issues, leading to fixes in major Linux distributions and an open-source testing toolset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Opal2 self-encrypting drives (SEDs) offer hardware-based disk encryption as an alternative or supplement to software-based solutions. Despite their growing adoption, the real-world security of Opal2 firmware and its integration with Linux had not been systematically evaluated, motivating a comprehensive black-box study across multiple vendors.

Method: The authors conducted a black-box case study on a testbed of 38 commercial off-the-shelf Opal2 drives from various vendors. They examined Linux integration compatibility and performed security analysis of the Opal2 firmware, followed by responsible disclosure of identified issues to the respective vendors.

Result: Multiple firmware security issues and Linux incompatibilities were discovered across different drive models. These findings prompted improvements in Linux disk encryption tools deployed across all major Linux distributions. The authors also released their test scenarios as an open-source toolset to enable independent public evaluation.

Conclusion: Opal2 self-encrypting drives, while valuable for hardware-based disk encryption, suffer from real-world firmware security weaknesses and integration gaps. Systematic third-party evaluation and open-source testing frameworks are essential to improve both drive firmware security and operating system interoperability.

Abstract: Opal2 self-encrypting drives provide hardware-based disk encryption serving as an additional layer of protection, or a replacement, for software-based solutions. This paper presents a case study of real-world Linux integration of Opal2 drives and the security of Opal2 firmware. The study was conducted on a testbed of 38 commercial off-the-shelf Opal2 drives from various vendors using a black-box approach. We identified several firmware security issues and incompatibilities, which we responsibly disclosed to respective vendors. Our findings led to improvements in Linux disk encryption tools used across all major Linux distributions. To enable independent evaluation for the public, we release our test scenarios for Opal2 drives as an open-source toolset.

</details>


### [201] [Cardano's Voltaire Governance: Complete Specification and Research Program](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11601)
*Nimrod Talmon,Oghenekaro Elem*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This technical report analyzes Cardano's Voltaire on-chain governance system (CIP-1694, enacted via the Chang hard fork in 2024), providing a complete specification of its mechanisms and proposing a research agenda for governance optimization through simulation, delegation dynamics, parameter optimization, and game-theoretic incentive design, including a formal governance kernel for safety/liveness analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Blockchain governance faces a fundamental trilemma of balancing adaptability, security, and stakeholder representation. Cardano's Voltaire system represents a live, large-scale experiment in on-chain governance (managing ~$235M treasury) that warrants rigorous formal analysis and principled optimization, yet lacks a complete technical specification and structured research program to advance blockchain governance science.

Method: The authors (1) provide a complete technical specification of Voltaire's three-body architecture, seven governance action types, voting rules, and constitutional framework; and (2) establish a research agenda spanning agent-based simulation platforms, delegation dynamics analysis, multi-objective parameter optimization, and game-theoretic incentive design, including a formal governance kernel modeled as a state-transition system for safety and liveness verification.

Result: The paper delivers a specification sufficient for implementation or formal analysis and proposes a structured research program with preliminary results including a minimal executable governance kernel that captures self-amending governance. No quantitative experimental results are reported in the abstract.

Conclusion: The report serves as both a comprehensive technical reference for Voltaire and a call to the research community to rigorously study Cardano's governance as a live, large-scale experiment, aiming to advance blockchain governance science through principled optimization and formal methods.

Abstract: Blockchain governance, the set of processes by which decentralized protocols evolve, remains a fundamental challenge in balancing adaptability, security, and stakeholder representation. This technical report analyzes Cardano's Voltaire governance system, the on-chain framework introduced via CIP-1694 and enacted through the Chang hard fork in September 2024, and lays down a corresponding research program.
  We make two contributions. First, we provide a complete technical specification of Voltaire's mechanisms, including its three-body architecture, seven governance action types, voting rules, and its constitutional framework; this specification is sufficient for implementation or formal analysis. Second, we establish a research agenda for principled governance optimization, including design of an agent-based simulation platform, analysis of delegation dynamics, optimization of multi-objective parameters, and game-theoretic incentive design; we provide preliminary results, including a formal governance kernel: a minimal executable model capturing self-amending governance as a state-transition system and enabling rigorous safety and liveness analysis.
  Our report offers a comprehensive technical overview and invites the research community to advance blockchain governance science through rigorous study of Voltaire as a live, large-scale experiment now managing a treasury valued at approximately \$235 million (1.47B ADA as of early July 2026).

</details>


### [202] [Closing the Loop: An Access-Control Architecture for Automated, Anomaly-Driven Network Revocation in IoT Deployments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11649)
*Muhammet Emir Korkmaz,Kemal Bicakci,Yusuf Uzunay*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper presents a closed-loop anomaly detection and automated enforcement architecture for IoT networks using only standard protocols (802.1X/EAP-TLS, RADIUS). An anomaly detector triggers a RADIUS-based disconnect-then-revoke response via certificate revocation, achieving eviction in ~336 ms and full revocation in ~448 ms, with the detector reaching an AUC of 0.9964 across 24 attack scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most IoT network-based anomaly detection systems stop at raising alerts without automated enforcement. Those that address enforcement rely on programmable data planes (e.g., SDN) that are rarely deployed in real networks. There is a gap between detection and actionable, automated response using existing, widely deployed protocols.

Method: The authors propose an access-control architecture with three components: (1) IEEE 802.1X/EAP-TLS device authentication with a RADIUS server as a continuous policy decision point, capable of issuing Change-of-Authorization Disconnect-Requests and certificate revocation; (2) a central contextual access policy engine that consumes anomaly detector output and actuates responses via a restricted channel to RADIUS; (3) a one-class anomaly detector adapted from a prior MUD/SDN design, replacing per-flow multi-model pipelines with passive traffic capture and a single fused model combining cluster-based, volumetric, and protocol-signature scores. The detector uses ~43× less training data than the reference design.

Result: The detector achieved an AUC of 0.9964 and detected all 24 evaluated attack scenarios (8 attack types × 3 intensities). The closed-loop response evicted a device from the network in 335.8 ms on average, with certificate revocation completing in a further 111.5 ms (total ~447.3 ms). Training data efficiency improved by ~43× over the reference design.

Conclusion: The closed-loop architecture effectively bridges detection and enforcement using only standard, already-deployed protocols. The evaluation serves as a demonstration of the architecture's viability rather than a full detector benchmark. Multi-device generalization is identified as the immediate next step for future work.

Abstract: Network-based anomaly detection for IoT devices has matured to the point of reporting strong detection accuracy, yet most published systems stop at raising an alert and leave the question of automated enforcement to future work or to a programmable data plane that few real networks operate. This paper presents an access-control architecture that closes that loop using only standard, already-deployed protocols. Devices authenticate via IEEE 802.1X with EAP-TLS, and a RADIUS server acts as a continuous policy decision point capable of evicting an active session via a Change-of-Authorization Disconnect-Request and permanently excluding a device through certificate revocation. A central, contextual access policy engine continuously consumes the anomaly detector's output and actuates this response over a narrowly restricted channel to the RADIUS server; the same engine is designed to be extensible to other access types, though this paper evaluates only the network access-control mechanism. This mechanism is driven by an anomaly signal from a one-class detector adapted from a prior MUD/SDN-based design, replacing its per-flow multi-model pipeline with passive traffic capture and a single fused model that combines a cluster-based, a volumetric, and a protocol-signature score. On a single testbed device, the detector reaches an AUC of 0.9964 and detects all 24 evaluated attack scenarios (eight attack types at three intensities) using roughly 43$\times$ less training data than the reference design, and the resulting alerts reliably trigger the automated disconnect-then-revoke response, which we measure to evict a device from the network in 335.8\,ms on average and complete certificate revocation in a further 111.5\,ms. We report this evaluation as a demonstration of the closed-loop architecture rather than of the detector itself, and discuss multi-device generalization as a concrete next step.

</details>


### [203] [Agent Hacks Agent: Autoresearch for Production-Agent Red-Teaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11698)
*Xutao Mao,Xiang Zheng,Cong Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AHA is a falsifiable discovery loop that automatically red-teams production LLM agents (Claude Code, Codex) by hypothesizing vulnerabilities, constructing attacks, executing them, and promoting confirmed findings into a Vulnerability Concept Graph (VCG). The frozen VCG outperforms baselines by 14.2 points and transfers across models, scenarios, and attack channels, providing auditable safety artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production LLM agents (e.g., Claude Code, Codex) operate over untrusted content, making safety failures directly actionable. Existing red-teaming methods optimize attack success but fail to capture the enabling conditions behind unsafe behavior — they record where attacks succeed, not why. There is a need for automated red-teaming that discovers reusable vulnerability knowledge rather than one-off attacks.

Method: AHA is a falsifiable discovery loop comprising: (1) proposing a vulnerability hypothesis, (2) constructing a falsifier, (3) instantiating a valid attack, (4) executing it in a sandboxed harness, (5) reflecting on the trajectory, and (6) promoting confirmed findings into a Vulnerability Concept Graph (VCG). Each VCG concept links an attacker-facing surface to an unsafe trajectory via a claim, enabling condition, falsifier, transfer prediction, and supporting evidence. The system uses one agentic research environment to discover knowledge about another.

Result: Across Claude Code and Codex on three scenarios (direct and indirect attacks), AHA-discovered concepts revealed a reusable vulnerability core. A frozen VCG (requiring no further search) outperformed the strongest frozen discovery baseline by 14.2 percentage points under a single-shot protocol and transferred successfully across scenarios and attack channels.

Conclusion: The VCG provides an auditable artifact for production safety teams to inspect vulnerabilities, validate patches, and accumulate reusable safety knowledge, advancing automated red-teaming from attack-centric to knowledge-centric approaches.

Abstract: Production LLM agents such as Claude Code and Codex operate over untrusted content, files, commands, and workspace state, making safety failures directly actionable. Red-teaming must therefore keep pace with evolving models and tools. Existing approaches mainly optimize attack success and preserve artifacts such as benchmarks, payloads, or attack programs, which record where attacks succeed but not the enabling conditions behind unsafe agent behavior. We study automated red-teaming for production LLM agents using one agentic research environment to discover reusable vulnerability knowledge about another. We present AHA, a falsifiable discovery loop that proposes a vulnerability hypothesis, constructs a falsifier, instantiates a valid attack, executes it in a sandboxed harness, reflects on the trajectory, and promotes confirmed findings into a Vulnerability Concept Graph (VCG). Each concept links an attacker-facing surface to an unsafe trajectory through a claim, enabling condition, falsifier, transfer prediction, and supporting evidence. Across Claude Code and Codex on three scenarios covering direct and indirect attacks, the discovered concepts reveal a reusable vulnerability core across models and agents. A frozen VCG requires no further search and outperforms the strongest frozen discovery baseline by 14.2 percentage points under the same single-shot protocol, while transferring across scenarios and attack channels. The resulting VCG provides an auditable artifact for production safety teams to inspect vulnerabilities, validate patches, and accumulate reusable safety knowledge. Our code is available at https://github.com/henrymao2004/Auto-research-red-teaming-in-sleep.

</details>

### [204] [The Individual-Targeting Assumption: A Systematic Review of Proactive Robots in Human Group Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09734)
*Tauhid Tanjim,Tasmia Mayen,Malte F. Jung,Susan R. Fussell*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A systematic review of 63 studies (2000–2025) reveals that 60.3% of proactive HRI research treats co-present people as independent targets (the Individual-Targeting Assumption). Group-aware approaches emerge only after interaction begins, leaving the robot's entry into pre-formed groups critically unaddressed. Three recurring failure modes are identified: engagement misdetection, social ratification blindness, and bystander neglect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proactive robots are increasingly deployed in public spaces where people form cohesive social groups, yet it is unclear whether prevailing HRI design paradigms account for the relational structure that defines groups as social units. The authors aim to examine whether and how existing proactive HRI research addresses group-level dynamics versus treating individuals in isolation.

Method: A systematic review of 63 proactive human-robot interaction studies conducted in group settings, spanning 2000 to 2025. The authors analyzed each study for the presence of the Individual-Targeting Assumption (ITA), cataloged when and how group-aware mechanisms were employed, and identified recurring failure patterns across the corpus.

Result: ITA was present in 60.3% of the reviewed corpus. Group-aware approaches appeared almost exclusively after the robot was already embedded in an ongoing interaction. The critical problem of how a robot should detect and negotiate entry into a pre-formed group before initiating contact remained entirely unaddressed. Three failure modes recurred: engagement misdetection, social ratification blindness, and bystander neglect.

Conclusion: Proactive HRI in group settings must be reframed not as an extension of dyadic interaction but as a qualitatively distinct design problem. The robot's approach to the group during the entry phase is identified as a critical, understudied open challenge requiring dedicated research attention.

Abstract: Proactive robots are increasingly deployed in public environments where people are encountered not as isolated individuals but as members of cohesive social groups. Yet whether the prevailing design paradigm in proactive human-robot interaction (HRI) accounts for the relational structure that defines a group as a social unit remains largely unexamined. Through a systematic review of 63 proactive HRI studies in group settings from 2000 to 2025, we identify a recurring tendency, the Individual-Targeting Assumption (ITA), in which robots treat co-present people as independent engagement targets. We find that ITA is present in 60.3% of the corpus, with group-aware approaches emerging almost entirely after the robot is already embedded in an ongoing interaction. Critically, how a robot should detect and negotiate entry into a pre-formed group before initiating contact remains unaddressed across the corpus. Three failure modes, engagement misdetection, social ratification blindness, and bystander neglect, emerge as recurring patterns when proactive robots interact with human groups. These findings reframe proactive HRI in group settings not as an extension of dyadic interaction but as a qualitatively distinct design problem, and they identify the robot's approach to the group during the entry phase as a critical and understudied open challenge.

</details>


### [205] [When LLM Tutoring Responses Work: Evidence from Student Programming Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09919)
*Mohammad Fahim Abrar,Shayla Sharmin,Roghayeh Leila Barmaki*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Analyzing 16,851 assistant-response interactions from the StudyChat dataset, this paper finds that LLM tutoring response styles significantly associate with student outcomes—verification feedback yields the highest productive continuation (82.4%), direct answers the lowest (62.7%)—and demonstrates that optimal response strategies are context-dependent, varying across help-seeking situations like debugging versus conceptual questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM tutors proliferate in CS education, it is unclear which response styles best support productive student continuation across different programming help-seeking contexts. Prior work studied student LLM usage broadly but lacked granular, context-sensitive analysis linking specific response styles to follow-up outcomes.

Method: The authors transformed the StudyChat dataset (203 students, 2,214 conversations) into 16,851 assistant-response interactions. Using local LLM-assisted annotation with Gemma 4, they labeled four dimensions: help-seeking situation, student state, assistant response style, and student next-turn outcome. Human validation achieved 82% agreement (Cohen's κ=.74). Chi-square tests and descriptive comparisons assessed associations between response styles and productive/unresolved continuation across contexts.

Result: Response style was significantly associated with both productive continuation (χ²(7)=100.39, p<.001, V=.078) and unresolved continuation (χ²(7)=125.77, p<.001, V=.087), though effect sizes were small. Verification feedback had the highest productive-continuation rate (82.4%); direct answers had the lowest (62.7%). Context-dependent patterns emerged: response-style score ranges were smallest in low-confusion conceptual contexts (.017) and largest in high-cognitive-load contexts (.203). Stepwise guidance reduced confusion best in high-load code requests; direct answers led to more unresolved continuation in high-load debugging.

Conclusion: Tutoring response styles matter for student outcomes in LLM-mediated programming help-seeking, but there is no one-size-fits-all optimal style. Effective AI tutoring requires context-aware response design—tailoring feedback type to the student's specific help-seeking situation (e.g., debugging vs. conceptual, cognitive load level) to maximize productive continuation.

Abstract: As students increasingly use LLM tutors in computer science education, one question becomes especially important: what kind of response helps a student continue productively? Prior work has studied how students use LLMs in computer science education, but less is known about how tutoring response styles are associated with student follow-up across programming help-seeking contexts. This paper analyzes StudyChat (UMass, 2026), a public dataset of student and ChatGPT tutoring conversations from an artificial intelligence course. We transformed StudyChat into 16,851 assistant-response interactions from 203 students and 2,214 conversations. Using local LLM-assisted annotation with Gemma 4, we labeled student help-seeking situations, student state, assistant response style, and student next-turn outcome. Human validation showed 82\% agreement with the LLM-assisted labels (Cohen's $κ=.74$). We analyzed productive continuation and unresolved continuation across the full dataset and across help-seeking contexts. Globally, response style was significantly associated with productive continuation, $χ^2(7)=100.39$, $p<.001$, $V=.078$, and unresolved continuation, $χ^2(7)=125.77$, $p<.001$, $V=.087$, though effect sizes were small. Verification feedback had the highest productive-continuation rate (82.4\%), while direct answers had the lowest (62.7\%). Descriptively, response-style score ranges were smallest in low-confusion conceptual contexts (.017) and largest in high-cognitive-load contexts (.203). More detailed comparisons showed situation-dependent response patterns. For example, stepwise guidance was followed by greater confusion decrease in high-cognitive-load code requests, while direct answers were followed by more unresolved continuation in high-load debugging. These findings support context-aware evaluation and design of AI tutoring responses for programming education.

</details>


### [206] ["Code Is Cheap. Show Me the Talk.": Lessons from Teaching and Managing AI Coding Tool Usage in a Visualization Course](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09938)
*Zhongzheng Xu,Taehyun Yang,Fumeng Yang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper reflects on integrating Generative AI coding tools into a university visualization course, reporting student behaviors like widespread unsanctioned AI use, reliance on refinement over explanation in prompting, preference for scaffolded instruction, and trade-offs between polished but homogeneous final projects. The authors advocate for clearer AI boundaries, explicit prompting instruction, and teaching critical adaptation of AI-generated designs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GenAI coding tools are increasingly used by students in visualization courses, potentially undermining pedagogical goals by allowing students to bypass intended learning. The authors sought to understand how students actually use these tools and to develop strategies for managing AI use effectively in an educational context.

Method: The authors conducted a retrospective case study of an upper-level visualization course where they: (1) injected prompts into assignments to detect unsanctioned AI use, (2) administered oral checkout questions to assess understanding, (3) delivered two dedicated AI coding labs (one with optional AI use, one mandatory), and (4) analyzed student prompting logs, submission choices, and final project outcomes compared to a prior offering.

Result: Key findings: (a) at least 50% of students used AI tools before any formal AI instruction; (b) in AI labs, ~50% of prompting logs involved refinement, while explanation-seeking was nearly absent; (c) in the optional lab, 56.4% (44/78) of submissions chose scaffolded instructions over crafting their own prompts; (d) final projects were more polished than the previous cohort's but exhibited greater visual homogeneity.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that visualization educators must establish clearer AI use policies, provide deliberate instruction on effective prompting strategies, and teach students to critically interrogate and adapt generic AI-generated visualizations to suit their specific data narratives, rather than accepting default outputs.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) coding tools are transforming visualization education. They can assist with implementation and design, but they can also let students bypass intended learning trajectories. In this paper, we share our retrospective experience managing and teaching AI use in an upper-level visualization course. We implemented prompt injections, asked oral checkout questions, and taught two AI coding labs. Prior to our coding labs, at least half of the students had already used AI tools in their assignments. In both AI coding labs, refinement accounted for about half of students' prompting logs, and explanation was almost absent. In the lab where AI coding was optional, 44 of 78 (56.4%) submissions preferred the scaffolded instructions over designing their own prompts. Students' final projects were more polished than in our previous offering, but also more visually homogeneous. Our reflections point to the need for clearer AI use boundaries and instruction on prompting, and for teaching students to question generic AI designs and adapt them to their data and story.

</details>


### [207] [SyncSpace: Layout-Conditioned 3D Gaussian Splatting for Space Reskinning in Mixed Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10050)
*Qinchuan Zhang,Weibo Xu,Yunge Wen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: SyncSpace generates 3D Gaussian splatting scenes spatially aligned and visually consistent with physical spaces by using depth-sensed layout as a geometric prior for a generative world model, then aligns output to the real world via coarse-to-fine registration with optional manual refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods lack joint spatial alignment and visual consistency when generating virtual worlds overlaid on physical spaces. Per-object control is cumbersome, and automatic registration may fail, necessitating a system that preserves room layout while enabling stylistic reskinning of a single physical space.

Method: The approach proceeds in stages: (1) depth sensing scans the physical space to extract 3D bounding boxes; (2) these boxes are rendered into a layout-only panorama serving as a geometric prior for a generative world model; (3) the model outputs a 3DGS scene where objects are re-semantized to match a target style without per-object control; (4) coarse-to-fine registration aligns the generated scene to physical space; (5) manual refinement via pinch gestures handles cases where automatic registration fails to converge.

Result: The system demonstrates hand-tracked engulfment interaction, where the virtual world rises to replace the physical space. A single physical space can be reskinned into multiple stylistically distinct worlds while preserving the original layout.

Conclusion: SyncSpace shows that combining depth-derived geometric priors with generative 3DGS and a hybrid automatic/manual registration pipeline enables compelling mixed-reality experiences where physical rooms are faithfully reskinned into diverse virtual environments with preserved spatial structure.

Abstract: We present SyncSpace, a system that achieves both spatial alignment and visual consistency between a generated 3DGS world and physical space. We first scan the space via depth sensing to extract 3D bounding boxes, which we render into a layout-only panorama and feed as a geometric prior to a generative world model, producing a Gaussian splat scene in which objects are re-semantized to fit a target style without per-object control. We then align the generated scene to physical space with a coarse-to-fine registration algorithm, refined manually via pinch gestures when automatic registration does not converge. We demonstrate a hand-tracked engulfment interaction in which the virtual world rises to replace the physical space, and show a single space reskinned into multiple stylistically distinct worlds with its layout preserved.

</details>


### [208] [Learning behavior accounts for background-related advantage in AI-assisted education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10101)
*Jingwei Yi,Yueqi Xie,Jiyan He,Rui Ye,Junming Huang,Bin Zhu,Sean Rintel,Yu Xie,Xing Xie,Fangzhao Wu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A study of 318 university students in structured learning experiments examined heterogeneity in AI-assisted learning. Findings show that proactive, critical engagement with AI predicts better outcomes, and learner profiles (university ranking, prior knowledge) shape who benefits — primarily through differences in how students interact with AI. Learning behavior largely mediates the relationship between background and outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on AI in education yields inconsistent evidence on average effects, and educational technology research shows average effects often mask substantial heterogeneity across student populations. This motivates a deeper investigation into which students benefit from AI assistance and how learner profiles and learning behaviors shape these patterns.

Method: Researchers recruited 318 university students to participate in structured learning experiments lasting up to 125 minutes. They examined associations between learner profiles (university ranking, prior knowledge), learning behaviors (proactive and critical engagement vs. limited engagement), and learning outcomes, including mediation analyses to assess whether behavior accounts for profile-outcome relationships.

Result: Learning behavior strongly predicts outcomes: proactive and critical engagement is associated with significantly better performance. Students from higher-ranking universities and those with greater prior knowledge benefit more, largely because they are more likely to adopt proactive interaction strategies. Accounting for learning behavior substantially weakens or eliminates the associations between learner profiles and outcomes, indicating behavior is a key mediating pathway.

Conclusion: How students use AI — not merely who they are — is the critical pathway linking background differences to learning gains. These insights can help educators and students better integrate AI into educational practice by focusing on fostering effective engagement strategies.

Abstract: Generative AI has been found, and will likely be found increasingly, useful in education. However, existing AI-for-education studies provide inconsistent evidence on its average effects. More broadly, research on prior educational technologies shows that average effects often mask substantial heterogeneity across student populations. Motivated by this evidence, this study examines heterogeneity in students' learning behavior with AI, which students benefit from AI assistance, and how learner profiles and learning behavior shape these patterns. To this end, we recruited 318 university students to participate in structured learning experiments lasting up to 125 minutes. Our findings indicate that students' learning behavior is strongly associated with learning outcomes, with behaviors characterized by proactive and critical engagement, rather than limited engagement, associated with significantly better performance. These behavioral differences are related to learner profiles, with students from higher-ranking universities and those with greater prior knowledge tending to benefit more, consistent with their greater likelihood of adopting proactive interaction strategies. Accounting for learning behavior substantially weakens or eliminates the associations between learner profiles and learning outcomes, suggesting that how students use AI is a key pathway through which background differences are linked to learning gains. Overall, this work provides a deeper understanding of AI assistance in education by showing how differences in learner profiles and learning behavior shape who benefits from AI-supported learning. These insights can help educators and students better navigate and integrate AI into educational practices.

</details>


### [209] [Intervenability as a Design Requirement for Autonomy and Oversight within Human-Centered AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10322)
*Thomas Herrmann*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces the concept of "intervenability" — a framework for human intervention in AI systems that goes beyond emergency shutdowns or reconfiguration, emphasizing continuous human oversight, autonomy, and mutual improvement between humans and AI in organizational contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mechanisms like emergency shutdowns and workarounds fail to adequately capture the nuanced ways humans need to interact with and override AI systems. There is a gap in conceptualizing how controllability, autonomy, and keeping humans in the loop can be systematically instantiated for AI-based decision-making, particularly for discrete case-related decisions rather than just real-time process control.

Method: The authors draw on literature review and practical AI application examples to develop a taxonomy of intervenability. This taxonomy categorizes intervention activities along dimensions of mental effort required from users, distinguishes between real-time process control and discrete decision-making contexts, and frames interventions as part of an iterative socio-technical improvement cycle within organizational practices.

Result: The paper delivers a taxonomy that maps the spectrum of possible human interventions in AI systems, differentiated by user mental effort. It shows how intervenability supports a dual improvement pathway: enhancing human capabilities through reflective practice and enabling technical AI reconfiguration. The concept also opens design space for AI systems that can self-initiate or facilitate interventions, enabling a smooth transition from human intervention to automated reconfiguration.

Conclusion: Intervenability is a necessary extension to human-centered AI, bridging the gap between emergency measures and full reconfiguration. Embedding collaborative reflection on intervention effects into organizational routines is essential for continuous improvement of both human operators and AI systems. The concept also motivates future AI designs capable of recognizing when intervention is needed and transitioning toward self-reconfiguration.

Abstract: Based on the literature and several practical examples of possible AI applica-tions, we outline the concept of intervenability. This new phenomenon is not covered by emergency shutdowns, workarounds, or the reconfiguration of automated systems. Intervenability instantiates the principles of control-lability, autonomy, oversight, and keeping humans in the loop in the context of AI. We provide a taxonomy that encompasses a range of possibilities for intervening activities and differentiates them regarding the mental effort of the users. This taxonomy extends the scope of interventions from real-time control of automated processes to AI-based discrete case-related decision-making. This is in accordance with human-centered AI, which seeks to combine human strengths with the usage of AI. We demonstrate how inter-venability can potentially contribute to the ongoing development of human capabilities on the one hand and to further technical improvement by recon-figuration of AI on the other. Exploring and collaboratively reflecting on the effects of interventions as an integral part of organizational practices is key to enabling this continuous improvement on both sides. Intervenability also provides further momentum for the design of an AI that can help realize in-terventions on its own and advance a smooth transition from intervention to reconfiguration of the AI.

</details>


### [210] [Spatula: Exploring On-Demand In-Situ Interfaces and Interaction for Attribute Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10405)
*Boyu Li,Linjie Qiu,Lin-Ping Yuan,Duotun Wang,Yue Jiang,Zeyu Wang,Hongbo Fu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Spatula is a proof-of-concept system that automatically generates on-demand, in-situ attribute control interfaces for motion graphics creation, framing attribute control as an explorable landscape across four dimensions: Discoverability, Resolution, Scope, and Expandability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current creative tools lack adequate support for iterative refinement of generative content, particularly in controlling attributes. Users need more intuitive and flexible ways to manipulate parameters during the creative process rather than being constrained by static, predefined control interfaces.

Method: The authors built Spatula, a technical probe system that automatically analyzes animation context to generate corresponding attributes and UI controls on-demand. They conceptualized attribute control along four key dimensions (Discoverability, Resolution, Scope, and Expandability) and evaluated the system through a user study with 12 participants, plus demonstrative applications in web design and 3D modeling.

Result: The user study (N=12) demonstrated that Spatula provides intuitive and convenient interactions while supporting diverse fine-grained parameter control needs. The plug-and-play design successfully generalized to other domains including web design and 3D modeling.

Conclusion: Spatula validates that automatically generated, context-aware attribute control interfaces can significantly improve the iterative creative workflow. Its generalizability beyond motion graphics suggests broad applicability across multiple creative domains.

Abstract: Controlling attributes is a critical step toward achieving the final creative outcome, yet current approaches fall short in supporting users in the iterative refinement of generative content. We propose Spatula, a proof-of-concept system that generates on-demand, in-situ attribute control interfaces and interactions for creating motion graphics. Building on a technical probe that automatically analyzes animation context and generates corresponding attributes and UI, we frame attribute control as an explorable landscape and explore the attribute control space along four key dimensions: Discoverability, Resolution, Scope, and Expandability. Findings from a user study (N=12) show that our system provides intuitive and convenient interactions while supporting diverse needs for fine-grained parameter control. Furthermore, our applications demonstrate that the plug-and-play design generalizes to other domains, such as web design and 3D modeling.

</details>


### [211] [How Data Narratives Go Wrong: A Taxonomy of Issues Across the Data Communication Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10523)
*Yu Fu,Jiawei Zhou,Sichen Jin,Munmun De Choudhury,Cindy Xiong Bearfield,John Stasko*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Introduces TIC, a taxonomy categorizing breakdowns in data narratives across six dimensions (data, analysis, visual encoding, text, reasoning, interpretation), grounded in a qualitative annotation of 700 real-world cases, to provide a holistic diagnostic lens for problematic data communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Failures in data narratives are not merely isolated errors but emerge from a broader meaning-making process. Existing work addresses these issues in silos (statistics, visualization, fact-checking), lacking a unified framework to explain how problems arise, propagate, and compound.

Method: Synthesized prior literature across disparate fields; qualitatively annotated 700 real-world data narratives sourced from fact-checking sites, research datasets, and controversial media; iteratively refined the taxonomy. Contributed an annotated case corpus with coding justifications and an interactive browsing interface.

Result: TIC organizes recurring breakdowns across six dimensions — data, analysis, visual encoding, text, reasoning, and interpretation — situated within a process framework spanning analysis, narrative construction, and audience reception.

Conclusion: TIC offers a structured diagnostic tool for identifying and understanding failures in data narratives, supporting future sociotechnical interventions aimed at trustworthy data communication.

Abstract: Data narratives increasingly shape public understanding, but their failures are rarely just isolated factual errors or deceptive charts. Instead, they emerge through a broader meaning-making process in which quantitative evidence is transformed into claims, representations, and arguments. While prior work has examined these failures across disparate fields (e.g., statistics, visualization, and fact-checking), the community lacks a holistic lens to explain how these issues arise, propagate, and compound. To address this gap, we introduce TIC, a Taxonomy of Issues in Data Communication, synthesized from prior literature and refined through the qualitative annotation of 700 real-world data narratives from fact-checking sites, research datasets, and controversial media. TIC organizes recurring breakdowns across six dimensions-data, analysis, visual encoding, text, reasoning, and interpretation-and situates them within a framework spanning analysis, narrative construction, and audience reception. Alongside the taxonomy and process framework, we contribute a qualitatively annotated case corpus with coding justifications and an interactive browsing interface. Collectively, these contributions provide a structured lens for diagnosing problematic data narratives and informing future sociotechnical support for trustworthy data communication.

</details>


### [212] [Motif: Discovering and Automating Personal Web Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10531)
*Shaokang Jiang,Daye Nam*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Motif passively observes browser activity to discover recurring interaction patterns, recommends automations to users, and generates executable programs upon confirmation. In a study with 8 participants, Motif discovered more automatable patterns than users identified through "vibe coding," and most generated automations were useful and aligned with participants' routines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing programming-by-demonstration and LLM-based automation systems require users to explicitly know what to automate and what is automatable. Additionally, LLM agent-based automation is computationally expensive compared to traditional programs. There is a need for a system that can proactively discover automation opportunities without user initiation.

Method: Motif is a system that passively observes everyday browser activity to detect recurring, programmable interaction patterns. When a pattern is discovered, it surfaces a recommendation to the user. After user confirmation, Motif generates a program (rather than relying on expensive LLM agents at runtime). Users can review and refine the generated program using natural language.

Result: In a multi-day study with 8 participants, Motif discovered more automatable patterns than users recognized when attempting to build automations via "vibe coding." Most discovered patterns matched participants' actual routines and were deemed useful. Follow-up surveys indicated that most participants would continue using Motif-generated programs.

Conclusion: Motif demonstrates that passive, ambient observation of browser activity can surface more automation opportunities than users can self-identify, and that generating static programs (rather than relying on persistent LLM agents) is a viable and user-accepted approach for browser automation.

Abstract: Recent advances in LLMs and existing work on programming by demonstration have made it possible for end users to create automations by explicitly demonstrating their behavior to LLMs. However, these approaches rely on the assumption that users know what to automate and what is capable of being automated. Additionally, automation via LLM agents is often expensive compared with programs. We introduce Motif, a system that passively observes everyday browser activity to discover recurring interaction patterns that are programmable, makes recommendations to users whenever a pattern is discovered and generate a program to install after user confirmation. Users can review, and refine the program using natural language. We evaluated Motif in a multi-day study, comparing its ambient discoveries against automations users attempted to build via ``vibe coding.'' With eight participants, Motif discovered more automatable patterns than users recognized. Most of them matched participants' routines and were useful. Follow-up surveys showed most would continue using Motif-generated programs.

</details>


### [213] [Navigating the Open-Source Model Ecosystem: An Empirical Study of Creator Practices in Artistic Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10538)
*Yiluo Wei,Yupeng He,Qiming Ye,Gareth Tyson*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: First large-scale empirical study of how creators use and combine open-source image generation models, analyzing 6M images with embedded metadata to map the ecosystem of 22.4K base models and 154K LoRA models, revealing strengths and obstacles in these emerging workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The open-source image generation ecosystem has grown rapidly with creators curating and combining community models, yet no large-scale study has examined these workflows. A gap exists between understanding closed-source (e.g., Midjourney) and open-source creation practices.

Method: The authors construct a novel dataset of 6 million images containing embedded generation metadata (model usage, prompts, creation parameters). They analyze the usage patterns of 22.4K base models and 154K LoRA models by linking model instances to generated images at scale.

Result: The study reveals the ecosystem's unique strengths (model composability, community-driven curation) and inherent obstacles, providing empirical evidence about actual creator workflows in open-source image generation.

Conclusion: The findings offer insights for improving ecosystem sustainability and innovation. The publicly released dataset serves as a practical reference for creators and a foundation for future research.

Abstract: The open-sourcing of powerful image generation models has created a vibrant ecosystem where creators curate and combine a vast array of community-contributed models. This practice stands in sharp contrast to using closed-source tools like Midjourney. Yet, little is known about these emerging creative workflows. To bridge this gap, this paper presents the first large-scale empirical study of creator model usage behavior within this open-source image generation ecosystem. We construct a novel dataset of 6 million images with their embedded generation metadata -- a detailed recipe of the creation process, including the models used and the prompts. By linking the usage of 22.4K base models and 154K LoRA models to the images, our findings underscore the ecosystem's unique strengths and its inherent obstacles. This provides valuable insights for making this ecosystem more sustainable and innovative. Moreover, we make our dataset publicly available, providing creators with practical references for producing better artworks and researchers to facilitate further studies.

</details>


### [214] [U-Lens: Supporting User Uncertainty Management in Long-Form LLM Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10604)
*Yu Mei,Qingyue Zhuang,Jie Cai,Chang Liu,Zhi Zheng,Zhoutong Ye,Chun Yu,Yuanchun Shi*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: U-Lens is a system that helps users manage uncertainty in LLM-generated long-form answers by organizing uncertain claims into contextual inspection targets, prioritizing them, and connecting each with evaluative context and response options — moving beyond simple confidence scores to support the full interpretation-evaluation-decision workflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Users of LLMs struggle to identify which parts of a long-form response are unreliable, understand why they may be unreliable, and decide what actions to take. Existing uncertainty communication methods (e.g., confidence scores) make uncertainty visible but fail to support the broader, multi-stage process of managing uncertainty distributed across lengthy responses.

Method: The authors conducted a formative study examining how users manage uncertainty across three stages: interpretation, evaluation, and decision. From this, they derived design guidelines (uncertainty target representation, evaluative explanation, response guidance, interactive presentation) and built U-Lens, a support system that instantiates these guidelines. U-Lens was evaluated in a controlled within-subjects study (n=18) against a confidence-cue baseline.

Result: U-Lens significantly improved verification efficiency and effort allocation, lowered perceived workload, and strengthened perceived support across all three stages (interpretation, evaluation, and decision) compared to the confidence-cue baseline.

Conclusion: The work reframes uncertainty support for generative AI from presenting isolated, text-centered cues toward supporting the user-centered process of interpreting, evaluating, and acting on uncertain information.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate long-form answers for knowledge-intensive tasks, but users often struggle to decide which parts of a response deserve scrutiny, why they may be unreliable, and what to do next. Prior work on uncertainty communication has largely focused on making uncertainty visible through cues such as confidence scores, leaving less support for the broader process of managing uncertainty distributed across a long response. Through a formative study, we examine how users manage such uncertainty across three stages: interpretation, evaluation, and decision. Based on these insights, we derive design guidelines that address both stage-specific and cross-stage needs: uncertainty target representation, evaluative explanation, response guidance, and interactive presentation. We instantiate these guidelines in U-Lens, an uncertainty-management support system that organizes uncertain information in long-form responses into contextual inspection targets, prioritizes them for attention, and connects each target with evaluative context and response options. We evaluated U-Lens in a controlled within-subjects study with 18 participants, comparing it against a confidence-cue baseline. Our results show that U-Lens improved verification efficiency and effort allocation, lowered perceived workload, and strengthened perceived support across interpretation, evaluation, and decision stages. This work reframes uncertainty support for generative AI from presenting isolated, text-centered cues toward supporting the user-centered process of interpreting, evaluating, and acting on uncertain information.

</details>


### [215] [Lottery and Sprint Arcade: Enabling Player-Driven Game Editing with Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10711)
*Maya Grace Torii,Takahito Murakami,Yoichi Ochiai*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A voice-driven, LLM-mediated game editing system allows players to modify a Space Invaders-style game during play. A user study reveals that players had positive experiences regardless of programming background, with distinct editing patterns: perceptible parameter edits correlated with usability, while core gameplay edits correlated with enjoyment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore how LLMs can enable play-driven game modification through natural language, shifting game generation from offline automation to real-time, interactive co-creation, and to understand how users experience such AI-mediated editing and how editing patterns relate to player experience.

Method: A play-driven game editing system was built where spoken natural-language commands are interpreted by an LLM and translated into structured updates of ~100 internal configuration parameters. A user study was conducted combining subjective evaluations, workload measures (NASA-TLX), and log-based analysis of editing behavior to investigate RQ1 (user experience) and RQ2 (editing patterns vs. experience).

Result: Participants reported generally positive experiences with moderate workload; outcomes did not strongly depend on prior programming experience. Log analysis revealed that edits to immediately perceptible parameters correlated with higher usability, while edits to core gameplay structures correlated more with enjoyment. Qualitative reflections identified diverse strategies: exploratory experimentation, goal-driven structural modification, and iterative parameter tuning.

Conclusion: Voice-driven, LLM-mediated editing supports accessible, play-driven human-AI co-creation in structured arcade game environments, enabling non-programmers to meaningfully participate in game modification through natural interaction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are shifting game generation from offline automation toward play-driven modification through natural language interaction. In this work, we present a play-driven game editing system that enables players to modify a retro Space Invaders - style arcade game through voice-based natural-language commands during play. Spoken instructions are interpreted by an LLM and translated into structured updates of internal configuration parameters, allowing iterative play - edit - feedback cycles in an invader-style game environment without exposing underlying system details. The game includes approximately 100 editable configuration fields controlling mechanics, visuals, interaction patterns, and audio behavior, enabling gameplay transformation through incremental parameter changes. To investigate how users experience play-driven AI-mediated editing (RQ1) and how emergent editing patterns relate to variations in player experience (RQ2), we conducted a user study combining subjective evaluations, workload measures, and log-based analysis of editing behavior. Participants were able to modify gameplay with generally positive experiences and moderate workload, and interaction outcomes did not strongly depend on prior programming experience. Editing-log analysis revealed distinct experiential tendencies: adjustments to immediately perceptible parameters were associated with higher usability, whereas edits affecting core gameplay structures were more closely associated with enjoyment. Post-session reflections further identified diverse editing strategies, including exploratory experimentation, goal-driven structural modification, and iterative parameter tuning. These findings demonstrate that voice-driven editing can support accessible, play-driven human - AI co-creation within a structured invader-style arcade game environment.

</details>


### [216] [FaciliTrain: Practicing Facilitation Skills through AI-Simulated Group Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10850)
*Hang Jiang,Yuanxin Zhu,Diyi Yang,Yoon Kim,Deb Roy,Jad Kabbara*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: FaciliTrain is a voice-based training system where learners practice facilitating AI-simulated multi-participant conversations, receiving structured AI feedback. A mixed-methods study (N=24) found treatment participants' self-rated comfort declined versus controls, while qualitative themes highlighted the taxonomy's externalization value, cognitive demands of the "Making Connections" technique, voice as a forcing function for deliberate responses, and strong preference for AI feedback over self-practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Skilled facilitation of inclusive small-group dialogue is critical but difficult to scale because it requires expert coaches, live practice partners, and iterative feedback. The authors aim to address this scalability bottleneck by leveraging AI simulation and feedback to support deliberate practice of facilitation techniques.

Method: The authors developed FaciliTrain, a voice-based training system where learners assume the facilitator role in an AI-simulated multi-participant conversation, apply five evidence-based facilitation techniques, and receive structured AI feedback. A mixed-methods study was conducted with 24 participants split into a formative study (N=12) and a controlled pilot (N=12; 6 treatment, 6 control). Evaluations included a live evaluation task and reflexive thematic analysis of qualitative data.

Result: Both treatment and control conditions achieved comparable accuracy on the live evaluation task. However, treatment participants' self-rated comfort declined significantly while control participants' comfort improved (p = .018). Thematic analysis yielded four themes: (1) the taxonomy externalizes implicit facilitation intuitions; (2) Making Connections is the most cognitively demanding technique; (3) voice acts as a deliberate-response forcing function; (4) participants overwhelmingly preferred AI feedback over self-practice.

Conclusion: Voice-based, AI-supported training systems like FaciliTrain show promise for scaling interpersonal skill development, but the decline in self-rated comfort among treatment participants suggests that increased metacognitive awareness may initially reduce confidence. Design implications center on balancing challenge with support and leveraging voice interaction as a mechanism for deliberate practice.

Abstract: Skilled facilitation supports inclusive small-group dialogue, but deliberate practice is hard to scale: it depends on expert coaches, live practice partners, and iterative feedback. We present FaciliTrain, a voice-based training system in which learners step into the facilitator role of an AI-simulated multi-participant conversation, apply five evidence-based techniques, and receive structured AI feedback to support reflection. We report findings from a mixed-methods study with 24 participants, conducted as a formative study (N = 12) and a controlled pilot (N = 12; 6 treatment, 6 control). Both conditions achieved comparable accuracy on a live evaluation task, though treatment participants' self-rated comfort declined significantly while control participants' comfort improved (p = .018). Reflexive thematic analysis identifies four themes: the taxonomy externalizes implicit facilitation intuitions; Making Connections is the most cognitively demanding technique; voice acts as a deliberate-response forcing function; and participants overwhelmingly preferred AI feedback over self-practice. We discuss design implications for voice-based, AI-supported interpersonal skill training at scale.

</details>


### [217] [What to Distinguish and How? Opportunities and Challenges of Augmenting Multiple, Cluttered Objects in Complex Scenes for People with Low Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10902)
*Yuheng Wu,Ruijia Chen,Jaewook Lee,Jia Li,Kexin Zhang,Mengfong Lio,Weibing Wang,Sanbrita Mondal,Jon E. Froehlich,Yapeng Tian,Yuhang Zhao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: SceneGlance is a wearable AR system that identifies and visually distinguishes objects by importance level for people with low vision. Studies with 25 participants in kitchen and outdoor settings showed the system shifted attention toward higher-importance objects and supported strategic perception, but augmenting many objects reduced overall scene recall, and adjacent augmentations interfered with each other.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People with low vision (PLV) struggle to perceive complex, cluttered, multi-object scenes. Existing AR systems focus on low-level visual enhancement or single-task object augmentation in simple settings, leaving multi-object augmentation in complex real-world scenes underexplored. There is a need to understand how importance-based augmentation can support PLV in navigating such environments.

Method: The authors first conducted a formative study to characterize what objects PLV consider important and how they perceive relative importance. They then built SceneGlance, a wearable AR system that recognizes important objects and visually distinguishes them by importance level. Two user studies were conducted: (1) a controlled lab study with 12 PLV in a mock-up kitchen scene, and (2) a free-form think-aloud study with 13 PLV navigating an outdoor route.

Result: AR distinction based on importance shifted PLV's attention toward higher-importance objects. Participants developed perception strategies such as building mental snapshots from augmentation distribution and hierarchical scanning by importance. However, augmenting many objects reduced overall scene recall (a tradeoff), and adjacent augmentations were found to blend or interfere with each other in complex scenes.

Conclusion: Importance-based AR augmentation can effectively guide PLV attention and support strategic scene perception, but designers must balance the number of augmented objects to avoid recall degradation and address spatial interference between adjacent augmentations. These findings yield design implications for building more practical AR vision enhancement systems for complex real-world environments.

Abstract: People with low vision (PLV) struggle to perceive complex scenes like busy kitchens and crowded streets, which contain many objects, visual clutter, and dynamic elements. Prior AR systems for low vision either enhance low-level visual features or augment task-relevant objects for single tasks in simple settings, leaving multi-object augmentation in complex scenes underexplored. Informed by a formative study characterizing important objects and their perceived importance for PLV, we built SceneGlance, a wearable AR system that recognizes important objects and visually distinguishes them by importance level. Through a controlled lab study with 12 PLV in a mock-up kitchen scene and a free-form think-aloud study with 13 PLV navigating an outdoor route, we found that AR distinction on object importance shifted PLV's attention toward objects of higher importance, and supported perception strategies such as building mental snapshots from the augmentation distribution and hierarchical scanning by importance. However, this attention shift came with a tradeoff, as augmenting many objects reduced overall scene recall. The studies also surfaced challenges posed by AR augmentations in complex scenes, such as adjacent augmentations blending or interfering with each other, yielding design implications for more practical AR vision enhancement systems in the complex real world.

</details>


### [218] [When Context Dominates: Multimodal Signatures of Takeover Readiness Under Varying Hazard and Cognitive Load Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10945)
*Shiva Azimi,Yasaman Hakiminejad,Luis Gomero,Elizabeth Pantesco,Irene P. Kan,Meltem Izzetoglu,Arash Tavakoli*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This driving simulator study found that hazard type (pedestrian vs. crash events) is the primary determinant of takeover performance in semi-automated driving, outweighing the effects of secondary task engagement. Multimodal sensing (vehicle dynamics, physiology, fNIRS) reveals the importance of jointly considering environmental context and driver state for designing adaptive monitoring systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle how distraction, hazard context, and drivers' cognitive/physiological states interact to shape takeover performance in semi-automated driving—an area that remains insufficiently understood despite its critical safety implications.

Method: A controlled, within-subjects driving simulator experiment crossing two hazard types (dynamic pedestrian, static crash) with three secondary task levels (no task, conversation, working memory load). Multimodal data collected: vehicle dynamics, subjective workload ratings, electrodermal activity, heart rate variability, and prefrontal cortical activation via fNIRS.

Result: Hazard context was the primary determinant of takeover behavior: pedestrian events elicited longer, more variable maneuvers; crash events produced faster, more stable responses. Secondary tasks had smaller effects on objective vehicle control, while internal-state measures showed more variable task-related patterns.

Conclusion: Environmental context and human state must be jointly considered when evaluating takeover readiness and designing driver monitoring systems. The study lays groundwork for adaptive, context-aware strategies that support safer human-automation collaboration in semi-automated vehicles.

Abstract: Semi-automated driving systems promise to reduce crashes by assisting with perception and control, yet they simultaneously introduce additional human factors challenges by requiring drivers to monitor automation and rapidly resume control when failures occur. Prolonged passive monitoring can degrade vigilance, delay reactions, and increase takeover risk, but the extent to which distraction, hazard context, and drivers' underlying cognitive and physiological states jointly shape takeover performance remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates these interacting factors using a controlled, within-subjects driving simulator experiment that crosses two hazard types (dynamic pedestrian and static crash events) with three levels of secondary task engagement (no task, conversation, and working memory load). Driver responses were assessed using a multimodal sensing framework that integrates vehicle-dynamics measures, subjective workload ratings, autonomic physiology (electrodermal activity and heart rate variability), and prefrontal cortical activation measured with functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Results show that hazard context is the primary determinant of takeover behavior, with pedestrian events producing longer and more variable maneuvers and crash events yielding faster and more stable responses. Secondary tasks exerted smaller effects on objective vehicle control, while internal-state measures showed more variable task-related patterns. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering environmental context and human state when evaluating takeover readiness and designing driver monitoring systems. This study lays the groundwork for adaptive, context-aware strategies that support safer human-automation collaboration in semi-automated vehicles.

</details>


### [219] [Same Stories, Different Journeys: From Social Comparison to Sensemaking in AI-Mediated Peer Career Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11039)
*Pengping Tan,Baoquan Zhao,Zhenhui Peng*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: JobMate transforms real social media career posts into persona-grounded conversational AI agents, shifting passive browsing to active dialogue. A between-subjects study (N=24) found this redirected detrimental upward social comparison toward constructive self-reframing while preserving authentic peer content for emotional grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Young job seekers rely on social media for peer comparison and career sensemaking, but passive feed browsing creates a paradox: authentic peer content provides emotional grounding yet triggers detrimental upward social comparison and cognitive overload. Prior work either structures content without changing the passive modality or builds AI career tools that ignore authentic human experiences.

Method: The authors developed JobMate, an interactive system that transforms real social media career posts into persona-grounded conversational AI agents. They conducted a between-subjects study (N=24, three disciplines) comparing JobMate with native RedNote browsing.

Result: JobMate's AI-mediated dialogue redirected social comparison from detrimental upward comparison toward constructive self-reframing and promoted sensemaking through active conversational engagement. However, users still relied on the authenticity of real peer content for emotional grounding.

Conclusion: AI systems that augment authentic online user-generated content can mitigate the negative effects of social comparison while preserving emotional grounding. The authors provide design implications for such systems across social comparison contexts.

Abstract: Young job seekers frequently turn to social media to compare themselves with peers and make sense of career possibilities. However, passive feed browsing creates a paradox: the authentic peer content that provides emotional grounding also triggers potentially detrimental upward social comparison and cognitive overload. Previous work has either structured online user-generated content to reduce noise without changing the passive browsing modality, or built AI-powered career exploration systems that disregard authentic human experiences. To address this gap, we developed JobMate, an interactive system that transforms real social media career posts into persona-grounded conversational AI agents, shifting the interaction from passive scrolling to active, personalized dialogue. We conducted a between-subjects study ($N$ = 24, three disciplines) comparing JobMate with native RedNote browsing. Our study shows that JobMate's AI-mediated dialogue redirected social comparison from potentially detrimental upward comparison toward constructive self-reframing, while promoting sensemaking through active conversational engagement. However, users still relied on the authenticity of real peer content for emotional grounding. We discuss design implications for AI systems that augment authentic online user-generated content consumption across social comparison contexts.

</details>


### [220] [DiffLens: A Visualization System to Explore Local Differences in Graph Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11424)
*Zhiguang Zhou,Yong Zhang,Yuming Ma,Yuqi Zhou,Ke Lu,Yong Wang,Yuhua Liu,Jingfang Mao,Yongheng Wang,Ying Zhao,Wei Chen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper proposes systematic quantitative measures for three categories of graph differences (neighbor-based, path-based, structure-based) caused by sampling, and presents DiffLens, a lens-based visualization system that helps users intuitively explore local differences between sampled and original networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph sampling inevitably introduces discrepancies between sampled and original networks, yet no systematic method exists to quantify and visualize these differences. This gap hinders users from comparing sampling techniques and prevents developers from properly evaluating their methods.

Method: First, the authors define systematic quantitative measures across three difference categories: neighbor-based (local connectivity changes), path-based (shortest path distortions), and structure-based (topological property deviations). Second, they build DiffLens, a visualization system featuring three novel lens-based visual designs — each tailored to display one category of difference — enabling interactive exploration of local discrepancies in user-selected regions of interest.

Result: Two case studies and one user study on real-world network datasets demonstrated DiffLens's effectiveness and usability in helping users explore local differences and compare different graph sampling strategies.

Conclusion: DiffLens provides the first systematic framework combining quantitative measures with interactive visualization to analyze graph sampling differences, filling a critical research gap and offering practical value for both users and developers of graph sampling techniques.

Abstract: Graph sampling techniques have been widely used to simplify network computation and visualization, which also results in inevitable differences between the sampled networks and the original networks in terms of nodes, edges and structures. Investigating such differences can inform graph sampling technique users of the pros and cons of different techniques and select the appropriate one, and can also help graph sampling developers evaluate their own technique. However, there are still no systematic ways to achieve such a goal. This paper fills this research gap by first proposing systematic and generic quantitative measures to quantify three categories of graph differences (i.e., neighbor-based, path-based, and structure-based). Built upon this, we further propose DiffLens, a novel visualization system to help graph sampling developers and users intuitively explore local differences at different regions of their interest within a sampled graph, where three new lens-based visual designs are presented to display the neighbor-based, path-based, and structure-based differences respectively. We conducted two case studies and a user study using real-world network datasets to evaluate DiffLens. The results confirmed its effectiveness and usability in helping users explore local differences and compare different graph sampling strategies.

</details>


### [221] [ManiScope: LLM-Assisted Visual Analytics of Cryptocurrency Manipulation Risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11451)
*Xiaolin Wen,Feng Liang,Yuanye Ma,Qishuang Fu,Zhengyu Sun,Feng Zhu,Can Liu,Yong Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ManiScope is an LLM-assisted visual analytics system for assessing trade-based manipulation risks in cryptocurrency markets, featuring a human-LLM collaborative framework where the LLM acts as a co-analyst that infers user intent and surfaces relevant evidence for hypothesis evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing manipulation detection methods rely on fixed rules or labeled data with limited flexibility. Current visual analytics tools require excessive manual effort to integrate holder relationships, suspicious behaviors, and market dynamics for comprehensive risk assessment.

Method: ManiScope combines coordinated visualizations (token distributions, holder relationships, holder behaviors, price dynamics, suspicious trading patterns) with a novel human-LLM collaborative framework where the LLM serves as a proactive co-analyst — inferring analytical intent and hypotheses from interaction context, then surfacing relevant visual, statistical, and synthesized evidence to support hypothesis evaluation.

Result: Evaluation through two case studies and a user study with 12 experienced cryptocurrency practitioners demonstrated that ManiScope supports effective manipulation risk assessment, reduces manual effort in evidence-seeking, and organizes findings around user hypotheses.

Conclusion: ManiScope demonstrates that positioning an LLM as a proactive co-analyst — rather than a reactive assistant — can significantly enhance evidence-based reasoning for cryptocurrency manipulation risk assessment, with positive results validated by domain practitioners.

Abstract: Cryptocurrency markets are vulnerable to trade-based manipulation, such as wash trading, which can distort price signals and mislead investors. Prior research has mainly focused on detecting manipulation using fixed rules or labeled examples, offering limited flexibility and interpretability for assessing potential risks. Existing visual analytics tools can reveal basic manipulation-related signals, such as token distribution, but still require substantial manual effort to integrate holder relationships, suspicious behaviors, and market dynamics for risk assessment. To address these limitations, we propose ManiScope, an LLM-assisted visual analytics system for analyzing trade-based manipulation risks in cryptocurrency markets. ManiScope provides coordinated views of token distributions, holder relationships, detailed holder behaviors, price dynamics, and suspicious trading patterns. To further enhance user analysis, ManiScope introduces a human-LLM collaborative visual analytics framework. Rather than acting as a basic reactive LLM assistant, the framework positions the LLM as a co-analyst that infers users' analytical intent and emerging hypotheses from interaction context and surfaces relevant visual, statistical, and synthesized evidence for hypothesis evaluation. This design reduces repetitive inspection and strengthens evidence-based reasoning. We evaluate ManiScope through two case studies and a user study with 12 experienced cryptocurrency practitioners. The results suggest that ManiScope supports effective risk assessment of manipulation, reduces manual effort in evidence-seeking, and organizes findings around user hypotheses.

</details>


### [222] [Toward Inclusive Avatar Design with Limb Differences Through Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11512)
*Fernanda Miyuki Yamada,João Paulo Gois,Hiroki Takahashi*

Main category: cs.HC
