TL;DR: This paper surveys technical approaches and design guidelines for creating inclusive 3D avatars that accurately represent people with limb differences, amputations, and non-normative body morphologies, identifying dataset scarcity and animation limitations as key challenges, and positioning AI as a promising solution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As extended reality (XR) grows for social interaction and entertainment, 3D avatar systems overwhelmingly default to normative body types, failing to represent the full spectrum of human morphological diversity — particularly people with limb differences, amputations, and other physical variations. This exclusion perpetuates underrepresentation in immersive digital spaces.

Method: The paper conducts a literature review of emerging technical approaches for inclusive 3D avatar customization, alongside an examination of current guidelines that promote respectful and accurate depiction of non-normative anatomies. It also surveys AI-driven methods as potential pathways to overcome existing barriers.

Result: The review identifies two persistent challenges: (1) a severe scarcity of diverse, high-quality 3D datasets capturing non-normative body morphologies, and (2) fundamental limitations in animation pipelines and rigging systems that assume normative skeletal structures and cannot accommodate morphological variations such as amputations or congenital limb differences.

Conclusion: Artificial intelligence — particularly generative models, neural rendering, and data-efficient learning techniques — is positioned as a promising path to synthesize diverse avatar representations, bridge dataset gaps, and enable adaptive animation systems that can handle non-normative anatomies, thereby advancing truly inclusive 3D avatar generation.

Abstract: As extended reality becomes more popular for social interaction and entertainment, 3D avatars must represent the full diversity of body types. Most 3D avatar systems only support normative bodies and do not accurately depict people with limb differences, amputations, or other morphological variations. This paper reviews emerging technical approaches for inclusive 3D avatar customization for this group and current guidelines that promote respectful and accurate representation. We highlight persistent challenges, including the scarcity of diverse datasets and the limitations in animation for non-normative anatomies. This paper positions artificial intelligence as a promising path to overcoming these limitations and advancing inclusive 3D avatar generation.

</details>


### [223] ["We are all in big trouble! *Shock Emoji": Personal Narratives in Expressing Emotions, Opinions, and Data Regarding Climate Change in TikTok Short Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11803)
*Chu Zhang,Simai Huang,Shaohua Wu,Yihuan Chen,Ray LC*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Analysis of 200 TikTok #climatechange videos reveals four content categories (expression-feelings, views-appeals, news-information, trend-hijacking). Creators use humor for indirect critique, personal narratives over complex discussions, and repackaged news for perceived scientific credibility. Viewer interactions foster empathetic, community-building engagement but risk echo-chamber effects on a platform lacking formal community structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Climate change generates future-oriented anxiety, and understanding how people express themselves about it on social media is critical for addressing public concerns. TikTok, as a rapidly growing short-form video platform, represents an underexplored context for climate communication research.

Method: Content analysis of 200 TikTok videos tagged with #climatechange, categorizing them into four content types: expression-feelings, views-appeals, news-information, and trend-hijacking. Analysis of viewer responses (comments, engagement patterns) was also conducted to examine audience interpretation and community dynamics.

Result: Four content categories were identified. Creators employ humor to deliver pointed critiques while avoiding direct confrontation; substitute complex climate discourse with relatable personal life stories (e.g., vegetarianism, deleting emails); and repurpose news media fragments to project scientific credibility, balancing accuracy with emotional appeal. Viewer responses showed empathetic engagement and reinterpretation of video content, which builds community but may also reinforce pre-existing beliefs.

Conclusion: Short-form video on TikTok enables distinctive climate communication strategies — personal narratives retelling science news, humor-mediated critique, and emotionally balanced credibility signaling. These practices foster community despite the platform's lack of formal community infrastructure, though they carry risks of ideological reinforcement.

Abstract: Climate change is a source of anxiety about the future. Understanding how people express themselves about climate change enables us to address such concerns. To study climate change expression on social media, we analyzed 200 TikTok videos tagged with #climatechange, identifying four categories of content: expression-feelings, views-appeals, news-information, and trend-hijacking. We found that creators use humor to package sharp critiques, avoiding direct confrontation. They replace complex discussions with life stories, such as adopting a vegetarian lifestyle or deleting emails. They borrow from news media to present fragmented information as scientific interpretations, creating a perception of scientific credibility, balancing scientific accuracy with emotionality. Analysis of viewer responses showed they engaged empathetically, reshaping interpretations of videos. These interactions risk reinforcing existing views but help build community on TikTok, which lacks community structure. This study reveals how creators may retell news on science using personal narratives, highlighting how short-form videos enable climate communication.

</details>


### [224] [HandPad: A Bimanual Hand Interface for Fluid Window Interactions in VR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11807)
*Wen Ying,Adil Rahman,Erzhen Hu,Seongkook Heo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: HandPad is a bare-hand interaction system for mobile VR that uses asymmetric bimanual coordination: the non-dominant hand sets spatial frames and modes, while the dominant hand performs precise manipulation, with the NDH palm serving as a physical touch surface for haptic feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mobile VR systems for productivity rely on external input devices, which hinders true on-the-go use. There is a need for device-free interaction techniques that enable efficient knowledge work anywhere without carrying additional hardware.

Method: HandPad leverages asymmetric bimanual coordination by assigning the non-dominant hand (NDH) to establish spatial reference frames and interaction contexts (acting as an input modifier), while the dominant hand (DH) handles fine-grained manipulation. NDH gestures switch modes and targets for DH actions across three interaction domains: multi-window navigation, in-window content interaction, and window management. The NDH palm doubles as a physical touch surface providing passive self-haptic feedback, and both hands are spatially remapped to the virtual window surface for direct, comfortable interaction.

Result: An exploratory study demonstrated that HandPad enables efficient and ergonomic interaction, validating its potential as a device-free approach for knowledge work in VR.

Conclusion: HandPad shows promise as a practical, device-free interaction paradigm for mobile VR productivity, eliminating the need for external controllers while maintaining efficient bimanual interaction through self-haptic support and spatial remapping.

Abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) offers potential for productivity work by creating expansive displays anywhere, yet current systems often rely on external input devices that limit the on-the-go use of mobile VR. We introduce HandPad, a suite of bare-hand interaction techniques that leverage the benefits of asymmetric bimanual coordination and self-haptic support. HandPad assigns the non-dominant hand (NDH) to establish spatial frames and interaction contexts, while the dominant hand (DH) performs fine-grained manipulation. Users can use NDH gestures as an input modifier to change the mode and target of DH interactions, including multi-window navigation, in-window content interaction, and window management. The palm surface of the NDH also serves as a physical touch surface, providing passive haptic feedback for effective DH touch interaction. Both hands and their interactions are spatially remapped to the window surface, enabling comfortable and direct interaction with virtual content. An exploratory study showed that HandPad enables efficient and ergonomic interaction, demonstrating its potential as a device-free approach for knowledge work in VR.

</details>


### [225] [Supporting Reflection in LLM-based Exploratory Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11810)
*Giulia Di Fede,Salvatore Andolina*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: TrailLM is an LLM-based search system that reconstructs exploration paths to support user reflection and metacognitive engagement, balancing the efficiency of LLM assistance with the need for sensemaking in unfamiliar domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs enhance search efficiency but risk undermining the reflective, iterative sensemaking critical when exploring unfamiliar domains. Existing tools prioritize rapid answers without helping users track how their understanding evolves or how their strategies align with their goals.

Method: TrailLM reconstructs and revisits users' exploration paths during information seeking, aligning LLM assistance with sensemaking workflows to foster reflection and metacognitive awareness.

Result: The paper presents TrailLM as a system design; specific empirical results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: Aligning LLM assistance with sensemaking workflows can preserve search efficiency while enhancing critical reflection on the search process itself, addressing a key tension in exploratory search.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make exploratory search more efficient but may undermine the reflection and iterative sensemaking needed in unfamiliar domains. Existing LLM tools often prioritize rapid answers over supporting users in tracking how their understanding evolves and how well their strategies align with their goals. We present TrailLM, a system that helps users reconstruct and revisit their exploration paths to support reflection and metacognitive engagement during information seeking. By aligning LLM assistance with users' sensemaking workflows, TrailLM aims to preserve the benefits of LLM-based search while enhancing opportunities for critical reflection on one's own search process.

</details>


### [226] [FIERO: Empowering Creative Writing Through Collaborative Game Play](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11837)
*Chu Zhang,XiaoKe Zeng,Jin Zhang,Ruoyu Wen,Vince Siu,Richard William Allen,Ray LC*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: FIERO is a multiplayer web-based card game that combines physical cards with a digital interface and generative AI to enhance in-person collaborative storytelling. A study (N=60) showed it significantly improved intuitive stimulation, idea fluency, novelty, and plot coherence compared to online collaborative writing alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Collaborative storytelling faces challenges such as disagreement over plot direction and fragmentation of ideas. Existing tools prioritize synchronous online text sharing but neglect the social dynamics of in-person collaboration, which are critical to creative synergy.

Method: The authors designed and developed FIERO, a hybrid system combining physical card-based gameplay with a digital interface. Physical cards provide tangible scaffolding and social interaction, while the digital component uses generative AI to produce contextual visuals, facilitate group decisions, maintain narrative coherence, and synthesize diverse contributions. The system was evaluated through a between-subjects experiment (N=60) comparing FIERO against online collaborative writing alone, measuring creativity outcomes and story quality.

Result: FIERO significantly outperformed online-only collaborative writing on multiple dimensions: intuitive stimulation, idea fluency, novelty generation, and plot coherence. The physical cards provided creative structure and social engagement, while the digital interface offered contextualized augmentation without undermining player agency.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that collaborative play, when supported by hybrid physical-digital design and generative AI, can effectively foster creative support, offering a promising direction for tools that leverage social dynamics in co-creative processes.

Abstract: Creativity often flourishes in collaboration, such as when designers brainstorm a new app together, or storytellers collectively build a world with elements of each person's narrative. However, collaborative storytelling can have challenges for its participants, such as when they disagree about the plot proposed, or when different ideas become fragmented when voiced individually. While current tools for creative collaboration focus on synchronous online text sharing, they often neglect the social dynamics of in-person collaboration critical to creative synergy. To address this, we created FIERO, a multiplayer web-based card game. Physical cards provide tangible scaffolding and social interaction, while the digital interface generates contextual visuals, facilitate group decisions, ensure narrative coherence, and synthesize different idea contributions using generative AI. Compared against online collaborative writing alone, the game significantly enhanced intuitive stimulation, idea fluency, and novelty generation, and also improved the content of the stories produced, leading to greater plot coherence (N=60). The cards provided creative structure and social engagement, while the interface provided contextualized augmentation without affecting player agency. This work shows how collaborative play can be utilized to foster creative support.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [227] [Knowledge Graphs Meet Graph Neural Networks: A Comprehensive Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09666)
*Chengcheng Sun,Jiayun Tian,Cheng Zhai,Zhixiao Wang,Yajie Song,Xiaobin Rui,Jian Zhang,Philip S. Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a systematic review of GNN-based methodologies across the entire knowledge graph technology pipeline, proposing a two-level taxonomy (KG pipeline stages × GNN model types) and analyzing advantages, limitations, and future directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the widespread adoption of GNNs for knowledge graph tasks, no systematic review exists that comprehensively covers GNN-based methodologies spanning the full KG technology pipeline (construction, embedding, reasoning, and applications). The authors aim to fill this gap.

Method: The authors propose a two-level taxonomy framework: (1) the KG technologies pipeline dimension — covering KG construction, KG embedding, knowledge reasoning, and KG applications; and (2) a GNN-based perspective — categorizing approaches by model type (e.g., GCN, GAT, HGNN). They conduct a structured literature review, analyzing how different GNN architectures suit different KG lifecycle tasks, summarizing strengths and limitations of existing models.

Result: The review provides a structured categorization of GNN-based KG technologies, identifies the advantages of specific GNN variants for different KG tasks, summarizes the strengths and limitations of reviewed models, and highlights unresolved challenges with corresponding future research directions.

Conclusion: GNNs offer significant advantages for KG technologies, but unresolved challenges remain. The proposed taxonomy provides a foundation for systematically understanding and advancing GNN-based KG research, with several promising directions outlined for future work.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm in Knowledge Graphs (KGs) due to their intrinsic ability to model graph-structured data. However, there remains a lack of a systematic review about GNN-based methodologies across the entire knowledge graph technologies pipeline. To address this gap, we first propose a novel two-level taxonomy framework for GNN-based knowledge graph technologies: the KG technologies pipeline and GNN-based perspective. Specifically, the knowledge graph technologies pipeline covers knowledge graph construction, knowledge graph embedding, knowledge reasoning and knowledge graph applications. Meanwhile, the GNN-based perspective provides a new categorization of knowledge graph technologies with GNN models, such as GCN, GAT, and HGNN. Then, we analyze the advantages of GNN technology based on the characteristics of different tasks in the knowledge graph lifecycle. Furthermore, we detailed review various GNN-based models for knowledge graph following the proposed taxonomy, and summarize strengths and limitations. Finally, we discuss unresolved challenges and outline promising directions for future research.

</details>


### [228] [Position: Every Ground Truth is a Human Construction, not an Objective Truth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09668)
*Charlotte Högberg,Ericka Johnson,Kiri L. Wagstaff*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ground truth datasets are not neutral or objective but are constructed through human and technological arrangements. The paper argues for acknowledging this contingency to improve model reliability, transparency, and accountability through the concept of "situated reliability."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The ML community treats ground truth datasets as neutral, objective reference values without acknowledging the subjective choices, human labor, and technological arrangements that construct them. This invisibility undermines reliability, limits appropriate use, and hinders interdisciplinary collaboration.

Method: This is a position paper that develops a conceptual argument drawing on insights from Science and Technology Studies (STS), critical data studies, and related fields to analyze how ground truths are sociotechnically constructed and to propose the framework of "situated reliability."

Result: The paper articulates that ground truth datasets are contingent rather than universal, proposes "situated reliability" as a framework for understanding where and how models can appropriately be used, and argues that surfacing the hidden construction processes of reference datasets enhances transparency, accountability, and interdisciplinary work.

Conclusion: The ML community should move beyond treating ground truths as naturally given and instead embrace their situated, constructed nature. Articulating the limits and strengths of both datasets and models through situated reliability leads to more responsible and context-aware machine learning practice.

Abstract: Ground truth datasets play a fundamental role as reference values in the training and evaluation of machine learning models. This position paper argues that ground truths are not neutral objective measurements that are naturally given, but instead that they are constructed by arrangements of humans and technologies. We argue that the ML community will benefit from articulating and discussing these often invisible or unreported choices and acknowledging that reference data sets are contingent, not universal. Focusing on the situated and context-dependent nature of ground truths can improve reliability by enabling a better informed perspective on where, when, and how the datasets, and the models they have shaped, can best be used. We argue for increasing `situated reliability' which includes articulating the limits and strengths of models and their truth claims. Finally, paying more attention to the construction of ground truths can support transparency, accountability, and interdisciplinary work.

</details>


### [229] [AuditWeave: A Tamper-Evident, Auditor-Navigable Evidence Layer for AI-Assisted and Data-Transformation Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09682)
*Vimal Nakrani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AuditWeave is a lightweight Python library that records AI-assisted workflow steps into an append-only, hash-chained ledger, enabling post-hoc reconstruction of which evidence informed a given decision with tamper-detection guarantees, all with negligible runtime overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations in regulated domains (auditing, finance, healthcare) face recurring obligations to reconstruct how AI systems reached consequential decisions and to prove that reasoning records were unaltered. Existing tools (model observability, drift monitoring, governance reporting) are designed for ML engineers operating systems, not for reviewers who need to trace one specific conclusion back to its supporting evidence.

Method: The authors designed AuditWeave as a zero-dependency Python library featuring: (1) a small, system-agnostic event vocabulary spanning both RAG pipelines and tabular/lakehouse transformations for end-to-end traceability; (2) an append-only, hash-chained ledger where each event is cryptographically linked to its predecessor, making any modification, reordering, insertion, or deletion detectable via chain verification.

Result: Integrity guarantees cost tens of microseconds per event. Verification successfully flagged every injected mutation across four mutation classes over 2,000 randomized trials.

Conclusion: AuditWeave provides a practical, low-overhead mechanism for tamper-evident audit trails in AI-assisted decision workflows, filling a gap between MLOps tooling and the needs of compliance reviewers.

Abstract: AI systems are increasingly used to assist consequential decisions in regulated domains such as auditing, finance, and healthcare. This creates a recurring obligation: an organization must be able to reconstruct, after the fact, which evidence informed a given conclusion, and to show that the record of that reasoning was not altered. Existing tools address related but distinct problems - model observability, drift monitoring, governance reporting - and are built for the machine-learning engineer operating a system, not the reviewer who must trace one specific conclusion back to its supporting evidence. We present AuditWeave, a lightweight Python library, with no runtime dependencies, that records the steps of AI-assisted and data-transformation workflows into a single append-only, hash-chained ledger. A small, system-agnostic event vocabulary spans both retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines and tabular/lakehouse transformations, so a conclusion that draws on both can be traced end-to-end through one record. Within a sealed ledger, any modification, reordering, insertion, or deletion of events is detectable through chain verification. We describe the design and evaluate recording overhead, scalability, and tamper-detection correctness on the reference implementation. The integrity guarantees cost tens of microseconds per event, and, as the hash-chain construction implies, verification flagged every injected mutation across four mutation classes over 2,000 randomized trials.

</details>


### [230] [Ablation, Statistical Inference, and Validation for KV-Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09683)
*Paolo D'Alberto,Ashish Siarasao,Elliott Delaye,Rajeev Patwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A systematic comparison of Turbo-Quant and SpectralQuant KV-cache compression schemes, evaluating WHT rotation with Beta Lloyd-Max and QJL, using statistical validation to disentangle codec differences from implementation variance. Eigenbasis methods fail under heavy tails but adapt their effective semantic dimension to calibration budgets in structured regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need to rigorously compare KV-cache compression methods (Turbo-Quant vs. SpectralQuant) while properly separating genuine algorithmic differences from noise due to implementation variance, and to understand when eigenbasis-based approaches succeed or fail.

Method: The authors employ a statistical validation methodology that isolates systematic codec-level differences from implementation variance. They evaluate non-dominated compression schemes including WHT rotation combined with Beta Lloyd-Max quantization and QJL, and analyze eigenbasis-based methods via the effective semantic dimension metric under varying calibration budgets.

Result: Eigenbasis-based methods fail on heavy-tailed data due to covariance instability. However, in structured regimes they perform well, with the effective semantic dimension (d_eff) adapting to calibration budget size rather than reflecting the true rank of the data.

Conclusion: Eigenbasis methods are not robust under heavy-tailed distributions but are viable in structured settings where d_eff flexibly adjusts to calibration constraints, highlighting the importance of statistical rigor in KV-cache compression benchmarking.

Abstract: This study systematically compares Turbo-Quant and SpectralQuant KV-cache compression, evaluating non-dominated schemes, including WHT rotation with Beta Lloyd-Max and QJL, through a statistical validation methodology that separates systematic codec differences from implementation variance. Key findings reveal that while eigenbasis-based methods fail on heavy-tailed data due to covariance instability, they excel in structured regimes, with the effective semantic dimension ($d_{eff}$) adapting to calibration budgets rather than true data rank. (this is an abstract of the abstract thank you )

</details>


### [231] [SciML in the Wild: A Diagnostic Study of When Structural Priors Help and When They Hurt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09684)
*Vrishank Sai Anand,Prathamesh Dinesh Joshi,Raj Abhijit Dandekar,Rajat Dandekar,Sreedath Panat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: When structural priors in SciML models (PINNs, UDEs) misalign with true data-generating processes, they act as "misregularizers." In macroeconomic forecasting with sparse annual data, simpler models (ARIMA, NODE) consistently outperform more-constrained heuristic-prior models (PINN, UDE), demonstrating that more structure is not always beneficial.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SciML methods like NODEs, PINNs, and UDEs rely on structural priors reflecting governing dynamics, but the consequences of violating this assumption are underexplored. The authors use macroeconomic forecasting — a domain with inherently unreliable structural priors — to stress-test whether imposing structure helps or hurts predictive performance.

Method: Five model families (ARIMA, LSTM, NODE, PINN, UDE) are evaluated on macroeconomic forecasting across 23 countries using sparse annual data, multiple temporal splits, and five random seeds. Models range from purely data-driven (ARIMA, LSTM) to heavily structure-constrained (PINN, UDE), with NODE representing an intermediate neural hybrid without strong mechanistic priors.

Result: No model achieves consistently strong forecasting performance, underscoring the inherent difficulty of low-frequency macroeconomic prediction. However, a clear relative hierarchy emerges: less-constrained models (ARIMA, NODE) consistently outperform more-constrained heuristic-prior models (PINN, UDE). Structural priors function as misregularizers when mismatched with the data-generating process.

Conclusion: The findings constitute a diagnostic message rather than a rejection of SciML: practitioners should empirically test whether structural priors help, rather than assuming that more structure is inherently beneficial. Failure modes include prior misalignment, regime shifts, structural breaks, and optimization instability.

Abstract: Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) methods such as Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs), Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), and Universal Differential Equations (UDEs) are most effective when structural priors reflect reliable governing dynamics. We ask what happens when this assumption is violated. Using macroeconomic forecasting as a stress-test domain, we evaluate five model families, ARIMA, LSTM, NODE, PINN, and UDE, across 23 countries using sparse annual data, multiple temporal splits, and five random seeds. Our results show that none of the evaluated models achieve consistently strong forecasting performance, highlighting the difficulty of low-frequency macroeconomic prediction. However, a clear relative hierarchy emerges: less-constrained models, particularly ARIMA and NODE, consistently outperform more-constrained heuristic-prior models such as PINN and UDE. Rather than treating this as a rejection of SciML, we interpret it as a diagnostic result: structural priors can act as misregularizers when they do not match the data-generating process. We identify failure modes including prior misalignment, regime shifts, structural breaks, and optimization instability, and argue that SciML practitioners should test whether structure helps before assuming that more structure is beneficial.

</details>


### [232] [MawForge: Memory-Bounded Expert Materialization for Local Mixture-of-Experts Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09686)
*Craig Opie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MawForge proposes a disk-backed execution strategy for local MoE inference on memory-constrained unified-memory machines, materializing expert tensors on demand into a bounded cache rather than requiring the full model in RAM. The approach works as an execution mechanism but falls short as a cache-maximization policy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse MoE models decouple total parameters from per-token compute, but local inference still demands that the full model, KV-cache, runtime buffers, and OS headroom all fit simultaneously in fast memory — a prohibitive requirement for consumer-grade unified-memory hardware.

Method: MawForge stores the full MoE model on disk, keeps shared (non-expert) tensors memory-resident, and materializes only routed expert tensors on demand into a bounded in-memory execution cache. This shifts the bottleneck from total model size to expert reuse patterns and cache management.

Result: The system is effective as both a bounded execution mechanism and a measurement substrate for characterizing local MoE inference behavior. However, it does not succeed as a cache-maximization policy. Performance is governed by the interplay of expert reuse, resident footprint, KV-cache sizing, quantization, routing locality, and macOS memory pressure.

Conclusion: Bounded on-demand expert materialization makes local MoE serving feasible on constrained hardware, but naive cache-maximization strategies are insufficient; careful tuning across multiple interdependent factors is required.

Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models separate total parameter count from per-token active computation, but local inference systems often still require the full model, key-value cache, runtime buffers, and operatingsystem headroom to fit in fast memory. MawForge tests a different systems hypothesis: local MoE serving can be made practical on constrained unified-memory machines by storing the full model on disk, keeping common tensors resident, and materializing routed expert tensors into a bounded execution cache on demand. The central finding is that MawForge is effective as a bounded execution mechanism and measurement substrate for local MoE inference, but not as a cache-maximization policy. Performance depends on balancing expert reuse against resident footprint, KV-cache size, quantization, route locality, and macOS memory pressure.

</details>


### [233] [Prioritizing Search Space Regions in the Low Autocorrelation Binary Sequences Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09688)
*Blaž Pšeničnik,Borko Bošković,Jan Popić,Janez Brest*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid search framework combining Thompson sampling (multi-armed bandit) with parallel self-avoiding walks for the LABS problem. It dynamically allocates computation across restriction classes, uses GPU parallelism and Bloom filters, and employs a two-stage optimization. The method improves best-known merit factors for 35 lengths (450≤L≤527) and L=573, including a new record merit factor >8.0 at L=451.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LABS is a hard combinatorial optimization problem with applications in communications, signal processing, and satellite navigation. Existing methods lack adaptive, online resource allocation across the search space's restriction classes, leaving potential merit factor improvements untapped for long sequences.

Method: A hybrid search framework that models restriction class partitions as arms in a multi-armed bandit with Thompson sampling to adaptively allocate computational effort. It employs parallel self-avoiding walks on GPU, shared posterior updates, efficient neighborhood evaluation, and a Bloom filter for cycle prevention. A two-stage strategy first searches constrained partitioned skew-symmetric spaces, then refines best candidates in unrestricted space.

Result: Improved best-known merit factors for 35 sequence lengths in 450≤L≤527 and for L=573. Achieved a new longest sequence with merit factor exceeding 8.0 at L=451. Thompson sampling effectively prioritized high-performing partitions, validating online data-driven resource allocation.

Conclusion: The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective strategy for high-performance merit factor maximization in LABS. Thompson sampling proves valuable for adaptive resource allocation in combinatorial optimization search spaces.

Abstract: Low autocorrelation binary sequences problem (LABS) is a hard combinatorial optimization challenge with important applications in communications, signal processing, and satellite navigation. This paper proposes a hybrid search framework that combines Thompson sampling with parallel self-avoiding walks to adaptively allocate computational effort across restriction classes of the LABS search space. By modeling partitions as arms in a multi-armed bandit setting, the proposed method dynamically shifts search resources toward partitions that empirically produce higher merit factors while maintaining exploration of less-sampled regions. The approach is further accelerated through GPU-parallel execution, shared posterior updates, efficient neighborhood evaluation, and a Bloom filter for cycle prevention. In addition, we use a two-stage optimization strategy that first searches constrained partitioned skew-symmetric spaces and then refines the best candidates in the unrestricted space. Experiments on long binary sequences show that the proposed method improves the previously best-known results for 35 sequence lengths in the range $450 \le L \le 527$ and for $L=573$. In particular, we report a new longest sequence with merit factor exceeding $8.0$, obtained for $L=451$. The results also show that Thompson sampling effectively prioritizes partitions with better observed performance, confirming the value of online, data-driven resource allocation in LABS optimization. Overall, the proposed framework provides a scalable and effective strategy for high-performance merit factor maximization.

</details>


### [234] [What Context Does a Coding Agent Actually Need to Act?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09691)
*Brian Sam-Bodden*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates what context a coding agent actually *needs* when editing code, finding that source code itself is the primary signal — natural-language summaries fail to answer most behavioral questions, surrounding file context beyond the edit site can be aggressively compressed or even deleted without harming resolution rates, and compressed context matches full-file performance at one-third the token cost. The study also identifies a ~9% outcome flip rate in temperature-0 API inference, establishing a noise floor for benchmark comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern coding agents can hold entire repositories in context, but most of that reading is wasted. The authors aim to determine what information is actually necessary when an agent edits code, separating the "finding" (localization) phase from the "acting" (editing) phase to isolate how code representation affects issue resolution.

Method: Using SWE-bench Verified, localization is held fixed via an oracle so only code representation varies. Three experiments are conducted: (1) comparing source code vs. natural-language summaries for answering behavioral questions about edits, evaluated by an independent judge on held-out repositories; (2) testing whether surrounding file context matters by rendering non-edit portions as UML skeletons/signatures vs. deleting them outright, with a pre-registered hypothesis and exact McNemar test (N=70); (3) measuring compressed context against whole files on token efficiency. A reproducibility instrument with gold-validated environments and deterministic patch construction is released.

Result: Source code vastly outperforms natural-language summaries on behavioral questions (27/45 vs. 4/45), with the gap attributable to representation, not summarizer quality (frontier and 3B model summaries score equally poorly). Deleting surrounding file context performs identically to UML skeletons (McNemar p=0.75), meaning surrounding context hardly matters. Compressed context matches whole-file performance at ~19K tokens per resolved issue vs. 94K. Temperature-0 API inference flips ~9% of per-instance outcomes between identical runs, a significant noise floor.

Conclusion: The signal for code editing lives almost entirely in the code being edited itself. Surrounding context can be largely discarded, and compressed representations are highly token-efficient. The field must account for a ~9% non-determinism noise floor in API-based evaluations. The released instrument enables rigorous, reproducible benchmarking with pre-registered hypotheses.

Abstract: A modern coding agent can hold an entire repository in its context window. Most of its reading is wasted -- and the interesting question is not how much context an agent can use, but what it actually \emph{needs}. We study that question at the moment it matters most: when the agent must \emph{edit} code. Separating \emph{finding} the work site from \emph{acting} on it, we hold localization fixed with an oracle, vary only how the code is represented, and score context against real issue resolution on SWE-bench Verified. The answer is starkly minimal. The signal lives in the code being edited itself: natural-language summaries of it answer almost none of the behavioral questions that the source answers ($4/45$ vs.\ $27/45$, held-out repositories, independent judge), and the gap belongs to the representation, not the summarizer -- a frontier model's summaries score exactly as poorly as a 3B model's. The surrounding context hardly matters either: across every multi-file instance in Verified, under a protocol frozen before any data, rendering a file's remainder as UML skeletons and signatures resolves no more issues than deleting that remainder outright ($N{=}70$, exact McNemar $p{=}0.75$). That was our registered hypothesis, and it failed. Compressed context, meanwhile, matches whole files at a third of the tokens: a resolved issue costs $19$K context tokens, not $94$K. The instrument also yielded a finding the field should keep: temperature-0 API inference flips ${\sim}9\%$ of per-instance outcomes between byte-identical runs. That is a noise floor under every small effect reported on this benchmark, including ours. We release the instrument -- gold-validated environments, per-instance proof that every reference edit is expressible from every arm's context, deterministic patch construction, and pre-registered hypotheses whose nulls we publish.

</details>


### [235] [Reference-Based Distillation Detection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09692)
*Rajat Rawat,Sizhe Chen,Akshay Anand,Michael Duan,Bob Rotsted,Sewon Min*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a reference-based membership inference method to detect whether a model was distilled from another teacher model. By comparing output alignment between a student checkpoint and an earlier reference checkpoint against candidate teachers, the method identifies the true teacher with near-perfect accuracy, even with unknown distillation pipelines. The approach also reveals new evidence about potential distillation relationships among models like QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model distillation from stronger third-party models is widespread but raises fairness and policy concerns. The fundamental question driving this work is: can we detect whether a model was distilled from another? While identifying a teacher in isolation is hard, the authors hypothesize it becomes tractable when a reference checkpoint from the same lineage is available.

Method: The method uses reference-based membership inference: given a student model and an earlier checkpoint from the same lineage, it compares how strongly the student preferentially aligns with outputs from candidate teachers relative to the reference. Key techniques include (1) inferring proxy prompt templates from model outputs to handle unknown distillation pipelines, (2) exploiting a distinctive glyph-level signal specific to o1/o3 models, and (3) statistical tests for teacher attribution and distillation detection, extended to open-world settings where no teacher is guaranteed among candidates.

Result: In both controlled distillation experiments and real-world evaluations, the approach recovers the true teacher with near-perfect accuracy in single-teacher distillation scenarios, even with largely unknown distillation pipelines. Applied to contemporary models, the method yields new evidence regarding potential distillation relationships involving QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS.

Conclusion: Distillation detection, while challenging in isolation, becomes highly tractable in a reference-based setting. The proposed method provides a robust framework for teacher attribution and distillation detection, with practical implications for auditing model provenance and enforcing policies around model distillation.

Abstract: Model distillation -- training on outputs from stronger third-party models -- is widely used to boost performance, but raises concerns about unfair advantages and policy violations. This motivates a fundamental question: can we detect whether a model was distilled from another? We show that, while identifying a teacher model from a student in isolation is highly challenging, it becomes tractable in a reference-based setting: given a model and an earlier-generation checkpoint from the same lineage, we can identify the teacher model used to train the later checkpoint. We introduce a distillation detection method based on reference-based membership inference. By comparing how strongly a student model preferentially aligns with outputs from different candidate teachers relative to a reference checkpoint, our method identifies the most likely teacher and detects evidence of distillation. To handle unknown distillation pipelines such as hidden prompts, we infer proxy prompt templates directly from model outputs. We additionally identify a distinctive glyph-level signal specific to o1/o3 models. Evaluating distillation detection is challenging because modern model lineages are already heavily entangled. To address this, we develop a hybrid evaluation spanning both controlled distillation experiments and real-world models. Across both settings, our approach recovers the true teacher with near-perfect accuracy in single-teacher distillation scenarios, even when the underlying distillation pipeline is largely unknown. We further introduce statistical tests for both teacher attribution and distillation detection, and extend our framework to open-world settings where no teacher is guaranteed to be present among the candidates. Applying our method to contemporary models yields new evidence regarding potential distillation relationships involving QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS.

</details>


### [236] [Depth-Entropy Guided Sampling for Training-Free LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09693)
*Zibin Meng,Peng Xie,Kani Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DEGS is a training-free, test-time method that improves LLM reasoning by sampling sequences based on both likelihood and a novel "collapse depth" signal — the layer at which entropy collapses in the forward pass. Instantiated within MCMC power-sampling (DEGS-MCMC), it achieves state-of-the-art training-free accuracy, sometimes surpassing RL-trained models out-of-domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL is expensive (training, curated data, reward signals). Existing test-time methods only use output-layer likelihoods, ignoring rich internal signals from the transformer's forward pass. The authors identify that stronger reasoners (including RL-trained ones) exhibit a distinctive "late collapse" pattern in layer-wise entropy, suggesting this internal dynamic can serve as a quality heuristic.

Method: DEGS defines a per-sequence collapse depth D(x) — the layer where logit-lens decoded entropy sharply drops — and combines it with sequence likelihood p(x) into a joint objective π(x) ∝ p(x)^α exp(βD(x)). This is instantiated within an MCMC power-sampling framework (DEGS-MCMC) that compounds the per-candidate signal over the sampling trajectory. No training, reward model, or labeled data is required.

Result: Across three open-weight models and four reasoning benchmarks, DEGS-MCMC achieves state-of-the-art training-free accuracy. Gains are largest out-of-domain and on harder splits — precisely where likelihood alone fails. DEGS narrowly trails an in-house GRPO reference on math splits GRPO was trained for, yet surpasses it out-of-domain on GPQA for all three models, at single-digit-percent wall-clock overhead.

Conclusion: Layer-wise entropy collapse depth is an effective, near-zero-cost intrinsic quality signal for reasoning. DEGS demonstrates that internal transformer dynamics can be exploited at test time to rival or even exceed RL-trained models out-of-domain, challenging the necessity of expensive RL post-training for reasoning improvements.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become the dominant paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but it requires expensive training, curated data, and reward signals. Recent work shows that sampling from sharpened base-model distributions at test time recovers much of the RL gain, yet existing methods rely solely on output-layer likelihoods and ignore the transformer's internal forward-pass dynamics. We introduce Depth-Entropy Guided Sampling (DEGS), a training-free, test-time method that exploits layer-wise entropy collapse as an intrinsic quality signal. We observe that stronger reasoners -- including RL-posttrained variants -- exhibit a distinctive "late collapse": logit-lens decoded entropy stays elevated until deeper layers before converging. We define a per-sequence collapse depth $D(\mathbf{x})$ and a joint objective $π(\mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x})^α\exp(βD(\mathbf{x}))$ that combines sequence likelihood with this depth-entropy structure, instantiated inside an MCMC power-sampling framework (DEGS-MCMC). Across three open-weight models and four reasoning benchmarks, this near-chance per-candidate signal compounds over the sampling trajectory into state-of-the-art training-free accuracy, with gains largest out of domain and on the harder splits -- exactly where likelihood alone falls short -- at single-digit-percent wall-clock overhead. DEGS narrowly trails an in-house GRPO reference on the math splits GRPO was trained for, yet surpasses it out of domain on GPQA for all three models, without any training, reward model, or labeled data.

</details>


### [237] [Low-Rank Attention Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09694)
*Jonathan Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Low-Rank Attention Residuals (LR-AttnRes), which decouples routing from representation in attention-based residual connections by using low-dimensional keys (r ≪ d) instead of full-dimensional ones, reducing computational cost while improving validation loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Attention Residuals use full-dimensional outputs as both keys and values for depthwise routing, coupling routing with representation and causing routing scores to scale with hidden width d. This is computationally expensive and conceptually suboptimal.

Method: Two variants are introduced: (1) Projected LR-AttnRes, which emits learned low-rank keys (dimension r ≪ d) from existing output projections, keeping full-dimensional residual values; (2) Sliced LR-AttnRes, which uses the last r dimensions of each value as the routing key, eliminating the auxiliary key-projection path entirely.

Result: Projected LR-AttnRes achieves the best validation loss among all tested variants. Sliced LR-AttnRes reduces residual-side FLOPs while still outperforming baselines. Comprehensive sweeps demonstrate that depthwise routing works effectively with far fewer dimensions than model width.

Conclusion: Decoupling routing keys from residual values via low-rank projections is both more efficient and more effective. The authors release code and models to support further investigation.

Abstract: Attention Residuals replace the fixed residual sum with depthwise attention over previous sub-layer outputs in large language models (LLMs), but use each output as both a full-dimensional key and value. This couples routing with representation and makes depth-routing scores scale with the hidden width $d$. We propose Low-Rank Attention Residuals (LR-AttnRes), which keep full-dimensional residual values while using $r$-dimensional keys, with $r \ll d$, for routing. Projected LR-AttnRes emits learned low-rank keys from existing output projections, decoupling routing from residual content and achieving the best validation loss among the variants tested. Sliced LR-AttnRes uses the last $r$ dimensions of each value as the routing key, removing the auxiliary key-projection path and reducing residual-side FLOPs while still improving performance. Comprehensive sweeps show that depthwise routing can be effective with far fewer dimensions than the model width. We release code and models to facilitate future research.

</details>


### [238] [FedCausal-Dyn: A Causal-Dynamic Paradigm for Federated Learning under Dynamic Feature Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09695)
*Kaijie Chen,Alex Johnson,Maria Garcia,Wei Zhang,Daniel Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedCausal-Dyn is a federated learning framework that tackles dynamic feature drift by separating causal domain-invariant features from spurious domain-specific variations, then performing reliability-weighted prototype aggregation with causal-feature guided collaborative regularization, achieving SOTA on three domain generalization benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated learning approaches assume static data distribution drift, which is inadequate for real-world non-stationary environments (e.g., fintech) where data distributions evolve across clients and over time dynamically.

Method: FedCausal-Dyn employs three core components: (1) causal-domain feature separation using specialized projection heads and adversarial training to disentangle invariant causal features from spurious domain-specific variations; (2) reliable dynamic prototype aggregation that weights local class prototypes by their estimated reliability before global aggregation; and (3) causal-feature guided collaborative regularization that unifies prototype contrastive alignment and domain invariance into a single cohesive objective.

Result: Extensive experiments on three federated domain generalization benchmarks show FedCausal-Dyn achieves state-of-the-art performance with the highest average accuracy and most stable results. Ablation studies validate the critical contribution of each component.

Conclusion: FedCausal-Dyn provides a robust, principled solution for federated learning under dynamic feature drift, with causal separation and dynamic prototype aggregation proving highly effective in non-stationary environments.

Abstract: This paper addresses the challenging problem of dynamic feature drift in federated learning, where data distributions evolve across clients and over time -- a common scenario in real-world applications like financial technology. Existing approaches often assume static drift, limiting their effectiveness in non-stationary environments. To overcome this, we propose \textbf{FedCausal-Dyn}, a novel federated learning framework built on a causal-dynamic paradigm. Its key innovation is \textit{causal-domain feature separation}, which disentangles domain-invariant causal features from spurious, domain-specific variations via specialized projection heads and adversarial training. This enables \textit{reliable and dynamic prototype aggregation}, weighting local class prototypes by estimated reliability before global aggregation. We further introduce \textit{causal-feature guided collaborative regularization}, unifying prototype contrastive alignment and domain invariance into a cohesive objective. Extensive experiments on three federated domain generalization benchmarks demonstrate that FedCausal-Dyn consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with the highest average accuracy and the most stable results. Ablation studies confirm each component's critical contribution. Our work provides a robust and principled solution for federated learning under dynamic feature drift.

</details>


### [239] [Mitigating Early Training Collapse in CTR Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09696)
*Ergun Biçici,Erkan Çetinyamaç*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deep CTR prediction models suffer from rapid post-first-epoch validation degradation. The study finds that controlling feature sparsity — by removing highly sparse features and aggregating infrequent feature values — is substantially more effective than learning rate reduction for stabilizing training and improving both offline and online performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep neural models for click-through rate (CTR) prediction commonly exhibit a sharp decline in validation performance immediately after the first training epoch, even as training loss continues to improve. This instability limits effective learning and constrains overall model performance. The authors seek to understand the root cause of this phenomenon using large-scale industrial datasets and to identify practical mitigation strategies.

Method: The authors analyze training instability on large-scale industrial CTR datasets. They evaluate two mitigation strategies: (1) reducing the learning rate, and (2) controlling feature sparsity. The sparsity control involves two techniques — removing highly sparse features entirely and aggregating infrequent feature values into more frequent buckets. Both offline evaluation metrics and online system performance are assessed.

Result: Reducing the learning rate yields only incremental improvements. In contrast, controlling feature sparsity produces substantial gains: training is stabilized, useful learning extends beyond a single epoch, and both offline evaluation metrics and online system performance improve significantly.

Conclusion: Feature sparsity, rather than learning rate, is the primary driver of the rapid post-first-epoch validation degradation in deep CTR models. Aggregating or removing sparse features is a practical and effective remedy that enables sustained multi-epoch training and delivers meaningful performance gains in real-world industrial systems.

Abstract: Deep neural models for click-through rate prediction often exhibit a sharp decline in validation performance immediately after the first training epoch despite continued improvement in training loss. This instability restricts effective learning and limits model performance. In this study, we analyze this behavior using large-scale industrial datasets and evaluate practical mitigation strategies. While reducing the learning rate provides only incremental gains, controlling feature sparsity yields substantial improvements. Removing highly sparse features and aggregating infrequent feature values stabilizes training, extends useful learning beyond a single epoch, and improves both offline evaluation metrics and online system performance.

</details>


### [240] [Safe responses matter: Output-aware safety guardrail mitigate over-refusal in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09697)
*Jiayi Li,Kun Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Output-aware safety guardrails that predict response harmfulness from hidden states drastically reduce over-refusal compared to input-aware methods while maintaining safety performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Input-aware safety guardrails for MLLMs suffer from severe over-refusal because they make safety decisions without considering the model's intrinsic ability to generate safe responses. MLLMs can often transform harmful inputs into harmless outputs, but input-side guardrails override this capability, degrading user experience.

Method: Proposes output-aware safety guardrails that operate in the model's hidden state space. A lightweight classifier, trained via multi-instance contrastive learning on hidden state representations, predicts whether the forthcoming generation will be unsafe before it is fully produced. This enables intervention only when the model's actual response would be harmful.

Result: Extensive experiments show the output-aware safety guardrail matches the safety performance of existing methods while drastically reducing over-refusal, thereby preserving both model utility and built-in safety capabilities.

Conclusion: Shifting from input-aware to output-aware safety guardrails resolves the fundamental safety-utility trade-off. By leveraging the model's intrinsic safety mechanisms and intervening only when truly necessary, the approach achieves robust safety without unnecessary refusal of benign queries.

Abstract: Existing safety mechanisms for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) face a fundamental trade-off between safety and utility. Model fine-tuning achieves robust safety but compromises general utility. Input-side safety guardrails offer a lightweight alternative, yet they suffer from severe over-refusal, indiscriminately blocking benign queries or those the model could have safely answered through refusal or advisory responses. We identify that the root cause of over-refusal lies in the input-aware paradigm: safety guardrails make safety decisions without considering whether the model itself is capable of generating safe responses. Usually, MLLMs already possess intrinsic safety mechanisms that can transform harmful inputs into harmless outputs, but input-side safety guardrails override this capability, degrading user experience. Motivated by this insight, we propose a paradigm shift toward output-aware safety guardrails. Our method operates within the model's hidden state space to predict whether the forthcoming generation will be unsafe before it is fully produced. By training a lightweight classifier via multi-instance contrastive learning on hidden state representations, our approach distinguishes between inputs that will lead to unsafe outputs and those that will not, even when the inputs themselves contain risky elements. This enables precise intervention only when the model's actual response would be harmful. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our output-aware safety guardrail matches the safety performance of existing methods while drastically reducing over-refusal, preserving the model's utility and built-in safety capabilities. Code is available at: https://github.com/kunzhan/OutGuard

</details>


### [241] [Quantum-Inspired Contextual Learning for Sparse-Ring Fraud Detection in Dynamic Transaction Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09704)
*Behnam Tonekaboni,Hiroshi Yamauchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exploratory benchmark using synthetic transaction graphs with sparse-ring fraud patterns, comparing GRU and quantum-inspired CML classifiers. Hybrid features combining graph features with persistent-homology summaries outperform topology-only or raw features alone, suggesting topology serves best as a contextual layer for dynamic fraud detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coordinated fraud in financial transaction networks often manifests as multi-period relational patterns (e.g., sparse-ring fraud) that are invisible in single transactions. Existing methods struggle to integrate evidence across both temporal and graph-structural dimensions simultaneously.

Method: A synthetic transaction simulator generates daily directed transaction graphs with injected sparse-ring fraud (completed cycles distributed over days) and broken-ring decoys. Daily graphs are aggregated into rolling windows and represented via (1) raw graph features, (2) persistent-homology summaries, or (3) hybrid vectors combining both. Sequence-level classification is performed using a GRU baseline and quantum-inspired Contextual Machine Learning (CML).

Result: Topology-only (persistent-homology) summaries are insufficient alone, as they discard account-pair identity and edge direction. Hybrid representations combining identity-preserving graph features with topological summaries yield the strongest classification performance. CML shows promise as a model for capturing fraud patterns with distributed temporal and relational evidence.

Conclusion: Topological features are most effective when used as a contextual layer augmenting identity-preserving graph features, rather than as a standalone representation. Quantum-inspired CML emerges as a promising approach for this class of temporally and relationally distributed fraud detection problems, though results remain exploratory given synthetic data and modest sample sizes.

Abstract: We present an exploratory benchmark and quantum-inspired modeling prototype for fraud screening in dynamic financial transaction graphs. Coordinated fraud may not be visible from individual transactions alone, but may emerge as a multi-period relational pattern. We focus on sparse-ring fraud, a stylized pattern in which a completed directed cycle is distributed across several days, requiring models to integrate evidence across both time and graph structure. We study this problem using a synthetic transaction simulator with completed sparse-ring injections and broken-ring decoys. Daily directed transaction graphs are aggregated into rolling windows and represented using raw graph features, persistent-homology summaries, or hybrid feature vectors that combine both. We compare a gated recurrent unit (GRU) baseline with quantum-inspired Contextual Machine Learning (CML) as sequence-level classifiers. Because the benchmark uses synthetic data, a modest sample size, and sequence-level labels, the results are exploratory. Within this scope, topology-only summaries are too compressed to solve the supervised ring-completion task by themselves, largely because they remove account-pair identity and edge direction. The strongest results come from hybrid representations that combine identity-preserving graph features with topological summaries. These findings suggest that topology is most useful as a contextual layer over dynamic graph features, and that CML is a promising candidate model for fraud patterns whose evidence is distributed across temporal and relational context.

</details>


### [242] [Manifold Constrained Tabular Deep Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09710)
*Tian Li,Lucy Robinson,Varun Ojha,Huizhi Liang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HDE-Net introduces a hyperbolic-space manifold-constrained DNN for tabular classification, using Latent Decision Nodes and Soft Decision Routing to better capture rule-based, tree-like decision boundaries, achieving state-of-the-art average rank on 30 datasets while surpassing GBDTs and recent tabular DNNs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular classification typically relies on local, condition-triggered rules (discrete, rule-partitioned structures) rather than smooth global patterns. Existing tabular DNNs use Euclidean representations that favor smooth variations and semantic locality, creating a geometric mismatch that hinders efficient representation of rule-based structures inherent to tabular data.

Method: HDE-Net operates in hyperbolic (Poincaré ball) space to model hierarchical decision structures. Key components: (1) heterogeneous features are abstracted into unified Latent Decision Nodes (LDNs) embedded in the Poincaré ball for tree-structured reasoning; (2) Soft Decision Routing approximates range-based local rules differentiably for numerical features, aligning their LDN semantics with categorical features; (3) entropy-aware capacity allocation adaptively controls the number of LDNs per numerical feature to balance expressiveness and complexity.

Result: On the TALENT-tiny-core benchmark (30 tabular classification datasets), HDE-Net achieved the best average rank, outperforming industrial GBDTs (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) and recent tabular DNNs while maintaining high efficiency.

Conclusion: Embedding tabular reasoning in hyperbolic space with LDNs and Soft Decision Routing effectively bridges the geometric gap between smooth Euclidean DNN representations and discrete rule-based tabular structures, yielding superior performance for tabular classification.

Abstract: Tabular classification is often governed by local, condition-triggered rules rather than smooth global patterns. However, tabular deep neural networks (DNNs) are typically built upon Euclidean representations that favor smooth variations and semantic locality. This potential geometric mismatch can make it challenging for tabular DNNs to efficiently represent the discrete, rule-partitioned structures often underlying tabular classification. To address this issue, we propose HDE-Net, a manifold-constrained DNN that enables hierarchical decision modeling in hyperbolic space. We first abstract heterogeneous features into unified Latent Decision Nodes (LDNs) and embed them in the Poincaré ball, forming a continuous representation that resembles tree-structured reasoning. For numerical features, we introduce a Soft Decision Routing mechanism that approximates range-based local rules in a differentiable manner, bringing their LDN semantics closer to those of categorical features. An entropy-aware capacity allocation algorithm further adapts the number of LDNs per numerical feature to balance expressiveness and complexity. On the TALENT-tiny-core classification benchmark (30 datasets), HDE-Net achieves the \textit{best average rank}, outperforming both industrial GBDTs and recent tabular DNNs while maintaining high efficiency.

</details>


### [243] [EvoClawBench: Can Agents Learn Reusable Skills from Their Own Runs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09711)
*Zhiyuan Peng,Xin Yin,Chenhao Ying,Zhe Cui,Zixiang Ding,Zhenhua Liu,Jiang Wu,Yuan Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoClawBench isolates closed-loop skill learning: whether agent runtimes can convert first-run evidence into reusable skills that improve second-run performance. Results show skill learning is selective and model/runtime-dependent, not an automatic benefit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks evaluate task completion or tool use but fail to isolate whether a runtime can extract reusable skills from its own execution traces and apply them to improve subsequent runs. The authors aim to fill this gap by testing closed-loop, self-improving skill acquisition.

Method: EvoClawBench provides 100 tasks with 502 sub-problems across coding, data, office, security, operations, and domain-document workflows. It compares three modes: direct execution (no skills), PreSkill (authoring before execution), and PostSkill (summarizing first-run evidence into skills for a fresh second execution). Experiments use OpenClaw and nanobot runtimes under local execution.

Result: Direct baseline is strongly runtime-dependent: OpenClaw <20% across models; nanobot ranges 56.45%–96.13%. Self-authored skills have mixed effects: nanobot GPT-5.4 stays >96% in all modes; MiniMax-M2.7 improves from 90.97% to 94.50% under PostSkill; nanobot DeepSeek-V4-Pro drops from 77.77% to 4.80% (PreSkill) and 0.99% (PostSkill). OpenClaw shows non-monotonic behavior with some skill runs near baseline and others collapsing.

Conclusion: Learning reusable skills from an agent's own runs is selective and cost-sensitive, not an automatic benefit. The utility of skill authoring depends heavily on the specific model–runtime combination, with some configurations suffering catastrophic performance degradation.

Abstract: Existing agent benchmarks primarily test task completion, tool use, or skill utility, but do not isolate whether a runtime can convert evidence from its own runs into reusable skills that improve fresh executions after authoring overhead. We introduce EvoClawBench, a benchmark for this closed-loop skill-learning question on repeated, fixture-backed tasks. EvoClawBench compares direct execution without skills, PreSkill authoring before execution, and PostSkill summarization from first-run evidence followed by a fresh second execution. The suite contains 100 tasks and 502 sub-problems across coding, data, office, security, operations, and domain-document workflows, with support for multiple agent runtimes. Experiments with OpenClaw and nanobot under local execution show that direct baseline performance is strongly runtime-dependent: OpenClaw remains below 20% across models, while nanobot ranges from 56.45% to 96.13%. Self-authored skills have mixed effects. nanobot GPT-5.4 stays above 96% in all modes and MiniMax-M2.7 improves from 90.97% to 94.50% under PostSkill, but nanobot DeepSeek-V4-Pro drops from 77.77% to 4.80% with PreSkill and 0.99% with PostSkill. OpenClaw shows similarly non-monotonic behavior, with some skill runs near baseline and others collapsing. These results indicate that learning reusable skills from an agent's own runs is selective and cost-sensitive, rather than an automatic benefit of adding skill authoring to an agent loop.

</details>


### [244] [ERP Data Provisioning Financial Control Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09712)
*Anitha Samudrala*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEQ-FCT is a governed data-provisioning framework for ERP financial control testing that integrates deterministic masking, synthetic scenario expansion, referential tokenization, policy-based release approval, and automated validation. Evaluated on a synthetic 186K-record dataset, it achieved 0.932 reconciliation F1, 0.887 fraud-trigger recall, and 0.914 control-failure F1 with a leakage-risk score of 0.018, outperforming several baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial control testing requires representative ERP data in quality environments, but direct production copies expose sensitive information (personal, supplier, banking, commercially sensitive records). Existing approaches treat masking, synthesis, and governance as independent utilities, which fails to preserve financial process behavior reliably.

Method: SEQ-FCT integrates five components into a unified release pipeline: (1) deterministic masking of sensitive fields, (2) synthetic scenario expansion for coverage, (3) referential tokenization preserving entity relationships, (4) policy-based release approval governance, and (5) automated validation for reconciliation, fraud-rule testing, and audit analytics. The framework is evaluated on a synthetic dataset of 186,000 finance-process records spanning six subsidiaries (2022–2025), covering AP invoices, payments, GL journals, AR receipts, and bank-statement lines.

Result: SEQ-FCT achieved: reconciliation F1 of 0.932, fraud-trigger recall of 0.887, control-failure F1 of 0.914, and leakage-risk score of 0.018. It was benchmarked against a production-clone upper bound, static masking, rules-only synthesis, conditional tabular generative synthesis, and a hybrid baseline.

Conclusion: Financial process behavior is preserved more reliably when masking, synthetic data generation, and governance checks are evaluated as a single integrated release pipeline rather than as independent, decoupled utilities.

Abstract: Financial control testing increasingly depends on representative enterprise resource planning (ERP) data in quality environments, yet direct production copies expose personal, supplier, banking, and commercially sensitive records. This work presents Secure ERP Quality Provisioning for Financial Control Testing (SEQ-FCT), a governed data-provisioning framework that combines deterministic masking, synthetic scenario expansion, referential tokenization, policy-based release approval, and automated validation for reconciliation, fraud-rule testing, and audit analytics. A single synthetic dataset is used for evaluation. It contains 186,000 finance-process records from six subsidiaries over 2022-2025, including accounts payable invoices, payments, general-ledger journals, accounts receivable receipts, and bank-statement lines. The dataset includes entity relationships, monetary values, approval paths, tax attributes, banking markers, exception labels, fraud-rule triggers, and control-failure outcomes. Because the dataset is synthetic, reported results demonstrate controlled internal consistency rather than production validation. Against a production-clone upper bound, static masking, rules-only synthesis, conditional tabular generative synthesis, and a hybrid baseline, SEQ-FCT achieved 0.932 reconciliation F1, 0.887 fraud-trigger recall, 0.914 control-failure F1, and an estimated leakage-risk score of 0.018. The analysis indicates that financial process behavior can be preserved more reliably when masking, synthetic data, and governance checks are evaluated as a single release pipeline instead of independent utilities.

</details>


### [245] [Gauge dependence and structured-output corruption in sign-branched repetition penalties: measurements across models, inference stacks, and alternative repetition controls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09791)
*Peter Hollows*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The multiplicative repetition penalty used across LLM inference engines has a critical flaw: it branches on the sign of raw logits, but logit zero-points are arbitrary and unconstrained by training. This causes inconsistent behavior across models and severely degrades structured output quality. Applying the penalty to normalized log-probabilities instead eliminates both problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper identifies a fundamental bug in the widely-deployed multiplicative repetition penalty: its sign-branching behavior depends on the arbitrary zero-point of a model's logits, which the training objective leaves completely unconstrained. This means the same penalty setting produces different operations on different models, and nobody in the ecosystem has noticed this flaw.

Method: The authors provide a mechanistic analysis showing that adding a constant to all logits is a no-op for softmax, making the zero-point arbitrary, yet the sign-branch in the repetition penalty reads that arbitrary point. They then conduct two empirical measurements: (1) testing how re-centering logits by a constant changes greedy token selection at theta=1.3 across models, and (2) evaluating structured output validity (JSON schema conformance) with and without the penalty on 200 real-world schemas. Five models up to 7B (base and RLHF) are tested on WikiText-103, plus two code models on HumanEval and JSONSchemaBench, with replication across vLLM and llama.cpp.

Result: At theta=1.3, re-centering logits changes 58-96% of greedy tokens, whereas subtractive and normalized penalties change none. Real checkpoints sit at widely different zero-points, confirming the penalty is model-dependent. On 200 JSON schemas, theta=1.3 drops valid schema-conformant output from 97% to 23%. Applying the penalty to normalized log-probabilities instead of raw logits removes both effects entirely.

Conclusion: The multiplicative repetition penalty's sign-branch is fundamentally broken because it depends on an arbitrary logit zero-point. The fix is to apply the penalty to normalized log-probabilities rather than raw logits. HuggingFace already ships this operator (LogitNormalization) but it is off by default and applied after the penalty; reversing this order resolves the issue.

Abstract: The multiplicative repetition penalty shipped across the LLM inference ecosystem (HuggingFace, vLLM, llama.cpp, and a dozen further engines) branches on the sign of each raw logit (divide positives by theta, multiply negatives). But the softmax is unchanged by adding a constant to every logit, so a model's logit zero-point is arbitrary, and the sign-branch reads that arbitrary point. The sign-branch is itself the accepted fix for an earlier bug, so the accepted fix branches on a quantity the training objective leaves unconstrained. Two measurable consequences follow. (1) The penalty is not well-defined: re-centring a model's logits by a constant is a provable no-op at theta=1, yet at a routine theta=1.3 it changes 58-96% of greedy tokens, where subtractive and normalized penalties change none; real checkpoints sit at widely different zero-points, so a fixed repetition_penalty is a different operation on every model. (2) It corrupts structured output: on 200 real-world JSON schemas, theta=1.3 drops the rate of valid, schema-conformant output from 97% to 23%. In our measurements, applying the penalty to normalized log-probabilities instead of raw logits removes both effects. HuggingFace already ships that operator (LogitNormalization); today it is off by default and applied after the penalty. This note gives the mechanism, the measurements (five models up to 7B, base and RLHF, on WikiText-103 prefixes; two code models on HumanEval and JSONSchemaBench; both effects replicated inside vLLM and llama.cpp through their own samplers on the same inputs), and the normalized variant.

</details>


### [246] [Metadata-Free Meta-Reweighted Direct Preference Optimization under Noisy Preference Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09796)
*Hua Qu,Yifan Li,Xiaodong Yuan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a bilevel optimization framework with meta-knowledge-driven weighting to make DPO robust against noisy preference data, using central-difference approximation and LoRA for scalable training, validated on summarization and dialogue tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
