Motivation: DPO's alignment performance degrades significantly under noisy, real-world preference data. Existing methods lack a principled mechanism to handle label noise without requiring high-quality metadata, motivating a robust, task-agnostic solution.

Method: A bilevel optimization framework is proposed that provably recovers the DPO optimum under clean data. A learnable weighting function with a derived prior form handles asymmetric label-flipping noise. When metadata is unavailable, a task-agnostic meta-knowledge-driven approach enables meta-learning. Scalability is achieved by combining central-difference approximation with LoRA fine-tuning to reduce higher-order gradient costs.

Result: Experiments on TL;DR summarization and Anthropic HH single-turn dialogue demonstrate improved training performance over multiple DPO baselines across various noise rates.

Conclusion: The proposed bilevel meta-learning framework with learnable instance weighting effectively mitigates the impact of noisy preferences in DPO, achieving robust alignment without relying on high-quality metadata, while remaining computationally scalable for LLMs.

Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become an important method for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences because it removes the need for explicit reward modeling and reinforcement learning optimization. However, its performance depends heavily on the quality of preference data, and noisy preference data in real-world settings can weaken alignment performance. To address this issue, we propose a bilevel optimization framework and prove, under certain assumptions, that this framework can recover the DPO optimum under clean data. We further derive a prior form for the learnable weighting function under asymmetric label-flipping noise. Considering that high-quality metadata may be difficult to obtain, we propose a task-agnostic meta-knowledge-driven method that enables meta-learning even when metadata is completely unavailable. To reduce the high cost of higher-order gradients in LLM meta-learning, we combine central-difference approximation with LoRA fine-tuning and develop a scalable training scheme. Experiments on TL;DR summarization and Anthropic HH single-turn dialogue show that the proposed method improves training performance over multiple DPO baselines under different noise rates.

</details>


### [247] [JEPA for AI-Native 6G: Predictive Representations and Open Challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09798)
*Sheikh Salman Hassan,Irshad A. Meer,Almoatssimbillah Saifaldawla,Yan Kyaw Tun,Mustafa Ozger,Madyan Alsenwi,Nguyen Van Huynh,Woong-Hee Lee,Cedomir Stefanovic,Mathini Sellathurai,Henk Wymeersch,Tharmalingam Ratnarajah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a tutorial on applying Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) — a self-supervised learning paradigm — to 6G networks, demonstrating through a beam-management case study that wireless-aware pretraining targets can improve label efficiency and robustness, while also outlining open challenges in deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 6G networks are evolving toward AI-native architectures where learning modules are embedded throughout the RAN, edge, and core. This poses challenges including limited labeled data, heterogeneous wireless/network data, partial observations, non-stationary propagation, and latency-constrained control loops — all of which demand a learning paradigm beyond traditional supervised or contrastive self-supervised methods.

Method: The authors adopt the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), a self-supervised paradigm that predicts missing or future representations in latent space rather than reconstructing raw measurements or using contrastive negative samples. They provide a wireless-oriented tutorial covering: (1) JEPA's training mechanism, (2) tokenization and masking strategies for CSI, beam measurements, KPIs, topology graphs, and sensing observations, and (3) positioning the learned encoder as a predictive representation layer for RAN/O-RAN/edge/core functions, with task-specific heads for final decisions. A beam-management case study evaluates a wireless-aware auxiliary target (future beam-energy prediction) during pretraining against a supervised baseline.

Result: The beam-management case study shows that using a wireless-aware auxiliary target — specifically, future beam-energy prediction during self-supervised pretraining — improves label efficiency and robustness under shifted deployment conditions compared to a purely supervised source-domain model.

Conclusion: JEPA is a promising self-supervised framework for 6G AI-native intelligence. The authors identify open challenges including multi-timescale prediction, action-conditioned modeling, distributed training, trustworthiness, efficient deployment, benchmarking, and standardization as critical areas for future work.

Abstract: Sixth-generation (6G) networks are moving toward AI-native operation, where learning modules are embedded across the radio access network (RAN), edge, and core. This transition requires learning from limited labels, heterogeneous wireless and network data, partial observations, non-stationary propagation, and latency-constrained control loops. Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) is a promising self-supervised paradigm for this setting because it predicts missing or future representations in latent space instead of reconstructing raw measurements or using contrastive negative samples. This article presents a wireless-oriented tutorial on JEPA for 6G intelligence. We define the JEPA training mechanism, describe how CSI, beam measurements, KPIs, topology graphs, and sensing observations can be tokenized and masked, and position the learned encoder as a predictive representation layer for RAN, O-RAN, edge, and core functions, with task-specific heads or controllers producing final decisions. Then we present an illustrative, beam-management case study suggesting that a wireless-aware target, specifically an auxiliary future beam-energy target during self-supervised pretraining, can improve label efficiency and robustness across shifted deployment conditions relative to a supervised source domain. Finally, we outline open challenges in multi-timescale prediction, action-conditioned modeling, distributed training, trustworthiness, efficient deployment, benchmarking, and standardization.

</details>


### [248] [The Silent Freeze: Predicting When Low-Precision Training Stops Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09800)
*Zekai Shang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Low-precision training can deterministically freeze weights when gradient updates fall below half the ULP of the quantized weight. This freeze is predictable from high-precision trajectories and mantissa length alone. Experiments on GPT-2 and other networks confirm the phenomenon, and stochastic rounding eliminates it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training in reduced floating-point precision is widely used for efficiency, but its failure modes are poorly understood. The authors identify a specific, deterministic mechanism—the "silent freeze"—by which low-precision weight representations cause coordinates to stop updating entirely while gradients remain nonzero, fundamentally limiting learning.

Method: The authors derive a per-coordinate half-ULP condition that governs when a weight update rounds to zero in low precision. They show this condition can be predicted a priori from a high-precision (fp32) training trajectory and the target mantissa length, without running low-precision training. Experiments test this on: (1) a small GPT with bf16-equivalent stored weights under AdamW+cosine schedule, (2) a 124M-parameter GPT-2 with weights constrained to 8-bit floating-point after every optimizer step (no master weights), (3) frozen-feature regression, a mantissa-truncation emulator spanning 128× in precision, small networks, and a CNN on MNIST. Stochastic rounding is evaluated as a remedy.

Result: In the small GPT, training freezes permanently just past mid-run within four steps of the a priori prediction. In the 124M GPT-2, dense weights freeze at initialization under both fp8 formats (E4M3 and E5M2), and validation loss plateaus while fp32 keeps improving—all predicted from the fp32 reference. Stochastic rounding removes the persistent freeze, also as predicted. The freeze condition transfers across diverse settings including the mantissa-truncation emulator, small networks, and MNIST CNNs, confirming this is a computable, systematic axis of low-precision training rather than diffuse noise.

Conclusion: The silent freeze is a deterministic, predictable failure mode of low-precision training governed by a simple half-ULP condition. It can be diagnosed from high-precision trajectories alone and remedied by stochastic rounding. This reframes low-precision training failures as computable rather than mysterious, with practical implications for mixed-precision training workflows.

Abstract: Training in reduced floating-point precision can silently halt learning: when a gradient-descent weight update falls below half the unit in the last place (ULP) of the weight, it rounds away and that coordinate freezes while its gradient is still nonzero. The freeze is deterministic, governed by a per-coordinate half-ULP condition, and predictable from a high-precision trajectory and the target mantissa length alone, without low-precision data. In a small GPT trained under the standard AdamW-plus-cosine recipe with bf16-equivalent stored weights, training proceeds normally and then permanently freezes just past mid-run, within four steps of the a-priori prediction. In a $124$-million-parameter GPT-2 transformer whose weights are constrained to the $8$-bit floating-point grid after every optimizer step, with no master weights, the dense weights freeze at initialization in both fp8 formats -- predicted \emph{a priori} from an fp32 reference -- and validation loss plateaus while full precision keeps improving. Stochastic rounding removes the persistent freeze, and the same reference predicts that too. The condition transfers across frozen-feature regression, a mantissa-truncation emulator spanning $128\times$ in precision, small networks, and a CNN on MNIST: a computable axis of low-precision training, not diffuse noise.

</details>


### [249] [Discovering Latent Response Laws in Forced Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09801)
*Yi Zhu,Su Chen,Xiaojun Li,Xiuli Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLARE is a forced latent autoencoder that discovers compact latent coordinates and sparse input-dependent dynamics from high-dimensional forced system measurements, enabling long-horizon prediction under unseen inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Governing equations are often simple in latent variables but obscured in high-dimensional measurements. This problem is exacerbated for forced systems, where responses depend on both intrinsic dynamics and time-dependent external inputs. Existing methods struggle to simultaneously learn compact representations and input-driven dynamics from observational data.

Method: FLARE (Forced Latent Autoencoder for Response Equations) learns a latent space where dynamics are sparse and explicitly depend on external forcing. It estimates latent dimension from data, separates state estimation from forcing, and decodes latent trajectories back to full responses. Forecasts are initialized from past responses and driven by prescribed future inputs.

Result: Across known dynamical systems, application-scale forced responses, and visual observations, FLARE recovers compact forced dynamics and predicts long-horizon high-dimensional responses under inputs not seen during training.

Conclusion: FLARE extends equation discovery to systems whose effective states are hidden within complex observations, offering interpretable modeling and prediction of high-dimensional forced dynamical systems by turning learned coordinates into a dynamical interface.

Abstract: Governing equations provide compact descriptions of physical systems, yet the variables in which they are simple are often hidden in high-dimensional measurements. This challenge is sharper for forced systems, whose responses depend on both intrinsic dynamics and time-dependent inputs. Here we introduce FLARE, a forced latent autoencoder for response equations that learns compact response coordinates, identifies sparse input-dependent latent dynamics and decodes equation rollouts to full responses. By estimating latent dimension from data and separating state estimation from external forcing, FLARE enables forecasts to be initialized from past responses and driven by prescribed future inputs. Across known dynamical systems, application-scale forced responses and visual observations, FLARE recovers compact forced dynamics and predicts long-horizon high-dimensional responses under inputs not used for training. By turning learned coordinates into a dynamical interface, FLARE extends equation discovery to systems whose effective states are hidden within complex observations, providing a route for interpretable modelling and prediction of high-dimensional responses in forced dynamical systems.

</details>


### [250] [Quota Marketplace: Dynamic Pricing for Efficient Allocation of ML Training Resources](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09802)
*Balasubramanian Sivan,Renato Paes Leme,Mihai Tiuca,Ian McFarlane,Vasilis Gkatzelis,Nehal Mehta,Soheil Hassas Yeganeh,Vahab Mirrokni,Amin Vahdat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Google developed Quota Marketplace, a market-based mechanism for allocating scarce ML training chips (GPUs) that handles heterogeneous workload values. Unlike prior systems like Karma, it preserves Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness by allowing users to express workload value and enabling dynamic pricing based on supply and demand. The paper covers design, implementation, deployment at Google, and theoretical analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing resource allocation mechanisms (e.g., Karma) guarantee Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness under dynamic user demands but fail when demands have heterogeneous values. Since organizations inherently assign different values to different ML workloads, an allocation policy must accommodate this heterogeneity to maximize ROI on scarce, expensive ML training resources.

Method: The authors propose Quota Marketplace, a market-based mechanism where users express the value of their workloads, and resource prices adjust dynamically based on supply and demand fluctuations. The paper provides theoretical analysis proving the mechanism achieves Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness, alongside a full-stack implementation and real-world deployment within Google.

Result: The Quota Marketplace was implemented and deployed at Google. Metrics demonstrate its practical impact, and the system effectively handles multiple business-critical requirements. The market-based approach unlocks new gains and opportunities by aligning resource allocation with organizational priorities.

Conclusion: A market-based mechanism like Quota Marketplace, which lets users express workload value and leverages dynamic pricing, can efficiently allocate scarce ML training resources while maintaining Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness — overcoming the limitations of prior mechanisms in heterogeneous-value settings.

Abstract: The escalating demand for Machine Learning (ML) training resources in recent years has resulted in a substantial gap between the high demand and the available supply. Efficient allocation of these scarce and expensive resources is crucial for organizations to maximize their return on investment. Existing resource allocation mechanisms, like Karma [OSDI'23], are designed to guarantee Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness in settings with dynamic (time-varying) user demands, but fail to preserve these key properties in the presence of demands with heterogeneous values. Given the ubiquity and inevitability of heterogeneity in organizational values of different workloads, effective resource allocation policies must accommodate these variations.
  In this paper, we describe the design, implementation, deployment, and theoretical analysis of Quota Marketplace, a market-based mechanism to efficiently allocate ML training chips (like GPUs), explicitly addressing scenarios with demands of heterogeneous value. We detail the implementation of this mechanism within Google and present metrics that demonstrate its impact. We also discuss many business-critical requirements that the Quota Marketplace handles quite effectively, and document the gains and opportunities it has unlocked. We establish theoretically how this market-based approach achieves the essential properties of Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness by allowing the users to express the value of their workloads and enabling dynamic resource pricing based on supply and demand fluctuations. Ultimately, the market facilitates resource allocation that aligns with organizational priorities.

</details>


### [251] [Spectral Origins of the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Autoregressive Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09803)
*Ingrid Petrova,Luan Vejsiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SPARC provides a formal spectral-algebraic theory explaining why LLMs exhibit a self-correction blind spot (fixing external errors but not their own). It defines an error-propagation operator via attention Jacobians, derives activation thresholds for correction markers, and proves RL convergence conditions, with predictions validated within 3.2% RMSE across four backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work empirically documents the self-correction blind spot in LLMs but lacks three things: (1) a formal model of why self-generation suppresses error detection, (2) a quantitative activation condition for correction markers, and (3) convergence guarantees for RL-based self-correction. SPARC aims to fill these theoretical gaps.

Method: SPARC constructs a spectral-algebraic framework centered on an error-propagation operator defined as the product of per-step attention Jacobians on the residual stream. Key analyses: (1) proving the blind spot occurs iff the spectral radius ≥ 1, (2) deriving a sharp activation threshold for correction markers as a function of spectral radius, (3) proving RL verifier-corrector training converges at rate proportional to squared coupling strength / √(samples) iff the coupling matrix's spectral norm < 1, and (4) showing this criterion is invariant across autoregressive modalities (text, image, video). Validation used four backbones plus a visual autoregressive probe.

Result: The spectral predictions matched measured blind-spot rates within 3.2% RMSE. A simple "Wait" marker achieved 89.3% blind-spot reduction, consistent with the derived activation threshold. The spectral norm criterion for RL convergence was empirically confirmed across all tested backbones and modalities.

Conclusion: The self-correction blind spot is a fundamental spectral property of autoregressive generation, governed by the spectral radius of the error-propagation operator. SPARC provides a unifying theory with sharp quantitative thresholds, modality-invariant convergence guarantees, and strong empirical validation, grounding previously empirical observations in formal spectral-algebraic principles.

Abstract: Large autoregressive language models exhibit a self-correction blind spot: they reliably fix identical errors when attributed to an external source yet fail to fix the same errors in their own outputs. Prior work has documented this phenomenon empirically, through controlled error injection, error-depth decompositions, RL-based verifier-corrector training, and intrinsic self-verification, but offers no formal model of why generating a token suppresses the ability to detect its error, no quantitative activation condition for correction markers, and no convergence guarantee for reinforcement-learning-based self-correction. We close these gaps with SPARC, a spectral-algebraic theory of self-correction in autoregressive generation. We define the error-propagation operator as the product of per-step attention Jacobians on the residual stream and prove that the blind spot arises if and only if the spectral radius of this operator is at least one. We derive a sharp activation threshold, given as a function of the spectral radius, that a correction marker must exceed, recovering the 89.3\% blind-spot reduction observed with a simple ``Wait'' marker. We further prove that RL-based verifier-corrector training converges at a rate proportional to the squared coupling strength over the square root of the number of samples if and only if the verifier-corrector coupling matrix has spectral norm below one, and that this criterion is invariant across residual-stream autoregressive modalities, unifying text LLMs and autoregressive image and video generation. Experiments across four backbones and a visual autoregressive probe validate every theorem, with spectral predictions matching measured blind-spot rates within 3.2\% RMSE.

</details>


### [252] [Serving the Long Tail: Training-Free LLM Candidate Generation for Vacation Rental Marketplaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09877)
*Syed Mohammed Arshad Zaidi,Eric Rincon,Shayan Hassantabar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Vrbo addresses the cold-start / sparse-interaction problem in vacation rental candidate generation by augmenting item-based kNN with a training-free LLM pipeline that synthesizes semantic queries from property metadata, retrieves candidates via ANN search, and fuses them via a Union strategy — extending coverage to tens of thousands of previously unreachable listings without degrading performance on well-served properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vacation rental marketplaces exhibit extreme supply-side imbalance: a small fraction of properties monopolize user interactions, while the long tail of new, niche, and seasonal listings lack sufficient behavioral signal for collaborative filtering. At Vrbo, the item-based kNN candidate generation channel leaves tens of thousands of properties with zero candidates and produces weak neighborhoods for sparsely interacted ones. The goal is to complement behavioral methods with a purely metadata-driven approach that requires no retraining and scales to an 11.7M-property catalog.

Method: A three-stage, training-free pipeline: (1) An off-the-shelf LLM generates diverse semantic queries per property from static metadata (title, description, amenities, location). (2) A pre-trained text encoder embeds these queries, and an approximate nearest-neighbor index retrieves semantically similar candidates from the full catalog. (3) A Union fusion strategy merges LLM candidates with IBKNN candidates, preserving the behavioral channel's ordering and guaranteeing no degradation on well-served properties. A downstream learning-to-rank model then re-scores the fused pool. The authors also compare open-weights (3B) versus frontier API-based LLMs and show Union fusion collapses the recall gap between them.

Result: Evaluated on 1.6 million focal properties: (1) The system extends candidate coverage to tens of thousands of properties that IBKNN cannot reach. (2) Largest gains occur on the long-tail segment where behavioral methods are weakest. (3) On shared properties, the LLM pipeline matches or beats IBKNN at every K. (4) Downstream LTR further lifts the fused pool. (5) Union fusion reduces the recall gap between a 3B open-weights LLM and frontier API models from 27–46% to under 1%, enabling cost-effective self-hosted deployment.

Conclusion: LLM-based semantic candidate generation using only static metadata is a practical, training-free complement to behavioral collaborative filtering for large-scale marketplaces. The Union fusion strategy ensures safe deployment — no regression on head properties — while dramatically improving coverage and relevance for the long tail. The approach also demonstrates that small, self-hosted LLMs can match frontier models when paired with appropriate fusion, making the solution economically viable at catalog scale.

Abstract: Vacation rental marketplaces face a structural imbalance on the supply side: a small fraction of properties receive most user interactions, while the long tail of new, niche, and seasonal listings generates too little behavioral signal for collaborative filtering to serve effectively. At Vrbo, item-based k-nearest neighbors (IBKNN) is a core candidate generation channel, but leaves tens of thousands of properties with no candidates and produces weak neighborhoods for sparsely interacted ones. We present a training-free, LLM-based candidate generation pipeline that complements IBKNN using static property metadata alone. An off-the-shelf LLM synthesizes diverse semantic queries per property, a pre-trained text encoder embeds them, and an approximate nearest-neighbor index retrieves candidates from an 11.7M-property catalog. A Union fusion strategy merges these with IBKNN while preserving the behavioral channel's ordering, guaranteeing no degradation on well-served properties, and a downstream learning-to-rank model re-scores the fused pool. Evaluated on 1.6M focal properties, the system extends candidate coverage to tens of thousands of properties IBKNN cannot reach, delivers its largest gains on the long-tail segment where behavioral methods are weakest, and matches or beats IBKNN at every K on shared properties. A downstream learning-to-rank stage further lifts the fused pool, yielding a complete candidate generation and re-ranking stack that serves the long tail without regressing well-served properties. We additionally show that Union fusion collapses the recall gap between a 3B open-weights LLM and frontier API-based models from 27-46% to under 1%, supporting self-hosted small-model deployment at marketplace catalog scale.

</details>


### [253] [RUBRIC: Realism--Utility Balanced Ranking for Imbalanced Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09816)
*Yanxuan Yu,Dong liu,Renata Borovica-Gajic,Ying Nian Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RUBRIC is a generator-agnostic filtering framework for imbalanced classification that selects synthetic samples by balancing realism (via a discriminator) and utility (via margin-based proximity to the decision boundary), yielding tightened generalization bounds and improved F1-macro/recall across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing oversampling methods for class imbalance generate many low-quality synthetic samples that distort decision boundaries, cause overfitting, and degrade generalization. A principled selection mechanism is needed to filter candidates based on quality rather than quantity.

Method: RUBRIC formulates synthetic sample selection as a quality-over-quantity optimization. Candidates are ranked via a realism-utility trade-off: (1) realism scored by a learned discriminator distinguishing real vs. synthetic samples; (2) utility scored by a concave margin-based function measuring proximity to the decision boundary. The authors prove the filtering strategy monotonically tightens the generalization bound for margin classifiers by reducing distribution shift and suppressing near-negative tail contributions.

Result: Extensive experiments on credit-card fraud detection and other imbalanced benchmarks show RUBRIC improves F1-macro and recall while maintaining comparable ROC-AUC across various generators. Lambda-sensitivity analysis demonstrates AUPRC recovery when ranking quality is prioritized.

Conclusion: RUBRIC offers a generator-agnostic, theoretically grounded filtering approach that enhances classifier performance on imbalanced data by prioritizing high-quality synthetic samples, with practical flexibility via its trade-off parameter.

Abstract: Class imbalance poses a fundamental challenge in risk-sensitive applications such as fraud detection and medical diagnosis, where minority-class samples are scarce yet critical for accurate classification. Existing oversampling methods generate synthetic samples to rebalance class distributions; however, they often produce large numbers of low-quality candidates that distort decision boundaries or introduce artifacts, leading to overfitting and degraded generalization.
  In this work, we introduce RUBRIC, a generator-agnostic filtering framework that formulates synthetic sample selection as a quality-over-quantity optimization problem. RUBRIC ranks candidates using a realism-utility trade-off: realism is quantified by a learned discriminator that distinguishes real samples from synthetic samples, while utility captures proximity to the decision boundary through a concave margin-based scoring function. We show that, under mild regularity conditions, the proposed filtering strategy monotonically tightens the generalization bound for margin-based classifiers by jointly reducing distribution shift and suppressing near-negative tail contributions.
  Through extensive experiments on credit-card fraud detection and other imbalanced benchmarks, we demonstrate that RUBRIC improves F1-macro and recall while maintaining comparable ROC-AUC across several generators. We also provide explicit lambda-sensitivity analysis to show how users can recover AUPRC when ranking quality is prioritized.

</details>


### [254] [Estimation, Prediction, and Assortment Optimization for Markov Chain Choice Models with Panel Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09817)
*Yalcin Akcay,Gerardo Berbeglia,Young-San Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an EM-based framework for Markov chain choice models with panel data that leverages partial-ordering preferences to capture inter-transaction dependencies, outperforming existing methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional choice models assume independent transactions per customer, ignoring the dependencies and partial-ordering preference information inherent in panel data (multiple transactions from the same customer over time). The authors aim to fill this gap by introducing the first MC-based choice modeling framework that explicitly accounts for such dependencies.

Method: Novel expectation-maximization (EM) algorithms for estimating Markov chain parameters that incorporate partial-ordering-based customer preference information derived from panel data. The framework also addresses conditional choice prediction and personalized assortment optimization, with accompanying hardness and computational results.

Result: On synthetic datasets and the sushi dataset, the proposed EM algorithms outperform the traditional EM algorithm of Simsek and Topaloglu (2018) and MNL-based partial-order benchmarks from Jagabathula and Vulcano (2018). Hardness and computational results for conditional choice prediction and assortment optimization are also provided.

Conclusion: The framework successfully initiates the study of Markov chain choice modeling with panel data, demonstrating that incorporating partial-ordering preferences via EM yields superior estimation performance. The computational landscape analysis for downstream tasks offers independent value.

Abstract: We propose a framework for the Markov chain (MC) choice model with panel data, including parameter estimation, personalized choice prediction, and personalized assortment optimization. In contrast to the traditional setting, which assumes that each transaction is independently drawn from a random utility model, our framework accounts for dependencies among transactions for the same customer in historical data, captured by partial-ordering preference information. To the best of our knowledge, our framework initiates the study of choice modeling with panel data under MC. As our primary result, we propose novel expectation-maximization (EM) algorithms for MC parameter estimation by incorporating partial-ordering-based customer preference information. On synthetic datasets and the sushi dataset, our EM algorithms outperform the traditional EM algorithm of Simsek and Topaloglu (Operations Research, 66, 2018) and multinomial-logit-based partial-order benchmarks adapted from Jagabathula and Vulcano (Management Science, 64, 2018). As our secondary contribution, we present hardness and computational results for conditional choice prediction and assortment optimization problems. These results complement our estimation framework and clarify the computational landscape of conditional choice and assortment optimization, which may be of independent interest.

</details>


### [255] [Learning Predictive Ambiguity Sets for Decision-Focused Distributionally Robust Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09820)
*Junjie Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Learned Predictive Ambiguity Sets (LPAS), a deep contextual model that outputs a state-dependent Wasserstein radius and nominal distribution for distributionally robust optimization, with the radius trained via quantile calibration, regularization, and decision loss. Applied to portfolio optimization, it achieves 26.28% annualized return and Sharpe ratio 1.30, outperforming fixed-radius DRO baselines while reducing unnecessary conservatism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional predict-then-optimize pipelines treat point forecasts as certain, ignoring distributional misspecification. Existing DRO methods center ambiguity sets at historical samples with a globally fixed radius, which is overly conservative in calm regimes and insufficiently robust in volatile regimes. The authors aim to make robustness adaptive and context-dependent.

Method: LPAS uses a deep neural network that takes contextual features and outputs three components: (1) a finite nominal scenario distribution, (2) a state-dependent Wasserstein radius, and (3) an optional anisotropic ground metric. These define a contextual ambiguity set fed into a DRO decision layer. The radius is trained through a loss combining conditional quantile calibration, size regularization, and downstream decision loss. The authors derive the finite dual form for the decision layer and propose a staged training algorithm. Evaluation is on distributionally robust portfolio optimization using 20 S&P 500 constituents from 2018–2026.

Result: LPAS substantially outperforms equal-weight, predict-then-optimize, and historical Wasserstein DRO baselines, achieving 26.28% annualized return, Sharpe ratio 1.30, final wealth 1.61, and lower tail loss than a deep fixed-radius DRO baseline while using a smaller average radius. It recovers most of the performance of strong fixed-radius DRO while reducing unnecessary conservatism and improving regime adaptivity.

Conclusion: Learned, state-dependent ambiguity radii can match or approach the performance of well-tuned fixed-radius DRO while being less conservative on average, demonstrating that adaptive robustness is both feasible and beneficial in contextual decision-making under uncertainty.

Abstract: Predict-then-optimize systems usually compress uncertainty into a point forecast and then solve a downstream optimization problem as if the forecast were reliable. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers protection against misspecification, but the ambiguity set is often centered at historical samples and uses a fixed radius. We propose \emph{learned predictive ambiguity sets} (LPAS): a deep contextual model outputs a finite nominal scenario distribution, a state-dependent Wasserstein radius, and optionally an anisotropic ground metric. These outputs define a contextual ambiguity set that feeds a DRO decision layer. The radius is trained by a combination of conditional quantile calibration, size regularization, and downstream decision loss, so that robustness is adaptive rather than globally fixed. We derive the finite dual form used by the decision layer, present a staged training algorithm, and evaluate the method on distributionally robust portfolio optimization with 20 S&P 500 constituents from 2018--2026. The proposed method substantially improves over equal-weight, predict-then-optimize, and historical Wasserstein DRO baselines, achieving 26.28% annualized return, Sharpe ratio 1.30, final wealth 1.61, and lower tail loss than a deep fixed-radius DRO baseline while using a smaller average radius. The results show that learned ambiguity radii can recover most of the performance of strong fixed-radius DRO while reducing unnecessary conservatism and improving regime adaptivity.

</details>


### [256] [A Strong Balanced-Softmax Classifier-Retraining Baseline for Long-Tailed Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09832)
*Juan Terven,Diana Margarita Córdova Esparza,Julio Alejandro Romero Gonzalez,Edgar Arturo Chávez Urbiola,Francisco Javier Willars Rodriguez,Juan Bautista Hurtado Ramos,Alfonso Ramirez Pedraza*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: After Balanced Softmax training, retraining only the classifier (frozen backbone) on balanced episodic batches — termed BS-cRT — consistently boosts Few-shot accuracy across multiple long-tailed benchmarks. The authors also analyze CBRM, revealing failure modes related to scaled-logit instability and head-class anchoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-tailed recognition methods typically modify losses, margins, or representations to mitigate head-class dominance. This work investigates whether residual tail error after Balanced Softmax training can be further reduced by retraining only the classifier, leaving the backbone frozen — questioning if representation learning is truly the bottleneck.

Method: A two-stage procedure: (1) train backbone + cosine classifier with Balanced Softmax; (2) freeze the backbone, then retrain only the classifier on balanced episodic batches, retaining the empirical-prior Balanced Softmax objective and using raw cosine logits at inference. The authors also analyze Counterfactual Boundary Risk Minimization (CBRM), a boundary-probe extension using prototype-based features near decision boundaries.

Result: BS-cRT yields consistent Few-shot accuracy gains: +5.15 (CIFAR-100-LT), +5.83 (CIFAR-10-LT), +6.92 (ImageNet-LT), +9.78 (Places-LT) at imbalance factor 100. A Top-1/Few-shot trade-off is observed on ImageNet-LT. CBRM analysis reveals two failure modes: scaled-logit cosine margins destabilize training, and corrected hardest-negative probes remain anchored to head classes.

Conclusion: BS-cRT serves as a simple yet effective classifier-side baseline, demonstrating that classifier-only retraining can meaningfully reduce tail error post-Balanced Softmax. Boundary supervision methods like CBRM must explicitly account for class frequency to avoid head-class anchoring and training instability.

Abstract: Long-tailed recognition methods often modify losses, margins, or representations to reduce the dominance of frequent classes. We ask whether, after Balanced Softmax training, the remaining tail error can be reduced by retraining only the classifier. We evaluate BS-cRT, a two-stage procedure that trains a backbone and cosine classifier with Balanced Softmax, freezes the backbone, and updates only the classifier on balanced episodic batches. The second stage keeps the empirical-prior Balanced Softmax objective and uses raw cosine logits at inference. Across CIFAR-100-LT, CIFAR-10-LT, ImageNet-LT, and Places-LT, this classifier-only step consistently improves Few-shot accuracy over the matched Balanced Softmax checkpoint. At imbalance factor 100, Few-shot gains are +5.15 points on CIFAR-100-LT and +5.83 on CIFAR-10-LT; on ImageNet-LT and Places-LT, gains are +6.92 and +9.78 points, respectively, with a Top-1/Few-shot trade-off on ImageNet-LT. We also analyze Counterfactual Boundary Risk Minimization (CBRM), a boundary-probe extension using prototype-based features near decision boundaries. CBRM identifies two failure modes: scaled-logit cosine margins destabilize training, and corrected hardest-negative probes remain head-class anchored. The results support BS-cRT as a practical classifier-side baseline and indicate that boundary supervision must account for class frequency.

</details>


### [257] [Context by Distinct Information: An Auditable Dirichlet-Process Working Memory for Long, Redundant Context Streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10441)
*Siddharth Pal,Viktoria Rojkova*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Context engineering should scale with distinct information rather than tokens. The paper proposes a novelty-gated cache that allocates memory only for novel keys, combined with a recurrent state for summary information and a recency window for locality. Experiments show this hybrid design matches full-attention performance at ~50% token attendance, with advantages growing as context lengthens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current context engineering designs (bounded recurrent states, per-token KV caches, sliding windows/eviction) all treat the token as the unit of memory, which is wasteful when streams are redundant and tasks depend on distinct information. The motivation is to shift the unit of memory from tokens to distinct informational items.

Method: Three memory components are organized by how a task depends on the past: (1) a content-addressed novelty cache that opens a slot only when an incoming key is novel (recall-carried information), (2) a recurrent state for summary-carried information, and (3) a recency window for locality-carried information. Experiments use character-level control tasks, synthetic Medicare claims for next-code prediction and cost forecasting.

Result: Novelty-gated attention reaches full-attention performance while attending to ~50% of tokens. Coupling the cache with a state-space summary matches full-attention coupling at reduced cost. The advantage grows with context length. On next-code prediction over synthetic Medicare claims at 1000-event horizon, the coupled component outperforms full attention and all fixed-budget eviction policies. For cost forecasting (summary-carried), the cache is neutral. Retained memory is an inspectable table rather than an opaque state.

Conclusion: Context can scale with distinct information rather than tokens using a content-addressable, auditable working memory. The experiments are small-scale and use only public data, establishing a primitive that decomposes context by informational dependency type (recall, summary, locality).

Abstract: Context engineering decides what information a model carries forward, and current designs meter it in tokens: compressing the past into a bounded recurrent state, keeping a key-value entry for every token, or imposing a fixed budget through a window or eviction rule. All three make the token the unit of memory even when the stream is redundant and the task depends on the distinct information it carries. Building on a companion mechanism paper that opens a cache slot only when an incoming key is novel, so memory scales with the number of distinct items rather than tokens, we develop that allocate-on-novelty cache as a working-memory component and organize context by how a task depends on the past: recall-carried information belongs in a content-addressed novelty cache, summary-carried information in a recurrent state, and locality-carried information in a recency window. The claim is empirical and bounded. On a matched character-level control, novelty-gated attention reaches full-attention performance while attending to about half the tokens, and coupling the cache with a state-space summary matches full-attention coupling at that reduced cost; the advantage grows as context lengthens, while a sliding window is preferable on short, locality-dominated spans. On next-code prediction over synthetic Medicare claims the coupled component leads full attention and every fixed-budget eviction policy at a thousand-event horizon, whereas cost forecasting over the same stream is summary-carried and the cache is neutral. The retained memory is an inspectable table of templates, codes, drugs, or places rather than an opaque state. The experiments are small-scale and use only public data; they establish the primitive that context can scale with distinct information rather than tokens, in a working memory that is content-addressable and auditable.

</details>


### [258] [From Direction to Magnitude: How Multimodal Instruction-Tuning Reorganizes the Geometric Encoding of Identity-Specifying Prompts in Transformer Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09842)
*Jorge A. Castillo,Marco Torres Yévenes,Juan Carlos Lanas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper examines whether system prompts that specify a model identity leave detectable geometric signatures in hidden-state trajectories. Across four open-weight models spanning base, multimodal RLHF, RL distillation, and SFT regimes, the key finding is a qualitative shift at the instruction-tuning boundary: identity encoding transitions from direction-based (angular) separation in the base model to magnitude-based (Euclidean) separation in the multimodal instruction-tuned model — a reorganization unique to multimodal RLHF and absent in other post-training regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether identity-specifying system prompts produce statistically distinguishable, geometrically measurable fingerprints in the hidden-state trajectories of transformer language models, and to understand how this encoding changes across different post-training regimes (base, multimodal RLHF, RL distillation, SFT).

Method: Hidden-state trajectories are extracted from four open-weight models (Gemma-4-E4B base, Gemma-4-E4B-it, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) under three prompt conditions: identity-specifying, length-matched generic-assistant, and a vanilla 26-token baseline. Five geometric metrics are applied, with the primary metric being the 1-Wasserstein distance between edge-wise distributions of Ollivier-Ricci curvature computed on k-NN trajectory graphs. Statistical claims are validated via trajectory-level permutation tests (B=5000) with multiple geometric controls including teacher-forced content controls, temporal-chain vs. k-NN topology, ABT-projected k-NN, and angular vs. Euclidean graph construction.

Result: In the base model, identity produces a direction-coded fingerprint: angular k-NN yields separation of 0.034 (p=0.002). In the multimodal instruction-tuned model, angular separation collapses (p=0.439) while Euclidean separation survives (p=0.042), and the mean norm of the first generated hidden state inverts its length ordering, becoming lowest for the identity prompt. This direction-to-magnitude reorganization is specific to the multimodal instruction-tuning (RLHF) regime and is absent in RL distillation and SFT models. A teacher-forced control attributes approximately 30% of the free-running cosine signal to prompt-driven effects.

Conclusion: Identity-specifying system prompts leave geometric fingerprints in hidden-state trajectories, but the nature of these fingerprints undergoes a qualitative reorganization across the instruction-tuning boundary — from directional coding in base models to magnitude-based coding in multimodal RLHF models. This shift is regime-specific, suggesting that multimodal instruction tuning fundamentally alters how models represent prompt-level identity information in their internal geometry. The use of 1-Wasserstein distance on edge-wise Ollivier-Ricci curvature distributions over k-NN trajectory graphs is proposed as a broadly applicable methodological contribution.

Abstract: We investigate whether identity-specifying system prompts produce statistically distinguishable geometric fingerprints in the hidden-state trajectories of four open-weight transformer language models spanning four post-training regimes: no training (Gemma-4-E4B base), multimodal RLHF (Gemma-4-E4B-it), RL distillation (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), and SFT (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Three prompt conditions (an identity-specifying axis prompt, a length-matched generic-assistant prompt, and a 26-token vanilla baseline) are compared via five geometric metrics, principally the 1-Wasserstein distance between edge-wise distributions of Ollivier-Ricci curvature on k-NN trajectory graphs. Claims rest on trajectory-level permutation tests with multiple geometric controls (teacher-forced content controls, temporal-chain vs k-NN topology, ABT-projected k-NN, angular vs Euclidean graph construction, B=5000 permutations on borderline statistics). The central finding is a qualitative reorganization of identity encoding across the instruction-tuning boundary: in the base model the fingerprint is direction-coded (separation 0.034, p=0.002 under angular k-NN); in the multimodal instruction-tuned model it migrates into the magnitude (angular separation collapses to p=0.439 while Euclidean survives at p=0.042, and the mean norm of the first generated state inverts its length-ordering, being lowest for the identity prompt). This direction-to-magnitude reorganization is specific to the multimodal instruction-tuning regime, absent under RL distillation and SFT. A teacher-forced control attributes ~30% of the free-running cosine signal to prompt-driven effects. We position W_1 on edge-wise Ollivier-Ricci distributions on k-NN trajectory graphs as a methodological contribution of independent interest.

</details>


### [259] [Nonlinear Axiomatic Attribution for Cooperative Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09869)
*Weida Li,Zhuanghua Liu,Yaoliang Yu,Bryan Kian Hsiang Low*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The Shapley value's linearity creates an excessively large null space that makes it unreliable for player ranking via inclusion AUC. The authors introduce a class of nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods inspired by the least core, which retain key axioms (consistency, equal treatment, efficiency) while replacing linearity, and demonstrate improved ranking performance experimentally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Shapley value, despite uniquely satisfying linearity, consistency, equal treatment, and efficiency, is unreliable for identifying positively participating players when evaluated by the inclusion AUC metric. The root cause is that its linearity implies an overly large null space, allowing non-negligible perturbations to go undetected, which undermines ranking quality.

Method: The authors propose a class of nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods inspired by the least core — a known nonlinear alternative to the Shapley value. Each method in this class is defined as the unique optimal solution to a minimization problem that approximates utility functions as faithfully as possible, while preserving the axioms of consistency, equal treatment, and efficiency (discarding linearity).

Result: Experiments using the inclusion AUC metric show that the proposed nonlinear methods are potentially more effective than Shapley value variants that relax only the efficiency axiom.

Conclusion: Nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods that retain consistency, equal treatment, and efficiency — while replacing linearity — offer a more reliable approach for player ranking than the standard Shapley value, addressing a fundamental limitation rooted in the Shapley value's linear null space.

Abstract: The Shapley value is a widely used concept in attribution problems, as it uniquely satisfies the axioms of linearity, consistency, equal treatment, and efficiency. Often, the inclusion AUC metric is used to evaluate the quality of player rankings, in order to identify positively participating players. However, it can be established that the Shapley value is not always reliable for this purpose. The core issue lies in its linearity: the Shapley value acts as a linear operator with an excessively large null space, which is likely to contain non-negligible perturbations that remain indistinguishable to the operator. To address this limitation, we explore the design of nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods. Inspired by the least core, which is a popular nonlinear substitute for the Shapley value, we introduce a class of nonlinear attribution methods that retain the remaining necessary axioms. Each method yields a contribution vector that is the unique optimal solution to a minimization problem, which aims to approximate utility functions as faithfully as possible. In terms of the inclusion AUC metric, our experiments demonstrate the potential effectiveness of these methods compared to Shapley value variants that relax only the efficiency axiom. Our code is available at https://github.com/watml/nonlinear-axiom.

</details>


### [260] [Nonparametric Bayesian Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Data-Parallel Gibbs Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09886)
*Sai Anirudh Katupilla,Shreeya Dasa Lakshminath*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A nonparametric Bayesian IRL method using Dirichlet Process priors that infers multiple latent reward functions from pooled expert demonstrations without knowing the number of expert types in advance, outperforming parametric MaxEnt IRL baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard inverse reinforcement learning assumes all demonstrations come from a single expert. When demonstrations are pooled from multiple experts with distinct preferences, parametric methods recover only an averaged reward function that poorly fits any individual expert. The work aims to automatically discover latent reward types and their number directly from heterogeneous demonstration data.

Method: The authors employ a Dirichlet Process prior over reward functions to enable nonparametric Bayesian IRL. Inference uses a collapsed Gibbs sampler that alternates between a Chinese Restaurant Process update for cluster assignments and a Metropolis-Hastings update for reward weights, with soft value iteration serving as the inner planning routine. The approach is parallelized across CPU cores using Ray, employing a consensus merge heuristic for state aggregation.

Result: On a 10×10 ObjectWorld grid with two ground-truth types, the sampler recovers K=2 with Adjusted Rand Index of 1.000 versus ARI=0.000 for MaxEnt IRL. With three types, K is correctly identified in all runs; assignment ARI ranges 0.48–0.58 due to behavioral overlap. Parallelization achieves 4.79× speedup on 8 workers, with a characterized throughput-versus-accuracy tradeoff from the merge heuristic.

Conclusion: The nonparametric Bayesian approach successfully infers both the number and parameters of latent reward types from mixed demonstrations. Reliable evaluation with more than two types requires controlled object placement. The parallelized implementation demonstrates practical scalability on HPC hardware, though the consensus merge heuristic introduces a tunable accuracy–throughput tradeoff.

Abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning recovers reward functions from expert demonstrations, but standard formulations assume that all demonstrations come from a single expert. When demonstrations are pooled from multiple experts with distinct preferences, parametric methods recover an averaged reward that fits no individual expert well. We implement Nonparametric Bayesian Inverse Reinforcement Learning with a Dirichlet Process prior over reward functions, allowing the number of latent reward types to be inferred jointly with the rewards themselves. Inference uses a collapsed Gibbs sampler combining a Chinese Restaurant Process update for cluster assignments with a Metropolis-Hastings update for reward weights, and soft value iteration as the inner planning routine. We evaluate on a 10x10 ObjectWorld grid with two and three ground-truth reward types. The serial sampler recovers K=2 with Adjusted Rand Index of 1.000, substantially outperforming a Maximum Entropy IRL baseline (ARI=0.000). Extension to K=3 shows that the sampler correctly identifies the number of clusters in all runs; assignment ARI of 0.48-0.58 reflects behavioral overlap between expert types that persists across grid instantiations, revealing that reliable K=3 evaluation on ObjectWorld requires controlled object placement rather than random seeding. We further parallelize the sampler across CPU cores using Ray on HPC hardware, achieving a peak speedup of 4.79x at 8 workers, and characterize a throughput-versus-accuracy tradeoff arising from the consensus merge heuristic used during state aggregation. Code and a containerized environment are available at https://github.com/dasashreeya/np_bayes_irl.

</details>


### [261] [Remembering Distinct Items, Not Tokens: A Learnable Dirichlet-Process Cache Between State-Space Models and Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09889)
*Siddharth Pal,Viktoria Rojkova*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a sparse key-value cache for sequence models that allocates memory slots only for novel/distinct inputs using DP-means clustering, achieving attention-like associative recall at a fraction of the memory cost, with the allocation rule being learnable end-to-end via a simple two-parameter gate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard attention mechanisms achieve unbounded associative recall by storing a key-value pair per token, but incur quadratic compute and linearly growing cache. Fixed-state models (e.g., SSMs) compress the past into a bounded state, capping recall capacity. The authors seek a middle ground: a sparse cache whose size scales with distinct items rather than sequence length.

Method: The authors use DP-means (the small-variance limit of a Dirichlet-process mixture) as a key-value memory operator: an input is assigned to an existing slot if sufficiently similar, otherwise a new slot is allocated. Two variants are developed — a static cache with fixed concentration parameter, and a surprise-adaptive variant where concentration tracks recent novelty rate. The allocation rule is implemented as a learnable two-parameter gate trained purely on task loss, providing an inductive bias toward novelty-gated storage.

Result: On controlled associative-recall benchmarks with redundancy, the sparse cache matches full-attention recall while storing only distinct items. It dominates fixed-budget eviction caches on the recall-vs-size frontier. On a state-space backbone, it handles both recall queries and long-range aggregation at the lowest memory cost. The two-parameter gate recovers the DP-means rule exactly when trained end-to-end, whereas over-parameterized gates fail. The distinct-items property is confirmed on four real-world streams: recommendation, systems logs, clinical events, and insurance claims.

Conclusion: The key insight is that sparse, novelty-gated caching with the right inductive bias (DP-means) can match full attention's associative recall at dramatically lower memory cost. The simplicity of the two-parameter learnable gate suggests that the inductive bias — not model capacity — is the operative ingredient, and the approach generalizes across diverse real-world data streams.

Abstract: Fixed-state sequence models compress an unbounded past into a bounded state, which caps their associative recall at roughly the state dimension; attention escapes the cap by keeping a key-value entry for every token, at quadratic compute and a cache that grows with the sequence. We study the middle ground: a sparse cache that allocates a slot only when an input is novel, so its size tracks the number of distinct items rather than the number of tokens. The allocation rule is the DP-means clustering rule, the small-variance limit of a Dirichlet-process mixture, used not as latent-variable inference but as the key-value memory operator for a deep recurrent backbone. We develop it in two forms, a static cache with a fixed concentration and a surprise-adaptive variant whose concentration follows the recent novelty rate. On a controlled associative-recall benchmark with redundancy we show that the cache matches full-attention recall while storing only the distinct items, that it dominates a fixed-budget eviction cache on the recall-versus-size frontier, and that on a state-space backbone it answers both a recall query and a long-range aggregate at the lowest memory of any model tested. The allocation is learnable end to end: a two-parameter novelty-threshold gate trained on the task loss alone recovers the rule exactly, whereas an over-parameterized gate fails, so the operative ingredient is the inductive bias rather than capacity. The evidence is a family of controlled mechanism studies at modest scale, with the distinct-items property confirmed on four real streams (recommendation, systems logs, clinical events, and insurance claims); a real-backbone, real-corpus language validation is pursued in a companion study.

</details>


### [262] [SMETA-ZSL:Semantic Meta-Alignment for Zero-Shot Threat Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09936)
*Ivan Alejandro Montoya Sanchez,Anantaa Kotal,Aritran Piplai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SMETA-ZSL is a generalized zero-shot learning framework for cybersecurity threat detection that uses LLM-derived semantic prototypes, contrastive finetuning, episodic meta-learning, and adaptive routing to overcome semantic overlap, feature heterogeneity, class imbalance, and open-set challenges, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 7 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cybersecurity systems face novel threats with no labeled training data. While generalized zero-shot learning (GZSL) and large language models (LLMs) can address this by converting CTI reports into semantic prototypes, applying them to cybersecurity is hindered by: (1) strong semantic overlap among threat descriptions, (2) heterogeneity between behavioral attributes and textual representations, (3) severe class imbalance, and (4) open-set conditions where unseen classes are entirely unknown during training.

Method: SMETA-ZSL addresses these via three components: (1) Contrastive finetuning of LLM-derived semantic prototypes to disambiguate overlapping threat descriptions; (2) Episodic meta-learning combined with knowledge distillation to align heterogeneous behavioral features with semantic prototypes; (3) Adaptive routing mechanism that dynamically balances generalization across seen and unseen threat classes under strict inductive settings.

Result: Evaluated across 7 benchmarks, SMETA-ZSL achieves the strongest overall generalized zero-shot performance under the strictest inductive setting. It surpasses prior methods by an average of 10.8 points, with maximum gains reaching 18.1 points.

Conclusion: SMETA-ZSL demonstrates that combining contrastive semantic prototype learning, meta-learning-based feature alignment, and adaptive routing effectively enables zero-shot threat recognition in cybersecurity, setting a new state-of-the-art for the domain.

Abstract: Cybersecurity systems must adapt rapidly to emerging threats. However, labeled data for new threat categories is unavailable when those threats first appear. Generalized zero-shot learning offers a natural solution by enabling recognition of unseen classes through auxiliary semantic knowledge rather than labeled examples. Large language models are particularly promising in this setting because they can convert unstructured CTI reports into semantic prototypes for emerging threats. However, applying language-driven zero-shot learning to cybersecurity is difficult due to strong semantic overlap between threat descriptions, heterogeneity between behavioral attributes and text, severe class imbalance, and open-set conditions where unseen threats are unknown during training. We propose SMETA-ZSL, that learns semantic prototypes from overlapping language descriptions through contrastive finetuning, aligns behavioral features through episodic meta-learning and knowledge distillation, and performs adaptive routing for generalization across seen-unseen classes. Across 7 benchmarks, SMETA-ZSL delivers the strongest overall generalized zero-shot performance under the strictest inductive setting, surpassing prior methods by 10.8 points on average, with gains up to 18.1 points. Github:https://github.com/Security-And-Intelligence-Lab-UTEP/SMETA-ZSL

</details>


### [263] [A Foundation Model for Multimodal Event Sequences in Financial Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09955)
*Nikita Rusakov,Vladislav Meshkov,Konstantin Zorin,Gleb Zaripov,Alexander Uglov,Alexey Vasilev,Anton Klenitskiy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A foundation transformer model pretrained on multimodal, chronologically ordered user event sequences via next-event prediction, producing general-purpose representations that, combined with existing tabular features, outperform task-specific models across multiple financial downstream tasks when deployed in a major Eastern European bank.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional financial predictive modeling relies on task-specific models with manually engineered tabular features, which limits cross-task reuse and fails to fully exploit heterogeneous data sources like transaction histories and digital interaction signals.

Method: Events from multiple data sources are unified into a single chronological sequence, enabling early fusion of heterogeneous modalities. A transformer-based foundation model is pretrained with a next-event prediction objective to learn general-purpose user representations. These learned representations are then concatenated with existing engineered user features, and lightweight task-specific neural heads are trained on top for multiple downstream tasks.

Result: The proposed system outperforms traditional task-specific models while reducing development overhead. In production deployment at one of the largest Eastern European banks, it yielded measurable improvements in business metrics.

Conclusion: Pretraining a transformer on multimodal user-event sequences with a next-event prediction objective is an effective strategy for building reusable foundation representations in financial services, enabling superior performance and operational efficiency compared to siloed task-specific modeling.

Abstract: Predictive modeling is a core component of modern financial services, where a wide range of tasks are traditionally addressed using separate models trained on manually engineered tabular features. This task-specific approach limits reuse and makes it difficult to fully exploit heterogeneous data sources such as transaction histories and digital interaction signals. In this paper, we present an approach based on pretraining a foundation transformer model on multimodal sequences of user events. Events from multiple data sources are unified into a single chronological sequence, enabling early fusion of heterogeneous modalities and learning of general-purpose representations via a next-event prediction objective. These representations are combined with existing engineered user features, on top of which lightweight neural models are trained for multiple downstream tasks. The proposed system outperforms traditional task-specific models while reducing development overhead. The approach was deployed in production at one of the biggest banks in Eastern Europe, resulting in measurable improvements in business metrics.

</details>


### [264] [Optimizing ARDL Models for Retail Sales Forecasting and Fair Pricing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09956)
*Sujay Uday Rittikar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a fairness-aware dynamic pricing framework for retail food products that embeds CPI-based price constraints into sales forecasting. Using a log-log ARDL model, the authors find that unconstrained optimization drives prices to upper bounds due to positive nominal elasticities (an inflation artifact), while Simulated Annealing finds interior prices that balance consumer welfare with sales targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retailers face a tension between maximizing profitability via dynamic pricing and ensuring consumer fairness. Most existing pricing models optimize purely for business objectives, overlooking the risk of consumer exploitation—particularly in essential goods like food. The paper addresses this gap by studying fairness-constrained pricing in the Canadian food retail context.

Method: The authors model total retail trade sales using a log-log Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) specification, where the price coefficient represents sales elasticity. The pricing problem is framed as maximizing forecast sales subject to CPI-anchored price bounds. They solve this via Linear Programming (LP) and Simulated Annealing (SA) under both single-product and multi-product configurations. Forecast accuracy is benchmarked against naive, seasonal-naive, ARIMA, and SARIMA baselines. A CPI-deflated re-specification isolates inflation effects on elasticity estimates.

Result: Fitted nominal elasticities are positive, meaning an unconstrained sales-maximizer pushes all prices to upper bounds—making the CPI ceiling the critical safeguard. Simulated Annealing yields conservative, interior prices that reduce consumer cost while still meeting sales targets. The CPI-deflated re-specification reveals that the positive nominal elasticities are largely an inflation-driven artifact rather than a structural demand relationship.

Conclusion: The framework delivers a transparent, fairness-aware pricing methodology that explicitly prevents consumer exploitation by embedding CPI-based constraints into the optimization. The contrast between LP (corner solutions at price ceilings) and SA (interior solutions) demonstrates that appropriately designed optimization can balance retailer sales objectives with consumer welfare.

Abstract: Pricing food products to balance profitability with consumer welfare is a central challenge for retailers. Dynamic pricing is widely used to maximize revenue, yet most pricing models optimize business objectives while overlooking consumer fairness. This paper studies the risk of consumer exploitation under dynamic food pricing in Canada and proposes a methodology that embeds fairness constraints directly into retail sales forecasting. We model total retail trade sales with a log--log Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) specification, in which the coefficient on a product price is a sales elasticity, and pose the pricing problem as maximizing forecast sales subject to price bounds anchored to the Consumer Price Index (CPI). We solve this problem with both Linear Programming (LP) and Simulated Annealing (SA), under single-product and multi-product configurations. A key finding is that the fitted nominal elasticities are positive. As a result, an unconstrained sales-maximizer would push every price to its upper bound, and the CPI ceiling is the safeguard that prevents this. Simulated Annealing instead settles on conservative, interior prices that lower consumer cost while still meeting the sales target. We benchmark forecast accuracy against naive, seasonal-naive, ARIMA, and SARIMA baselines, and a CPI-deflated re-specification shows that the positive nominal elasticities are largely an inflation-driven artifact. The result is a transparent, fairness-aware pricing framework.

</details>


### [265] [Learning in Curved Weight Space:Exponential-Linear Weight Reparameterization for Improved Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09967)
*Ethan Smith*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces AdaCurv, a weight reparameterization that combines a symmetric-exponential pathway with a linear pathway. Additive updates in log-space become magnitude-proportional changes in weight-space, creating a curved parameter geometry. Training transformers on OpenWebText shows 1.32–1.49× faster convergence to matched validation loss across various width×depth configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural network operations are often multiplicative in nature, yet standard optimizers (including adaptive ones like Adam) apply additive updates. This means weights of different magnitudes receive similarly-sized absolute changes, leading to very different relative perturbations — a mismatch with the multiplicative structure of many network components.

Method: AdaCurv reparameterizes weights using two parallel pathways: (1) a sign-aware symmetric-exponential pathway that maps additive updates in log-space to magnitude-proportional changes in effective weight space, and (2) an identity-like linear pathway providing a direct optimization route. Learnable scale, curvature, and offset parameters control the balance between pathways. A mismatched initialization strategy is also used: raw weights are initialized to match Xavier statistics under a symmetric transform, but training uses an asymmetric forward transform where positive weights remain at full strength while negative weights are reduced in magnitude.

Result: On OpenWebText, AdaCurv-trained transformers reach matched validation loss in 1.32–1.49× fewer training steps compared to standard linear parameterization, with the largest width configurations showing the greatest gains. Small-model ablations indicate the mismatched initialization improves early optimization, possibly acting as symmetry breaking.

Conclusion: The curved parameter-space geometry created by AdaCurv's dual-pathway reparameterization empirically accelerates loss descent over standard linear parameterization, with benefits scaling favorably with model width. The mismatched initialization provides additional early-optimization advantages, meriting further investigation as a symmetry-breaking mechanism.

Abstract: Many neural networks operations have a multiplicative nature rather than additive: halving or doubling a norm are analogous relatively but require unequal optimization distances when taking linear steps. Adaptive optimizers such as Adam normalize updates per coordinate, but update steps remain additive; weights with very different magnitudes receive similarly sized absolute changes, producing very different relative perturbations. We introduce \textbf{\method} (\textbf{\methodshort}), a weight reparameterization for neural networks that combines a sign-aware symmetric-exponential pathway with an identity-like linear pathway. The symmetric-exponential pathway is near-linear for small raw weights but increasingly curved at larger magnitudes. Additive updates in logarithmic space map to magnitude-proportional changes in effective weight space. The linear pathway provides a direct route through the transform that we hypothesize stabilizes optimization, while learnable scale, curvature, and offset parameters control balance between pathways and the curvature of the exponential pathway. These components create a curved parameter-space geometry that empirically improves speed of loss descent over standard linear parameterization. We also identify a useful \emph{mismatched initialization}: raw weights are chosen so a symmetric version of the transform matches Xavier statistics, but training uses an asymmetric forward transform that leaves positive weights at full strength while making negative weights smaller in magnitude; in small-model ablations, this improves early optimization and may act as a form of symmetry breaking. We train transformers on OpenWebText over nine width$\times$depth configurations, \methodshort reaches matched validation loss in 1.32--1.49$\times$ fewer training steps, with the largest widths seeing the biggest gains.

</details>


### [266] [Multimodal Routing for Interpretable, Robust, and Auditable Clinical Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09982)
*Nikkie Hooman,Zhongjie Wu,Eric C. Larson,Mehak Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an explicit multimodal routing framework for clinical prediction using EHR data (structured variables, clinical notes, chest X-rays). The model constructs discrete unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal routes, enabling interpretable and auditable reasoning. Inference-time route masking simulates missing modalities to assess robustness without retraining. Evaluated on MIMIC-IV for phenotype prediction and ICU mortality, the approach reveals systematic differences in modality reliance across clinical conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal EHR models rely on deep fusion, which obscures individual modality contributions and limits interpretability. The authors aim to create a transparent framework where modality-level reasoning is explicit, auditable, and robust to missing data.

Method: An explicit multimodal routing framework that constructs discrete routes: unimodal (L, N, or I alone), directional bimodal (e.g., L→N, N→I), and trimodal. Cross-modal interactions are asymmetric and directional. A novel inference-time route masking technique simulates missing modalities and reweights remaining routes without retraining, enabling robustness analysis through performance and routing weight changes.

Result: Evaluated on MIMIC-IV for multi-label phenotype prediction (K=25) and binary ICU mortality prediction using trimodal patient stays. Results reveal systematic differences in modality reliance across clinical condition groups, demonstrating the framework's ability to surface which modalities drive predictions for different outcomes.

Conclusion: The explicit multimodal routing framework offers a transparent, auditable, and practical approach to multimodal clinical prediction, providing interpretability, robustness to missing modalities, and mechanistic insights into modality-level decision-making in clinical contexts.

Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) data are inherently multimodal, and leveraging multiple modalities can improve predictive performance. However, most existing approaches rely on deep fusion, which obscures how individual modalities contribute to predictions and limits the interpretability of multimodal reasoning. We propose an explicit multimodal routing framework for clinical prediction that enables interpretable, robust, and auditable reasoning across three EHR modalities: structured longitudinal variables (L), clinical notes (N), and chest X-rays (I). Our model constructs discrete unimodal, directional bimodal, and trimodal routes to capture both individual modality signals and asymmetric cross-modal interactions. To audit multimodal reasoning and assess robustness, we introduce inference-time route masking, which simulates missing modalities and reweights the remaining routes without retraining. We analyze changes in performance and routing weights under these scenarios to understand model decision-making. We evaluate our framework on multi-label phenotype prediction (K = 25) and binary ICU mortality prediction using trimodal patient stays from MIMIC-IV, revealing systematic differences in modality reliance across clinical condition groups. Overall, our framework offers a transparent, auditable, and practical approach to multimodal clinical prediction, providing interpretability, robustness, and insights into how different data sources drive model decisions.

</details>


### [267] [Vilya-1: An all-atom foundation model for macrocycle structure prediction and design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09998)
