*Vilya Research,:,Pascal Sturmfels,Milad Salem,Naozumi Hiranuma,Stephen Rettie,Xiaoliang Pan,Benjamin D. Sellers,Adam P. Moyer,Patrick J. Salveson,Ivan Anishchanka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Vilya-1 is a deep learning foundation model for macrocyclic peptides that accurately predicts 3D conformations across diverse chemistries and estimates developability properties like membrane permeability, outperforming physics-based and existing deep learning methods while also enabling generative design of novel macrocycles with tailored property profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Macrocyclic peptides are a growing therapeutic modality, but current computational methods for modeling their structures and properties are limited in chemical scope and fail to generalize across synthetically accessible chemical space. There is an unmet need for a unified model that can both sample biologically relevant conformations and predict key drug-like properties across arbitrary macrocycle chemistries.

Method: The authors developed Vilya-1, a deep learning model using a uniform all-atom representation trained on heterogeneous structural datasets encompassing diverse topologies and chemical classes (both canonical and non-canonical residues). The model addresses two tasks: (1) sampling biologically relevant conformations across arbitrary chemistries, and (2) predicting developability properties such as membrane permeability. Training data spans macrocycles and small molecules, giving it broad chemical coverage.

Result: Vilya-1 substantially improves geometric accuracy relative to physics-based methods, co-folding networks, and deep-learning conformer generators across a broad set of macrocycles composed of both canonical and non-canonical residues. It maintains broad chemical coverage extending to small molecules. The model also demonstrates generative capabilities for designing novel macrocycles with tailored chemical, structural, and property profiles.

Conclusion: Vilya-1 represents a foundation model for macrocycle therapeutics, unifying conformational sampling and property prediction across diverse chemistries with state-of-the-art accuracy, while enabling generative design. This establishes a new computational paradigm for accelerating the development of next-generation macrocycle-based drugs.

Abstract: Macrocyclic peptides are an increasingly important therapeutic modality, but existing computational methods for modeling their structures and properties are limited in scope and do not generalize well across the synthetically accessible chemical space. In this work, we introduce Vilya-1, a deep learning model that addresses two central challenges in macrocycle design: sampling biologically relevant conformations across arbitrary chemistries and predicting key developability properties such as membrane permeability. Vilya-1 operates on a uniform all-atom representation and is trained on heterogeneous structural datasets spanning diverse topologies and chemical classes. Across a broad set of macrocycles composed of canonical and non-canonical residues, Vilya-1 substantially improves geometric accuracy relative to physics-based methods, co-folding networks, and deep-learning conformer generators, while maintaining broad chemical coverage that extends to small molecules. Vilya-1 also supports generative applications, enabling the design of novel macrocycles with tailored chemical, structural, and property profiles. Together, these capabilities establish Vilya-1 as a foundation model for accelerating the development of next-generation macrocycle therapeutics.

</details>


### [268] [MLPs are Hebbians: Constructing Efficient Fact-Storing MLPs for Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10034)
*Roberto Garcia,Jerry Liu,Ronny Junkins,Sabri Eyuboglu,Atri Rudra,Christopher Ré*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a theoretical explanation for why LLMs store factual knowledge at an information-theoretically optimal rate in MLP layers. The authors construct the first Transformer-compatible closed-form MLP that achieves optimal fact storage scaling, handles arbitrary embedding geometries, and functions within Transformers, requiring 10-104× fewer parameters than prior constructions while enabling modular fact editing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior constructive and mechanistic interpretability models of fact storage in LLMs cannot explain the empirical observation that LLMs store facts at an information-theoretically optimal rate. Existing constructions fail to simultaneously achieve optimal scaling, handle arbitrary input/output geometries, and operate within Transformer architectures.

Method: The authors develop a closed-form MLP construction and analyze the decoding margin of MLPs (rather than just storage). Under isotropic embeddings, they prove optimal storage capacity scaling. For arbitrary key/value embeddings, they derive scaling up to penalization factors based on embedding geometries. They also integrate the construction into Transformer blocks and validate it for factual recall tasks.

Result: The construction achieves information-theoretically optimal storage capacity scaling, requiring 10-104× fewer parameters than prior constructions under isotropic embeddings and 15-63× fewer when integrated into Transformers. The method also enables modular fact editing by swapping MLPs.

Conclusion: The proposed MLP construction successfully bridges theory and practice by matching the empirically observed optimal fact storage scaling in LLMs, offering both a theoretical account of the phenomenon and practical benefits in parameter efficiency and modular editability.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store factual knowledge in their parameters. While recent work has shown that this knowledge resides in MLP layers, existing constructive and mechanistic interpretability models of fact-storage in LLMs fail to explain the surprising empirical phenomenon that they store facts at an information-theoretically optimal rate. In this work, we develop a theoretical account of this phenomenon. We develop the first Transformer-compatible fact-storing MLP closed-form construction that satisfies the following three properties empirically observed in LLMs: it (i) attains optimal fact storage scaling, (ii) handles arbitrary input/output geometries, and (iii) works inside Transformers. Key to our work is to analyze the decoding margin of MLPs, whereas prior work only studies MLP fact storage. Under isotropic embeddings, our construction achieves information-theoretically optimal storage capacity scaling and requires $10$-$104\times$ fewer parameters at matched fact count than prior constructions. For arbitrary key and value embeddings, we show that our construction attains the same storage capacity scaling, up to penalization factors depending on the embedding geometries. Moreover, we demonstrate that our constructed MLPs can be used within Transformer blocks for factual recall tasks at optimal capacity scaling, requiring $15$-$63\times$ fewer parameters at matched fact count than prior constructions. Finally, as a proof-of-concept, we show that fact-storing MLPs enable modular fact editing by swapping a Transformer's MLP with a new one.

</details>


### [269] [FlashTrie: A GPU-Accelerated Constrained Beam Search for Generative Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10044)
*Dakshitha Anandakumar,Anurag Mukkara,Wenxiang Hu,Jiusheng Chen,M Akash Kumar,Ting Ye,Qiang Lou,Jian Jiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlashTrie accelerates constrained beam search for generative retrieval by moving trie-based decoding entirely onto GPUs, using a compressed integer-aware trie layout and cooperative CUDA kernels. It achieves up to 24x speedup over CPU baselines, scales beam widths to 1000 with sub-3ms latency, and delivers +0.71% revenue lift in a commercial search engine A/B test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constrained decoding in large-scale generative retrieval requires validating generated document IDs against a predefined trie. Existing CPU-based implementations suffer from limited parallelism, causing trie traversal and candidate validation to become serving bottlenecks as beam width scales. This limits beam size and hinders latency-critical applications like sponsored search.

Method: FlashTrie introduces three key innovations: (1) an integer-aware succinct trie layout using bit compression to fit the full index in GPU high-bandwidth memory, reducing memory stalls; (2) a cooperative CUDA kernel that performs beam expansion, validation, and pruning entirely on-device without per-step CPU orchestration; and (3) GPU-aware parallel primitives that replace irregular CPU-style lookup and heap maintenance, improving warp utilization and reducing thread divergence.

Result: On an 800M-keyword library with beam widths up to 1000, FlashTrie achieves sub-3ms trie-search latency and up to 24x speedup over a highly optimized multi-threaded CPU baseline. It enables scaling beam sizes by up to 5x in latency-critical applications. In a large-scale online A/B test on a commercial search engine, it yields a statistically significant +0.71% revenue lift.

Conclusion: FlashTrie demonstrates that GPU-native constrained decoding can overcome the parallelism bottlenecks of CPU-based trie traversal, enabling real-time, large-beam generative retrieval at scale — previously feasible only offline — with significant business impact in commercial search settings.

Abstract: Constrained decoding is essential in generative retrieval, where document identifiers generated directly from a query must exactly match a predefined library of valid IDs. At scale, decoding is often constrained using a trie with beam search but most implementations run on CPU. Limited parallelism then makes trie traversal and candidate validation a serving bottleneck as beam width grows.
  We present FlashTrie, which addresses this limitation by optimizing constrained beam search on GPUs. It introduces an integer-aware succinct trie layout that uses bit compression to reduce memory footprint while keeping the full index in GPU high-bandwidth memory reducing memory stalls, and a cooperative CUDA kernel that performs beam expansion, validation, and pruning entirely on-device without per-step host orchestration. It further replaces CPU-style irregular lookup and heap maintenance with GPU-aware parallel primitives, improving warp utilization and reducing divergence.
  Together, these designs significantly reduce decoding latency and increase throughput while preserving retrieval quality. On a library of 800M keywords with beam widths up to 1000, FlashTrie reduces trie-search latency to under 3 ms, achieving up to 24x speedup over a highly optimized multi-threaded CPU baseline. These improvements enable FlashTrie to scale beam sizes by up to 5x in latency-critical applications such as sponsored search. In a large-scale online A/B experiment on a popular commercial search engine, it delivers a statistically significant +0.71% revenue lift, enabling real-time constrained decoding at a scale previously feasible only offline. The FlashTrie code will be publicly released after the review process.

</details>


### [270] [Conservation Laws for Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10067)
*Ziv Aharoni,Henry D. Pfister*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper develops conservation laws via GEXIT functions for memoryless noise processes, showing cross-entropy can be expressed as an integral of local information-theoretic derivatives along the noise path. This unifies likelihood characterization for discrete and continuous diffusion (Gaussian case recovers I-MMSE), implies a locality property enabling training via marginal posterior learning, and validates predictions on synthetic and standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive models optimize exact data likelihood via the chain rule, while diffusion models rely on denoising objectives — lacking a unified likelihood characterization across discrete and continuous noise processes. The authors seek to bridge this gap by establishing fundamental information-theoretic relationships (conservation laws) that characterize cross-entropy for broad classes of diffusion models.

Method: The authors develop conservation laws based on generalized extrinsic information transfer (GEXIT) functions applicable to a broad class of memoryless noise processes. They show that data-model cross-entropy can be expressed as an exact integral of local information-theoretic derivatives along the noise path. The locality property — that these derivatives depend only on marginal posteriors — reduces training to learning marginal posteriors by minimizing negative log-likelihood. The Gaussian case is shown to reduce to the classical I-MMSE relationship.

Result: The conservation law implies entropy is independent of the noise path, but finite-capacity denoisers approximate posteriors with varying accuracy across noise types, causing performance differences. Predictions are validated on synthetic Markov sources and standard benchmarks (text8, CIFAR-10).

Conclusion: The unified GEXIT-based framework provides a likelihood characterization for both discrete and continuous diffusion models. While entropy is path-independent in theory, practical performance depends on how well finite-capacity models approximate marginal posteriors under different noise types, explaining empirical performance variations across diffusion model designs.

Abstract: While autoregressive models optimize the exact data likelihood via the chain rule, diffusion models are typically trained with denoising objectives. We develop conservation laws based on generalized extrinsic information transfer (GEXIT) functions for a broad class of memoryless noise processes, showing that the data--model cross-entropy (CE) can be characterized exactly as an integral of local information-theoretic derivatives along the noise path. This yields a unified characterization of the likelihood for discrete and continuous diffusion, with the Gaussian case reducing to the well-known mutual information--minimum mean-square error (I-MMSE) relationship. An immediate implication is a locality property: one can compute the information-theoretic derivatives using only the marginal posteriors along the noise path. As a result, training reduces to learning the marginal posteriors by minimizing the negative log-likelihood. While the conservation law implies that the entropy does not depend on the noise path, finite-capacity denoisers approximate the posteriors with varying accuracy across noise types, leading to differences in performance. We validate these predictions on synthetic Markov sources and standard benchmarks, including text8 and CIFAR-10.

</details>


### [271] [Error Aware Distribution Prediction for Lightweight Implicit Neural Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10068)
*Zhimin Li,Jake D. Balla,Joshua A. Levine*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a lightweight uncertainty estimation method for implicit neural representations (INRs) by reformulating regression-based training as a classification task via target discretization into bins, enabling flexible multimodal distribution modeling with competitive reconstruction quality and error awareness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Implicit neural representations inevitably produce prediction errors as lossy approximators, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods are either computationally expensive or rely on restrictive parametric assumptions (e.g., Gaussian). The authors seek a lightweight alternative that captures complex, multimodal predictive distributions without these limitations.

Method: The method reformulates regression-based INR training into a classification task by discretizing continuous target values into discrete bins. This enables flexible, non-parametric distribution modeling that can naturally capture multimodal behaviors. The approach simultaneously encodes relative error scales through the predicted categorical distributions over bins.

Result: The classification-based INR training achieves high reconstruction quality and competitive error awareness compared to regression-based approaches, while providing more flexible uncertainty estimates without computational overhead or restrictive distributional assumptions.

Conclusion: Reformulating INR training as classification via target discretization offers an effective lightweight strategy for uncertainty estimation, balancing reconstruction fidelity with meaningful error awareness while avoiding the drawbacks of parametric distribution assumptions.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) offer compact encoding of volumes, but as lossy approximators, inevitably have prediction errors. We consider INRs that can simultaneously encode relative error scales by predicting distributions using tools from uncertainty estimation. Typically, uncertainty estimation relies on computationally expensive approaches or on predefined parametric assumptions about the predictive distribution (e.g., Gaussian). In this study, we propose a lightweight method that reformulates regression-based INR training as a classification task by discretizing continuous targets into bins, enabling flexible distribution modeling to capture complex multimodal behaviors. We analyze the trade-off between regression and classification for INR training and demonstrate that the classification setting tends to achieve high reconstruction quality and competitive error awareness through uncertainty estimation, compared to regression-based approaches.

</details>


### [272] [Knowledge-Conditioned, Single-Pass LLM Synthesis of Executable Unity Game Scenes: A Compiler Error Census across 26 Goal Playable Concepts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10187)
*Hugh Xuechen Liu,Kıvanç Tatar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether LLMs can generate Unity C# code that compiles in a single pass (no iterative repair). Across 10,400 generations from four open-weight models under various conditions, zero produced a runnable scene. All 90,673 compiler errors were categorized as Grounding (invented/misused Unity types) or Hygiene (plain C# structural defects), revealing that missing engine-specific knowledge is the primary bottleneck.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior LLM code-generation evaluations for game scenes rely on iterative repair loops that conflate what the model initially generates with what the loop corrects, introducing survivorship bias. The authors aim to isolate parametric knowledge through single-pass generation — the most stringent test of unaided model capability.

Method: Four open-weight models (7B–30B parameters) generated Unity C# code across two generation modes, four intermediate-representation (IR) conditioning levels, 26 goal patterns, and 20 seeds, yielding 10,400 generations. The "Goal Playable Concepts" framework maps goal patterns to playable counterparts. All compiler errors (90,673 occurrences, 99 distinct error codes) were classified as either "Grounding" (invented/misused Unity-specific types/APIs) or "Hygiene" (general C# structural errors requiring no engine knowledge), with breakdowns analyzed per goal pattern, model size, IR condition, and generation mode.

Result: Zero generations compiled into a runnable scene, eliminating survivorship bias entirely. The Grounding/Hygiene split differed sharply by goal pattern: Stealth primarily failed on invented engine references, while Capture failed on plain C# structure. Larger models, stricter IR conditioning, and different generation modes shifted error distributions but never produced a compiling scene. The bottleneck is definitively missing engine-specific knowledge rather than general coding ability. A census orders the 26 goal patterns by their demand on Unity-specific knowledge.

Conclusion: Single-pass LLM generation of Unity C# scenes fails universally due to insufficient parametric knowledge of engine-specific APIs and types. Iterative repair loops are essential for current models, and the per-goal-pattern error census provides actionable guidance for designers on where single-pass generation breaks down. The Grounding vs. Hygiene taxonomy offers a useful diagnostic framework for evaluating code generation in domain-specific environments.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write Unity C\# for game scenes. Yet nearly all demonstrations rest on an iterative repair loop that regenerates code until it compiles, conflating what the model writes with what the loop fixes. We remove the loop and evaluate a single pass, where the first draft is final. This isolates the model's parametric knowledge, the most stringent test of unaided generation. Models instantiate Goal Playable Concepts, playable counterparts of goal patterns, across 10,400 generations (four open-weight models, 7B--30B; two generation modes; four intermediate-representation (IR) conditioning levels; 26 goal patterns; 20 seeds). None compiled into a runnable scene, leaving no survivorship bias. To understand how the generated C\# scripts fail, we categorize the 99 error codes behind 90{,}673 compiler-error occurrences as Grounding (invented or misused Unity types and APIs) or Hygiene (structural defects needing no Unity knowledge). The split differs sharply by goal pattern (e.g., Stealth fails mostly on invented engine references; Capture on plain C\# structure). Larger models, stricter IRs, and different generation modes move the errors but never yield a compiling scene. The bottleneck is missing engine-specific knowledge. The census orders goal patterns by that demand, showing designers where single-pass generation breaks.

</details>


### [273] [Distance-Preserving Embeddings in Inhomogeneous Random Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10074)
*My Le,Luana Ruiz,Souvik Dhara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes landmark-based graph embeddings on inhomogeneous random graphs, establishing tighter dimension-distortion trade-offs than classical worst-case bounds. It unifies analysis across finite-type and continuous latent space models via a metric sandwiching framework, extends guarantees to global averages, and introduces a GNN-augmented variant that learns distance-preserving features from small-scale graphs, generalizing robustly to real-world networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior distortion guarantees for distance-preserving graph embeddings rely on worst-case analyses that produce overly pessimistic bounds, failing to reflect the behavior of typical large-scale networks. The authors aim to provide tighter, more realistic guarantees by exploiting structural properties of inhomogeneous random graphs and to replace expensive exact shortest-path computations with learnable neural surrogates.

Method: The authors analyze landmark-based shortest-path embeddings on inhomogeneous random graphs with type-dependent edge probabilities. They model neighborhood expansion via multi-type branching processes to derive tighter dimension-distortion trade-offs. A novel metric sandwiching framework unifies analysis across finite-type and continuous latent space models, establishing universal distortion bounds for general L² kernel models. Finally, they propose a GNN-augmented variant where neural message-passing surrogates replace exact shortest-path queries, leveraging alignment between message-passing and dynamic programming principles of shortest-path algorithms.

Result: The analysis yields significantly tighter dimension-distortion trade-offs than classical worst-case bounds by exploiting structural heterogeneity. Universal distortion bounds are established for general L² kernel models, including heavy-tailed and power-law networks. The GNN-augmented approach, trained on small-scale random graphs, achieves robust generalization to large-scale real-world networks, matching or exceeding the fidelity of exact landmark-based embeddings.

Conclusion: Landmark-based embeddings on inhomogeneous random graphs admit substantially tighter distortion guarantees than worst-case analyses suggest, enabled by controlled neighborhood expansion in branching process models. The metric sandwiching framework provides a unified theoretical foundation, and GNN-based neural surrogates offer a scalable, generalizable alternative to exact shortest-path computation for distance-preserving graph embeddings.

Abstract: Graph machine learning provides powerful tools for understanding complex networks and learning meaningful node representations. A central challenge, however, is designing embeddings with minimal distortion of both local and global functionals, such as shortest path lengths. Prior distortion guarantees for distance-preserving embeddings are worst-case in nature, producing overly pessimistic bounds that fail to capture the structure of typical large-scale networks. To address this, we analyze shortest-path approximation via landmark-based embeddings on inhomogeneous random graphs, a general model with type-dependent edge probabilities. By retaining shortest paths to a small set of reference nodes called landmarks, landmark-based methods effectively function as virtual graph spanners, where structural heterogeneity and controlled neighborhood expansion modeled via multi-type branching processes enable significantly tighter dimension-distortion trade-offs than classical worst-case bounds. We extend these guarantees to global, component-wide averages and unify the analysis across finite-type and continuous latent spaces through a novel metric sandwiching framework, establishing universal distortion bounds for general $L^2$ kernel models, including heavy-tailed and power-law networks. Finally, we introduce a GNN-augmented variant that replaces rigid, computationally expensive exact shortest-path queries with flexible, structure-aware neural surrogates. By leveraging the inherent alignment between graph neural message-passing and the dynamic programming principles of shortest-path algorithms, our approach demonstrates that models trained on small-scale random graphs learn to extract universal distance-preserving features, achieving robust generalization to large-scale, real-world networks that match or exceed the fidelity of classical, exact landmark-based embeddings.

</details>


### [274] [TabLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Low-Rank Ensemble Learning for Large-Scale Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10077)
*Jiaqi Luo,Shixin Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TabLoRA introduces parameter-efficient neural ensembles for large-scale tabular learning by sharing a common backbone and adding predictor-specific low-rank adaptations, achieving competitive performance against GBDTs while reducing computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Applying deep tabular models to large-scale datasets is challenging due to high computational costs from large sample sizes, high feature dimensionality, or many target classes. Existing neural ensembles duplicate full parameters, making them impractical at scale.

Method: TabLoRA shares a single common backbone across all ensemble predictors and introduces predictor-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) matrices. This enables ensemble-style diversity and prediction without full parameter duplication, significantly reducing memory and compute overhead.

Result: TabLoRA achieves a favorable balance between predictive performance and practical efficiency compared to GBDT methods and recent deep tabular baselines under identical resource constraints. Memory analysis and ablation studies confirm improved feasibility of neural ensemble learning while preserving most benefits of full ensembles.

Conclusion: Low-rank adaptation is an effective strategy for scaling neural ensembles to large tabular datasets, making deep tabular models more practical without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Tabular learning is still dominated by gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs), while recent deep learning approaches have become increasingly competitive. However, applying deep tabular models to large-scale datasets remains challenging, as large sample sizes, high feature dimensionality, or many target classes can introduce substantial computational cost. We propose TabLoRA, a parameter-efficient trainable neural ensemble for large-scale tabular learning. Instead of using fully independent ensemble backbones, TabLoRA shares a common backbone across predictors and introduces predictor-specific low-rank adaptations, enabling ensemble-style prediction without full parameter duplication. Across benchmarks, TabLoRA achieves a favorable balance between predictive performance and practical efficiency compared with GBDT methods and recent deep learning baselines under the same resource constraints. Memory analysis and ablation studies further show that the proposed design improves the feasibility of neural ensemble learning while preserving much of the benefit of full ensembles.

</details>


### [275] [When Data Imbalance Helps: Robust Generalization Through Shortcut Saturation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10116)
*Cheng-Ting Chou,Duc Binh Hoang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Under spurious correlations, data imbalance (higher spurious ratio) promotes robust generalization in sufficiently capable models, contrary to intuition. A 2-layer transformer achieves 100% adversarial accuracy far more often at r=0.90 than r=0.50, while 1-layer models fail. Mechanistic analysis reveals gradient conflict dynamics and circuit evolution drive this effect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate how models learn robust features versus shortcut features under spurious correlations, specifically how the spurious ratio (r) and model capacity interact to affect adversarial generalization. The counterintuitive hypothesis: data imbalance may help rather than hurt generalization in capable models.

Method: Synthetic task: true label = sum parity of integer sequence; shortcut = parity of max element. Varying spurious ratio r (0.50 to 0.90) and model depth (1-layer vs 2-layer, 2-head transformers). Evaluation via adversarial held-out split (shortcut anti-correlated with label). Mechanistic analysis: gradient conflict dynamics between true and shortcut circuits, circuit evolution trajectories, and QK/OV circuit causal ablations.

Result: At r=0.50, 0% of 2-layer transformer seeds achieved 100% adversarial accuracy; at r=0.90, 77% of seeds did. 1-layer models showed opposite behavior — imbalance trapped them on the shortcut. Mechanistic analyses revealed a consistent pathway: high imbalance reduces gradient conflict early in training, allowing the true-label circuit to dominate before the shortcut circuit strengthens, enabling robust generalization.

Conclusion: Data imbalance can be beneficial for robust generalization in sufficiently expressive models by altering gradient dynamics to favor the true feature circuit. This has implications for understanding and mitigating spurious correlations in deep learning, suggesting that balanced data is not always optimal.

Abstract: We study robust generalization under spurious correlations: tasks where a shortcut feature is correlated with the true label in training but anti-correlated in an adversarial held-out split. Varying the spurious ratio $r$ (the fraction of training examples where shortcut = true label) and model capacity, we find a counterintuitive result: data imbalance promotes generalization in sufficiently capable models. On a synthetic task where the true label is sum parity of an integer sequence and the shortcut is the parity of the maximum-valued element, a 2-layer, 2-head transformer generalized (reached $100\%$ adversarial accuracy) in 0% of seeds at $r{=}0.50$ but 77% of seeds at $r{=}0.90$. The effect is absent in 1-layer models, where imbalance instead traps the model on the shortcut. Through mechanistic analysis -- gradient conflict dynamics, circuit evolution, and QK/OV circuit ablations -- we characterize a mechanistic pathway consistent with imbalance promoting generalization.

</details>


### [276] [GAE: Graph-Augmented Evolution for Scientific Discovery via Reinforcement Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10127)
*Xuanzhou Chen,Taoli Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GAE introduces a graph-augmented evolutionary framework that uses GNN-based program embeddings, an RL meta-controller for directed parent/mutation selection, and online GRPO fine-tuning of LLM mutation operators, achieving SOTA symbolic regression on nonlinear oscillator systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-guided evolutionary program search suffers from three key bottlenecks: (1) structurally blind parent selection that ignores program topology, (2) sparse whole-program evaluation rewards that provide weak learning signals, and (3) static mutation operators that cannot adapt or improve during the search process.

Method: GAE employs a three-pillar architecture: (1) a relational GNN that parses programs into typed computation graphs to produce structure-aware embeddings; (2) an RL-optimized meta-controller that uses these embeddings to dynamically select parents and mutation directions based on reward history, replacing blind sampling; and (3) an online GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) fine-tuning loop that continuously updates the LLM mutation operator at test-time using group-normalized evaluation rewards to align generation with high-fitness structural edits.

Result: On symbolic regression for complex nonlinear oscillator systems, GAE consistently matches or outperforms static LLM-driven baselines and achieves state-of-the-art out-of-distribution performance by transforming stochastic search into a directed, self-improving trajectory that efficiently discovers closed-form physical equations.

Conclusion: The tightly coupled integration of graph-structured program representations, RL-driven search policies, and online LLM fine-tuning effectively overcomes the core limitations of prior LLM-guided evolutionary methods, enabling more efficient and generalizable scientific discovery.

Abstract: Evolutionary program search guided by Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automated scientific discovery. However, current approaches are fundamentally constrained by three bottlenecks: structurally blind parent selection, sparse whole-program evaluation rewards, and static mutation operators that fail to adapt during search. We present GAE (Graph-Augmented Evolution), a framework that resolves these limitations through a tightly coupled, three-pillar architecture. First, a relational graph neural network (GNN) parses programs into typed computation graphs, producing structure-aware embeddings. Second, an RL-optimized meta-controller leverages these embeddings to replace blind evolutionary sampling with a directed policy, dynamically selecting optimal parents and mutation directions based on reward history. Third, an online GRPO fine-tuning loop continuously updates the LLM mutation operator at test-time using group-normalized evaluation rewards, directly aligning the model's generation distribution with high-fitness structural edits. We evaluate GAE on a challenging scientific discovery task: symbolic regression for complex nonlinear oscillator systems. By transforming stochastic search into a directed, self-improving trajectory, GAE efficiently discovers closed-form physical equations, consistently matching or outperforming static LLM-driven baselines and achieving state-of-the-art out-of-distribution performance.

</details>


### [277] [Energy-guided Recursive Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10128)
*Yifei Zhao,Ying Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ERM introduces explicit Hopfield energy functions as an intrinsic selection principle for recursive reasoning models, replacing heuristic voting or q-heads with energy-based techniques like parallel tempering, achieving strong results on Sudoku, PPBench, and Maze.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing recursive reasoning models scale test-time computation by increasing depth or stochastic breadth but lack a principled criterion for selecting among candidate trajectories, relying instead on ad-hoc q-heads or heuristic voting.

Method: ERM uses Hopfield-type memories encoding valid local/global structures to define an explicit energy function over candidate trajectories. This energy serves as an intrinsic selector and integrates with energy-based techniques (e.g., parallel tempering) to improve sampling and ranking, with D=64 recurrent steps and K=128 candidates.

Result: ERM achieves 98.97% on Sudoku, 88.04% on PPBench, and 99.30% on Maze, outperforming Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model and Equilibrium Reasoners.

Conclusion: Incorporating explicit energy functions into recursive reasoning provides a principled, effective path toward improved test-time inference.

Abstract: Recursive reasoning models address structured problems by repeatedly updating latent states of small neural networks. However, their test-time scaling lacks a principled inference mechanism: increasing depth or stochastic breadth generates more trajectories without a clear criterion for selection, and existing methods predominantly rely on additional q-heads or heuristic voting. Here, we develop the Energy-guided Recursive Model (ERM), which introduces an intrinsic selection principle based on explicit Hopfield energies. ERM leverages Hopfield-type memories of valid local or global structures to define the selector over candidate trajectories. The resulting energy seamlessly integrates with energy-based techniques such as parallel tempering to enhance sampling efficiency and ranking. With $D=64$ recurrent steps and $K=128$ candidates, ERM reaches optimal solutions on Sudoku ($98.97\%$), Pencil Puzzle Bench (PPBench, $88.04\%$) and Maze ($99.30\%$), improving upon recent Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model and Equilibrium Reasoners. These results suggest that incorporating explicit energy functions into recursive reasoning offers a principled path toward more effective inference.

</details>


### [278] [SALT-GNN: Handling Dense Neighborhoods in Anti-Money Laundering Graphs via Statistics-Aware Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10131)
*Lidia Losavio,Francesco Sovrano,Dario Fenoglio,Martin Gjoreski,Marc Langheinrich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GNN-based AML models fail in dense recipient contexts due to multiset non-discriminability, cardinality blindness, and attention attenuation. The authors propose SALT-GNN, which fuses degree-aware statistical aggregation with attention at each layer, achieving 3–20 point F1 gains in dense contexts with up to 77% fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard aggregate metrics (e.g., overall F1) mask a critical operational problem in AML: high-activity recipient accounts create dense transaction neighborhoods where suspicious signals become harder to isolate and costlier to investigate. Existing GNN-based AML models degrade significantly in these dense recipient contexts, but this failure mode is undiagnosed and unaddressed.

Method: First, the authors introduce a recipient-degree stratified evaluation framework that reports standard AML metrics across recipient-context density, exposing consistent degradation in dense contexts. They trace this to three GNN limitations: (1) multiset non-discriminability, (2) cardinality blindness, and (3) attention attenuation in dense neighborhoods. They then propose SALT-GNN, a lightweight architecture that fuses degree-aware statistical aggregation with attention at each message-passing layer, allowing distributional and cardinality information to shape node representations used by subsequent attention steps. The approach is agnostic to the attention operator (Transformer- or GAT-style).

Result: On HI-Small and HI-Medium, SALT-GNN uses up to 77% fewer parameters than task-specific graph-transformer baselines while improving dense-context F1 by 3–6 points. On AMLSim-32k-5%, highest-degree F1 improves by 16–20 points. Ablations confirm that fusion placement (where statistical and attentional evidence are combined) is the key factor driving dense-context performance gains, not the choice of attention operator.

Conclusion: Recipient-degree stratified evaluation reveals a previously hidden failure mode in AML GNNs. SALT-GNN demonstrates that injecting degree-aware statistical information directly into the message-passing layers—rather than using it only for initial features or final prediction—substantially improves performance in dense recipient contexts, offering a parameter-efficient solution for real-world AML deployment.

Abstract: Money laundering threatens financial stability and exposes institutions to penalties, motivating automated detection. Because laundering schemes often emerge through relational patterns, graph neural networks (GNNs) are increasingly used for anti-money laundering (AML). Yet AML GNNs are typically evaluated with aggregate metrics such as overall F1 score, which hide an operational issue: high-activity recipient accounts concentrate many incoming transactions, making suspicious signals harder to isolate and costlier to investigate. We introduce a recipient-degree stratified evaluation that reports standard AML metrics across recipient-context density. Across three datasets (HI-Small, HI-Medium, and AMLSim-32k-5%), it reveals consistent degradation in dense recipient contexts, which we trace to three GNN characteristics: two known limitations that AML amplifies, i.e., (1) multiset non-discriminability and (2) cardinality blindness, and (3) an attention-specific effect: in dense neighborhoods, normalized attention attenuates weak but pattern-relevant multi-hop signals. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose SALT-GNN, a lightweight statistics-aware architecture that fuses degree-aware statistical aggregation with attention at each message-passing layer, so distributional and cardinality information shapes the node states used by subsequent attention steps. Ablations support fusion placement as a key factor in dense-context performance. On HI-Small and HI-Medium, SALT-GNN uses up to 77% fewer parameters than task-specific graph-transformer baselines while improving dense-context F1 score by 3-6 points; on AMLSim-32k-5%, it improves highest-degree F1 score by 16-20 points. The gains hold for both Transformer- and GAT-style attention, indicating that the benefit comes from where statistical and attentional evidence is fused rather than from a specific attention operator.

</details>


### [279] [LeRoPE: Learnable RoPE Frequencies Improve Language Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10134)
*Petros Karypis,Sean O'Brien,Shreyas Kadekodi,Rui Zhu,Julian McAuley*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Learned Rotary Positional Encodings (LeRoPE), which treats the per-frequency rotation rates in RoPE as learnable parameters instead of fixed hyperparameters. Experiments across model scales (52M–2.5B parameters) show LeRoPE consistently outperforms standard RoPE and partial RoPE, with RoPE requiring 3.4% more compute to match LeRoPE's performance at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RoPE uses a fixed geometric sequence of rotation frequencies governed by a base-frequency hyperparameter. Prior work has only coarsely tuned this (e.g., increasing the base or applying RoPE partially), but the optimal per-frequency rotation rates may not follow a rigid geometric progression. The authors hypothesize that making each frequency learnable could yield better position-sensitive representations.

Method: The authors introduce LeRoPE, which parameterizes the rotation frequencies as learnable scalars (one per frequency/dimension pair) rather than fixing them via a geometric schedule. They train a ladder of decoder-only language models from scratch (52M, 150M, 500M, 1.2B, 2.5B parameters) using LeRoPE and compare against standard RoPE and partial RoPE baselines. They also analyze the emergent properties of the learned frequency parameters.

Result: LeRoPE consistently outperforms both RoPE and partial RoPE across all model scales. At the 2.5B scale, RoPE requires 3.4% more FLOPs to match LeRoPE's performance. The authors also observe the emergence of a distinctive "high-norm, positional LeRoPE band" — a subset of learned frequencies that develop unusually large magnitudes and appear to specialize in encoding positional information.

Conclusion: Making RoPE frequencies learnable provides consistent and meaningful gains over fixed-geometric scheduling. The emergence of the high-norm band suggests that certain positional frequencies are more critical than others, and learning them adaptively yields more compute-efficient position encoding.

Abstract: Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE) are currently the most popular positional encodings used in modern language models. RoPE rotates two-dimensional chunks of query and key vectors, operating as a function of their relative positional offset. The position-wise rates of rotation in RoPE typically follow a geometric sequence specified by a fixed base-frequency hyperparameter. Prior work has improved performance by either increasing this parameter to slow rotation or by applying RoPE to only a subset of QK dimensions. In this work we modify RoPE by learning a scalar per frequency, treating frequencies as learnable parameters rather than hyperparameters. We validate Learned RoPE by training a ladder of language models from scratch, ranging from 52M to 2.5B parameters. We observe and analyze the emergence of a high-norm, positional LeRoPE band. LeRoPE consistently outperforms RoPE and partial RoPE across all scales, with RoPE requiring 3.4% more compute (FLOPs) to match LeRoPE at the largest scale.

</details>


### [280] [RDQ: Residual Distribution Quantization for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10137)
*Prateek Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training quantization below 4-bit fails due to residual stream distributional drift accumulating across layers. The authors propose RDQ with Cascaded Error Compensation (CEC), which calibrates each layer using activations from already-quantized upstream layers and folds correction scales into RMSNorm, achieving state-of-the-art perplexity with zero inference overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM post-training quantization degrades sharply below 4-bit, but the root cause is poorly understood. The authors aim to rigorously diagnose this failure and develop a principled mitigation that maintains practical deployability.

Method: 1. Diagnostic analysis: KL divergence, per-layer variance growth (6,548×), and KS normality tests on residual streams across LLaMA-3-8B layers. 2. RDQ framework with Cascaded Error Compensation (CEC): sequential calibration where each layer receives activations produced by already-quantized upstream layers (capturing actual drift), then per-channel AWQ-style scales are fitted against these drifted inputs and folded into preceding RMSNorm weights for mathematically equivalent, zero-overhead deployment. Standard group-128 asymmetric quantization throughout.

Result: Residual stream drift correlates with log-perplexity (Pearson r=0.999, p<0.001). 84% of LLaMA-3-8B layers show non-Gaussian residuals. RDQ achieves SOTA: LLaMA-3-8B 7.55/5.62 PPL (W3/W4); Qwen-2.5-7B 7.46/6.38; Mistral-7B 6.88/5.73. Beats LeanQuant/SpinQuant at all model/bit-width combos, up to -46.4% vs. RTN at W3A16.

Conclusion: Residual distributional drift is the primary failure mechanism in low-bit LLM PTQ. Cascaded Error Compensation directly addresses this by calibrating on drifted activations, and the scale-folding trick ensures zero runtime overhead. RDQ sets new SOTA across multiple architectures while remaining fully deployable on standard inference stacks.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models degrades sharply below 4-bit precision. We identify the root cause as residual stream distributional drift: quantization noise injected at each transformer layer accumulates in the shared residual representation, causing KL divergence from the FP16 baseline to grow super-linearly with depth (Pearson r=0.999 with log-perplexity, p<0.001, confirmed across all tested methods and bit-widths). We discover that 84% of LLaMA-3-8B layers exhibit non-Gaussian residual distributions (KS test, p<=0.05), and that per-layer residual stream variance grows 6,548x across depth. We propose RDQ (Residual Distribution Quantization), a PTQ framework whose central contribution is Cascaded Error Compensation (CEC): a sequential calibration procedure that captures the actual drifted activations each layer receives (computed by running calibration data through already-quantized upstream layers) and fits per-channel AWQ-style scales against those drifted inputs, with scales folded into preceding RMSNorm weights for exact mathematical equivalence at zero inference overhead. RDQ achieves state-of-the-art results on all three tested architectures: LLaMA-3-8B: 7.55 / 5.62 PPL (W3/W4); Qwen-2.5-7B: 7.46 / 6.38 PPL; Mistral-7B: 6.88 / 5.73 PPL. RDQ beats the best published baseline (LeanQuant/SpinQuant) at every model and bit-width combination, with gains up to -46.4% vs. RTN at W3A16 on LLaMA-3-8B. All output is standard group-128 asymmetric quantization, deployable on Qualcomm AIMET, GGUF, and any standard inference stack at zero runtime overhead.

</details>


### [281] [LLMs as a Jury: Cross-Model Consensus Can Outperform Process Reward Models for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10139)
*Ning Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-model consensus — treating independently trained LLMs as a jury where agreement structure, not scoring, serves as a free verification signal at inference time — outperforms self-consistency and trained reward models, with a closed-form law predicting its accuracy from panel statistics and characterizing its failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing test-time answer selectors have significant limitations: self-consistency (majority voting) propagates errors from a single model's biased reasoning, while trained reward models require expensive labeled data and generalize poorly out-of-distribution. The authors seek a free, distribution-robust verification signal available at inference time.

Method: The authors propose using cross-model consensus: a panel of independently trained LLMs each solve a problem once, and the answer with the highest agreement count across models is selected — treating the panel as a jury where only agreement structure matters, never one model scoring another. They derive a parameter-free closed-form law that predicts consensus accuracy from three observable panel statistics (model accuracy, inter-model agreement rates, and a shared-error term). They benchmark against self-consistency, self-scoring, and four trained verifiers (discriminative, outcome, and generative reward models) across seven benchmarks.

Result: On competition math, cross-model consensus closed the entire gap to an oracle selector (while self-scoring closed almost none). Across seven benchmarks, it outperformed self-consistency and self-scoring. Against trained verifiers, the free LLM-jury matched the strongest reward model within its math training domain and was the top selector outside it. The derived law predicts consensus accuracy with a mean absolute error of 0.03. The method's ceiling is a "shared-error floor" where models share common misconceptions — near zero on math but non-trivial on science.

Conclusion: Cross-model consensus is a principled, free verification signal that decouples errors through independent training. It is analytically characterized by a predictive law and a shared-error floor, making it a verifier whose reliability can be determined in advance.

Abstract: Selecting the correct answer from a pool of candidate reasoning chains is the engine of test-time scaling, yet the standard selectors each carry a cost: self-consistency inherits the errors of the single model it resamples, and trained reward models need labeled data and transfer poorly off-distribution. We study a third signal, free at inference time: cross-model consensus, the degree to which independently trained models, each solving the problem once, agree on a final answer. We treat the panel as an LLM-jury, in which the structure of agreement, not any model's score of another, is the verification signal. Across seven benchmarks it selects correct answers better than self-consistency and far better than a model scoring its own candidates: on competition math it closes the entire gap to an oracle selector, while self-scoring closes almost none. The mechanism is error decorrelation: independently trained models err differently, so their wrong answers scatter while the correct one accumulates agreement. We make this precise with a parameter-free law, derived in closed form, that predicts consensus accuracy from three measured panel statistics to a mean absolute error of $0.03$ and exposes the method's ceiling: a shared-error floor where models share a misconception, near zero on math but non-trivial on science. Against four trained verifiers spanning discriminative, outcome, and generative reward models, the free LLM-jury matches the strongest inside their math training domain and is the top selector outside it. Cross-model consensus is thus a verifier we can characterize in advance: a law that says when to trust it, and a floor that marks where it cannot.

</details>


### [282] [Beyond Euclidean Clipping: Overcoming Exploration Collapse in LLM RL via Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10169)
*Zhicheng Cai,Xinyuan Guo,Hanlin Wu,Mingxuan Wang,Wei-Ying Ma,Ya-Qin Zhang,Hao Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PPO-Clip fails due to a geometric mismatch: it uses Euclidean distance to measure policy discrepancy, which is inconsistent with the Riemannian geometry of the policy manifold. The authors propose Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization (RIPO), which enforces isometric updates on the Riemannian manifold, achieving better exploration-exploitation balance and up to 60% improvement over GRPO on AIME24.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior RL algorithms for LLMs (e.g., PPO-Clip) suffer from exploration collapse, and existing heuristic remedies fail to identify the root cause. The authors aim to diagnose the fundamental flaw and provide a principled geometric solution.

Method: The paper analytically shows that PPO-Clip implicitly measures policy discrepancy via Euclidean metric, conflicting with the Riemannian manifold structure of probability distributions. RIPO is proposed to enforce isometric (distance-preserving) policy updates on the policy Riemannian manifold, respecting the intrinsic geometry. It also achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off for optimization stability.

Result: RIPO significantly outperforms existing LLM RL algorithms across seven competition-level benchmarks, achieving up to 60% improvement over GRPO on AIME24.

Conclusion: The geometric inconsistency in PPO-Clip is the fundamental cause of exploration collapse. RIPO corrects this by aligning policy updates with the Riemannian manifold geometry, yielding superior and more stable optimization for LLM reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. However, RL algorithms with PPO-Clip are inherently limited by exploration collapse. Subsequent works remain primarily heuristic and fail to identify the essential cause of PPO-Clip's failure. This work reveals the fundamental flaw of PPO-Clip: it implicitly measures policy discrepancy using Euclidean metric, which is theoretically inconsistent with the intrinsic geometry on the policy Riemannian manifold. This geometric mismatch results in overly conservative updates in low-probability regions while aggressive in high-probability regions, ultimately collapsing exploration. To correct this geometric flaw, we propose Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization (RIPO), which guarantees isometric policy updates on the Riemannian manifold, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation. We further show that RIPO achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off, which stabilizes optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RIPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across seven competition-level benchmarks (up to 60% improvement over GRPO on AIME24).

</details>


### [283] [PhysMRV: Physical Memory Retrieval and Verification for Physics Plausibility Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10190)
*Wenyuan Wang,Lianyu Hu,Hao Wang,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PhysMRV is a training-free framework that enhances VLMs' physical plausibility reasoning by retrieving structured physical knowledge from a Hierarchical Memory Bank (scene descriptions, physical-event graphs, and physics-rule summaries), achieving consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs perform well on video understanding but remain unreliable in physical plausibility reasoning — understanding object interactions, causal dynamics, and fundamental physical principles. Existing benchmarks reveal a persistent gap in physical commonsense reasoning that retrieval-augmented methods using semantically similar videos fail to adequately address.

Method: PhysMRV constructs a Hierarchical Memory Bank from training videos with three levels: (1) scene descriptions capturing visual context, (2) physical-event graphs modeling object interactions and causal structure, and (3) physics-rule summaries distilling reusable physical principles. During inference, physically relevant memories are retrieved and their structured evidence guides a frozen VLM in verifying physical plausibility, requiring no fine-tuning or parameter updates.

Result: Evaluated on ImplausiBench, IntPhys2, and GRASP Level 2 across multiple state-of-the-art VLMs, PhysMRV demonstrated consistent improvements over direct prompting across diverse VLMs and benchmarks.

Conclusion: Structured physical memories provide an effective and scalable means of enhancing physical plausibility reasoning in VLMs without requiring additional training, suggesting a promising direction for improving physical commonsense in video-language models.

Abstract: Video-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on video understanding and visual question answering, yet they remain unreliable in reasoning about physical plausibility, where understanding object interactions, causal dynamics, and fundamental physical principles is essential. This limitation is particularly evident on challenging physical reasoning benchmarks, revealing a persistent gap in physical commonsense reasoning. To address this challenge, we propose PhysMRV, a training-free physical memory and verification framework for physical plausibility reasoning. Unlike retrieval-augmented VLMs that retrieve semantically similar videos as additional context, PhysMRV transforms training videos into a Hierarchical Memory Bank of structured physical knowledge comprising three complementary levels: scene descriptions capturing visual context, physical-event graphs modeling object interactions and causal structure, and physics-rule summaries distilling reusable physical principles and cues. During inference, PhysMRV retrieves physically relevant memories and leverages their structured physical evidence to guide a frozen VLM in verifying physical plausibility, requiring neither fine-tuning nor parameter updates. We evaluate PhysMRV on three challenging physical reasoning benchmarks, ImplausiBench, IntPhys2, and GRASP Level 2, across multiple state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over direct prompting across diverse VLMs and evaluation benchmarks, showing that structured physical memories provide an effective and scalable means of enhancing physical plausibility reasoning without additional training.

</details>


### [284] [Generative Augmentation of Raman Spectra for Glioma Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10196)
*Andrei Iuşan,Iulian Vasile,Daria Voiculescu,Ion Petre,Andrei Păun,Bogdan Oancea,Mihaela Păun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A conditional variational autoencoder (β-CVAE) generates synthetic Raman spectra to augment small glioma biopsy datasets. While synthetic-only training underperforms real data, augmenting real training data with synthetic spectra consistently improves IDH status and methylation subtype classification. A reconstruction-based inference strategy (Classification by Reconstruction) is also explored.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biomedical Raman spectroscopy datasets, particularly for glioma analysis, are typically small, heterogeneous, and affected by acquisition-specific variability, hindering effective machine learning. This work investigates whether deep generative augmentation can mitigate these limitations in small-cohort settings.

Method: A β-CVAE generates class-conditioned synthetic Raman spectra from 58 glioma biopsy samples. Evaluation uses strict patient-isolated cross-validation under TS/TR and TSR/TR settings for binary IDH classification and 6-class methylation subtype classification. A Classification by Reconstruction (CbR) strategy is also investigated.

Result: Synthetic-only training (TS/TR) underperforms real data training due to domain gap. However, TSR/TR augmentation consistently improves classification across multiple models. The CbR approach provides an alternative inference strategy based on reconstruction error.

Conclusion: Deep generative augmentation provides useful regularization for downstream classifiers even with limited patient samples, supporting its practical use for improving ML robustness in Raman spectroscopy with small biomedical datasets.

Abstract: Access to sufficiently large biomedical datasets remains a major obstacle for machine learning in Raman spectroscopy-based diagnostics. In particular, for glioma analysis, datasets are typically small and heterogeneous, affected by acquisition-specific variability. This work investigates the utility of deep generative augmentation in such a small-cohort setting. We analyze glioma biopsy spectra acquired from 58 tumor samples and consider both binary IDH-status classification and 6-class methylation subtype classification problems. To address the limited size and imbalance of the dataset, we develop a conditional variational autoencoder ($β$-CVAE) capable of generating class-conditioned synthetic Raman spectra. The generated data are evaluated in Train-on-Synthetic, Test-on-Real (TS/TR) and Train-on-Synthetic+Real, Test-on-Real (TSR/TR) settings under a strict patient-isolated cross-validation protocol. Models trained exclusively on synthetic data underperform models trained on real spectra, indicating a substantial domain gap between synthetic and real distributions. However, augmenting the real training data with synthetic spectra consistently improves classification performance across multiple models. These findings indicate that, even with a limited number of independent patient samples, generative models can capture sufficient structure to provide useful regularization for downstream classifiers. We also investigate a reconstruction-based inference strategy, termed Classification by Reconstruction (CbR), in which class prediction is based on reconstruction error under different class conditions. Overall, the results support the use of deep generative augmentation as a practical strategy for improving machine learning robustness in Raman spectroscopy applications characterized by limited biomedical datasets.

</details>


### [285] [The Differential Neural Tangent Kernel and Its Positivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10200)
*Bangti Jin,Longjun Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Differential Neural Tangent Kernel (DNTK), an extension of the NTK framework tailored for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). It establishes the positivity of the infinite-width DNTK for both shallow and deep networks with a broad class of activation functions (including RePU and smooth non-polynomial activations) across all linear differential operators, addressing a key theoretical challenge posed by the presence of multiple differential operators in PINNs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The NTK framework has been successfully applied to analyze over-parameterized neural networks, and recently extended to PINNs for solving linear PDEs. However, establishing NTK positivity for PINNs is fundamentally challenging due to multiple differential operators acting on the network. Without positivity guarantees, convergence analyses of gradient-based training for PINNs lack a rigorous foundation.

Method: The authors propose the Differential Neural Tangent Kernel (DNTK), a novel theoretical framework that reformulates the NTK analysis for PINNs. They analyze the infinite-width limit of this kernel and prove its positivity for both shallow and deep neural networks. The analysis covers a wide class of activation functions, including RePU and smooth non-polynomial activations, and applies to all linear differential operators.

Result: The paper establishes the positivity of the infinite-width DNTK for shallow and deep neural networks across a broad family of activation functions and all linear differential operators. This provides the necessary theoretical groundwork for analyzing gradient-type algorithms when training PINNs.

Conclusion: The DNTK framework successfully resolves the positivity challenge that hindered NTK-based analysis of PINNs. These results lay a rigorous foundation for future convergence analyses of gradient-type training algorithms for physics-informed neural networks in over-parameterized settings.

Abstract: The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) is one powerful tool for analyzing the training dynamics of neural networks in the over-parameterized regime. Recently, the theoretical framework has been extended to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving linear PDEs, one highly popular class of neural PDE solvers. In the analysis, the positivity of the associated NTK plays a fundamental role. However, establishing the positivity of the NTK for PINNs is highly challenging, due to the presence of multiple differential operators. In this work, we propose a new theoretical framework, called Differential Neural Tangent Kernel (DNTK), for analyzing PINNs through the lens of the NTK, and establish the positivity of the infinite width DNTK for both shallow and deep neural networks for a wide class of activation functions, including RePU and smooth but non-polynomial activations, for all linear differential operators. These theoretical results lay the foundation for the analysis of gradient type algorithms for training PINNs.

</details>


### [286] [Two Confounds in Cross-Model Value Comparison: Response Determinism and the Access Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10202)
*Hong-In Won,Jinseok Jang,Hyoseop Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-model comparisons of values conflate genuine value differences with response determinism (decisiveness). The authors introduce a decomposition protocol that separates these, finding determinism varies widely across models and that deployment harnesses (e.g., system prompts) act as a distinct value-shaping confound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work interprets divergence in value dispositions across language models as evidence of individuated values, but single-draw forced-choice measurement confounds a genuine difference in central tendency with a difference in response determinism (how sharply a model commits to a choice). The authors aim to disentangle these two quantities and identify additional confounds in value measurement pipelines.

Method: They introduce a separation protocol using no-rule value dilemmas with counterbalanced, repeated forced-choice measurement, along with a determinism index. A determinism-corrected decomposition splits apparent cross-model distance into a direction-flip component (genuine disagreement) and a same-side-more-extreme component (determinism). They further isolate the deployment harness confound by re-collecting model responses through both raw provider APIs and deployment clients, including a white-box causal control using an agent system prompt.

Result: Determinism varies substantially across nine models (0.66-0.95 among engaging models). Correcting for determinism shrinks apparent individuation, though a few cross-family disagreements survive. Deployment clients shift value profiles substantially and client-specifically: one CLI moves a profile by 0.31, flips 4/18 items, and inflates apparent softness (0.34 via CLI vs 0.66 via raw API). An agent system prompt causally makes a base model compliant that otherwise refuses 10% of forced choices.

Conclusion: Single-draw value distance rankings conflate determinism with genuine disagreement and are further confounded by the deployment harness. The authors contribute both a determinism-corrected decomposition method and the identification of the deployment harness as a distinct, causally demonstrated value-shaping layer.

Abstract: Cross-model comparisons read divergence in value dispositions as evidence that language models hold individuated values. Under single-draw measurement this conflates two quantities: a difference in central tendency (a genuine value difference) and a difference in response determinism (how sharply a model commits to a forced choice). We introduce a separation protocol -- no-rule value dilemmas with counterbalanced, repeated forced-choice measurement and a determinism index -- and a determinism-corrected decomposition that splits an apparent cross-model distance into a direction-flip component (genuine disagreement) and a same-side-more-extreme component we label determinism. Across nine models, determinism varies substantially (0.66-0.95 among engaging models); whether it is a per-model trait or tracks provider and scale is a question our method makes measurable but our sample leaves open. Correcting for determinism shrinks apparent individuation, while a few cross-family disagreements survive a strict test. We then isolate a second confound: the access harness serving each model. Re-collecting the same models through raw provider APIs, we find the deployment client shifts a model's value profile substantially and client-specifically: one subscription CLI moves a profile by 0.31, flips four of eighteen items, and inflates the flagship's apparent softness (0.34 via CLI vs 0.66 via raw API), whereas another provider's client is clean, confounding provider family with access client. The harness is a value-shaping layer: a base model that refuses one-in-ten forced choices is made compliant by an agent system prompt, established causally in a white-box control. An audit ranking models by single-draw value distance thus ranks a determinism-inflated quantity, confounded further by the client used. We contribute the decomposition and identify the deployment harness as a distinct value confound.

</details>


### [287] [When Does Depth Survive Composition? Compute--Quality Regimes in Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10203)
*Achyuthan Sivasankar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether deeper world models genuinely produce better autoregressive rollouts. Using a "shallow penalty" metric ρ across nine DeepMind Control tasks, the authors find three regimes: intrinsic (depth helps), inversion (shallow exits outperform full depth), and flat. The inversion regime is shown to be created by multi-step training supervision — a "routability catch-22" where training early exits to be routable causes them to outperform the full stack in rollouts. Regime is partially predictable from task properties (dimensionality, one-step error).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adaptive-compute world models assume that (1) deeper computation yields better per-step predictions and (2) this precision survives composition across autoregressive rollouts. The second assumption — compositional fidelity — had not been systematically tested. The authors aim to empirically characterize when and why depth helps or hurts in multi-step rollouts.

Method: A pre-registered instrument: the shallow penalty ρ = err(shallowest-exit rollout) / err(full-depth rollout). Tested across 9 DeepMind Control tasks under matched single-step (K=1) and multi-step (K=4) training, with 3 seeds each. An ablation on the cheetah inversion task supervises early exits only at the first rollout step. A CEM planner evaluates whether ρ's sign predicts planning benefits from depth. Pre-registered correlations tested between ρ and observation/action dimensionality plus one-step model error.

Result: Three regimes identified: intrinsic (6/9 tasks, ρ up to 4.7×), inversion (2/9 tasks, ρ down to 0.85×), and flat (1 task). The robust inversion (cheetah) is erased by first-step-only supervision (ρ: 0.87→1.18, Δ=+0.31), while intrinsic tasks are unaffected — a double dissociation. Regime is partially predictable a priori: observation/action dimensionality and one-step error correlate with ρ at |Spearman|≈0.75 (n=9). In CEM planning, ρ's sign predicts whether depth benefits planning, most sharply on inversion tasks where shallow planning beats deep.

Conclusion: The routability catch-22 reveals a fundamental tension: the multi-step supervision that makes early exits usable as routers is precisely what trains them to outperform the full stack in rollouts. Three cautions are emphasized: a task's regime depends on the metric space, rollout horizon, and encoder choice. All thresholds and gates were fixed before the compute campaign.

Abstract: Adaptive-compute world models -- early-exit or mixture-of-depths predictors that spend variable depth per step -- assume depth buys better predictions and can be routed adaptively. In autoregressive rollouts, the first assumption requires depth's per-step precision to survive composition. We test this with a pre-registered instrument, the shallow penalty $ρ=\mathrm{err}(\text{shallowest-exit rollout})/\mathrm{err}(\text{full-depth rollout})$, across nine DeepMind Control tasks under matched single-step ($K=1$) and multi-step ($K=4$) training, three seeds each. We find three regimes: on 6/9 tasks depth helps rollouts (intrinsic, $ρ$ up to $4.7\times$), on 2/9 the shallow exits beat the full stack (inversion, $ρ$ down to $0.85\times$), and one is flat. The robust inversion (cheetah) is not a property of the dynamics but is created by training: an ablation supervising early exits only at the first rollout step erases it ($ρ: 0.87\to1.18$, $n=8$, $Δ=+0.31$), while an intrinsic-tradeoff task is unaffected -- a double dissociation we call the routability catch-22, since the supervision that makes exits routable is what trains them to out-roll the full stack. The regime is partly predictable a priori: observation/action dimensionality and one-step model error correlate with $ρ$ at $|\text{Spearman}|\approx0.75$ ($n=9$). Inside a CEM planner, $ρ$'s sign predicts whether planning benefits from depth, most sharply on the inversion task, where shallow planning beats deep. Finally, three cautions: a task's regime depends on the metric space, the rollout horizon, and the encoder. All thresholds and gates were fixed before the compute campaign, including a pre-registered negative for the hypothesis that motivated the study.

</details>


### [288] [Exploratory Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Forecasting Meteorological Parameters in the Agricultural Sector](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10208)
*Piotr Sikora,Sotirios Kontogiannis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Comparative evaluation of recurrent (GRU, LSTM) and hybrid (1D-CNN-GRU, 1D-CNN-LSTM) deep learning architectures for multivariate meteorological forecasting (ET₀, VPD, wind speed/direction) at 24h and 168h horizons, showing hybrid CNN-GRU achieves best overall performance, with convolutional front-ends providing greater benefit for short-term forecasts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate meteorological forecasting is critical for agriculture, irrigation, and environmental decision-making. The study aims to identify optimal deep learning architectures for multivariate forecasting of key agro-meteorological variables across different time horizons.

Method: Comparative evaluation using 134,376 hourly ERA5 observations (2011–2026) from Ioannina, Greece. Benchmarked single/multi-layer GRU and LSTM against hybrid 1D-CNN-GRU and 1D-CNN-LSTM on two forecasting tasks (24h next-day, 168h week-ahead). Assessed via NRMSE, R², and a composite Weighted Quotient Score (WQS).

Result: Best purely recurrent: 64-unit LSTM (WQS=0.816755, 24h) and 1024-unit GRU (WQS=0.779465, 168h). Best overall: CNN-GRU (WQS=0.827535 at 24h; 0.782863 at 168h) but with more parameters; CNN-LSTM achieved near-identical results with substantially fewer parameters. Hybrid models improved WQS over recurrent baselines by 1.22–1.63% (24h) and 0.44–0.45% (168h).

Conclusion: Hybrid 1D-CNN-recurrent architectures outperform purely recurrent models for multivariate meteorological forecasting, with convolutional feature extraction conferring greater relative gains at shorter (24h) than longer (168h) horizons. CNN-LSTM offers a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

Abstract: Accurate meteorological forecasting is essential for agricultural planning, irrigation management, and environmental decision support. This study conducts a comparative evaluation of recurrent and hybrid deep learning architectures for multivariate forecasting of reference evapotranspiration ($ET_0$), vapour pressure deficit (VPD), wind speed, and the sine and cosine components of wind direction. The analysis utilizes 134,376 hourly observations from Ioannina, Greece, spanning January 2011 to April 2026, sourced from ERA5 via the OpenMeteo Historical Weather API. Single and multi-layer GRU and LSTM networks are compared with hybrid 1D-CNN-GRU and 1D-CNN-LSTM models for two forecasting tasks: a 24-hour next-day forecast and a 168-hour week-ahead forecast. Performance is evaluated using normalized root mean squared error, the coefficient of determination, and a composite Weighted Quotient Score (WQS). The most effective purely recurrent models are a 64-unit LSTM for the 24-hour horizon, with a WQS of 0.816755, and a 1024-unit GRU for the 168-hour horizon, with a WQS of 0.779465. The hybrid CNN-GRU models achieved the highest overall scores of 0.827535 and 0.782863 for the 24-hour and 168-hour horizons, but with additionally more number of units respectively to LSTM models, while the CNN-LSTM models yield nearly identical results with substantially fewer parameters. Compared to the corresponding recurrent baselines, the hybrid models improve WQS by 1.22--1.63\% at 24 hours and by 0.44--0.45\% at 168 hours, indicating that convolutional feature extraction is more beneficial for short-term forecasting.

</details>
