### [289] [DSSMs: State Space Models with Explicit Memory via Delay Differential Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10244)
*Yixiao Qian,Song Chen,Jiaxu Liu,Shengze Cai,Chao Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSSMs augment diagonal state space models with explicit delayed-state feedback inspired by delay differential equations, enabling better long-range retrieval. The authors provide stability parameterization, history management, and FFT-based frequency-domain training, achieving improvements on delayed-retrieval tasks while remaining competitive on standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SSMs compress unbounded history into a fixed-size state, limiting long-range context retention and precise retrieval. The authors aim to overcome this by explicitly incorporating delayed-state feedback into the recurrence.

Method: DSSMs introduce delayed-state feedback into diagonal SSM recurrences using a delay differential equation framework. Key technical contributions include: (1) a practical discretization with a delay-independent stability condition for parameterization; (2) deriving the DSSM transfer function to compute kernels in the frequency domain via FFT, avoiding direct time-domain construction; and (3) a kernel contour shift technique to suppress aliasing and enable accurate FFT-based training.

Result: DSSMs substantially improve performance on targeted delayed-retrieval tasks. They outperform S4D on most standard sequence metrics and remain close on the rest.

Conclusion: Explicit delayed-state feedback is a viable and effective mechanism for enhancing long-range modeling in SSMs, addressing a fundamental limitation of fixed-size state compression without sacrificing performance on standard tasks.

Abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for efficient long-sequence modeling, offering parallel training and fast linear-time recurrent inference. However, like other recurrent architectures, SSMs must compress an unbounded history into a fixed-size state, which limits context retention and makes precise retrieval over long-range context inherently difficult. To overcome this limitation, we propose Delay State Space Models (DSSMs), a delay differential equation (DDE)-inspired extension of diagonal SSMs that augments discrete SSM recurrences with explicit delayed-state feedback. Making explicit delayed feedback practical requires new stability parameterization, history management, and FFT-training tools. We address these challenges with a practical discretization and parameterization grounded in a simple delay-independent stability condition. To bypass direct time-domain kernel construction, we derive the DSSM transfer function and compute kernels in the frequency domain, using a kernel contour shift to suppress aliasing and recover accurate FFT training. Empirically, DSSMs substantially improve targeted delayed-retrieval tasks while outperforming S4D on most standard sequence metrics and remaining close on the others.

</details>


### [290] [Data-Driven Telecom Marketing Optimization: A Machine Learning-Based Churn Prediction and Customer Segmentation Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10260)
*Nada Ali,Lina Ahmed,Tahani Abdalla Attia Gasmalla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A data-driven marketing framework combining gradient boosting churn prediction (CatBoost selected), K-Means customer segmentation by value, and segment-specific ROI strategies, operationalized via a Streamlit web app, using the IBM Telco dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Telecom companies rely on generic retention programs that fail to identify high-risk customers with precision. There is a need for personalized, data-driven marketing that integrates churn risk with customer value to enable profitable, targeted interventions.

Method: Using the IBM Telco dataset (7043 customers, 21 features), three gradient boosting ensembles (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) were trained with stratified 5-fold CV, class weighting, and F1-driven threshold optimization to address 73.4%/26.6% class imbalance. CatBoost was selected (77.68% accuracy, F1 0.6366, PR AUC 0.6553, ROC AUC 0.8403). K-Means clustering (Elbow-validated, PCA-visualized) segmented customers into High/Medium/Low Value tiers, cross-tabulated with churn risk labels to form four actionable clusters. Segment-specific retention, upsell, and engagement strategies were designed, with a theoretical ROI/CLV framework. The pipeline was deployed as an interactive Streamlit app with SHAP explainability and automated reporting.

Result: CatBoost achieved 77.68% accuracy, F1 0.6366, PR AUC 0.6553, and ROC AUC 0.8403 on the held-out test set. Customer segmentation yielded four actionable clusters combining value tiers and churn risk, each with tailored marketing strategies. The Streamlit app enables upload, filtering, SHAP visualization, and automated report generation.

Conclusion: Combining predictive churn modeling with value-aware segmentation produces more actionable and profitable marketing decisions than churn prediction alone.

Abstract: Customer churn is a major challenge for telecommunication companies, directly eroding revenue and long term customer relationships. Traditional retention programs rely on generic, not personalized incentives and lack the precision to identify high risk customers before they leave. This paper presents a data driven marketing optimization framework integrating machine learning based churn prediction, customer segmentation combining churn risk with customer value, and tailored, segment specific marketing and Return on Investment ROI strategies. Using the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset with 7043 customers and 21 features, three gradient boosting ensembles, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, were trained and tuned via randomized search with stratified 5 fold cross validation, class weighting, and F1 score driven decision threshold optimization to counter a class imbalance of 73.4% versus 26.6%. CatBoost was selected as the deployment model, achieving 77.68% accuracy, an F1 score of 0.6366, a PR AUC of 0.6553, and a ROC AUC of 0.8403 on the held out test set. Customers were partitioned with K Means clustering, validated via the Elbow method and visualized with Principal Component Analysis, into High, Medium, and Low Value segments, cross tabulated against churn risk labels to define four actionable clusters. Segment specific retention, upsell, and engagement strategies were designed for each cluster, and a theoretical ROI and CLV framework quantifies the financial impact of the proposed interventions. The pipeline was operationalized in an interactive Streamlit web application allowing marketing teams to upload data, filter by segment, visualize churn drivers via SHAP, and download automated segment reports. Results confirm that combining predictive churn modeling with value aware segmentation yields more actionable and profitable marketing decisions than churn prediction alone.

</details>


### [291] [Sharper Analysis of Single-Loop Methods for Bilevel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10263)
*Yubo Zhou,Jun Shu,Luo Luo,Junmin Liu,Deyu Meng,Guang Dai,Haishan Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Decoupled Norm Analysis (DNA), a novel analytical framework that establishes sharper convergence guarantees for single-loop bilevel optimization methods. For AID, the rate improves from O(κ⁶/K) to O(κ⁵/K); for ITD, the asymptotic error bound improves from O(κ³) to O(κ²), matching the known lower bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There exists a gap between theoretical convergence guarantees and practical single-loop implementations of hypergradient-based bilevel optimization methods. Existing analyses yield suboptimal dependence on the condition number κ, failing to match known lower bounds, particularly for iterative differentiation (ITD).

Method: The authors introduce Decoupled Norm Analysis (DNA), an analytical framework that decouples the analysis of coupled variables in bilevel optimization. This framework is applied to sharpen the convergence analysis of two single-loop methods: approximate implicit differentiation (AID) and iterative differentiation (ITD).

Result: For AID, the convergence rate improves from O(κ⁶/K) to O(κ⁵/K). For ITD, the asymptotic error bound improves from O(κ³) to O(κ²), which exactly matches the known lower bound. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks validate these theoretical improvements.

Conclusion: The DNA framework successfully bridges the theory-practice gap in single-loop bilevel optimization by providing tighter, matching bounds. The improved rates suggest that single-loop methods are more efficient than previously believed, with implications for hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, and related applications.

Abstract: Bilevel optimization underpins many machine learning applications, including hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, neural architecture search, and reinforcement learning. While hypergradient-based methods have advanced significantly, a gap persists between theoretical guarantees and practical single-loop implementations required for efficiency. We bridge this gap by establishing sharper convergence results for single-loop approximate implicit differentiation (AID) and iterative differentiation (ITD) methods, leveraging our proposed analytical framework, decoupled norm analysis (DNA). For AID, we improve the convergence rate from $\mathcal{O}(κ^6/K)$ to $\mathcal{O}(κ^5/K)$, where $κ$ is the condition number of the inner-level problem. For ITD, we prove that the asymptotic error is $\mathcal{O}(κ^2)$, exactly matching the known lower bound and improving upon the previous $\mathcal{O}(κ^3)$ guarantee. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real tasks corroborate our theoretical findings.

</details>


### [292] [Interpreting learning dynamics of autoencoders: Transient scaling and emerging concepts of the Ising model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10285)
*Max Weinmann,Miriam Klopotek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using Ising model spin configurations, this study reveals that unsupervised autoencoders learn macroscopic variables through two distinct dynamical regimes—magnetization-dominated and energy-dominated—controlled by model depth, width, and learning rate. Deep models at moderate/fast rates arrest before reaching these regimes. A recursive-dynamic trajectory analysis shows prediction errors create universal flow-field topology, framing learning as a nonequilibrium process driven by data fluctuations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how unsupervised autoencoders, without embedded domain knowledge, learn macroscopic, theory-relevant variables from microscopic data, and to characterize the learning dynamics as a physically interpretable process.

Method: Autoencoders are trained on microscopic spin configurations from the Ising model. The authors quantify learning across multiple spatial (coarse-graining) scales, systematically vary hyperparameters (depth, width, learning rate), and introduce a novel recursive-dynamic trajectory analysis to track representation evolution during training.

Result: Two dynamical regimes emerge: (1) a transient magnetization-dominated regime with dynamical scaling and ordering-to-scale fluctuations, and (2) an energy-dominated regime that shifts resolution toward smaller scales. Deep models at moderate/fast learning rates arrest prematurely. Prediction errors induce flow fields that produce a common trajectory topology across all representation spaces.

Conclusion: Learning in autoencoders can be framed as a nonequilibrium process driven by fluctuations from training data and the optimizer. Intrinsic dynamical properties expose the effects of forced representation changes, providing an interpretive bridge between physical systems and the machine models that represent them.

Abstract: We study how unsupervised autoencoders trained on microscopic spin configurations from the Ising model learn macroscopic, theory-relevant variables underlying the data-generating process. Without embedding domain knowledge, we mimic a typical discovery setting: We quantify learning across multiple spatial (coarse-graining) scales and reveal two distinct dynamical regimes controlled by main hyperparameters (model depth, width, and learning rate) -- a magnetization-dominated regime and an energy-dominated regime characterized by trade-offs in their representation quality. The first regime is a transitory state exhibiting dynamical scaling and fluctuations that follow an ordering-to-scale; the second gradually shifts resolution towards smaller scales relevant for the energy representation. Deep models trained at moderate and fast rates become arrested before reaching these regimes. With a novel analysis of recursive-dynamic trajectories, we demonstrate that prediction errors induce flow fields that produce a common trajectory topology across all representation spaces. A dynamical viewpoint of learning is established in which intrinsic properties expose the effects of forced changes in representation during training. We utilize the intuition that learning operates as a process driven far from equilibrium by fluctuations from the training data and optimizer to provide an interpretive basis grounded in both the physical world and the machine models that represent it.

</details>


### [293] [Empowering Long-form Omni-modal Understanding with Robust Audio Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10299)
*Kaiying Yan,Luoyi Sun,Xiao Zhou,Weidi Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces AVDC, a large-scale audio-visual dataset with decoupled captions (visual-only, audio-only, joint AV), created via an automated annotation pipeline. It also presents AVDC-QA-CoT, a reasoning-focused QA dataset. A two-stage training paradigm (omni-modal pre-training followed by instruction tuning) yields consistent performance gains across video captioning, audio analysis, and omni-modal benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Comprehensive omni-modal understanding remains under-explored due to the scarcity of datasets with rich, explicitly aligned auditory cues. Existing vision-language models lack well-annotated data that disentangles visual and auditory semantics, limiting progress in true audio-visual reasoning.

Method: (1) An automated pipeline using off-the-shelf models to annotate videos with tripartite decoupled captions: visual-only (V), audio-only (A), and joint audio-visual (AV). (2) Construction of AVDC-QA-CoT, a Chain-of-Thought augmented question-answering dataset for audio-visual reasoning. (3) A two-stage training paradigm: omni-modal caption generation pre-training on AVDC, followed by instruction tuning on AVDC-QA-CoT.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse downstream tasks — including video captioning, audio-centric analysis, and omni-modal benchmarks — demonstrate consistent and significant performance gains, validating the efficacy of both the proposed datasets and the two-stage training strategy.

Conclusion: The AVDC dataset and AVDC-QA-CoT, coupled with the two-stage training paradigm, effectively advance omni-modal perception by explicitly disentangling visual and auditory semantics and fostering cross-modal reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Recent advances in large-scale multimodal models have drivenremarkable progress in vision-language tasks; however, comprehensiveomni-modal understanding remains under-explored, largely due to thescarcity of datasets with rich, explicitly aligned auditory cues. To bridgethis gap, we present AVDC (Audio-Visual Decoupled Captions), a large-scaledataset designed to disentangle visual and auditory semantics. Specifi-cally, we propose an automated pipeline that leverages off-the-shelf mod-els to annotate videos with tripartite captions: visual-only (V), audio-only (A), and joint audio-visual (AV). This decoupled structure explic-itly captures both modality-specific nuances and complex cross-modalinteractions. Building upon this, we introduce AVDC-QA-CoT, a Chain-of-Thought augmented question-answering dataset to foster audio-visualreasoning. To fully exploit these resources, we employ a two-stage train-ing paradigm: omni-modal caption generation pre-training on AVDC, fol-lowed by instruction tuning on AVDC-QA-CoT. Extensive experiments acrossdiverse downstream tasks, spanning video captioning, audio-centric anal-ysis, and omni-modal benchmarks, demonstrate consistent and signifi-cant performance gains, showing the efficacy of our proposed datasetsand training strategy in advancing omni-modal perception. Code anddataset are related on https://radiant0726.github.io/AVDC-web/.

</details>


### [294] [A Control Theory of Predictability in Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10362)
*Hanzhe You,Yonggang Zhang,Maohao Ran,Zhiqin Yang,Zhenyuan Zhang,Wei Xue,Jun Song,Xinmei Tian,Yike Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prediction error on held-out data is an unreliable proxy for planning performance in latent world models because planners query off-manifold states not covered by the training distribution. The authors reframe the objective as plan-cost discrepancy, prove it bounds planner suboptimality (unlike data-averaged error), and decompose it into an on-manifold spectral term and a dominant off-manifold divergence term.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current practice in latent world model training uses single- or multi-step rollout prediction error on held-out data as the optimization and model-selection criterion, implicitly assuming lower prediction error yields better downstream control. The authors identify a structural flaw in this assumption: planners roll out candidate actions that push states off the training manifold, so data-averaged error cannot govern control quality.

Method: The authors reframe the objective as the discrepancy between predicted and true plan-cost at the committed plan. They formally prove that planner suboptimality is bounded by twice this plan-cost discrepancy, while data-averaged prediction error neither bounds nor tracks it. Under a linear-control premise, they decompose the discrepancy into: (1) a small on-manifold residual priced by spectral non-normality of the latent transition operator, and (2) an off-manifold divergence term where actions carry states off the manifold — this term dominates and is not bounded by any data-averaged error. Synthetic experiments validate the pricing formulas, and latent MPC experiments across seeds confirm the decoupling empirically.

Result: Single-step validation error is essentially uncorrelated with control success across seeds, while a fidelity score computed on the planner-reachable measure reliably tracks control performance. The off-manifold divergence term dominates and is not captured by standard data-averaged metrics.

Conclusion: Model selection and training for latent world models should shift from data-averaged prediction error to metrics defined on the planner-reachable measure, as the structural off-manifold nature of planner queries renders the standard objective unreliable for governing control.

Abstract: Latent world models are trained to predict future states in a learned representation and are then deployed inside a planner that selects actions by simulating them forward. Current practice adopts the prediction error, the single- or multi-step rollout loss on held-out data, as the training and model-selection objective, on the assumption that a lower prediction error yields better control. We show that this assumption is unreliable for a structural reason: a planner does not query the model on the training distribution but on the states that its candidate actions reach, which generally leave the data manifold, so an error averaged over the data cannot by itself govern control. We therefore reframe the objective as the discrepancy between the predicted and the true plan-cost at the plan the planner commits to, and prove that the planner's suboptimality is bounded by twice this discrepancy, whereas the data-averaged prediction error neither bounds nor tracks it. Under a linear-control premise the discrepancy separates into two terms. The first is a small on-manifold residual, on which the predicted and true dynamics agree and which a spectral tax prices through the non-normality of the latent transition operator. The second is an off-manifold divergence, on which an action carries the state off the manifold and the two dynamics diverge; this divergence is the binding term and is bounded by no data-averaged error. Synthetic operators confirm the pricing formulas, and latent model-predictive control experiments confirm the decoupling: across seeds, the single-step validation error is essentially uncorrelated with control success, whereas a fidelity score on the planner-reachable measure tracks it.

</details>


### [295] [A Hyperbolic Neural Closure for M1 Radiation Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10364)
*Bongseok Kim,Jiahao Zhang,Johannes Krotz,Dinshaw Balsara,Ryan McClarren,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a hyperbolic neural closure for M1 radiative transfer that guarantees real eigenvalues by parameterizing the Jacobian via a symmetric matrix network and a convex entropy network, ensuring numerical stability in simulations while improving accuracy over classical closures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning closures for M1 radiative transfer can improve accuracy over analytic closures, but unconstrained learned closures may produce non-real characteristic speeds, causing numerical solver breakdown. A method is needed to guarantee hyperbolicity (real eigenvalues) of the resulting system.

Method: Instead of directly predicting closure terms, the Jacobian is parameterized through two neural networks: (1) a symmetric matrix network and (2) a strictly convex entropy network whose Hessian provides a positive definite symmetrizer. These are combined to produce a Jacobian similar to a symmetric matrix, guaranteeing real eigenvalues. The closure is then reconstructed via numerical integration of the learned Jacobian field along a prescribed path.

Result: The proposed closure achieves higher closure accuracy than classical analytic closures, improves solution accuracy, and remains stable in discontinuous Galerkin simulations for radiative transfer problems.

Conclusion: The hyperbolic neural closure successfully enforces the structural property of hyperbolicity in learned M1 closures, enabling stable and accurate radiation transfer simulations that outperform classical analytic closures.

Abstract: In radiation transfer simulations, an M1 method achieves substantial computational savings by replacing the full angular transport equation with a low-order moment system. Because this reduced system is not closed, a closure model is required to represent the unknown higher-order moments using lower-order moments. While machine learning (ML)-based closures can improve accuracy beyond classical analytic closures, unconstrained learned closures may produce non-real characteristic speeds and consequently cause numerical solver breakdown. To guarantee real eigenvalues of the Jacobian associated with ML closures, we propose a hyperbolic neural closure for the M1 radiative transfer system. Rather than directly predicting closure terms, we parameterize the Jacobian through two neural networks: (i) a symmetric matrix network and (ii) a strictly convex entropy network whose Hessian defines a positive definite symmetrizer. These components are combined to yield a Jacobian that is similar to a symmetric matrix, thereby ensuring real eigenvalues. The closure is then reconstructed by numerical integration of the learned Jacobian field along a prescribed integration path. Numerical experiments show that the proposed closure not only achieves higher closure accuracy than classical analytic closures, but also improves solution accuracy and remains stable in discontinuous Galerkin simulations for radiative transfer problems.

</details>


### [296] [Machine Learning-based Correlation of Charpy Impact Properties Between Sub-sized and Standard-sized Specimens for Nuclear Structural Materials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10412)
*Yugandhar Kasala Sreenivasulu,Isshu Lee,John W. Merickel,Fei Xu,Yalei Tang,Joshua E. Rittenhouse,Aleksandar Vakanski,Rongjie Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A machine learning framework is proposed to correlate Charpy impact test results between sub-sized and full-sized specimens, using temperature shift and scaled residual projection to align energy curves across the ductile-to-brittle transition region. Validated on 389 matched tests of SA533B steel, it achieves R² of 0.942 for USE and 0.892 for DBTT, outperforming conventional methods without requiring full-sized data during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing analytical correlation methods for converting sub-sized to full-sized Charpy impact results (per ASTM A370, BS 7910) suffer from limited accuracy and narrow applicability across materials, treatments, and geometries. This is especially critical in nuclear applications where spatial constraints and limited material volume force the use of sub-sized specimens.

Method: An ML-based framework that maps absorbed energy values across the full ductile-to-brittle transition region via (1) a temperature shift combined with scaled residual projection to align sub-sized data with full-sized response, and (2) fitting the resulting temperature-energy profiles with a hyperbolic tangent model to extract USE and DBTT. The framework does not require full-sized data at inference.

Result: Validated on 389 matched sub-sized/full-sized Charpy tests on SA533B steel, the ML approach achieves R² = 0.942 for upper shelf energy and R² = 0.892 for ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, significantly outperforming conventional analytical correlation methods.

Conclusion: The proposed ML framework provides a robust, accurate, and practical tool for correlating Charpy impact properties across specimen sizes, suitable for material surveillance programs, accelerated irradiation testing, and other small-specimen applications where full-sized data are unavailable.

Abstract: Reliable correlations of Charpy impact test results between sub-sized and full-sized specimens are essential for structural integrity assessments, particularly in nuclear applications, where spatial constraints and limited material volume restrict specimen size. Although standards such as ASTM A370 and BS 7910 provide guidance on conversion methodologies, and numerous analytical correlation methods have been proposed in prior studies, these approaches generally have limited accuracy and their applicability is often constrained to specific materials, treatment conditions, and specimen geometries. In this study, a Machine Learning (ML)-based framework is proposed for correlating Charpy impact properties across specimen sizes. The proposed approach maps absorbed energy values across the full ductile-to-brittle transition region by applying a temperature shift combined with scaled residual projection, to align sub-sized test data with full-sized response. From the resulting temperature-energy profiles, the correlated values for upper shelf energy (USE) and ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) are extracted by fitting data with a hyperbolic tangent model. The framework is validated using a dataset comprising 389 matched sub-sized and full-sized Charpy impact tests on SA533B steel. This ML-based approach demonstrates an improved correlation performance relative to conventional analytical methods, achieving R2 values of 0.942 for USE and 0.892 for DBTT. The trained ML models do not require access to full-sized Charpy data during inference, making this approach suitable for material surveillance programs, accelerated irradiation testing, and other applications involving small-size Charpy impact testing.

</details>


### [297] [Pitfalls of Administrative Censoring in Survival Models with Time-Indexed Inputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10466)
*Yanqi Xu,Hui Dai,Carlos Fernandez-Granda,Krzysztof J. Geras,Yiqiu Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies and characterizes "administrative-cutoff leakage," a failure mode in survival models where models inadvertently infer the calendar date of data acquisition from input features, thereby learning to predict available follow-up time rather than true event risk. The authors distinguish this from informative censoring and temporal risk shifts, propose detection methods, and demonstrate inflated discrimination metrics in both simulations and real mammography data. They recommend that datasets provide at least n years of potential follow-up after the latest input date for n-year prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In large retrospective clinical datasets, input data (images, labs, EHR snapshots) are collected over many calendar years and may contain subtle temporal signals (e.g., changes in devices, protocols, or documentation). When outcomes are observed only up to a fixed study end date, more recent records have less potential follow-up than older ones. A survival model that infers the record date can exploit this to predict how much follow-up was available, rather than true patient risk, producing spuriously inflated performance metrics and biased predictions.

Method: The authors (1) formally characterize the conditions under which administrative-cutoff leakage occurs, (2) distinguish it from informative censoring and genuine temporal shifts in baseline risk, (3) propose practical detection methods, (4) conduct simulation studies to quantify the impact on fixed-horizon AUC and Harrell's C-index under realistic follow-up patterns, and (5) validate findings in a real-world mammography cohort.

Result: Simulations demonstrate that administrative-cutoff leakage can artificially inflate both fixed-horizon AUC and Harrell's C-index under realistic follow-up patterns. The same behavior is confirmed in a real mammography cohort. The magnitude of bias depends on how strongly inputs encode temporal information and on the follow-up distribution.

Conclusion: The paper proposes a simple design principle: for an n-year prediction task, every record in the dataset should have at least n years of potential follow-up after its input date. Without this safeguard, survival models risk learning follow-up availability rather than true risk, yielding biased performance estimates and potentially flawed clinical decision support.

Abstract: Survival models can model time-to-event outcomes using partially observed data. They are widely used in clinical prediction, including cancer risk, disease progression, treatment response, and mortality. Recent models often rely on rich inputs collected at a specific clinical encounter, such as medical images, laboratory tests, electronic health record snapshots, or sensor measurements. In large retrospective datasets, these inputs are usually collected over many calendar years. As a result, they may contain clues about when they were acquired through changes in devices, protocols, documentation, patient mix, or clinical practice. This creates a potential failure mode when outcomes are observed only up to a fixed study end date. More recent records necessarily have less potential follow-up than older records. A model that can infer the record date from the input may therefore learn to predict how much follow-up was available rather than the patient's true risk of experiencing the event. We call this failure mode administrative-cutoff leakage. In this paper, we characterize when this leakage can occur, distinguish it from classical informative censoring and genuine temporal changes in risk, and propose practical ways to detect it. In simulations, we show that administrative-cutoff leakage can inflate fixed-horizon AUC and can also affect Harrell's C-index under realistic follow-up patterns. We then demonstrate the same behavior in a real mammography cohort. These results motivate a simple design principle for survival prediction: for an n-year prediction task, the dataset should provide at least n years of potential follow-up after the latest input date. Otherwise, the models may be subject to bias induced by administrative-cutoff leakage.

</details>


### [298] [Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Physics: Post-training LLMs with Continuous Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10474)
*Pengfei Cai,Utkarsh Utkarsh,Alan Edelman,Christopher Vincent Rackauckas,Rafael Gomez-Bombarelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLVP introduces a reinforcement learning framework for generating PDE solver code, using a hybrid verifier that combines binary program-validity checks with continuous physics-based accuracy rewards. Post-training a single policy across diverse PDE families improves solver generation, transfers zero-shot to held-out PDEs, and enables smaller models to outperform frontier LLMs on in-distribution tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based PDE solver generation operates only at inference time (prompting, debugging, self-refinement) without adapting the model. Meanwhile, RL with verifiable rewards for code/math uses only binary signals (compiles/passes), discarding the graded structure of scientific correctness where two executable solvers can differ in accuracy by orders of magnitude.

Method: RLVP (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Physics) post-trains an LLM policy with a hybrid verifier: (1) hard program-validity checks for executability, and (2) continuous physics rewards that score function-space accuracy and PDE-residual consistency. A single policy is RL post-trained across multiple PDE families (hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic, incompressible flow).

Result: RLVP outperforms pre-trained and supervised-only baselines on PDE benchmarks, exhibits zero-shot improvement transfer to held-out PDEs, and a smaller RLVP-post-trained LLM surpasses frontier-model prompting on in-distribution solver generation. The policy additionally shows compositional generalization, recombining learned numerical motifs (stencils, time-stepping schemes, boundary primitives) for unseen PDEs.

Conclusion: RL post-training with continuous, physics-grounded verifiers is a viable and effective paradigm for scientific code generation, bridging the gap between binary code verification and the graded nature of numerical accuracy in computational science.

Abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are foundational to modeling in science and engineering, but constructing reliable numerical solvers remains labor-intensive, demanding expert knowledge of discretization schemes, stability conditions, and boundary treatments. Recent work has begun to frame PDE solving as a code-generation task for large language models (LLMs), yet existing approaches operate primarily at inference time: relying on prompting, debugging, self-refinement, and test-time scaling rather than adapting the model itself. In parallel, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has emerged as a post-training paradigm for code and math reasoning, but its verifiers are typically binary: a compiler runs, or a test passes. Such signals discard the graded structure of scientific correctness, where two solvers may both execute and yet differ in solution accuracy by orders of magnitude. In this work, we introduce RLVP: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Physics, an RL post-training framework for multi-PDE solver code generation. RLVP addresses this verifiability gap with a hybrid verifier: hard program-validity checks ensure executability, while continuous physics rewards score function-space accuracy and PDE-residual consistency. A single policy is post-trained across diverse PDE families spanning hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic, and incompressible-flow systems. RLVP improves over both pre-trained and supervised-only baselines on PDE benchmarks, and shows zero-shot improvement transfer to held-out PDEs. We show that a smaller LLM post-trained with RLVP can outperform prompting a frontier model on in-distribution PDE solver generation. The trained policy shows evidence of compositionality in numerical motifs: it recombines stencils, time-stepping schemes, and boundary-handling primitives learned from the PDEs used in training into generated solvers for unseen PDE problems.

</details>


### [299] [ARMOR: Stabilizing On-Policy LLM RL with Off-Policy Anchor Samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10481)
*Kexin Huang,Junkang Wu,Jinda Lu,Shuo Yang,Chiyu Ma,Jiancan Wu,Xiang Wang,Xiangnan He,Guoyin Wang,Jingren Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RL training for LLM reasoning suffers from over-optimization instability. Standard reverse KL regularization is insufficient because it fails to cover the reference distribution comprehensively. The authors propose ARMOR, combining Anchor Rollout (off-policy data from the reference policy) and Mixed Optimization (reformulated objective for controlled exploration), which mitigates validation collapse and sustains performance over long training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-based reasoning training for LLMs is notoriously fragile due to over-optimization, where models exploit training heuristics rather than learning generalizable reasoning. Existing defenses like reverse KL regularization are often inadequate because they do not ensure comprehensive coverage of the reference distribution.

Method: ARMOR (Anchor Rollout and Mixed Optimization for RL) consists of two components: (1) Anchor Rollout — uses off-policy data sampled from the reference policy to preserve established solution patterns and maintain coverage of the reference distribution; (2) Mixed Optimization — reformulates the policy objective to enable controlled exploration, eliminating the need for auxiliary loss terms.

Result: Extensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ARMOR effectively mitigates validation collapse and enables sustained performance improvements over extended training horizons, outperforming standard reverse KL regularization approaches.

Conclusion: ARMOR shifts the paradigm from passive penalty-based regularization to active sample stabilization, providing a more robust solution to over-optimization in RL-based LLM reasoning training and enabling longer, more stable training runs with continued gains.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet the training process remains notoriously fragile. In this work, we investigate a critical source of this instability: over-optimization, where models exploit training heuristics at the expense of generalizable reasoning. While reverse KL regularization is the standard defense against such degradation, our analysis reveals that it is often insufficient in this regime, as it fails to ensure comprehensive coverage of the reference distribution. To address this, we propose ARMOR (Anchor Rollout and Mixed Optimization for RL), a framework that shifts the paradigm from passive penalty to active sample stabilization. ARMOR comprises two key components: (1) Anchor Rollout, which leverages off-policy data from the reference policy to preserve established solution patterns; and (2) Mixed Optimization, which reformulates the policy objective to enable controlled exploration without relying on auxiliary losses. Extensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks validate that ARMOR effectively mitigates validation collapse, enabling sustained performance improvements over extended training horizons.

</details>


### [300] [EvidentialRAG: Quantifying and Mitigating Information Conflict in Multi-Source Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Evidential Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10491)
*S M Asif Hossain,Ruksat Khan Shayoni,M. F. Mridha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ERAG introduces uncertainty-aware retrieval-augmented generation by converting retrieved chunks into probabilistic evidence using Dirichlet distributions and Dempster-Shafer fusion, enabling a generator to answer, resolve conflicts, or abstain based on epistemic uncertainty. It reduces hallucination and improves conflict resolution on ambiguous queries compared to deterministic RAG baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG pipelines treat retrieved passages as deterministic and mutually consistent, ignoring real-world disagreements caused by temporal drift, source error, ambiguity, or genuine uncertainty. This leads to hallucination or overconfident answers when sources conflict.

Method: ERAG uses three components: (1) a lightweight evaluator that extracts candidate claims from chunks and maps support to Dirichlet evidence distributions; (2) a conflict-preserving Dempster-Shafer fusion rule that combines evidence while retaining unresolved disagreement as epistemic uncertainty (rather than normalizing it away); and (3) a generator routed to one of three modes — direct answering, conflict-aware answering, or abstention — based on the fused uncertainty score.

Result: On CRAG's ambiguous subset, ERAG reduced hallucination from 45.3% (Corrective RAG) to 34.8%, increased conflict resolution from 35.2% to 51.2%, and achieved an expected calibration error of 0.122. It remained competitive with the strongest matched baseline on standard QA tasks (ConflictQA, MuSiQue).

Conclusion: Evidential modeling via Dirichlet evidence and Dempster-Shafer fusion is a practical mechanism for making foundation-model retrieval systems more trustworthy, particularly under information conflict.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds large language models in external evidence, but most pipelines still treat retrieved passages as deterministic and mutually consistent context. In open information environments, retrieved sources may disagree because of temporal drift, source error, ambiguity, or genuine uncertainty. This paper introduces ERAG, an uncertainty-aware RAG framework that converts retrieved chunks into probabilistic evidence before generation. A lightweight evaluator extracts candidate claims and maps chunk-level support to Dirichlet evidence. A conflict-preserving Dempster-Shafer fusion rule then transfers unresolved disagreement into epistemic uncertainty rather than normalizing it away. The generator is routed to direct answering, conflict-aware answering, or abstention according to the fused uncertainty score. Experiments on CRAG, ConflictQA, and MuSiQue show that ERAG remains competitive with the strongest matched baseline on standard question answering while improving behavior under conflict. On the CRAG ambiguous subset, hallucination decreases from 45.3% for Corrective RAG to a human-calibrated estimate of 34.8%, conflict resolution increases from 35.2% to 51.2%, and expected calibration error improves to 0.122. These results suggest that evidential modeling is a practical mechanism for trustworthy information processing in foundation-model-based retrieval systems.

</details>


### [301] [Learning from Noise: Effective-Rank Collapse and Out-of-Distribution Rejection in Restricted Boltzmann Machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10506)
*Oshada Rathnayake,Nikhil Shukla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RBMs fail under OOD inputs by absorbing them into learned class basins. The paper shows that training with auxiliary random binary images assigned to a rejection label causes the effective rank of the visible–visible interaction matrix J=WW^T to collapse toward that of the data covariance matrix, depleting weak bulk modes and enabling structured OOD rejection while preserving MNIST accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Restricted Boltzmann Machines used discriminatively are brittle under out-of-distribution inputs — OOD samples get absorbed into learned class basins rather than being rejected. The authors aim to understand this failure mode through spectral analysis of the induced interaction matrix and to develop a principled remedy.

Method: The authors analyze the spectrum of the visible–visible interaction matrix J=WW^T, using the Marchenko–Pastur random-matrix distribution as a reference. They introduce a training procedure where auxiliary random binary images are assigned to a rejection label, then study how this affects the eigenspectrum, effective rank, and free-energy landscape of the RBM.

Result: Conventional training spreads spectral weight into many weak, bulk-compatible directions, inflating the effective rank of J. Adding random auxiliary rejection data causes effective-rank collapse: weak bulk modes are depleted, spectral weight concentrates into fewer dominant eigendirections, and the effective rank approaches that of the empirical data covariance matrix. The resulting RBM successfully rejects structured OOD image datasets while maintaining MNIST classification accuracy.

Conclusion: Random auxiliary exposure reshapes both the interaction spectrum and the free-energy landscape of energy-based classifiers, providing a spectral mechanism for robust OOD rejection. The effective-rank collapse toward the data covariance rank serves as a diagnostic for when an RBM will generalize appropriately to unknown inputs.

Abstract: Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) represent data by shaping an energy landscape over visible and hidden configurations, but their discriminative use is fragile under out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs: samples outside the training distribution can be absorbed into one of the learned class basins rather than rejected. Here, we analyze this failure mode through the spectrum of the induced visible--visible interaction $J=WW^{T}$, where \(W\) is the visible--hidden weight matrix. Relative to a Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix reference, conventional training spreads spectral weight into many weak, bulk-compatible directions, increasing the effective rank of $J$. When auxiliary random binary images are assigned to a rejection label during training, the learned interaction undergoes effective-rank collapse: weak bulk-like modes are depleted, spectral weight concentrates into fewer dominant eigendirections, and the effective rank of $J$ approaches that of the empirical data covariance matrix. The resulting RBM rejects structured OOD image datasets while preserving MNIST classification accuracy, showing that random auxiliary exposure can reshape both the interaction spectrum and the free-energy landscape of an energy-based classifier.

</details>


### [302] [Conditional Optimal Bridge for Riemannian Activation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10517)
*Seyed Arshan Dalili,Ajay Narayanan Sridhar,Vijaykrishnan Narayanan,Mehrdad Mahdavi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cobras reformulates activation steering as a Schrödinger Bridge on the residual-stream hypersphere, yielding the first principled derivation of the log-density-ratio objective via entropic optimal transport. The resulting steering directions are query-adaptive, outperforming baselines across four models and three alignment axes while avoiding OOD degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing activation steering methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) they optimize a log-density-ratio objective heuristically rather than deriving it from a principled optimization framework, and (2) they produce query-independent steering directions that degrade performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs.

Method: The authors cast activation steering as a Schrödinger Bridge problem on the residual-stream hypersphere. They solve this bridge via entropic optimal transport and extract the probability flow ODE. This recovers the widely used density-ratio gradient as a special case when Sinkhorn potentials are uniform. The key novelty is that the Schrödinger potentials are evaluated at the current activation, making steering directions inherently query-adaptive.

Result: Across four models and three alignment axes (helpfulness, truthfulness, detoxification), Cobras consistently outperforms prior activation steering baselines while avoiding the OOD degradation commonly observed in existing methods.

Conclusion: Cobras provides a theoretically grounded, query-adaptive alternative to heuristic activation steering methods, offering consistent performance gains and robustness to distribution shift.

Abstract: Activation steering offers a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language models at inference time. While many existing methods implicitly optimize a log-density-ratio objective between desired and undesired activation distributions, they do so heuristically rather than deriving it from a principled optimization problem. Moreover, these methods produce query-independent steering directions that can degrade performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. We introduce \textsc{Cobras} (Conditional Optimal Bridge for Riemannian Activation Steering), which addresses both limitations by casting activation steering as a Schrödinger Bridge on the residual-stream hypersphere. This formulation yields, to our knowledge, the first principled derivation of the log-density-ratio steering objective from a well-posed optimization problem. Solving the bridge via entropic optimal transport and extracting the probability flow ODE recovers the widely used density-ratio gradient as a special case when the Sinkhorn potentials are uniform. Crucially, the Schrödinger potentials are evaluated at the current activation, making the resulting steering direction inherently query-adaptive. Empirically, across four models and three alignment axes (helpfulness, truthfulness, and detoxification), \textsc{Cobras} consistently outperforms prior activation steering baselines while avoiding the OOD degradation commonly observed in existing methods. The code can be found at https://github.com/arshandalili/cobras.

</details>


### [303] [LLM-PDESR: Robust PDE Discovery via Subdomain Weighted Residuals and LLM-Guided Symbolic Hypothesis Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10546)
*Jinyang Du,Hao Ma,Xiaohu Shi,Bo Yang,Yanchun Liang,Heow Pueh Lee,Chunguo Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM-PDESR integrates LLM-based hypothesis generation with C⁴-continuous quintic splines and subdomain weighted residuals to discover governing PDEs from noisy data. A Pareto-driven feedback loop refines candidate equations, balancing accuracy and parsimony. The framework outperforms existing methods on 28 PDEs, including novel equations designed to prevent memorization, and successfully extracts interpretable dynamics from ERA5 climate reanalysis data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional symbolic regression for PDE discovery suffers from two critical bottlenecks: (1) inability to incorporate domain-specific prior knowledge within vast combinatorial search spaces, and (2) reliance on pointwise evaluations and discrete finite differences that amplify high-frequency noise, creating deceptive fitness landscapes that derail optimization. These limitations motivate an approach that combines the inductive reasoning capabilities of LLMs with mathematically rigorous numerical methods for robust differentiation and evaluation.

Method: LLM-PDESR comprises three key components: (1) an LLM-driven structural hypothesis generator that proposes candidate PDE forms, leveraging domain knowledge; (2) a mathematically rigorous evaluation environment using C⁴-continuous quintic splines for robust numerical differentiation and subdomain weighted residuals as natural low-pass filters to suppress noise amplification; and (3) a Pareto-driven feedback loop that iteratively refines candidates by balancing predictive accuracy against structural parsimony, mitigating equation bloat and spurious complexity.

Result: Evaluated on 23 canonical PDEs and 5 structurally novel equations (including a multivariate system) specifically designed to preclude dataset memorization. The framework successfully extracts a consistent structural skeleton for an interpretable 1D dynamical surrogate (1D-CACE) from noisy ERA5 reanalysis data. Out-of-distribution testing confirms significant outperformance over state-of-the-art methods in structural recovery, noise resilience, and avoidance of spurious complexity and equation bloat.

Conclusion: The integration of LLM-based structural reasoning with rigorous spline-based numerical methods and Pareto-driven refinement offers a robust, generalizable framework for PDE discovery from noisy observational data. The approach demonstrates both strong benchmark performance and real-world applicability on climate data, suggesting a promising direction for data-driven scientific discovery where noise resilience and structural interpretability are paramount.

Abstract: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from noisy observational data is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning. Traditional symbolic regression (SR) methods often struggle to identify accurate equations within vast combinatorial search spaces, largely due to their inability to incorporate essential domain-specific prior knowledge. Furthermore, reliance on pointwise evaluations and discrete finite differences inherently amplifies high-frequency noise, creating deceptive fitness landscapes that derail the optimization process. To resolve these bottlenecks, we propose LLM-PDESR, a framework that integrates the structural hypothesis generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) with a mathematically rigorous evaluation environment. By employing C^4-continuous quintic splines for robust differentiation and subdomain weighted residuals as natural low-pass filters, our approach effectively mitigates the fitness landscape distortion that plagues existing methods. A Pareto-driven feedback loop then enables the LLM to iteratively refine candidate equations, balancing predictive accuracy with structural parsimony. We evaluate LLM-PDESR on 23 canonical PDEs and five structurally novel equations (including a multivariate system) specifically designed to preclude dataset memorization and test true discovery capabilities. Demonstrating real-world applicability, the framework successfully extracts a consistent structural skeleton for an interpretable 1D dynamical surrogate (1D-CACE) directly from noisy ERA5 reanalysis data. Extensive experiments and out-of-distribution testing confirm that LLM-PDESR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methodologies in structural recovery, noise resilience, and the avoidance of spurious complexity and equation bloat.

</details>


### [304] [Learning from Local Walks on Dynamic Graphs with Bandit Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10571)
*Sourav Chakraborty,Amit Kiran Rege,Claire Monteleoni,Lijun Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies stochastic multi-armed bandits on time-varying graphs where the learner can only move locally. It identifies a sliding-window mixing condition ensuring stable navigation, analyzes local explore-then-commit algorithms, and proves sublinear regret with both safety and performance guarantees for a reward-aware strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many real-world applications (e.g., mobile sensor networks, robotic exploration, dynamic social networks), the learner's access to arms is constrained by an evolving graph topology. This creates a fundamental decoupling between identifying the optimal arm and physically reaching it — a challenge not addressed by classical bandit models. The work aims to characterize when and how effective learning is still possible under such dynamic, locality-constrained settings.

Method: The authors introduce a process-agnostic structural condition called sliding-window mixing, which ensures the time-varying graph's random walk process remains sufficiently stable over sliding time windows for both exploration and exploitation. Under this condition, they analyze a family of local explore-then-commit (ETC) algorithms: the learner first explores by performing a random walk to gather reward estimates, then commits to navigating toward the empirically best arm. One variant is reward-aware, adaptively adjusting the exploration-commitment tradeoff based on observed rewards.

Result: The authors prove that under the sliding-window mixing condition, the proposed local ETC algorithms achieve sublinear expected regret. For the reward-aware strategy specifically, they establish two key theorems: (1) a worst-case safety theorem guaranteeing bounded regret even under adversarial graph dynamics, and (2) a performance gain theorem showing that the reward-aware variant strictly improves over reward-agnostic baselines when reward gaps are large.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sublinear regret is achievable in dynamic-graph bandits under a mild, structural mixing condition, despite the decoupling of arm identification and reachability. The reward-aware strategy provides a principled way to balance exploration and commitment, offering both safety and improved performance. This framework opens the door to bandit learning in broader classes of constrained, time-varying environments.

Abstract: We study stochastic multi-armed bandits on dynamic graphs, where arms correspond to the vertices of a network with time-varying edges. In this setting, the learner is restricted to local movement, selecting only its current node or an immediate neighbor at each round. This constraint decouples best-arm identification from exploitation: even after the optimal arm is identified, the learner may remain unable to reach it through the evolving topology. We identify a process-agnostic structural condition, based on sliding-window mixing, that ensures the graph's intrinsic walk remains stable for both exploration and navigation. Under this regime, we analyze a family of local explore-then-commit algorithms and establish sublinear expected regret. Our framework includes a reward-aware strategy, for which we prove a worst-case safety theorem and a separate performance gain theorem.

</details>


### [305] [MemDecay: Region-Aware KV Cache Eviction for Efficient LLM Agent Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10582)
*Venkatesha Matam,Keon Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MemDecay is a training-free, region-aware KV-cache eviction policy for LLM agents that assigns tokens region-specific priorities and decay rates based on semantic structure (e.g., system instructions vs. scratchpad), preserving critical information under fixed cache budgets. Experiments with Qwen2.5 models show system tokens have ~10× longer attention half-lives than scratchpad tokens, and region-aware pinning preserves system facts at full-cache accuracy while recency-based baselines collapse at longer contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents accumulate heterogeneous context from multiple sources (system instructions, user turns, tool outputs, retrieved documents, reasoning traces), causing KV-cache memory bottlenecks. Existing eviction policies apply uniform attention- or recency-based rules to every token, ignoring the semantic structure already known to the orchestrator. The authors argue this structural information should be exploited for smarter cache management.

Method: MemDecay assigns each token a region-specific base priority and exponential decay rate, refreshes retention scores when tokens receive attention, and evicts lowest-scoring KV-cache pages under a fixed budget. Critical regions (e.g., system prompts) can be pinned. The method includes a calibration procedure that estimates decay rates from empirically measured attention lifetimes per region. Evaluated on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B at ~450 and ~1,700 token contexts.

Result: (1) Attention lifetimes differ by an order of magnitude across regions: system-token half-lives range 148–189 decoding steps vs. 14–16 for scratchpad tokens. (2) Pinning preserves system-region facts at full-cache accuracy across all settings; no baseline preserves more than 13 of 24 facts. (3) Region-aware retention remains effective as context grows, while recency-based retention collapses. (4) Accumulated-attention retention performs better on unpinned content, with ablations identifying attention-score normalization as the main limitation of MemDecay's current formulation.

Conclusion: Semantic prompt structure is a robust signal for KV-cache management in LLM agents. Region-aware eviction substantially outperforms uniform policies, particularly for preserving critical facts in pinned regions. However, the best overall strategy should combine region-awareness with attention-based importance, as the latter better handles unpinned content. The authors identify attention-score normalization as the key limitation to address in future work.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents accumulate heterogeneous context, including system instructions, plans, user turns, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and intermediate reasoning, whose key-value (KV) cache can become a major memory bottleneck. Existing eviction policies generally apply the same attention- or recency-based rule to every token, ignoring semantic structure already available to the agent orchestrator.
  We introduce MemDecay, a training-free, region-aware KV-cache eviction policy. MemDecay assigns tokens region-specific base priorities and decay rates, refreshes retention scores when tokens receive attention, and evicts the lowest-scoring pages under a fixed cache budget while allowing critical regions to be pinned. We also provide a procedure for calibrating decay rates from measured attention lifetimes.
  We evaluate MemDecay at approximately 450 and 1,700 token contexts using Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B. Across all settings, attention lifetimes differ by an order of magnitude across regions: system-token half-lives range from 148 to 189 decoding steps, compared with 14 to 16 for scratchpad tokens. Pinning preserves system-region facts at full-cache accuracy in every setting, while no baseline preserves more than 13 of 24. Region-aware retention remains effective as context grows, whereas recency-based retention collapses. Accumulated-attention retention performs better on unpinned content, however, and ablations identify attention-score normalization as the main limitation of the current formulation. These results establish semantic prompt structure as a robust signal for KV-cache management while clarifying how it should be combined with attention-based importance.

</details>


### [306] [Sharp Concentration Bounds for Bundle-Valued Statistics on Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10592)
*Swagatam Das,Vaclav Snasel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Develops non-asymptotic concentration theory for empirical means of fiber-valued observations on manifolds, where transport to a common reference fiber introduces curvature- and holonomy-driven effects. Derives Hoeffding/Bernstein-type bounds, quantifies a deterministic holonomy bias from path-dependent transport, and establishes a bias-variance decomposition with a curvature-driven error floor. Validated experimentally on spheres.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many geometric statistics and manifold learning pipelines produce observations (tangent vectors, local frames) that live in varying fibers over different base points rather than a single vector space. Classical concentration theory assumes a shared vector space, so it fails to account for curvature and holonomy effects introduced when transporting these observations to a common reference fiber for empirical averaging. The work aims to fill this gap by developing concentration inequalities that explicitly incorporate geometric structure.

Method: The authors derive finite-sample, dimension-free Hoeffding- and Bernstein-type concentration bounds using sharp Hilbert-space inequalities applied to transported empirical means. They characterize path-dependent transport when shortest paths are non-unique, isolating a deterministic holonomy bias expressed through bundle curvature and loop geometry, with closed-form formulas for the round sphere's tangent bundle. They prove a bias-variance decomposition separating stochastic fluctuation (decaying at rate n^{-1/2}) from an irreducible curvature-driven error floor, confirmed via minimax lower bounds. They further propose a robust median-of-means estimator for heavy-tailed settings and establish a CLT in the reference fiber.

Result: The theory yields dimension-free Hoeffding and Bernstein bounds that explicitly quantify curvature and holonomy effects. The bias-variance decomposition reveals a curvature-driven error floor that no amount of additional data can eliminate, with minimax lower bounds confirming both the stochastic and geometric terms are unavoidable. The median-of-means estimator achieves optimal rates under heavy tails. All predictions are validated through controlled experiments on the sphere.

Conclusion: Concentration theory for fiber-valued data on manifolds must account for geometry-induced bias from transport. The curvature-driven error floor is a fundamental limitation — it cannot be overcome by increasing sample size. The robust median-of-means estimator and CLT provide practical tools for inference in geometric statistics pipelines.

Abstract: Many geometric statistics and manifold learning pipelines routinely produce observations -- such as tangent vectors or local frames -- whose natural home is a varying family of fibers attached to different points of a base manifold, rather than a single shared vector space. Forming empirical averages requires transporting these observations to a common reference fiber, thereby introducing curvature- and holonomy-driven effects that are absent from classical concentration theory. We develop a non-asymptotic concentration theory for such transported empirical means, deriving finite-sample, dimension-free Hoeffding- and Bernstein-type bounds via sharp Hilbert-space inequalities. When shortest paths to the reference point are non-unique, transport becomes path-dependent and introduces a deterministic holonomy bias; we isolate and quantify this bias through bundle curvature and loop geometry, with sharp closed-form formulas for the tangent bundle of a round sphere. The resulting bias-variance decomposition separates the stochastic fluctuation decaying at the classical $n^{-1/2}$ rate in sample size $n$, from a curvature-driven error floor that no amount of additional data can eliminate; minimax lower bounds confirm both terms are unavoidable. We further establish a robust median-of-means estimator achieving optimal rates under heavy tails and the central limit theorem in the reference fiber. Controlled experiments on the sphere validate all theoretical predictions.

</details>


### [307] [AutoNorm: Understanding Adaptive Normalization in Transformers through Differentiable Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10593)
*Piyush Kaushik Bhattacharyya,Divyanshu Rai,Swastik Singh,Kumar Aakash,Ayush Ranjan,Krutika Verma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Investigates optimization instability in Gumbel-Softmax-based differentiable normalization gating for Transformers. Proposes AutoNorm-S, a gate-freezing schedule that mitigates gradient variance, achieving strong NLP performance while maintaining competitiveness on vision tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Differentiable normalization gating using Gumbel-Softmax suffers from high gradient variance that hinders convergence on stationary vision tasks, causing learned gates to underperform random selection. The authors aim to understand and resolve this optimization challenge to enable robust adaptive normalization across diverse task types.

Method: The authors first diagnose the problem through experiments comparing stationary (vision) vs. non-stationary (language) tasks, identifying gradient variance from Gumbel-Softmax as the root cause of poor routing convergence. They then propose AutoNorm-S (Stabilized), which introduces a gate-freezing schedule: normalization selection gates are progressively frozen during training to decouple routing decisions from ongoing optimization noise, thereby stabilizing the learning of per-layer normalization policies.

Result: AutoNorm-S achieves competitive or improved performance across benchmarks. On NLP datasets (PTB, SST-2), it outperforms adaptive normalization baselines. On standard vision benchmarks, it remains competitive without degradation. The results validate that decoupling normalization selection from optimization noise is effective.

Conclusion: Decoupling normalization selection from optimization noise via gate freezing is a practical and principled strategy for adaptive normalization in Transformers. The approach bridges the gap between static (e.g., LayerNorm) and adaptive normalization methods across both vision and language domains.

Abstract: Normalization is a critical component for stabilizing Transformer training, yet the choice between static strategies such as Layer Normalization (LN) and adaptive alternatives remains largely task-dependent. In this paper, we investigate a key optimization challenge in differentiable normalization gating. Our experiments show that, on relatively stationary vision tasks, the high gradient variance introduced by Gumbel-Softmax gating can hinder convergence of the routing mechanism, causing learned gates to underperform simple random selection. In contrast, on non-stationary language modeling and classification tasks, sustained gating diversity enables the model to learn more effective layer-wise normalization policies. Motivated by these observations, we propose AutoNorm-S (Stabilized), a training strategy that mitigates optimization instability through a gate-freezing schedule. AutoNorm-S achieves competitive or improved performance across multiple benchmarks, outperforming adaptive normalization baselines on NLP datasets, including PTB and SST-2, while remaining competitive on standard vision benchmarks. These results suggest that decoupling normalization selection from optimization noise provides a practical and principled approach for adaptive normalization in Transformer architectures.

</details>

### [308] [Transfer Learning Across Policy Regimes in Adaptive Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09685)
*Roberto Garrone*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Policy-outcome relationships can shift after regulatory change. This paper models regime change as transfer learning in multi-agent systems, showing that reusing structural knowledge from prior regimes helps when the policy-outcome mapping is preserved, but harms when it introduces misspecification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard policy models assume stable mappings between instruments and outcomes across institutional conditions. In adaptive socio-technical systems, regulatory change can alter incentives, strategic behavior, and the policy-outcome relationship itself — violating this assumption. The paper addresses the question of when prior regulatory experience should be reused versus discarded.

Method: The authors formalize a policy regime as a learning problem with an observable input distribution and a target function mapping policy variables to outcomes. They compare two learners: a blank-slate learner using a flexible hypothesis class in the new regime, and a transfer learner whose hypothesis class is constrained by structural knowledge from the previous regime. Transfer is beneficial when the constraint preserves the true target function while reducing effective complexity; it is harmful when the constraint excludes the target (misspecification). Validation uses a stylized emissions-regulation environment and a dynamic agent-based model robustness experiment.

Result: When the target regime preserves an affine monotone tax-emissions relationship, transfer learning improves empirical small-sample performance. When the target regime introduces a threshold break, the same transferred structure produces negative transfer: held-out error remains high, online prediction generates more mistakes, and repeated online streams show larger cumulative and final-window error under misspecification.

Conclusion: Prior regulatory experience should be reused when it captures stable structural invariants in the policy-outcome relationship, but treated cautiously — or discarded — when policy change fundamentally alters that relationship. The contribution is methodological, providing a transfer-learning lens for reasoning about regime change in policy design.

Abstract: Policy models often assume that the relationship between a policy instrument and its outcome remains stable across institutional conditions. In adaptive socio-technical systems this assumption may fail: regulatory change can alter incentives, agents can respond strategically, and the mapping from policy variables to aggregate outcomes can change. This paper studies such regime change as a transfer-learning problem in adaptive multi-agent systems. A policy regime is represented as a learning problem induced by an observable input distribution and a target function mapping policy variables to outcomes. We compare a blank-slate learner that searches a flexible hypothesis class in the new regime with a transfer learner whose effective hypothesis class is restricted by structural knowledge from the previous regime. Transfer is beneficial when this restriction preserves the new target function while reducing effective complexity; it is harmful when the restriction excludes the new target and creates misspecification. A stylized emissions-regulation experimental environment and a dynamic ABM robustness experiment support the claim. When the target regime preserves an affine monotone tax-emissions relation, transfer improves empirical small-sample performance. When the target regime introduces a threshold break, the same transferred structure produces negative transfer: held-out error remains high, online prediction generates more mistakes, and repeated online streams show larger cumulative and final-window error under misspecification. The contribution is methodological: previous regulatory experience should be reused when it captures stable structural invariants, but treated cautiously when policy change alters the policy-outcome relationship.

</details>


### [309] [RideGym: A Standardized Interface for Real-World Large-Scale Ride-Sharing System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10173)
*Zijian Zhao,Yulong Hu,Sen Li*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: RideGym is the first open-source, standardized Gym-style interface for MARL-based ride-sharing order dispatch, decoupling environment from algorithm to enable reproducible, fair benchmarking on real road networks at city scale, while revealing that exploration noise significantly impacts MARL performance and ranking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ride-sharing simulation platforms are tailored to specific studies or tightly coupled to particular dispatch algorithms, lacking standardized, learning-friendly interfaces. This forces researchers to build custom environments from scratch, undermining reproducibility, fair comparison, and wasting redundant effort.

Method: The authors present RideGym, an open-source Gym-style interface that fully decouples the simulation environment from dispatch algorithms. It supports large-scale city-level simulations on real road networks with flexible configurations for vehicle attributes, order specifications, and automatic shortest-path routing. The platform enables both learning-based (MARL) and model-based methods under identical, fully specified conditions.

Result: RideGym reproduces several baselines and demonstrates high efficiency: a one-hour simulation with thousands of vehicles and tens of thousands of orders completes within one minute across all methods. Additionally, the choice of exploration noise significantly affects both absolute performance and relative ranking of MARL solutions, a previously overlooked factor.

Conclusion: RideGym fills a critical gap in ride-sharing research by providing a standardized, efficient, and flexible benchmarking platform. It highlights the underappreciated role of exploration noise in MARL evaluation and promotes reproducible, fair comparisons across dispatch methods.

Abstract: Ride-sharing has become an essential component of modern urban transportation and has attracted significant attention across computer science, transportation, and management science. While the field spans a broad range of problems, such as driver relocation, dynamic pricing, and vehicle charging or fueling dispatch, the core challenge remains order assignment and trip bundling, which directly affect urban traffic efficiency and carbon emissions. Despite its importance, existing simulation platforms are typically tailored to specific operational studies or tightly coupled to a particular dispatch algorithm, and rarely expose a standardized, learning-friendly interface. As a result, most researchers still build customized environments from scratch, raising serious concerns about reproducibility and fair comparison, and incurring substantial redundant effort. To address this gap, we present RideGym, the first open-source, standardized Gym-style interface tailored to MARL-based order dispatch in real-world ride-sharing systems. By fully decoupling the environment from the dispatch algorithm, RideGym enables diverse learning-based and model-based methods to be developed and compared under identical, fully specified conditions. It supports efficient, large-scale city-level simulations on real road networks, and offers flexible configurations for vehicle attributes, order specifications, and automatic shortest-path routing. We validate RideGym by reproducing several baselines, and demonstrate its high efficiency, with a one-hour simulation involving thousands of vehicles and tens of thousands of orders completed within one minute across all methods. Moreover, we reveal that the choice of exploration noise can significantly affect both the performance and the relative ranking of MARL solutions, an aspect often overlooked in prior work.

</details>


### [310] [Distributed Agent System: Fault-Tolerant Collaboration Among Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10811)
*Kai Yu,Lu Chen,Hanqi Li*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Proposes a Distributed Agent System (DAS) with device-edge-cloud architecture and two-layer fault tolerance (agent-level alignment + cross-agent semi-formal protocols) to address cumulative error propagation in long-horizon heterogeneous agent collaboration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI engineering is transitioning from passive LLM text generation to agent-driven task execution, where conventional error-elimination strategies fail against cumulative error propagation in long-horizon tasks under resource constraints and environmental uncertainty.

Method: DAS, a device-edge-cloud framework with a two-layer fault-tolerance architecture: (1) single-agent execution reliability via fault-tolerant alignment, and (2) cross-agent communication reliability via semi-formal language protocols.
