This paper presents emerging results from an exploratory study investigating the relationship between trust in GenAI and perceived productivity, motivated by Global South contexts. We conducted a systematic literature review, complemented by a grey literature analysis and a survey study. The literature review identified no peer-reviewed evidence at the intersection of GenAI trust, productivity, and Global South settings, while the grey literature revealed only limited insights. At the time of writing, the survey has received 36 valid responses from participants across both the Global North and Global South, including individuals with cross-regional experiences. Preliminary results suggest that respondents born and working in the Global South tended to trust AI more, but did not usually report clear productivity gains from using it. In contrast, respondents born and working outside the Global South reported stronger productivity gains and greater time savings, even though they showed less trust in generative AI. These findings suggest that trusting AI is not enough on its own; productivity also depends on access, the type of task, and how much users need to check the output.

</details>


### [332] [Question Answering for Diagram-Rich Technical Meeting Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10494)
*Zhuoran Xu,Jia Li,Dayuan Tan,Mark Cole,Ish Ashraf,Sandeep Puri,Mehrdad Sabetzadeh,Shiva Nejati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LMVQA is an LLM-based multimodal QA system for technical meeting videos that grounds answers in audio and visual evidence, achieving dramatic improvements in accuracy (31%→94%) and response time (81.3s→3.3s) while reducing API costs by ~75%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software engineering teams increasingly rely on recorded meetings containing diagrams (requirements, UML, system behavior) where stakeholders discuss rationale and decisions. However, extracting knowledge from these recordings is difficult because relevant evidence is dispersed across speech, slides, and technical diagrams, and recordings are prohibitively long for manual review.

Method: LMVQA processes each video once to build a reusable time-stamped evidence corpus. It grounds answers in both audio and visual modalities, with explicit handling of diagram-rich content (requirements and UML diagrams). The system was developed collaboratively with engineers at Ciena and evaluated on both a proprietary Ciena dataset and a public dataset, compared against a state-of-the-art baseline.

Result: LMVQA improved answer accuracy from 31% to 94% on the Ciena dataset and from 21% to 88% on the public dataset, with larger gains on diagram-rich videos. After one-time indexing, average response time dropped from 81.3s to 3.3s (Ciena) and from 98.4s to 9.2s (public), while token-based LLM API costs decreased by approximately 75%. Interviews with three domain experts confirmed engineers value the system for locating SE-relevant information, revisiting rationale, and tracing answers to specific video segments.

Conclusion: LMVQA demonstrates that multimodal, evidence-grounded QA systems can effectively unlock knowledge from diagram-rich technical meeting recordings, offering substantial improvements in accuracy, latency, and cost over existing approaches. The system is particularly valued by practitioners for rationale recovery and fine-grained answer traceability.

Abstract: Software engineering increasingly relies on asynchronous communication artifacts, including recorded meetings where stakeholders discuss concerns, rationale, and decisions. These meetings often include diagram-based representations of requirements, system behavior, component interactions, and trace dependencies. Accessing knowledge from these meetings is challenging because recordings are long and relevant evidence is distributed across speech, slides, and technical diagrams. This paper reports our industrial experience developing and evaluating LMVQA, an LLM-based multimodal question-answering system for technical meeting videos. Developed in collaboration with engineers at Ciena, LMVQA supports the understanding of requirements and design intent by grounding answers in audio and visual evidence, with explicit handling of diagram-rich content such as requirements and UML diagrams. It processes each video once to build a reusable time-stamped evidence corpus for grounded question answering. Across a Ciena dataset and a public dataset, we show that LMVQA significantly improves answer accuracy compared to a state-of-the-art baseline, from 31% to 94% on the Ciena dataset and from 21% to 88% on the public dataset, with larger gains on diagram-rich videos. We further show that, after one-time indexing, LMVQA reduces average response time from 81.3s to 3.3s on Ciena and from 98.4s to 9.2s on the public dataset, while lowering average token-based LLM API cost by about 75%. Finally, our interviews with three domain experts show that engineers particularly value LMVQA for locating software-engineering-relevant information, revisiting rationale, and tracing answers to specific video segments.

</details>


### [333] [When Does Restricting a Coding Agent to execute_code Help? A Regime $\times$ Agent-Design Ablation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10569)
*Hong Yang,Qi Yu,Travis Desell*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper conducts a controlled three-arm ablation study comparing tool surfaces (baseline with all tools, bash-only, and code-only via MCP) across two coding agents and two task regimes. It finds that restricting agents to a single execute_code MCP tool is generally cheaper or statistically tied with richer tool surfaces, with pass rates invariant across conditions. The key insight is that cost differences are driven by failure-trajectory costs on doomed runs, not per-edit taxes, and that the optimal tool surface depends jointly on task regime and agent design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The coding agent field has produced three contradictory claims about which tool surface matters most (IDE primitives, bash, or MCP code-execution), but no prior work has conducted a clean, controlled comparison holding model, harness, and prompts constant. The authors aim to resolve this contradiction through a rigorous ablation study.

Method: A three-arm ablation (baseline with all tools / bash_only / code_only) is run on synthetic computation tasks (Artifact) and SWE-bench Mini modification tasks using two agents (Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI), producing four (regime × agent) cells. The comparison is integrity-clean: model, harness, and prompts are held fixed. A conditional-cost analysis decomposes costs on successful vs. failed trajectories to localize cost differences.

Result: In three of four (regime, agent) cells, restricting to a single execute_code MCP tool is cheaper or statistically tied with the cheapest tool-rich rival — significantly on Artifact/Claude and SWE-bench/Codex, directionally on Artifact/Codex. Pass rates are statistically tied within each cell. The lone exception is SWE-bench/Claude, where code_only is directionally costlier (+14.4%, not significant); this gap is localized to failure-cost on doomed-run trajectories, not a per-edit tax on successful runs.

Conclusion: The cheapest tool surface is jointly determined by task regime and agent design, not by either axis alone. The headline cost signal lives in cache-adjusted cost rather than pass rate, which is invariant across surfaces at the evaluated model sizes. The findings challenge the assumption that richer tool surfaces always improve efficiency.

Abstract: Modern coding agents expose multiple tool surfaces -- IDE primitives, bash, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) code-execution -- and the field has shipped three contradictory claims about which one matters. We run the missing crossed comparison: an integrity-clean three-arm ablation (baseline / bash_only / code_only) on synthetic computation tasks and SWE-bench Mini modification tasks, holding model, harness, and prompts fixed, with two agents (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI) so the comparison spans both regime and agent-design axes. Across the four resulting (regime, agent) cells, restricting the agent to a single execute_code MCP tool is cheaper than -- or statistically tied with -- its cheapest tool-rich rival in three cells (significantly on Artifact/Claude and SWE-bench/Codex; directionally on Artifact/Codex), with pass rates statistically tied within each cell. The lone exception is SWE-bench/Claude, where code_only is directionally costlier (+14.4%, not significant); a conditional-cost analysis localizes that gap to failure-cost on doomed-run trajectories, not a per-edit tax on successful runs. Two implications: the cheapest tool surface is jointly determined by task regime and agent design rather than by either axis alone, and the headline cost signal lives in cache-adjusted cost -- not pass rate, which is invariant across surfaces at the model sizes we evaluate. The benchmark harness, task suite, and analysis code are available at https://github.com/hyang0129/onlycodes.

</details>


### [334] [WebDesignIter: Co-Evolving Design Knowledge for Repository-Level Front-End Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10621)
*Zheng Pei,Mingwei Liu,Zhenxi Chen,Zihao Wang,Yanlin Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: WebDesignIter introduces a persistent knowledge graph (WebAppArchKG) that encodes architectural design knowledge alongside repository structure, enabling LLM coding agents to maintain coherent, maintainable code across multi-iteration front-end development tasks. On Web-Bench, it achieves a 9.55 pp Pass@2 gain over baselines and outperforms general-purpose agents while consuming fewer tokens. Ablation shows design knowledge is the most critical component.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM coding agents are tuned for single-shot tasks and fail to track complex cross-file dependencies across multiple development iterations, leading to functional regressions and unmaintainable code. The authors argue that what is missing is explicit design knowledge — architectural principles, module responsibilities, and structural constraints — that human developers use to keep evolving codebases readable and maintainable.

Method: The framework, WebDesignIter, is built around WebAppArchKG, a persistent knowledge graph that fuses repository structure with design knowledge and keeps both synchronized across development cycles. It operates in two stages: (1) design-informed planning retrieves historical context and architectural overviews from the KG to produce implementation plans with test scripts; (2) design-aware generation executes the plan via targeted diff-based patches, validated by sandbox execution and automatic syntax repair.

Result: On the Web-Bench benchmark, WebDesignIter yields an average Pass@2 improvement of 9.55 percentage points across nine foundation models over existing baselines. It outperforms every general-purpose coding agent (Claude Code, OpenHands, SWE-Agent, Codex CLI) on all model configurations, achieving the highest Pass@1 and Pass@2 while consuming 25–30 fewer input tokens. Ablation reveals design knowledge as the dominant component: removing it causes an 11.40 pp drop in Pass@1, far exceeding the impact of removing code-graph retrieval, patch-based generation, or sandbox verification.

Conclusion: Explicit, persistent design knowledge encoded in a knowledge graph provides a fundamentally more efficient and reliable path to repository-level code generation than current approaches. The ablation results confirm that architectural understanding — not just retrieval or generation mechanics — is the key enabler for multi-iteration front-end development with LLMs.

Abstract: Front-end development accumulates change after change at the repository level, weaving complex cross-file dependencies that current LLM coding agents tuned for single-shot tasks cannot reliably track across multiple iterations, leading to functional regressions and code that resists maintenance. We argue the missing piece is design knowledge: architectural principles, module responsibilities, and structural constraints that developers lean on to keep code readable, maintainable, and evolvable as a system scales. To operationalize this, we propose WebDesignIter, a framework built around a persistent knowledge graph (WebAppArchKG) that fuses repository structure with design knowledge and keeps both in sync across development cycles. WebDesignIter works in two stages: design-informed planning pulls historical context and architectural overviews from WebAppArchKG to produce an implementation plan with corresponding test scripts, and design-aware generation executes that plan through targeted diff-based patches, validated by sandbox execution and automatic syntax repair. On Web-Bench, WebDesignIter delivers an average Pass@2 gain of 9.55 percentage points across nine foundation models over existing baselines. More importantly, WebDesignIter outperforms every general-purpose coding agent Claude Code, OpenHands, SWE-Agent, Codex CLI on every model configuration, posting the highest Pass@1 and Pass@2 while consuming 2530 fewer input tokens. Ablation singles out design knowledge as the most impactful component: stripping it drops Pass@1 by 11.40 percentage points, a degradation far larger than removing code-graph retrieval, patch-based generation, or sandbox verification, confirming that design knowledge provides a fundamentally more efficient and reliable path to repository-level code generation.

</details>


### [335] [Commenting with Copilot: A Taxonomy and Multi-Year Analysis of Student Code-Generation Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10674)
*Nasser Giacaman,Valerio Terragni,Paul Denny,Viraj Kumar*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Analysis of a four-year dataset of student comments in AI-assisted programming reveals a taxonomy of comment types, expression levels, and code constructs. Students predominantly write natural-language "What" comments, shift toward "How" comments for procedural constructs, and prioritize verification over iterative comment rewriting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI code generation tools become pervasive in programming education, the role of students shifts from writing code to writing specifications (comments). However, little is known about the nature and quality of comments students write as specifications in AI-assisted programming tasks.

Method: The authors analyzed a four-year dataset of undergraduate programming submissions and student reflections from tasks where students wrote comments to guide AI code generation and iteratively refined solutions using test-case feedback. They developed a three-dimensional taxonomy (comment type, code expression level, code construct) and applied automated classification to examine patterns across attempts and student reflections.

Result: Students predominantly wrote natural-language "What" comments (describing desired behavior). They shifted toward "How" comments (procedural descriptions) when dealing with more procedural code constructs. Students focused more on verifying AI-generated code against test cases rather than iteratively rewriting and refining their comments.

Conclusion: The findings highlight a gap in current AI-assisted programming pedagogy: students underutilize specification refinement as a strategy, defaulting instead to verification of generated code. This has implications for designing instructional approaches that teach effective specification writing in AI-augmented programming environments.

Abstract: As AI code tools become integrated into programming environments, students increasingly describe intended behavior in natural language and rely on these tools to generate code, shifting emphasis from code writing to specification. Yet little is known about the comments students write as specifications in AI-assisted programming tasks. We analyze a four-year dataset of undergraduate programming submissions and reflections from tasks in which students wrote comments to guide code generation and refined solutions using test-case feedback. We introduce a taxonomy spanning three dimensions: comment type, code expression level, and code construct. Using automated classification, we examine how these dimensions vary across attempts and how students describe the process in their reflections. Our findings show that students mostly wrote natural-language What comments, shifted toward How comments for more procedural constructs, and focused more on verifying generated code than on repeatedly rewriting comments.

</details>


### [336] [Maintenance and Support in Community-Driven Scientific Pipeline Ecosystems: A Cross-Platform Empirical Study of nf-core](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10839)
*Khairul Alam,Kowsik Roy,Md Shamimur Rahman,Banani Roy*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study of the nf-core ecosystem analyzing 15,760 issues, 35,411 pull requests, and 895 forum discussions to understand how maintenance and support operate across repository and community spaces, identifying factors that predict resolution outcomes and revealing limited cross-platform traceability between GitHub artifacts and community forum discussions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Community-driven scientific pipeline ecosystems face sustainability challenges beyond technical infrastructure — they depend on effective maintenance, contribution integration, and user support across heterogeneous environments. Understanding how these activities manifest and what drives successful outcomes is critical for ecosystem health.

Method: Cross-platform empirical study combining quantitative analysis and qualitative coding of 15,760 GitHub issues, 35,411 pull requests, and 895 Seqera Community Forum discussions from the nf-core ecosystem. Statistical modeling is used to identify factors associated with resolution outcomes (issue closure, PR integration, forum accepted answers), and cross-platform traceability patterns are examined.

Result: (1) Issues serve repository-level problem reporting and coordination; PRs capture implementation, review, testing, dependency, and template updates; forums handle user-facing execution, container, cloud/HPC, MultiQC, and Nextflow usage support. (2) Issue closure correlates with assignees, comments, milestones, bug labels, error mentions, and version information. (3) PR integration varies by author role, automation type, draft status, checklists, linked issues, and review routing. (4) Forum accepted answers associate with code blocks, sustained interaction, and concrete evidence; cloud/HPC/workflow-semantics questions resist resolution. (5) GitHub shows strong internal traceability, but explicit forum-to-repository linkage is limited.

Conclusion: Sustainable pipeline ecosystems require coordinated attention to both repository-centered maintenance and community-centered user support. The weak cross-platform traceability between forums and repositories represents a gap that, if addressed, could improve knowledge flow, reduce duplicate effort, and strengthen ecosystem sustainability.

Abstract: Community-driven scientific pipeline ecosystems are increasingly important for reproducible data-intensive research, but their sustainability depends on more than workflow engines, templates, and testing infrastructure. It also depends on how communities maintain pipelines, integrate contributions, and support users across heterogeneous execution environments. This paper presents a cross-platform empirical study of maintenance and support in nf-core, a large ecosystem of standardized Nextflow pipelines. We analyze 15,760 GitHub issues, 35,411 GitHub pull requests, and 895 Seqera Community Forum discussions to examine what maintenance and support concerns arise, how they differ across artifact types, which factors are associated with resolution outcomes, and how problems and solutions flow between repository-centered and community-centered spaces. We find that issues primarily capture repository-level problem reporting and maintenance coordination; pull requests capture implementation, review, testing, dependency, and template-update work; and forum discussions capture user-facing support around execution failures, containers, cloud and HPC environments, MultiQC reporting, and Nextflow usage. Resolution outcomes are associated with actionability, coordination, and diagnostic evidence. Issue closure is linked to assignees, comments, milestones, bug labels, error mentions, and version information. Pull request integration varies by author role, automation type, draft status, checklists, linked issues, and review routing. Forum accepted answers are more likely when discussions include code blocks, sustained interaction, and concrete technical evidence, while cloud, HPC, and workflow-semantics questions are harder to resolve. Cross-platform analysis reveals strong repository-internal traceability within GitHub, but limited explicit linkage between forum discussions and repository artifacts.

</details>


### [337] [How Do Practitioners Build SE Agents? Insights from a Mixed-Methods Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10856)
*Yunbo Lyu,David Williams,Jieke Shi,Zhensu Sun,Chao Peng,Zhou Yang,Federica Sarro,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Through interviews (20 practitioners) and a survey (80 practitioners), this first-of-its-kind study reveals how SE agent development shifts bottlenecks from coding to non-coding tasks like requirements, review, and evaluation. It characterizes a seven-stage workflow centered on evaluation-driven development and identifies six key challenges, including unreliable evaluation signals, comprehension debt, and provider-side model update issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite rapid advances in LLM-based SE agents, there is no empirical understanding of how practitioners actually build these systems. Existing studies focus on mining repositories or deployment, leaving a gap in knowledge about the construction process and the challenges developers face when building SE agents.

Method: Mixed-methods empirical study combining semi-structured interviews with 20 practitioners from 12 organizations and an online survey of 80 practitioners who build SE agents.

Result: Key findings: (1) As implementation becomes cheaper, bottlenecks shift to non-coding work (requirements, coordination, review, deployment); (2) Reviewing/evaluating agent output becomes a new central activity; (3) A seven-stage evaluation-driven development workflow emerges where evaluation steers iteration and specifications become versioned artifacts for both humans and agents; (4) Six challenges identified: unreliable evaluation signals, comprehension debt (code outpaces understanding), behavioral changes from provider-side model updates, and three others.

Conclusion: The development of SE agents fundamentally reshapes software engineering processes, shifting emphasis toward evaluation-driven workflows and non-coding activities. Practitioners face novel challenges requiring new practices, highlighting the need for better tooling, evaluation infrastructure, and strategies to manage comprehension debt and model instability.

Abstract: The rise of Software Engineering (SE) agents, i.e., LLM-based agents that can understand large codebases and carry out engineering tasks with limited human intervention, has been marked by rapid advances and adoption, but little is known about how developers build these systems in practice: existing studies mine repositories or examine deployment, but few investigate how SE agents are constructed. Through semi-structured interviews with 20 practitioners from 12 organizations and an online survey of 80 practitioners, this paper is the first to study how SE processes are changing in the development of SE agents and what challenges developers face. We find that as implementation becomes cheaper, bottlenecks shift rather than disappear: long-standing non-coding work such as requirements, coordination, review, and deployment becomes more visible, while reviewing and evaluating agent output becomes new and central. We characterize a seven-stage workflow and a shift toward evaluation-driven development, in which evaluation steers iteration and specifications become versioned artifacts read by both humans and agents. We further identify six challenges that teams face, together with the practices they adopt to address them, including unreliable evaluation signals, comprehension debt as code outpaces understanding, and behavioral changes introduced by provider-side model updates.

</details>


### [338] [BackendForge: Benchmarking Agentic End-to-End Code Generation with Backend Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11042)
*Yuzhe Guo,Mengzhou Wu,Yuan Cao,Jialei Wei,Dezhi Ran,Wei Yang,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: BackendForge is a benchmark of 56 backend service generation tasks using OpenAPI contracts, where LLMs must produce Dockerized services evaluated via HTTP tests. GPT-5.5 achieves 55.4% under the base oracle but only 28.6% under a co-evolved final oracle, revealing that LLMs can handle local API behaviors but struggle with complete, deployable backend services.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in agentic coding settings with file inspection, command execution, and iterative revision capabilities. Existing evaluations lack rigorous assessment of whether an agentic LLM can generate an end-to-end software artifact that is both deployable and behaviorally correct under execution. Backend services are ideal for this because they expose application-level semantics via APIs and correctness can be deterministically verified through black-box HTTP interactions against an OpenAPI contract.

Method: BackendForge comprises 56 contract-defined backend generation tasks derived from real open-source applications. Each task provides a specification and an OpenAPI contract; the LLM must generate a Dockerized service evaluated solely through HTTP tests. To strengthen evaluation without introducing hidden requirements, the benchmark employs a co-evolution process: a test agent proposes specification-grounded backend tests while a code agent repairs the reference implementation, yielding progressively stronger test oracles (base oracle vs. final oracle).

Result: GPT-5.5, the best-performing model, succeeds on 55.4% of tasks under the base oracle but drops to only 28.6% under the final oracle. This 26.8 percentage point gap highlights a significant disparity between implementing individual API behaviors and delivering a fully correct, deployable backend service.

Conclusion: Current LLMs demonstrate competence in implementing isolated, local API behaviors but remain unreliable at producing complete, deployment-ready backend services. The co-evolution approach to oracle construction provides a more rigorous evaluation without leaking hidden requirements, and the benchmark reveals substantial room for improvement in end-to-end software artifact generation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in agentic coding settings, where they can inspect files, execute commands, run tests, observe failures, and iteratively revise code. This shift raises a central evaluation question: can an agentic LLM generate an end-to-end software artifact that is both deployable and behaviorally correct under execution? Backend services provide a controlled but realistic substrate for this evaluation. Their APIs expose application-level executable semantics, and deployed behavior can be checked deterministically against an OpenAPI contract through black-box HTTP interactions. We introduce BackendForge, a benchmark of 56 contract-defined backend generation tasks rewritten from real open-source applications. Given a visible specification and an OpenAPI contract, an LLM must generate a Dockerized service that is built, deployed, and evaluated only through HTTP tests. To strengthen evaluation without introducing hidden requirements, BackendForge uses a test agent and a code agent to co-evolve the test oracle and reference service, where the test agent proposes specification-grounded backend tests and the code agent repairs the reference implementation. Although the best-performing model, GPT-5.5, succeeds on 55.4\% of tasks under the base oracle, it succeeds on only 28.6\% under the final oracle. This gap suggests that current LLMs can implement many local API behaviors, but still struggle to produce complete backend services.

</details>


### [339] [Retrieval-Oriented Code Representations in Agentic Bug Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11046)
*Genevieve Caumartin,Tse-Hsun,Chen,Diego Elias Costa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how different code representations (file paths, raw source code, LLM-generated summaries) affect file-level bug localization in LLM-based agents. Role-aware summaries achieve the best cost-effectiveness trade-off, outperforming file-path representations by up to 40% Hit@5 while being 10-20x smaller than raw source code. Combining representations and using LLM-based re-ranking further improves results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents for software development rely on accurate code context retrieval, yet existing work focuses narrowly on file paths and raw source code for localization. The role of textual code representations—particularly LLM-generated summaries—in retrieval and localization remains underexplored, creating a gap in understanding how to optimally balance effectiveness and cost.

Method: The authors frame file-level bug localization as a representation-driven retrieval problem. They compare five code representations (file paths, raw source code, and three LLM-generated textual representations: structure summaries, role-aware summaries, and monolithic summaries) across LCA and SWE-bench Verified datasets. Retrieval methods include lexical (BM25), semantic (embedding-based), and LLM-based approaches, followed by LLM-based post-retrieval ranking. They introduce the "representation footprint" metric to quantify representation cost. They also conduct a case study integrating their techniques into the Agentless pipeline.

Result: Role-aware summaries outperform file-path representations by up to 40% Hit@5 with 10.4–20.9x smaller footprint than raw source code. Combining complementary representations yields up to 31.9% improvement; LLM-based re-ranking adds up to 42.0% gains. Raw source code offers competitive effectiveness in some settings but at significantly higher cost. In the Agentless case study, the approach reaches 94% Hit@6 (+4.7% over baseline).

Conclusion: Code representation should be treated as a first-class design choice in agentic localization pipelines. Role-aware summaries offer the best cost-effectiveness trade-off, and the choice of representation should be guided by the pipeline stage and cost-accuracy requirements.

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly being used to support software development, yet their performance in repository-level tasks depends on retrieving the right code context. Existing studies have explored file-level localization using traditional information retrieval over file paths and raw source code. However, the role of textual code representations in retrieval and localization remains underexplored.
  We study file-level bug localization as a representation-driven retrieval problem. Across the Long Code Arena (LCA) and SWE-bench Verified (SWE) datasets, we compare five code representations: file paths, raw source code, and three LLM-generated textual representations. Our experiments include lexical, semantic, and LLM-based retrieval, followed by LLM-based post-retrieval ranking. We quantify the cost incurred by a representation through the representation footprint. We find that the choice of code representation affects both localization effectiveness and cost. Role-aware summaries outperform file-path representations by up to 40% Hit@5 while requiring a representation footprint 10.4 to 20.9x smaller than raw source code. Combining complementary representation results and ranking retrieved candidates with an LLM provides further gains of up to 31.9% and 42.0%, respectively. Overall, role-aware summaries provide the best cost-effectiveness trade-off, while raw source code offers effectiveness in some settings at a significantly higher cost. A case study with Agentless reveals the utility of our techniques within a well-known pipeline, reaching 94% Hit@6 on file localization (+4.7% against the baseline). Our findings suggest that code representation should be treated as a first-class design choice in agentic localization pipelines, guided by pipeline stage and cost-accuracy requirements.

</details>


### [340] [AgentCheck: A Reproduce-Intervene-Mitigate Workbench for LLM Agents over MCP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11098)
*Aritra Mazumder,Nusrat jahan Lia*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentCheck is an open-source workbench that turns MCP servers into intervention surfaces, enabling developers to reproduce, test, and verify fixes for tool failures in LLM agents by injecting 12 fault types into recorded tool responses and re-running agents in a reproduce-intervene-confirm loop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent evaluation assumes all tools function correctly, but real-world deployments face tool timeouts, stale data, and poisoned descriptions. Developers lack a controlled method to reproduce these failures, test mitigations, and confirm fixes before deployment.

Method: AgentCheck records an agent's tool responses during an initial run, then re-runs the agent with a fault injector that perturbs responses using one of 12 fault types. Matching tool calls replay from cache until the agent diverges, after which calls go live. Evaluation combines deterministic pass/fail rules with an LLM judge validated against human annotations.

Result: Across five agents tested on 120 scenarios, the best agent passed 105 and the weakest only 77. Failures are predominantly silent misuses of incorrect tool outputs rather than crashes. On the weakest agent, retry mitigation improved timeout success from 30% to 100%, while stale-data faults remained at 3-4/10 regardless of mitigation.

Conclusion: AgentCheck makes tool-failure modes reproducible, comparable, and verifiable before deployment, revealing that silent, confident reliance on faulty tool outputs is the dominant failure pattern, and that mitigations are fault-type-dependent in their effectiveness.

Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are mostly evaluated assuming all tools work. When a tool times out, returns a week-stale value, or has its description poisoned in deployment, the developer needs a controlled way to reproduce the failure, test a fix, and confirm the fix worked before deployment. We present AgentCheck, an open-source web workbench that turns an MCP server into an intervention surface. AgentCheck runs an agent against its real tools and records every tool response, then re-runs the agent with the response perturbed by a fault (12 types) injector. Matching tool calls are replayed from cache, and later tool calls go live after the agent diverges. This yields a reproduce-intervene-confirm loop: the developer toggles a mitigation, re-runs against the identical fault, and sees if the failure goes away. Scoring has two parts: deterministic pass/fail rules, plus an LLM judge for interpretive labels, validated against human annotations. Across five agents, the best passes 105/120 scenarios and the weakest only 77. The failures are usually silent, confident use of incorrect tool outputs rather than crashes. On the weakest agent, a retry mitigation raises success on timeout error faults from as few as 30% of cases to 100%, whereas stale-data faults remain near 3-4 of 10 regardless of the mitigation. AgentCheck makes these failure modes reproducible, comparable, and verifiable before deployment.

</details>


### [341] [Know Before Fix: QA-Driven Repository Knowledge Acquisition for Software Issue Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11111)
*Haotian Lin,Silin Chen,Xiaodong Gu,Yuling Shi,Chengxi Pan,Jiaqi Ge,Mengfan Li,Jianghong Huang,Mengchieh Chuang,Beijun Shen,Haibing Guan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ACQUIRE is a QA-driven framework that explicitly acquires repository knowledge before patch generation, using a Questioner-Answerer collaboration to bridge the agent's knowledge gaps, achieving up to 4.4 pp Pass@1 improvement on SWE-bench Verified.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based coding agents suffer from factual errors due to insufficient repository understanding. Existing pre-repair exploration methods are fix-driven and fail to identify the agent's specific knowledge gaps, resulting in imprecise context that doesn't resolve the underlying understanding deficit.

Method: ACQUIRE decouples knowledge acquisition from patch generation into two stages: (1) A Questioner agent poses targeted questions about the repository, and an Answerer agent produces evidence-grounded answers through autonomous exploration, collaboratively building structured QA knowledge; (2) A Resolver agent leverages this acquired knowledge to generate informed patches.

Result: On SWE-bench Verified, ACQUIRE consistently outperforms representative pre-repair methods, achieving up to 4.4 percentage points improvement in Pass@1 with only modest additional cost and time overhead.

Conclusion: Transforming implicit knowledge gaps into explicit, factually reliable understanding via a QA-driven approach effectively accelerates knowledge-intensive repair stages and enables more accurate automated software issue resolution.

Abstract: LLM-based coding agents have significantly advanced automated software issue resolution, yet they remain highly prone to factual errors caused by insufficient repository understanding. Recent methods attempt to mitigate this limitation through pre-repair repository exploration; however, their fix-driven strategies explore repositories without identifying the agent's knowledge gaps, often yielding imprecise context that fails to bridge the underlying understanding deficit. In this paper, we propose ACQUIRE, a QA-driven framework for software issue resolution. Mirroring how experienced developers first comprehend unfamiliar code before attempting a fix, ACQUIRE explicitly acquires repository knowledge prior to repair. The framework decouples knowledge acquisition from patch generation through two stages: in the first stage, a Questioner and an Answerer collaborate to acquire structured repository knowledge, where the Questioner poses targeted questions and the Answerer produces evidence-grounded answers through autonomous exploration; in the second stage, the Resolver leverages the resulting QA knowledge to generate informed patches. By transforming implicit knowledge gaps into explicit, factually reliable understanding, ACQUIRE accelerates knowledge-intensive repair stages and enables more accurate resolution. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified demonstrate that ACQUIRE consistently outperforms representative pre-repair methods, raising Pass@1 by up to 4.4 percentage points with modest additional cost and time.

</details>


### [342] [RepTran: Search-Based Repair of Transformer Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11193)
*Yuta Ishimoto,Paolo Arcaini,Fuyuki Ishikawa,Masanari Kondo,Naoyasu Ubayashi,Yasutaka Kamei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: RepTran is a search-based repair method targeting feed-forward networks in Transformer models, using variance-based and bidirectional scores to identify suspicious weights, then optimizing them via differential evolution. It achieved a 74.7% average repair rate, significantly outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As Transformer models are increasingly integrated into AI-enabled software, their misbehaviors become critical. Existing DNN repair methods overlook Transformer-specific architectural structures, particularly the feed-forward networks (FFNs), motivating a targeted repair approach.

Method: RepTran targets FFN weights in Transformers by combining a variance-based neuron score with an existing bidirectional score to identify suspicious weights, then applies differential evolution for iterative weight optimization. Evaluation used 18 fault benchmarks from CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet, compared against random selection, Arachne, and ArachneW baselines.

Result: RepTran achieved a 74.7% average repair rate, statistically outperforming both random weight selection and Arachne across all benchmarks. Effect size analysis showed RepTran surpassed ArachneW regardless of the number of selected weights.

Conclusion: RepTran effectively enhances Transformer model reliability, demonstrating that targeting FFN-specific structures with search-based repair yields superior results compared to generic DNN repair methods.

Abstract: To ensure the overall quality of AI-enabled software, not only traditional software components but also AI components need to be tested and repaired. Among AI components, Transformer models are increasingly integrated into software systems, which makes their misbehaviors critical. Although prior work in the software engineering community has proposed deep neural network (DNN) repair methods, most overlook Transformer-specific structures. We propose RepTran, a search-based repair method for Transformer models. It targets their feed-forward networks (FFNs), which play a central role in the architecture. RepTran identifies suspicious weights by combining two types of scores: a variance-based neuron score and an existing bidirectional score. It then iteratively optimizes these weights using differential evolution. Our evaluation includes 18 fault benchmarks constructed from CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet. We compare RepTran against three baselines: random weight selection, Arachne (a state-of-the-art DNN repair method), and ArachneW, which enables Arachne to control the number of selected weights. RepTran achieved an average repair rate of 74.7%, statistically outperforming random selection and Arachne across all benchmarks. Effect size analysis revealed that RepTran achieved higher repair rates than ArachneW regardless of the number of selected weights. These results suggest that RepTran is effective for enhancing the reliability of AI-enabled software.

</details>


### [343] [An Empirical Study for GUI Test Migration from Android to OpenHarmony System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11245)
*Yakun Zhang,Xinjia Chen,Yiyun Chen,Yuxia Zhang,Mingyi Zhou,Xiang Gao,Shaokun Zhang,Li Li,Yunming Ye*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: First systematic empirical study of GUI test migration from Android to OpenHarmony. Evaluates two SOTA approaches (ReSPlay, ITeM) on a benchmark of 36 apps/108 test cases, finding low success rates (15%, 26%). Identifies OpenHarmony-specific characteristics as primary failure causes. Proposes ITeM-HM, an enhanced approach achieving 81% success rate (214% relative improvement over ITeM).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Migrating GUI tests from Android to OpenHarmony requires substantial engineering effort, yet no existing research provides tailored solutions or systematic evaluation for this platform. Developers lack empirical guidance, creating a critical gap as OpenHarmony adoption grows.

Method: (1) Constructed the ATH Benchmark: 36 commercial applications (avg. 9B+ downloads) with 108 manually designed test cases. (2) Adapted two SOTA migration approaches (ReSPlay and ITeM) to run on OpenHarmony. (3) Evaluated both approaches across three dimensions: testing performance, failure root causes, and impact of OpenHarmony-specific characteristics. (4) Developed ITeM-HM by augmenting ITeM with OpenHarmony-specific system features based on failure analysis findings.

Result: ReSPlay achieved 15% success rate; ITeM achieved 26% success rate on Android-to-OpenHarmony migration. Failures primarily stem from OpenHarmony-specific characteristics: technical architecture differences and unique ecosystem traits. ITeM-HM achieved an 81% success rate, representing a 214% relative improvement over the original ITeM.

Conclusion: Existing test migration approaches are significantly less effective for Android-to-OpenHarmony scenarios due to platform-specific characteristics. Incorporating OpenHarmony system features into migration tools can dramatically improve success rates, as demonstrated by ITeM-HM. This work provides the first empirical guidance for OpenHarmony test migration.

Abstract: To reduce the substantial engineering effort required to test the corresponding applications from Android to OpenHarmony, migrating existing GUI test cases has become a critical problem. However, current research neither proposes solutions tailored for OpenHarmony nor provides a systematic evaluation of migration approaches on this system, leaving developers with limited empirical guidance in practice. In this paper, we present the first systematic empirical study of test migration from Android to OpenHarmony. Specifically, we first construct a dataset referred to as the ATH Benchmark, comprising 36 commercial applications with an average of over 9 billion downloads, along with 108 manually designed test cases. Second, we select two state-of-the-art test migration approaches (i.e., ReSPlay and ITeM) and adapt these two approaches to enable their execution on OpenHarmony. Third, we use the preceding infrastructure to evaluate these two approaches from three perspectives, including testing performance, root causes of failures, and the impact of OpenHarmony characteristics. Our results reveal that existing test migration approaches are less effective (15% success-rate on ReSPlay and 26% success-rate on ITeM) in Android-to-OpenHarmony scenarios. Through an in-depth analysis of failed cases, we identify that test performance is primarily hindered by OpenHarmony-specific characteristics, including technical architecture differences and unique ecosystem traits. Utilizing these findings, we propose an enhanced approach based on ITeM, referred as ITeM-HM, which incorporates specific OpenHarmony system features. As a result, ITeM-HM successfully achieves a 214% success-rate relative improvement over the original ITeM (from 26% to 81%).

</details>


### [344] [Hidden or Formal Architects: Understanding Who Makes Architectural Decisions in Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11251)
*Klara Borowa,Dominik Nowak,Mikołaj Nowak*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study investigates who actually makes architectural decisions in practice, finding that many decision-makers lack the formal "software architect" title. Formal architects are deemed necessary primarily in large companies and teams, suggesting prior research focusing only on titled architects may have overlooked significant contributors to architecture decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior empirical research on software architecture has often focused on individuals with the formal title of "software architect," yet many companies do not employ anyone in that role. Since all systems have architectures, someone must be making architectural decisions. This gap motivates the study to identify who actually performs this role and under what conditions a formal architect is considered necessary.

Method: A mixed-methods approach combining a questionnaire with 54 participants from diverse companies and seven follow-up interviews to gather qualitative and quantitative data on architectural decision-making practices.

Result: Architectural decisions are frequently made by practitioners who do not hold the formal title of software architect. The presence of a formal architect is perceived as essential primarily in large companies and large teams, not universally.

Conclusion: Research that focuses exclusively on individuals holding the formal "software architect" title may systematically omit a substantial portion of practitioners who participate in architectural decision-making (ADM), introducing sampling bias into empirical software architecture studies.

Abstract: Empirical research on software architecture sometimes focuses on individuals holding the formal title of software architect. However, not all companies have individuals hired in such roles. Despite no formal architects, all systems have architectures, and there must be practitioners making the architectural decisions. This study aims to identify who, in practice, makes architectural decisions and in what environments the existence of a formal architect is perceived as necessary. This research employed a method consisting of a questionnaire with 54 participants from different companies and seven follow-up interviews. The findings indicate that architectural decisions are often made by individuals without a formal architect title. A formal architect is perceived as essential mainly in large companies and large teams. The results of this study show that many practitioners taking part in ADM may have been omitted by previous research, particularly if it focused on formal architects.

</details>


### [345] [Extending Decision Maps for Sustainable Safety and Security in Self-Adaptive Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11274)
*Marco Stadler,Wesley K. G. Assunção,Michael Vierhauser,Iris Groher,Michael Riegler,Johannes Sametinger*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper extends Decision Maps (DMs), a sustainability-driven visual modeling notation for Self-Adaptive Systems, by adding safety incident modeling and temporal security mode viewpoints, then validates the extension through an industry case study, demonstrating improved accuracy in capturing safety and security scenarios across the self-adaptation lifecycle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decision Maps (DMs) effectively model sustainability-driven long-term behavior in Self-Adaptive Systems (SASs), but they lack adequate modeling support for safety and security concerns — critical properties for systems intended to endure over time.

Method: The authors extend the DM notation along two axes: (1) introducing an additional modeling dimension to account for safety incidents, and (2) adopting a fine-grained divide-and-conquer approach that models security from distinct temporal viewpoints called "security modes." The extended notation is evaluated through a real-world use case provided by an industry partner.

Result: The extended DM notation captures security and safety scenarios more accurately and provides holistic support for the self-adaptation lifecycle phases, confirming its feasibility and suitability for practitioners.

Conclusion: Extending DMs with safety and security dimensions fills a critical gap in sustainability-driven SAS modeling, offering practitioners a more comprehensive notation for engineering self-adaptive systems that must endure safely and securely over time.

Abstract: Sustainability refers to a system's ability to maintain its functionality and endure over time. Hence, sustainability is a highly desirable property of software systems, including Self-Adaptive Systems (SASs). SASs can change (adapt) their behavior at runtime to continue achieving their objectives despite external or internal impacts. SASs' intended long-term system behavior can be expressed through a sustainability-driven visual modeling notation called Decision Maps (DMs). Although DMs have been proven helpful, they lack adequate modeling support for safety and security concerns. We address this limitation by extending the current notation for sustainability-driven modeling of SASs to better accommodate the unique characteristics of safety and security scenarios. First, we introduce an additional modeling dimension to account for safety incidents. Second, we adopt a fine-grained divide-and-conquer approach, modeling from distinct temporal security viewpoints ("security modes") to address security. We employ the extended DM notation in a real-world use case scenario provided by our industry partner to assess its feasibility and suitability for practitioners. Our results indicate that our modeling notation helps capture security and safety scenarios more accurately and provides holistic support for the self-adaptation life cycle phases.

</details>


### [346] [FlowArk: Boosting Agentic Data-flow Analysis for Android Apps via Context-Aware Knowledge Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11308)
*Yiming Zhang,Jiangrong Wu,Yuhong Nan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FlowArk is a knowledge-reuse system for batch agentic data-flow analysis that reduces redundant re-analysis of shared code fragments across context-isolated agent instances. By distilling, packaging, and injecting reusable analysis knowledge from completed tasks into subsequent agent contexts, FlowArk achieves 26.83% API cost reduction while maintaining analysis quality, and completes 36.66% more tasks under a fixed budget compared to standard setups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Batch agentic data-flow analysis for Android privacy/security auditing suffers from high re-analysis costs. Because different taint sources often converge on shared code fragments (due to code reuse), multiple context-isolated agent instances redundantly analyze the same program logic. This repetition wastes API budget and limits scalability, motivating a knowledge-sharing mechanism across agent instances.

Method: FlowArk introduces a three-stage knowledge-reuse pipeline: (1) it distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates; (2) it packages these candidates into matchable knowledge entries; and (3) it injects matched entries into the context of later agent instances, enabling them to leverage prior analysis results rather than re-analyzing shared code fragments. The system is implemented on top of OpenCode.

Result: Evaluated on 4,685 source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks across 50 open-source Android apps, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode maintained comparable analysis quality to standard OpenCode while reducing end-to-end API cost by 26.83%. Under a $100 budget constraint, FlowArk completed 1,060 tasks versus 776 for standard OpenCode — a 36.66% improvement.

Conclusion: FlowArk demonstrates that knowledge reuse across agent instances is an effective strategy for scaling agentic data-flow analysis, significantly improving cost efficiency and throughput without sacrificing analysis quality.

Abstract: Data-flow analysis is foundational to Android app privacy and security auditing. Recent coding agents can assist with non-trivial source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks by searching, reading, and reasoning over repository code. However, when these tasks are executed as a batch workload, current agentic analysis setups incur substantial re-analysis cost. Agent instances assigned to different taint sources may inspect shared code fragments, because code reuse in the target app can cause different data-flow paths to converge on shared program logic. Since these agent instances are context-isolated, analysis of these shared code fragments can be repeated within a batch, unnecessarily consuming API budget and limiting scalability.
  We propose FlowArk, a knowledge-reuse system that reduces re-analysis cost in batch agentic data-flow analysis by making knowledge from completed analyses available to later agent instances. Specifically, FlowArk distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates, packages these candidates into matchable knowledge entries, and injects matched entries into a later agent instance's context. We implement FlowArk on OpenCode and evaluate it on 4,685 source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks from 50 open-source Android apps. Compared with standard OpenCode, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode maintains comparable analysis quality while reducing end-to-end API cost by 26.83%. In addition, under a USD 100 budget, FlowArk completes 36.66% more tasks (1,060 vs. 776).

</details>


### [347] [Fail-Aware and Explainable Test Oracle Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11342)
*Yue Zhao,Binish Tanveer,Jelena Zdravkovic*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FOCAL is a code LLM-based discriminative oracle predictor that directly predicts whether a test prefix passes or fails, emphasizing failing cases during training and grounding predictions in statement-level behavioral evidence, significantly improving failure detection on unseen projects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test oracles are central to fault detection yet challenging to construct effectively. Prior learning-based assertion generation methods produce syntactically correct but often ineffective assertions. Discriminative oracles like SEER collapse on unseen projects, leaving a gap in reliable failure prediction for automated test generation pipelines.

Method: FOCAL trains an emerging code LLM on labeled pairs of (test prefix, method under test). Key design elements include: (1) loss functions that emphasize failing cases during training, (2) statement-level behavioral evidence grounding for predictions, and (3) direct pass/fail prediction rather than assertion generation.

Result: FOCAL substantially outperforms SEER on failing cases for unseen projects, achieves high accuracy within its training distribution, provides richer behavioral explanations, and passes explanation checks. Preliminary evaluation on fault-detection benchmarks and automated test-generation artifacts confirms these gains.

Conclusion: Fail-aware discriminative oracle prediction can complement fuzzing, search-based testing, and LLM-based test generation by attaching fault-aware predicted oracles to generated test prefixes, turning high-volume input generation into executable tests more likely to expose semantic failures.

Abstract: Despite their central role in fault detection, test oracles remain challenging to construct effectively. Recent learning based methods address this challenge by automatically generating test assertions, yet even if syntactically correct, they are often ineffective in revealing bugs. Rather than generating assertions, this study explores a different approach by training a model to directly predict whether a given test prefix passes or fails. We present FOCAL, an emerging code LLM-based discriminative oracle predictor. It learns from labeled pairs of test prefixes and methods under test, employs losses that emphasize failing cases during training, and grounds its predictions in statement level behavioral evidence. Compared with the baseline method SEER, we substantially improve performance on failing cases for unseen projects and provide richer explanations. A preliminary evaluation on fault-detection benchmarks and automated test-generation artifacts shows that our approach is highly accurate within its training distribution and substantially improves failure detection on previously unseen projects where prior discriminative oracles collapse. Moreover, the highlighted statements are supported by behavioral explanation checks. These early results suggest that fail-aware discriminative oracle prediction can complement existing approaches such as fuzzing, search-based testing, and LLM-based test generation. These techniques produce test prefixes at scale but often lack fault oriented oracles. In future work, FOCAL could take generated test prefixes and attach fault-aware predicted oracles to them, turning high-volume input generation into executable tests that are more likely to expose semantic failures.

</details>


### [348] [Understanding the Impact of AI Code Assistants on Security API Usage: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11348)
*Zahra Mousavi,Chadni Islam,M. Ali Babar,Alsharif Abuadbba,Kristen Moore*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A study with 44 professional developers found that GitHub Copilot improves functional correctness but does not significantly improve secure API usage. Developers rarely raised security concerns and often failed to recognize insecurities in their final code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While AI code assistants are widely adopted, their impact on security API usage remains unexplored from a developer-centered perspective. Security APIs are critical yet complex, and incorrect usage leads to serious vulnerabilities. An evidence-based understanding is needed to inform mitigation strategies.

Method: Empirical user study with 44 professional developers who completed security API programming tasks both with and without GitHub Copilot assistance (within-subjects design). Both functional correctness and security properties of the resulting code were analyzed.

Result: Copilot improved functional correctness and marginally reduced certain insecure patterns, but did not significantly improve secure API usage. Developers rarely raised security concerns when interacting with Copilot, and many did not recognize that their final implementations remained insecure.

Conclusion: Current AI code assistants are insufficient for ensuring secure API usage. The authors recommend enhancing developer security awareness and propose future research directions for safer AI-assisted software development.

Abstract: AI code assistants are transforming software development, but their implications for software security remain a major concern, particularly in the context of security APIs. These APIs are critical for safeguarding software systems, yet their complexity often leads to incorrect use and serious vulnerabilities. Developing an evidence-based understanding of how AI assistants influence developers' use of these APIs is therefore essential for informing effective mitigation strategies. While a few user studies have examined the broader impact of AI assistants on software vulnerabilities, the use of security APIs remains unexplored from a developer-centered perspective. This study addresses this gap by presenting the first empirical investigation into how AI code assistants affect professional developers' use of security APIs. We conducted a study with 44 developers who completed security API programming tasks with and without GitHub Copilot assistance. Our findings show that, while Copilot improves functional correctness and marginally reduces certain insecure patterns, it does not significantly improve secure API usage. We also found that developers rarely raised security concerns when engaging with Copilot, and many did not recognize that their final implementations remained insecure. Finally, we offer recommendations for enhancing security awareness among developers and propose future research directions to support safer AI-assisted software development.

</details>


### [349] [Predicting Program Comprehension with Foundation Models of Human Cognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11372)
*Yannick Lehmen,Marvin Wyrich,Anna-Maria Maurer,Norman Peitek,Marvin Wyrich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper evaluates Centaur, a foundation model trained on 160 psychological experiments, against 9 program-comprehension studies. It finds Centaur aligns more closely with human response patterns than its base Llama 3.1 model, relies less on prior trial data, and benefits more from task-related context — suggesting cognitive regularities learned from general psychological data can transfer to modeling developer behavior in software engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting how developers understand code remains an open challenge. Existing methods are limited: simplified proxy measures lack accuracy, while non-trivial measurements require elaborate, hard-to-scale experimental setups. The authors propose an alternative inspired by psychology — leveraging cognitive regularities learned from large-scale behavioral data rather than directly modeling task-specific phenomena.

Method: The authors evaluate Centaur, a foundation model pre-trained on 160 general psychological experiments, against 9 previously published program-comprehension studies. They assess the alignment between Centaur's predicted response distributions and actual human responses, comparing performance against the base model (Llama 3.1). Ablation studies isolate contributions from three information sources: code artifacts, task-related context, and prior trials/participant responses.

Result: Centaur aligns more closely with human response patterns than Llama 3.1. It is significantly less reliant on information from prior trials and participant responses, and benefits more from task-related information. These results hold across multiple program-comprehension studies.

Conclusion: Behavioral patterns learned from general psychological data can transfer to complex software engineering tasks like program comprehension. The findings support foundation models of human cognition as a viable basis for modeling developer behavior, offering a scalable alternative to traditional approaches.

Abstract: Software engineering depends on the ability of developers to understand code, yet predicting how they do so remains an open challenge despite decades of research. Existing approaches rely either on simplified proxy measures that limit accuracy or on non-trivial measurements requiring elaborate experimental setups that are difficult to scale and apply in practice. In contrast, recent work in psychology suggests an alternative perspective: Instead of modeling task-specific phenomena directly, human behavior can be captured through cognitive regularities learned from large-scale behavioral data. This idea treats complex human behavior as the observable outcome of underlying cognitive processes that manifest consistently across tasks and domains. In this paper, we explore this perspective in the context of program comprehension. We evaluate Centaur, a foundation model trained on 160 general psychological experiments, on 9 previously published program-comprehension studies. We assess how well its predicted response distributions align with human response data and compare Centaur's performance to its base model, Llama 3.1. To better understand the source of its performance, we conduct ablation studies to isolate the contribution of different sources of information, such as the code artifacts, task-related context, and prior trials and participant responses. In a nutshell, we find that Centaur more closely aligns with human response patterns than its base model, is significantly less reliant on information from prior trials and responses, and benefits more from task-related information. These findings suggest that behavioral patterns learned from general psychological data can transfer to complex software engineering tasks such as program comprehension. More broadly, they point toward foundation models of human cognition as a basis for modeling developer behavior in software engineering.

</details>


### [350] [From GUI Tests to Conversational Interaction: A New Perspective on App-Specific Voice Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11387)
*Xue Qin,Sumesh Surendran Letha*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: GUI test code can be repurposed via LLMs to automatically synthesize app-specific voice assistants, grounding conversational interaction in existing executable specifications rather than requiring manual reimplementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System-level voice assistants are poorly aligned with app-specific behavior, forcing developers to manually reimplement application logic for voice interaction, which incurs high development and maintenance costs.

Method: An LLM-driven pipeline that reinterprets GUI test methods (behavior-preserving, executable specifications) into voice assistant artifacts — including voice intents, capability descriptions, and executable action plans — demonstrated through the AppVA prototype on Android.

Result: Preliminary evaluation across five open-source Android applications shows that GUI test code can be successfully reused to synthesize app-specific voice assistants.

Conclusion: The approach reveals a broader research direction at the intersection of software testing, interaction design, and LLM-enabled automation, where test code serves as a reusable bridge between application behavior and conversational interfaces.

Abstract: Voice assistants are widely deployed on mobile platforms, yet most are designed as system-level services that remain poorly aligned with application-specific behavior. As a result, enabling voice interaction at the app level requires developers to manually reimplement application logic, leading to high development and maintenance costs.
  We propose an LLM-driven approach to automating the development of app-specific voice assistants by repurposing GUI test code, which encodes behavior-preserving, executable specifications of application functionality. In this paper, we present a perspective in which large language models reinterpret GUI tests as bridges between application behavior and conversational interaction. By transforming test methods into app-specific VA artifacts, such as voice intents, capability descriptions, and executable action plans, our approach grounds voice assistants directly in existing application logic rather than external specifications.
  We illustrate this vision through AppVA, a research prototype on Android. Our preliminary results across five open-source applications suggest that GUI test code can be reused beyond testing, enabling the synthesis of app-specific voice assistants and highlighting a broader research direction at the intersection of software testing, interaction design, and LLM-enabled automation.

</details>


### [351] [TerraRepair: A Tool-Grounded LLM Agent for Infrastructure-as-Code Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11390)
*Minase Mekete Mengistu,Juri Di Rocco,Phuong T. Nguyen,Davide Di Ruscio*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TerraRepair is a tool-grounded LLM agent that improves automated repair of Terraform IaC misconfigurations by retrieving dependency context, consulting provider schemas, and re-running scanners. It achieves substantial fix-rate improvements (26.6%→78.4% on Checkov; 44.8%→72.4% on Trivy) over a one-shot baseline, while escalating rather than hallucinating when deployment-specific context is missing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current IaC scanners can detect cloud misconfigurations in Terraform before deployment, but repair remains manual. Existing LLM-based repair approaches suffer from two critical failure modes: (1) hallucinating unsupported Terraform constructs, and (2) suppressing scanner warnings without actually resolving the underlying misconfiguration. The authors aim to address these limitations through tool grounding and principled escalation.

Method: TerraRepair is a tool-grounded LLM agent that: (1) retrieves dependency context from Terraform cross-references, (2) consults the installed provider schema for valid attribute types and resource definitions, (3) re-runs the IaC scanner (Checkov or Trivy) to verify that the candidate repair actually resolves the flagged finding, and (4) escalates findings when required deployment-specific context is unavailable, rather than fabricating plausible but incorrect fixes. The approach is compared against a controlled one-shot LLM baseline.

Result: On vulnerable-by-design Terraform repositories spanning AWS, Azure, and GCP, TerraRepair improved scanner-verified fix rates from 26.6% to 78.4% (Checkov) and from 44.8% to 72.4% (Trivy) on the combined AWS benchmark compared to the one-shot baseline. Repairs were labelled as correct under a majority-vote protocol.

Conclusion: Tool grounding substantially improves scanner-verified LLM-based IaC repair on the studied benchmarks. The primary remaining knowledge boundary for full autonomy is the absence of deployment-specific context, which the escalation mechanism explicitly handles rather than masking with hallucinated fixes.

Abstract: Background: Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) scanners detect cloud misconfigurations in Terraform and other IaC languages before deployment, but repairing the flagged configurations remains largely manual. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based repair approaches can repair some findings, but may hallucinate unsupported constructs or suppress warnings without fixing the issue. Aims: We study whether tool grounding can improve LLM-based Terraform repair, and when a finding should be escalated because the required deploymnet-specific context is not availble. Method: We present TerraRepair, a prototype of a tool-grounded LLM agent for Terraform repair with structured escalation. TerraRepair retrieves dependency context from Terraform references, consults the installed provider schema, and re-runs the scanner before returning a candidate repair. Then teh required context is absent, TerraRepair escalates instead of fabricating a plausible fix. Results: We evaluate our tool on two vulnerable-by-design Terraform repositories using two IaC security scanners, Checkov and Trivy, across AWS, Azure, and GCP. On the combined AWS benchmark, TerraRepair improves scanner-verified fix rates from 26.6% to 78.4% on Checkov and from 44.8% to 72.4% on Trivy, compared with a controlled one-shot baseline. It repairs are labelled as correct under a majority-vote protocol. Conclusions: These emerging results show that tool grounding can substantially improve scanner-verified LLM-based IaC repair on the studied benchmarks, while missing deployment-specific context remains the main knowledge boundary for full autonomy.

</details>


### [352] [Knowledge-Guided Synthetic Bug Feedback for LLM-Based Unit Test Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11573)
*Ziheng Wang,Maike Li,Chen Zhi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework that leverages historical real-bug mechanisms — transformed into retrievable, executable synthetic bugs — to guide LLM-based unit test generation toward detecting actual defects, demonstrating improved bug detection over multiple baseline approaches on the Defects4J benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can generate executable unit tests, these tests often fail to reveal real defects because they lack alignment with the specific mechanisms that cause bugs. The authors aim to bridge this gap by exploiting historical bug-fix knowledge to produce tests that target genuine defect patterns.

Method: The framework first constructs structural and semantic representations from historical real-bug records. For a given focal method, it retrieves applicable bug mechanisms and instantiates them as synthetic bugs injected into the code. These synthetic bugs serve as executable feedback targets, guiding an iterative test-generation loop where LLM-generated tests are refined until they can detect the synthetic bugs, thereby aligning them with real defect patterns.

Result: Evaluated on method-level bug detection tasks from Defects4J, the mechanism-guided synthetic-bug feedback approach outperformed five categories of baselines: execution-based, coverage-based, mutation-based, knowledge-based, and search-based test generation strategies.

Conclusion: Organizing real-bug mechanisms as retrievable and executable feedback targets is an effective strategy for steering LLM-generated tests toward producing both bug-triggering inputs and accurate behavioral oracles, thereby improving real defect detection.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for unit test generation, but executable tests do not necessarily reveal real defects. This paper studies how historical real-bug mechanisms can be transformed into executable feedback targets for LLM-based unit test generation. The proposed framework constructs structural and semantic representations of real-bug records, retrieves mechanisms applicable to a focal method, and instantiates them as synthetic bugs that guide iterative test enhancement. We evaluate the approach on method-level real-bug detection tasks from Defects4J and show that mechanism-guided synthetic-bug feedback improves real-bug detection over execution-, coverage-, mutation-, knowledge-, and search-based baselines. The results suggest that organizing real-bug mechanisms as retrievable and executable feedback targets is an effective way to guide generated tests toward bug-triggering inputs and behavioral oracles.

</details>


### [353] [ThinkLog: Leveraging Reasoning for Log Statement Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11615)
*Kazuki Kusama,Honglin Shu,Masanari Kondo,Tao Xiao,Yasutaka Kamei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ThinkLog is an LLM-based method for end-to-end log statement generation that incorporates reasoning into prompts as few-shot examples, achieving 20.55% accuracy (a 15.4% improvement over the best existing method) at roughly half the inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Developers spend significant effort on log statement generation — identifying log locations, assigning severity levels, and writing messages — yet existing end-to-end automated methods exhibit limited accuracy.

Method: ThinkLog injects reasoning into LLM prompts as few-shot examples, guiding the model to make decisions about log insertion, severity level assignment, and message generation in an end-to-end fashion.

Result: Evaluated on 9,619 Java methods from public GitHub repositories, ThinkLog achieves 20.55% log statement generation accuracy, a 15.4% relative improvement over the best existing method, at approximately 50% of the inference cost (USD).

Conclusion: Incorporating reasoning into LLM prompts is an effective and cost-efficient approach to improving end-to-end log statement generation accuracy.

Abstract: Runtime logs are an important source of information that supports software maintenance. To obtain useful logs, developers spend significant effort identifying appropriate log locations, assigning correct severity levels, and writing concise yet informative messages. Therefore, end-to-end automated log statement generation can help reduce this burden, and prior work has proposed many methods for this task. However, existing methods still exhibit limited accuracy. To address this problem, we propose ThinkLog, an LLM-based end-to-end log statement generation method. The core idea of ThinkLog is to incorporate reasoning that helps LLMs make decisions about log insertion, severity level assignment, and message generation, thereby improving log statement generation accuracy. ThinkLog injects reasoning into prompts as few-shot examples and guides LLMs to generate appropriate log statements. Evaluated on 9,619 Java methods extracted from public GitHub repositories, ThinkLog achieves 20.55% log statement generation accuracy, representing a 15.4% improvement over the best existing method. Moreover, these improvements were achieved at approximately 50% of the inference cost (USD) compared to the best existing method. These results show that leveraging reasoning is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve the accuracy of end-to-end log statement generation.

</details>


### [354] [Which Optimizer, At What Budget? A Tournament of Optimizers for Search-Based SE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11705)
*Kishan Kumar Ganguly,Tim Menzies*

Main category: cs.SE
