TL;DR: A large-scale tournament of 20 optimizers across 106 software engineering optimization tasks reveals no single best optimizer; the optimal choice depends on labeling budget. A cheap lookup table based on two task attributes can predict the best optimizer, matching or beating a hindsight oracle on ~75% of tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software configuration and tuning is expensive and error-prone, with hundreds of interacting options. While automated optimization is the standard solution, practitioners face a confusing landscape of many optimizers with misleading guidance (e.g., NSGA-II is widely recommended despite being 20x less sample-efficient than alternatives). There is no principled way to select the right optimizer for a given task and budget.

Method: The authors cluster 20 optimizers based on six assumptions about the data. They run a tournament across all 20 optimizers on 106 SE optimization tasks at four different labeling budgets (total: 14,000+ CPU hours). They then derive a predictive model using two cheap-to-compute task attributes plus labeling budget, enabling optimizer selection via a simple table lookup.

Result: No single optimizer dominates across all budgets. The best optimizer shifts with budget: a geometric active learner wins when labels are scarce, while differential evolution excels when labels are plentiful. An optimizer crowned best at one budget is wrong at another on up to 50% of tasks. The proposed lookup table ties or beats a hindsight oracle on approximately 75% of held-out tasks, eliminating the need for costly per-domain tournaments.

Conclusion: Practitioners should select optimizers based on labeling budget and task characteristics rather than relying on one-size-fits-all recommendations. The lookup table approach makes this selection practical and cost-effective. All artifacts are open-sourced to support reproducibility and adoption.

Abstract: Configuring and tuning modern software is unavoidable, expensive, and error-prone: a single system can expose hundreds of interacting options, and scoring one setting can mean a full build or test run. The standard response is automated optimization, but the number of available optimizers is large and growing. And some of the guidance for selecting among them is misleading: NSGA-II, for example, is widely recommended, yet other algorithms reach the same results using only 1/20th as many evaluations.
  To help practitioners make better choices about tools to configure their systems, we cluster 20 optimizers, based on six assumptions about the data. Next, we run a tournament across those optimizers, using 106 SE optimization tasks at four labeling budgets (taking 14,000+ CPU hours). We find that no optimizer wins outright. The best one migrates with the budget (from a geometric active learner when labels are scarce to differential evolution when labels are plentiful) so a winner "crowned" at one budget is wrong at another on up to half our tasks.
  Running such a tournament for every new domain is impractical due to its CPU cost. Fortunately, we find that those 14,000 hours can be replaced by a table lookup over two cheap-to-obtain task attributes (plus the labeling budget). Predictions from this table tie or beat a hindsight oracle on $\approx 75%$ of held-out tasks.
  To support open science, our tournament and replication package are open-sourced for SBSE researchers and practitioners at https://github.com/KKGanguly/OptimizerTournament.

</details>


### [355] [Evaluating RE Practices for Explainability: Synthesizing Insights from Daimler Truck into an Explainable RE Framework Proposal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11771)
*Umm-e- Habiba,Lucas Mauser,Jonas Fritzsch,Justus Bogner,Stefan Wagner*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An industrial study at Daimler Truck reveals that current Requirements Engineering practices inadequately support explainability requirements across elicitation, specification, and validation, due to conceptual ambiguity, limited testability, and regulatory uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite explainability being critical for AI systems in safety-critical domains, there is little empirical understanding of how existing RE practices support explainability requirements in industrial settings across the full RE lifecycle.

Method: A multi-phase qualitative study with eight practitioners at Daimler Truck, using think-aloud protocols and moderated group discussions across three RE steps: requirements elicitation, specification, and validation.

Result: Recurring challenges were identified: conceptual ambiguity during elicitation, limited testability and expressiveness during specification, and fragmented validation stemming from vague criteria and regulatory uncertainty.

Conclusion: Current RE practices offer limited systematic support for explainability requirements. The paper contributes empirical insights into step-specific and cross-cutting challenges and proposes a research vision for an empirically grounded RE framework for explainable AI systems.

Abstract: Explainability has emerged as a critical requirement for AI-based systems, particularly in safety-critical and regulated domains. Although prior research has proposed frameworks, patterns, and user-centered approaches to support explainability, there is limited empirical understanding of how existing Requirements Engineering (RE) practices support explainability requirements across the RE lifecycle, especially in an industrial context. This paper reports early findings from an ongoing industry-based study investigating how explainability requirements are elicited, specified, and validated using established RE techniques. We conducted a multi-phase qualitative study with eight practitioners at Daimler Truck, employing think-aloud protocols and moderated group discussions across requirements elicitation, specification, and validation steps. Our preliminary analysis reveals recurring challenges across all steps, including conceptual ambiguity during elicitation, limited testability and expressiveness during specification, and fragmented validation due to vague criteria and regulatory uncertainty. These findings indicate that current RE practices provide limited support to systematically address explainability requirements. The paper contributes empirical insights into step-specific and cross-cutting challenges and outlines a research vision toward developing an empirically grounded RE framework for explainable AI-based systems.

</details>

### [356] [An LLM-powered Agentic Recommendation System for Connected TV Content Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09988)
*Lei Shi,Di Wang,Harry Tran,Helsing Xu,Yuchen Lu,Dhara Ghodasara,Wilson Chaney,Xueting Liao,Jerry Yu,Huayu Ding,Mingze Gao,Shike Mei,Shuo Tang,Zhe Zhang,Jianming He,Abhishek Kumar,Haotian Wu,Hamed Firooz,Li Li*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Presents an LLM-powered agentic recommendation system for Connected TV that uses a hybrid architecture combining LLM reasoning for heterogeneous contextual signals with traditional ML for retrieval efficiency and personalization, addressing practical challenges like inference latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional recommendation systems struggle to incorporate diverse, unstructured contextual signals (trending topics, breaking news, cultural events) because they rely on structured behavioral data with fixed schemas. Incorporating such signals typically requires heavy feature engineering, custom data pipelines, and manual heuristics. LLMs offer natural reasoning over unstructured data but fall short on retrieval efficiency, personalization precision, and scalability compared to traditional ML models.

Method: An agentic architecture that orchestrates specialized components, delegating sub-tasks to either LLM-based or traditional ML methods depending on suitability. LLMs handle processing and synthesizing heterogeneous contextual signals, while traditional ML components manage retrieval and ranking tasks requiring efficiency and precision. The key engineering contribution is overcoming LLM inference latency through architectural design choices.

Result: The hybrid agentic system successfully integrates diverse contextual signals into the recommendation pipeline while maintaining performance. The paper shares practical insights, trade-offs, and lessons learned from building this system, particularly around mitigating LLM inference latency in production.

Conclusion: A hybrid agentic architecture that combines LLM flexibility with traditional ML performance is a viable path for incorporating unstructured contextual signals into production recommendation systems. The main contribution is the engineering approach to overcoming LLM practical limitations, especially inference latency.

Abstract: Recommendation systems, from traditional multi-stage to recent unified generative architectures, face challenges in incorporating diverse contextual signals, such as trending topics, breaking news, cultural events, and cross-surface user activities, into their ranking pipelines. These systems are designed to consume structured behavioral signals with consistent schemas, and lack the reasoning capability to naturally process unstructured or heterogeneously formatted contextual information. Incorporating such signals typically requires feature engineering, bespoke data pipelines, and carefully tuned heuristics. In this paper, we present an LLM-powered agentic recommendation system designed for Connected TV (CTV) content discovery that addresses these limitations. Our system leverages the reasoning capabilities of large language models to naturally process and synthesize diverse signals across varying schemas and structures, eliminating much of the manual integration inherent in traditional ranking and retrieval systems. Recognizing that current LLM-based solutions still fall short of traditional machine learning models in several recommendation tasks, including retrieval efficiency, personalization precision, and scalability, we adopt an agentic architecture that orchestrates specialized components, allowing each sub-task to be handled by the most suitable method, whether LLM-based or traditional ML. The main contribution of this work is our engineering approach to successfully overcoming the practical limitations of enabling LLM for recommendation, particularly inference latency. We share insights from our work and discuss the trade-offs and lessons learned in building a hybrid system that combines the flexibility of LLMs with the performance of established recommendation techniques.

</details>


### [357] [Tokenizing Numerical and Embedding Features for LLM RecSys](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10016)
*Zhe Xu,Ankit Peshin,Chiyu Zhang,Feng Qi,Johnson Lui,Anil Ramakrishna,Justin Johnson,Carl Hu,Kaushik Rangadurai,Luke Simon*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Proposes a soft-token fusion framework that maps numerical and dense embedding features into the LLM embedding space, enabling LLM-based recommenders to leverage heterogeneous non-textual signals through the standard token interface, with experiments showing improved retrieval performance on Amazon benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most LLM-based recommenders operate on discrete textual tokens, but real-world recommendation pipelines depend heavily on continuous numerical features and dense embeddings from upstream feature engineering or pretrained encoders. This mismatch prevents LLM-based models from exploiting fine-grained non-textual signals, motivating a unified interface for heterogeneous feature types.

Method: A soft-token fusion framework that projects numerical and embedding features into the LLM's token embedding space, treating them as "soft tokens." The framework is instantiated in a shared-parameter LLM-based two-tower retrieval model with an interaction-based fusion module that refines embedding and numerical soft tokens before insertion into the LLM input, rather than naive concatenation.

Result: Experiments on three Amazon recommendation benchmarks demonstrate that soft-token fusion improves retrieval performance over LLM-based baselines, and that the interaction-based fusion approach outperforms direct concatenation of heterogeneous soft tokens.

Conclusion: Integrating numerical and embedding features via soft-token fusion effectively bridges the gap between discrete text and continuous non-textual signals in LLM-based recommenders, with interaction-based refinement yielding further gains over simple concatenation strategies.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as backbone architectures for recommender systems because of their strong sequence modeling and representation learning capabilities. However, most LLM-based recommenders operate primarily on discrete textual tokens, whereas practical recommendation pipelines also rely on continuous numerical features and dense embedding features produced by upstream feature engineering or pretrained encoders. This mismatch limits the ability of LLM-based models to exploit fine-grained non-textual signals. We propose a soft-token fusion framework that maps numerical and embedding features into the LLM embedding space, allowing heterogeneous recommendation signals to be consumed through the standard token interface. We instantiate the framework in a shared-parameter LLM-based two-tower retrieval model and introduce an interaction-based fusion module that refines embedding and numerical soft tokens before they are inserted into the final LLM input. Experiments on three Amazon recommendation benchmarks show that soft-token fusion improves retrieval performance over LLM-based baselines, and that interaction-based fusion is more effective than direct concatenation of heterogeneous soft tokens.

</details>


### [358] [The Effect of Multi-Lingual and Keyword Adversarial Injection on LLM Relevance Judgment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10080)
*Nguyen Khoi Vo,Duy Duong Tuong,Oleg Zendel,Mark Sanderson*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Cross-lingual prompt injection attacks effectively manipulate LLM-based relevance judgments, inflating scores while evading defenses across 8 languages, revealing a critical robustness gap in LLM-as-a-judge systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as automated judges for relevance evaluation in IR, but their robustness to adversarial manipulation — especially cross-lingual prompt injection — is poorly understood, particularly in multilingual contexts.

Method: The authors evaluate instruction-based and content-based cross-lingual prompt injection attacks across 8 languages (varying resource levels) on two open-weight LLMs using TREC Deep Learning collections under established prompting frameworks. They also test existing defenses and adapted variants.

Result: Multilingual query-based injections significantly inflate relevance scores while evading current defenses. Although defenses can be modified to mitigate attacks, injections are easily adapted to bypass these modifications. Language generalization itself serves as an effective attack vector.

Conclusion: Current defense mechanisms are insufficient against cross-lingual prompt injection attacks on LLM relevance judges. More robust, proactive evaluation frameworks are urgently needed, as linguistic diversity can be exploited to undermine LLM-as-a-judge reliability.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as automated judges
  for relevance evaluation in information retrieval, yet their robustness to
  adversarial manipulation remains insufficiently understood, particularly in
  multilingual settings. In this work, we investigate the impact of
  cross-lingual prompt injection attacks on LLM-based relevance judgments using
  TREC Deep Learning collections and two open-weight models under established
  prompting frameworks. We examine both instruction-based and content-based
  injection strategies in 8 languages spanning different resource levels. Our
  results demonstrate that multilingual query-based injections are highly
  effective in inflating relevance scores while simultaneously evading existing
  prompt-injection defenses. We further found that, although existing defense
  mechanisms can be modified to mitigate such attacks, these injections can be
  easily adapted to bypass them. These findings highlight a critical gap in
  current defense approaches and demonstrate that language generalization can
  act as an attack vector, underscoring the need for more robust and proactive
  evaluation frameworks for LLM-as-a-judge systems.

</details>


### [359] [Scaling and Stabilizing Large-Scale Embedding-Based Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10096)
*Zhen Yang,Juexin Lin,Hongwei Shang,Kaihao Li,Feng Liu,Satya Chembolu,Xunfan Cai,Xinyi Liu,Cun Mu,Tony Lee,Ciya Liao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Walmart's unified EBR pipeline combines hybrid hard negative mining (online cross-batch + offline cross-encoder/metadata heuristics) with legacy-aware distillation to transition from DistilBERT to GTE-base, achieving +7.34% NDCG@5 and +0.50% gross revenue lift in production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two core challenges in large-scale e-commerce EBR: (1) training-inference gap where dual-encoders are optimized on narrow candidate pools but must discriminate against hundreds of millions of items at inference; (2) replacing mature but lower-capacity encoders with higher-capacity backbones risks losing domain-specific knowledge and causing inconsistent retrieval behavior.

Method: (1) Hybrid Hard Negative Mining: Online Cross-Batch Sampling expands negative diversity by an order of magnitude; Hybrid Offline Mining leverages cross-encoder predictions combined with metadata heuristics to surface nuanced mismatches. (2) Legacy-Aware Distillation: A Warm-Start Distillation technique transfers domain-specific expertise from the legacy DistilBERT model to the new GTE-base encoder, ensuring smooth transition and knowledge retention.

Result: Offline experiments and online A/B testing validated the pipeline. In live production deployment: +7.34% improvement in NDCG@5 and +0.50% lift in gross revenue.

Conclusion: The unified pipeline effectively addresses both signal quality and model evolution challenges in production-scale e-commerce EBR. The combination of diversified hybrid hard negative mining and legacy-aware warm-start distillation enables seamless upgrades to higher-capacity encoders while retaining valuable domain knowledge, yielding significant business impact at Walmart scale.

Abstract: Embedding-based retrieval (EBR) is foundational to large-scale e-commerce search, yet its effectiveness is often constrained by the quality of training signals and the representational capacity of the encoder. Standard dual-encoders suffer from a training-inference gap: they are optimized on narrow candidate pools but must discriminate against hundreds of millions of items during inference. Furthermore, while transitioning to higher-capacity backbones can mitigate this gap, simply replacing a mature model can lead to inconsistent retrieval behavior and a loss of the domain-specific knowledge established in previous iterations. In this paper, we present a unified pipeline deployed at Walmart that addresses both signal quality and model evolution. Our contributions are two-fold: (1) Hybrid Hard Negative Mining: We integrate Online Cross-Batch Sampling to increase negative diversity by an order of magnitude and Hybrid Offline Mining, which combines cross-encoder predictions with metadata heuristics to identify nuanced mismatches. (2) Legacy-Aware Distillation: We transition from DistilBERT to a higher-capacity GTE-base encoder. To ensure a smooth and superior transition, we introduce a Warm-Start Distillation technique that transfers domain-specific expertise from the legacy model to the new backbone. Validated through extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing, the proposed pipeline is deployed in live production, delivering a +7.34% improvement in NDCG@5 and a +0.50% lift in gross revenue.

</details>


### [360] [Adaptive Model Compression (AMC): Saliency-Driven Resource Allocation for Ultra-Low-Power Transformer Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10109)
*Jiayin Hu,Kai Yuan,Vanessa Hu,Xuetao Yin,Jianhua Li,Sean Suchter*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Adaptive Model Compression (AMC) is a saliency-driven framework that dynamically allocates hardware resources based on token importance, achieving 59.2% energy reduction and 2.24× throughput increase on 45nm CMOS with only 3.6% accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static inference in large-scale transformer models imposes uniform computational intensity on both simple and complex tokens, causing excessive energy and memory overhead that hinders deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

Method: AMC employs a multi-tier architecture that uses saliency detection to identify high-importance tokens for full-precision processing, while aggressively reducing the rank (low-rank approximation) and bit-width (quantization) of less significant tokens, thereby dynamically allocating hardware resources based on token-level importance.

Result: On 45nm CMOS hardware, AMC achieves a 59.2% reduction in system energy and a 2.24× increase in throughput, with only a marginal 3.6% accuracy degradation compared to the uncompressed baseline.

Conclusion: By confining high-definition computation to salient tokens, AMC effectively extends mobile device battery life while maintaining robust performance, demonstrating that dynamic, importance-aware resource allocation is a viable strategy for deploying transformers at the edge.

Abstract: Deploying large-scale transformer models on resource-constrained edge devices remains a challenge due to the high energy and memory overhead inherent in static inference, which processes simple and complex tokens with uniform intensity. To address this, we propose Adaptive Model Compression (AMC), a saliency-driven framework that dynamically allocates hardware resources based on token importance. By implementing a multi-tier architecture, our system identifies critical high-saliency information for full-precision processing while aggressively reducing the rank and bit-width of less significant data. Experimental results demonstrate that AMC achieves a 59.2% reduction in system energy and a 2.24x increase in throughput on 45nm CMOS hardware. This approach effectively extends the battery life of mobile devices by utilizing high-definition compute only where necessary, maintaining robust performance with a marginal 3.6% accuracy trade-off.

</details>


### [361] [MC-RAG System: A Structure-Driven RAG System for Multi-Constraint Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10151)
*Xiao Zhang,Yang Wan,Yi Li,Miao Xie,Chunli Lv*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MC-RAG is a structure-driven Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that addresses multi-constraint queries by reformulating retrieval as subgraph matching over a knowledge graph, enabling interpretable and constraint-consistent answer generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG systems often fail on complex multi-constraint queries, producing answers with constraint violations, factual inconsistencies, or hallucinations. There is a need for a more structured, interpretable approach that ensures constraint satisfaction during retrieval and generation.

Method: MC-RAG reformulates retrieval as a subgraph matching problem over a knowledge graph. It integrates semantic and structural embeddings with path-level indexing to perform structure-aware, constraint-consistent retrieval. The system parses multi-constraint queries, matches them structurally against the knowledge graph, and generates answers grounded in the matched subgraphs.

Result: The paper presents a demonstration system where users can input medical or encyclopedic multi-constraint queries, visualize constraint parsing, structural matching, and answer generation in an end-to-end, interactive, and explainable RAG pipeline. A demo video accompanies the submission.

Conclusion: MC-RAG provides an interpretable and structurally grounded alternative to traditional RAG systems, effectively handling multi-constraint queries through knowledge graph-based subgraph matching, with demonstrable applicability in medical and encyclopedic domains.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are widely adopted in question answering, yet they often fail to satisfy complex multi-constraint queries, leading to constraint violations, factual inconsistencies, or hallucinations. We present Structure-Driven RAG System for Multi-Constraint Queries(MC-RAG), a structure-driven RAG system that reformulates retrieval as a subgraph matching problem over a knowledge graph. By integrating semantic and structural embeddings with path-level indexing, MC-RAG performs interpretable, structure-aware, and constraint-consistent retrieval and generation. During the demonstration, participants can input medical or encyclopedic multi-constraint queries, visualize how the system parses constraints, performs structural matching, and generates answers, thereby experiencing an end-to-end, interactive, and explainable RAG pipeline. A demo video is available at https://youtu.be/J8kahzmAnu0.

</details>


### [362] [From Patent Expiry to Business Pathways: AI Workflows for Activating Innovation Archives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10179)
*Sidney Shapiro,Mark Price*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper proposes an AI-enabled framework to surface expired/lapsing patents, identify technology trends, and translate patent disclosures into structured commercialization pathways. A proof of concept using CIPO records and a local Qwen3.6 model demonstrates reproducible ingestion, stable scoring, and schema-conformant outputs, while highlighting gaps in legal-status coverage and the necessity of expert review.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Patent databases contain vast technical knowledge that becomes difficult to access and reuse once patents expire or lapse. Current approaches treat patent expiry primarily as a legal problem rather than as a business opportunity signal. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reframing expiry as both a business signal and an archival transition, enabling entrepreneurs and organizations to convert dormant technical disclosures into actionable commercialization pathways.

Method: The framework integrates multiple components: patent metadata, maintenance-fee records, legal-status indicators, semantic search, patent-family analysis, market signals, and generative AI workflows. A transparent scoring model ranks patent candidates based on customer need, implementation feasibility, channel access, and market timing. A proof of concept was conducted on 378 records from a weekly CIPO ST.96 archive, identifying 20 expired/lapsed/near-expiry candidates. A locally hosted Qwen3.6 model was used to populate structured review packets. Stability was tested via weight perturbation experiments.

Result: The proof of concept demonstrated (1) reproducible ingestion of patent records, (2) stable rankings under weight perturbation of the scoring model, and (3) schema-conformant output from the generative AI component. However, the evaluation also exposed incomplete legal-status coverage in available data sources and confirmed that register verification and expert review remain necessary components of any practical system.

Conclusion: AI can serve as an effective discovery and translation layer for dormant technical knowledge in patent archives, but deployed systems must explicitly represent and communicate legal uncertainty, data limitations, and commercialization risk rather than presenting outputs as definitive.

Abstract: Patent databases represent one of the largest public archives of technical knowledge, yet much of this knowledge remains difficult to identify, interpret, and reuse once patent rights expire or lapse. This paper proposes an AI-enabled framework for discovering expired and lapsing patents, identifying technology trends, and translating patent disclosures into business pathways. We use pathways to mean structured commercialization routes such as SaaS products, services, licensing packages, consulting playbooks, training offerings, data products, or internal process tools. The framework treats patent expiry as both a business signal and an archival transition, not primarily as a legal problem. Legal status remains important, but it is one risk-screening input alongside customer need, implementation feasibility, channel access, and market timing. We describe a system architecture that combines patent metadata, maintenance-fee records, legal-status indicators, semantic search, patent-family analysis, market signals, and generative AI workflows. A proof of concept parses all 378 records in an official weekly CIPO ST.96 archive, identifies 20 expired, lapsed, or near-expiry candidates, tests the stability of the transparent scoring model, and uses a locally hosted Qwen3.6 model to populate structured review packets. The evaluation demonstrates reproducible ingestion, stable rankings under weight perturbation, and schema-conformant model output, while also exposing incomplete legal-status coverage and the need for register and expert review. We argue that AI can function as a discovery and translation layer for dormant technical knowledge, but that such systems must explicitly represent legal uncertainty, data limitations, and commercialization risk.

</details>


### [363] [Multilingual Semantic Retrieval for Apple Music Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10239)
*Vishalaksh Aggarwal,Kevin Sebastian,Vivek Kanojiya,Leo Le,Nick Tucey,Santosh Shankar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Apple Music deployed a 305M-parameter multilingual bi-encoder for semantic retrieval across 150+ storefronts, achieving a 2.28% conversion-rate lift, 86% reduction in no-result searches, and 7.93% CR lift on tail queries — with no regressions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: At Apple Music's scale (150+ storefronts, dozens of languages, hundreds of thousands of new tracks daily), misspelled, transliterated, and cross-lingual queries dominate search failures. Tail queries — the majority of unique queries — suffer most from token-based retrieval limitations. The goal is to improve recall for these hard queries without degrading performance on well-served head queries or requiring retraining of downstream rankers.

Method: A 305M-parameter Siamese bi-encoder is fine-tuned from GTE-multilingual-base using curriculum-scheduled multi-objective training. The model is integrated via a hybrid retrieval architecture that blends dense nearest-neighbor results with the existing token-based index using quantile distribution matching — crucially, this allows deployment without retraining downstream LTR rankers. The system operates across all storefronts and languages simultaneously.

Result: Offline: 69% relative improvement in Hit@10 over GTE-multilingual-base. Online A/B test (worldwide): 2.28% relative CR lift overall; 86% reduction in no-result rate; gains across every storefront with zero regressions. Stratified by query frequency: tail queries saw 7.93% relative CR lift, mid-frequency 0.89%, head queries 0.14% — confirming targeted improvement on hard queries without disturbing popular ones.

Conclusion: Semantic retrieval via a multilingual bi-encoder significantly improves search quality at scale, with disproportionate benefits for tail queries. The quantile distribution matching approach enables safe deployment without downstream retraining. This represents one of the largest search-quality improvements ever deployed on Apple Music.

Abstract: Apple Music serves listeners across 150+ storefronts in dozens of languages, with a catalog that grows by hundreds of thousands of new tracks daily. At this scale, search recall on misspelled, transliterated, and cross-lingual queries becomes a dominant driver of session quality, particularly for tail queries that account for the majority of unique queries. We present a multilingual semantic retrieval system built on a 305M-parameter Siamese bi-encoder fine-tuned from GTE-multilingual-base with curriculum-scheduled multi-objective training. The model is integrated into the search stack via a hybrid retrieval architecture that blends dense nearest-neighbor results with the existing token-based index using quantile distribution matching, enabling deployment without retraining downstream rankers. Offline, the model achieves a 69% relative improvement in Hit@10 over GTE-multilingual-base. In a worldwide online A/B test, the system delivers a 2.28% relative conversion-rate (CR) lift overall, an 86% reduction in the no-result rate, and gains across every storefront with no observed regressions. The improvement is concentrated where it is needed most: tail queries see a 7.93% relative CR lift, compared with 0.89% for mid-frequency queries and 0.14% for head queries -- evidence that semantic retrieval improves recall on hard queries without disturbing well-served popular ones. To our knowledge, this is one of the largest search-quality improvements deployed on the platform.

</details>


### [364] [SVD-RAG: Efficient Tree-Organized Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Singular Value Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10316)
*Zhihui Sun*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SVD-RAG proposes using Singular Value Decomposition on dense sentence embeddings for extractive summarization in hierarchical RAG systems, replacing costly LLM-based abstractive summarization with a deterministic, efficient method that achieves comparable retrieval quality while being 317x faster in tree construction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hierarchical RAG systems like RAPTOR use expensive LLM-based abstractive summarization at each internal tree node, making large-scale deployment prohibitively costly. A cheaper, deterministic alternative is needed that preserves retrieval quality.

Method: SVD-RAG applies Singular Value Decomposition directly on dense sentence embedding matrices (not sparse TF-IDF as in classical LSA) to perform extractive summarization. It selects the most informative sentences based on their energy contribution in the principal components, using an energy-ratio threshold τ to adaptively control compression based on content complexity.

Result: In head-to-head comparison, SVD-RAG achieves MRR of 0.867 vs. RAPTOR's 0.875 and Recall@1 of 0.483 vs. 0.458 — within 1-5% of LLM-based summarization quality — while building trees 317x faster (0.1s vs. 31.7s) and reducing token consumption by ~85%. On a multi-topic benchmark, it achieves 4.2x improvement in Recall@1 and 3.1x improvement in MRR over flat embedding retrieval.

Conclusion: SVD-based extractive summarization is a viable, cost-efficient, and deterministic alternative to LLM-based abstractive summarization for hierarchical RAG, offering near-equivalent retrieval performance with dramatic speed and cost improvements.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models by retrieving relevant documents from external knowledge bases. Recent work by Sarthi et al. (2024) introduced RAPTOR, which organizes documents into hierarchical tree structures for efficient retrieval, but requires expensive LLM-based abstractive summarization at each internal node -- making large-scale deployment prohibitively costly.
  We present SVD-RAG, the first method to apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on dense sentence embedding matrices for extractive summarization in hierarchical RAG. Unlike classical LSA which operates on sparse TF-IDF matrices, SVD-RAG exploits the rich semantic representations of modern embedding models, identifying the most informative sentences through their energy contribution in the principal components. Our approach is (1) deterministic -- unlike LLM-based summarization, SVD produces identical results for the same input; (2) cost-efficient -- tree construction requires no additional API calls beyond the initial embedding, reducing token consumption by ~85%; and (3) content-adaptive -- the energy-ratio threshold tau automatically adjusts compression based on content complexity. In a controlled head-to-head comparison using identical corpora, clustering, and beam search, SVD-RAG achieves retrieval quality within 1-5% of RAPTOR with LLM summarization (MRR 0.867 vs. 0.875, Recall@1 0.483 vs. 0.458) while building the tree 317x faster (0.1s vs. 31.7s). On a scaled multi-topic benchmark with 205 chunks and 100 queries across 20 topic variations, SVD-RAG achieves a 4.2x improvement in Recall@1 and 3.1x improvement in MRR over flat embedding retrieval. We provide a detailed cost analysis and parameter sensitivity study. Our implementation is released as an open-source Python package.

</details>


### [365] [Implicit Fine-tuning via Context Engineering: A Curriculum Learning Framework for Multimodal Entity Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10532)
*Yunpeng Hong,Chenyang Bu,Di Wu,Yi He,Xindong Wu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: PTFEA theoretically unifies context engineering and fine-tuning for Multimodal Entity Alignment, then proposes a curriculum-learning-inspired framework that translates fine-tuning strategies into interpretable context engineering, achieving superior performance with dramatically reduced runtime and token consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MMEA methods rely on black-box context engineering strategies that depend on LLM parameter capacity and lack theoretical interpretability. There is no theoretical framework explaining why context engineering works in MMEA, nor a systematic way to translate fine-tuning principles into interpretable prompt design.

Method: The authors (1) theoretically prove the mathematical equivalence between context engineering (prompt components) and contrastive learning-based sequential fine-tuning in MMEA; (2) propose PTFEA, which uses adaptive difficulty modulation with confidence thresholds to dynamically adjust information injection stages (equating curriculum learning weights with context sample selection); and (3) employs three-stage progressive inference that processes entity information from simple to complex cases, mirroring the gradient descent process of fine-tuning.

Result: PTFEA consistently outperforms strong baselines across five public datasets. On ICWIKI, it narrows the H@1 gap between Qwen2.5-72B and 14B to only 0.6%. Compared to MM-ChatAlign, PTFEA reduces Qwen2.5-72B runtime from 21 hours to 1 hour and token consumption from 2200–3000 to 200–400 (over 80% reduction).

Conclusion: This is the first theoretical framework unifying context engineering and fine-tuning in MMEA, establishing a foundation for translating additional fine-tuning strategies into context engineering paradigms. The dramatic efficiency gains demonstrate the practical value of theoretically-grounded prompt design.

Abstract: Multimodal Entity Alignment (MMEA) aims to identify equivalent entities across different modalities. While existing methods enhance MMEA performance through black-box context engineering strategies, their reliance on LLM parameter capacity and lack of theoretical interpretability remain unresolved. To this end, we first theoretically validate the mathematical equivalence between context engineering and model fine-tuning in MMEA tasks, demonstrating that prompt components simulate contrastive learning-based sequential fine-tuning in MMEA. Building on this foundation, we then propose PTFEA, a curriculum-learning-inspired framework that translates fine-tuning strategies into interpretable context engineering. Specifically, adaptive difficulty modulation dynamically adjusts information injection stages using confidence thresholds, establishing mathematical equivalence between curriculum learning weights and context sample selection; and three-stage progressive inference incorporates entity information from simple to complex cases, mirroring the gradient descent process in fine-tuning. Experiments on five public datasets demonstrate that PTFEA consistently outperforms strong baselines. In particular, on the ICWIKI dataset, PTFEA narrows the H@1 gap between Qwen2.5-72B and 14B to 0.6%. Moreover, compared with the representative context-engineering-based MMEA method MM-ChatAlign, PTFEA reduces the runtime of Qwen2.5-72B from 21 hours to 1 hour and lowers token consumption from 2200-3000 to 200-400, achieving over 80% reduction on the ICWIKI dataset. This work provides the first theoretical framework unifying context engineering and fine-tuning in MMEA, paving the way for future research that seeks to translate additional fine-tuning strategies into context engineering paradigms. Our code is available at https://github.com/DMiC-Lab-HFUT/PTFEA.

</details>


### [366] [RecRec: Recursive Refinement for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10541)
*Pervez Shaik,Prosenjit Biswas,Abhinav Thorat,Ravi Kolla,Niranjan Pedanekar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: RecRec proposes a lightweight sequential recommender that models user preferences as a persistent latent state recursively refined through an evidence-anchored correction mechanism, matching or outperforming SOTA models with only 3.9M–14M parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current sequential recommenders rely on single-pass encoding with increasingly deep architectures, lacking iterative refinement. The authors ask whether user preferences can instead be modeled as a persistent latent state that undergoes recursive refinement, offering a more scalable alternative.

Method: RecRec maintains a compact latent state updated by a shared recursive module conditioned on interaction evidence. The key innovation is an evidence-anchored correction mechanism that grounds each recursive update in the original interaction context, preventing semantic drift during deep recursive reasoning. The model operates under standard evaluation protocols on three benchmark datasets.

Result: RecRec matches or exceeds state-of-the-art sequential, graph-based, and reasoning-enhanced recommenders while using only 3.9M to 14M parameters. Ablation studies confirm that both recursive refinement and the evidence-anchored correction gate contribute significantly to performance.

Conclusion: Recursive latent inference with evidence-anchored correction is an effective, scalable alternative to deeper or language-based architectures for sequential recommendation, achieving competitive performance with substantially fewer parameters.

Abstract: Sequential recommender systems typically infer user preferences through single-pass encoding of interaction histories without iterative refinement, relying on increasingly deep architectures to capture complex patterns. In this work, we revisit sequential recommendation from a recursive inference perspective: can user preferences be modeled as a persistent latent state that is recursively refined? We propose RecRec (Recursive Recommendation), a lightweight model that maintains a compact latent state and updates it through a shared recursive module conditioned on interaction evidence. Unlike prior recursive models, RecRec introduces an evidence-anchored correction mechanism that stabilizes refinement by grounding each update in the original interaction context, preventing semantic drift during deep recursive reasoning. Experiments on three benchmark datasets under standard evaluation protocols show that RecRec matches or outperforms state-of-the-art sequential, graph-based, and reasoning-enhanced recommenders while using only 3.9M to 14M parameters. Ablation studies demonstrate that both recursive refinement and the evidence-anchored correction gate contribute significantly to performance, highlighting the effectiveness of recursive latent inference as a scalable alternative to deeper or language-based architectures. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RecRec-6B67/README.md.

</details>


### [367] [Tool-Adaptive LLM Reranker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10555)
*Zichuan Liu,Ruijin Hua*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TALRanker frames relevance scoring as a Markov decision process with a two-stage training paradigm (language-preserving warm-up + cost-aware RL), enabling LLM rerankers to autonomously decide when to invoke external search tools — matching pointwise reranker throughput while achieving SOTA on both standard and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from factual hallucinations on complex queries beyond their knowledge boundaries. Tool-calling can help, but indiscriminately invoking search for every document during reranking causes prohibitive latency. This creates an accuracy-efficiency dilemma: how to selectively use external evidence only when needed.

Method: TALRanker formalizes pointwise relevance scoring as an agentic Markov decision process. Training proceeds in two stages: (1) a warm-up phase using a language-preserving hybrid loss to prevent catastrophic forgetting of generative capacities; (2) reinforcement learning with an asymmetric cost-aware reward that incentivizes the policy to bypass tools when confident and retrieve external evidence when uncertain, penalizing severe hallucinations heavily.

Result: TALRanker achieves state-of-the-art performance on both standard and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks. It matches the throughput of pointwise rerankers while outperforming parameter-heavy reasoning models.

Conclusion: TALRanker demonstrates that reinforcement learning with cost-aware rewards can effectively train LLM-based rerankers to make autonomous, efficient tool-use decisions, resolving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in retrieval-augmented reranking.

Abstract: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized information retrieval, yet their strictly parametric nature frequently leads to severe factual hallucinations when confronted with complex queries beyond their epistemic boundaries. While external tool-calling can mitigate this, indiscriminately invoking search tools for every document during reranking incurs prohibitive latency overheads, creating an intractable accuracy-efficiency dilemma. To address this challenge, we propose TALRanker, a novel framework that formalizes pointwise relevance scoring as an agentic Markov decision process. We optimize it via a two-stage training paradigm. An initial warm-up utilizes a language-preserving hybrid loss to prevent the catastrophic forgetting of native generative capacities. Subsequently, an asymmetric cost-aware reward equipped in reinforcement learning forces the policy to autonomously bypass tools for maximum efficiency when confident, while selectively retrieving external evidence to avert severe hallucination penalties when uncertain. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TALRanker achieves state-of-the-art performance across standard and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, matching throughput with pointwise rerankers while outperforming parameter-heavy reasoning models.

</details>


### [368] [Stream-aware Side Adaptation for Large Pre-trained Multimodal Embedding Models in Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10909)
*Junchen Fu,Kaiwen Zheng,Ioannis Arapakis,Wenhao Deng,Xin Xin,Joemon M. Jose,Xuri Ge*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Stresa is a stream-aware side-adaptation framework that addresses two key challenges in adapting frozen multimodal embedding models for sequential recommendation: inadequate residual fusion selection and degraded historical representation preservation. It introduces SHAF (Stream-aware Hidden-Adapter Fusion) and ReSA (Residual Stream Adapter), outperforming existing adapters and baselines across multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large pretrained multimodal embedding models (e.g., Qwen3-VL Embedding) offer reusable semantic representations for sequential recommendation, but direct use suffers from domain misalignment. Existing side adapters degrade with depth, forcing layer dropping and losing useful hidden states. Two core issues remain unsolved: (1) no mechanism for selecting fused representations during residual addition, and (2) insufficient preservation of earlier representations during progressive sigmoid fusion.

Method: The authors propose Stresa, comprising two components: (1) Stream-aware Hidden-Adapter Fusion (SHAF), which preserves historical side memory during fusion by maintaining a stream of hidden representations across layers; and (2) Residual Stream Adapter (ReSA), which produces selective residual updates across layers, enabling effective use of all backbone layers without degradation.

Result: Stresa consistently outperforms standard side adapters and state-of-the-art baselines on public datasets across multiple backbone embedding models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed stream-aware adaptation framework.

Conclusion: The work highlights the promise of adapting large frozen multimodal embedding models for sequential recommendation and shows that properly designed side adaptation can unlock their full potential. Code is publicly released.

Abstract: Recently, large pretrained multimodal embedding models such as Qwen3-VL Embedding have shown strong promise for sequential recommendation, as they provide reusable semantic item representations across modalities and domains. However, directly using these embeddings often leads to suboptimal performance because of domain misalignment. Efficient side adaptation is therefore an attractive solution. Although adapting all backbone layers should help, existing side adapters often degrade with depth, prompting layer dropping despite the loss of useful hidden states. This is due to two major challenges: (1) the lack of modeling in selecting fused representations during residual addition, and (2) the insufficient preservation of earlier representations during progressive sigmoid fusion. This paper therefore asks a practical question: How can we design a side adaptation approach that effectively unlocks the potential of large pre-trained multimodal embedding models?
  To address this question, we propose Stresa, a stream-aware side-adaptation framework for frozen large pre-trained multimodal embedding models in sequential recommendation. Stresa introduces Stream-aware Hidden-Adapter Fusion (SHAF) to preserve historical side memory during fusion and Residual Stream Adapter (ReSA) to produce selective residual updates across layers. Empirically, Stresa consistently outperforms standard side adapters and state-of-the-art baselines on public datasets across multiple backbone embedding models. These results highlight the promise of adapting large embedding models for sequential recommendation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/GAIR-Lab/Stresa.

</details>


### [369] [ZoRRO: A Zero-Weight Personalized Recommender System for Scalable News Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10910)
*Johannes Kruse,Ryotaro Shimizu,Kasper Lindskow,Jon Tofteskov,Michael Riis Andersen,Julian McAuley,Jes Frellsen*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: ZoRRO is a training-free, zero-weight framework for personalized news recommendation that matches deep learning models in online CTR while being 600x faster, highlighting gaps between offline and online evaluation and the need for metrics beyond accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural recommender systems are computationally expensive to train and serve at scale for news recommendation. The authors aim to develop a lightweight, training-free alternative that can achieve competitive performance without the overhead of deep learning models, while also investigating the discrepancies between offline benchmarks and online deployment outcomes.

Method: ZoRRO is a zero-weight, training-free recommendation framework. It eschews learned parameters entirely, instead relying on efficient, pre-defined mechanisms for personalized news recommendation. The approach is designed for scalable deployment, operating over 600 times faster than comparable deep learning models. The authors evaluate using both offline ranking metrics and online A/B testing with click-through rate, and further analyze recommendation distribution differences between models with similar CTR.

Result: ZoRRO outperforms strong neural baselines in offline ranking evaluations. In online A/B testing, it achieves CTR nearly on par with a state-of-the-art deep learning model while being 600x faster. The experiments also reveal that models with similar CTR can produce markedly different recommendation distributions, affecting overall news flow, and expose gaps between offline and online performance.

Conclusion: ZoRRO is a practical, efficient solution for large-scale news recommendation, demonstrating that training-free approaches can rival deep learning in production settings. The findings underscore the importance of evaluating recommender systems using metrics beyond accuracy alone, as models with comparable CTR can shape content distribution in divergent ways.

Abstract: We present ZoRRO (Zero-Weight Personalized Recommender System), a zero-weight, training-free framework for personalized news recommendation designed for scalable real-world deployment. ZoRRO outperforms strong neural baselines in offline ranking evaluations and achieves click-through rate performance in online A/B testing that is nearly on par with a state-of-the-art deep learning model, while operating more than 600 times faster. Our experiments reveal gaps between offline and online performance and demonstrate that models with similar click-through rate outcomes can produce markedly different recommendation distributions, thereby influencing the overall news flow. These findings position ZoRRO as a practical and efficient solution for large-scale news recommendation and highlight the importance of evaluating recommender systems using metrics beyond accuracy alone.

</details>


### [370] [Normative Alignment of Recommender Systems via Internal Label Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10915)
*Johannes Kruse,Kasper Lindskow,Michael Riis Andersen,Ryotaro Shimizu,Julian McAuley,Pierre-Alexandre Mattei,Jes Frellsen*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: NAILS is a scalable, retraining-free method that adjusts recommendation outputs to match target attribute distributions (e.g., fairness, diversity) by applying internal label shift within a hierarchical classification framework, achieving normative alignment with minimal engagement loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recommender systems optimized purely for user engagement often neglect broader normative goals such as fairness, diversity, and editorial values. Existing solutions typically require model retraining or complex architectural changes, motivating a lightweight, post-hoc alignment mechanism.

Method: NAILS frames recommendation as hierarchical classification and applies internal label shift — reweighting the user-conditional item distribution to match a desired marginal distribution over item attributes — without retraining the base recommender. It adopts a stakeholder-centric perspective to encode global normative objectives as target attribute distributions.

Result: NAILS consistently improves attribute-level alignment with specified normative targets while preserving user engagement, demonstrating only minimal impact on recommendation quality across empirical evaluations.

Conclusion: NAILS offers a practical, scalable mechanism for value-driven recommendation, enabling post-hoc alignment with normative objectives without costly model retraining, and opens avenues for stakeholder-centric governance of recommender outputs.

Abstract: We introduce NAILS (Normative Alignment of Recommender Systems via Internal Label Shift), a simple and scalable method for aligning recommendation outputs with target distributions over item-level attributes, such as categories. Recommender systems optimized solely for user engagement often fail to satisfy broader normative objectives, including fairness, diversity, and editorial values. NAILS modifies the user-conditional item distribution to induce a specified marginal distribution over attributes while preserving the preferences learned by an existing recommender system and requiring no model retraining. We formulate this problem as a form of label shift applied internally within a hierarchical classification framework. By adopting a stakeholder-centric perspective, NAILS enables recommendation outputs to be aligned with global normative objectives. Empirically, we show that NAILS consistently improves attribute-level alignment with minimal impact on user engagement, providing a practical mechanism for value-driven recommendation.

</details>


### [371] [MMRM: A Multiplex Multimodal Representation Model for Product Ranking in E-commerce Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11030)
*Zhen-Lin Chen,Maosen Sheng,Peng Lin,Jianmin Chen,Zhuojian Xiao,Dongyue Wang,Xiwei Zhao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MMRM is a unified framework that aligns MLLMs with multiple collaborative signals to generate multiplex item representations in a single pass, then uses these for task-specific user modeling in e-commerce search ranking. Deployed at JD.com with significant gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal ranking approaches have two key limitations: (1) they fine-tune MLLMs using only a single collaborative signal, missing the benefits of heterogeneous signals needed for multitask ranking; and (2) they treat multimodal representations as static item features, failing to leverage their potential for dynamic user behavior modeling.

Method: MMRM employs a shared MLLM backbone with task-specific tokens and projection layers to simultaneously learn from multiple collaborative signals, producing multiplex item representations in one inference pass. For ranking, it introduces a multiplex user representation strategy that derives task-specific user representations through search-based behavior sequence modeling over the multiplex item representations.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate MMRM's superior efficiency and effectiveness. The framework has been successfully deployed in JD's e-commerce search engine, delivering significant performance improvements for millions of daily users.

Conclusion: MMRM effectively addresses the limitations of single-signal MLLM fine-tuning and static multimodal feature usage by enabling multitask-aligned multiplex representations and task-specific user modeling, achieving both academic and industrial validation.

Abstract: Multimodal information is pivotal for e-commerce search ranking. Existing works leverage multimodal data typically by fine-tuning general Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) via collaborative signals, subsequently integrating the derived representations into ranking models as item features. Despite their efficacy, these methods face two primary limitations: (1) they rely on a single collaborative signal for MLLM fine-tuning, failing to exploit the heterogeneous signals essential for multitask ranking; and (2) they treat multimodal representations as regular item features in ranking models, underutilizing their latent potential for user behavior modeling. To address these challenges, we propose the Multiplex Multimodal Representation Model (MMRM), a unified framework that aligns MLLMs with diverse collaborative signals. By employing a shared backbone with task-specific tokens and projection layers, MMRM simultaneously learns from multiple signals and generates comprehensive multiplex item representations in a single inference pass. Furthermore, we introduce a multiplex user representation strategy in ranking models, which derives task-specific user representations via search-based behavior sequence modeling leveraging multiplex item representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate MMRM's superior efficiency and effectiveness. Notably, MMRM has been successfully deployed in the JD e-commerce search engine, yielding significant performance gains for millions of daily users.

</details>


### [372] [Generative Chinese Statute Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11109)
*Yiteng Tu,Zitao Su,Weihang Su,Xuanyi Chen,Yueyue Wu,Yiqun Liu,Min Zhang,Qingyao Ai*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: GCSR reformulates statute retrieval as a sequence generation problem using multi-granularity structured document IDs encoding legal hierarchy and semantics, trained with a multi-task strategy, outperforming sparse, dense, and legal-domain baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing statute retrieval methods struggle to bridge the gap between colloquial legal queries and formal statutory language, limiting effective legal information access.

Method: GCSR, a generative statute retrieval framework that (1) reformulates retrieval as sequence generation, (2) internalizes statutory knowledge into a generative model via multi-granularity structured docids encoding both legal hierarchy and semantic information, and (3) employs a multi-task training strategy.

Result: GCSR consistently outperforms strong sparse, dense, and legal-domain baselines across experiments.

Conclusion: Generative retrieval is effective for statute retrieval and shows strong potential for broader legal information access and downstream legal reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Statute retrieval is a fundamental task in legal information retrieval, yet existing approaches struggle to bridge the gap between colloquial legal queries and formal statutory language. In this paper, we propose GCSR, a generative statute retrieval framework that reformulates statute retrieval as a sequence generation problem and internalizes statutory knowledge into a generative model. Specifically, we propose a multi-granularity structured docid that encodes legal hierarchy and semantic information, together with a multi-task training strategy. Experiments show that GCSR consistently outperforms strong sparse, dense, and legal-domain baselines. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of generative retrieval for statute retrieval and highlight its potential for broader legal information access and downstream legal reasoning tasks.

</details>


### [373] [NGM-RAG: Neural Graph Matching based Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11159)
*Guo Chen,Ziwen Li,Maolin Zheng,Hao Gao,Junjie Huang,Tao Jia*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: NGM-RAG is a novel framework that uses neural graph matching with GNNs to improve retrieval-augmented generation for multi-hop reasoning tasks, outperforming traditional RAG and existing graph-enhanced methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional RAG methods rely on text-based retrieval and struggle with complex questions requiring multi-hop reasoning. Existing graph-enhanced methods lack effective integration of relational knowledge.

Method: NGM-RAG unifies graph construction, graph matching, and answer generation. It employs neural graph matching combining text-based matching with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), using an adaptive weighting strategy to fuse multiple matching signals for selecting optimal contextual nodes.

Result: NGM-RAG achieves superior performance over NaiveRAG baselines and state-of-the-art graph-enhanced approaches (GraphRAG, LightRAG) on multi-hop QA and long-context summarization tasks.

Conclusion: Integrating neural graph matching into RAG via GNNs and adaptive weighting effectively addresses multi-hop reasoning limitations, establishing NGM-RAG as a strong alternative to both text-only and existing graph-based RAG paradigms.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly enhances the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide accurate and contextually relevant answers by dynamically integrating external databases. However, traditional RAG methods are primarily constrained by their reliance on text-based retrieval strategies, which often struggle with complex questions requiring multi-hop reasoning. To address this limitation, we introduce Neural Graph Matching based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (NGM-RAG), a novel framework that leverages graph structures to effectively capture and utilize relational knowledge for improved retrieval and answer generation. NGM-RAG explicitly incorporates graph construction, graph matching, and answer generation into a unified process. Within this framework, we propose a neural graph matching approach that combines text-based matching with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). By employing an adaptive weighting strategy, NGM-RAG efficiently integrates multiple matching methods to select the most relevant contextual node information for answer generation. Experimental results on multi-hop question answering and long-context summarization tasks demonstrate that our NGM-RAG model achieves superior performance compared to both traditional NaiveRAG methods and state-of-the-art graph-enhanced approaches such as GraphRAG and LightRAG.

</details>


### [374] [Enhancing LLMs through human feedback: a journey towards self-improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11267)
*Tatiana Pelc,Gila Kamhi,Asaf Avrahamy,Adi Fledel-Alon*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A novel methodology that integrates an auxiliary feedback RAG system with a primary RAG system, using human-in-the-loop feedback collection and classification to iteratively improve response accuracy and relevance, validated across three benchmark datasets using LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RAG systems lack robust mechanisms for continuous self-improvement through user feedback. The authors identify a gap in adaptive information retrieval where systems fail to systematically harness human-generated feedback to refine response quality, accuracy, and relevance over time.

Method: The study proposes a dual-RAG architecture comprising: (1) a primary RAG system for inference, and (2) an auxiliary feedback RAG system that collects, classifies, and integrates human-generated feedback into the inference workflow. This human-in-the-loop approach enables iterative learning and self-improvement. Evaluation uses LLM-as-a-Judge across three benchmark datasets covering general and custom domain knowledge.

Result: The paper reports that the feedback-driven dual-RAG methodology demonstrates enhanced response accuracy, relevance, and overall quality. However, the abstract does not provide specific quantitative metrics or performance comparisons against baseline systems.

Conclusion: The feedback-driven enhancement framework demonstrates transformative potential for RAG systems and sets a precedent for future research in adaptive, self-improving information retrieval technologies, advancing toward autonomous refinement through user engagement.

Abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of information retrieval systems, the ability to adapt and improve through user feedback is paramount. This study introduces a novel methodology for refining the performance of a primary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system by strategically integrating an auxiliary feedback RAG system. By systematically harnessing human-generated feedback, the approach aims to enhance the accuracy, relevance, and overall quality of responses, driving the system towards self-improvement. Central to this methodology is a human-in-the-loop implementation, where user feedback is continuously collected, classified, and integrated into the inference workflow, enabling the system to learn and evolve iteratively. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, the study employs rigorous testing against three diverse benchmark datasets focused on general and custom domain knowledge, utilizing a LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation strategy. This comprehensive framework not only underscores the transformative potential of feedback-driven enhancements in RAG systems but also sets a precedent for future research in adaptive information retrieval technologies, marking a significant step in the journey towards autonomous refinement and optimization through user engagement.

</details>


### [375] [Prompt Generation Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11326)
*Dan Ou,Gui Ling,Hao Wan,Hongbin Zhou,Jialiang Cheng,Jiangnan Pang,Silu Zhou,Wei Shi,Weichen Ye,Wenming Zhang,Yang Wang,Yu Li,Yuliang Yan,Zhan Fa,Zhihong Chen,Zongyuan Wu,Bo Zheng,Changfa Wu,Dunxian Huang,Haihong Tang,Jinlong Guo,Kaixuan Zhang,Kun Ma,Lin Qu,Longbo Zhong,Tao Lan,Tong Xiong,Zhibo Wu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: PG decouples feature engineering from model architecture via declarative JSON configurations, enabling fast iteration, deployment, and inference for generative retrieval. Deployed on Taobao Search, it yielded +0.47% transactions and +0.51% GMV uplift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feature engineering in industrial generative retrieval is tightly coupled with model architecture, causing slow offline iteration, heavy/scenario-specific online deployment, and difficulty in reuse — all exacerbated by tight latency budgets. The authors seek to break this coupling to accelerate experimentation and standardize serving.

Method: Prompt Generation (PG), a configuration-driven framework using two declarative JSON files as the single source of truth for both training and serving. Features are organized into four types with three composable processing components for assembling and compressing heterogeneous features. PG provides built-in token compression for ultra-long sequences and a universal pipeline that new scenarios plug into via schema conformance, with unified engine-side optimizations for inference.

Result: Statistically significant online A/B gains on Taobao Search: +0.47% transaction count and +0.51% GMV. PG has been adopted across multiple Taobao search and recommendation teams as the standard iteration framework for generative retrieval.

Conclusion: PG successfully decouples feature processing from model architecture in industrial generative retrieval systems, delivering acceleration across training iteration, deployment, and inference. Its configuration-driven approach reduces engineering overhead and enables consistent, reusable feature pipelines at scale.

Abstract: Generative retrieval has become an increasingly adopted paradigm for industrial search, recommendation, and advertising systems, delivering significant online gains. Most existing work combines user behavior sequences with large language models (LLMs) to model user preferences. In practice, feature engineering remains critical to model effectiveness, yet its complexity slows offline iteration and makes online deployment heavy and hard to reuse, all under tight online latency budgets. The root cause is a tight coupling between feature-processing logic and model architecture, where every feature change touches the training and serving code and resists reuse across scenarios. To break this coupling, we present Prompt Generation (PG), a high-level tokenizer and configuration-driven framework that decouples feature-processing logic from model architecture through two declarative JSON files, which serve as the single source of truth for both offline training and online serving, ensuring feature consistency across the two stages. Organizing features under four types with three composable processing components to assemble and compress heterogeneous features, PG delivers acceleration at three levels: (1)fast training iteration: feature experiments require only configuration changes, with built-in token compression for ultra-long sequences; (2)fast deployment: a new scenario only needs to conform to the PG schema and plug into a universal pipeline, with no scenario-specific engineering; (3)fast online inference: engine applies unified optimizations over the standardized configuration, reducing PG's overhead to a negligible level. PG has been deployed on Taobao Search with statistically significant online A/B uplifts of +0.47% in transaction count and +0.51% in GMV, and has been applied across multiple Taobao search and recommendation teams as the iteration framework for generative retrieval.

</details>


### [376] [User Preference Induction with LLMs for Offline Top-N Recommendation Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11354)
*David Otero,Javier Parapar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes using LLMs to expand sparse relevance judgments in offline recommender evaluation. An LLM first summarizes user history into a profile, then judges unlabeled items from a pooled candidate set, reducing the "missing-as-negative" bias and improving evaluation robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline evaluation of top-N recommender systems suffers from the missing-as-negative assumption, where unjudged user-item pairs are treated as non-relevant. This biases metrics, penalizes plausible but unobserved recommendations, and favors algorithms that recommend popular/overexposed items.

Method: A two-stage LLM-based framework: (1) Preference Induction — an LLM summarizes each user's historical interactions into a textual profile capturing tastes and interests; (2) Relevance Judging — conditioned on that profile, the LLM judges candidate items lacking observed labels. To maintain tractability, judgment expansion is restricted to a pooled candidate set built from top-ranked outputs of multiple recommenders. Enriched judgments then enable more complete ranking metric computation.

Result: The proposed approach proves promising for improving offline top-N evaluation robustness and mitigating popularity-sensitive distortions introduced by sparse feedback.

Conclusion: LLM-based relevance judgment expansion is a viable strategy to address evaluation bias in sparse feedback settings, offering a more complete basis for computing ranking metrics without requiring exhaustive human annotation.

Abstract: Offline evaluation is the standard methodology for comparing top-N recommender systems, yet it relies on incomplete relevance information. In most benchmark datasets, only a small subset of user--item preferences is observed, and unjudged items are commonly treated as non-relevant. This missing-as-negative assumption can bias evaluation, penalize plausible recommendations with no recorded feedback, and favour algorithms that concentrate on popular or highly exposed items. We propose an LLM-based framework to expand relevance judgements for offline recommender evaluation. Our approach uses large language models in two complementary roles. First, a preference induction stage summarizes each user's historical interactions into a textual profile that captures their tastes and interests. Second, conditioned on this profile, an LLM acts as a relevance judge for candidate recommended items that lack observed labels in the original test data. To make this process tractable and evaluation-focused, we apply judgement expansion to a pooled candidate set built from the top-ranked outputs of multiple recommenders. The resulting enriched judgements provide additional relevance evidence for previously unobserved user--item pairs, enabling ranking metrics to be computed on a more complete basis. Experimental results show that this approach is a promising strategy for improving the robustness of offline top-N evaluation and mitigating the popularity-sensitive distortions caused by sparse feedback.

</details>


### [377] [Boolean queries are all you need?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11362)
*Charles L. A. Clarke,Mark D. Smucker*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: An LLM-based search agent using only Boolean retrieval and substring matching achieved NDCG@10 of 0.6863 on TREC 2024 RAG track topics, outperforming many dense and sparse neural retrievers, suggesting that simple pattern matching may suffice for agentic search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether a simple, unsupervised pattern-matching approach — where an LLM agent queries a Boolean retrieval engine — can achieve competitive retrieval performance compared to dense, sparse, and learned-sparse neural retrievers, without requiring supervised training, global statistics, or term weighting.

Method: An LLM-based search agent was given access to a Boolean retrieval engine over the MS MARCO V2.1 deduped segment collection (TREC 2024 RAG track). Under a budget of 100 model calls per topic across 86 topics, the agent formulates Boolean queries. Documents are scored solely based on the number and length of corpus substrings matching a query — a query language expressing a strict subset of regular languages. No supervised learning, global statistics (e.g., IDF), or term weights are used.

Result: The agent achieved an NDCG@10 of 0.6863, which would rank above many dense, sparse, and learned-sparse first-stage retrievers on this benchmark.

Conclusion: Simple pattern matching via Boolean retrieval, when driven by an LLM-based agent, may be sufficient for effective search. However, the results are exploratory rather than definitive, as they rely on a single publicly available test collection that was likely included in the LLM's training data.

Abstract: We equipped an LLM-based search agent with access to a Boolean retrieval engine to search the MS MARCO V2.1 deduped segment collection used by the TREC 2024 RAG track. Over a standard track subset of 86 topics, and operating under a budget of 100 model calls/topic, the agent achieved an NDCG@10 of 0.6863, which would place it above many dense, sparse, and learned-sparse first-stage retrievers. Ranking is based solely on the density of corpus substrings matching a query, with no requirement for supervised learning, global statistics, or term weights. Formally, the query language expresses a strict subset of the regular languages, with a document's score based on the number and length of matches it contains. Although the results are more exploratory than definitive, because they are based on a single test collection that was publicly available during model training, they suggest that simple pattern matching may be sufficient for agentic search.

</details>


### [378] [Beyond Semantic IDs: Encoding Business-Value Ranking into Document Identifiers for Generative Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11392)
*Gui Ling,Zhihong Chen,Yu Li,Tong Xiong,Kunhai Lin,Kaixuan Zhang,Yuliang Yan,Dan Ou,Haihong Tang,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: CRID decouples document identifiers into semantic clustering and business-value ranking components, producing collision-free, incrementally updatable DocIDs for generative retrieval. On a 300M-item Taobao corpus, it outperforms embedding-based baselines on Hitrate and delivers +1.06% GMV in full deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing discrete representation learning schemes for GR suffer from (1) inherent collision issues in DocID assignment and (2) a mismatch between DocID encoding objectives and business optimization targets. These limitations degrade retrieval quality in large-scale industrial settings.
